The general commissioners had the power of choosing a superintendent or master of police for the whole city and suburbs included in the act, and to appoint a clerk who shall do the duty of clerk to the general meetings, as well as to the court of police to be held by the superintendent. The general commissioners also were authorized to fix the number of officers and watchmen to be employed in the different wards. The superintendent of police having been appointed by the commissioners, was to receive from the sheriff depute of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Edinburgh the authority of a sheriff substitute, as well as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of sheriff depute within the city and liberties from the lord provost, who was principal sheriff within these bounds, that the superintendent acting as master or judge of police may have the full powers of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> in the execution of his duty. By the powers with which the superintendent was invested, he might commit offenders to the tolbooth or to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDEWELL">bridewell</a> for a period not exceeding 60 days, and impose fines for offences not exceeding 40 shillings sterling, and give judgment in damages for any sum not exceeding three pounds sterling with the expenses in either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. From the sentences of the superintendent there was no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the sheriff depute of the county, or to the lord provost as sheriff principal within the city. The superintendent of police was also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a>-master within his bounds, and the inspectors of wards were billet-masters within their several wards. The inspectors also had the powers of procurator fiscals with respect to all prosecutions for offences committed within their bounds. The expenses necessary to carry the above act into execution, were to be defrayed from a fund raised by assessment on the inhabitants, of three per cent. on the free rent of houses, shops, or warehouses; and for the expenses of clothing and alimenting the persons committed to bridewell a farther assessment, not exceeding 2½ per cent. of the free rent of such houses, &c. For the purpose of ascertaining rents, surveyors were appointed; and if the rent fixed by them should be overrated, an appeal might be made to a committee of the general commissioners specially appointed. After a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of seven years this bill was found objectionable in many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; and therefore in 1812 a new bill was procured, which abolished the office of judge of police, divided the city into 26 wards, with three resident commissioners for each. The sheriff of the county, and magistrates of Edinburgh, were appointed judges. A superintendent, with a salary of £500 a-year, was appointed, assisted by a clerk with £200, and three lieutenants at £80 each. The total expense of the establishment in 1817 was £18,482. The number of inhabitants in the city of Edinburgh is somewhat uncertain, and has been very variously calculated. By a survey made in the year 1775, it appears that the number of families in the city, Canongate, and other suburbs, and the town of Leith, amounted to 13,806. The difficulty therefore is to fix the number of persons in a family. Dr Price fixes this number at 4½; Mr Maitland, at 5½; and Mr Arnot, at 6½; so that, according to this last <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, the whole number of inhabitants is 82,836; to which he thinks 1400 more may be added for those in the garrisons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, &c. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> exhibits a comparative view of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the city of Edinburgh with Leith and suburbs taken in different years. The enumeration made in 1801 by act of parliament is supposed to be considerably defective in the real amount of the inhabitants, as an alarm was industriously spread that it was done with a view to the imposition of new taxes. | Year | Population | |------|------------| | 1678 | 35,500 | | 1722 | 49,420 | | 1755 | 57,195 | | 1775 | 70,430 | | 1791 | 84,886 | | 1801 | 82,560 | | 1811 | 102,987 | According to this last enumeration the males were 43,982, the females 59,005, a most surprising <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, if correct. The number of families was 23,104. There are in Edinburgh 14 incorporations, capable of choosing their own deacons, viz. The royal college of surgeons; the corporations of goldsmiths, skinners, furriers, hammermen, wrights and masons, taylors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>, butchers, shoemakers, weavers, waukers, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a>-makers, and merchant company. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> of Edinburgh are plentifully supplied with all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Fresh <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> meat, as well as fowl and fish, if the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> permit, may be had every day; and no city can be better supplied with garden stuffs. The Edinburgh strawberries particularly are remarkably large and fine. A striking instance of the plenty of provisions with which Edinburgh is supplied was observed in the year 1779, when several large fleets, all of them in want of necessaries, arrived in the Forth, to the amount of about 500 sail, and having on board at least 20,000 men; yet the increased consumption of provisions, which certainly ensued upon the arrival of so many strangers, made not the least increase in the rate of the markets, insomuch that several victualling ships sent down by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> board returned without opening their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a>. The city <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> are let to the corporation of bakers in Edinburgh: and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> made in the city is remarkable for its good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Edinburgh is supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> brought from miles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, and lodged in two reservoirs, from whence it is distributed through the city both to public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and private families. A revenue accrues to the town from the latter, which must undoubtedly increase in proportion as the city extends in magnitude. There are but few merchants in Edinburgh, most of them residing at the port of Leith: so that the support of the city depends on the consumption of the necessaries as well as the superfluities of life. There are five different sorts of people on whom the shopkeepers, publicans, and different trades depend: 1. The people of the law, who are a very respectable body in the city. 2. The number of young people of both sexes who come to town for their education, many of the parents of whom come along with them. 3. The country gentlemen, gentlemen of the army and navy, and people who have made their fortunes abroad, &c., all of whom come to attend the public diversions, or to spend their time in such a manner as is most agreeable to them. 4. The vast concourse of travellers from all parts. 5. Most of the money drawn for the rents of country gentlemen is circulated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> or other agents. See Edinburgh, Supplement.

CARRIERS

Pages 31-31

those who dress and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> after it comes from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a>-yard. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TANNING">TANNING</a>.

CIRCULATING DECIMALS

Pages 117-117

called also recurring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> repeating decimals, are those in which a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or several figures are continually repeated. They are distinguished into single and multiple, and these again into pure and mixed. A pure single circulate is that in which one figure only is repeated; as '222, &c. and is marked thus '2. A pure multiple circulate is that in which several figures are continually repeated; as '232323, &c. marked '23; and '524524, &c. marked '524. A mixed single circulate is that which consists of a terminate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and a single repeating figure; as 4'222, &c. or 4'2. And A mixed multiple circulate is that which contains a terminate part with several repeating figures; as 45'524. That part of the circulate which repeats is called the repetend; and the whole repetend, supposed infinitely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, is equal to a vulgar fraction, whose numerator is the repeating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or figures, and its denominator the same number of nines: so '2 is =\(\frac{2}{9}\); and '23 is =\(\frac{23}{99}\); and '524 is =\(\frac{524}{999}\). Dr Wallis, it appears, was the first who distinctly considered or treated of infinite circulating decimals, as he himself informs us in his Treatise of Infinites. Since his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> many other authors have treated on this part of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of those, however, to whom the art is mostly indebted, are Messrs <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, Cunn,

CUBA

Pages 11-12

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and very important <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the West Indies, belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. On the south-east it begins at 25° 10' N. Lat., touches the tropic of Cancer on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and extends from 74° to 85° W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. It is 764 miles long, lies 60 miles to the west of Hispaniola, 25 leagues north of Jamaica, 100 miles to the south of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>; and commands the entrance of the gulfs both of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and Florida, as also the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>. By this situation it may be called the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the West Indies. It was discovered by Columbus in 1492, who gave it the name of Ferdinand, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Ferdinand of Spain; but it quickly after recovered its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of Cuba. The natives did not regard Columbus with a very favourable eye at his landing; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> proving very tempestuous, he soon left this island, and sailed to <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HAYTI">Hayti</a>, now called Hispaniola, where he was better received. The Spaniards, however, soon became masters of it. By the year 1515 it was totally conquered; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they had destroyed, according to their own accounts, several millions of people. But the possession of Cuba was far from answering the expectations of the Spanish adventurers, whose avarice could be satiated with nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. These monsters, finding that there was gold upon the island, concluded that it must come from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and therefore tortured the few inhabitants they had left, in order to extort from them a discovery of the places where these mines lay. The miseries endured by these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> creatures were such that they almost unanimously resolved to put an end to their own lives; but were prevented by one of the Spanish tyrants called Vasco Porcellos. This wretch threatened to hang himself along with them, that he might have the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, as he said, of tormenting them in the next world worse than he had done in this; and so much were they afraid of the Spaniards, that this threat threat diverted these poor savages from their desperate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. In 1511, the town of Havana was built, now the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the island. The houses were at first built only of wood; and the town itself was for a long time so inconsiderable, that in 1536 it was taken by a French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, who obliged the inhabitants to pay 700 ducats to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> it from being burnt. The very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the pirate's departure, three Spanish ships arrived from Mexico, and having unloaded their cargoes, sailed in pursuit of the pirate ship. But such was the cowardice of the officers, that the pirate took all the three ships, and returning to the Havana, obliged the inhabitants to pay 700 ducats more. To prevent misfortunes of this kind, the inhabitants built their houses of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and the place has since been strongly fortified. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVANNAH">HAVANNAH</a>. According to the Abbé Raynal, the Spanish settlement at Cuba is very important, on three accounts: 1. The produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which is considerable. 2. As being the staple of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade; 3. As being the key to the West Indies. The cultivation of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> is carried on to a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; no fewer than 480 sugar engines having been erected, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> exported having amounted on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> from 1801 to 1810 to 644,000 cwt. per annum. Coffee began to be planted in Cuba after the destruction of the coffee plantations in St Domingo; and in 1823 it produced about 12,000 quintals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 18 millions of pounds. In 1763 some emigrants introduced bees, which multiplied with such rapidity in the hollows of old trees, that the inhabitants had ample supplies of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> for their own consumption, besides a surplus for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Although the surface of the island is in general uneven and mountainous, yet it has plains sufficiently extensive, and well enough watered, to supply the consumption of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> with sugar. The incredible fertility of its new lands, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> properly managed, would enable it to surpass every other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, however they may have now got the start of it: yet such is the indolence of the Spaniards, that to this day they have comparatively but few plantations, where, with the finest canes, they make but a small quantity of coarse sugar at a great expense. This serves partly for the Mexican market, and partly for the mother-country. It has been expected with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> imported from Cuba would compensate this loss; for after furnishing Mexico and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, there was sufficient, with the little brought from Caracca and Buenos Ayres, to supply all Spain. But this trade too has declined through the mismanagement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. The article is monopolized for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and the planters have been exposed to such vexations, that its cultivation in 1823 had declined to 3,750,000 pounds, from 7,873,000 its amount in 1794. Cuba furnished considerable quantities of gold when the Spaniards first seized it, and it still yields some small supplies of this metal. The Spanish colonies have an universal trade in skins; and Cuba supplies annually about 10 or 12 thousand. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> might easily be increased in a country abounding with wild cattle, where some gentlemen possess large tracts of ground, that for want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> can scarce be applied to any other purpose than that of breeding cattle. The hundredth part of this island is not yet cleared. The true plantations are all confined to the beautiful plains of the Havannah, and even those are not what they might be. The number of inhabitants has increased rapidly. In 1774 they amounted to 220,000; but in 1824, the number was 432,000, including 108,000 slaves. The food of these different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> consists of excellent pork, very bad beef, and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CASSAVA">cassava</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. The colony would be still more flourishing, if its productions had not been made the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, whose exclusive privilege operates as a constant and invariable principle of discouragement. If any thing could supply the want of an open trade, and alone for the grievances occasioned by this monopoly at Cuba, it would be the advantage which this island has for such a long time enjoyed, in being the rendezvous of almost all the Spanish vessels that sail to the new world. This practice commenced almost with the colony itself. Ponce de Leen, having made an attempt upon Florida in 1512, became acquainted with the new canal of Bahama. It was immediately discovered that this was the best route the ships bound from Mexico to Europe could possibly take; and to this the wealth of the island is principally, if not altogether, owing.

CUBE

Pages 12-12

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body consisting of six equal sides. See GEOMETRY. CUBE-Root of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">Number</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">Quantity</a>, is such a number or quantity, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> multiplied into itself, and then again the product thence arising by that number or quantity, being the cube-root, this last product shall be equal to the number or quantity whereof it is the cube-root; as 2 is the cube-root of 8; because two times two is 4, and two times 4 is 8; and \(a + b\) is the cube-root of \(a^3 + 3ab + 3a^2b + b^3\). See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">ALGEBRA</a>.

CUBEBS

Pages 12-12

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a small dried fruit resembling a grain of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, but often somewhat longer, brought into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>. In aromatic warmth and pungency, they are far inferior to pepper. CUBIC EQUATION. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">ALGEBRA</a>.

CUBIDIA

Pages 12-12

a genus of spars. The word is derived from κύβος, "a die;" and is given them from their being of the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> die, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of a cubic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. These bodies owe this shape to an admixture of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and there are only two known <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the genus. 1. A colourless crystalline one, with thin flakes, found in the lead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and some other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and, 2. A milky <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> one with thicker crusts. This is found in the lead-mines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a> and Yorkshire, but is usually small, and is not found plentifully.

CUBIT

Pages 12-12

in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, equal to the length of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s arm, from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. Dr Arbuthnot makes the English cubit equal to 18 inches; the Roman cubit equal to 1 foot 5.466 inches; and the cubit of the Scripture equal to 1 foot 9.888 inches. CUBITÆUS MUSCLES, the name of two muscles of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. See ANATOMY, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

CUBITUS

Pages 12-12

in Anatomy, a bone of the arm, reaching from the elbow to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>; otherwise called ulna, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the greater fossile. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word for all that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the arm between the elbow and the wrist; including the ulna or cubitus, properly so called, and the radius.

CUCKING-STOOL

Pages 12-13

an engine invented for punishing scolds and unquiet women, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCKING">ducking</a> them in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; called in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times a tumbrel, and sometimes a trebuchet. In Domesday, it is called cathedra stercoris; and it was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> even in the Saxon times, by whom it was described to be cathedra in qua rixose mulieres sedentes aquis demergebantur. It was anciently also a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted upon brewers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> transgressing the laws; who were thereupon in such a stool immersed over head and ears in stercor, some stinking water. Some think it a corruption from ducking-stool; others from choking-stool, quia hoc modo demersae aquis fere suffocantur. See CASTIGATORY. CUCKOW. See CUCULUS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cuckow-Spit, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROTH">froth</a>-spit. See Froth-Spit, and Cicada.

CUCUBALUS

Pages 13-13

BERRY-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">BEARING</a> CHICK-WEEED, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 22nd order, Caryophyllaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CUCULUS

Pages 13-13

the CUCKOW, a genus of birds belonging to the order of piece. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CUCUMBER. See CUCUMIS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

CUCUMIS

Pages 13-13

the CUCUMBER: a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocota class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Cucurbitaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Four varieties of the cucumis sativus are chiefly cultivated in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They are raised at three different seasons of the year: 1. on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>, for early fruit; 2. under <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-glasses, for the middle crop; 3. on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ground, which is for a late crop, or to pickle. The cucumbers which are ripe before April are wholesome; being raised wholly by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the dung without the assistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Those raised in April are good, and are raised in the following manner. Towards the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-dung must be procured with the litter among it; and a small proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coal ashes should be added to it. In four or five days the dung <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> begin to heat; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a little of it may be drawn flat on the outside, and covered with two inches thickness of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>: this must be covered with a bell glass; and after two days, when the earth is warm, the seeds must be sown on it, covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch of fresh earth, and the glass then set on again. The glass must be covered with a mat at night, and in four days the young plants will appear. When these are seen, the rest of the dung must be made up into a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> for one or more lights. This must be three feet thick, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, and covered three inches deep with fine fresh earth; the frame must then be put on, and covered at night, or in bad <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, with mats. When the earth is hot enough, the young plants from under the bell must be removed into it, and set two inches distant. The glasses must be now and then a little raised, to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> to the plants, and turned often, to prevent the wet from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> of the dung from dropping <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon them. The plants must be watered at proper times; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> used for this purpose must be set on the dung till it becomes as warm as the air in the frame: and as the young plants increase in bulk, they must be earthed up, which will give them <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> additional strength. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the bed is not hot enough, some fresh litter should be laid round its sides: and if too hot, some holes should be bored into several parts of it with a stake, which will let out the heat; and when the bed is thus brought to a proper coolness, the holes are to be stopped up again with fresh dung. When these plants begin to shoot their third or rough <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, another bed must be prepared for them like the first; and when it is properly warm through the earth, the plants of the other bed must be taken up, and planted in this, in which there must be a hole in the middle of each <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, about a foot deep, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches over, filled with light and fine fresh earth laid hollow in form of a basin: in each of these holes there must be set four plants: these must be, for two or three days, shaded from the sun, that they may take firm root; after which they must have all the sun they can, and now and then a little fresh air, as the weather will permit. When the plants are four or five inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, they must be gently pegged down towards the earth, in directions as different from one another as may be; and the branches afterwards produced should be treated in the same manner. In a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after this the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> will appear, and soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the fruit. The glasses should now be carefully covered at night; and in the daytime the whole plants should be gently sprinkled with water. These will produce fruit till about midsummer; at which time the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> crop will come in to supply their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; these are to be raised in the same manner as the early crop, only they do not require so much care and trouble. This second crop should be sown in the end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> or beginning of April. The season for sowing the cucumbers of the last crop, and for pickling, is towards the latter end of May, when the weather is settled: these are sown in holes dug to a little depth, and filled up with fine earth, so as to be left in the form of a basin; eight or nine seeds being put into one hole. These will come up in five or six days; and till they are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> old, are in great danger from the sparrows. After this they require only to be kept clear of weeds, and watered now and then. There should be only five plants left at first in each hole; and when they are grown a little farther up, the worst of these is to be pulled up, that there may finally remain only four. The plants of this crop will begin to produce fruit in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>.

CUCURBIT

Pages 13-13

the name of a chemical vessel employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, when covered with its head. Its name comes from its elongated form in shape of a gourd: some cucurbits, however, are shallow and wide-mouthed. They are made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, glass, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the substances to be distilled. A cucurbit, provided with its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, constitutes the vessel for distillation called an alembic.

CUCURBITA

Pages 13-14

the GOURD, and POMPION; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocota class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Cucurbitaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. All the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of gourds and pompions, with their respective varieties, are raised from seed sown annually. Cucurbita in April <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the beginning of May, either with or without the help of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> heats. But the plants sowed in a hot <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> till about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> old, produce fruit a month or six weeks earlier on that account, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> proportionally sooner. The first species particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarce ever produce tolerably sized fruit in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, without the treatment above mentioned. In this country these plants are cultivated only for curiosity; but in the places where they are natives, they answer many important purposes. In both the Indies, bottle-gourds are very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> cultivated and sold in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. They make the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, particularly in the warm months of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and August. The Arabians call this kind of gourd charrah. It grows commonly on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in their deserts. The natives boil and season it with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>; and sometimes, filling the shell with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and meat, make a kind of pudding of it. The hard shell is used for holding <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and some of them are capacious enough to contain 22 gallons; these, however, are very uncommon. The fruit of the pompion likewise constitutes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the food of the common people during the hot months, in those places where they grow. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> gathered when not much bigger than a hen or goose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and properly seasoned with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, vinegar, &c., they make a tolerable good sauce for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s meat, and are also used in soups. In England they are seldom used till grown to maturity. A hole is then made in one side, through which the pulp is scooped out; after being divested of the seeds, it is mixed with sliced apples, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and grated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>, and thus a kind of pudding is made. The whole is then baked in the oven, and goes by the name of a pumpkin pie. For this purpose the plants are cultivated in many places in England by the country people, who raise them upon old dung-hills. The third species is also used in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> for culinary purposes. The fruit is gathered when about half grown, boiled and eaten as sauce to butcher's meat. The squashes are also treated in the same manner, and by some people esteemed delicate eating. CUCURBITACEÆ, the name of the 34th order in Linnæus's fragments of a natural method, consisting of plants which resemble the gourd in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, virtues, and sensible qualities. This order contains the following genera, viz. Gronovia, Melothria, Passiflora, Anguria, Bryonia, Cucumis, Cucurbita, Sevilia, Momordica, Sicyos, Trichosanthes.

CUCURUCU

Pages 14-14

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> found in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, growing 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It is also very thick in proportion to its length, and is of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, strongly variegated with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spots, which are irregularly mixed among the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and often have spots of yellow within them. It is a very poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and greatly dreaded by the natives; but its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is a very rich food, and much esteemed among them, when properly prepared.

CUDDALORE

Pages 14-15

a town on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Coromandel in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, belonging to the English, very near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where Fort St. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> once stood. N. Lat. 11° 30'. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 79° 53'. 30". This place was reduced by Coddalore, the French in the year 1781; and in 1783 underwent a severe siege by the British forces commanded by General Stuart. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was become the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> place of arms held by the enemy on that coast; they had exerted themselves to the utmost in fortifying it; and it was garrisoned by a numerous body of the best forces of France, well provided with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, and every thing necessary for making a vigorous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Previous to the commencement of the siege, they had constructed strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of defence all along the fort, excepting one place where the town was covered by a wood, supposed to be inaccessible. Through this wood, however, General Stuart began to cut his way; on which the besieged began to draw a line of fortification within that also. The British commander then determined to attack these fortifications before they were quite completed; and for this purpose a vigorous attack was made by the troops under General Bruce. The grenadiers assailed a redoubt which greatly annoyed them, but were obliged to retire; on which the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> advanced to the attack of the lines. The French defended themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; and as both parties <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> each other with fixed bayonets, a dreadful slaughter ensued. At last the British were obliged to retreat; but the French having imprudently come out of their lines to pursue them, were in their turn defeated, and obliged to give up the lines they had constructed with so much pains, and so gallantly defended. The loss on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the British amounted to near 1000 killed and wounded, one half of whom were Europeans; and that of the French was not less than 600. Though the British proved victorious in this contest, yet the victory cost so dear that there was not now a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to carry on the siege with any effect. The troops also became sickly; and their strength diminished so much, that the besieged formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of not only obliging them to raise the siege, but of totally destroying them. For this purpose 4000 men were landed from the squadron commanded by M. Suffrein; and the conduct of the enterprise committed to the Chevalier de Damas, an experienced and valiant officer. On the 25th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1783, he sallied out at the head of the regiment of Aquitaine, supposed to be one of the best in the French <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and of which he was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>; with other troops selected from the bravest of the garrison. The attack was made by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>; but though the British were at first put into some disorder, they quickly recovered themselves, and not only repulsed the enemy, but pursued them so warmly, that the Chevalier de Damas himself was killed, with about 200 of his countrymen, and as many taken prisoners. This engagement was attended with one of the most remarkable circumstances that happened during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, viz. a corps of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPOYS">sepoys</a> grenadiers encountering the French troops opposed to them with fixed bayonets, and overcoming them. This extraordinary bravery was not only noticed with due applause, but procured for that corps a provision for themselves and families from the presidencies to which they belonged. No other operation of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> took place. Cuddaloe place during the siege, which was now soon ended by the news of peace having taken place between the bel- ligerent powers of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

CUDDY

Pages 15-15

in a first-rate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> lying between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>'s cabin and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>- deck; and divided into partitions for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and other officers. It denotes also a kind of cabin near the stern of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> barge of burden. CUDWEED. See GNAPHALIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> In- dex.

CUDWORTH

Pages 15-15

RALPH, a very learned divine of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England in the 17th century. In Janu- ary 1657, he was one of the persons nominated by a committee of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to be consulted about the English translation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>. In 1678 he published his True Intellectual System of the Universe; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which met with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> opposition. He likewise publish- ed a treatise, entitled, Deus justificatus: "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>," The divine goodness of God vindicated, against the asser- tions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and unconditional <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>." He embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> or corpuscular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>: but with regard to the Deity, spirits, genii, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, he followed the Platonists. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> in 1688. The editor of the new edition of the Biogra- phia Britannica observes, that it is not easy to meet with a greater storehouse of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> literature than the "Intellectual System;" and various writers, we believe, have been indebted to it for an appearance of learning which they might not otherwise have been able to maintain. That Dr Cudworth was fanciful in some of his opinions, and that he was too devoted a follower of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and the Platonists, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarcely be denied even by those who are most sensible of his gene- ral merit. The reflections that have been <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> as the author, by bigotted writers, are al- together contemptible. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of distinguished merit to be thus treated. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>, speaking on this subject, has given an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> testimony to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Dr Cudworth." "You know (says his lordship) the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fate of those who dare to appear fair authors. What was that pious and learned man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, who wrote the Intellectual System of the Uni- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>! I confess it was pleasant enough to consider, that though the whole world were not less satisfied with his capacity and learning, than with his sincerity in the cause of Deity; yet he was accused of giving the upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">atheists</a>, for having only stated their reasons, and those of their adversaries, fairly to- gether." It is observed by Dr Birch, that Dr Cudworth's Intellectual System of the Universe has raised him a reputation, to which nothing can add but the publi- cation of his other writings still extant in manuscript. That these writings are very valuable cannot be doubt- ed. We may be assured that they display a great compass of sentiment and a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of learning. Nevertheless, from their voluminous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, from the abstruseness of the subjects they treat upon, and from the revolutions of literary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, it is morally certain that the publication of them would not be successful in the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Dr Cudworth's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Damaris, who married Sir Francis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASHAM">Masham</a> of Oates in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, was a lady of genius and learning; she had a great friendship for Mr Locke, who resided several years at her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Oates, where he died in Cudworth 1724.

CUENZA

Pages 15-15

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in New Castile, and in the territory of the Sierra, with a bishop's see. It was taken by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Peterborough in 1796, but retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Berwick. It is seated on the river Xucar, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 45. N. Lat. 40. 10.

CUERENHERT

Pages 15-15

THEODORE VAN, a very extra- ordinary person, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, where he was born in 1522. It appears, that early in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; but the motives of his journey are not ascertained. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of science, and according to report, a good poet. The sister arts at first he considered as an amusement only; but in the end he was, it seems, obliged to have re- course to engraving alone for his support. And though the different studies in which he employed his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prevented his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his profession being so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as it ought to have been, yet at least the marks of genius are discoverable in his works. They are slight, and hastily executed with the graver alone; but in an open careless style, so as greatly to resemble de- signs made with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>. He was established at Haer- lem; and there pursuing his favourite studies in litera- ture, he learned Latin, and was made secretary to that town, from whence he was sent several times as ambas- sador to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, to whom he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>- ed a famous manifesto, which that prince published in 1566. Had he stopped here, it had been well; but directing his thoughts into a different channel, he undertook an argument as dangerous as it was absurd. He maintained, that all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> communions were corrupted; and that, without a supernatural mission, accompanied with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, no person had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to administer in any religious office: he therefore pro- nounced that man to be unworthy the name of a Christian who would enter any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of public wor- ship. This he not only advanced in words, but strove to show the sincerity of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> by practice; and for that reason would not communicate with either Pro- testant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Papist. His works were published in three volumes folio in 1630; and though he was several times imprisoned, and at last sentenced to banishment, yet he does not appear to have altered his sentiments. He died at Dergoude in 1590, aged 68 years. It is no small addition to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this singular man, that he was the instructor of that justly celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> Henry Goltzius. Cuerenbert worked jointly with the Galles and other artists, from the designs of Mar- tin Henskerck. The subjects are from the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, and consist chiefly of middling-sized plates lengthwise. He also engraved several subjects from Franc. Floris. CUERPO. To walk in cuerpo, is a Spanish phrase for going without a cloak; or without all the formali- ties of a full dress.

CUIRASS

Pages 15-16

a piece of defensive armour made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plate, well hammered, serving to cover the body, from the neck to the girdle, both before and behind. Some derive the word, by corruption, from the Italian cuore, "heart," because it covers that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; others from the French cuir, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Latin corium, "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>;" whence coriaceus; because defensive arms were originally made of leather. The cuirass was not brought into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> till about the year 1300, though they were known both to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in different forms.

CUIRASSIERS

Pages 16-16

cavalry armed with cuirasses, as many of the Germans are: The French have regiments of cuirassiers; but we have had none in the British <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> since the Revolution.

CULDEE

Pages 16-16

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a sort of monkish priests formerly inhabiting Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Being remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> exercises of preaching and praying, they were called, by way of eminence, cultores Dei; from whence is derived the word culdees. They made choice of one of their own fraternity to be their spiritual head, who was afterwards called the Scots bishop.

CULEMBACH

Pages 16-16

a town of Germany, in Franconia, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the marquisate of the same name. It has good fortifications, and is seated at the confluence of two branches of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>. It was pillaged and burnt by the Hussites in 1432, and by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> in 1573. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 28. N. Lat. 50. 12.

CULEUS

Pages 16-16

in Roman antiquity, the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity for things liquid, containing 20 amphorae, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 40 urnae. It contained 143 gallons 3 pints, English wine-measure, and was 11,095 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> inches.

CULEX

Pages 16-16

the GNAT; a genus of insects belonging to the order of diptera. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CULIACAN

Pages 16-16

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the audience of Guadalajara. It is bounded on the north by New <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, on the east by New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a> and the Zacatecas, on the south by Chiametlan, and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is a fruitful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and has rich <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>.

CULLEN

Pages 17-21

Dr William, an eminent physician and distinguished medical teacher, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANARKSHIRE">Lanarkshire</a>, in the west of Scotland, 11th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, 1712. His father was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of the town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>; but though a very respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, his circumstances were not such as to permit him to lay out much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his son. William therefore, after serving an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> to a surgeon-apothecary in Glasgow, went several voyages to the West Indies as a surgeon in a trading vessel from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>: but of this employment he tired, and settled himself, at an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> surgeon in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Shotts, where he staid a short time practising among the farmers and country people, and then went to Hamilton with a view to practise as a physician, having never been fond of operating as a surgeon. While he resided near Shotts, it chanced that Archibald <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle, who at that time bore the chief <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> sway in Scotland, made a visit to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in that neighbourhood. The duke was fond of literary pursuits, and was then particularly engaged in some chemical researches, which required to be elucidated by experiment. Eager in these pursuits, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, while on his visit, found himself much at a loss for the want of some small chemical <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, which his landlord could not furnish: but happily recollecting young Cullen in the neighbourhood, he mentioned him to the duke as a person who could probably furnish it. —He was accordingly invited to dine; was introduced to his grace,—who was so much pleased with his knowledge, his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, that he formed an acquaintance which laid the foundation of all Dr Cullen's future advancement. The name of Cullen by this time became familiar at every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in that neighbourhood; and thus he came to be known, by character, to the duke of Hamilton, who then resided, for a short time, in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the country: and that nobleman having been suddenly taken ill, the assistance of young Cullen was called in; which proved a fortunate circumstance in serving to promote his advancement to a station in life more suited to his talents than that in which he had hitherto moved. The duke was highly delighted with the sprightly character and ingenious conversation of his new acquaintance. Receiving instruction from him in a much more pleasing, and an infinitely easier way than he had ever before obtained, the conversation of Cullen proved highly interesting to his grace.—No wonder then that he soon found means to get his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, who was already the esteemed acquaintance of the man through whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> all fermentations in Scotland were obliged to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, appointed to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the university of Glasgow, where his singular talents for discharging the duties of the station he now occupied soon became very conspicuous. During his residence in the country, however, several important incidents occurred, that ought not to be passed over in silence. It was during this time that was formed a connection in business in a very humble line between two men, who became afterwards eminently conspicuous in much more exalted stations. William, afterwards Doctor Hunter, the famous lecturer on anatomy in London, was a native of the same part of the country; and not being in affluent circumstances more than Cullen, these two young men, stimulated by the impulse of genius to prosecute their medical studies with ardour, but thwarted by the narrowness of their fortune, entered into a copartnery business as surgeons and apothecaries in the country. The chief end of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> being to furnish the parties with the means of prosecuting their medical studies, which they could not separately so well enjoy, it was stipulated, that one of them alternately should be allowed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in what <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> he inclined, during the winter, while the other should carry on the business in the country, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> advantage. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this agreement, Cullen was first allowed to study in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> for one winter; but when it came to Hunter's turn next winter, he, preferring London to Edinburgh, went thither. There his singular neatness in dissecting, and uncommon dexterity in making anatomical preparations, his assiduity in study, his mildness of manner, and pliability of temper, soon recommended him to the notice of Dr Douglas, who then read lectures upon anatomy and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">midwifery</a> there; who engaged Hunter as an assistant, and whose <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> he afterwards filled with so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to himself and satisfaction to the public. Thus was dissolved, in a premature manner, a copartnery perhaps of as singular a kind as is to be found in the annals of literature: nor was Cullen a man of that disposition to let any engagement with him prove a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to his partner's advancement in life. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> were freely departed from by him; and Cullen and Hunter ever after kept up a very cordial and friendly correspondence; though, it is believed, they never from that time had a personal interview. During the time that Cullen practised as a country surgeon and apothecary, he formed another connection of a more permanent kind, which happily for him, was not dissolved till a very late period of his life. With the ardour of disposition he possessed, it cannot be supposed he beheld the fair <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a> with indifference. Very early in life he took a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to an amiable woman, a Miss Johnston, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to a clergyman in that neighbourhood, nearly of his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, who was prevailed on to join with him in the sacred bonds of wedlock, at a time when he had nothing else to recommend him to her except his person and dispositions. After giving to him a numerous family, and participating with him the changes of fortune which he experienced, she died in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> 1766. In the year 1746, Cullen, who had now taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of doctor in physic, was appointed a lecturer in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> in the university of Glasgow: and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of October began his lectures in that science. His singular talents for arrangement, his distinctness of enunciation, his vivacity of manner, and his knowledge of the science he taught, rendered his lectures interesting to the students to a degree that had been till then unknown at the university. He became, therefore, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, adored by the students. The former professors were eclipsed by the brilliancy of his reputation; and he had to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> all those little rubs that envy Cullen and disappointed ambition naturally threw in his way. Regardless, however, of these secret chagrins, he pressed forward with ardour in his literary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>; and, supported by the favour of the public, he consoled himself for the contumely he met with from a few individuals. His practice as a physician increased from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to day; and a vacancy having occurred in the year 1753, he was then appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> professor of medicine in that university. This new appointment served only to call forth his powers, and to bring to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> talents that it was not formerly known he possessed; so that his fame <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to increase. As, at that period, the patrons of the university of Edinburgh were constantly on the watch for the most eminent medical men to support the rising fame of the college, their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was soon directed towards Cullen; who, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr Plummer, professor of chemistry, was, in 1756, unanimously invited to accept the vacant chair. This invitation he accepted; and having resigned all his employments in Glasgow, he began his academical career in Edinburgh in the month of October of that year; and there he resided till his death. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the admission of Cullen into the university of Glasgow gave <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> spirit to the exertions of the students, this was still, if possible, more strongly felt in Edinburgh. Chemistry, which had been till that time of small account in that university, and was attended to by very few of the students, instantly became a favourite study; and the lectures upon that science were more frequented than any others in the university, anatomy alone excepted. The students, in general, spoke of Cullen with the rapturous ardour that is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to youth when they are highly pleased. These eulogiums appeared extravagant to moderate men, and could not fail to prove disgusting to his colleagues. A party was formed among the students for opposing this new favourite of the public; and these students, by misrepresenting the doctrines of Cullen to others who could not have an opportunity of hearing these doctrines themselves, made even some of the most intelligent men in the university think it their duty publicly to oppose these imaginary tenets. The ferment was thus augmented; and it was some time before the professors discovered the arts by which they had been imposed upon, and universal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> restored. During this time of public ferment, Cullen went steadily forward, without taking any part himself in these disputes. He never gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to any tales respecting his colleagues, nor took any notice of the doctrines they taught: That some of their unguarded strictures might at times come to his knowledge is not impossible; but if they did, they seemed to make no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on his mind. These attempts of a party of students to lower the character of Cullen on his first outset in the university of Edinburgh having proved fruitless, his fame as a professor, and his reputation as a physician, became more and more respected every day. Nor could it well be otherwise: Cullen's professional knowledge was always great, and his manner of lecturing singularly clear and intelligible, lively and entertaining; and to his patients, his conduct in general as a physician was so pleasing, his address so affable and engaging, and his manner so open, so kind, and so little regulated by pecuniary considerations, that it was impossible for those who had occasion to call once for his medical assistance, ever to be satisfied on any future occasion without it. He became the friend and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of every family he visited; and his future acquaintance could not be dispensed with. But if Dr Cullen in his public capacity deserved to be admired, in his private capacity by his students he deserved to be adored. His conduct to them was so attentive, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> he took in the private concerns of all those students who applied to him for advice, was so cordial and so warm, that it was impossible for any one who had a heart susceptible of generous emotions, not to be enraptured with a conduct so uncommon and so kind. Among ingenious youth, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> easily degenerates into rapture—into respect nearly allied to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>. Those who advert to this natural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be at no loss to account for that popularity which Cullen enjoyed—a popularity, that those who attempt to weigh every occurrence by the cool standard of reason alone, will be inclined to think excessive. It is fortunate, however, that the bulk of mankind will ever be influenced in their judgment not less by feelings and affections than by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and phlegmatic dictates of reason. The adoration which generous conduct excites, is the reward which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> hath appropriated exclusively to disinterested beneficence. This was the secret <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> that Cullen ever carried about with him, which fascinated such numbers of those who had intimate access to him. This was the power which his envious opponents never could have an opportunity of feeling. The general conduct of Cullen to his students was this. With all such as he observed to be attentive and diligent, he formed an early acquaintance, by inviting them by twos, by threes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by fours at a time, to sup with him, conversing with them on these occasions with the most engaging ease, and freely entering with them on the subject of their studies, their amusements, their difficulties, their hopes, and future prospects. In this way, he usually invited the whole of his numerous class, till he made himself acquainted with their abilities, their private character, and their objects of pursuit. Those among them whom he found most assiduous, best disposed, or the most friendless, he invited the most frequently, till an intimacy was gradually formed, which proved highly beneficial to them. Their doubts, with regard to their objects of study he listened to with attention, and solved with the most obliging condescension. His library, which consisted of an excellent assortment of the best books, especially on medical subjects, was at all times open for their accommodation; and his advice, in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of difficulty to them, they always had it in their power most readily to obtain. They seemed to be his family; and few persons of distinguished merit have left the university of Edinburgh in his time, with whom he did not keep up a correspondence till they were fairly established in business. By these means, he came to have a most accurate knowledge of the state of every country, with respect to practitioners in the medical line; the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> he made of which knowledge, was to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> students in their choice of places, where they might have an opportunity of engaging in business with a reasonable prospect of success. Cullen, success. Many, very many, able men has he thus put into a good line of business, where they never could have thought of it themselves; and they are now reaping the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of this beneficent foresight on his part. Nor was it in this way only that he befriended the students at the university of Edinburgh. Possessing a benevolence of mind that made him ever think first of the wants of others, and recollecting the difficulties that he himself had to struggle with in his younger days, he was at all times singularly attentive to their pecuniary concerns. From his general acquaintance among the students, and the friendly habits he was on with many of them, he found no difficulty in discovering those among them who were rather in embarrassed circumstances, without being obliged to hurt their delicacy in any degree. To such persons, when their habits of study admitted of it, he was peculiarly attentive. They were more frequently invited to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> than others; they were treated with more than usual kindness and familiarity; they were conducted to his library, and encouraged by the most delicate address to borrow from it freely whatever books be thought they had occasion for: and as persons in these circumstances were usually more shy in this respect than others, books were sometimes pressed upon them as a sort of constraint, by the doctor insisting to have their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of such or such <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> they had not read, and desiring them to carry the book home for that purpose. He, in short, behaved to them rather as if he courted their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and stood in need of their acquaintance than they of his. He thus raised them in the opinion of their acquaintance to a much higher degree of estimation than they could otherwise have obtained; which, to people whose minds were depressed by penury, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of honour was sharpened by the consciousness of an inferiority of a certain kind, was singularly engaging. Thus they were inspired with a secret sense of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, which elevated their minds, and excited an uncommon ardour of pursuit, instead of that melancholy inactivity which is so natural in such circumstances, and which too often leads to despair. Nor was he less delicate in the manner of supplying their wants, than attentive to discover them. He often found out some polite excuse for refusing to take payment for a first course, and never was at a loss for one to an after course. Before they could have an opportunity of applying for a ticket, he would sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the conversation to some subject that occurred in the course of his lectures; and as his lectures were never put in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> by himself, he would sometimes beg the favour to see their notes, if he knew they had been taken with attention, under a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of assisting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Sometimes he would express a wish to have their opinion of a particular part of his course, and presented them with a ticket for that purpose; and sometimes he refused to take payment, under the pretext that they had not received his full course the preceding year, some part of it having been necessarily omitted for want of time, which he meant to include in this course. By such delicate address, in which he greatly excelled, he took care to forerun their wants. Thus he not only gave them the benefit of his own lectures, but by refusing to take their money, he also enabled them to attend those of others that were necessary to complete their course of studies. These were particular devices he adopted to individuals to whom economy was necessary; but it was a general rule with him, never to take money from any student for more than two courses of the same set of lectures, permitting him to attend these lectures as many years longer as he pleased gratis. He introduced another general rule into the university, that was dictated by the same principle of disinterested beneficence, that ought not to be here passed over in silence. Before he came to Edinburgh, it was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of medical professors to accept of fees for their medical assistance, when wanted, even from medical students themselves, who were perhaps attending the professor's own lectures at the time. But Cullen never would take fees as a physician from any student at the university, though he attended them, when called in as a physician, with the same assiduity and care as if they had been persons of the first rank, who paid him most liberally.
