This gradually induced others to adopt a similar practice: so that it is now become a general rule for medical professors to decline taking any fees when their assistance is necessary to a student. For this useful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>, with many others, the students of the university of Edinburgh are solely indebted to the liberality of Dr Cullen. The first lectures which Cullen delivered in Edinburgh were on chemistry; and for many years he also gave clinical lectures on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> which occurred in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> infirmary. In the month of February 1763, Dr Alston died, after having begun his usual course of lectures on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>; and the magistrates of Edinburgh, as patrons of that professorship in the university, appointed Dr Cullen to that chair, requesting that he would finish the course of lectures that had been begun for that season. This he agreed to do; and though he was under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of going on with the course in a few days after he was nominated, he did not once think of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the lectures of his predecessor, but resolved to deliver a new course entirely his own. The popularity of Cullen at this time may be guessed at by the increase of new students who came to attend his course in addition to the eight or ten who had entered to Dr Alston. The new students exceeded 100. An imperfect copy of these lectures thus fabricated in haste, having been published, the doctor thought it necessary to give a more correct edition of them in the latter part of his life. But his faculties being then much impaired, his friends looked in vain for those striking beauties that characterised his literary exertions in the prime of life. Some years afterwards, on the death of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, the magistrates once more appointed Dr Cullen to give lectures on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of physic in his stead. And it was on that occasion Dr Cullen thought it expedient to resign the chemical chair in favour of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>, his former pupil, whose talents in that department of science were then well known, and who filled the chair till his death with great satisfaction to the public. Soon after, on the death of Dr Rutherford, who for many years had given lectures with applause on the practice of physic, Dr John Gregory (whose name can never be mentioned by any one who had the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of his acquaintance without the warmest tribute of a grateful respect) having become a candidate for this place along with Dr Cullen, a sort of compromise took place between them, by which they agreed each to give lectures alternately on the theory and on the practice of physic during their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> lives, the longest survivor being allowed to hold either of the classes he should incline. In consequence of this agreement, Dr Cullen delivered the first course of lectures on the practice of physic in winter 1766, and Dr Gregory succeeded him in that branch the following year. Never perhaps did a literary arrangement take place that could have proved more beneficial to the students than this. Both these men possessed great talents, though of a kind extremely dissimilar. Both of them had certain failings or defects, which the other was aware of, and counteracted. Each of them knew and respected the talents of the other. They co-operated, therefore, in the happiest manner, to enlarge the understanding, and to forward the pursuits of their pupils. Unfortunately this arrangement was soon destroyed by the unexpected death of Dr Gregory, who was cut off in the flower of life by a sudden and unforeseen event. After this time, Cullen continued to give lectures on the practice of physic till a few months before his death, which happened on the 5th of February 1790, in the 77th year of his age. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the character of Dr Cullen, his biographer, Dr Anderson observes, that in scientific pursuits men may be arranged into two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> classes, which, though greatly different from each other in their extremes, yet approximate at times so near as to be blended indiscriminately together; those who possess a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for detail, and those who are endowed with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of arrangement. The first may be said to view objects individually as through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. The field of vision is confined; but the objects included within that field, which must usually be considered singly and apart from all others, are seen with a wondrous degree of accuracy and distinctness. The other takes a sweeping view of the universe at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, considers every object he perceives, not individually, but as a part of one harmonious whole: His mind is therefore not so much employed in examining the separate parts of this individual object, as in tracing its relations, connections, and dependencies on those around it.—Such was the turn of Cullen's mind. The talent for arrangement was that which peculiarly distinguished him from the ordinary class of mortals; and this talent he possessed perhaps in a more distinguished degree than any other person of the age in which he lived. Many persons exceeded him in the minute knowledge of particular departments, who, knowing this, naturally looked upon him as their inferior; but possessing not at the same time that glorious faculty, which, "with an eye wide roaming, glances from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to heaven," or the charms which this talent can infuse into congenial minds, felt disgust at the pre-eminence he obtained, and astonishment at the means by which he obtained it. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> have had their talents in like manner appreciated; and many are the persons who can neither be exalted to sublime <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, nor ravished with the natural touches of a Shakespeare. Such things are wisely ordered, that every department in the universe may be properly filled by those who have talents exactly suited to the task assigned them by heaven. Had Cullen, however, possessed the talents for arrangement alone, small would have been his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of applause he has attained. Without a knowledge of facts, a talent for arrangement produces nothing but chimeras; without materials to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon, the structures which an over-heated imagination may rear up are merely "the baseless fabric of a vision." No man was more sensible of the justness of this remark than Dr Cullen, and few were at greater pains to avoid it. His whole life, indeed, was employed, almost without interruption, in collecting facts. Whether he was reading, or walking, or conversing, these were continually falling into his way. With the keen perception of an eagle, he marked them at the first glance; and without stopping at the time to examine them, they were stored up in his memory, to be drawn forth as occasion required, to be confronted with other facts that had been obtained after the same manner, and to have their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> ascertained, or their falsity proved by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> which should appear when carefully examined at the impartial bar of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Without a memory retentive in a singular degree, this could not have been done; but so very extraordinary was Dr Cullen's memory, that till towards the very decline of life, there was scarcely a fact that had ever occurred to him which he could not readily recollect, with all its concomitant circumstances, whenever he had occasion to refer to it. It was this faculty which so much abridged his labour in study, and enabled him so happily to avail himself of the labour of others in all his literary speculations. He often reaped more by the conversation of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> than another man would have done in whole weeks of laborious study. In his prelections, Dr Cullen never attempted to read. His lectures were delivered sine voce, without having been previously put into writing, or thrown into any particular arrangement. The vigour of his mind was such, that nothing more was necessary than a few short notes before him, merely to prevent him from varying from the general order he had been accustomed to observe. This gave to his discourses an ease, a vivacity, a variety, and a force, that are rarely to be met with in academical discourses. His lectures, by consequence, upon the same subject, were never exactly the same. Their general tenor indeed was not much varied; but the particular illustrations were always new, well suited to the circumstances that attracted the general attention of the day, and were delivered in the particular way that accorded with the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of mind the prelector found himself in at the time. To these circumstances must be ascribed that energetic artless elocution, which rendered his lectures so generally captivating to his hearers. Even those who could not follow him in those extensive views his penetrating mind glanced at, or who were not able to understand those apt allusions to collateral objects which he could only rapidly point at as he went along, could not help being warmed in some measure by the vivacity of his manner. But to those who could follow him in his rapid career, the ideas he suggested were so numerous, the views he laid open were so extensive, and the objects to be attained were so important—that every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> faculty of the mind was roused; and such an ardour of enthusiasm was excited in the prosecution of study, as appeared to be perfectly inexplicable to those who were merely unconcerned spectators. In consequence of this unshackled freedom in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and delivery of his lectures, tures, every circumstance was in the nicest unison with the tone of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of countenance, which the particular cast of mind he was in at the time inspired. Was he joyous, all the figures introduced for illustration were fitted to excite hilarity, and good humour; was he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, the objects brought under view were of a nature more solemn and grand: and was he peevish, there was a peculiarity of manner in thought, in word, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which produced a most striking and interesting effect. The languor of a nerveless uniformity was never experienced, nor did an abortive attempt to excite emotions that the speaker himself could not at the time feel, ever produce those discordant ideas which prove disgusting and unpleasing. It would seem as if Dr Cullen had considered the proper business of a preceptor to be that of putting his pupils into a proper train of study, so as to enable them to prosecute those studies at a future period, and to carry them on much farther than the short time allowed for academical prelections would admit. He did not, therefore, so much strive to make those who attended his lectures deeply versed in the particular details of objects, as to give them a general view of the whole subject; to shew what had been already attained respecting it; to point out what remained yet to be discovered; and to put them into a train of study that should enable them at a future period, to remove those difficulties that had hitherto obstructed our progress, and thus to advance themselves to farther and farther degrees of perfection. If these were his views, nothing could be more happily adapted to them than the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> he invariably pursued. He first drew, with the striking touches of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, a rapid and general outline of the subject, by which the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> was seen at once to start boldly from the canvas, distinct in all its parts, and unmixed with any other object. He then began anew to retrace the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, to touch up the lesser parts, and to finish the whole in as perfect a manner as the state of our knowledge at the time would permit. Where materials were wanting, the picture there continued to remain imperfect. The wants were thus rendered obvious; and the means of supplying these were pointed out with the most careful discrimination. The student whenever he looked back to the subject, perceived the defects; and his hopes being awakened, he felt an irresistible impulse to explore that hitherto untrodden path which had been pointed out to him, and fill up the chasm which still remained. Thus were the active faculties of the mind most powerfully excited; and instead of labouring himself to supply deficiencies that far exceeded the power of any one man to accomplish, he set thousands at work to fulfil the task, and put them into a train of going on with it. It was to these talents, and to this mode of applying them, that Dr Cullen owed his celebrity as a professor; and it was in this manner that he has perhaps done more towards the advancement of science than any other man of his time, though many individuals might perhaps be found who were more deeply versed in the particular departments he taught than he himself was. Dr Cullen's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, though striking and not unpleasing, was not elegant. He had an expressive countenance and a lively eye. In his person he was tall and thin, stooping much about the shoulders; and when he walked he had a contemplative look, seemingly regarding little the objects around him. According to the observation of one who was well acquainted with the character of Cullen, he was eminently distinguished as a professor for three things. "The energy of his mind, by which he viewed every subject with ardour, and combined it immediately with the whole of his knowledge. "The scientific arrangement which he gave to his subject, by which there was a lucidus ordo to the dullest scholar. He was the first person in this country who made chemistry cease to be a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>. "A wonderful art of interesting the students in everything which he taught, and of raising an emulative enthusiasm among them." Life of Dr Cullen, by Dr Anderson, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>.

a barbarous and immoral practice, whereby the lords of manors anciently assumed a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the first night of their vassals' brides.

CULLODEN

Pages 21-21

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Scotland within two miles of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, chiefly remarkable for a complete victory gained over the rebels on the 16th of April 1746. That <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, commanded by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, began their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> from Nairn, formed into five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of three battalions each; headed by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>-general Huske on the left, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Sempill on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and Brigadier Mordaunt in the centre; flanked by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> under the generals Hawley and Bland, who at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> covered the cannon on the right and left. In this order they marched about eight miles, when a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>'s horse, and of the Highlanders, having advanced before the rest of the army, discovered the van of the rebels commanded by the young Pretender. Both armies immediately formed in the order and numbers shown in the annexed scheme. About two in the afternoon the rebels began to cannonade the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s army; but their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> being ill served, did little execution; while the fire from their enemies was severely felt, and occasioned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disorder. The rebels then made a push at the right of the royal army, in order to draw the troops forward; but finding themselves disappointed, they turned their whole force on the left; falling chiefly on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">Barrel</a>'s and Munro's regiments, where they attempted to flank the king's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> line. But this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> also was defeated by the advancing of Wolfe's regiment, while in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the cannon kept playing upon them with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTRIDGE">cartridge</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. General Hawley, with some Highlanders, had opened a passage through some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls to the right for the horse which advanced on that side; while the horse on the king's right wheeled off upon their left, dispersed their body of reserve, and met in the centre of their front line in their rear; when being repulsed in the front, and great numbers of them cut off, the rebels fell into very great confusion. A dreadful carnage was made by the cavalry on their backs; however, some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foot still preserved their order; but Kingston's horse, from the reserve, gallopped up briskly, and falling upon the fugitives, did terrible execution. A total defeat instantly took place, with the loss of 2500 killed, wounded, and prisoners, on the part of the rebels, while the royalists lost not above 200. The young Pretender had his horse shot under him during the engagement; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>

CULM

Pages 21-22
or Culmus, among botanists, a straw or haulm; defined by Linnæus to be the proper trunk of the grasses, which elevates the leaves, flower, and fruit. This sort of trunk is tubular or hollow, and has frequently knots or joints distributed at proper distances through its whole length. The leaves are long, sleek, and placed either near the roots in great numbers, or proceed singly from the different joints of the stalk, which they embrace at the base, like a sheath or glove. The haulm is commonly garnished with leaves; sometimes, however, it is naked; that is, devoid of leaves, as in a few species of cypress-grass. Most grasses have a round cylindrical stalk; in some species of Schoenus, Scirpus, cypress-grass, and others, it is triangular. The stalk is sometimes entire, that is, has no branches; sometimes branching, as in Schoenus aculeatus et copensis; and not seldom consists of a number of scales which lie over each other like tiles. Lastly, in a few grasses the stalk is not interrupted with joints, as in the greater part. The space contained betwixt every two knots or joints, is termed by botanists internodium and articulus culmi. This species of trunk often affords certain marks of distinction in discriminating the species. Thus, in the genus Eriocaulon, the species are scarce to be distinguished. Those of the above, who have only guns, and Kilmarnock's guards. Second column 800. Ld. Lewis Gordon's and Glenbucket's, to be ready to succour when needful. Third column 800. CULMIFEROUS PLANTS

Pages 22-23

(from culmus, a straw <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> haum) : <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> so called, which have a smooth jointed stalk, usually hollow, and wrapped about at each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> with single, narrow, sharp-pointed leaves, and the seeds contained in chaffy husks; such are oats, wheat, barley, rye, and the other plants of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> family of the Grasses.

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the passage of any heavenly body over the meridian, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> its greatest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> for that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>.

CULPRIT

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the clerk of the arraignments, when a person is indicted for a criminal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. CULROSS

Pages 23-23

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough town in Scotland, situated on the river Forth, about 23 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. Here is a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which was built about the year 1590 by Edward <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kinloss, better known in England by the name of Lord Bruce, slain in the noted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a> between him and Sir Edward Sackville. Some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains of the Cistercian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> are still to be seen here, founded by Malcolm <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Fife in 1217. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was jointly dedicated to the Virgin and St. Serf confessor. The revenue at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> was 768 pounds Scots, besides the rents paid in kind. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of monks, exclusive of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1611 in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 34'. N. Lat. 56° 8'.

CULVERIN

Pages 23-23

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender piece of ordnance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, serving to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. Manege derives the word from the Latin culubrina: others from culuber, "snake;" either on account of the length and slenderness of the piece, or of the ravages it makes. There are three kinds of culverins, viz. the extraordinary, the ordinary, and the least sized. 1. The culverin extraordinary has 5½ inches bore; its length 32 calibers, or 13 feet; weighs 4800 pounds; its load above 12 pounds; carries a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> 5½ inches diameter, weighing 20 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. 2. The ordinary culverin is 12 feet long; carries a ball of 17 pounds 5 ounces; caliber 5½ inches; its weight 4500 pounds. 3. The culverin of the least size, has its diameter 5 inches; is 12 feet long; weighing about 4000 pounds; carries a shot 3½ inches diameter, weighing 14 pounds 9 ounces.

CULVERTAILED

Pages 23-23

among shipwrights, signifies the fastening <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> letting of one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> into another, so that they cannot slip out, as the corlings into the beams of a ship.

CUMA

Pages 23-23
or CUMÆ, in Ancient Geography, a town of Æolia in Asia Minor. The inhabitants have been accused of stupidity for not laying a tax upon all the goods which entered their harbour during 300 years. They were called Cumani. CUMÆ, or CUMA, in Ancient Geography, a city of Campania near Puteoli, founded by a colony from Chalcis and Cumae of Æolia before the Trojan war. The inhabitants were called Cumæi. One of the Sibyls fixed her residence in a cave in the neighbourhood, and was called the Cumæan Sibyl.

CUMBERLAND

Pages 23-23

Richard, a learned English divine in the end of the 17th century, was son of a citizen of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. In 1672 he published a Treatise of the Laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>; and in 1686, An <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> toward the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">Weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">Measures</a>. After the Revolution he was nominated by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William to the bishopric of Peterborough. He wrote on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and was as remarkable for humility of mind, benevolence of temper, and innocence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as for his extensive learning. He died in 1718.

CUMBRAY

Pages 23-23
GREAT and LITTLE, two islands in the frith of Clyde, in Scotland. The first is about six miles in circumference, and lies between the isle of Bute and the coast of Ayrshire. The other is of smaller extent, and has a light-house.

CUMINUM

Pages 23-23

CUMIN; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, umbellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CUNÆUS, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> in 1586, was distinguished by his knowledge in the learned languages, and his skill in the Jewish antiquities. He also studied <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which he taught at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1615; and read politics there till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1638. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is a treatise, in Latin, on the republic of the Hebrews.

CUNEIFORM

Pages 23-23

in general, an appellation given to any body having the shape of a wedge. CUNEIFORM Bone, in Anatomy, the seventh bone of the cranium, called also os basilaris, and os sphenoides. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CUNEOUS

Pages 23-24

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of infantry drawn CUNICULUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPUS">LEPUS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cuniculus, in mining, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by authors in distinction from puteus, to express the several sorts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> and cuts in these subterranean works. The cuniculi are those <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> passages in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> where they walk on horizontally; but the putei are the perpendicular cuts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> descents. The miners in Germany call these by the name stollen, and schacht; the first word expressing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the perpendicular cuts.

CUNILA

Pages 24-24

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONANDRIA">monandria</a> class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CUNINA

Pages 24-24

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> who had the care of little children.

CUNITZ

Pages 24-24
or CUNITIA, MARIA, astronomer, was the eldest daughter of Hendric Cunitz, doctor of medicine in Silesia, and was born about the beginning of the 17th century. She learned languages with amazing facility; and understood Polish, German, French, Italian, Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. She attained a knowledge of the sciences with equal ease: she was skilled in history, physic, poetry, painting, music, and playing upon instruments; and yet these were only an amusement. She more particularly applied herself to the mathematics, and especially to astronomy, which she made her principal study, and was ranked in the number of the most able astronomers of her time. Her Astronomical Tables acquired her a prodigious reputation: she printed them in Latin and German, and dedicated them to the emperor Ferdinand III. She married Elias de Lewin, M.D. and died at Pistehen in 1664.

CUNNINGHAM

Pages 24-24

Alexander, author of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> from the Revolution to the accession of George I. was born in the south of Scotland about the year 1654, in the regency of Oliver Cromwell. His father was minister at Ettrick, in the presbytery and shire of Selkirk. He was educated, as was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> among the Scottish presbyterian gentlemen of those times, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; where he imbibed his principles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and lived much with the English and Scots refugees at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> before the revolution, particularly with the earls of Argyle and Sunderland. He came over to England with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and enjoyed the confidence and intimacy of many leading men among the whig party, that is, the friends and abettors of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William and the revolution. He was employed, at different times, in the character of a travelling <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>; first, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Hyndford, and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Mr William Carmichael, solicitor-general, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, for Scotland; secondly, with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Lorne, afterwards so well known under the name of John <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle; and thirdly, with the lord viscount Lansdale. In his travels, we find him, at the German courts, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the celebrated Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Addison, whose virtues he celebrates. Lord Lorne, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was under the tuition of Mr Cunningham, though not seventeen years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> of a regiment, which his father, the earl of Argyle, had raised for his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. Mr Cunningham's connection with the duke of Argyle, with whom he had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of maintaining an intimacy as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived, together with the opportunities he enjoyed of learning, in his travels, what may be called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, naturally tended to qualify him for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> on military affairs. Mr Cunningham, both when he travelled with the nobleman above mentioned, and on other occasions, was employed by the English ministry in transmitting secret intelligence to them on the most important subjects. He was also, on sundry occasions, employed by the generals of the confederate armies, to carry intelligence, and to make representations to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Britain. In Carstairs's State Papers, published by Dr Macormick, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the United <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of St Andrew's, in 1774, there are two letters from our author, dated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the 22d and 26th of August 1701, giving an account of his conferences with the marquis de Torcy, the French minister, relative to the Scots trade with France. This commercial negotiation, from the tenor of Cunningham's letters compared with his history, appears to have been only the ostensible object of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>: for he sent an exact account to King William, with whom he was personally acquainted, of the military preparations throughout all France. Mr Cunningham's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> friends, Argyle, Sunderland, Sir Robert Walpole, &c. on the accession of George I. sent him as British envoy to the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. He arrived in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1715; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there, in the character of resident, till the year 1720, when he returned again to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He lived many years after, which he seems chiefly to have passed in a studious retirement. In 1735, he was visited in London by Lord Hyndford, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of his lordship's father, to whom he had been tutor, when he appeared to be very old. He seems to have lived about two years after: for the body of an Alexander Cunningham lies interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of St Martin's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who died in the 83d year of his age, on the 15th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of May 1735; and who was probably the same person. His "History of Great Britain, from the revolution in 1688 to the accession of George I." was published in two volumes 4to, in 1787. It was written by Mr Cunningham in Latin, but was translated into English by the reverend William Thomson, L.L.D. The original manuscript came into the possession of the reverend Dr Hollingberry, archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, some of whose relations had been connected with the author. He communicated it to the earl of Hardwicke, and to the reverend Dr Douglas, now bishop of Carlisle, both of whom recommended the publication. In a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the archdeacon says, "My first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to have produced it in the original; but knowing how few are sufficiently learned to understand, and how many are indisposed to read two quarto volumes in Latin, however interesting and entertaining the subject may be, I altered my purpose, and intended to have sent it into the world in a translation."

CUNODONTES

Pages 24-25

a people mentioned by Solinus and Isidorus, and by them supposed to have the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of dogs. They were probably denominated, says Dr Bryant, from the object of their worship, the deity Chan-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADON">Adon</a>, which the Greeks expressed Κούρασις, and thence called his votaries Cunodontes.

CUNONIA

Pages 25-25

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CUOGOLO

Pages 25-25

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> much used by the Venetians in glass-making, and found in the river Tesino. It is a small stone of an impure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, of a shattery texture, and is of the shape of a pebble.

CUP

Pages 25-25

a vessel of capacity of various forms and materials, chiefly to drink out of. In the Ephem German, we have a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of a cup made of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>-corn by Oswald Nerlinger, which holds 1200 other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> cups, having each its several handle, all gilt on the edges; with room for 400 more. Cup, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Calyx, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cup-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">Galls</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by authors to a very singular kind of galls, found on the leaves of the oak and some other trees. They are of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a cup, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> drinking-glass without its foot, being regular cones adhering by their point or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>; and the top or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is hollowed a little way, so that it appears like a drinking-glass with a cover, which was made so small as not to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> it at the mouth, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> a little way into it. This cover is flat, and has in the centre a very small protuberance, resembling the nipple of a woman's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. This is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> green, as is also the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a>, excepting only its rim that runs round the top: this is of a scarlet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and that very beautiful. Besides this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of gall, the oak leaves furnish us with several others, some of which are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, some round and others flatted; these are of various sizes, and appear on the leaves at various seasons of the year. They all contain the worm of some small fly; and this creature passes all its changes in this its habitation, being sometimes found in the worm, sometimes in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>, and sometimes in the fly state, in the cavity of it.

CUPANIA

Pages 25-25

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monococca class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricoccæ. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CUPEL

Pages 25-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, a small vessel which absorbs metallic bodies when changed by fire into a fluid scoria; but retains them as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as they continue in their metallic state. One of the most proper materials for making a vessel of this kind is the ashes of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; there is scarcely any other substance which so strongly resists vehement fire, which so readily imbites metallic scoriae, and which is so little disposed to be vitrified by them. In want of these, some make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of vegetable ashes, freed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from their saline <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which would cause them melt in the fire. The bones, burnt to perfect whiteness, so that no particle of coaly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inflammable matter may remain in them, and well washed from filth, are ground into moderately fine powder; which in order to its being formed into cupels, is moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as much water as is sufficient to make it hold together when strongly pressed between the fingers; some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> glutinous liquids, as whites of eggs or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water, in order to give the powder a greater tenacity; but the inflammable matter, however small in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, which accompanies these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and cannot be easily burnt out from the internal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, is apt to revive a part of the metallic scoria that has been absorbed, and to occasion the vessel to burst or crack. The cupel is formed in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, from three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch to two inches diameter, and not quite so deep, placed upon some smooth support: the ring being filled with moistened powder, which is pressed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> with the fingers; a round-faced pestle, called a monk, is struck <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into it with a few blows of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a>, by which the mass is made to cohere, and rendered sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and a shallow cavity formed in the middle: the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the cavity is nearly that of a sphere, that a small quantity of metal melted in it may run together into one bead. To make the cavity the smoother, a little of the same kind of ashes levigated into an impalpable powder, and not moistened, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sprinkled on the surface, through a small fine sieve made for this purpose, and the monk again struck down upon it. The ring or mould is a little narrower at bottom than at top; so that by pressing it down on some of the dry powder spread upon a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, the cupel is loosened, and forced upwards a little; after which it is easily pushed out with the finger; and is then set to dry in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> free from dust.

CUPELLATION

Pages 26-27

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of refining <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver by means of a cupel. For this purpose another vessel, called a muffle, is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, within which one or more cupels are placed. The muffle is placed upon a grate in a proper <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, with its mouth facing the door, and as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it as may be. The furnace being filled up with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, some lighted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> is thrown on the top, and what fuel is afterwards necessary is supplied through a door above. The cupels are set in the muffle; and being gradually heated by the successive kindling of the fuel, they are kept <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that the moisture which they strongly retain may be completely dissipated: for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any vapours should issue from them after the metal is put in, they would occasion it to sputter, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it to be thrown off in little drops. In the sides of the muffle are some perpendicular slits, with a knob over the top of each, to prevent any small pieces of coals or ashes from falling in. The door, or some apertures made in it, being kept open, for the inspection of the cupels, fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> enters into the muffle, and passes off through these slits: by laying some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> charcoal on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plate before the door, the air is heated before its admission; and by removing the charcoal or supplying more, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in the cavity of the muffle may be somewhat diminished or increased more speedily than can be effected by suppressing or exciting the fire in the furnace on the outside of the muffle. The renewal of the air is also necessary for promoting the scorification of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. The cupel being of a full red heat, the lead <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into a smooth bullet, that it may not scratch or injure the surface, is laid lightly in the cavity; it immediately melts; and then the gold or silver to be cupelled is cautiously introduced either by means of a small iron ladle, or by wrapping them in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and dropping them on the lead with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of tongs. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of lead should be at least three or four times that of the fine metal; but when gold is very impure, it requires 10 or 12 times its quantity of lead for cupellation. It is reckoned that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> requires for its scorification about 10 times its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of lead: that when copper and gold are mixed in equal quantities, the copper is so much defended by the gold, as not to be separable with less than 20 times its weight of lead; and that when copper is in very small proportion, as a 20th or 30th part of the gold or silver, upwards of 60 parts of lead are necessary for one of the copper. The cupel must always weigh at least half as much as the lead and copper; for otherwise it would not be sufficient for receiving half the scoria; there is little danger, however, of cupels being made too small for the quantity of a gold <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a>. The mixture being brought into thin fusion, the heat is to be regulated according to the appearances; and in this consists the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> nicety in the operation. If a various coloured skin rises to the top, which liquefying, runs off to the sides, and is there absorbed by the cupel, visibly staining the parts it enters; if a fresh scoria continually succeeds, and is absorbed nearly as fast as it is formed, only a fine circle of it remaining round the edge of the metal; if the lead appears in gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and throws up a fume a little way from the surface; the fire is of the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> goes on successfully. Such a fiery brightness of the cupel as prevents its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from being distinguished, and the fumes of the lead rising up almost to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the muffle, are marks of too strong a heat; though it must be observed, that the elevation of the fumes is not always in proportion to the degree of heat; for if the heat greatly exceeds the due limits, both the fumes and ebullition <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> entirely cease. In these circumstances the fire must necessarily be diminished: for while the lead boils and smokes vehemently, its fumes are apt to carry off some part of the gold; the cupel is liable to crack from the hasty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of the scoria, and part of the gold and silver is divided into globules, which lying discontinued on the cupel after the process is finished, cannot easily be collected; if there is no ebullition or fumes, the scorification does not appear to go on. Too weak a heat is known by the dull redness of the cupel; by the fume not rising from the surface of the lead; and the scoria like bright drops in languid motion, or accumulated, or growing consistent all over the metal. The form of the surface affords also an useful mark of the degree of heat; the stronger the fire, the more convex is the surface; and the weaker, the more flat: in this point, however, regard must be had to the quantity of metal; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity being always flatter than a small one in an equal fire. Towards the end of the process, the fire must be increased; for the greatest part of the fusible metal lead being now worked off, the gold and silver will not continue melted in the heat that was sufficient before. As the last remains of the lead are separating, the rainbow colours on the surface become more vivid, and variously intersect one another with quick motions. Soon after, disappearing all at once, a sudden <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> brightness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> of gold and silver shows the process to be finished. The cupel is then drawn forwards towards the mouth of the muffle; and the button, as soon as grown fully <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, taken out. **CUPELLING FURNACE.** See Cupelling Furnace. **CUPID,** in Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the god of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. There seems to have been two Cupids; one the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Venus, whose delight it was to raise sentiments of love and virtue; and the other the son of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> and the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, who inspired base and impure desires. The first of these, called Eros, or true love, bore <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> arrows, which caused real joy, and a virtuous affection; the other, called Anteros, had leaden arrows, that raised a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> founded only on desire, which ended in satiety and disgust. Cupid was always drawn with wings, to represent his inconstancy; and naked, to show that he has nothing of his own. He was painted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, to denote that love sees no fault in the object beloved; and with a bow and quiver of arrows, to show his power over the mind. Sometimes he is placed between <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, to show the prevalence of eloquence and valour in love; and at others is placed near Fortune, to signify that the success of lovers depends on that inconstant goddess. Sometimes he is represented with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> on his head and a spear on his shoulder, to signify that love disarms the fiercest men; he rides upon the backs of panthers and lions, and uses their manes for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>, to denote that love tames the most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> beasts. He is likewise pictured riding upon a dolphin, to signify that his empire extends over the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> no less than the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. **CUPOLA,** in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a spherical vault, or the round top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, in the form of a cup <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>. **CUPPING,** in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the operation of applying cupping-glasses for the discharge of blood and other humours by the skin. See Surgery. **CUPRESSUS,** the Cypress Tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the coniferae class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 51st order, Coniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The wood of the sempervirens, or evergreen cypress, is said to resist <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, moths, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, and to last many centuries. The coffins in which the Athenians were wont to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their heroes, were made, says <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, of this wood; as were likewise the chests containing the Egyptian mummies. The doors of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s church at Rome were originally of the same materials. These, after lasting upwards of 600 years, at the end of which they did not discover the smallest tendency to corruption, were removed by order of Pope Eugenius IV. and gates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> substituted in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The same tree is by many eminent authors recommended as improving and meliorating the air by its balsamic and aromatic exhalations; upon which account many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians of the eastern countries used to send their patients who were troubled with weak lungs to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Candia, where these trees grow in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance; and where, from the salubrious air alone, very few failed of a perfect cure. In the same island, says Miller, the cypress-trees were so lucrative a commodity, that the plantations were called das filiae; the felling of them being reckoned a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>'s portion. Cypress, says Mr Pococke, is the only tree that grows towards the top of Mount Lebanon, and being nipped by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, grows like a small oak. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s ark is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed to have been made of this kind of wood. **CUPRUM AMMONIACALE.** See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is recommended in some kinds of spasmodic diseases, given in the dose of one or two grains.

CUPRUM

Pages 27-28
or Copper.** See Copper, Chemistry Index. **CURACOA,** or Curassow, one of the larger Antilles islands, formerly subject to the Dutch; situated in W. Long. 68. 30. N. Lat. 12. 30. This island is little else than a bare rock, about ten leagues long and five broad; lying three leagues off the coast of Venezuela. It has an excellent harbour, but the entrance is difficult. The basin is extremely large, and convenient in every respect; and is defended by a fort skillfully constructed, and always kept in repair. The reason of forming a settlement upon this barren spot, was to carry on a contraband trade with the Spanish colonies on the continent; but after some time the method of managing this trade was changed. Curassow itself became an immense magazine, to which the Spaniards resorted in their boats to exchange gold, silver, vanilla, cocoa, cochineal, bark, skins, and mules, for negroes, linen, silks, India stuffs, spices, laces, ribbands, quicksilver, steel, and iron-ware. These voyages, though continual, did not prevent a number of Dutch sloops from passing from Curassow to the continent. But the modern substitution of register-ships, instead of galleons, has made this communication less frequent; but it will be revived whenever, by the intervention of war, the communication with the Spanish Main shall be cut off. The disputes between the courts of London and Versailles also prove favourable to the trade of Curassow. At these times it furnishes provisions to the southern parts of St Domingo, and takes off all its produce. Even the French privateers, from the windward islands, repair in great numbers to Curassow, notwithstanding the distance. The reason is, that they find there all kinds of necessary stores for their vessels; and frequently Spanish, but always European goods, which are universally used. Every commodity without exception, that is landed at Curassow, pays one per cent. port-duty. Dutch goods are never taxed higher; but those that are shipped from other European ports pay nine per cent. more. Foreign coffee is subject to the same tax, in order to promote the sale of that of Surinam. Every other production of America is subject only to a payment of three per cent. but with an express stipulation, that they are to be conveyed directly to some port belonging to the republic. This island is now in possession of Great Britain. **CURATE,** the lowest degree in the church of England; land; he who represents the incumbent of a church, parson, or vicar, and performs divine service in his stead: and in case of pluralities of livings, or where a clergyman is old and infirm, it is requisite there should be a curate to perform the cure of the church. He is to be licensed, and admitted by the bishop of the diocese, or by an ordinary having episcopal jurisdiction; and when a curate hath the approbation of the bishop, he usually appoints the salary too; and in such case, if he be not paid, the curate hath a proper remedy in the ecclesiastical court, by a sequestration of the profits of the benefice; but if the curate is not licensed by the bishop, he is put to his remedy at common law, where he must prove the agreement, &c. A curate having no fixed estate in his curacy, not being instituted and inducted, may be removed at pleasure by the bishop or incumbent. But there are perpetual curates as well as temporary, who are appointed where the tithes are inappropriate, and no vicarage endowed: these are not removable, and the impropreitors are obliged to find them; some whereof have certain portions of the tithes settled on them. Every clergyman that officiates in a church (whether incumbent or substitute) in the liturgy is called a curate. Curates must subscribe the declaration according to the act of uniformity, or are liable to imprisonment, &c.

CURATELLA

Pages 28-28

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CURATOR

Pages 28-28

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, an officer under the emperors, who regulated the price of all kinds of merchandise and vendible commodities in the cities of the empire. They had likewise the superintendence of the customs and tributes; whence also they were called logistae. Curator, among civilians, a trustee <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> person nominated to take care of the affairs and interests of a person emancipated or interdicted. In countries where the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> prevails, between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14 and 24 years, minors have curators assigned them; till 14, they have tutors. Curator of an University, in the United Provinces, is an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> office, to which belongs the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the affairs of the university; as, the administration of the revenues, the inspection of the professors, &c. The curators are chosen by the states of each <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>: The university of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> has three; the burghermasters of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> have a fourth.

CURB

Pages 28-28

in the manege, a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> made fast to the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> in a hole called the eye, and running over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. It consists of these three parts; the hook fixed to the eye of the branch; the chain of SS's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> links; and the two rings or mailles. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">Large</a> curbs, provided they be round, are always most gentle; but care is to be taken, that it rest in its proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, a little above the beard, otherwise the bit-mouth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not have the effect that may be expected from it. English watering bits have no curbs; the Turkish bits, called genettes, have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> that serves instead of a curb. See Genettes. Curb, in Farriery, is a hard and callous swelling on the hind part of the hock, attended with stiffness, and sometimes with pain and lameness. See Spavin.

CURCAS

Pages 28-28

a name given in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESCULENT">esculent</a> root, approaching to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and virtues of the colocasia. It is also a name used in Malabar for a small fruit of the shape and size of a hazel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>. Both these things have the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of being strong provocatives; and it is very probable that the curcas of the East Indies may be the fruit called beld by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, and said to possess the same virtues. Gracias has been led into a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> by this similarity of names and virtues; and supposes the curcas of Egypt the same with that of the East Indies.

CURCUMA

Pages 28-28

Turmeric, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monoandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 8th order, Scitaminæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CURDISTAN

Pages 28-28

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated between the Turkish empire and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, lying along the eastern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the river Tigris, and comprehending <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>. Some of the inhabitants live in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, and others rove from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, having tents like the wild Arabs, and are also robbers like them. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is partly Christian, and partly Mahometanism.

CURDLING

Pages 28-28

the coagulating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fixing any fluid body; particularly <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. See Cheese, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Pausanias says, that Aristaeus son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the river Peneus, were the first who found out the secret of curdling milk. At <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> they curdle their milk for the making of cheese with artichoke <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, in lieu of the rennet used for the same purpose among us. The Balsithe, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, Rochfort observes, live wholly upon curded milk, i.e. on curds. He adds, that curds are the whole food of the people of Upper Auvergne in France, and whey their only drink.

CURETES

Pages 28-29

in antiquity, a sort of priests <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> people of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, called also Corybantes. See Corybantes and Crete. The Curetes are said to have been originally of Mount Ida in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>; for which reason they were also called Idi Dactyli. See Dactyl. Lucian and Diodorus Siculus represent them as very expert in casting of darts; though other authors give them no weapons but bucklers and pikes: but all agree in furnishing them with tabors and castanettas: and relate, that they used to dance much to the noise and clashing thereof. By this noise, it is said, they prevented <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> from hearing the cries of young <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, whereby he was saved from being destroyed. Some authors, however, give a different account of the Curetes. According to Pezron and others, the Curetes were, in the times of Saturn, &c. and in the countries of Crete and Phrygia, what the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> were afterwards among the Gauls, &c. i.e. they were priests who had the care of what related to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and the worship of the gods. Hence, as in those days it was supposed there was no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the gods but by divinations, auguries, and the operations of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, the Curetes passed for magicians and enchanters: to these they added the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the stars, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, Vossius, de Idolat, distinguishes three kinds of Curetes, those of Ætolia, those of Phrygia, and those of Crete, who were originally derived from the Phrygians. The first, he says, took their name from sagres, tonsure; in regard, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> wherein the enemy seized their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, they always kept it cut. Those of Phrygia and Crete, he supposes, were so called from sagres, young men, in regard they were young, or because they nursed Jupiter when he was young.

CUREYNY

Pages 32-32

(Curtana), was the name of Edward the Confessor's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, which is the first sword carried before the kings of England at their coronation; and it is said the point of it is broken as an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of mercy.

CURFEU

Pages 29-29

CURFEW, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> COURFEW, a signal given in cities taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, &c., to the inhabitants to go to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASQUIN">Pasquin</a> says, it was so called, as being intended to advertise the people to secure themselves from the robberies and debaucheries of the night. CURFEW-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a> in French couvrefeu, and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Latin of the middle ages, ignitium, or pyritium, was a signal for all persons to extinguish their fires. The most eminent curfew in England was that established by William the Conqueror, who appointed, under severe penalties, that, at the ringing of the bell at 8 o'clock in the evening, every one should put out their lights and fires and go to bed; whence to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> a bell rung about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is called a curfew-bell. This law was abolished by Henry I. in 1100. This practice was highly necessary to prevent accidents in those ages when the fires were placed in a hole in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, under an opening in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> to allow the escape of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. This hole was covered up when the family went to bed. The same practice still exists in some countries, and particularly in some parts of Scotland. But besides securing houses against accidents by fire, the law which was very generally established in England for extinguishing or covering fires, was probably meant also to check the turbulence which frequently prevailed in the middle ages, by forcing the people to retire to rest, or to keep within doors. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> practice, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Beckmann, has arisen a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> of saying, when people wish to go home sooner than the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> choose, that they hear the bürgerglocke, the burgheer's bell. The ringing of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> bell, as it is called, which is still practised in some Protestant countries, according to Beckmann, originated in that of the curfew-bell. Pope John XXIII., dreading that some misfortunes were to befall him, ordered every person on hearing the ignitium to repeat the Ave <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> three times, with a view to avert them. When the appearance of a comet, and a dread of the Turks, alarmed all Christendom, Pope Calixtus VIII. increased these periodical times of prayer, by ordering the prayer-bell to be rung also at noon. Hist. of Invent. ii. 101.

CURGULIO

Pages 28-28

a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CURIA

Pages 29-29

in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> customs.—It was usual for the kings of England to summon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to some particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> festivals in the year; and this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> is called by our historians curia; because there they consulted about the weighty affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; whence it was sometimes also called solemnis curia, generalis curia, augustalis, and curia publica, &c. See WITNESS-Mot. CURIA Borenum. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">COURT</a>-BARON. CURIA Claudiana is a writ that lies against him who should <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> and inclose the ground, but refuses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> defers to do it.

CURIATII

Pages 29-29

three brothers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who had declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against those of Alba. The two armies being equal, three brothers on each side were chosen to decide the contest; the Curiati by those of Alba, and the Horatii by the Romans. The three first were wounded, and two of the latter killed; but the third joining policy to valour, ran away; and having thus tired the Curiati, he took them one after another, and killed them all three.

CURING

Pages 29-29

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for the preserving fish, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and other animal substances, by means of certain additions of things, to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. One <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> method of doing this is by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the bodies to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rubbing them with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, nitre, &c.

CURIOS

Pages 29-29
