the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURIA">curia</a>.—<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, upon dividing the people into curiae, gave each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> a chief, who was to be priest of that curia, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of curio and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMEN">flamen</a> curialis. His business was to provide and officiate at the sacrifices of the curia, which were called curioria; the curia furnishing him with a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> on that consideration, which pension <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appointment was called curiorium. Each division had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of its curia; but all these particular curios were under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a superior or general, called curio maximus, who was the head of the body, and elected by all the curios assembled in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> curialis. All these institutions were introduced by Romu-

CURIOSUS

Pages 29-30

an officer of the Roman empire during the middle <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, appointed to take care that no frauds and irregularities were committed; particularly no abuses in what related to the posts, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, &c. and to give intelligence to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of what passed in the provinces. This made the curious people of importance, and put them in a condition of doing more harm than they prevented; on which account, Honorius cashiered them, at least in some parts of the empire, anno 415. The curious came pretty near to what we call controllers. They had their name from cura, "care," quod curis agendis et evocationibus curae publici inspicendi operam darent. CURLEW. See SCOLOPAX, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CURLA

Pages 29-29

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, also denoted a portion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a tribe. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, a tribe consisted of ten curiae, or a thousand men; each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURIA">curia</a> being one hundred. That <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> made the first division of his people into thirty curiae. Afterwards curia, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">domus</a> curialis, became used for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where each curia held its assemblies. Hence also curia passed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and it is from hence the moderns came to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word curia, "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>," for a place of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and for the judges, &c., there assembled. Varro derives the word from cura, "care," q. d. an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of people <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the care of public affairs. Others deduce it from the Greeks; maintaining, that at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> they called sagres the place where the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> held his assizes, and the people used to assemble; sagres, again, may come from xevres, authority, power; because it was here the laws were made.

CURMI

Pages 30-30

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a sort of malt liquor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ale. It was made of barley, and was drunk by the people of many nations instead of wine, according to Dioscorides's account. He accuses it of causing pains in the head, generating bad juices, and disordering the nervous system. He also says, that in the western <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IBERIA">Iberia</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, such a sort of liquor was in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prepared from wheat instead of barley. See ALE.

CURNOCK

Pages 30-30

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of corn containing four bushels, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>.

CURRANS

Pages 30-30
or CURRANTS, the fruit of a species of grossularia. See GROSSULARIA, BOTANY Index. The white and red sort are mostly used; for the black, and chiefly the leaves, upon first coming out, are in use to flavour English spirits, and counterfeit French brandy. Currants greatly assuage drought, cool and fortify the stomach, and help digestion; and the jelly of black currants is said to be very efficacious in curing inflammations of the throat. Currants also signify a smaller kind of grapes, brought principally from Zante and Cephalonia. They are gathered off the bushes, and laid to dry in the sun, and so put up in large butts. They are opening and pectoral; but are more used in the kitchen than in medicine.

CURRENT

Pages 30-31
or Currant, a term used to express the present time. Thus the year 1804 is the current year, the 20th current is the 20th day of the month now running.—With regard to commerce, the price current of any merchandise is the known and ordinary price accustomed to be given for it. The term is also used for any thing that has course or is received in commerce; in which sense we say, current coin, &c. Current, in Navigation, a certain progressive movement of the water of the sea, by which all bodies floating therein are compelled to alter their course or velocity, or both, and submit to the laws imposed on them by the current. In the sea, currents are either natural and general, as arising from the diurnal rotation of the earth about its axis; or accidental and particular, caused by the waters being driven against promontories, or into gulfs and straits, where, wanting room to spread, they are driven back, and thus disturb the ordinary flux of the sea. Currents are various, and directed towards different parts of the ocean, of which some are constant, others periodical. The most extraordinary current of the sea is that by which part of the Atlantic or African ocean moves about Guinea from Cape Verd towards the curvature or bay of Africa, which they call Fernando Poo; viz. from west to east, contrary to the general motion; and such is the force of the current, that when ships approach too near the shore, it carries them violently towards that bay, and deceives the mariners in their reckoning. There is a great variety of shifting currents, which do not last, but return at certain periods: and these do, most of them, depend upon and follow the anniversary winds or monsoons, which by blowing in one place may cause a current in another. Varenus informs us, that at Java, in the straits of Sunda, when the monsoons blow from the west, viz. in the month of May, the currents set to the eastward, contrary to the general motion. Between the island of Celebes and Madora, when the western monsoons set in, viz. in December, January, and February, or when the winds blow from the north-west, or between the north and west, the currents set to the south-east, or between the south and east. At Ceylon, from the middle of March to October, the currents set to the southward, and in the other parts of the year to the northward: because at this time the southern monsoons blow, and at the other the northern. Between Cochin-China and Malacca, when the western monsoons blow, viz. from April to August, the currents set eastward against the general motion; but the rest of the year they set westward, the monsoon conspiring with the general motion. They run so strongly in these seas, that unexperienced sailors mistake them for waves that beat upon the rocks, known usually by the name of breakers. So for some months after the 15th of February, the currents set from the Maldives towards India on the east, against the general motion of the sea. On the shore of China and Cambodia, in the months of October, November, and December, the currents set to the north-west, and from January to the south-west, when they run with such rapidity about the shoals of Parcel, that they seem swifter than an arrow. At Pulo Condore, upon the coast of Cambodia, though the monsoons are shifting, yet the currents set strongly towards the east, even when they blow to a contrary point. Along the coasts of the bay of Bengal, as far as the Cape Romania, at the extreme point of Malacca, the current runs southward in November and December. When the monsoons blow from China to Malacca, the sea runs swiftly from Pulo Cambi to Pulo Condore on the coast of Cambodia. In the bay of Sans Bras, not far from the Cape of Good Hope, there is a current particularly remarkable, where the sea runs from east to west to the landward; and this more vehemently, as it is opposed by winds from a contrary direction. The cause is undoubtedly owing to some adjacent shore which is higher than this. In the straits of Gibraltar the currents almost constantly drive to the eastward, and carry ships into the Mediterranean; they are also found to drive the same way into St George's channel. The setting or progressive motion of the current may be either quite down to the bottom, or to a certain determinate depth. As the knowledge of the direction and velocity of currents is a very material article. Current tide in navigation, it is highly necessary to discover both, in order to ascertain the ship's situation and course with as much accuracy as possible. The most successful method which has been hitherto practised by mariners for this purpose, is as follows: A common iron-pot, which may contain four or five gallons, is suspended by a small rope, fastened to its ear or handles, so as to hang directly upright, as when placed upon the fire. This rope, which may be from 70 to 100 fathoms in length, being prepared for the experiment, is coiled in the boat, which is hoisted out of the ship at a proper opportunity, when there is little or no wind to ruffle the surface of the sea. The pot being then thrown overboard into the water, and immediately sinking, the line is slackened till about 70 or 80 fathoms of the line are run out; after which the line is fastened to the boat's stern, by which she is accordingly restrained and rides at an anchor. The velocity of the current is then easily tried by the log and half-minute glass, the usual method of discovering the rate of a ship's sailing at sea. The course of the stream is next obtained by the compass provided for this operation. Having thus found the setting and drift of the current, it next remains to apply this experiment to the purposes of NAVIGATION; for which see that article. Under-CURRENTS, are distinct from the upper or apparent, and in different places set or drive a contrary way. Dr Smith makes it highly probable, that in the Downs, in the straits of Gibraltar, &c., there is an under-current, whereby as much water is carried out as is brought in by the upper currents. This he argues from the offing between the North and South Foreland, where it runs tide and half-tide, i.e. it is ebb or flood in that part of the Downs three hours before it is so off at sea: a certain sign, that though the tide of flood runs aloft, yet the tide of ebb runs under-foot, i.e. close by the ground; and so at the tide of ebb it will flow under foot. This he confirms by an experiment in the Baltic sound, communicated to him by an able seaman present at the making of it. Being there then with one of the king's frigates, they went with their pinnace into the mid-stream, and were carried violently by the current. Soon after that, they sunk a basket with a large cannon bullet to a certain depth of water, which gave a check to the boat's motion; and sinking it still lower and lower, the boat was driven a-head to the windward against the upper current, the current aloft not being above four or five fathom deep. He added, that the lower the basket was let down, the stronger the under-current was found. From this principle, it is easy to account for that continual indraught of water out of the Atlantic into the Mediterranean through the straits of Gibraltar, a passage about 20 miles broad; yet without any sensible rising of the water along the coasts of Barbary, &c. or any overflowing of the land, which there lies very low.—Dr Halley, however, solves the currents setting in at the straits without overflowing the banks, by the great evaporation, without supposing any under current.

CURRICULUS

Pages 31-31

in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, denotes the year <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> course of a year. Actum est hoc annorum Dominice incarnationis quater quinquagenis et quin- quies quinis lastris, et tribus curriculis, i.e. In the year Cerciculus 1028; for four times fifty make two hundred, and five times two hundred make one thousand; five lustres are twenty-five years, and three curricula are three years.

CURRODREPANUS

Pages 31-31

(formed of currus, "chariot," and ἀγρίανος, "scythe" <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "sickle"), in antiquity, a kind of chariot armed with scythes. The driver of these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> was obliged to ride on one of the horses, as there was no other seat for him; the usual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for him being all armed with knives, as was likewise the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the chariot. There were no scythes pointing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, either from the beam or axle-tree; but these were fixed at the head of the axle-tree in such a manner as to be moveable by means of a rope, and thereby could be raised or let down, and drawn forward or let <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> backward.

CURRYING

Pages 31-31

the method of preparing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, tallow, &c. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> business is to soften cow and calve-skins, which make the upper leather and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of shoes, covering of saddles, coaches, and other things which must keep out <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. 1. These skins, after coming from the tanner's yard, having many fleshy fibres on them, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a> soaks them some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> water. 2. He takes them out, and stretches them on a very even wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; then with a paring <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> he scrapes off all the superfluous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and puts them in to soak again. 3. He puts them wet on a hurdle, and tramples them with his heels till they begin to grow soft and pliant. 4. He soaks thereon train-oil, which by its unctuous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is the best liquor for this purpose. 5. He spreads them on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tables, and fastens them at the ends. There, with the help of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called a pummel, which is a thick piece of wood, the under side of which is full of furrows crossing each other, he folds, squares, and moves them forwards and backwards several times, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of this instrument, which breaks their too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stiffness. This is what is properly called currying. The order and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these operations is varied by different carriers, but the material <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is always the same. 6. After the skins are curried, there may be occasion to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> them. The colours are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, green, &c.; the other colours are given by the skinners, who differ from carriers in this, that they apply their colours on the flesh side; the carriers on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> side. In order to whiten skins, they are rubbed with lumps of chalk <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> white <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and afterwards with pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. 7. When a skin is to be made black, after having oiled and dried it, he passes over it a puff dipt in water impregnated with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and after his first wetting, he gives it another in water prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOOT">soot</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-arabic. These different dyes gradually turn the skin black, and the operations are repeated till it be of a shining black. The grain and wrinkles, which contribute to the suppleness of calves and cows' leather, are made by the reiterated folds given to the skin in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and by the care taken to scrape off all hard parts on the colour side.

CURSING AND SWEARING

Pages 31-31

an offence against God and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and a sin of all others the most extravagant.

CURSITOR

Pages 31-32

a clerk belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, whose business it is to make out original writs. In the statute 18 Edw. III., they are called clerks of course, and are 24 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, making a corporation of themselves. To each of them is allowed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of certain counties, into which they issue out the original writs required by the subject.

CURTATE DISTANCE

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the distance of a planet from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to that point, where a perpendicular let <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the planet meets with the ecliptic.

CURTATION

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between a planet's distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the curtate distance.

CURTIN

Pages 32-32

CURTAIN, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Courtin, in Fortification, is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the rampart of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which is betwixt the flanks of two bastions, bordered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, behind which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> stand to fire upon the covered way and into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>.

CURTIUS

Pages 32-32

MARCUS, a Roman youth, who devoted himself to the gods manes for the safety of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, about 365 years before the Augustan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. A wide <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a> had suddenly opened in the forum, and the oracle had said that it never would <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> before Rome threw into it whatever it had most precious. Curtius immediately perceived that no less than a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sacrifice was required. He armed himself, mounted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and solemnly threw himself into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, which instantly closed over his head. Curtius, Quintus, a Latin historian, who wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> in 10 books, of which the two first are not indeed extant, but were so well supplied by Freinsheimius, that the loss is scarcely regretted. Where this writer was born, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even when he lived, are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> no one pretends to know. By his style he is supposed to have lived in or near the Augustan age; while some are not wanting, who imagine the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to have been composed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> about 300 years ago, and the name of Quintus Curtius to be fictitiously added to it. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> du Perron was so great an admirer of this work, as to declare one page of it to be worth 30 of Tacitus; yet, M. le Clerc, at the end of his Art of Criticism, has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> the writer with great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and many contradictions. He has nevertheless many qualities as a writer, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> always make him admired and applauded. CURVATURE OF A LINE, is the peculiar manner of its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> or flexure, by which it becomes a curve of any form and properties. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the curvature of a circle is such, as that every point in the periphery is equidistant from a point within, called the centre; and so the curvature of the same circle is everywhere the same. But the curvature in all other curves is continually varying.

CURULE CHAIR

Pages 32-32

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> magistrates of Rome had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to sit and be carried. The curule magistrates were the sediles, the praetors, censors, and consuls. The chair was fitted in a kind of chariot, whence it had its name. The senators who had borne the offices of sediles, praetors, &c., were carried to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in this chair, as were all

CURVE

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a line which running on continually in all directions, may be cut by one <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line in more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> than one. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">CONIC SECTIONS</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">FLUXIONS</a>. CURVE OF EQUABLE APPROACH. Leibnitz first proposed to find a curve, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> which a body descending by the force of gravity, shall make equal approaches to the horizon in equal portions of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. This curve, as it has been found by Bernoulli and others, is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> cubical parabola placed with its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a> uppermost, and which the descending body must enter with a certain determinate velocity. The question was rendered general by Varignon for any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of gravity, by which a body may approach towards a given point by equal spaces in equal times. Maupertuis also resolved the problem in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a body descending in a medium whose resistance is as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the velocity.

CURVES

Pages 32-32

Transcendental, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">Mechanical</a>, are those which cannot be defined or expressed by an algebraic equation.

CURVET

Pages 32-32
or CORVET, in the manege, an air in which the horse's legs are raised higher than in the demi-volt; being a kind of leap up, and a little forwards, wherein the horse raises both his fore-legs at once, equally advanced, (when he is going straight forward, and not in a circle); and as his fore-legs are falling, he immediately raises his hind legs, equally advanced, and not one before the other: so that all his four legs are in the air at once; and as he sets them down, he marks but twice with them.

CURVILINEAR

Pages 32-32
or CURVILINEAL, is said of figures bounded by curves or crooked lines. CURVIROSTRA. See Loxia, Ornithology Index.

CURZOLA

Pages 32-33

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, lying on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. It is about 25 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and has a small town of the same name, with a bishop's see. It now belongs to the Austrians. E. Long. 17° 15'. N. Lat. 43° 6'.

CUSA

Pages 33-33

NICHOLAS DE, a learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, born of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> parentage, and named from Cusa, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth. He was made a cardinal in 1448; and being appointed governor of Rome by Pope Pius II. during his absence at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, he was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> concerer and manager of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Turks. He founded a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and a noble library of Greek and Latin authors, at Cusa; and left many excellent works behind him, which were collected and published in three volumes at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1565. In these he has made no scruple to detect the lying traditions and sophistries of the Roman church.

CUSCO

Pages 33-33

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome town of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, formerly the residence of the Incas. It is seated at the foot of a mountain, and is built in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> form, in the middle of which there is the best market in all America. Four large streets terminate in this square, which are all as straight as a line, and regard the four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the world. The Spaniards tell us wonderful things of the richness of the Inca's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and of the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; but more sober travellers, judging from what remains, think most of them to be fabulous. At present it contains eight large parishes, and five <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, the best of which belongs to the Jesuits; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants may be about 20,000, of which three-fourths are the original natives, Americans. From this town there is a very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, which runs along the Cordilleras; and, at certain distances, there are small houses for resting places, some parts of which are so artificially wrought, that it is surprising how a people who had no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> tools could perform such workmanship. There are streams of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> run through the town, which are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> convenience in so hot a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where it never rains. It is 375 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>. W. Long. 71° 47'. S. Lat. 13° 40'.

CUSCUTA

Pages 33-33

DODDER; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CUSH

Pages 33-33

the eldest son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>, and father of Nimrod; the other sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabtecha, Gen. x. 6—8. Though we know of no other person in Scripture that is called by this name, yet there are several countries that are called by it; whether the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may have dwelt in them all at different times, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that there were some other men of this name, we are ignorant. The Vulgate, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, and other interpreters, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, generally translate Cush, Ethiopia; but there are many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> wherein this translation cannot take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Cush is the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> watered by the Araxes. They who, in translating the situation of Eden, have made Cush Ethiopia, gave rise to that unwarrantable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which Josephus and several others have entertained of the river Gihon's being the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. In this place (Gen. ii. 13.) the LXX translation renders the word Cush by the name of Ethiopia; and, in this mistake, is not only here followed by our English version, but in the same particular in several other places. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTH">Cuth</a> is the same as Cush. The Chaldees generally put the tau where the Hebrews <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the shin: they say cuth instead of cush. See CUTH. But Ethiopia is frequently in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> called Cush; and Josephus says, that they called themselves by this name, and that the same name was given them by all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. St Jerome tells us that the Hebrews call the Ethiopians by the same name, and the Septuagint give them no other. Jeremiah (xiii. 23.) says, "Can the Cushcan, or Ethiopian, change his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>?" In <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> (xxxix. 10.) the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> threatens to reduce "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, from the tower of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYENE">Syene</a> even unto the border of Cush, or Ethiopia;" and in Isaiah, (xi. 11.) he says, "he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and from Egypt, and Pathros, and from Cush." All these marks agree with Ethiopia properly so called, which lies to the south of Egypt. Bochart has shown very clearly that there was a country called the "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Cush" in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, bordering upon Egypt; that this country extended itself principally upon the eastern shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and at its extremity to the point of the sea, inclining towards Egypt and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. Thus there are three countries of the name of Cush, described in Scripture, and all confounded by interpreters under the general name of Ethiopia.

CUSHION

Pages 33-33

in gilding, is made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, fastened to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> board, from 14 inches square to 10, with a handle. The vacancy between the leather and board is stuffed with fine tow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, so that the outer surface may be flat and even. It is used for receiving the leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in order to its being cut into proper sizes and figures.

CUSPIDATED

Pages 33-33

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, are such <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> whose leaves are pointed like a spear.

CUSPINIAN

Pages 33-34

JOHN, a German, was born at Swinfurt in 1473, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> in 1529. He was first physician to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian I. and employed by that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in several delicate negotiations. We have of his in Latin, 1. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Roman emperors from Julius Caesar to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Maximilian I. Degory Wheare, in his Methodus Legendae Historiae, calls this "luculentum sane opus, et omnium lectionis dignissimum." 2. A history of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; being a kind of continuation of the preceding. 2. A history of... CUS Customian of the origin of the Turks, and of their cruelties towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Gerard Vossius calls Cuspinian magnum suo eo historice lumen.

CUSSO

Pages 34-34

the name given by the natives to a tree which is indigenous to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. It is particularly described by Mr Bruce; but as this celebrated traveller was totally unacquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, it is impossible to discover to what class, order, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> genus, it belongs. It grows nearly to the height of 20 feet, and the seed is employed by the Abyssinians as a vermicide. From the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which Mr Bruce has given of this plant, it would appear to be most nearly allied to the palms.

CUSTOM

Pages 34-34

a very comprehensive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, denoting the manners, ceremonies, and fashions of a people, which having turned into a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and passed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, obtain the force of laws; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it implies such usages, as, though voluntary at first, are yet by practice become necessary. Custom is hence, both by lawyers and civilians, defined lex non scripta, "a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> not written," established by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> usage, and the consent of our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; in which sense it stands opposed to the lex scripta, or "the written law." See Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Custom and Habit, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> economy. The former is often confounded with the latter. By custom we <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> a frequent reiteration of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>; and by habit, the effect that custom has on the mind or body. This curious subject falls to be considered first in a moral, and secondly in a physical, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. I. Influence of Custom and Habit on the Mind, &c. Custom hath such influence upon many of our feelings, by warping and varying them, that its operations demand the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of all those who would be acquainted with human <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The subject, however, is intricate. Some pleasures are fortified by custom; and yet custom begets familiarity, and consequently indifference: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> all the year were playing holidays, To sport would be as tedious as to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>: But when they seldom come, they wish'd-for come, And nothing pleaseth but rare accidents.

CUSTOMS

Pages 41-44

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> economy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the duties, toll, tribute, or tariff, payable to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> upon merchandise exported and imported, form a branch of the perpetual taxes. See Tax. The considerations upon which this revenue (or the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, which arose only from exports) was invested in the king, were said to be two: 1. Because he gave the subject leave to depart the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and to carry his goods along with him. 2. Because the king was bound of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to maintain and keep up the port and havens, and to protect the merchant from pirates. Some have imagined they are called with us customs, because they were the inheritance of the king by immemorial usage and the common <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and not granted him by any statute; but Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> hath clearly shown, that the king's first claim to them was by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> 3 Edw. I., though the record thereof is not now extant. And indeed this is in express words confessed by statute 25 Edw. I. c. 7., wherein the king promises to take no customs from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, without the common assent of the realm, "saving to us and our heirs the customs on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, skins, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, formerly granted to us by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> aforesaid." These were formerly called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> customs of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and were due on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> only of the said three commodities, and of none other: which were styled the staple commodities of the kingdom, because they were obliged to be brought to those parts where the king's staple was established, in order to be there first rated, and then exported. They were denominated in the barbarous Latin of our ancient records, custuma (an appellation which seems to be derived from the French word coutum or coutum, which signifies toll or tribute, and owes its own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> to the word cost, which signifies price, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, or as we have adopted it in English, cost); not consuetudines, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of our law whenever it means merely usages. The duties on wool, sheep-skins or woollfells, and leather exported, were called custuma antiqua sine magna, and were payable by every merchant, as well native as stranger: with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that merchant-strangers paid an additional toll, viz. half as much again as was paid by natives. The custuma parva et nova were an impost of 3d. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, due from merchant-strangers only, for all commodities as well imported as exported; which was usually called the aliens duty, and was first granted in 31 Edw. I. But these ancient hereditary customs, especially those on wool and woollfells, came to be of little account, when the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> became sensible of the advantages of a home manufacture, and prohibited the exportation of wool by statute 11 Edw. III. c. 1. Other customs payable upon exports and imports were distinguished into subsidies, tonnage, poundage, and other imposts. Subsidies were such as were imposed by parliament upon any of the staple commodities before mentioned, over and above the custuma antiqua et magna: tonnage was a duty upon all wines imported, over and above the prisage and butlerage aforesaid: poundage was a duty imposed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> valorem, Customs, at the rate of 12d. in the pound, on all other merchandise whatsoever; and the other imposts were such as were occasionally laid on by parliament, as circumstances and times required. These distinctions are now in a manner forgotten, except by the officers immediately concerned in this department; their produce being in effect all blended together, under the one denomination of the customs. By these we understand, at present, a duty or subsidy paid by the merchants at the quay upon all imported as well as exported commodities, by authority of parliament; unless where, for particular national reasons, certain rewards, bounties or drawbacks, are allowed for particular exports or imports. The customs thus imposed by parliament are chiefly contained in two books of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>, set forth by parliamentary authority; one signed by Sir Harbottle Grimstone, speaker of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II.'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the other an additional one, signed by Sir Spencer Compton, speaker in the reign of George I., to which also subsequent additions have been made. Aliens pay a larger proportion than <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> subjects, which is what is now generally understood by the aliens duty; to be exempted from which is one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of the frequent applications to parliament for acts of naturalization. These customs are then, we see, a tax immediately paid by the merchant, although ultimately by the consumer. And yet these are the duties felt least by the people; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> prudently managed, the people hardly consider that they pay them at all. For the merchant is easy, being sensible he does not pay them for himself; and the consumer, who really pays them, confounds them with the price of the commodity; in the same manner as Tacitus observes, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Nero gained the reputation of abolishing the tax of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of slaves, though he only transferred it from the buyer to the seller: so that it was, as he expresses it, remissum magis specie, quam vi: quia cum venditor pendere iubetur, in partem pretii emptoribus accrescet. But this inconvenience attends it on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that these imposts, if too heavy, are a check and cramp upon trade; and especially when the value of the commodity bears little or no proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the duty imposed. This in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> gives rise also to smuggling, which then becomes a very lucrative employment; and its natural and most reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, viz. confiscation of the commodity, is in such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> quite ineffectual; the intrinsic value of the goods, which is all that the smuggler has paid, and therefore all that he can lose, being very inconsiderable when compared with his prospect of advantage in evading the duty. Recourse must therefore be had to extraordinary punishments to prevent it; perhaps even to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> ones: which destroys all proportion of punishment, and puts <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> upon an equal footing with such as are really guilty of no natural, but merely a positive offence. There is also another ill consequence attending <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> imposts on merchandise, not frequently considered, but indisputably certain; that the earlier any tax is laid on a commodity, the heavier it falls upon the consumer in the end; for every trader, through whose Customs whose bands it passes, must have a profit, not only upon the raw materials and his own labour and time in preparing it, but also upon the very tax itself, which he advances to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; otherwise he loses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which he so advances. To instance in the article for foreign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. The merchant pays a duty upon importation, which he does not receive again till he sells the commodity, perhaps at the end of three months. He is therefore equally entitled to a profit upon that duty which he pays at the customhouse, as to a profit upon the original price which he pays to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a> abroad; and considers it accordingly in the price he demands of the stationer. When the stationer sells it again, he requires a profit of the printer or bookseller upon the whole sum advanced by him to the merchants: and the bookseller does not fail to charge the full proportion to the student or ultimate consumer; who therefore does not only pay the original duty, but the profits of these three intermediate traders who have successively advanced it for him. This might be carried much farther in any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>, or more complicated branch of trade. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">Custom</a>-House, an office established by the king's authority in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> cities, or port <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, for the receipt and management of the customs and duties of importation and exportation, imposed on merchandises, and regulated by books of rates. Custos brevium, the principal clerk belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a>, whose business it is to receive and keep all the writs made returnable in that court, filing every return by itself; and, at the end of each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, to receive of the prothonotaries all the records of the nisi prius, called the postea. Custos Rotulorum, an officer who has the custody of the rolls and records of the session of peace, and also of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of the peace itself. He usually is some person of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and always a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, of the quorum, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> where he is appointed. Custos Spiritualium, he that exercises the spiritual jurisdiction of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, during the vacancy of any see, which by the canon law, belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>; but at present, in England, to the archbishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>. Custos Temporalium, was the person to whom a vacant see or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> was given by the king, as supreme <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>. His office was, as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the goods and profits, to give an account to the exchequer, who did the like to the exchequer. Cut-feather, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-language. If a ship has too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> a bow, it is common to say, she <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not cut a feather; that is, she will not <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> so swift as to make it foam or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROTH">froth</a>. Cut-Purse, in Law; if any person clam et secreta, and without the knowledge of another, cut his purse or pick his pocket, and steal from thence above the value of twelve pence, it is felony excluded clergy. Cut-purses, or saccularii, were more severely punished than common thieves by the Roman and Athenian laws. Cut-Water, the sharp part of the head of a ship below the beak. It is so called, because it cuts or divides the water before it comes to the bow, that it may not come too suddenly to the breadth of the ship, which would retard it. Cutaneous, in general, an appellation given to whatever belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTIS">cutis</a> or skin. Thus, we say, cutaneous eruptions: the itch is a cutaneous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTH">Cuth</a>, or Cuthah, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a province of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, which, as some say, lies upon the Araxes, and is the same with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSH">Cush</a>; but others take it to be the same with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which the Greeks call Susiana, and which to this very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, says Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, is by the inhabitants called Chusistan. F. Calmet is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that Cuthah and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a> are the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and that the Cuthites who were removed into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a> by Salmaneser (2 Kings xvii. 24.) came from Cush or Cuth, mentioned in Gen. ii. 23. See the article Cush. The Cuthites worshipped the idol Nergal, Id. ibid. 39. These people were transplanted into Samaria in the room of the Israelites, who before inhabited it. Calmet is of opinion, they came from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Cush, or Cuthah upon the Araxes; and that their first settlement was in the cities of the Medes, subdued by Salmaneser and the kings of Assyria his predecessors. The Scripture observes, that the Cuthites, upon their arrival in this new country, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to worship the gods formerly adored by them beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who succeeded Sennacherib, appointed an Israelitish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> to go thither, and instruct them in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Hebrews. But these people thought they might reconcile their old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> with the worship of the true God. They therefore framed particular gods for themselves, which they placed in the several cities where they dwelt. The Cuthites then worshipped both the Lord and their false gods together, and chose the lowest of the people to make priests of them in the high places; and they continued this practice for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time. But afterwards they forsook the worship of idols, and adhered only to the law of Moses, as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, who are descended from the Cuthites, do at this day. Cuticle, the Scarf Skin. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cuticular, the same with Cutaneous. Cutis, the Skin. See Anatomy Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTLERY">Cutlery</a>, a general term which includes all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> tools. See Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">Cutter</a>, a small vessel, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> navigated in the channel of England. It is furnished with one mast, and rigged as a sloop. Many of these vessels are used in an illicit trade, and others are employed by government to take them; the latter of which are either under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> or custom-house. Cutter, is also a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> used by ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Cutter of the Tallies, an officer of the exchequer, whose business is to provide wood for the tallies, to cut or notch the sum paid upon them; and then to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> them into court, to be written upon. See Tally. Cutting, a term used in various senses and various arts; in the general it implies a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> or separation. Cutting is particularly used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, where the shield is divided into two equal parts, from right to left, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, or in the fesse-way. The word also is applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> ordinances, and even to animals and moveables, when they are divided equally the same way; so, however, as that one Cutting: one moiety is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, the other metal. The ordinaries are said to be cut, couped, when they do not come full to the extremities of the shield. Cutting, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, denotes the operation of extracting the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> out of the bladder by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITHOTOMY">Lithotomy</a>, Surgery Index. Cutting, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a>. When the laminae or plates of the metal, be it <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, are brought to the thickness of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> to be coined, pieces are cut out, of the thickness, and nearly of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, of the intended <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>; which are now called planchets, till the king's image hath been stamped on them. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> wherewith they cut, consists of two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, very sharp, and placed over one another; the lower a little hollow, representing a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, the other a pestle. The metal put between the two, is cut out in the manner described under Coinage. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>. Medallions, where the relievo is to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, are not cut, but cast or moulded. Cutting, in the manege, is when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s feet interfere; or when with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> of one foot he beats off the skin from the pastern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of another foot. This is more frequent in the hind feet than the fore: the causes are either weariness, weakness in the reins, not knowing how to go, or ill shoeing. Cutting, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, the laying one strong lively colour over another, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> or softening. The cutting of colours has always a disagreeable effect. Cutting in wood, a particular kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> or engraving; denominated from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> wherein it is employed. It is used for various purposes; as for figured letters; head and tail pieces of books; and even for schemes and other figures, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the expences of engraving on copper; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> and stamps for paper, calicoes, linens, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of cutting in wood, as well as that in copper, is ascribed to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>; but it is to Albert Durer and Lucas they are both indebted for their perfection. See Engraving and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>. One Hugo de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CARPI">Carpi</a> invented a manner of cutting in wood, by means whereof the prints appeared as if painted in clair-obscuré. In order to this, he made three kinds of stamps for the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; which were drawn one after another through the press for the same print: they were so conducted, as that one served for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> lights, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> for the demi-teints, and a third for the outlines and the deep shadows. The art of cutting in wood was certainly carried to a very great pitch above two hundred years ago; and might even vie, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and justness, with that of engraving in copper. At present it is in a low condition, as having been long neglected, and the application of artists wholly employed on copper, as the more easy and promising province; not that wood- en cuts have the advantage of those in copper on many accounts; chiefly for figures and devices in books; as being printed at the same time and in the same press as the letters; whereas for the other there is required a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. In the representation of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and in designs for paper-hangings, where the outline only is wanted to be printed in a bold full manner, this method will be found cheaper and more effectual than the use of copperplates. The cutters in wood begin with preparing a plank or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of the size and thickness required, and very even and smooth on the side to be cut: for this, they usually take beech, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-tree, or box; though the latter is the best, as being the closest, and least liable to be worm-eaten. The wood being cut into a proper form and size, should be planed as even and truly as possible: it is then fit to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> or chalking of the design to be engraved. But the effect may be made more apparent, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, if any be used in drawing, be prevented from running, by spreading thinly on the surface of the wood <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> tempered with water, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and afterwards rubbing it well with a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> rag whilst it is wet: and when it is dry, brushing off any loose or powdery part with a soft pencil. On this block they draw their design with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> or pencil, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they would have it printed. Those who cannot draw their own design, as there are many who cannot, make use of a design furnished them by another; fastening it upon the block with paste made of flour and water, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> tragacanth; the strokes or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> turned towards the wood. When the paper is dry, they wash it gently over with a sponge dipped in water; which done, they take off the paper by little and little, still rubbing it a little first with the tip of the finger; till at length there be nothing left on the block but the strokes of ink that form the design, which mark out so much of the block as is to be spared or left standing. Figures are sometimes cut out of prints, by taking away all the white part or blank paper, and cemented with gum-water to the surface of the wood. The rest they cut off, and take away very curiously with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of very sharp knives, or little chisels or gravers, according to the bigness or delicacy of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>: for they need no other instruments. It differs from engraving in copper, because in the former the impression comes from the prominent parts or strokes left uncut; whereas in the latter, it comes from the channels cut in the metal. The manner of printing with wooden prints is much more expeditions and easy than that of copper-plate: because they require only to be dipt in the printing-ink, and impressed on the object in the same manner and with the same <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-printing is managed: and for purposes that do not require great correctness, the impression is made by the hand only, a proper handle being fixed to the middle of the print, by which it is first dipped in the ink, spread by means of a brush on a block of proportionable size covered with leather; and then lifted up instantly, and dropped with some little force on the paper which is to receive the impression. Most of our readers are probably not ignorant that the art of engraving on wood has been revived of late years, and has been carried to great perfection by Messrs Bewick of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and other ingenious artists. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> we may mention Messrs Nesbit and Anderson of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">Quadrupeds</a>; in one volume 8vo, and the Natural History History of British Birds, in two volumes, published with engravings cut in wood by Messrs Bewick, are excellent specimens of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection at which this art has arrived. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">Cuttings</a>, or slips, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the branches or sprigs of trees or plants, cut or slipped off to set again; which is done in any moist fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The best season is from August to April; but care is to be taken, when it is done, the sap be not too much in the top, lest the cut die before that part in the earth have root enough to support it: nor yet must it be too dry or scanty; the sap in the branches assisting it to take root. In providing the cuttings, such branches as have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, knots, or burrs, are to be cut off two or three inches beneath them, and the leaves to be stripped off so far as they are set in the earth. Small top branches, of two or three years growth, are fittest for this operation. CUTTLE-FISH. See Sepia. The bone of the cuttle-fish is hard on one side, but soft and yielding on the other; so as readily to receive pretty neat impressions from medals, &c. and afterwards to serve as a mould for casting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, which thus take the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the original; the bone is likewise frequently employed for cleaning or polishing silver. This fish contains in a certain distinct vessel a fluid as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> as ink; which it is said to emit when pursued, and thus to conceal itself by discolouring the water. The particular qualities of this liquor are not yet determined. Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a> says, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a letter which had been written with it ten years before, and which still continued. Some report that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> made their ink from it; and others, that it is the basis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ink; but both these accounts appear to have little foundation. Pliny, speaking of the inks made use of in his time, after observing that the cuttle-fish is in this respect of a wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, adds expressly, that ink was not made from it.

CUTTS

Pages 44-44

JOHN <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">LORD</a>, a soldier of most hardy bravery in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William's wars, was son of Richard Cutts, Esq. of Matching in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>; where the family were settled about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Henry VI. and had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> estate. He entered early into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Monmouth, was aid-de-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> to the duke of Lorraine in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and signalized himself in a very extraordinary manner at the taking of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUDA">Buda</a> by the Imperialists in 1686; which important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> had been for near a century and a half in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks. Mr Addison, in a Latin poem worthy of the Augustan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, plainly hints at Mr Cutts's distinguished bravery at that siege. Returning to England at the revolution, he had a regiment of foot; was created baron of Gower in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, Dec. 6. 1690; appointed governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Wight, April 14. 1693; was made a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general; and, when the assassination project was discovered, in 1695-6, was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. In 1698 he was complimented by Mr John Hopkins, as one to whom "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> was due," as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> and a poet. He was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLDSTREAM">Coldstream</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> regiment of guards, in 1701; when Mr Steele, who was indebted to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to him his first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, "The Christian Hero." On the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, he was made a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general of the forces in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; commander in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the forces in Ireland, under the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 23. 1704-5; and afterwards one of the lords justices of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, to keep him out of the way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; a circumstance which broke his heart. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, Jan. 26. 1706-7, and is buried there in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Christ <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He wrote a poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; and published, in 1687, "Poetical Exercises, written upon several occasions, and dedicated to her <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> highness Mary princess of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>." It contains, besides the dedication signed J. Cutts, verses to that princess; a poem on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a>; another to Mr Waller on his commending it; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> more copies of verses (one of them called La Muse Caroulier, which had been ascribed to Lord Peterborough, and as such mentioned by Mr Walpole in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of that nobleman's writings), and 11 songs; the whole composing but a very thin volume. A specimen of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> is here added: Only tell her that I <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, Leave the rest to her and fate; Some kind planet from above May perhaps her pity move; Lovers on their stars must wait; Only tell her that I love. Why, oh, why should I despair? Mercy's pictur'd in her eye; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> she once vouchsafe to hear, Welcome hope, and welcome fear. She's too good to let me die; Why, oh, why should I despair?

CUVETTE

Pages 44-44
or CUNETTE, in Fortification, is a ditch within a ditch, being a pretty deep trench, about four fathoms broad, sunk, and running along the middle of the great dry ditch, to hold water; serving both to keep off the enemy, and prevent him from missing.

CYANOMETER

Pages 44-44

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for measuring the intensity of the blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the sky. See Supplement.

CYATHUS

Pages 44-44

κυάθος (from the verb κύων, to pour out), was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, both of the liquid and dry kind. It was equal to an ounce, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a pint. The cyathus was made with a handle like our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a> ladle. The Roman topers used to drink as many cyathi as there were <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>; also as many as there were letters in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>'s name. Thus, they had modes of drinking similar to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>-drinking or toasting. The cyathus of the Greeks weighed 10 drachms; but Galen says that a cyathus contains 12 drachms of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, 13 drachms and one scruple of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and 18 drachms of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; and he adds that among the Veterinarii the cyathus contained two ounces.

CYAXARES

Pages 44-44

son of Phraortes, was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Media and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. He bravely defended his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which the Scythians had invaded. He made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against Alyattes king of Lydia; and subjected to his power all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> beyond the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a>. He died after a reign of 40 years, in the year of Rome 165. Cyaxares II. is supposed by some to be the same as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> the Mede. He was son of Astrages king of Media. He added <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> provinces to his father's dominions,

CYBELE

Pages 44-45

in Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Coelus and Terra, and wife of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>.
