She is supposed to be the same as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, Rhea, Ops, Vesta, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">Bona</a> Mater, Magna Mater, Berecynthia, Dindymene, &c. According to Diodorus, she was the daughter of a Lydian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and as soon as she was born she was exposed on a mountain. She was preserved by sucking some of the wild beasts of the forest, and received the name of Cybele from the mountain where her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> had been preserved. When she returned to her father's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, she had an intrigue with Atys, a beautiful youth, whom her father mutilated, &c. All the mythologists are unanimous in mentioning the amours of Atys and Cybele. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> the festivals of Cybele were observed with the greatest solemnity. Her priests, called Corybantes, Galli, &c., were not admitted in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> without a previous mutilation. In the celebration of the festivals, they imitated the manners of madmen, and filled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with shrieks and howlings mixed with the confused noise of drums, tabrets, bucklers, and spears. This was in commemoration of the sorrow of Cybele for the loss of her favourite Atys. Cybele was generally represented as a robust woman far advanced in her pregnancy, to intimate the fecundity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. She held keys in her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and her head was crowned with rising turrets, and sometimes with the leaves of an oak. She sometimes appears riding in a chariot drawn by two tame lions: Atys follows by her side, carrying a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> in his hand, and supporting himself upon a fir-tree which is sacred to the goddess. Sometimes she is represented with a sceptre in her hand, with her head covered with a tower. She is also seen with many breasts, to show that the earth gives aliment to all living creatures; and she generally carries two lions under her arms. From Phrygia the worship of Cybele passed into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and was solemnly established at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a> under the name of the Eleusinian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of Ceres. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, by order of the Sibylline books, brought the statue of the goddess from Pessinus into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and when the ship which carried it had run on a shallow <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tiber, the virtue and innocence of Claudia were vindicated in removing it with her girdle. It is supposed that the mysteries of Cybele were first known about 257 years before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1580 years before the Augustan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The Romans were particularly superstitious in washing every year, on the 6th of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a> of April, the shrine of this goddess in the waters of the river Almon. There prevailed many obscenities in the observation of the festivals; and the priests themselves were the most eager to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> indecent expressions, and to show their unbounded licentiousness by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a> of their actions.

CYBELICUM MARMOR

Pages 45-45

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of marble dug in a mountain of that name in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. It was of an extremely bright <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> veins of bluish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>.

CYCAS

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order, Palmae. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This is a valuable tree to the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, Cycas as it not only furnishes a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their constant <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, but also supplies them with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> article of trade. The pith consists of a farinaceous substance, which is extracted from it and made into bread in this manner: they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the body into small pieces, and after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, pour <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; this is left for some hours to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>. When fit, it is strained through a cloth, and the finer particles of the mealy substance running through with the water, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> ones are left behind and thrown away. After the farinaceous part is sufficiently subsided, the water is poured off, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> being properly dried, is occasionally made into cakes and baked. These cakes are said to eat nearly as well as wheaten bread, and are the support of the inhabitants for three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four months in the year. The same meal more finely pulverized, and reduced into granules, is what is called sago, which is sent into all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and sold in the shops as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strengthener and restorative. There is a sort of sago made in the West Indies, and sent to Europe in the same manner as that from the East; but the West India sago is far inferior in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to the other. It is supposed to be made from the pith of the areca or arecaea. See Areca. The brood <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOOM">boom</a> (or bread-tree) of the Hottentots, a plant discovered by Professor Thunberg, is described as a new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus, by the name of cycas Cafrria, in the Nova Acta Reg. Soc. Scient. Ups. vol. ii. p. 283. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> V. The pith, or medulla, which abounds in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of this little palm, Mr Sparrman informs us, is collected and tied up in dressed calf or sheep-skins, and then buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> for the space of several weeks, till it becomes sufficiently mellow and tender to be kneaded up with water into a paste, of which they afterwards make small loaves or cakes, and bake them under the ashes. Other Hottentots, not quite so nice, nor endured with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> enough to wait this tedious method of preparing it, are said to dry and roast the pith or marrow, and afterwards make a kind of frumenty of it.

CYCEON

Pages 45-45

from σκεῖν, "to mix;" a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets and physicians to a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and sometimes of other ingredients. These constituted the two kinds of cyceon; the coarser being of water and meal alone; the richer and more delicate composed of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, flour, water, and cheese. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, in the 11th Iliad, talks of cyceon made with cheese and the meal of barley mixed with wine, but without any mention either of honey <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> water; and Ovid, describing the draught of cyceon given by the old woman of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, mentions only flour and water. Dioscorides understood the word in both these senses; but extolled it most in the coarse and simple kind: he says, when prepared with water alone, it refrigerates and nourishes greatly.

CYCLAMEN

Pages 46-46

Soweread; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 21st order, Preciae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYCLE

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of numbers, which regularly proceed from the first to the last, and then return again to the first, and so circulate perpetually. See Chronology, No. 26. Cycle of Indiction, is a series of 15 years, returning constantly around, like the other cycles, and commenced from the third year before Christ; whence it happens, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> 3 be added to any given year of Christ, and the sum be divided by 15, what remains is the year of the indiction. Cycle of Indication, a period of 15 years, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It has no connection with the celestial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, but was instituted, according to Baronius, by Constantine; who having reduced the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> which the Romans were obliged to serve to 15 years, he was consequently obliged every 15 years to impose, or indicere according to the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, an extraordinary tax for the payment of those who were discharged; and hence arose this cycle, which, from the Latin word indicere, was styled indication. Cycle of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>, called also the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the Masonic cycle, from its inventor Meton the Athenian, is a period of 19 years, which when they are completed, the new moons and full moons return on the same days of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, so that on whatever days the new and full moons <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> this year, 19 years hence they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> happen on the very same days of the month, though not at the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, as Meton and the fathers of the primitive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> thought; and therefore, at the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, when the method of finding the time for observing the feast of Easter was established, the numbers of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> cycle were inserted in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, which, upon the account of their excellent use, were set in golden letters, and the year of the cycle called the golden number of that year. Cycle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, a revolution of 28 years, which being elapsed, the dominical or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> letters return to their former <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and proceed in the same order as before, according to the Julian calendar.

CYCLISUS

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in the form of a half <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, used in scraping the skull, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fractures on that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>.

CYCLOID

Pages 46-46

a curve on which the doctrine of pendulums, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>-measuring instruments, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> depends. Mr Huygens demonstrated, that from whatever point <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> height, a heavy body, oscillating on a fixed centre, begins to descend, while it continues to move in a cycloid, the time of its falls or oscillations <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be equal to each other. It is likewise demonstrable, that it is the curve of quickest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, i.e. a body falling in it, from any given point above, to another not exactly under it, will come to this point in a less time than in any other curve passing through those two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. This curve is thus <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>: suppose a wheel or circle to roll along a straight line till it has completed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> one revolution; a nail or point in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the circumference of the circle, which at the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> touches the straight line, will, at the end of the revolution, have described a cycloid on a vertical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>. CYCLOPÆDIA, or Encyclopædia, denotes the circle or compass of arts and sciences. A cyclopaedia, say the authors of the French Encyclopédie, ought to explain as much as possible the order and connexion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> knowledge. See Encyclopædia.

CYCLOPS

Pages 46-46

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of whom were Brontes, Steropes, and Persaces; but their whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> amounted to above a hundred. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> threw them into Tartarus as soon as they were born; but they were delivered at the intercession of Tellus, and became the assistants of Vulcan. They were of prodigious stature, and had each only one eye, which was placed in the middle of their foreheads. Some mythologists say, that the Cyclops signify the vapours raised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which occasion <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>: on which account they are represented as forging the thunderbolts of Jupiter. Others represent them as the first inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, who were cruel, of a gigantic form, and dwelt round Mount Etna.

CYCLOPTERUS

Pages 46-46

the Sucker, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a> nantes. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYDER

Pages 46-48
or Cider, an excellent drink made of the juice of apples, especially of the more curious table kinds; the juice of these being esteemed more cordial and pleasant than that of the wild or harsh kinds. In making this drink, it hath long been thought necessary, in every part of England, to lay the harder cyder-fruits in heaps for some time before breaking their pulps; but the Devonshire people have much improved this practice. In other countries, the method is to make these heaps of apples in a house, or under some covering inclosed on every side. This method hath been found defective, because, by excluding the free air, the heat soon became too violent, and a great perspiration ensued, by which in a short time the loss of juice was so great, as to reduce the fruit to half their former weight, attended with a general rottenness, rancid smell, and disagreeable taste. In the South-hams, a middle way has been pursued, to avoid the inconveniences and loss attending the above. They make their heaps of apples in an open part of an orchard, where, by the means of a free air and less perspiration, the desired maturity is brought about, with an inconsiderable waste of the juices and decay of the fruit entirely free of rankness; and though some apples rot even in this manner, they are very few, and are still fit for use; all continue plump and full of juices, and very much heighten the colour of cyders, without ill taste or smell. In pursuing the Devonshire method it is to be observed, 1. That all the promiscuous kinds of apples that have dropped from the trees, from time to time, are to be gathered up and laid in a heap by themselves, and to be made into cider after having so lain about ten days. 2. Such apples as are gathered from the trees, having already acquired some degree of maturity, are likewise to be laid in a heap by themselves for about a fortnight. 3. The later hard fruit, which are to be left on the trees till the approach of frost is apprehended, are to be laid in a separate heap, where they are to remain a month or six weeks, by which, notwithstanding frost, rain, &c., their juices will receive such a maturation, as will prepare them for a kindly fermentation, and which they could not have attained on the trees by means of the coldness of the season. It is observable, that the riper and mellower the fruits are at the time of collecting them into heaps, the shorter should be their continuance there; and on the contrary, the harsher, immaturest, and harder they are, the longer they should rest. These heaps should be made in an even and open part of an orchard, without any regard to covering from rain, dew, or what else may happen during the apples staying there; and whether they be carried in and broke in wet or dry weather, the thing is all the same. If it may be objected, that during their having lain together in the heap, they may have imbibed great humidity, as well from the air as from the ground, rain, dews, &c., which are mixed with their juices; the answer is, this will have no other effect than a kindly diluting, natural to the fruit, by which means a speedier fermentation ensues, and all heterogeneous humid particles are thrown off. The apples are then ground, and the pumice is received in a large open-mouthed vessel, capable of containing as much thereof as is sufficient for one making, or one cheese. Though it has been a custom to let the pumice remain some hours in the vessel appropriated to contain it, yet this practice is by no means commendable; for if the fruits did not come ripe from the trees, or otherwise matured, the pumice remaining in the vat too long will acquire such sharpness and coarseness from the skins as is never to be got rid of; and if the pumice is of well ripened fruit, the continuing too long there will occasion it to contract a sharpness that very often is followed with want of spirit and pricking: nay, sometimes it even becomes vinegar, or always continues of a wheyish colour; all which proceeds from the heat of fermentation that it almost instantly falls into on lying together; the pumice therefore should remain no longer in the vat than until there may be enough broke from one pressing, or that all be made into cheese, and pressed the same day it is broken. See farther on this subject Agriculture Index. In Plate CLXVIII. is a perspective view of the cider press and apple-mill. A, B, the bottom or lower-beam; C, D, the upper beam; 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, the rights; 4, 4, e, e, spars; Z, 2, 12, braces, or cross-pieces; a, b, capitals; X, blocks; g, the screw; E, the back or receiver; F, the cheese or cake of pumice, placed on the stage or bason; G, the stage or bason; I, I, beams that support the pieces of which the bason is composed; H, perpendicular pieces for supporting these beams; H, the buckler; R, S, Q, a circular trough of the apple-mill; T, L, V, compartments or divisions, for different sorts of apples; M, the mill-stone; L, M, axis of the mill-stone; N, the spring-tree bar. Cyder-Spirit, a spirituous liquor drawn from cyder by distillation, in the same manner as brandy from wine. The particular flavour of this spirit is not the most agreeable, but it may with care be divested wholly of it, and rendered a perfectly pure and insipid spirit upon rectification. The traders in spirituous liquors are well enough acquainted with the value of such a spirit as this: they can give it the flavour of some other kinds, and sell it under their names, or mix it in large proportion with the foreign brandy, rum and arrack, in the sale, without any danger of a discovery of the cheat. Cyder-Wine. See Agriculture Index. Cyderkin. See Agriculture Index. Cydius, a painter who made a painting of the Argonauts in the 11th Olympiad. This celebrated piece was bought by the orator Hortensius for 164 talents. Cydnus, in Ancient Geography, a river of Cilicia; rising in Mount Taurus, to the north of Tarsus, through whose middle it ran, in a very clear and cold stream, which had almost proved fatal to Alexander on bathing in it; falling into the sea at a place called Rhegan, a breach, the sea breaking in there, and affording the people of Tarsus a station or port for their ships. The water of the Cydnus is commended by Strabo, as of service in nervous disorders and the gout. Cydonia, in Ancient Geography, one of the three most illustrious cities of Crete, situated in the north-west of the island, with a locked port, or walled round. The circumstances of the founding of Cydon are uncertain. Stephen of Byzantium says, that it was at first named Apollonia from Cydon the son of Apollo. Pausanias ascribes the founding of it to Cydon the son of Tegetus, who travelled into Crete. Herodotus affirms, that it was founded by the Samians, and that its temples were erected by them. Alexander, in the first book of the Cretans, informs us, that it received its name from Cydon the son of Mercury. Cydon was the largest city in the island; and was enabled to hold the balance between her contending neighbours. She sustained some famous sieges. Phaleucus, general of the Phocians, making an expedition into Crete with a fleet and a numerous army, invested Canea both by sea and land, but lost his army and his life before its walls. In succeeding times when Metellus subdued the island, he assaulted Cydon with all his forces; and after combating an obstinate resistance, subjected it to the power of Rome. Cydon occupied the present situation of Canea; only extending half a league farther towards St Odero; where on the sea-shore the remains are still to be seen of some ancient walls which appear to have been of a very solid construction. See Canea. Cydonia, the Quince; so called from Cydon, a town of Crete, famous for its abounding with this fruit. Linnaeus has joined this genus to the apple and pear; but as there is such a remarkable difference between between the fruits, Mr Miller treats the quince as a genus by itself. The species are, 1. The oblonga, with an oblong fruit, lengthened at the base. 2. The mali-forma, with oval leaves, wholly on the upper side, with some other varieties. The Portugal quince is the most valuable; its pulp turns to a fine purple when stewed or baked, and becomes much softer and less austere than the others; so is much fitter for making marmalade. The trees are also easily propagated, either by layers, suckers, or cuttings; which must be planted in a moist soil. Those raised from suckers are seldom so well rooted as those which are obtained from cuttings or layers, and are subject to produce suckers again in greater plenty; which is not so proper for fruit-bearing trees. These trees require very little pruning: the chief thing to be observed is, to keep their stems clear from suckers, and cut off such branches as cross each other; likewise all upright luxuriant shoots from the middle of the tree should be taken off, that the head may not be too much crowded with wood, which is of ill consequence to all fruit trees. These sorts may also be propagated by building or grafting upon stocks raised by cuttings; so that the best sorts may be cultivated this way in greater plenty than by any other method. These are also in great esteem to bud or graft pears upon; which for summer or autumn fruits are a great improvement to them, especially those designed for walls and espaliers; for the trees, upon these stocks do not shoot so vigorously as those upon free-stocks, and therefore may be kept in less compass, and sooner produce fruit: but hard winter fruits do not succeed so well upon these stocks, their fruit being subject to crack, and are commonly stony, especially all the breaking pears: therefore these stocks are only fit for melting pears and a moist soil.

CYGINNIS

Pages 45-46

a Grecian dance, so called from the name of its inventor, one of the satyrs belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. It consisted of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and gay movements. CYCLADES INSULE: <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> anciently so called, as Pliny informs us, from the cyclus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> orb in which they <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a>; beginning from the promontory Gerestum of Euboea, and lying round the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Delos, (Pliny). Where they are, and what their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, is not so generally agreed. Strabo says, they were at first reckoned 12, but that many others were added: yet most of them lie to the south of Delos, and but few to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; so that the middle or centre, ascribed to Delos, is to be taken in a loose, not a geometrical, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Strabo recites them after Artemidorus, as follows: Helena, Ceos, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CYNTHIA">Cynthia</a>, Seriphus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELOS">Melos</a>, Siphnos, Cimolus, Prepesinthus, Olearus, Naxus, Parus, Syrus, Myconus, Tenus, Andrus, Gyarus; but he excludes from the number Prepesinthus, Olearus, and Gyarus.

CYGNUS

Pages 48-48

the Swan, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the northern hemisphere, between Lyra and Cepheus. The stars in the constellation Cygnus, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 195; in Tycho's 18; in Hevelius's 47; in the Britannic catalogue 81.

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of a parallelogram. Rolling <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Loaded CYLINDER, a cylinder which rolls up an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>; the phenomena of which are explained under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">MECHANICS</a>.

CYLINDROID

Pages 48-48

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body approaching to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, but differing from it in some respects, as having the bases elliptical, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> and equal.

CYLINDRUS

Pages 48-48

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of a genus of shell-fish, of which there are many elegant and precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.

CYMA

Pages 48-48
or CYMATIUM, in Architecture, a member or moulding of the corniche, the profile of which is waved, that is, concave at top, and convex at bottom. Cymbal, (κυμβαλον), a musical instrument in use among the ancients. The cymbal was made of brass, like our kettle-drums, and, as some think, in their form, but smaller, and of different use. Ovid gives cymbals the epithet of genialia, because they were used at weddings and other diversions. Cassiodorus and Isidore call this instrument acetabulum, the name of a cup or cavity of a bone wherein another is articulated; and Xenophon compares it to a horse's hoof; whence it must have been hollow; which appears, too, from the figure of several other things denominated from it; as a basin, caldron, goblet, cask, and even a shoe, such as those of Empedocles, which were of brass. In reality, the ancient cymbals appear to have been very different from our kettle-drums, and their use of another kind: to their exterior cavity was fastened a handle; whence Pliny compares them to the upper part of the thigh, and Rabanus to phials. They were struck against one another in cadence, and made a very acute sound. Their invention was attributed to Cybele; whence their use in feasts and sacrifices: setting aside this occasion, they were seldom used but by dissolute and effeminate people. M. Lampe, who has written expressly on the subject, attributes the invention to the Curetes, or inhabitants of Mount Ida in Crete; it is certain these, as well as the Corybantes or guards of the kings of Crete, and those of Rhodes and Samothracia, were reputed to excel in the music of the cymbal. The Jews had their cymbals, or at least instruments which translators render cymbals; but as to their matter and form, critics are still in the dark. The modern cymbal is a mean instrument, chiefly in use among vagrants, gypsies, &c. It consists of steel wire in a triangular form, whereupon are passed five rings, which are touched and shifted along the triangle with an iron rod held in the left hand, while it is supported in the right by a ring, to give it the freer motion. Durandus says, that the monks used the word cymbal for the cloister-bell, used to call them to the refectory.

CYME

Pages 48-48

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> built by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPS">Pelops</a> on his return to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Cyme the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMAZON">Amazon</a> gave it name, on expelling the inhabitants, according to Mela. Latin authors, as Nepes, Livy, Mela, Pliny, Tacitus, retain the appellation Cyme, after the Greek manner. It stood in Aëolia, between Myrina and Phocæa (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, in Peutinger's map, is set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles distant from Myrina.—From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was the Sibylla Cumæa, called Erythrea, from Erythra, "a neighbouring place." It was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Ephorus. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> was a Cumean originally (Stephanus); his father coming to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at Ascrea in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>.

CYMENE

Pages 48-49

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks to a plant with which they used to dye woollen stuffs <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and with which the women of those times used also to tinge the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> yellow, which was then the favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The cymene of the Greeks is evidently the same plant with the lutea herba of the Latins; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> what is now called dyers weed. See RESEDA, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CYNÆGIRUS, an Athenian, celebrated for his extraordinary courage. He was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the poet Æschylus. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a> he pursued the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Persians to their ships, and seized one of their vessels with his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, which was immediately severed by the enemy. Upon this he seized Cynagirus the vessel with his left hand, and when he had lost that also, he still kept his hold with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>.

CYNANCHE

Pages 49-49

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, in which the throat is inflamed and swelled to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as sometimes to threaten suffocation. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYNANCHUM

Pages 49-49
BASTARD DOGBANE;** a genus of plants, belonging to the pentandria class; and in the natural method ranking under the 30th order, Con- torce. See Botany Index.

CYNARA

Pages 49-49

the ARTICHOKE;** a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The varieties of the artichoke are propagated by slips <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suckers, arising annually from the stool or root of the old plants in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, which are to be taken from good plants of any present plantation in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> or the beginning of April, and planted in the open <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> garden, in rows five feet asunder: and they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce artichokes the same year in autumn. It should, however, be remarked, that though artichokes are of many years <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, the annual produce of their fruit will gradually lessen in the size of the eatable parts after the third or fourth year, so that a fresh plantation should be made every three or four years. The cardoon is a very hardy plant, and prospers in the open <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the kitchen-garden. It is propagated by seed sown annually in the full ground in March; either in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> for transplantation, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they are designed to remain. The plants are very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, so must stand at considerable distances from one another. By this means you may have some small temporary crops between the rows, as of lettuce, spinach, endive, cabbage, savoy, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCCOLI">broccoli</a> plants. In the latter end of September, or in October, the cardoons will be grown very large, and their footstalks have acquired a thick substance; you must then tie up the leaves of each plant, to admit of earthing them closely all round for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANCHING">blanching</a>, which will take up six or eight weeks; and thus the plants will come in for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in November and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, and continue all winter. **CYNEUS,** of Thessaly, the scholar of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, flourished 275 years before Christ. Pyrrhus had so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an esteem for him, that he sent him to Rome to solicit a peace; and so vast was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after his arrival he saluted all the senators and knights by name. Pyrrhus and he wrote a Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, quoted by Tully. **CYNICS,** a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, who valued themselves upon their contempt of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and state, arts and sciences, and every thing, in short, except virtue or morality. The Cynic philosophers owe their origin and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to Antisthenes of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>; who being asked of what use his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> had been to him, replied, "It enables me to live with myself." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> was the most famous of his disciples, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the system of this philosophy appears in its greatest perfection. He led a most wretched life, a tub having served him for a lodging, which he rolled before him wherever he went. Yet he was nevertheless not the more humble on account of his ragged cloak, bag, and tub; for one day entering <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when there was a splendid entertainment there for several persons of distinction, he jumped upon a very rich couch in all his dirt, saying, "I trample on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of Plato." "Yes (replied Plato), but with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pride, Diogenes." He had the utmost contempt for all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; for he walked the streets of Athens at noon-day with a lighted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, telling the people, "He was in search of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>." Among many excellent maxims of morality, he held some very pernicious opinions: for he used to say that the uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> of Harpalus, who generally passed for a thief and a robber, was a testimony against the gods. He regarded chastity and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> as weaknesses. Hence Laertius observes of him, that he did everything openly, whether it belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> or Venus; though he adds, that Diogenes only ran to an excess of impudence to put others out of conceit of it. But impudence was the characteristic of these philosophers; who argued, that what was <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to be done, might be done at all times, and in all places. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> principle of this sect in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the Stoics, was, that we should follow <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. But they differed from the Stoics in their explanation of that maxim; the Cynics being of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that a man followed nature that gratified his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> motions and appetites; while the Stoics understood right reason by the word nature. **Cynic-Spasms,** a kind of convulsion, wherein the patient imitates the howlings of dogs. **CYNIPS,** a genus of insects belonging to the hymenoptera order. See Entomology Index. **CYNOCEPHALUS,** in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Simia. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index.

CYNOGLOSSUM

Pages 49-51
Hound's Tongue;** a genus of plants belonging to the pentandria class, and in the natural method ranking under the 41st order, Asperiflorae. See Botany Index. **CYNOMETRY,** in Botany, a genus of plants belonging to the decandria class, and in the natural method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See Botany Index. **CYNOMORIUM,** in Botany, a genus of plants belonging to the monocota class, and in the natural method ranking under the 50th order, Amentaceae. See Botany Index. **CYNOPHONTIS,** in antiquity, a festival observed in the dog days at Argos, and so called ἀπὸ τῶν κυνῶν φονέων, i.e. from killing dogs: because it was usual on this day to kill all the dogs they met with. **CYNOREXY,** an immoderate appetite, to the degree of a disease, called also fames canina and bulimy. **CYNOSARGES,** a place in the suburbs of Athens, named from a white or swift dog, who snatched away part of the sacrifice offering to Hercules. It had a gymnasium, in which strangers or those of the half-blood performed their exercises; the case of Hercules, to whom the place was consecrated. It had also a court of judicature to try illegitimacy, and to examine whether persons were Athenians of the whole or half blood. Here Antisthenes set up a new sect of philosophers called Cynics, either from the place, or from the snarling or the impudent disposition of that sect. **CYNOSCEPHALÆ,** in Ancient Geography, a place in Thessaly near Scotussa; where the Romans, under Q. Flamininus, gained a great victory over Philip, son of Demetrius king of Macedon. These Cynoscephalæ... Cynossema, the tomb of Hecuba, on the promontory Mastusia, over against Dardanus, in the south of the Chersonesus Thracica; named either from the figure of a dog, to which she was changed, or from her sad reverse of fortune (Pliny, Mela). Cynosura, in Astronomy, a denomination given by the Greeks to ursa minor, "the little bear," by which sailors steer their course. The word is formed of κυνος, q.d., the dog's tail. This is the constellation next our pole, consisting of seven stars; four whereof are disposed like the four wheels of a chariot, and three lengthwise representing the beam; whence some give it the name of the chariot, or Charles's chain. Cynosura, Cynosure, or Cynosurus, in Ancient Geography, a place in Laconia; but whether maritime or inland, uncertain. Here Æsculapius, being thunderstruck, was buried (Cicero). Cynosura was also the name of the promontory of Marathon in Attica, opposite to Euboea. Cynosura, in Mythology, a nymph of Ida in Crete. She nursed Jupiter, who changed her into a star which bears the same name. It is the same as the ursa minor. Cynosurus, in Botany, a genus of plants belonging to the triandra class, and in the natural method ranking under the 4th order, Gramineae. See Botany Index. Cynthus, in Ancient Geography, a mountain of the island Delos, so high as to overshadow the whole island. On this mountain Latona brought forth Apollo and Diana: hence the epithet Cynthus (Virgil), and Cynthia (Lucan, Statius). Cynuria, or Cynurius Ager, in Ancient Geography, a district of Laconia, on the confines of Argolis. A territory that proved a perpetual bone of contention between the Argives and Spartans (Thucydides). For the manner of deciding the dispute, see Thryea. Cyperus, in Botany, a genus of plants belonging to the triandra class, and in the natural method ranking under the 3d order, Calamariae. See Botany Index. Cyphon, in antiquity, a kind of punishment used by the Athenians. It was a collar made of wood; so called because it constrained the criminal who had this punishment inflicted on him to bow down his head. Cyphonism (Cyphonismus), from κυφων, which has various significations; derived from κυφων, crooked; a kind of torture or punishment in use among the ancients. The learned are at a loss to determine what it was. Some will have it to be that mentioned by Jerome in his Life of Paul the Hermit, chap. x. which consisted in smearing the body over with honey, and thus exposing the person, with his hands tied, to the warm sun, to invite the flies and other vermin to persecute him. Cypræa, or Cowrie, a genus of shells belonging to the order of vermes testacea. See Conchology Index. This genus is called cypra and venera from its being peculiarly dedicated to Venus, who is said to have endowed a shell of this genus with the powers of a remora, so as to impede the course of the ship which was sent by Periander tyrant of Corinth, with orders to emasculate the young nobility of Coreya. Cypress. See Cupressus, Botany Index. Cyprianus, Thascius-Cæcilius, a principal father of the Christian church, was born at Carthage in Africa, at the latter end of the second or beginning of the third century. We know nothing more of his parents than that they were Heathens; and he himself continued such till the last 12 years of his life. He applied himself early to the study of oratory; and some of the ancients, particularly Lactantius, inform us, that he taught rhetoric in Carthage with the highest applause. Cyprian's conversion is fixed by Pearson to the year 246; and was at Carthage, where, as St Jerome observes, he had often employed his rhetoric in the defence of paganism. It was brought about by one Cecilius, a priest of the church of Carthage, whose name Cyprian afterwards took; and between whom there ever after subsisted so close a friendship, that Cecilius at his death committed to Cyprian the care of his family. Cyprian was also a married man himself; but as soon as he was converted to the faith, he resolved upon a state of continence, which was thought a high degree of piety, as not being yet become general. Being now a Christian, he was to give the usual proof of the sincerity of his conversion; and that was by writing against Paganism and in defence of Christianity. With this view he composed his piece De Gratia Dei, or "concerning the grace of God," which he addressed to Donatus. It is a work of the same nature with the Apologetic of Tertullian, and the Octavius of Minutius Felix. He next composed a piece De Idolorum Vanitate, or "upon the vanity of idols." Cyprian's behaviour, both before and after his baptism, was so highly pleasing to the bishop of Carthage, that he ordained him a priest a few months after. It was rather irregular to ordain a man thus in his very noviciate; but Cyprian was so extraordinary a person, and thought capable of doing such singular service to the church, that it seemed allowable in this case to dispense a little with the form and discipline of it. For besides his known talents as a secular man, he had acquired a high reputation of sanctity since his conversion; having not only separated himself from his wife, as we have observed before, which in those days was thought an extraordinary act of piety, but also consigned over all his goods to the poor, and given himself up entirely to the things of God. It was on this account no doubt, too, that when the bishop of Carthage died the year after, that is, in the year 248, none was judged so proper to succeed him as Cyprian. The quiet and repose which the Christians had enjoyed during the last 40 years, had, it seems, greatly corrupted their manners; and therefore Cyprian's first care, after his advancement to the bishopric, was to correct disorders and reform abuses. Luxury was prevalent among them; and many of their women were not so strict as CYPRIANUS as they should be, especially in the article of dress. This occasioned him to draw up his piece De habitu virginitum, "concerning the dress of young women;" in which, besides what he says on that particular head, he inculcates many lessons of modesty and sobriety. In the year 249, the emperor Decius began to issue out very severe edicts against the Christians, which particularly affected those upon the coast of Africa; and in the beginning of 250, the Heathens in the circus and amphitheatre of Carthage, insisted loudly upon Cyprian's being thrown to the lions: a common method of destroying the primitive Christians. Cyprian upon this withdrew from the church at Carthage, and fled into retirement, to avoid the fury of the persecutions. He wrote, in the place of his retreat, pious and instructive letters to those who had been his hearers; and also to the libellatici, a name by which those pusillanimous Christians were called, who procured certificates of the Heathen magistrates, to show that they had complied with the emperor's orders in sacrificing to idols. At his return to Carthage, he held several councils on the repentance of those who had fallen during this persecution, and other points of discipline; he opposed the schemes of Novatus and Novatianus; and contended for the rebaptizing of those who had been baptized by heretics. At last he died a martyr in the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, in 258. Cyprian wrote 81 letters, and several treatises. The best edition of his works are those of Pamelius in 1658; of Rigaltius in 1648; and of Oxford in 1682. His works have all been translated into English by Dr Marshal.

CYPRINUS

Pages 51-51

a genus of fishes, belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYPRIPEDIUM

Pages 51-51

the Lady's Slipper; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 7th order, Orchideae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYPRUS

Pages 51-52

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> most easterly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between 33 and 36 degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and 35 and 36 of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times this island was known by the names of Acamis, Cerastis, Aspalix, Amathus, Macaria, Cryptos, Colinia, Sphecia, Paphis, Salaminis, Ærosa, and Cyprus. The etymologies of these names are neither very easily found, nor are they of much importance. The name by which it was most generally known is that of Cyprus, said to be derived from cypros, the name of a shrub or tree with which the island abounds; supposed to be the cypress. Cyprus, according to Eratosthenes, was first discovered by the Phoenicians, two or three generations before the days of Asterius and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, kings of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>; that is, according to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's computation, 2006 years before the Christian era. It was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> so full of wood that it could not be tilled, and the Phoenicians first cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> that wood for melting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, with which the island abounded; and afterwards, when they began to sail without fear on the Mediterranean, that is, after the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, they built <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> navies of the wood produced on this island. Josephus, however, informs us, that the descendants of Cittim, the son of Javan, and grandson of Japhet, were the original inhabitants of Cyprus. According to his account, Cittim, seeing his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Tarshish settled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, where he built the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">Tarsus</a>, settled with his followers in this opposite island; and either he or his descendants laid the foundation of the city of Cittim, which, according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, was the most ancient in the island. As Cyprus was too narrow to contain the great numbers who attended him, he left here as many as might serve to people the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and with the rest passed over to Macedon. The island of Cyprus was divided among several petty kings till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> the Great. He subdued them all; but left each in possession of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, obliging them only to pay him an annual tribute, and to send supplies of men, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and ships when required. The Cyprian princes lived thus subject to the Persians till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hystaspes, when they attempted to shake off the yoke, but with bad success; their forces being entirely defeated, and themselves again obliged to submit. They made another more successful attempt about the year before Christ 337; but, however, could never totally free themselves from their subjection. It is very probable that they submitted to Alexander the Great, though historians are silent as to that event. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the Macedonian conqueror, the dominion of Cyprus was disputed by Antigonus and Ptolemy the son of Lagus. At last Antigonus prevailed, and the whole island submitted to him about 304 years before Christ. He and his son Demetrius kept possession of it for 11 years, when it was recovered by Ptolemy, and quietly possessed by him and his descendants till 38 years before Christ, when it was most unjustly seized by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. In the time of Augustus, it began to be ranked among the proconsular provinces, and to be governed by magistrates sent thither by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. In the year 638 it was conquered by the Saracens; but recovered by the Romans in 937. They held it, however, but for a very short time, and the barbarians kept possession of it till the time of the croisades. It was then reduced by the croisaders; and Richard I. of England gave it to the princes of the Lusignan family, who held it till the year 1570. They divided it into 12 provinces, in each of which was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city, from which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was denominated. So considerable was the island at this time, that besides the cities above mentioned, and others of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, it contained 800 villages. In 1570 it was taken by the Turks, and though it hath ever since <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under their tyrannical yoke, is still so considerable as to be governed by a beglerbeg, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sangias under him. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in this island is for the most part very unwholesome, on account of the many fens and marshes with which the country abounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is an excellent fertile clay; and would produce all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in abundance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> properly cultivated. There are but few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in this island; so that when the rains do not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> plentifully at the usual seasons, the inhabitants are much distressed by the scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. By reason of the uncultivated state of the country, they are also greatly infested with poisonous reptiles of various kinds. The people are extremely ignorant and lascivious, as indeed they are remarked to have been from the remotest antiquity. Anciently the worship of Venus was established in this island, whence her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> among the poets of the Cyprian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>; and such an inclination had the inhabitants to become become the votaries of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, both in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice, that the young women used to prostitute themselves in her temple in order to raise themselves portions. The exports of the island are silks, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, cotton, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and turpentine; the imports are French and Venetian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloths; and sometimes a few bales of English manufacture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> wares, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, tin, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants at present is believed not to exceed 60,000. Knights of Cyprus, an order instituted by Guy de Lusignan, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, to whom Richard I. of England, after conquering this island, made over his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>.

CYRANO

Pages 52-52

Bergerac, a French author, born in Gascony, about the year 1620. He first entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, where his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> courage engaged him frequently in duels in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; which, with other rash actions, procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Intrepid. But the little prospect he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> of preferment made him renounce the trade of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. His comic histories of the states and empires in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, show him well acquainted with the Cartesian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and to have a lively imagination. Our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a> classes him with Swift for his turn of humour, which he says the latter adopted and pursued.

CYRENAICA

Pages 52-52

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, corresponding to the present kingdom and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCA">Barca</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>. It was originally inhabited by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of barbarous nations, differing little from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> gangs of robbers. Afterwards some colonies from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> settled here, and Cyrenaica became so powerful a state, that it waged <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, often with success. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hystaspes, Arcesilaus, the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in Cyrenaica, was driven from the throne; on which his mother Pheretima applied for assistance to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Cyprus. Her son afterwards returning to Barca, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, was there assassinated, together with his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Pheretima finding herself disappointed by the king of Cyprus, applied to Darius Hystaspes, and by the assistance of the Persians reduced Barca. Here she behaved with the utmost cruelty, causing all those who had been concerned in her son's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to be impaled, and the breasts of their wives to be cut off and affixed near them. She is said to have been afterwards devoured by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>; which was looked upon as a divine judgment for her excessive cruelty. The prisoners in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time were sent to Darius, who settled him in a district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BACTRIA">Bactria</a>, from them called Barca. Cyrenaica, however, seems to have remained free till the time of Alexander the Great, who conquered it along with Egypt. Soon after his death the inhabitants recovered their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; but were in a short time reduced by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> king of Egypt. Under these kings it remained till Ptolemy Physcon made it over to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> son Apian, who in the 658th year of Rome left it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> permitted all the cities to be governed by their own laws; and this immediately filled the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with tyrants, those who were most potent in every city <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> district endeavouring to assume the sovereignty of it. Thus the kingdom was thrown into great confusion; but Lucullus in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> restored the public tranquillity on his coming thither during the first Mithridatic war. It was found impossible, however, totally to suppress these Cyrenaic disturbances till the country was reduced to the form of a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, which happened about 20 years after the death of Apian, and 76 before Christ. Upon a revolt, the city of Cyrene was ruined by the Romans; but they afterwards rebuilt it. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time it fell to the Arabs; and then to the Turks, who are still the nominal masters of it.

CYRENAICS

Pages 52-52

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, so called from their founder Aristippus of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> principle of their doctrine was, that the supreme good of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; whereby they not only meant a privation of pain, and a tranquillity of mind, but an assemblage of all mental and sensual pleasures, particularly the last. Cicero makes frequent mention of Aristippus's school, and speaks of it as yielding debauchees. Three disciples of Aristippus, after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, divided the sect into three branches; under which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> it languished and sunk; the first called the Hegesian school; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the Amicercism; and the third the Theodran; from the names of their authors.

CYRENE

Pages 52-52

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, and one of the cities called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTAPOLIS">Pentapolis</a>, distant from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLONIA">Apollonia</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port, 10 miles, situated on a plain, of the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, according to Strabo: A colony of the Therans. Though they were descendants of the Lacedemonians, yet they differed from them in their turn of mind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disposition, applying themselves to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and hence arose the Cyrenaic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, at the head of which was Aristippus, who placed all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The Cyreanacs were a people much given to auriugation, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the chariot, from their excellent breed of horses, (<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>, Ephorus, Strabo).

CYRIL

Pages 52-53

St., <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Alexandrin, succeeded Theophilus, his uncle, in 412. Scarce was he installed, when he began to exert his authority with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rigour; he drove the Novatians and Jews from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, permitting their wealth and synagogues to be taken from them. This proceeding highly displeased Orestes, the governor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the bishop's authority was not soon suppressed, it might grow too strong for that of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. Upon which a kind of civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> broke out between Orestes and the bishop; many tumults were raised, and some battles fought in the very streets of Alexandria. St Cyril also distinguished himself by his zeal against <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NESTORIUS">Nestorius</a> bishop of Constantinople, who in some of his homilies had asserted that the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> ought not to be called the mother of God. The dispute at first proved unfavourable to Cyril, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was not only condemned, but himself deprived of his bishopric and thrown into prison. But he was soon after released, and gained a complete victory over Nestorius, who in 431 was deposed from his see of Constantinople. Cyril returned to his see at Constantinople, where he died in 444. St Cyril also wrote against Theodorus of Mopsuestia, Diodorus of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">Tarsus</a>, and Julian the apostate. He composed commentaries on St John's gospel, and wrote several other books. His works were published in Greek and Latin in 1638, in six volumes folio.

CYRUS

Pages 53-54

the son of Cambyses the Persian, by Mandane, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Medes. The two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> historians, who have written the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Cyrus, are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> and Xenophon; but their accounts of him are different, in as much as the latter makes his father a king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and the former a meaner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The account of Herodotus, as Dr Prindeaux observes, indeed contains narratives that are much more strange and surprising, and consequently more diverting and agreeable to the reader: and for this reason more have chosen to follow him than Xenophon. Herodotus informs us, that Astyages king of the Medes dreamed that a vine sprung from the womb of his daughter Mandane, the branches whereof overshadowed all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; whereupon having consulted the soothsayers, he was told that his dream portended the future power and greatness of a child who should be born of his daughter: and further that the same child should deprive him of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Astyages, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of this prediction, instead of marrying his daughter to some powerful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, gave her to Cambyses, a Persian of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> condition, and one who had no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> capacity for forming any important <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, nor for supporting the ambition of his son by his own <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and authority. Nor did Astyages stop here: the apprehensions he was under lest Mandane's son might perhaps find that assistance in his own courage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some lucky circumstance which his family was not able to supply him with, induced him to take a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of despatching the child, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there should be any. As soon, therefore, as he understood his daughter was with child, he commanded one of his officers, whose name was Harpagus, to destroy the infant as soon as it came into the world. Harpagus, fearing the resentment of Mandane, put the child into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of one who was the king's shepherd, in order to expose him. The shepherd's wife was so extremely touched with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of Cyrus, that she desired her husband rather to expose her own son, who was born some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before, and preserve the young prince. After this manner Cyrus was preserved, and brought up among the king's shepherds. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, as the neighbouring children were at play together, Cyrus was chosen king; and having punished one of his little playfellows with some severity, for disobeying his commands, the child's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> complained of Cyrus to Astyages. This prince sent for young Cyrus, and observing something great in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, his manner and behaviour, together with a great resemblance of his daughter Mandane, he made particular inquiry into the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and discovered that, in reality, Cyrus was no other than his grandson. Harpagus, who was the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of preserving him, was punished with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his own son: however, Astyages believing that the royalty which the soothsayers had promised to the young prince, was only that which he had lately exercised among the shepherd's children, troubled himself no more about it. Cyrus being grown up, Harpagus disclosed the whole secret of his birth to him, together with the manner wherein he had delivered him from the cruel resolution of his grandfather. He encouraged him to come into Media, and promised to furnish him with forces, in order to make him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and depose Astyages. Cyrus hearkened to these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>; engaged the Persians to take up arms against the Medes, marched at the head of them to meet Astyages, defeated him, and possessed himself of Media. He carried on many other wars; and at length sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, which after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> siege he took. The relation of Cyrus's life from Xenophon is as follows: Astyages king of Media married his daughter Mandane to Cambyses king of Persia, son to Achemenes king of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Cyrus was born at his father's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and was educated with all the care his birth required. When he was about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 12 years, his grandfather Astyages sent for him to Media, together with his mother Mandane. Some time after, the king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>'s son having invaded Media, Astyages, with his son <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYAXARES">Cyaxares</a> and his grandson Cyrus, marched against him. Cyrus distinguished himself in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and defeated the Assyrians. Cambyses afterwards recalled him, that he might have him near his own person; and Astyages dying, his son Cyaxares, uncle by the mother's side to Cyrus, succeeded him in the kingdom of Media. Cyrus, at the age of 30 years, was, by his father Cambyses, made general of the Persian troops; and sent at the head of 30,000 men to the assistance of his uncle Cyaxares, whom the king of Babylon, with his allies the Cappadocians, Carians, Phrygians, Cilicians, and Paphlagonians were preparing to attack. Cyaxares and Cyrus prevented them, by falling upon them and dispersing them. Cyrus advanced as far as Babylon, and spread terror throughout the country. From this expedition he retired to his uncle, towards the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> and Assyria, and was received by Cyaxares in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> of the Assyrian king whom he had defeated. After this Cyrus carried the war into the countries beyond the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a>; entered Cappadocia, and subdued it entirely. From thence he marched against Croesus king of Lydia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> him in the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; then besieged him in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a> his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; and after a siege of fourteen days obliged him to surrender.
