See Croesus. After this, Cyrus having reduced almost all Asia, repassed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, and made war upon the Assyrians. He marched directly to Babylon, took it, and there prepared a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for his uncle Cyaxares, whither he might retire, if at any time he had an inclination to come to Babylon; for he was not then in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. After all these expeditions, Cyrus returned to his father and mother into Persia, where they were still living: and going some time after to his uncle Cyaxares into Media, he married his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> the only daughter and heiress of all Cyaxares's dominions, and went with her to Babylon, from whence he sent men of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to govern all the several nations which he had conquered. He engaged again in several wars, and subdued all the nations which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. He died at the age of 70 years, after a reign of 30; but authors differ very much concerning the manner of his death. Herodotus, Justin, and Valerius Maximus relate, that he died in the war against the Scythians; and that falling into an ambush which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Tomyris had laid for him, she ordered his head to be cut off, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into a vessel full of blood, saying, "Thou hast always thirsted after <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood, now glut thyself with it." Diodorus the Sicilian says, that he was taken in an engagement and hanged. Ctesias assures us, that he died of a wound which he received in his thigh: but by Xenophon's account he died peaceably in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, amidst his friends and his servants; and certain it is, that in Alexander's time his monument was shown at Pasagarda in Persia. From all this it is easy to conclude, that we are but imperfectly acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this great prince, the founder of the Persian, and destroyer of the Chaldean empire. We learn fewer particulars of it from Scripture, but then they are more certain than any that we have produced. Daniel (viii. 3—20.) in the famous vision wherein God showed him the ruin of several great emperors, which were to precede the birth of the Messiah, represents Cyrus to us under the idea of "a ram, which had two horns; and the two horns were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, but the one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last. This ram pushed westward, and northward, and southward, so that no beasts might stand before him; neither was there any that could deliver out of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, but he did according to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and became great." The ram's two horns signify the two empires which Cyrus reunited in his person; that of the Medes, and that of the Persians. The last was greater and more powerful than the empire of the Medes; or otherwise, these two horns signify the two branches of Cyrus's successors. His son Cambyses dying, the empire was transferred to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> the son of Hystaspes, and was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> down to Darius Codomannus, who, as Calmet thinks, is the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> which the he-goat, that denotes Alexander, run against. In chap. vii. 5. Daniel compares Cyrus to a bear, with three ribs in the mouth of it, to which it was said, "Arise, devour much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>." Cyrus succeeded his father Cambyses in the kingdom of Persia, and Darius the Mede, by Xenophon called Cyaxares, and Astyages in the apocryphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> (xiii. 1.) of Daniel, in the kingdom of the Medes and empire of Babylon. He was monarch of all the east; or as he speaks (2 Chr. xxxvi. 22, 23, and Ezr. i. 1, 2.) "of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>," when he permitted the Jews to return to their own country, in the year of the world 3466, before <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ 538. The enemies of the Hebrews, making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this prince's affection to his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, prevailed with him to put a stop by his orders to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; (<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> iv. 5.) The prophets frequently foretold the coming of Cyrus; and Isaiah (xlv. 28.) has been so particular as to declare his name 200 years before he was born. Josephus (Antiq. lib. ii. c. 2.) says, that the Jews of Babylon showed this passage of the prophet to Cyrus; and that this prince, in the edict which he granted them for their return, acknowledged that he received the empire of the world from the God of Israel; and that the same God had described him by name in the writings of the prophets, and foretold that he should build a temple to him at Jerusalem. Cyrus is pointed out in Scripture under the name of the righteous man and the shepherd of Israel, (Isaiah xlii. 2. &c. xlvii. 28.) and xlii. 11. Notwithstanding this, God says of him (Isaiah xlv. 5.) "I girded thee, though thou hast not known me." And Jeremiah calls Cyrus and his people who overthrew the Babylonish empire, thieves and robbers. The taking of Babylon by Cyrus is clearly set down by the prophets, and may be seen under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> BABYLON and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELSHAZZAR">BELSHAZZAR</a>. Archbishop Usher fixes the birth of Cyrus to the year of the world 3405; his first year at Babylon to 3466, and his death to 3475. The eastern people will have it, that Cyrus by his mother's side was descended from some of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> prophets: as also that his wife was a Jew, which is the reason (say they) that this prince so attached himself to the Jews, to whom he was so nearly allied. CYRUS II. was the younger son of Darius Nothus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a>. He was sent by his father at the age of 16 to assist the Macedonians against <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. Artaxerxes succeeded to the throne at the death of Nothus; and Cyrus, who was of an aspiring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, attempted to assassinate him. He was discovered, and had been punished with death, had not his mother Parysatis saved him from the hands of the executioner by her tears and entreaties. This circumstance did not in the least check the ambition of Cyrus; he was appointed over Lydia and the sea-coasts, where he secretly fomented rebellion and levied troops under various pretences. At last he took the field with an army of 100,000 barbarians, and 13,000 Greeks under the command of Clearchus. Artaxerxes met him with 900,000 men near Cunaxa. The battle was long and bloody; and Cyrus might have perhaps obtained the victory, had not his uncommon rashness proved his ruin. It is said that the two <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> brothers met in person, and their engagement ended in the death of Cyrus, 401 years before the Augustan age. Artaxerxes was so anxious of its being universally reported that his brother had fallen by his hand, that he put to death two of his subjects for boasting that they had killed Cyrus. The Greeks, who were engaged in the expedition, obtained much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in the battle; and after the death of Cyrus they remained victorious in the field without a commander. They were not discouraged though at the distance of above 600 leagues from their country, and surrounded on every side by a powerful enemy. They unanimously united in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of commanders, and traversed all Asia, in spite of the continual attacks of the Persians; and nothing is more truly celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> history than the bold retreat of the ten thousand. The journey that they made from the time of their first embarkation till their return, has been calculated at 1155 leagues, performed in the space of 15 months, including all the time which was devoted to take rest and refreshment. This retreat has been celebrated by Xenophon, who was one of their leaders, and among the friends and supporters of Cyrus.

CYSTIC

Pages 54-55

in Anatomy, a name given to two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> and two veins. Cystic Duct. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYTHERA

Pages 55-55

-orum, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> opposite to Malles, a promontory, and to Boire a town of Lascinia. The island was sacred to Venus, with a very ancient temple of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> exhibited in armour at Cythera, as in Cyprus. It is now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CERIGO">Cerigo</a>, and forms one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIAN_ISLANDS">Ionian <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. See Ionian Islands, Supplement.

CYTHEREA

Pages 55-55

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Venus, so called from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYTHERA">Cythera</a> an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, where she had a temple esteemed the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and on the shores of which she was believed to be borne by the Zephyrs, surrounded by the Loves, the Tritons, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>, reclining in a languishing posture in a seashell. They give the name of Cytherades to the Graces which attended her on the shore without quitting her, except on those occasions when she rather chose to be waited upon by the Pleasures.

CYTINUS

Pages 55-55

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th order, Sarmentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYTISUS

Pages 55-55

TREE TREFOIL, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32nd order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CYZICENS

Pages 55-55

CYZICENA, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks, were a sort of magnificent banqueting houses, always looking toward the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and usually opening upon gardens. They had their name from Cyzicus, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> very considerable for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of its buildings; situated in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same name.

CYZICUM

Pages 55-55
or CYZICUS, in Ancient Geography, one of the noblest cities of the hither Asia; situated in a cognominal island of the Propontis, on the coast of Mysia; joined to the continent by two bridges (Strabo); the first by Alexander; the city, a colony of the Milesians (Pliny). Rendered famous by the siege of Mithridates, which was raised by Lucullus.—The inhabitants were made a free people by the Romans, but forfeited their freedom under Tiberius. It was adorned with a citadel and walls round it; had a port and marble towers; and three magazines, one for arms, another for warlike engines, and a third for corn. Cyziceni, the people; noted by the ancients for their timidity and effeminacy; hence the proverb in Zenodotus and others, Tinctura Cyzenica, applied to persons guilty of an indecency through fear; but Statutes Cyzenici, nummi Cyzenici, denote things executed to perfection.

CZACKTHURN

Pages 55-55

a strong town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and near the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It is seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Drave and Muhir, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 19' N. Lat. 46° 24'.

CZAR

Pages 55-55

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, assumed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> dukes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as they are now styled, emperors of Russia. The natives pronounce it tsar, or zar; and this, by corruption (it has been fancied), from Caesar, "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>," from some imagined relation to the Roman emperors. But this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> does not seem correct. When the czar <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> formerly required of the European courts an acknowledgement of his imperial titles, and that the appellation of Emperor should never be omitted, there was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty made about it, especially at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>; which occasioned him to produce the famous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, written in the German tongue, from Maximilian I., emperor of Germany, to Vassili Ivanovitch, confirming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> offensive and defensive against Sigismund <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. In this dispatch, which is dated August the 4th, 1514, and is ratified with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bull, Maximilian addresses Vassili by calling him Kaiser and Herrscher aller Russen, "emperor and ruler of all the Russias." But independently of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a>, there could be no doubt that the foreign courts, in their intercourse with that of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, styled the sovereigns indiscriminately Great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a>, Czar, and Emperor. With respect to England in particular, it is certain that in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a>'s Account of Russia, so early as the middle of the 16th century, Ivan Vassilievitch II. is called <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> and Emperor of all Russia; and in the English dispatches, from the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> to that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, he is generally addressed under the same appellation. When the European powers, however, styled the czar Emperor of Muscovy, they by no means intended to give him a title similar to that which was peculiar to the emperor of Germany; but they bestowed upon him that appellation as upon an Asiatic sovereign, in the same manner as we now say the emperors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. When Peter, therefore, determined to assume the title of emperor, he found no difficulty in proving that it had been conferred upon his predecessors by most of the European powers; yet when he was desirous of affixing to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> the European <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it was considered as an innovation, and was productive of more negotiations than would have been requisite for the termination of the most important state affair. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it occasioned a curious controversy among the learned, concerning the rise and progress of the titles by which the monarchs of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> have been distinguished. From their researches it appeared, that the early sovereigns of Russia were called great dukes, and that Vassili Ivanovitch was probably the first who styled himself tsar, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which in the Slavonian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies king; and that his successors <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to bear within their own dominions that title as the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> appellation, until Peter the Great first took that of Perelitel, or emperor. After many delays and objections, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> courts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> consented, about the year 1722, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> the sovereign of Russia with the title of Emperor; without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, nevertheless, to the other crowned heads of Europe.

CZASLAU

Pages 55-55

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has the highest tower in Bohemia; and near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> gained a victory over the Austrians in 1742. It is seated on the river Crudenka, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 33' N. Lat. 49° 50'.

CZENSTOKOW

Pages 55-55

a town of Russian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of Cracovia, with a fort, in which they keep a rich <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> called "the treasure of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>." The pilgrims flock hither so much for the sake of a convent near it, that it is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORETTO">Loretto</a> of Poland. The town is situated on the river Warte. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 15' N. Lat. 50° 48'.

CZERNIC

Pages 55-56

D, THE fourth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, and the third consonant. Grammarians generally reckon D among the lingual letters, as supposing the tongue to have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> share in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> thereof; though the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">Abbot</a> de Dangeau seems to have reason in making it a palatal letter. The letter D is the fourth in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Chaldee, Samaritan, Syriac, Greek, and Latin alphabets; in the five first of which languages it has the same name, though somewhat differently spoke, e.g., in Hebrew, Samaritan, and Chaldee, Daleth, in Syriac Doth, and in Greek Delta. The form of our D is the same with that of the Latins, as appears from all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> medals and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, and the Latin D is no other than the Greek Δ, rounded a little, by making it quicker and at two strokes. The Δ of the Greeks, again, is borrowed from the ancient character of the Hebrew Daleth: which form it still retains, as is shown by the Jesuit Societ, in his dissertation on the Samaritan Medals. D is also a numerical letter, signifying five hundred, which arises hence, that in the Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, the D is half the M, which signifies a thousand, hence the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, Litera D velut A quingentos significabit. A dash added a-top D, denotes it to stand for five thousand. Used as an abbreviation, it has various significations: thus D stands for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>; as, M. D. for Doctor of Medicine; D. T. Doctor of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>; D. D. implies Doctor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "done dedit;" D. D. D. is used for "dat, dicit, dedicat;" and D. B. D. D. for "dignum Deo donum dedit."

D'URFEY

Pages 428-428

THOMAS, an eminent English satirist and songster, whose name, though as well known as that of any writer extant, yet there are very few particulars of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to be collected. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>; but when, where, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of what family, are all uncertain. He was bred to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which he forsook for the more agreeable employment of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> plays and songs; and the latter he had so happy a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> both of writing and singing, that he received many favours from persons of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> on that account. Even crowned heads did not disdain his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The writer of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>, No 67, tells us, he remembered to have seen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. leaning on Tom D'Urfey's shoulder more than once, humming over a song with him. This indeed was not extraordinary in so merry a monarch; but even the phlegmatic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William could relax his muscles on hearing him sing. He was certainly by all accounts a cheerful, honest, good-natured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; but as this character does not include <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, D'Urfey grew <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> as he grew old: and prevailing on the managers of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of the Plotting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">Sisters</a> for his benefit, Mr Addison wrote the above-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in the Guardian, with another, No 82, representing him in a good-humoured <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, to procure him a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. He died very old, in 1723.

DABUL

Pages 56-56

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, and to the south of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Cambaye, on a navigable river. It was formerly very flourishing, but is now much decayed. It belongs to the Maharrats, and its trade consists principally in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72° 50' N. Lat. 17° 30'.

DACCA

Pages 56-56

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> in the East Indies, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 92° 10', N. Lat. 23° 45'.—The advantages of the situation of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> round it, long since made it the centre of an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a> and Muxadavud were furnished from thence with the cottons wanted for their own consumption; and it was formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of each to maintain an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> on the spot to superintend the manufacture, who had an authority, independent of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, over the brokers, weavers, embroiderers, and all of the workmen whose business had any relation to the object of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. These unhappy people are forbidden, under pecuniary and corporeal penalties, to sell, to any person whatever, a piece exceeding the value of three guineas. Dacca was for eighty years the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Bengal. In this, as in all the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, the Europeans treat with the Moorish brokers settled upon the spot, and appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. They likewise lend their name to the individuals of their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, as well as to Indians and Armenians living in their settlements, who, without this precaution, would infallibly be plundered. The Moors themselves, in their private transactions, sometimes avail themselves of the same pretence, that they may pay only two, instead of five per cent. A distinction is observed, in their contracts, between the cottons that are bespoke and those which the weaver ventures, in some places, to manufacture on his own account. The length, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of threads, and the price, of the former are fixed: nothing further than the commission for the latter is stipulated, because it is impossible to enter into the same detail. These nations that make a point of having fine goods, take proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> that they may be enabled to advance <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to their workmen at the beginning of the year. The weavers, who in general have but little employment at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, perform their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with less hurry than in the months of October, November, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, when the demand is pressing. Some of the cottons are delivered unbleached, and others half bleached. It were to be wished that this custom might be altered. It is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to see cottons that look very beautiful go off in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>. Perhaps the manufacturers and brokers foresee how they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn out; but the Europeans have not so exquisite a touch, nor such an experienced eye, to discern this. It is a circumstance peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, that cottons, of what kind soever they are, can never be well bleached and prepared but in the place where they are manufactured. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they have the misfortune to get damage before they are shipped for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, they must be sent back to the places from whence they came.

DACE

Pages 56-57

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Cyprinus. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This fish is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and gives the expert angler <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diversion. The dace <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> bite at any fly; but he is more than ordinarily fond of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> caddis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> May fly, which is plentiful in the latter end of April and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May. Great quantities of these may be gathered among the reeds or sedges by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-side, and on the hawthorn bushes near the waters. These are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome bait; but as they only last a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year in season, recourse is to be had to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANT">ant</a>-fly. Of these the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> ones found in large <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>-hills or ant-hills are the best. These may be kept alive a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a bottle, with a little of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> of the hill, and some roots of grass; and they are in season throughout the months of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, August, and September. The best season of all is when they swarm, which is in the end of July or beginning of August; and they may be kept many months in a vessel washed out with a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and water, even longer than with the earth and grass-roots in the vial; though that is the most convenient method with a small parcel taken for one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. In warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> this fish very seldom refuses a fly at the top of the water; but at other times he must have the bait sunk to within three inches of the bottom. The winter fishing for dace requires a very different bait: this is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGGOT">maggot</a> with a reddish head, which is the produce of the eggs of the beetle, and is turned up with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> in great abundance. A parcel of these put in any vessel, with the earth they were taken in, will keep many months, and are an excellent bait. Small dace may be put into a glass jar with fresh water; and there preserved alive for a long time, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the water is properly changed. They have been observed to eat nothing but the animalcula of the water. They will grow very tame by degrees.

DACHAW

Pages 57-57

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> in Germany. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, well built, and seated on a mountain, near the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBER">Amber</a>, 10 miles N. W. of Munich. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and fine gardens. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 30' N. Lat. 48° 20'.

DACIA

Pages 57-57

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which Trajan, who reduced it to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, joined to Moesia by an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. This country lies extended between the Danube and Carpathian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, from the river Tibiscus, quite to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the Danube; so as to extend thence in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line to the mouth of the Danube and to the Euxine; on the north side, next the Carpathes, terminated by the river Hierasus, now the Pruth; on the west by the Tibiscus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Teiss; comprising a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, all Transylvania and Wallachia, and a part of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>. Daci, the people; a name which Strabo takes to be the same with the Daci of comedies; neighbours, on the west, to the Getar, an appellation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> also in comedies. Josephus mentions a set of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> men among the Daci, whom he calls Plisti, and compares with the Esseni: of these Plisti no other author makes any mention. Dacicus, the epithet assumed by some emperors (Juvenal). There was a Dacia Aureliana, a part of Illyricum, which was divided into the eastern and western; Sirmium being the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the latter, and Sardica of the former. But this belongs to the lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

DACIER

Pages 57-58
ANNE, daughter of Tannegui le Fevre, professor of Greek at Saumur in France. She early showed a fine genius, which her father cultivated with great care and satisfaction. After her father's death she went to Paris, whether her fame had already reached; she was then preparing an edition of Callimachus, which she published in 1674. Having shown some sheets of it to Mr Huet, preceptor to the dauphin, and to several other men of learning at the court, the work was so highly admired, that the duke of Montausier made a proposal to her of publishing several Latin authors for the use of the dauphin. She rejected this proposal at first, as a task to which she was not equal—But the duke insisted upon it; so that at last he gained her consent; upon which she undertook an edition of Florus, published in 1674. Her reputation being now spread over all Europe, Christina, queen of Sweden, ordered Count Konigsmark to make her a compliment in her name; upon which Mademoiselle le Fevre sent the queen a Latin letter with her edition of Florus; to which her majesty wrote an obliging answer, and not long after sent her another letter, to persuade her to abandon the Protestant religion, and make her considerable offers to settle at her court. In 1683 she married Mr Dacier; and soon after declared her design to the duke of Montausier and the bishop of Meaux of reconciling herself to the church of Rome, which she had entertained for some time: but as Mr Dacier was not yet convinced of the reasonableness of such a change, they retired to Castres in 1684, where they had a small estate, in order to examine the points of controversy between the Protestants and the Roman Catholics. They at last determined in favour of the latter, and made the public abjuration in 1685. After this, the king gave both husband and wife marks of of his favour. In 1693, she applied herself to the education of her son and daughter, who made a prodigious progress: the son died in 1694, and the daughter became a nun in the abbey of Longchamp. She had another daughter, who had united in her all the virtues and accomplishments that could adorn the sex; but she died at 18. Her mother has immortalized her memory in the preface to her translation of the Iliad. Madame Dacier was in a very infirm state of health the two last years of her life; and died, after a very painful sickness, August 17, 1720, aged 69. She was remarkable for her firmness, generosity, equality of temper, and piety.

DACTYL

Pages 58-58

(<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DACTYLUS">dactylus</a>), a foot in the Latin and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>, followed by two short ones; as *carmina*. Some say it is derived from *δάκτυλος*, "a finger," because it is divided into three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, the first of which is longer than the other two. The dactyl is said to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Dionysius <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, who delivered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a>, before <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. The Greeks call it *τριπάτης*. The dactyl and spondee are the most considerable of the poetical feet; as being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> used in heroic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, &c. These two are of equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but not equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. The spondee has an even, strong, and steady pace, like a trot; the dactyl resembles the nimble strokes of a gallop.

DACTYLI IDEI

Pages 58-58

the Fingers of Mount Ida. Concerning these, Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> give very different accounts. The Cretans paid divine worship to them, as those who had nursed and brought up the god <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; whence it appears that they were the same as the Corybantes and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURETES">Curetes</a>. Nevertheless Strabo makes them different; and says, that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> was, that "the Curetes and Corybantes were descended from the Dactyli Idei; that there were originally an hundred men in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, who were called Dactyli Idei; from whom sprang <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> Curetes, and each of these nine produced ten men, as many as the fingers of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and that this gave the name to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of the Dactyli Idei." He relates another <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, which is, that there were but five Dactyli Idei; who, according to Sophocles, were the inventors of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>: that these five brothers had five <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, and that from this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> they took the name of Fingers of Mount Ida, because they were in number ten; and that they worked at the foot of this mountain. Diodorus Siculus reports the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> a little differently. He says, "the first inhabitants of the island of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> were the Dactyli Idei, who had their residence on Mount Ida; that some said they were an hundred; others only five in number, equal to the fingers of a man's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, whence they had the name of Dactyli: that they were magicians, and addicted to mystical ceremonies: that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a> was their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, and carried their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>: that the Dactyli invented the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of iron and fire, and that they had been recompensed with divine honours." <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a> the grammarian says, the Dactyli Idei were priests of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Cybele: called *Idai*, because that goddess was chiefly worshipped on Mount Ida in Phrygia; and *Dactyli*, because that, to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> from hearing the cries of infant Jupiter, whom Cybele had committed to their custody, they used to sing certain verses of their own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, in the Dactylic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. See Curetes and Corybantes.

DACTYLIC

Pages 58-58

something that has a relation to dactyls. Anciently there were dactylic as well as spondaic flutes, *tibiae dactylicae*. The dactylic flutes consisted of unequal intervals; as the dactylic foot does of unequal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. **DACTYLIC Verses** are hexameter verses, ending in a dactyl instead of a spondee; as spondaic verses are those which have a spondee in the fifth foot instead of a dactyl. An instance of a dactylic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> we have in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>: *Bis patriae cessidere manus; quin protinus omnia Pergerent ocellis.*—Aen. vi. 33.

DACTYLIOMANCY

Pages 58-58

(Dactyliomantia), a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> performed by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. The word is composed of the Greek *δάκτυλος*, "ring," of *ἀναγνώσεις*, "a finger," and *μαντεία*, "divination." Dactyliomancy consisted principally in holding a ring, suspended by a fine thread, over a round <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, on the edge whereof were made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> marks with the twenty-four letters of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. The ring in shaking, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vibrating over the table, stopped over certain of the letters, which, being joined together, composed the answer required. But the operation was preceded and accompanied by several superstitious ceremonies: for first the ring was to be consecrated with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of mystery; the person who held it was to be clad in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> garments to the very shoes; his head was to be shaved all round; and in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> he was to hold vervain. And before he proceeded, the gods were first to be appeased by a formulary of prayers, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a> gives the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in his 29th book.

DACTYLIS

Pages 58-58

Cock's-foot Grass, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Gramino. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DACTYLUS

Pages 58-58

a name given by Pliny to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Pholas. See Pholas, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DADUCHI

Pages 58-63

in antiquity, priests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>. That <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> having lost her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Proserpine, say mythologists, began to make search for her at the beginning of the night. In order to do this in the dark, she lighted a torch and thus set forth on her travels throughout the world: for which reason it is that she is always seen represented with a lighted torch in her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. On this account, and in commemoration of this pretended exploit, it became a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the priests, at the feasts and sacrifices of this goddess, to run about in the temple, with torches after this manner; one of them took a lighted torch from off the altar, and holding it with his hand, ran with it to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the temple where he gave it to another, saying to him, *Tibi tradis*: this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> ran after the like manner to another part of the temple, and gave it to the third, and so of the rest. From this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> the priests became denominated daduchi, *dadux*. Dædali, q. d., "torch-bearers;" from ἀνά, "an unctuous resinous wood, as pine, fir," &c., whereof the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> made torches; and ἔχω, "I have, I hold."—The Athenians also gave the name Dædalus to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. Dædala, a mountain and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lycia, where Dædalus was buried, according to Pliny.—Also two festivals in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, so called; one of them observed at Alalcomenae by the Plateans in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, where they exposed in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> pieces of boiled <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and carefully observed whither the crows that came to prey upon them directed their flight. All the trees upon which any of these birds alighted were immediately cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and with them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> were made, called Dædalia, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Dædalus. The other festival was of a more solemn kind. It was celebrated every 60 years by all the cities of Boeotia, as a compensation for the intermission of the smaller festivals, for that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years, during the exile of the Plateans. Fourteen of the statues called Dædalia were distributed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> among the Plateans, Lebedians, Coroneans, Orchomenians, Thessians, Thebans, Tanagraeans, and Cheronceans, because they had effected a reconciliation among the Plateans, and caused them to be recalled from exile about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that Thebes was restored by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASSANDER">Cassander</a> the son of Antipater. During this festival a woman in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a bridemaid accompanied a statue which was dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> garments, on the banks of the Eurotas. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> was attended to the top of Mount Citheron by many of the Boeotians, who had places assigned them by lot. Here an altar of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pieces of wood cemented together like <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> was erected, and upon it were thrown large quantities of combustible materials. Afterwards a bull was sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and an ox <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> heifer to Juno, by every one of the cities of Boeotia, and by the most opulent that attended. The poorer citizens offered small cattle; and all these oblations, together with the Dædalia, were thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> heap and set on fire, and totally reduced to ashes. They originated in this: When Juno, after a quarrel with Jupiter, had retired to Euboea, and refused to return to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, the god, anxious for her return, went to consult Citheron <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Platea, to find some effectual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> her obstinacy. Citheron advised him to dress a statue in women's apparel, and carry it in a chariot, and publicly to report it was Platea the daughter of Asopus, whom he was going to marry. The advice was followed; and Juno, informed of her husband's future <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, repaired in haste to meet the chariot, and was easily united to him, when she discovered the artful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to effect a reconciliation. Dædalus, an Athenian, son of Eupalamus, descended from Erichtheus king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He was the most ingenious <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and to him we are indebted for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the wedge and many other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> instruments, and the sails of ships. He made statues which moved of themselves, and seemed to be endowed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Talus his sister's son promised to be as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as himself by the ingenuity of his inventions; and therefore from envy he threw him down from a window and killed him. After the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of this youth, Dædalus, with his son <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ICARUS">Icarus</a>, fled from Athens to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> king of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> gave him a cordial reception. Dædalus made a famous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a> for Minos, and assisted Pasiphaë Danae, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> to gratify her unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for a bull. For this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> Dædalus incurred the displeasure of Minos, who ordered him to be confined in the labyrinth which he had constructed. Here he made himself wings with feathers and wax, and carefully fitted them to his body and that of his son, who was the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of his confinement. They took their flight in the air from Crete; but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> melted the wax on the wings of Icarus, whose flight was too high, and he fell into that part of the ocean which from him has been called the Icarian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The father, by a proper management of his wings, alighted at Cumae, where he built a temple to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and thence directed his course to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where he was kindly received by Cocalus, who reigned over part of the country. He left many monuments of his ingenuity in Sicily, which still existed in the age of Diodorus Siculus. He was despatched by Cocalus, who was afraid of the power of Minos, who had declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against him because he had given an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to Dædalus. The flight of Dædalus from Crete with wings is explained by observing that he was the inventor of sails, which in his age might <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at a distance for wings. He lived 1400 years before the Christian era. There were two statuaries of the same name; one of Sicyon, son of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>; the other a native of Bithynia. Dæmon, (Δαιμων,) a name given by the ancients to certain spirits or genii, which they say appeared to men, either to do them <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> or to hurt them. The Greek word Δαιμων is derived (according to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, in his Cratylus, p. 398, ed. Serrani, vol. i.) from Δαίμων, "knowing or intelligent;" but according to others from Δαίμων, "to distribute," (see the Scholiast on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, II. i. ver. 222.) Either of these derivations agrees with the office ascribed to demons by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heathens, as the spirit intrusted with the inspection and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of mankind. For, according to the philosophers, demons held a middle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> between the celestial gods, and men on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and carried on all intercourse between them; conveying the addresses of men to the gods, and the divine benefits to men. It was the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of many, that the celestial divinities did not themselves interpose in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs, but committed the entire administration of the government of this lower world to these subaltern deities: Neque enim pro majestate deum celestium fuerit, haec curare; (Apuleius de dio Socratis, p. 677.) Cuncta celestium voluntate, numine, et authore, sed daemonum obsequio, et <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> et ministerio fieri arbitramur est; (Id. p. 675.) Hence they became the objects of divine worship. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> idols are nothing," says Celsus (apud <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>. cont. Cel. lib. viii. p. 393.) "what harm can there be to join in the public festivals? If they are demons, then it is certain that they are gods, in whom we are to confide, and to whom we should offer sacrifices and prayers to render them propitious." Several of the heathen philosophers held that there were different kinds of demons; that some of them were spiritual substances of a more noble origin than the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, and that others had once been men. But those demons who were the more immediate objects of the established worship among the ancient nations nations were human spirits, such as were believed to become demons or deities after their departure from their bodies. Plutarch teaches (Vit. Romul. p. 36. ed. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>), "that according to a divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the souls of virtuous men are advanced to the rank of demons; and that from demons, if they are properly purified, they are exalted into gods, not by any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, but according to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> reason." The same author says in another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> (de Is. et Osir. p. 361.), "that Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> were, for their virtue, changed from good demons into gods, as were Hercules and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> afterwards, receiving the united honours both of gods and demons." <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and other poets, who have recorded the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> or traditions on which the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and worship were founded, assert, that the men of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> age, who were supposed to be very good, became demons after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and dispensers of good things to mankind. Though demon is often used in a general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a deity, and is accordingly applied to fate or fortune, or whatever else was regarded as a god; yet those demons who were the more immediate objects of divine worship amongst the heathens, were human spirits; as is shown in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>, chap. iii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 2. The word demon is used indifferently in a good and a bad sense. In the former sense, it was very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used among the ancient heathens. "We must not (says <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>) think any demon to be evil, hurtful to a good life, but every god to be good." Nevertheless, those are certainly mistaken who affirm, that demon never signifies an evil being till after the times of Christ. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> held demons who sent diseases to men and cattle (Diog. Laert. Vit. Pitthagor. p. 574. ed. Amstel.) Zaleucus, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his Laws (apud Stoerum, Serm. 42.) supposes that an evil demon might be present with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, to influence him to injustice. The demons of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEDOCLES">Empedocles</a> were evil spirits, and exiles from heaven; (Plutarch Mæt. de usu daemoniorum). And in this life of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> (p. 938.), he says, "It was the opinion of the ancients that evil and mischievous demons, out of envy and hatred to good men, oppose whatever they do." Scarce did any opinion more generally prevail in ancient times than this, viz. that as the departed souls of good men became good demons, so the departed souls of bad men became evil demons. It has been generally thought, that by demons we are to understand devils, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> version of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Others think the word is in that version certainly applied to the ghosts of such dead men as the heathens deified, in Deut. xxxii. 17. Ps. civ. 37. That demon often bears the same meaning in the New Testament, and particularly in Acts xvii. 18. 1 Cor. x. 21. 1 Tim. iv. 1. Rev. ix. 13, is shown at large by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Mede (Works, p. 623, et seq.). That the word is applied always to human spirits in the New Testament, Mr Farmer has attempted to show in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on daemoniacs, p. 208, et seq. As to the meaning of the word demon in the fathers of the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, it is used by them in the same sense as it was by the heathen philosophers, especially the latter Platonists; that is, sometimes for departed human spirits, and at other times for such spirits as had never inhabited human bodies. In the fathers, indeed, the word is more commonly taken in an evil sense, than in the ancient philosophers. Besides the two forementioned kinds of demons, the fathers, as well as the ancient philosophers, held a third, viz. such as sprang from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of superior beings with the daughters of men. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the fathers, these were the worst kind of demons. Different orders of demons had different stations and employments assigned them by the ancients. Good demons were considered as the authors of good to mankind; evil demons brought innumerable evils both upon men and beasts. Amongst evil demons there was a great distinction with respect to the offices assigned them; some compelled men to wickedness, others stimulated them to madness. See Daemoniac. Much has been said concerning the daemon of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. He pretended to his friends and disciples, and even declared to the world, that a friendly spirit, whom he called his daemon, directed him how to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> on every important occasion in his life, and restrained him from imprudence of conduct. In contemplating the character of this great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, while we admire him as the noblest pattern of virtue and moral <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> that appeared in the heathen world, we are naturally led to inquire, whether what he gave out concerning his daemon were a trick of imposture, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVERIE">reverie</a> of a heated imagination, or a sober and true account of a favour which heaven deigned to confer on so extraordinary a man. To ascertain in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the object of our inquiries, is by no means so easy as the superficial thinker may be apt to imagine. When we consider the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of sentiment and simplicity of manners which Socrates displayed through the general tenor of his life, we cannot readily bring ourselves to think that he could be capable of such a trick of imposture. Nothing of the wildness of an enthusiast appears in his character; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of his pretensions, and the respect which in his conversation and conduct he uniformly testified for the ordinary duties of social life, sufficiently prove that he was free from the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> enthusiasm: we cannot infer, therefore, that, like the astronomer in Iaselas, he was deceived with respect to his daemon by an overheated imagination. It is no less difficult to believe, that God would distinguish a heathen in so eminent a manner, and yet leave him uninstructed in the principles of true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Surely, if ever scepticism be reasonable, it must be in such matters as the present. Yet, if it be still insisted, that some one of these three notions concerning the daemon of Socrates must be more probable than the others; we would rather esteem Socrates an enthusiast in this instance, than degrade him to the base character of an imposter, or suppose that a spiritual being actually revealed himself to the philosopher, and condescended to become his constant attendant and counsellor. People are often under the influence of an overheated imagination with regard to some one thing, and cool and sober as to everything else. Daemoniac (from daemon), a human being whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">Definition</a> volition and other mental faculties are overpowered and restrained, and his body possessed and actuated by some created spiritual being of superior power. Such seems to be the determinate sense of the word; It is generally agreed, that neither good nor evil spirits are known to exert such authority at present over the human race; but in the ancient heathen world, and among the Jews, particularly in the days of our Saviour, evil spirits at least are thought by many to have been more troublesome. The Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> imagined that their deities, to reveal future events, frequently entered into the prophet or prophetess who was consulted, overpowered their faculties, and uttered responses with their organs of speech. Apollo was believed to enter into the Pythoress, and to dictate the prophetic answers received by those who consulted her. Other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> besides that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> were supposed to unfold futurity by the same machinery. And in various other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> either malignant demons or benevolent deities were thought to enter into and to actuate human affairs. The Lymphatici, the Cerriti, the Larvati, of the Romans, were all of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>; and the Greeks, by the use of the word σαρκομετάσχειν, show that they referred to this cause the origin of madness. Among the ancient heathens, therefore, it appears to have been a generally received opinion, that superior beings entered occasionally into men, overpowered the faculties of their minds, and actuated their bodily organs. They might imagine that this happened in instances in which the effects were owing to the operation of different causes; but an opinion so generally prevalent had surely some plausible foundation. The Jews, too, if we may trust the sacred writings and Josephus, appear to have believed in demoniacal possession. The case of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> may be recollected as one among many in which superior created beings were believed by the Jews to exert in this manner their influence over human life. The general tenor of their history and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and their doctrines concerning good and evil spirits, prove the opinion of demoniacal possession to have been well known and generally received among them. In the days of our Saviour, it would appear that demoniacal possession was very frequent among the Jews and the neighbouring nations. Many were the evil spirits whom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> is related in the gospels to have ejected from patients that were brought unto him as possessed and tormented by those malevolent demons. His apostles too, and the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who were most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and successful in the propagation of Christianity, appear to have often exerted the miraculous powers with which they were endowed on similar occasions. The demons displayed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of knowledge and malevolence which sufficiently distinguished them from human beings: and the language in which the demoniacs are mentioned, and the actions and sentiments ascribed to them in the New Testament, show that our Saviour and his apostles did not consider the idea of demoniacal possession as being merely a vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> concerning the origin of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> or diseases produced by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes. The more enlightened cannot always avoid the use of metaphorical modes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>; which, though founded upon error, have yet been so established in language by the influence of custom, that they cannot be suddenly dismissed. When we read in the book of Joshua, that the sun on a certain occasion stood still, to allow that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> time to complete a victory; we easily find an excuse for the conduct of the sacred historian, in accommodating his narrative to the popular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the Jews concerning the relative motions of the heavenly bodies. In all similar instances, we do not complain much of the use of a single phrase, originally introduced by the prevalence of some groundless opinion, the falsity of which is well-known to the writer. But in descriptions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of facts, and in the laying down of systems of doctrine, we require different rules to be observed. Should any person, in compliance with popular opinions, talk in serious language of the existence, dispositions, declarations, and actions of a race of beings whom he knew to be absolutely fabulous, we surely could not praise him for candid integrity: we must suppose him to be either exulting in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRONY">irony</a> over the weak credulity of those around him, or taking advantage of their weakness, with the dishonest and the selfish views of an impostor. And if he himself should pretend to any connexion with this imaginary system of beings, and should claim, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his connexion with them, particular honours from his contemporaries; whatever might be the dignity of his character in all other respects, nobody could hesitate even for a moment to brand him as an impostor of the basest character. Precisely in this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> must we regard the conduct of our Saviour and his apostles, if the ideas of demoniacal possession were to be considered merely as a vulgar error. They talked and acted as if they believed that evil spirits had actually entered into those who were brought to them as possessed with devils, and as if those spirits were actually expelled by their authority out of the unhappy persons whom they had possessed. They expected, they demanded too, to have their profession and declarations believed, in consequence of their performing such mighty works, and to be honoured as having thus triumphed over the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. The reality of demoniacal possession stands upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> with the gospel system in general. Neither is there any thing absurd or unreasonable in Reasoning this doctrine. It does not appear to contradict those ableness of ideas which the general appearance of nature and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of events suggest concerning the benevolence and wisdom of the Deity, and the councils by which he regulates the affairs of the universe. We often fancy ourselves able to comprehend things to which our understanding is wholly inadequate: we persuade ourselves, at times, that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the works of the Deity must be well-known to us, and that his designs must always be such as we can fathom. We are then ready, whenever any difficulty arises to us, in considering the conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> things according to our own ideas; to deny that the Deity can possibly be the author of things which we cannot reconcile; and to assert, that he must act on every occasion in a manner consistent with our narrow views. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of reason; and it seems to have suggested the strongest objections that have been at any time urged against the reality of demoniacal possession. But the Deity may surely connect one order of his creatures with another. We perceive mutual relations and a beautiful connexion to prevail through all that part of nature which falls within the sphere of our observation. The inferior animals are connected with mankind, and subjected to their authority, not only in instances in which it is exerted for their advantage, but even where it is tyrannically abused to their destruction. Among the evils to which mankind have been subjected, why might not their being liable to demoniacal possession be one? While the Supreme Being retains the sovereignty of the universe, he may employ whatever agents he thinks proper in the execution of his purposes; he may either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> an angel or let loose a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>; as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, or communicate any particular impulse to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. All that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> makes known, all that human reason can conjecture, concerning the existence of various orders of spiritual beings, good and bad, is perfectly consistent with, and even favourable to, the doctrine of demoniacal possession. It was generally believed through the ancient heathen world; it was equally well known to the Jews, and equally respected by them; it is mentioned in the New Testament in such language, and such narratives are related concerning it, that the gospels cannot well be regarded in any other light than as pieces of imposture, and Jesus Christ must be considered as a man who dishonestly took advantage of the weakness and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of his contemporaries, if this doctrine be nothing but a vulgar error: it teaches nothing inconsistent with the general conduct of Providence; it is not the caution of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, but the pride of reason, that suggests objections against this doctrine. Those, again, who are unwilling to allow that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> or devils have ever intermeddled so much with the concerns of human life, urge a number of specious arguments in opposition to these. The Greeks and Romans of old, say they, did believe in the reality of demoniacal possession. They supposed that spiritual beings did at times enter into the sons or daughters of men, and distinguish themselves in that situation by capricious freaks, deeds of wanton mischief, or prophetic enunciations. But in the instances in which they supposed this to happen, it is evident that no such thing took place. Their accounts of the state and conduct of those persons whom they believed to be possessed in this supernatural manner, show plainly that what they ascribed to the influence of demons were merely the effects of natural diseases. Whatever they relate concerning the larvati, the cerviti, and the lymphatici, shews that these were merely people disordered in mind, in the same unfortunate situation with those madmen and idiots and melancholy persons whom we have among ourselves. Festus describes the Larvati as being furvissi et mente moti. Horace says, "Hellade percussa, Marius cum præcipit se, Cervitus fuit."
