Plato, in his Timaeus, says that the demons are like lunatics, and as staring with their eyes, foaming at the mouth, and being speechless. It appears still more evidently, that all the persons spoken of as possessed with devils in the New Testament, were either mad or epileptic, and precisely in the same condition with the madmen and epileptics of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. The Jews, among other reproaches which they threw out against our Saviour, said, "He hath a devil, and is mad: why hear ye him?" The expressions, "he hath a devil, and is mad," were certainly used on this occasion as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>. With all their virulence, they would not surely ascribe to him at once two things that were inconsistent and contradictory. Those who thought more favourably of the character of Jesus, asserted concerning his discourses, in reply to his adversaries, "These are not the words of him that hath a daemon;" meaning, no doubt, that he spoke in a more rational manner than a madman could be expected to speak. The Jews appear to have ascribed to the influence of demons, not only that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of madness in which the patient is raving and furious, but also melancholy madness. Of John, who secluded himself from intercourse with the world, and was distinguished for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> and acts of mortification, they said, "He hath a daemon." The youth, whose father applied to Jesus to free him from an evil spirit, describing his unhappy condition in these words, "Have mercy on my son, for he is lunatic and sore vexed with a daemon; for oft times he falleth into the fire, and oft into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, was plainly epileptic. Every thing indeed that is related in the New Testament concerning demoniacs, proves that they were people affected with such natural diseases as are far from being uncommon among mankind in the present age. When the symptoms of the disorders cured by our Saviour and his apostles as cases of demoniacal possession, correspond so exactly with those of diseases well known as natural in the present age, it would be absurd to impute them to a supernatural cause. It is much more consistent with common sense and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> philosophy to suppose, that our Saviour and his apostles wisely, and with that condescension to the weakness and prejudices of those with whom they conversed, which so eminently distinguished the character of the Author of our holy religion, and must always be a prominent feature in the character of the true Christian, adopted the vulgar language in speaking of those unfortunate persons who were groundlessly imagined to be possessed with demons, though they well knew the notions which had given rise to such modes of expression to be ill-founded; than to imagine that diseases, which arise at present from natural causes, were produced in days of old by the intervention of demons, or that evil spirits still continue to enter into mankind in all cases of madness, melancholy, or epilepsy. Besides, it is by no means a sufficient reason for receiving any doctrine as true, that it has been generally received through the world. Error, like an epidemic disease, is communicated from one to another. In certain circumstances, too, the influence of imagination predominates, and restrains the exertions of reason. Many false opinions have extended their influence through a very wide circle, and maintained it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. On every such occasion as the present, therefore, it becomes us to inquire, not so much how generally any opinion has been received, or how long it has prevailed, as from what causes it has originated, and on what evidence it rests. When we contemplate the frame of nature, we behold a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and beautiful simplicity prevailing through the whole: Notwithstanding its immense extent, and though it contains such numberless diversities of being; yet the simplest machine constructed by human art does not display easier simplicity, or an happier connection of parts. We may therefore venture to draw an inference, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, from what is observable of the order of nature in general to the present case. To permit evil spirits to intermeddle with the concerns of human life, would be to break through that order which the Deity appears to have established through his works; it would be to introduce a degree of confusion unworthy of the wisdom of Divine Providence. Such are the most rational arguments that have been urged on both sides in this controversy. Perhaps the demonianists have the stronger probabilities on their side; but we will not presume to take upon ourselves the office of arbitrators in the dispute. DÆMONIACS, in church history, a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>; whose distinguishing tenet is, that the devils shall be saved at the end of the world. DAFFODIL. See NARCISSUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DAGELET

Pages 63-63

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COREA">Corea</a>, discovered by La Perouse in the year 1787. It is about three leagues in circumference, and is encircled with steep rocks, excepting a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> creeks, which form convenient landing-places. The island is covered with fine trees; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the French navigator visited it, some boats were found on the stocks of a Chinese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. The workmen, who were supposed to be Corean carpenters, were employed upon them, but fled to the woods on the approach of the ships. La Perouse supposes that the island is uninhabited, and that these people go from Corea, and live there only during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> boats. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east point of this island is in N. Lat. 33° 15', E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 129° 2'. from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>.

DAGHESTAN

Pages 63-63

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, bounded by Circassia on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the east, by Chirvein a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> on the south, and by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> on the west. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Tarku and Derbent, both situated on the Caspian sea.

DAGNO

Pages 63-63

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, with a bishop's see. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the district of Ducagini, and is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Drino and Nero, near their confluence. It is 15 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCUTARI">Scutari</a>, and 15 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Alessio. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 48'. N. Lat. 42° 0'.

DAGON

Pages 63-63

the false god of Ashdod*, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as the Greeks call it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZOTUS">Azotus</a>. He is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> represented as a monster, half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and half fish; whence most learned men derive his name from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> dag, which signifies "fish." Those who make him to have been the inventor of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> corn, derive his name from the Hebrew Dagon, which signifies frumentum; whence Philo Biblius calls him Zieg Agelus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Aratrius. This deity <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to have a temple at Ashdod during all the ages of idolatry to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>; for the author of the first book of Maccabees tells us, that "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>, one of the Maccabees, having beaten the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Apollonius, Demetrius's general, they fled to Azotus, and entered into Bethdagon (the temple of their idol): but that Jonathan set fire to Azotus, and burnt the temple of Dagon and all those who had fled into it." Dagon, according to some, was the same with Jupiter, according to others <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, according to others, Venus, and according to most, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. DAHALAC is the largest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and is placed by Mr Bruce, who has given a minute <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it, between 15° 27' and 15° 54' N. Lat. It is a low, flat island, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, mixed with shells, and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> destitute of every kind of herbage, excepting a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of bent grass, which is barely sufficient to feed a few antelopes and goats. In many places the island is covered with extensive plantations of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a> trees, which rarely exceed eight feet in height, spreading wide, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> flat at top, probably from the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which blows from the sea. No <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> falls in Dahalac from the end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> to the beginning of October; but in the intermediate months there are heavy showers, during which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is collected in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> cisterns, to serve the inhabitants during the ensuing summer. Of these cisterns, which are said to be the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the Persians, or, as some suppose, of the first Ptolemies, 370 yet remain, cut out of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock. The inhabitants of Dahalac are a simple, fearful, and inoffensive people. It is the only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> where no one is furnished with arms of any kind. After the rains <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, the grass <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> up with great luxuriance, and then the goats give the inhabitants a copious supply of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, which in winter is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part of their subsistence. The poorer sort live entirely on shell and other fish. The sole employment of the inhabitants is to work the vessels which trade to the different parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. Dahalac contains 12 villages or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, each of which is surrounded with a plantation of doom trees. Of the leaves of this tree, which are of a glossy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> when dried, the inhabitants make baskets of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and neatness. This seems to be the only thing like manufacture in the island. Dahalac, as well as the other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Red sea is dependent upon Masuah. Each of the 12 villages furnishes a goat monthly to the governor, and every vessel putting in there for Masuah, pays him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of coffee, and every one from Arabia a dollar. These are his principal revenues. In the time of the Ptolemies, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> fishery in the vicinity of Dahalac flourished greatly, as well as another valuable fishery, namely that of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TORTOISES">tortoises</a>.

DAHNPEPHORIA

Pages 95-95

a festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, celebrated every ninth year by the Boeotians. It was then usual to adorn an olive bough with garlands of laurels and other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the top a brazen globe, on which were suspended smaller ones. In the middle was placed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of crowns, and a globe of inferior size, and the bottom was adorned with a saffron-coloured garment. The globe on the top represented the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Apollo. That in the middle was an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and the others of the stars. The crowns, which were 65 in number, represented the sun's annual revolution. This bough was carried in solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> by a beautiful youth of an illustrious family, and whose parents were both living. The youth was dressed in rich garments which reached to the ground, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hung loose and dishevelled, his head was covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and he wore on his feet shoes called <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPHICRATES">Iphicrates</a>, from Iphicrates an Athenian, who first invented them. He was called Δανπεφορος, laurel-bearer; and at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he executed the office of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Apollo. He was preceded by one of his nearest relations, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a rod adorned with garlands, and behind him followed a train of virgins with branches in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. In this order the procession advanced as far as the temple of Apollo, surnamed Ismenius, where supplicatory hymns were sung to the god. This festival owes its origin to the following circumstance.—When an oracle advised the Ætolians who inhabited Arne and the adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to abandon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> possessions, and go in quest of a settlement, they invaded the Theban territories, which at that time were pillaged by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Pelasgians. As the celebration of Apollo's festival was near, both nations, who religiously observed it, laid aside all hostilities, and according to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> laurel boughs from Mount <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, and in the neighbourhood of the river Melas, and walked in procession in honour of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> that this solemnity was observed, Polematas the general of the Boeotian army <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a youth in a dream, that presented him with a complete <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of armour, and commanded the Boeotians to offer solemn prayers to Apollo, and walk in procession with laurel boughs in their hands every ninth year. Three days after this dream, the Boeotian general made a sally, and cut off the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the besiegers, who were compelled by this blow to relinquish their enterprise. Polematas immediately instituted a nonennial festival to the god, who seemed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the Boeotians.

DAHOMY

Pages 63-64
or DAUMA, a powerful kingdom of Africa, on the coast of Guinea. Aboméy, the modern capital, lies in N. Lat. 7° 59'. This kingdom occurs in its true position, in the maps of Sanson, Plancius, and Mercator, where Dawhee, the ancient capital, is denominated Daumia. In 1700, it was erased from the maps of Africa, and the existence of the ancient nation of Dauma denied, till 1727, when it emerged from obscurity, and became known by the conquests of the maritime states of Whidah and Ardra. Between Dahomy, Dauma and Gago the lake Sigesmes, or Guarda, (which extends about 100 leagues from east to west, and 50 from north to south, which lies about 370 miles N. N. E. of Arada, and is represented as the source of various large rivers, which descend into the gulf of Guinea) is placed by Barbot and Snellgrave, who derived their authority from the native traders. It neither occurs in Edrisi nor Leo, though it is found in the maps to Ruscelli's edition of Ptolemy, in 1561. Dahomy is a fertile cultivated country; the soil is a deep rich reddish clay, intermixed with sand, scarcely containing a stone of the size of an egg in the whole country. It is extremely productive of maize, millet, beans, yams, potatoes, cassava, plantain, and the banana; indigo, cotton, tobacco, palm-oil, and sugar, are raised, as well as a species of black pepper. Bread, and a species of liquor, or rather diluted gruel, are formed of the lotus-berry. Animals, both wild and tame, are numerous, and the lakes abound in fish. The maritime districts of Whidah and Ardra, before they were ruined by the Dahomans, were highly cultivated and beautiful. The character of the Daumanese, or Dahomans, is original and strongly marked; they have retained peculiar manners, and have had little intercourse with either Europeans or Moors. They exhibit the germ of peculiar institutions and modifications of manners, that have appeared incredible to modern nations, when they perused the ancient records of the Egyptians, Hindus, and Lacedemonians. Like the Lacedemonians, they display a singular mixture of ferocity and politeness, of generosity and cruelty. Their conduct towards strangers is hospitable, without any mixture of rudeness or insult. Their appearance is manly, and their persons strong and active; and though they are less addicted to the practice of tattooing than their neighbours, their countenance rather displays ferocity than courage. Their government is the purest despotism; every subject is a slave; and every slave implicitly admits the right of the sovereign to dispose of his property and of his person. "I think of my king," said a Dahoman to Mr Norris, "and then I dare engage five of the enemy myself. My head belongs to the king, not to myself: if he pleases to send for it, I am ready to resign it; or if it be shot through in battle, I am satisfied—if it be in his service." This attachment continues unshaken, even when their nearest relations become the victims of the avarice or caprice of the king, and his enormities are always attributed to their own indiscretions. With this devoted spirit, the Dahoman rushes fearless into battle, and fights as long as he can wield his sabre. The modern history of the Dahomans realizes all that history has recorded of ancient Lacedemon, and of those Lacedemonians of the north, the inhabitants of Jomsburgh, who were forbidden to mention the name of Feur, even in the most imminent dangers, and who proudly declared that they would fight their enemies, though they were stronger than the gods. Saxo relates, that when Frotho, king of Denmark, was taken prisoner in battle, he obstinately refused to accept of life, declaring, that the restoration of his kingdom and treasures could never restore his honour, but that future ages would always say, Frotho has been taken by his enemy. The palace of the king of Dahomy is an extensive building of bamboo and mud-walled huts, surrounded by a mud-wall about 20 feet high, enclosing a quadrangular space of about a mile square. The entrance to the king's apartment is paved with human skulls, the lateral walls adorned with human jaw-bones, with a few bloody heads intermixed at intervals. The whole building resembles a number of farm-yards, with long thatched barns and sheds for cattle, intersected with low mud-walls. On the thatched roofs, numerous human skulls are ranged at intervals, on small wooden stakes. In allusion to these, when the king issues orders for war, he only announces to his general, that his house wants thatch. In this palace, or large house, as it is termed by the Dahomans, above 3000 females are commonly immured, and about 500 are appropriated by each of the principal officers. From this injurious and detestable practice, originate many flagrant abuses; the population is diminished, the sources of private happiness destroyed, and the best feelings of human nature being outraged, the energies of passion are converted into bitterness and ferocity. The religion of Dahomy is vague and uncertain in its principles, and rather consists in the performance of some traditional ceremonies, than in any fixed system of belief, or of moral conduct. They believe more firmly in their amulets and fetiches, than in the deity; their national fetich is the Tiger; and their habitations are decorated with ugly images, tinged with blood, stuck with feathers, besmeared with palm-oil, and bedaubed with eggs. As their ideas of deity do not coincide with those of Europeans, they imagine that their tutelary gods are different. "Perhaps," said a Dahoman chief to Snellgrave, "that god may be yours, who has communicated so many extraordinary things to white men; but as that god has not been pleased to make himself known to us, we must be satisfied with this we worship." The Dahomans manufacture and dye cotton-cloth, and form a species of cloth of palm-leaves. They are tolerably skilful in working in metals. The bards, who celebrate the exploits of the king and his generals, are likewise the historians of the country.

DAILLE

Pages 64-64

John, a Protestant minister near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, was one of the most learned divines of the 17th century, and was the most esteemed by the Catholics of all the controversial writers among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to two of the grandsons of the illustrious M. Du Plessis Morain. M. Daille having lived 14 years with so excellent a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with his two pupils; one of them died abroad; with the other he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and England, and returned in 1621. He was received minister in 1623, and first exercised his office in the family of M. Du Plessis Morain; but this did not last <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, for that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> died soon after. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> employed M. Daille the following year. In 1625 he was appointed minister of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>, and in 1626 removed to Paris. He spent all the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of this last church, and composed several works. His first piece was his masterpiece, and an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">Use</a> of the Fathers, printed 1631. It is a strong chain of reasoning, which forms a moral demonstration against those who would have <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> disputes decid-

DAIRY

Pages 65-65

in rural affairs, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> appropriated for the management of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and the making of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, cheese, &c. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The dairy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> should always be kept in the neatest order, and so situated as that the windows <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lattices never <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> the south, south-east, or south-west. Lattices are also to be preferred to windows, as they admit a more free circulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> than glazed lights possibly can do. It has been objected, that they admit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> air in winter and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; but the remedy is easily obtained, by making a frame the size of or somewhat larger than the lattice, and constructing it so as to slide backward and forward at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Packthread strained across this frame, and oiled <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> pasted thereon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and keep out the sun and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. It is hardly possible in the summer to keep a dairy-house too cool; on which account none should be situated far from a good <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> or current of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They should be neatly paved either with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> brick or smooth hard <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and laid with a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, so that no water may lodge. This pavement should be well washed in the summer every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and all the utensils belonging to the dairy should be kept perfectly clean. Nor should we ever suffer the churns to be scalded in the dairy, as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> that arises from hot water will injure the milk. Nor should cheese be kept therein, nor rennet for making cheese, nor a cheese-press be fixed in a dairy, as the whey and curd will diffuse their acidity throughout the room. The proper receptacles for milk are earthen pans, or wooden vats or trundlers; but none of these should be lined with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, as that mineral certainly contains a poisonous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and may in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> affect the milk: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> people are so obstinate as to persist in using them, they should never forget to scald them, scrub them well with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and water, and to dry them thoroughly, before they deposit the milk therein. Indeed all the utensils should be cleaned in like manner before they are used; and if after this, they in the least degree smell sour, they must undergo a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> scrubbing. See Dairy, Supplement.

DAKIR

Pages 65-65

in our statutes, is used for the twentieth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a last of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>. According to the statute of 31 Hen. III. Decompositio ponderum et mensurarum, a last of hides consists of twenty dakis, and every daki of ten hides. But by 1 Jac. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 33, one last of hides <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skins is twelve dozen. See Dicker.

DALACA

Pages 65-65

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which is said to be very fertile, populous, and remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> fishery. It is probably the same with Dahalac, Dalaca, which see.

DALBERGIA

Pages 65-65

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DALEA

Pages 65-65

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, bounded on the west by Dalecarlia, on the east by the Wermeland and the lake Wener, on the south by Gothland, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

DALEBURG

Pages 65-65

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Dalea, seated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the lake Wener, 50 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GOTTENBURG">Gottenburg</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13°. N. Lat. 59°.

DALECARLIA

Pages 65-65

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, so called from a river of the same name, on which it lies, near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. It is divided into six districts, and is about 175 miles in length and 100 in breadth. It contained 124,806 inhabitants in 1811. It is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which abound in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, some of which are of a prodigious depth. Idra is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. The inhabitants are rough, robust, and warlike: and all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> revolutions in Sweden had their rise in this province.

DALECHAMP

Pages 65-65

JAMES, a physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> in Normandy, in 1515. He was distinguished for his industry in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, as well as in other branches of literature. He wrote notes on Pliny's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, and translated Athenaeus into Latin. He added 30 plates of rare <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to the Dioscorides of Ruellius, printed in 1552. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> appeared his "Historia generalis Plantarum in xviii. libros digesta," Lugd. 1587, two vols folio. In this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is said to have been the labour of 30 years, the author proposed to include all the botanical discoveries previous to his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as well as those which he had made himself in the vicinity of Lyons and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. He also published editions of Paulus Aegineta, and Caelius Aurelianus, with notes; a work on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, and another De Peste, lib. iii. He practised physic at Lyons from 1552 to 1558, when he died, aged 75.

DALECHAMPIA

Pages 65-65

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monoecea class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricoccer. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DALEM

Pages 65-65

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district of the same name. It was taken by the French in 1672, who demolished the fortifications. It is seated on the river Bervine, five miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5°. 43'. N. Lat. 50°. 40'. D'ALEMBERT. See Alembert.

DALGARNO

Pages 65-65

GEORGE, an old and unjustly neglected Scottish writer. See Supplement.

DALKEITH

Pages 65-65

a town of Scotland, in Mid-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>, six miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2°. 22'. N. Lat. 55°. 50'. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Buccleugh, who has here a noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and extensive parks. In this house, which at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was the head <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of General Monk, the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. was planned.—The duke's eldest son has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Dalkeith. Here is a considerable corn market weekly on Thursdays. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 4799 in 1811.

DALRYMPLE

Pages 65-67

Sir <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, a Scottish lawyer and judge, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, on the 28th October new style, 1726. His father was Sir James Dalrymple, of Hailes, Bart., and his mother Lady Christian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HADDINGTON">Haddington</a>. His grandfather Sir David Dalrymple was the youngest son of the first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Stair, and is said to have been the ablest of that family, so much distinguished for ability. He was lord advocate for Scotland, in the reign of George I. and his son, Sir James, had the auditorship of the exchequer for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Sir David Dalrymple was bred at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school, where he was distinguished as a scholar, and remarkable as a virtuous and orderly youth; from thence he went to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, where he remained till after the rebellion in 1745. He was called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> at Edinburgh, 23rd February 1748; where he was much admired for the elegant propriety of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> he drew. He did not attain indeed to the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as a practising lawyer, but his character for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> knowledge and probity in the profession was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. He was appointed one of the judges of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of Session in the room of Lord Nesbit, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 6th 1776, with the warmest approbation of the public; and in May 1776, one of the lords commissioners of Justiciary, in the room of Lord Coalston, who resigned. He took his seat on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, according to the usage of the Court of Session, by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Lord Hailes, the name by which he is generally known among the learned of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. As a judge of the supreme civil and criminal courts, he acted in the view of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; from which he merited and obtained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> confidence and approbation. But he was not only conspicuous as an able and upright judge, and a sound lawyer; he was also eminent as a profound and accurate scholar; being a thorough <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of classical learning, the belles lettres, and historical antiquities, particularly of his own country, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of which he was led by his profession. Indefatigable in the prosecution of the studies he cultivated, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was sedulously devoted to the promotion of useful learning, piety, and virtue. Numerous are the works that have issued from his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, all of them distinguished by uncommon accuracy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and learning. Besides some occasional papers, both serious and humorous, of his composing, that appeared in the World; and a variety of communications, critical, and biographical, in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, and other publications of like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; he allotted some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his time to the illustration and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of primitive Christianity. In the year 1771 he composed a very learned and ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, in the disputed peirage of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a>. He was one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of the Lady <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, the daughter of the last earl; and being then a judge, the names of two eminent lawyers were annexed to it. In that case, he displayed the greatest accuracy of research, and the most profound knowledge of the antiquities and rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, in this country; which he managed with such dexterity of argument, as clearly to establish the Dalrymple <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his pupil, and to form a precedent, at the same time, for the decision of all such questions in future. In the year 1773, he published a small volume, entitled, "Remarks on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland." These appeared to be the gleanings of the historical research which he was making at that time, and discovered his lordship's turn for minute and accurate inquiry into doubtful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of history, and at the same time displayed the candour and liberality of his judgment. This publication prepared the public for the favourable reception of the Annals of Scotland, in 2 vols 4to, the first of which appeared in 1776, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1779, and fully answered the expectations which he had raised. The difficulties attending the subject, the want of candour, and the spirit of party, had hitherto prevented our having a genuine history of Scotland, in times previous to those of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; which had been lately written, in a masterly manner, by the elegant and judicious Dr Robertson. Lord Hailes carried his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the Scottish history, as far back as to the accession of Malcolm Canmore, in 1057, and his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> contains the annals of 14 princes, from Malcolm III. to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of David II. And happy it was that the affairs of Scotland attracted the talents of so able a writer, who to the learning and skill of a lawyer, joined the industry and curiosity of an antiquarian; to whom no object appears frivolous or unimportant, that serves to elucidate his subject. Lord Hailes has so well authenticated his work by references to historians of good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, or deeds and writings of undoubted authority; and has so happily cleared it from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, uncertainty, and conjecture, that every Scotsman, since its appearance, has been able to trace back, with confidence in genuine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, the history of his country, for 736 years, and may <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVERIE">reverie</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the respectable judge, who with indefatigable industry, and painful labour, has removed the rubbish under which the precious remains were concealed. Lord Hailes at first intended, as appears by an advertisement prefixed to his work, to carry <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his Annals to the accession of James I. but to the great disappointment of the public, he stopped short at the death of David II. and a very important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of our history still remains to be filled up by an able writer. Lord Hailes's Annals of Scotland, it is believed, stand unrivalled in the English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, for a purity and simplicity of style, an elegance, perspicuity, and conciseness of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>, that particularly suited the form of his work; and is entirely void of that false ornament and stately gait, which makes the works of some other writers appear in gigantic, but fictitious majesty. In 1786, Lord Hailes came forward with the excellent Dr Watson, and other writers in England, to repel Mr Gibbon's attack on Christianity, and published a 4to volume, entitled, "An Enquiry into the Secondary causes which Mr Gibbon has assigned for the rapid Progress of Christianity," in which there is a great display of literary acumen, and of zeal for the cause he espouses, without the rancour of theological controversy. This was the last work he sent from the press, except a few biographical sketches of eminent Scotchmen, designed as specimens of a Biographia Scotiae, which he justly considered as a desideratum in our literature; Dalrymple literature; and which, it is much to be regretted, the infirmities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, increasing fast upon him, did not allow him to supply; for he was admirably qualified for the undertaking, not only by his singular diligence and candour, but from the uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and accuracy of his literary and biographical knowledge: in which, it is believed, he excelled all his contemporaries. Although his lordship's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> had been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in an enfeebled state, he attended his duty on the bench till within three days of his death, which happened on the 29th of November 1792, in the 66th year of his age. His lordship was twice married. By his first wife, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, daughter of Lord Coniston; he left issue one daughter, who inherits the family estate. His second <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, of which there is issue also one daughter, was to Helen Fergusson, youngest daughter of Lord Kilkerran, who survived him. Though our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> does not encourage funeral discourses in general, because they are liable to much abuse, a very laudable endeavour was made, in these degenerate times, to render his lordship's pre-eminent talents and virtues a theme of instruction to mankind, in a sermon preached, soon after his death, in the church of Inveresk, by his learned friend, and venerable pastor, Dr Carlyle; from which we shall transcribe a summary view of his character as a judge, a scholar, a Christian, and a citizen. "His knowledge of the laws was accurate and profound, and he applied it in judgment with the most scrupulous integrity. In his proceedings in the criminal court, the satisfaction he gave to the public could not be surpassed. His abhorrence of crimes, his tenderness for the criminals, his respect for the laws, and his reverential awe of the Omniscient Judge, inspired him on some occasions, with a commanding sublimity of thought, and a feeling solemnity of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, that made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> seem <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, as the doom of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, to the criminals themselves, and raised a salutary horror of crimes in the breasts of the audience. Conscious of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and importance of the high office he held, he never departed from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a> that becomes that reverend character; which indeed it cost him no effort to support, because he acted from principle and sentiment, both public and private. Affectionate to his family and relations, simple and mild in his manners, pure and conscientious in his morals, enlightened and entertaining in his conversation; he left <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> only to regret, that, devoted as he was to more important employments, he had so little time to spare for intercourse with them. He was well known to be of high rank in the republic of letters, and his loss <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be deeply felt through many of her departments. His labours in illustration of the history of his country, and many other works of profound erudition, remain as monuments of his accurate and faithful research for materials, and his sound judgment in the selection of them. Of his unfeigned piety and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, you have very often been witnesses where we now are. I must add, however, that his attendance on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ordinances, was not merely out of respect to the laws, and for the sake of example, (motives which should never fail to have influence on persons of superior rank, for the most obvious reasons); but from principle and conviction, and the most conscientious regard to his duty: for he not only practised all the virtues and charities in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, but he demonstrated the sincerity of his zeal, by the uncommon pains he took to illustrate primitive Christianity, and by his elaborate and able defences of it against its enemies. His profound researches into history, and his thorough knowledge of the laws, made him perfectly acquainted with the progress of the constitution of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, from the first dawn of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, which precede all written records, and afterwards in the origin and establishment of parliaments, through all its vicissitudes and dangers, till at last, by the blessing of divine Providence, which brought many wonderful events to concur to the same end, it was renewed, strengthened, and finally confirmed by the Revolution. It was this goodly and venerable fabric of the British constitution, which the deceased most respectable character contemplated with admiration and delight, (of late indeed with a mixture of anxiety and fear) as the temple of piety, as the genuine source of greater <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and freedom, to a larger portion of mankind, than ever flowed from any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Ill indeed can the times bear the loss of such an affectionate patriot, and able <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the laws of his country. But we must not murmur at the will of Providence, which in its mercy may have withdrawn the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> from the evil to come. In mercy, I say, to him, whose righteous spirit was so deeply grieved, when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the wicked rage, and the people imagine a vain thing." Such is the memorial which, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of recent sorrow, followed this excellent man to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>! Beside the works already mentioned, Lord Hailes published a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of others, which consisted chiefly of re-editions and translations of old works, and editions of MS. papers.

DALTON

Pages 67-67

John, D.D. an eminent divine and poet, was the son of the Rev. Mr John Dalton, rector of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITEHAVEN">Whitehaven</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, where he was born in 1709. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and became <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governor to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Beauchamp, only son of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a>, late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Somerset; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he adapted <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>'s admirable mask of Comus to the stage, by a judicious insertion of several songs and different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> selected from other of Milton's works, as well as of several songs and other elegant additions of his own, suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and to the manner of the original author. During the run of this piece he industriously sought out a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Milton's, who was then oppressed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> and poverty; and procured her a benefit from it, the profits of which amounted to a very considerable sum. He was promoted by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to a prebend of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>; where he died on the 22d of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1763. Besides the above, he wrote a descriptive poem, addressed to two ladies at their return from viewing the coal-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> near Whitehaven; and Remarks on 12 historical designs of Raphael, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> Graecum et Egyptianum.

DAMAGE

Pages 68-68

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is generally understood of a hurt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hinderance attending a person's estate; but, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of what the jurors are to inquire of in giving verdict for the plaintiff or defendant in a civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, whether real or personal; for after giving verdict on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause, they are likewise asked their consciences touching costs and damages, which contain the hinderances that one party hath suffered from the wrong done him by the other. See Costs.

DAMAN

Pages 68-68

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of the East Indies, at the entrance into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Cambay. It is divided by the river Daman into two parts; one of which is called New Daman, and is a handsome town, well fortified, and defended by a good Portuguese garrison. The other is called Old Daman, and is very ill built. There is a harbour between the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, defended by a fort. It was taken by the Portuguese in 1535. Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is carried on here to a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, the teak forests being at no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73° N. Lat. 20° 22'.

DAMASCENUS

Pages 68-68

John, an illustrious father of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the 8th century, born at Damascus, where his father, though a Christian, enjoyed the office of counsellor of state to the Saracen caliph; to which the son succeeded. He retired afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Sabas, and spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> books of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. His works have been often printed: but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> edition in 1712, two vols folio, is esteemed the best.

DAMASCUS

Pages 68-70

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, seated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36° 40' N. Lat. 33° 20'. Some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> suppose this city to have been built by one Damascus, from whom it took its name; but the most generally received <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that it was founded by Uz the eldest son of Aram. It is certain, from Gen. xiv. 5, that it was in being in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and consequently may be looked upon as one of the most ancient cities in the world. In the time of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> it seems to have been a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; as the sacred historian tells us, that the Syrians of Damascus sent 20,000 men to the relief of Hadadezer king of Zobah. We are not informed whether at that time it was governed by kings, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> was a republic. Afterwards, however, it became a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> which proved very troublesome to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Israel, and would even have destroyed it entirely, had not the Deity miraculously interposed in its behalf. At last this monarchy was destroyed by Tiglath Pileser king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and Damascus was never afterwards governed by its own kings. From the Assyrians and Babylonians it passed to the Persians, and from them to the Greeks under Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> it belonged, with the rest of Syria, to the Seleucidae; till their empire was subdued by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, about 70 years before Christ. From them it was taken by the Saracens in 633; and it is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks.—Notwithstanding the tyranny of the Turks, Damascus is still a considerable place, and is supposed to contain 200,000 inhabitants. It is situated in a plain of so great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, that one can but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> discern the bounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It stands on the west side of the plain, about two miles from the head of the river Barady, which waters it. It is of a long, straight <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, extending about two miles in length, adorned with mosques and steeples, and encompassed with gardens computed to be full 30 miles round. The river Barady, as soon as it issues from the clefts of the Antilibanus into the plain, is divided into three streams, whereof the middlemost and biggest runs directly to Damascus, and is distributed to all the cisterns and fountains of the city. The other two seem to be <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>; and are drawn round, one to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and the other to the left, on the borders of the gardens, into which they are let by little currents, and dispersed everywhere. The houses of the city, whose streets are very narrow, are all built on the outside either with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-burnt brick or Flemish wall: and yet it is no uncommon thing to see the gates and doors adorned with marble portals, carved and inlaid with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and variety; and within these portals to find <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> courts beautified with fragrant trees and marble fountains, and compassed round with splendid apartments. In these apartments the ceilings are usually richly painted and gilded; and their duans, which are a sort of low stages seated in the pleasantest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the room, and elevated about 16 or 18 inches above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, whereon the Turks eat, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, say their prayers, &c., are floored, and adorned on the sides with variety of marble mixed in mosaic knots and mazes, spread with carpets, and furnished all round with bolsters and cushions, to the very height of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>. In this city are shown the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of John the Baptist, now converted into a famous mosque; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Ananias, which is only a small grotto or cellar, wherein is nothing remarkable; and the house of Judas with whom Paul lodged. In this last is an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, supposed to be that of Ananias; which the Turks hold in such veneration, that they keep a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> continually <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> over it. There is a castle belonging to Damascus, which is like a little town, having its own streets and houses; and in this castle a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of the famous Damascus <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> was formerly kept. The fruit-tree called the damascene, and the flower called the damask rose, were transplanted from the gardens belonging to this city; and the silks and linens known by the name of damask, were probably invented by the inhabitants. **Damascus Steel.** See Damask. **Damasia**, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Vindelicia, on the Licus. Afterwards called Augusta. Now Augsburg in Swabia, on the Lech. E. Long. 10° 50' N. Lat. 48° 20'. **Damask**, a sort of silken stuff, having some parts rising above the ground, representing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> or other figures. Damask should be of dressed silks, both in warp and woof. It has its name from its being originally brought from Damascus in Syria. There is also a stuff in France called the caffart-damask, made in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the true damask, having woof of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, thread, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, or cotton. Some have the warp of silk and the woof of thread; others are all thread or all wool. Damask is also a kind of wrought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, made in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; so called, because its large flowers resemble those of damasks. It is chiefly used for tables; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-cloth and a dozen of napkins are called a damask-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Damask is also applied to a very fine steel, in some parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, chiefly at Damascus in Syria; whence its name. It is used for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and cutlass blades, and is finely tempered. Damaskeening, or Damasking, the art or operation of beautifying <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, steel, &c., by making incisions therein, and filling them up with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver wire; chiefly used for adorning sword-blades, guards and grips, locks of pistols, &c. Damaskeening partakes of the mosaic, of engraving, and of carving: like the mosaic, it has inlaid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; like engraving, it cuts the metal, representing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> figures; and, as in chasing, gold and silver are wrought in relievo. There are two ways of damasking: the one, which is the finest, is when the metal is cut deep with proper instruments, and inlaid with gold and silver wire: the other is superficial only. Damelopre, a kind of bilander, used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> for conveying merchandise from one canal to another; being very commodious for passing under the bridges. Damianists, in church-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a branch of the ancient accephali-severitae. They agreed with the catholics in admitting the sixth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, but disowned any distinction of persons in the Godhead; and professed one single <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, incapable of any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>: yet they called God "the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost." Damien, Robert François, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSASSIN">assassin</a> by whom <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. of France was wounded in the year 1757. He was born in the suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAS">Arras</a>, in the year 1714; and seems rather to have been actuated by frenzy or insanity in the perpetration of the horrid deeds of which he was guilty, than by any of the motives to which they have been ascribed. This spirit appeared in the early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and such were the extravagance and violence of his conduct, that he was distinguished, while a boy, by the appellation of Robert the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a>. When he grew up he entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, served as a soldier at the siege of Philippsburgh, and was present at several engagements. He returned afterwards to France, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Jesuits at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He married in 1738, which rendered it necessary for him to resign this service. He was then employed in the same capacity by different masters, one of whom, it is said, he poisoned; and having robbed another, he was obliged to abscond to escape the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to his crimes. During a period of five months after the discovery of the robbery, he lurked in the neighbourhood of St Omer, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>; and was observed to express himself in an absurd and incoherent manner concerning some disputes which at this time prevailed in France. The following soliloquy is said to have been uttered by him in a small town near Ypres: "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> I return to Damien, France—Yes, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> return, I will die there, and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> shall die likewise, and you shall hear news of me." These expressions were uttered in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August 1756; and it is probable that they were regarded at the time only as the ravings of a madman. He spoke indeed in a similar strain in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following, at the house of a relation, at Falesque near Arras, saying, "That the kingdom, his wife, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, were all ruined!" It was about this time that he set out for Paris, and arrived there on the 31st of December. He was seen at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, on the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1757. To blunt his feelings, and to prepare himself for the perpetration of the horrid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, it is said that he swallowed opium for several days. But the state of mind in which Damien is described to have been for some time before, seemed to render such auxiliaries unnecessary. It was on the 5th of January, between five and six in the evening, that Louis XV. was wounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of this frantic assassin. He struck with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> the right side of the king, while he was surrounded with his courtiers, and just as he was entering his carriage to go to Trianon. Damien was instantly seized, examined at Versailles, and afterwards sent to Paris and confined in the tower of Montgommery, in an apartment prepared for him, near to that which was formerly occupied by Ravailiac the murderer of Henry IV. The great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> by the king to institute his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>; and although he was subjected to the most cruel tortures, which he bore with unexampled fortitude, no confession or acknowledgment could be extorted which afforded the smallest ground for suspicion that he had a single <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a>. When it was found that the torture failed of the purpose for which it was inflicted, he was condemned to die by the same punishment which Ravailiac suffered. The 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> following was fixed as the day of his execution. On that day he was brought to the Place de Greve, where the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> and instruments of his destruction were prepared. All these he beheld with an undismayed countenance and a tearless eye, although he must have known well that new and more dreadful tortures yet awaited him. His punishment commenced with burning his right hand; his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> was then torn with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot pincers; and the wounds were filled with melted wax, pitch, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. In attempting to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> his body, the four horses which were employed pulled in vain for 50 minutes. All their efforts seemed to be ineffectual, till the executioners cut with knives the ligaments with which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> are attached to the body. Even after the legs were cut he was still alive, and it was only after the arms were treated in the same way that he ceased to breathe, and his body was dismembered. The period of his punishment, from the time he was put upon the scaffold till his death, was not less than an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> and a half; during the greater part of it he seemed to retain his recollection; for he raised his head many times, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his eyes on his mangled and burned limbs, and on the horses which were then exerting their whole force to tear his body asunder. And even during the severest of his tortures, the firmness of his mind was so little shaken, that he affected some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of jocularity. Damiers. Thus perished this unfortunate assassin, the history of whose life, considered in itself, is scarcely worthy of a place even for the shortest sketch; and indeed we should probably not have introduced it here, were it not for the purpose of rectifying the mistaken views of some of his biographers. While we are told that he was an insane assassin, he is charged with the same degree of guilt, as if he had been all his life in full possession of every rational <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>. But the events of his life leave no doubt of his insanity; and the last horrid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> which he perpetrated strongly confirms it. He was not actuated by either public or private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>; he had no accomplices; and it does not appear that he had any purpose whatever to serve by taking away the life of the monarch, even if he had succeeded and escaped. In the midst of his most cruel tortures, he obstinately persisted that it was not his intention to kill the king. According to his own fanatical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, he wished that God would touch his heart to induce him to give peace to his kingdom. Our readers will probably anticipate us in remarking the needless excess of lingering punishment which was inflicted on the insane Damiers; and some of them will perhaps be surprised to be told that the execution was attended by some of the ladies of the court. Many of them too will naturally compare this event with what has happened more lately in our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and recollect, that a Nicholson and a Hadfield, influenced by a similar frenzy which urged them to a similar attempt, have been only doomed to perpetual confinement, not as a punishment, but merely to preclude the possibility of perpetrating such deeds; because in such a state of mind they are not recognized by our milder and more equitable laws as rational beings; and therefore they are improper objects of punishment.

DAMIETTA

Pages 70-71

a port-town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, situated on the eastern mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, four miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and 100 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 31° 49' and N. Lat. 31° 25'. The present town stands upon a different site from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Damietta, so repeatedly attacked by the European princes. The latter, according to Abulfeda, was "a town surrounded by walls, and situated at the mouth of the eastern branch of the Nile." Stephen of Byzantium informs us, that it was called Thamiatis under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Greeks of the lower empire, but that it was then very inconsiderable. It increased in importance every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in proportion as <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELUSIUM">Pelusium</a>, which was frequently plundered, lost its power. The total ruin of that ancient town occasioned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the eastern parts of the Delta to be transferred to Damietta. It was, however, no longer a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of strength, when, towards the year 238 of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, the emperors of Constantinople took possession of it a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The importance of a harbour so favourably situated opened the eyes of the caliphs. In the year 244 of the Hegira, Elmetouakkel surrounded it with strong walls.
