This obstacle did not prevent Roger <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> from taking it from the Mahometans in the year 550 of the Hegira. He did not, however, long enjoy his conquest. Salah Eddin, who about that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> mounted the throne of Egypt, expelled the Europeans from Damietta. Fifteen years after they returned to besiege it; but this able <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> baffled all their efforts. Notwithstanding their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was supported by a fleet of 1200 sail, they were obliged to make a disgraceful retreat. It was the fate of this place to be constantly besieged. In the year 615 of the Hegira, under the reign of Eladel, the crusaders attacked it with a very considerable force. They landed on the western shore of the Nile; and their first care was to surround their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> with a ditch and pallisado. The mouth of the river was defended by two towers, furnished with numerous garrisons. An enormous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chain, stretching from one side to the other, hindered the approach of vessels. The crusaders carried by storm the tower on the same side with their camp, broke the chain, and opened the entrance of the river for their fleet. Nejm Eddin, the sultan's son, who was encamped near Damietta, covered it with an army. To stop the enemies vessels he threw a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Nile. The Franks overturned it, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of choking up the mouth of the river, which he almost rendered impassable by several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> boats he sunk there. After <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> and various successes, many bloody battles, and a siege of 17 months, the Christian princes took Damietta by storm. They did not, however, long enjoy the fruit of so much blood spilt, and of an armament which had cost immense sums. Completely invested near the canal of Achmoun, by the waters of the Nile and by the Egyptian army, they purchased their lives and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> by the sacrifice of their conquest. One-and-thirty years after this defeat St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> carried Damietta without striking a stroke. The Arabs, however, soon recovered it; but tired of keeping a place which continually drew upon them the most warlike nations of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, they totally destroyed it, and rebuilt it further up in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Damietta, first called Menchic, as Abulfeda tells us, has preserved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of its origin in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> still called by that name. Writers in general have confounded these two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, ascribing to the one the attributes of the other. The modern Damietta is rounded in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Nile, two leagues and a half from the mouth of it. The eye, placed at one of the extremities of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, takes in its whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Savary reckoned it to contain 80,000 souls, others reduce it to 40,000. It has several squares, the most considerable of which has retained the name of Menchic. Spacious okals <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> khans, collecting under their porticoes the stuffs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the silks of Mount Lebanon, sal ammoniac, and pyramids of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, proclaim that it is a commercial town. The houses, those in particular which are on the banks of the river, are very lofty. They have in general handsome saloons built on the top of their terraces, which are cheerful belvederes, open to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, where the Turk, effeminately reclining on a sofa, passes his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in smoking, in looking on the sea, which bounds the horizon on one side, on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lake that extends itself on the other, and on the Nile, which, running between them, traverses a rich country. Several large mosques, adorned with lofty minarets, are dispersed over the town. The public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, lined with marble, are distributed in the same manner as those of Grand Cairo. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> you are served with is clean, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> very pure. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and the treatment in them, so far from injuring the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, serve to strengthen, may even to improve it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> used with moderation. Damietta. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, founded on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, is general in Egypt. The port of Damietta is continually filled with a multitude of boats and small vessels. Those called sekhern serve to convey the merchandise on board the ships in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and to unload them; the others carry on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a>-trade. This town carries on a great trade with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, with Cyprus, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>. The rice called mezclouni, of the finest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> there is in Egypt, is cultivated in the neighbouring plains. The exports of it amount annually to about six millions of livres. The other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the produce of the country are linens, sal ammoniac, corn, &c. A ruinous policy for the country prohibits the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of this last article; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> is evaded, and it passes under the name of rice. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> and Damascus, settled in this town, have for several ages carried on its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> commerce. Turkish indolence, content with extorting from them from time to time, suffers them to become rich. The exportation of rice to foreign countries is prohibited; but by means of some douceurs to the customhouse-officers, the people of Provence load annually several ships with it. The Bogazz preventing them from entering the Nile, their cargoes are conveyed on board by the boats of the country. This inconvenience is the source of endless vexation and abuse. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, which is loaded in the evening with rice of the first quality, is frequently not that which arrives at the ship; an inferior quality is substituted for it during the night. The Marseilles captains, aware of these ruses, without being able to prevent them, endeavour to play off trick against trick, so that this commerce has become a general <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of knavery. But the badness of the port is still more detrimental to Damietta. The road where the vessels <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> being exposed to every wind, the slightest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">gale</a> obliges the captains to cut their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> and take shelter at Cyprus, or to stand off to sea. It would be easy, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> a canal only of half a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, to open a passage for ships into the Nile, where there is deep water. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which might be executed at very little expense, would render Damietta a noble harbour; but despotism, insensible to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the people, is always surrounded by destruction in its progress, and wants both the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> and the power to create. The tongue of land on which Damietta is situated, straitened on one side by the river, and on the other by the western extremity of Lake Menzaleh, is only from two to six miles wide from east to west. It is intersected by innumerable rivulets in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, which render it the most fertile spot in Egypt. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> there produces, communibus annis, 80 bushels of rice for one. The other produce is in the same proportion. It is there that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, lavishing profusely her pomp and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, presents <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and harvests, at every season of the year. Winter never deprives it of these advantages; its beauties are never impaired by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Destructive heats, as well as chilling colds, are equally unknown in that happy spot. The thermometer varies only from 9 to 24 degrees above the freezing point. Damietta is indebted for this charming temperature to the immense <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water with which it is surrounded. The verdure is nowhere so fresh; the trees are nowhere covered with such quantities of fruit. The rivulets around the Damietta fields of rice are lined with several kinds of reeds, some of which rise to a great height. The reed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALAMUS">calamus</a> is here found in abundance, which is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> by the orientals. Its slender stalks bear long narrow leaves, which hang gracefully, and spreading branches covered with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flowers. Here also are to be seen forests of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPYRUS">papyrus</a>, of which the ancient Egyptians made their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. Strabo, who calls it biblins, gives an accurate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. It is here also that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTUS">lotus</a>, of which the Arabs have preserved the primitive name of nuphar, exalts its lofty stalk above the waters. Its large calyx blows either of an azure blue or of a brilliant white, and it appears with the majesty of the king of the aquatic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The marshes and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> in the interior parts of the country are filled with this superb flower, which diffuses a most agreeable odour. There are a great many villages around Damietta, in most of which are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> where the most beautiful linens of the country are fabricated. The finest napkins in particular are made there, fringed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. You are served at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with them, but especially on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a> visits, when the slave presents you with one to wipe your mouth with, after you have drank your sherbet, or eaten the sweetmeats, which are carried round on a silver plate to all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. These small towns, generally surrounded with little woods, or trees promiscuously planted, form a whimsical and picturesque assemblage. By the side of the sycomore and the melancholy tamarind, one sees the elegant cassia-tree, with its clusters of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flowers, like those of the cytisus. The top of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>-tree, loaded with enormous bunches, rises above the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. The cassia, with its sweet-scented flower, grows under its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and lemon trees cover the labourer's cabin with their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> fruit. The banana tree with its long leaves, the pomegranate with its scarlet flower, and the fig-tree with its sugary fruit, throw a vast variety into these landscapes.

DAMNII

Pages 71-71

anciently a people of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; situated between the Selgovae to the south and the Caledonii to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Now Clydesdale. DAMNONII. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANMONII">Danmonii</a>.

DAMOCLES

Pages 71-71

one of the flatterers of Dionysius the Elder of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. He admired the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>'s wealth, and pronounced him the happiest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Dionysius prevailed upon him to undertake for a while the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of royalty, and be convinced of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> which a sovereign enjoyed. Damocles ascended the throne, and while he gazed upon the wealth and splendour that surrounded him, he perceived a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> hanging over his head by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. This so terrified him that all his imaginary felicity vanished at once, and he begged Dionysius to remove him from a situation which exposed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to such fears and dangers.

DAMON

Pages 71-71

the name of several illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; particularly of a Pythagorean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> very intimate with Pythias. When he had been condemned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by Dionysius, he obtained from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> leave to go and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> affairs, on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of returning at a stated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of execution. Pythias pledged himself to undergo the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> which was to be inflicted on Damon, should he not return in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and he consequently delivered himself in

DAMPIER

Pages 71-73

WILLIAM, an English navigator, was born at East Coker in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, about the year 1652. His parents died while he was young, and having thus become an orphan, he was removed from the Latin school, and placed with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a ship at Weymouth. In this ship he made a voyage to Newfoundland; but, on his return, he left his master, with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, as he himself observes, of never again <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> himself to the pinching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of that northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. As the acquisition of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> was ever his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> object, he engaged himself as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sailor in a voyage to the East Indies. He served in the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> under Sir Edward Sprague, and was present at two engagements. The declining state of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> would not permit him to remain on board the fleet; he therefore came on shore, and removed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where he remained some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The year following he accepted an offer of employment in Jamaica as an under manager of an estate; but he only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a short time in that situation; after which he engaged in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> trader, and thus acquired an accurate knowledge of all the ports and bays of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Soon after he entered on board a vessel bound to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPEACHY">Campeachy</a>, and returning a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time to the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, he remained with the log-wood-cutters, and engaged himself as a common workman. During his stay in this country he collected the materials for the minute and interesting account which he has given of the laborious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of these people, as well as of the geographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the tract which they occupy. Satisfied with the knowledge which he had obtained of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the trade and country, he returned to Jamaica, and from thence to England, where he arrived in 1678. About the beginning of the year following he went out to Jamaica as a passenger, with the intention of revisiting the bay of Campeachy; but he was persuaded to associate himself with a body of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>, as they were called, who were then lying in several vessels in a bay of that island. These people who were called privateers, were pirates, who, having no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> whatever from any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, undertook a predatory warfare on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and settlements of the Spaniards. This body of plunderers was composed of English, Dutch, and French. In this expedition Dampier crossed the isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a> with his associates, and spent the year 1680 on the Peruvian coast, and was occasionally successful in plundering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The following year, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a dissension which arose among them, Dampier, and the minority with whom he had joined, recrossed the isthmus, and entered with another fleet of privateers, which was then stationed on the Spanish main; and, having spent another year among the West <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, he, with some others, proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> in a single ship to dispose of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> goods. Here he remained for a year; and afterwards engaged with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, who, with about 70 men, undertook an expedition against the Spaniards in the South seas. They sailed in 1683 in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August, touched at the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and then proceeded round <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. Having fallen in with a ship from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, which had sailed on a similar expedition, they joined <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and, having touched at the island of Juan Fernandez, they made the coast of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, cruising along <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. They took some prizes, and with them they proceeded to the Mexican coast, which they fell in with near Cape <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANCO">Blanco</a>. While they lay here Captain Cook died, and the command devolved on Captain Davis. Having separated from the London ship, they were joined by another commanded by Captain Swan. An attempt to plunder the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUAYAQUIL">Guayaquil</a> was unsuccessful, but at the mouth of the river they took some vessels which had about 1000 slaves on board. With these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> Dampier proposed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in the neighbourhood of Santa <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> on the isthmus of Darien, from which the Spaniards had been driven away by some privateers. But this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was not attempted. The next object of plunder was the Spanish fleet having on board the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of the Peruvian mines; but the English being ill supported by some French ships which had joined them, the fleet, after a running fight, got safe into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>. The English ships afterwards cruising along the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, landed, took the town of Puebla Nova, and burnt two others. Dampier leaving Davis, went on board of Swan's ship, and proceeded with him along the northern parts of Mexico, as far as the southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CALIFORNIA">California</a>. During this expedition they frequently landed for the purpose of plunder, but particularly when they were in want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Returning from the plunder of one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, 50 of the party were killed by the Spaniards. This disaster so discouraged them that they relinquished all farther attempts on these coasts. Swan then proposed to run across the Pacific ocean, and return by the East Indies; and in hopes of a successful cruise off the Manillas the crew were persuaded, with a very slender provision, to risk this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> passage. On the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1686, they took their departure from Cape Corrientes, and on the 52d day reached <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUAM">Guam</a>, one of the Ladrones islands. About this time the crew talked of killing and eating Swan and the officers, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> their stock of provision should be exhausted before it could be supplied. From Guam they proceeded to Mindanao. While the ship lay here a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> arose among the crew, and the majority carried her off. Swan and some of his people being left on the island. Among the former was Dampier, although it is said that he had no concern in the mutiny. After cruising some time off <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a>, and having careened their vessel at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLO">Polo</a> Condore, in 1687 they were driven to the Chinese coast, made the circuit of Luzonia and Mindanao, passed through the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of Spice islands, and reached the coast of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in the beginning of 1688. They left this in March, and having passed along the west coast of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, they arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOBAR_ISLANDS">Nicobar islands</a>, where Dampier, at his own request, and two other Englishmen, a Portuguese, and some Malays, were set on shore. Dampier's object was to establish a trade in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>. Attempting to navigate a canoe to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACHEEN">Acheen</a> in Sumatra, they were overtaken by a severe storm, in which they experienced great hardships. Dampier. They at last reached Sumatra; but the fatigues and distress of the voyage proved fatal to several of them, who were carried off by a fever. Dampier himself was scarcely recovered at the end of a twelvemonth. After making several voyages to different places of the East Indies, he acted for some time as gunner at the English fort of Bengoolen. In 1697, wishing to revisit his native country, he embarked on board a ship for England, where he arrived in September. At this time he brought with him a native of Meangis, one of the Spice islands, who was supposed to be the son of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, and after being exhibited as a sight, died of the smallpox at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. It is not known in what manner Dampier was employed for some years after this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. It appears, however, that he was at last engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He had the command of the Roebuck, a sloop of 12 guns and 50 men. This vessel, it is supposed, was fitted out for some voyage of discovery, for she had 20 months provisions on board. He sailed from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in 1699, touched at the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, and then ran across to the coast of New Holland, and arrived there on the 1st of August, about latitude 26°. He proceeded northwards along the coast, exploring the country in different places where he landed. To procure refreshments he found it necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his course towards Timor; and from this he sailed to the coast of New Guinea, where he arrived on the 3rd of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. By sailing along to its easternmost extremity, he discovered that it was terminated by an island, which he circumnavigated, and named <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NEW_BRITAIN">New Britain</a>. Here it would appear from his own journal that he encountered considerable difficulties from the small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his men, and their eager desire to hasten home. On account of these difficulties he was prevented from prosecuting his discoveries. In May he returned to Timor, and from thence proceeded homeward by Batavia and the Cape of Good Hope. In February 1701 he arrived off the island of Ascension, when the vessel sprung a leak and foundered; and it was with much difficulty that the crew reached the island. They remained at Ascension till they were taken away by an East India ship, and conveyed to England. This closes the account of Dampier's life and adventures, as it is detailed by himself. It appears, however, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the third volume, that he was preparing in 1703 for another voyage. It is mentioned also in Woodes Rogers' Voyage round the World, that Dampier had the command of a ship in the South seas about the year 1705, along with Captain Stradling, whose vessel foundered at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Dampier accompanied Woodes Rogers in his voyage round the world, in the years 1708, 1709, 1710, and 1711; but only in the capacity of pilot, which is supposed to be owing to something faulty in his conduct. During this expedition Guayaquil was taken, and Dampier had the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. Nothing farther is known of the life of Dampier; and we are equally ignorant of the place and time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The works of Dampier are well known, and have been often reprinted. They consist of: 1. A Voyage round the world, 3 vols octavo. 2. A Supplement to it, describing the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TONQUIN">Tonquin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, &c. 3. Two Voyages to Campeachy. 4. A Course of Trade-winds, Seasons, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">Tides</a>, &c. in the Torrid Zone. 5. A Voyage to New Holland. His observations are curious and important, and conveyed in a plain manly style. His nautical remarks discover a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of professional knowledge. His knowledge in natural history is not scientific; but it appears to be accurate, and has been frequently quoted.

DAMPS

Pages 73-76

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, (from the Saxon word damp, signifying vapour <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exhalation), are certain noxious exhalations issuing from some parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and which prove almost instantly fatal to those who breathe them. These damps are chiefly observed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and coal-pits; though vapours of the same kind often issue from old lavas of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and, in those countries where volcanoes are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, it is said that they fill the houses, and destroy people suddenly without the least warning of their approach. In mines and coal-pits they are chiefly of two kinds, called by the miners and colliers the choke and fire damps; and both go under one general name of foul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The choke-damps, known in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> by the name of fixed air, or carbolic acid <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, usually infests those places which have been formerly worked, but <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> neglected, and are called by the miners wastes. No <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, however, can be reckoned safe from this kind of damps, except where there is a due circulation of air; and the procuring of this is the only proper means of preventing accidents from damps of all kinds. The choke-damp suffocates the miners suddenly, with all the appearances found in those that are suffocated by fixed air. Being heavy, it descends towards the lowest parts of the workings, and thus is dangerous to the miners, who can scarce avoid breathing it. The fire-damp, which is inflammable air, hydrogen gas, rises to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the workings, as being specifically <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; and hence, though it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> suffocate as well as the other, it seldom proves so dangerous in this way as by its inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, by which it often takes fire at the candles, and explodes with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> violence. In the Phil. Trans. No. 119, there is an account of some explosions by damps of this kind, on which we have the following observations. 1. Those who are in the place where the vapour is fired suddenly find themselves surrounded with flames, but hear little or no noise; though those who are in places adjacent, or above ground, hear a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> one. 2. Those who are surrounded by the inflamed vapour feel themselves scorched or burnt, but are not moved out of their places, though such as unhappily stand in the way of it are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> killed by the violence of the shock, and often thrown with great force out at the mouth of the pit; nor are the heaviest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> found able to resist the impetuosity of the blast. 3. No smell is perceived before the fire, but a very strong one of brimstone is afterwards perceptible. 4. The vapour lies towards the roof, and is not perceived <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the candles are held low; but when these are held higher, the damp descends like a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a>, and catches hold of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, lengthening it to two or three handfuls; and this appearance ceases when the candles are held nearer the ground. 5. The flame continues in the vault for several minutes after the crack. 6. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is blue, something inclining to green, and very bright. 7. On the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> of the vapour, vapour, a dark <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> like that proceeding from fired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> is perceived. 8. Damps are generally observed to come about the latter end of May, and to continue during the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. They return several times during the summer season, but observe no certain rule. Besides these kinds of damps, which are very common, we find others described in the Philosophical Transactions, concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which we can say nothing. Indeed the account seems somewhat suspicious. They are given by Mr Jessop, from whom we have the foregoing observations concerning the fire-damp, and who had these from the miners in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. After describing the common damp, which consists of fixed air, "They call the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort (says he) the peace-bloom damp, because, as they say, it smells like peace-bloom. They tell me it always comes in the summer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and those grooves are not free which are never troubled with any other sort of damps. I never heard that it was mortal; the scent, perhaps, freeing them from the danger of a surprise: but by reason of it many good grooves <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> idle at the best and most profitable time of the year, when the subterraneous waters are the lowest. They fancy it proceeds from the multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-trefoil <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, by them called honeysuckles, with which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> meadows in the Peake do much abound. The third is the strangest and most pestilential of any; if all be true which is said concerning it. Those who pretend to have seen it (for it is visible) describe it thus: In the highest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the roof of those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> which branch out from the main <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a>, they often see a round thing hanging, about the bigness of a foot-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, covered with a skin of the thickness and colour of a cobweb. This, they say, if it is broke by any accident, as the splinter of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or the like, disperseth itself immediately, and suffocates all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Therefore, to prevent casualties, as soon as they have espied it, they have a way, by the help of a stick and long rope, of breaking it at a distance; which done, they purify the place well with fire, before they dare enter it again. I dare not avouch the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this story in all its circumstances, because the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of it seems impossible, since they say it kills all that are likely to bear witness to the particulars: neither do I deny but such a thing may have been seen hanging on the roof, since I have heard many affirm it."—Some damps, seemingly of the same nature with those last mentioned, are noticed by the author of the Chemical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, under the word Damps. "Amongst the noxious mineral exhalations (says he), we may place those which are found in the mines of sal gem in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. These frequently appear in form of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> flocks, threads, and spiders webs. They are remarkable for their property of suddenly catching fire at the lamps of the miners with a terrible noise and explosion. They instantly kill those whom they touch. Similar vapours are found in some mines of fossil coal." With regard to the formation of damps we have as yet no certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>; nor, though the experiments of aerologists are abundantly able to show the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and manner of forming these noxious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> artificially, have they yet thrown much light on the method by which nature prepares them on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. There are two general ways in which we may suppose this to be done: one by the stagnation of atmospheric air in old waste places of mines in coal-pits, and its conversion into these mephitic exhalations; the other by their original formation from the phlogistic or other materials found in the earth, without any interference of the atmosphere. In favour of the former <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> it may be urged, that old wastes are never free from damps, especially those of the kind resembling fixed air; nor are they always deficient in the inflammable kind. The same is also true of old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, or even cellars, and in short every place where the air stagnates for any considerable time. But, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, we have many instances of fixed air coming out of the earth, and that in vast quantities, where no considerable stagnation of the atmosphere could be suspected; as for instance, in the grotto del Cani in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where a continual stream of it has issued from time immemorial. The same seems to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the tops of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountains, particularly Mont Blanc, the highest in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; on the top of which M. Saussure found the atmosphere so much impregnated with fixed air, that lime <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> exposed to it very quickly gathered a crust on its surface. Sir-William <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, in his account of the eruptions of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, informs us, that the inhabitants in the neighbourhood of that mountain are infested with a kind of pestilential vapours named by them mofetes, which issue from the old <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> thrown out by the volcano. These are of the nature of the damps in our mines or coal-pits, and issue forth in such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> as either to infect the atmosphere for a very considerable way round, or to do mischief by being carried from place to place by the atmospherical currents, which are not strong enough to dissipate them for some time. From some late accounts the samiel (or scorching winds, as they have been represented) in the eastern countries, seem to be no other than streams of fixed air of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, which exert their usual and fatal effects on those who breathe them. A strong argument in favour of this opinion is, that these winds cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> a river, it being the nature of water to absorb fixed air, and thus destroy them. Hence it is rendered probable that these mephitic vapours are often to be met with in the open atmosphere, and consequently cannot always be the effect of stagnation; nor indeed does it at all appear that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> stagnation can affect the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the atmosphere either one way or other. This fluid cannot have its properties altered but by something immersed in it upon which it can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, and by means of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> its component parts may be changed or separated. While this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is going on, there is generally, if not always, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of air, accompanied indeed frequently with an emission of some aerial fluid equal in quantity to that which is absorbed. Mr Scheele, in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Fire, has shown by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> certain substances to the action of air, both on the substances themselves and on the aerial fluid. The result of all these is no other than what we might expect from a very slow <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a>, and which perhaps may on inquiry be found to be the only way by which air can be decomposed. If the substance exposed to the air was capable of absorbing that part of the fluid which had undergone a change, there was always an evident diminution Damp nution, but not otherwise. Thus, on inclosing some caustic fixed alkali in a phial of atmospheric air, a considerable diminution took place; and the alkali, by becoming saturated with fixed air, showed that a decomposition had taken place, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> part of the air had separated from the other, attached itself to the fixed alkali, and become fixed air by uniting with a certain proportion of phlogistic <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Hence we may conceive, that in any place where the air was confined over a vast quantity of caustic alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, it would soon become unfit for the purposes of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and we might say that a damp would be formed. But this would be a damp of a very different kind from that usually met with in mines; for here the dephlogisticated part of the atmosphere being converted into fixed air, and absorbed by the salt, only the azotic gas, or, as it has been called, phlogisticated air, would remain, so that no fixed air could ever be separated from it. Let us now suppose, that instead of the alkaline salt a quantity of burning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> is confined in a place where there is not a proper circulation of air, and we shall soon see that a damp of the very same kind with that called by miners the choke-damp will be formed. But this takes place by reason of the dissipation of the charcoal by heat, and its union with the pure part of the atmosphere, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> gas, which always constitutes fixed air. In this case, however, the damp must be but of short continuance, and will soon be dissipated after the charcoal is extinguished; but if, instead of the charcoal, we substitute a large quantity of fermenting liquor, from whence the fixed air is naturally emitted, a damp will be formed much more difficult to be dissipated than the former, because it renews itself in a very short time; and, unless there is a very constant circulation of air, it will be dangerous to enter the place where it is. From the last example we may form an idea of the manner in which these damps, consisting chiefly of fixed air, are formed. We know not indeed thoroughly the nature of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>; but we are assured, that it is always accompanied by an internal heat; which, in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, is raised to the utmost height, insomuch that large quantities of moist vegetable substances, packed together, will sometimes burst out into flame. It is not, however, at all times necessary for the extrication of fixed air, that the heat should come to this extremity. The example of fermenting liquors shows, that in some cases a very moderate heat is sufficient for the purpose. Now, though the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> may seem somewhat inadequate between the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substance of the earth and a fermenting liquid, yet we know that a gentle heat constantly takes place in the bowels of the earth; and that almost all terrestrial substances will emit fixed air on being exposed to heat. It is not at all improbable, therefore, that, on the large scale of nature, the quantity of materials may compensate for the weakness of the heat, and thus occasion a constant emission of fixed air; which, though slow in comparison of what is effected in our experiments by a violent <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> heat, may yet accumulate in the narrow spaces of mines in such a manner as to be very troublesome. In volcanic countries, where the heat of the earth is much greater, the emission of fixed air is in proportion: and thus we may account for that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> stream of it, which issues from the grotto del Cani, and perhaps other places. The mofettes, which are said to proceed from old lavas, can only be accounted for by supposing the heat, which originally took place in them, to be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> renewed; or that they have been again, by some means or other, disposed to take fire as formerly: but this we offer merely as a conjecture; there not being as yet sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a> to determine anything positively upon the subject. It may be objected to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, that, if there is a continual disposition in the earth to produce fixed air, the whole surface of it must pour out such a quantity as would destroy every living creature upon it. This indeed might be granted, were the surface of the earth quite bare, and destitute of vegetation: but there is no absurdity, in supposing that the fixed air may be continually decomposed by the vegetables which grow all over the surface of the earth; and the atmosphere not only thus preserved from any taint from it, but supplied with a quantity of pure air, which it is certain vegetables give out. It is also certain, that wherever the atmosphere is suffered to be in contact with the bare surface of the ground for some time, a considerable quantity of fixed air will be produced, unless there is a constant circulation of atmospherical air to carry off the former before it has time to produce any sensible effect. Hence we may account for the damps in wells, cellars, and even in the confined places of old castles and ruinous buildings, where the air is not in contact with the surface of the ground itself, but with mere heaps of rubbish and old walls. With regard to what is called the fire-damp, the case seems to be more plain. In the Phil. Trans. No. 136, we have the following account of one of this kind, which seemed evidently to issue from the earth: "This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is upon a coal of five yards in thickness, and hath been begun upon about six or eight and thirty years ago. When it was first found, it was extremely full of water, so that it could not be wrought down to the bottom of the coal; but a witchet, or cave, was driven out of the middle of it, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, for gaining room to work, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> down the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of water that lies in the coal to the eye of the pit. In driving of which witchet, after they had gone a considerable way under ground, and were scantied of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, the fire-damps began by little and little to breed, and to appear in crevices and slits of the coal, where water had lain before the opening of the coal, with a small bluish flame, working and moving continually; but not out of its first seat, unless the workmen held their candles to it; and then being weak, the blaze of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> would drive it out with a sudden fizz away to another crevice, where it would soon after appear blazing and moving as formerly. This was the first knowledge of it in this work, which the workmen made but a sport of, and so partly neglected, till it had gotten some strength; and then upon a morning the first collier that went down, going forwards in the witchet with his candle in his hand, the damp presently darted out so violently at his candle, that it struck the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> clear down, singed all his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and clothes, and disabled him from working for a while after. Some other small warnings it gave them, inso- much that they resolved to employ a man on purpose that was more resolute than the rest, to go down a while before them every morning, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> it from place to place, and so to weaken it. His usual manner was to put on the worst rags he had, and to wet them all in water, and when he came within the danger of it, then he fell down grovelling upon his belly, and so went forward, holding in one hand a long wand or pole, at the head whereof he tied candles burning, and reached them by degrees towards it; then the damp would fly at them, and, if it missed of putting them out, would quench itself with a blast, and leave an ill-scented smoke behind. Thus they dealt with it till they had wrought the coal down to the bottom, and the water following, and not remaining as before in the body of it, among sulphureous and brassy metal that is in some veins of the coal, the fire-damp was not seen nor heard of till the latter end of the year 1675, which happened as followeth: "After long working of this coal, it was found upon the rising grounds that there lay another reach of coal at the depth of 14 yards under it, which proved to be 3½ yards thick, and something more sulphureous. This encouraged us to sink in one of the pits we had formerly used on the five-yards coal. As we sunk the lower part of it, we had many appearances of the fire-damp in the watery crevices of the rocks we sunk through, flashing and darting from side to side of the pit, and showing rainbow-like colours upon the surface of the water in the bottom; but upon drawing up of the water with buckets, which stirred the air in the pit, it would leave burning, till the colliers at work, with their breath and sweat, and the smoke of their candles, thickened the air in the pit, and then it would appear again; they lighted their candles at it sometimes when they went out; and so in this pit it did no farther harm." In another pit, however, it soon appeared, and at last produced a most terrible explosion. This was occasioned by one of the workmen going imprudently down with a lighted candle, after a cessation of work for some days, and the force exerted by it seemed equal to that of gunpowder. The formation of inflammable air in mines is to be ascribed, according to the doctrines of modern chemistry, to the decomposition of water, a process which is constantly going on in places where metallic substances are exposed to its action. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are oxidated by their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> with the oxygen, one of the component parts of water, the hydrogen, its other component parts, is set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and accumulates in those places where it is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>. A much more important consideration than the formation of damps, however, is the proper method of avoiding their pernicious effects. The inflammability of one kind affords an easy method of preventing it from accumulating, viz. by setting fire to it. This may be done with safety, unless it has been suffered to go too far before the experiment is made; for the inflammable air being much lighter than any other kind will naturally rise to the top; so that a man, lying flat on the ground to avoid the force of the explosion, and holding up a lighted candle fixed upon a pole, may at once free the mine from such a troublesome guest. But where it has been allowed to accumulate in too great quantity, so that this method cannot be used, or in the other kind, which is not inflammable, the method commonly practised is to produce a constant circulation of air as much as possible through all parts of the mine. To procure this, they make a perpendicular opening, which they call a shank, or shaft, so that the mine may have two or more openings; and thus by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of temperature between the open atmosphere and that in the mine, there is a continual draught of air through them both. This current will always be stronger in proportion to the difference between the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> atmosphere and that of the mine; and likewise in proportion to the difference between the depth of the two shafts. But as the temperature of the atmosphere is variable, it happens at certain seasons of the year, that there is not a sufficient difference between that of the atmosphere and in the mine to produce the necessary circulation. This happens principally in the spring and autumn; at which seasons it is necessary to light fires in the shafts, which are always efficacious for the purpose desired. Among the other uses to which deplogisticated air might be applied, Mr Cavallo reckons that of securing people from the dangerous effects of damps in mines, and other subterraneous places. "If a large bladder," says he, "into which a solution of lime in water is introduced, be filled with deplogisticated air, and a small wooden or glass pipe be adapted to its neck, a man may hold that pipe in his mouth, and may breathe the deplogisticated air; and thus equipped, he may enter into these subterranean places, amidst the various <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> contained in them. A large bladder of deplogisticated air will serve for above a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, which is a length of time sufficient for various purposes; besides, if longer time is required to be spent in these places, a person may have two or more bladders of deplogisticated air along with him, and may shift as soon as the air of one is contaminated. Without the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of any more complicated <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, the bladders full of deplogisticated air may be kept stopped by putting corks into the glass or wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> that are tied to their necks. This air might also be used for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVING">diving</a>-bells."

DAMSEL

Pages 76-76

from the French damoisel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> damoisette, an appellation anciently given to all young people of either <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, that were of noble or gentle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, as the sons and daughters of princes, knights, and barons; thus we read of Damsel Pepin, Damsel <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> le Gros, Damsel Richard <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. From the sons of kings this appellation first passed to those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords and barons, and at length to those of gentlemen who were not yet knights. At present damsel is applied to all maids or girls not married, provided they be not of the vulgar.

DANDINI

Pages 90-94

PIETRO, an eminent painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1646, and received his first instructions in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> from Valero Spada, who excelled in small drawings with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>. Whilst he was under the care of that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, he gave such evident proofs of a ready genius, that he was then placed as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> with his uncle Vincenzo Dandini, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation through all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, who had been bred up under Pietro da Cortona. He afterwards travelled through most of the cities of Italy, studying the works of those who were most distinguished; and resided for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, where he copied the paintings paintings of Titian, Tintoretto, and Paolo Veronese. He next visited Parma and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> the works of Corregio; omitting no opportunity that might contribute to improve his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his judgment. When he returned to Florence, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> Cosmo III. the grand duchess Victoria, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> Ferdinand, kept him perpetually employed, in fresco painting as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; his subjects being taken not only from sacred or fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, but from his own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and fancy, which frequently furnished him with such as were odd and singular, and especially with whimsical caricatures. He died in 1712.—This master had a most extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for imitating the style of even the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> painters of every school, particularly Titian, Veronese, and Tintoretto; and with a force and elegance, equal to his subjects of history, he painted portraits, landscapes, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, fruit, battles, animals of all kinds, and likewise <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> pieces; proving himself an universal artist, and excellent in every thing he undertook. He had a son, Octavio, who proved not inferior to him in any branch of his profession, and was an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his family and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Dandini, Cesare, history painter, was born at Florence; and was the elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and first instructor of Vincenzo Dandini, the uncle of Pietro. This master had successively studied as a disciple with Cavalier Curradi, Passignano, and Cristofano Allori; from whom he acquired a very pleasing manner of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> and colouring. He was extremely correct in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, and finished his pictures highly. Several noble altarpieces in the churches of Florence are the productions of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>; and one, which is in the chapel l'Annunciata, is particularly admired. Dandola, Henry, doge of Venice, a brave <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> and politician. With a Venetian fleet he took Constantinople in 1203, and had the moderation to refuse to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. He died in 1250. Danegelt, an annual tax laid on the Anglo-Saxons, first of 1s. afterwards of 2s. for every hide of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> throughout the realm, for maintaining such a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of forces as were thought sufficient to clear the British seas of Danish pirates, which heretofore greatly annoyed our coasts. Danegelt was first imposed as a standing yearly tax on the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, under <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>, A.D. 991. That prince, says Camden, Britan. 142, much distressed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> invasions of the Danes, to procure a peace, was compelled to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> his people with heavy taxes called Danegelt.—At the first he paid 10,000l. then 16,000l. then 24,000l. after that 36,000l. and lastly 48,000l. Edward the Confessor remitted this tax: William I. and II. reassumed it occasionally. In the reign of Henry I. it was accounted among the king's standing revenues; but King Stephen, on his coronation <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, abrogated it for ever. No <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> or church-land paid a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> to the danegelt; because, as is set forth in an ancient Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the people of England placed more confidence in the prayers of the church than in any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> they could make. Danet, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of St Nicholas de Verdun, was one of the persons chosen by the duke of Montau- Vol. VII. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. Daniel, only what should happen to his own church and nation, but events in which foreign princes and kingdoms were concerned. **Daniel, Samuel**, an eminent poet and historian, was born near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in the year 1562, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; but leaving that university without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, he applied himself to English history and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>'s family. He was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the lady <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Clifford; and, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Spenser, was created poet-laureat to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. In King James's reign he was appointed <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> extraordinary, and afterwards one of the grooms of the privy-chamber to the queen consort, who took great delight in his conversation and writings. He wrote a history of England, several dramatic pieces, and some poems; and died in 1619. **Daniel, Gabriel**, a celebrated Jesuit, and one of the best French historians, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in 1649. He taught polite literature, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, among the Jesuits; and was superior of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he died in 1728. There are a great number of his works published in French, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are, 1. A History of France, of which he also wrote an abridgement in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> volumes, 12mo. 2. A History of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">Militia</a>, in two vols 4to. 3. An Answer to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">Provincial</a> Letters. 4. A Voyage to the World of Descartes. 5. Letters on the doctrines of the Theorists, and on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">Probability</a>. 6. New difficulties relating to the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">Brutes</a>: And, 7. A Theological treatise on the Efficiency of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANMONII">Danmonii</a>**, an ancient British nation, supposed to have inhabited that tract of country which is now called Cornwall and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, bounded on the south by the British ocean, on the west by St George's channel, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> sea, and on the east by the country of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUROTRIGES">Durotriges</a>. Some other British tribes were also seated within these limits; as the Cosini and Ostidamii; and, according to Mr Baxter, they were the keepers of their flocks and herds. As the several tribes of the Danmonii submitted without much resistance to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and never joined in any revolt against them, that people were under no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> many forts, or keeping many garrisons in their country. This is the reason why so few Roman antiquities have been found in that country, and so little mention is made of it and its ancient inhabitants by Roman writers. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> names a few places, both on the sea coasts and in the inland parts of this country, which were known to, and frequented by, the Romans. The most considerable of these places are the two famous promontories of Bolerium and Ocrynnum, now the Land's end and the Lizard; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Isca Danmoniorum and Tamare, now <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTASH">Saltash</a>. As the Danmonii submitted so tamely to the Romans, they might perhaps permit them to live, for some time at least, under their own princes and their own laws; a privilege which we know they granted to some other British states. In the most perfect state of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the country of the Danmonii made a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> called Flavia Caesariensis, and was governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of that province. After the departure of the Romans, kingly government was immediately revived among the Danmonii in the person of Vortigern, who was perhaps descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of their ancient princes, as his name signifies in the British <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> a chieftain or the head of a family. **Dante, Alighieri**, one of the first poets of Italy, was born at Florence in 1265, of an ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> family. Beccacio, who lived in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, has left a very curious and entertaining treatise, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the studies, and manners of this extraordinary poet, whom he regarded as his master, and for whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> he professed the highest veneration. This biographer relates, that Dante, before he was nine years old, conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for the lady whom he has immortalized in his singular poem. Her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> was near his own; and her name was Beatrice, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Folco Portinari, a noble citizen of Florence. The passion of Dante, however, like that of his successor Petrarch, seems to have been of the chaste and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">platonic</a> kind, according to the account he has himself given of it; in one of his early productions, entitled *Vita Nova*: a mixture of mysterious poetry and prose; in which he mentions both the origin of his affection and the death of his mistress, who, according to Beccacio, died at the age of 24. The same author asserts, that Dante fell into a deep melancholy in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this event, from which his friends endeavoured to raise him, by persuading him to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. After some time he followed their advice, and repented it; for he unfortunately made choice of a lady who bore some resemblance to the celebrated Xantippe. The poet, not possessing the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, separated himself from her with such vehement expressions of dislike, that he never afterwards admitted her to his presence, though she had borne him several children. In the early part of his life he gained some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> in a military character; distinguishing himself by his bravery in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> where the Florentines obtained a signal victory over the citizens of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>. He became still more eminent by the acquisition of civil honours; and at the age of 25 he rose to be one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates of Florence, when that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> was conferred by the suffrages of the people. From this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> the poet himself dated his principal misfortunes, as appears from the fragment of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> quoted by Leonardo Bruni, one of his early biographers, where Dante speaks of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> failure with that liberal frankness which integrity inspires. Italy was at that time distracted by the contending factions of the Ghibellins and the Guelphs; the latter, among whom Dante took an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> part, were again divided into the Blacks and the Whites. Dante, says Gravina, exerted all his influence to unite these inferior parties; but his efforts were ineffectual, and he had the misfortune to be unjustly persecuted by those of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>. A powerful citizen of Florence, named Corso Donati, had taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to terminate these intestine broils, by introducing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> of Valois, brother to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the Fair king of France. Dante, with great vehemence, opposed this disgraceful project, and obtained the banishment of Donati and his partizans. The exiles applied to the pope (Boniface VIII.), and by his assistance succeeded in their design. Charles of Valois entered Florence in triumph, and those who had opposed his admission were banished in their turn. Dante had been dispatched to Rome as the ambassa- Dante, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of his party; and was returning, when he received intelligence of the revolution in his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. His enemies, availing themselves of his absence, had procured an iniquitous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> against him, by which he was condemned to banishment, and his possessions were confiscated. His two enthusiastic biographers Boccaccio and Manetti, express the warmest indignation against the injustice of his country. Dante, on receiving this intelligence, took refuge in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, and afterwards in Arezzo, where many of his party were assembled. An attempt was made to surprise the city of Florence, by a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> which Dante is supposed to have attended: the design miscarried, and our poet is conjectured to have wandered to various parts of Italy, till he found a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> in the great Cangello Scala, prince of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, whom he has celebrated in his poem.
