DARTOS

Pages 103-106

in Anatomy, one of the coats which form the scrotum. It is called the dartos muscle; but Dr Hunter says, that no such muscle can be found, and Albinius takes no notice of it in his tables. Darwin, Erasmus, a physician, a poet, and medical writer, was born at Elston, near Newark, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, on the 12th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1731. He was the fourth son of Robert Darwin, Esq. He received the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Chesterfield school, under the reverend Mr Burrows, of whom he always spoke with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect. He was entered, with two of his elder brothers, at St John's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; and, being intended for the practice of medicine, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M. B. in 1755, defending in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the heart and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> is produced by the immediate stimulus of the blood. During his residence in Cambridge, Mr Darwin was elected to one of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>'s scholarships, worth about 16l. per annum, which, from the meagreness of his father's income at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was esteemed a desirable acquisition. After having prepared himself for his future profession, by an attendance on the lectures of Dr Hunter, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and by a severe course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, he contemplated the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> as the proper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> for his exertions. Deterred, however, by the want of an immediate introduction, and the improbability of obtaining immediate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, Dr Darwin thought it altogether more advisable to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to which he went, in the capacity of a physician, was <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, where he was entirely disappointed in his hopes of practice; he removed, therefore, to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>, with letters of introduction to Lady Gresley and the reverend Mr Seward. Here his great capacity and various acquirements were most justly appreciated: he resided at Litchfield during a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years, in the enjoyment of a very extensive reputation, and a very profitable practice, the foundation of which is supposed to have been laid by his success in restoring to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of fortune in the neighbourhood, whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> was despaired of by a numerous circle of friends and acquaintances. In the year 1757 Dr Darwin married Miss <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Howard, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Howard, Esq. by his wife, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Foley: she died in 1770. By this lady he had five children, two of whom died in their infancy: the eldest son, Charles, he educated to his own profession, but he died in the 20th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, very soon after he had finished his course of studies at Edinburgh, where he gained considerable reputation, by endeavouring to furnish a criterion for distinguishing pus from mucus. Soon after the decease of his wife, Dr Darwin commenced his laborious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the Zoonomia, which, however, he did not think proper to publish till about eight years since. In 1778 he obtained a lease of a picturesque spot of ground, about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from Litchfield, where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> bath was erected by Sir John Flayler, an eminent physician in the beginning of the last century: there is a grotto, surrounded by projecting rocks, from the edges of which trickles a perpetual shower of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This place became his favourite retreat and amusement: here he formed a botanic garden, and began his poem on the "Loves of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>," the scenery of which, Darwin. "as adapted to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-scenes, and being thence a proper residence for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>," is taken from these sequestered shades: And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> with thee some hapless maid should stray, Disastrous Love <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of her way, Gh <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> her timid steps to yonder glade, Whose arching cliffs depending alders <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>: There as meek Evening <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a> her temperate breeze, And moonbeams glimmer through the trembling trees, The rills, that guggle round, shall soothe her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>; The weeping rocks shall number tear for tear, &c. &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANTO">Canto</a> 1, line 25. In 1780, Dr Darwin was called to attend <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Sacheverel Pole, of Radbourne-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, four miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>; and a few months after the decease of the colonel, he married his relict, Mrs Pole, with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a> of £600 per annum. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Dr Darwin occasioned his immediate removal from Litchfield to Radbourne, where he resided two years, till he got accommodated with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Derby. In this last situation he remained till about two months before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, when he removed to Breadwall Priory about three miles from Derby, which was a commodious and peaceful retirement for his old age. During the last few years, Dr Darwin was much subject to inflammation in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and lungs; and had a very serious attack of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> in the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1801, from which, after repeated bleedings, he with difficulty recovered. On the 10th of April 1802, he was attacked with a severe shivering fit, followed by a correspondent hot one, and accompanied with symptoms of inflammation in his lungs: his surgeon, Mr Hadley, took from him, in the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, 25 ounces of blood. The fever was removed, and in two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three days he became, to all appearance, quite well. On the 17th as he was walking in his garden with Mrs Darwin, and a lady of about his own age, the latter remarked, that he would have sufficient employment for ten years in bringing all his plans about the place to perfection. "You madam (he replied) have as good a prospect as any body I know, of your age, of living ten years; I have not." Mrs Darwin remarked his good looks, spirits, and strength. He said, "I always appear particularly well immediately before I become ill." He sat with his family in the evening, conversing with his usual cheerfulness; went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and rose at six on the following morning; wrote some letters till after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, when he was seized with a chilly fit, which increased, and was attended with thirst. He then sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> fire and drank a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; but feeling himself much indisposed, he lay down on a sofa, when becoming more cold and torpid, he was raised up, and placed in an arm-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, where, without pain or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, he expired a little before <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, in the 71st year of his age. Dr Darwin left a widow and six children, three boys and three girls, by his last marriage. There was also another child, who died an infant. Besides these, he left two <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> daughters, whom he had established in a school at Ashbourne, and for whose instruction and assistance he composed and published his "Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> Education." During the whole of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, Dr Darwin was remarkable for great benevolence of disposition, and it was particularly conspicuous in the care he took even of the lowest animals. The keenness of his feelings on this subject has been attributed to the strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> made upon his mind by a representation of the tortures of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, which was shown to him at an early age. He had frequently expressed a strong desire, that the termination of his existence might be without pain, having always looked upon death as the less evil of the two. He was of a middle stature, in person <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and corpulent; his features were coarse, and his countenance heavy; if not wholly void of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a>, it certainly was by no means expressive. In his gait and dress he was rather clumsy and slovenly, and frequently walked with his tongue hanging out of his mouth. His conversation abounded with very unequal sallies of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>: when he found himself engaged with a powerful antagonist in argument, he had sometimes recourse to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, a weapon which he did not always handle with dexterity, for he was affected with an impediment in his speech which rendered his enunciation scarcely intelligible. About the age of twenty-one, Dr Darwin was seized with a fit of the gout; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he totally abstained from all fermented liquors, not even tasting small beer, or a drop of any kind of wine; but he ate plentifully of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-meat, and all kinds of vegetables and fruit, using for his drink, at meals, chiefly water alone, or cream and water, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> and coffee between them, as usual. By this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from fermented liquors, he kept quite free from gout for 15 years, and from some other complaints to which he had been subject. He then indulged himself occasionally with a little wine and water; cider and water, &c. but was speedily admonished into his former <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, by a paroxysm of the gout. He was in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of eating a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of food, and his stomach possessed a strong power of digestion. His advice frequently was, "Eat, or be eaten;" but he took every opportunity to impress a dread of all fermented liquors on the minds of his patients, whose diseases he was too ready to represent as originating in the frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them. In the "Botanic Garden," he has also taken an opportunity to express his strong antipathy against fermented and spirituous liquors, by comparing their effects to that of the Promethean fire: "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> story of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMETHEUS">Prometheus</a>, who concealed in his bosom the fire he had stolen, and afterwards had a vulture perpetually gnawing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, afford so apt an allegory for the effects of drinking spirituous liquors, that one should be induced to think the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, as well as some other chemical processes (such as calcining <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>) had been known in times of great antiquity, and lost again. The swallowing drams cannot be better represented in hieroglyphic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, than by taking fire into one's bosom; and certain it is, that the general effect of drinking fermented or spirituous liquors is an inflamed, schirrous, or paralytic liver, with its various critical or consequential diseases, as leprous eruptions on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, gout, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>, epilepsy, and insanity." The various productions of Dr Darwin's fanciful and philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> since been exposed to public criticism, and received an ample share, as well of obloquy as applause. Still, however, he has claims to celebrity from the literary lustre which adorns his character, as a medical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a philosophical agriculturist, and a poet. The pretensions of Dr Darwin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as a medical philosopher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, of course, substantiate themselves in the merit, numerous and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> as they are, of the "Zoonomia." In whichever point of view this work shall be considered, whether as a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> repository of curious natural and medical facts, or as a scheme and system of pathological and physiological disquisition, is probably <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of trifling import, so far as the reputation of its author is concerned. By either <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of appreciation, it is unquestionably, a noble effort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> labour or of human wit; and though its illustrious author may have sometimes erred from excess of ingenuity, and been occasionally blinded by too great a love of system, the Zoonomia will ever be considered as a production of transcendent merit. As a philosophical agriculturist Dr Darwin must ever be entitled to the highest consideration. In order to profit by the multitudinous experiments of Hales, Grew, Malpighi, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">Bonnet</a>, Du Hamel, Buffon, Spallanzani, Priestley, &c. collected in the "Phytologia," it is not necessary to take possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-built <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of vegetation which is there constructed, and securely inhabit it as an edifice whose solidity is equal to its elegance. Whether the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> is in fact so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> between the parts and functions of animal and vegetable beings;—whether the anatomy of the one so strictly corresponds with that of the other, as to induce a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that the latter are in reality an inferior order of the former, possessed of a brain, uterus, muscles, and complete nervous system, is an inquiry, which, however curious, must surely be subordinate in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with those <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and indisputable discoveries which the application of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> has brought to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. A small portion only of the Phytologia is devoted to this fanciful system of vegetable physiology: the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part, divided into three sections, treats on the economy of vegetation; and the third, on agriculture and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORTICULTURE">horticulture</a>, is divided into six sections. Dr Darwin, in his character as a poet, does not stand very high in the estimation of some. The ear is fascinated and seduced by the mellifluence of his numbers, but there is a barbility in his embellishments which is unchaste. His cadences are not sufficiently varied for a poem of such length as the "Botanic Garden;" indeed there is an evident mechanism in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> which it is by no means pleasant to detect. But an imagination of unrivalled richness; a felicity of allusion to whatever can throw lustre on his subject, to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> and modern discoveries, to the works of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and of art; if these are some of the essentials of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, Dr Darwin may certainly claim them as his own. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, perhaps, was ever happier in the selection and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of his epithets, had a more imperial command of words, or could elucidate with such accuracy and elegance the most complex and intricate machinery. Who but Dr Darwin would have thought of describing a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> manufactory in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; the powers and construction of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> engine; the mechanism of a watch; and the complexity of a cotton-mill? These, and many similar descriptions, to be found in the Botanic Garden, are inimitable in their way. In some of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> effusions he is particularly happy: the beautiful little song "to May," is exquisitely finished; and it would be difficult to find thirty lines in the Botanic Garden to rival in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and pathos the "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">Address</a> to Swilcar's Oak," introduced in the Phytologia. As a prose writer, Dr Darwin was incorrect; his grammatical errors are numerous, and he was even deficient in orthography. In the year 1758, he published, in the Philosophical Transactions, "An attempt to confute the opinion of Henry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a>, concerning the ascent of vapour;" and "An account of the cure of a periodical haemoptoe, by keeping the patient awake." This was followed by "Experiments on animal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> in the exhausted receiver." He inserted in the Derby <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, an elegy written at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATLOCK">Matlock</a>, and addressed to Mrs Darwin; another piece occasioned by the appearance of a most fatal distemper among horned cattle, at Calke, near Derby; and a third article on occasion of the earthquake, which several years ago was felt at Derby, and in the surrounding country. In 1782, the Botanical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Litchfield published a translation of Linnæus's Systema Vegetabilium, the execution of which was principally confided to Dr Darwin. His other works have already been mentioned in the course of this biographical sketch. He left a poem entitled "The Temple of Nature," which was published after his death. Next to medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, and almost every branch of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He not only pursued these studies with great ardour and diligence himself, but also embraced every opportunity of cultivating and encouraging them among his numerous connexions and acquaintance. Very soon after he settled in Derby, he instituted and established a philosophical society and library, both of which were in a flourishing state at the time of his decease. He also took <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in encouraging works in natural history. But though the learning, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and genius of Dr Darwin, were eminently displayed in these pursuits, yet there was one great end, to the attainment of which all his talents and views were directed. He did not hesitate openly and repeatedly to declare, that the acquisition of wealth was the leading object of all his literary undertakings. However, he was by no means insensible to the value of reputation. During the last years of his life, the love of fame was a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> which had a great power over his mind; and the incense of praise was so pleasant to him, that flattery was found to be the most successful means of gaining his notice and favour. There are reasons for suspecting that Dr Darwin was not a believer in Divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. A few days before his death, a gentleman endeavoured to discover whether he entertained a belief and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of a future state of existence; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> was observed to speak with a considerable degree of sedateness on the subject, and remarked, that it was natural to extend our wishes and views beyond the present <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, and that that it was <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to pursue such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> as are likely to secure our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in another world; "but," he added, "let us not hear any thing about <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>."

DASYPUS

Pages 106-106

the ARMADILLO <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tatou, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of Bruta. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DATA

Pages 106-106

among mathematicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> for such things <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities as are given or known, in order to find other things thereby that are unknown. The data of Euclid is the first in order of the books that have been written by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> geometers, to facilitate and promote the method of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>. In general, a thing is said to be given which is either actually exhibited, or can be found out, that is, which is either known by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, or that can be demonstrated to be known: and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> in the book of Euclid's data shew what things can be found out or known, from those that by hypothesis are already known: so that in the analysis or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of a problem, from the things that are laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as given or known, by the help of these propositions, it is demonstrated that other things are given, and from these last that others again are given, and so on, till it is demonstrated that that which was proposed to be found out in the problem is given; and when this is done, the problem is solved, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is made and derived from the compositions of the data which were employed in the analysis. And thus the data of Euclid are of the most general and necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the solution of problems of every kind. Marinus, at the end of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the data, is mistaken in asserting that Euclid has not used the synthetical, but the analytical method in delivering them: for though in the analysis of a theorem, the thing to be demonstrated is assumed in the analysis; yet in the demonstrations of the data, the thing to be demonstrated, which is, that something is given, is never once assumed in the demonstration; from which it is manifest, that every one of them is demonstrated synthetically; though indeed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a proposition of the data be turned into a problem, the demonstration of the proposition becomes the analysis of the problem. Simpson's Preface to his edition of the Data. From the primary use of the word data in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, it has been transplanted into other arts; as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, medicine, &c., where it expresses any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, which, for the sake of a present calculation, is taken for granted to be such, without requiring an immediate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> for its certainty; called also the given quantity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, or power. And hence also such things as are known, from whence, either in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, the animal mechanism, or the operation of medicine, we come to the knowledge of others unknown, are now frequently in physical writers called data.

DATE

Pages 106-106

an addition <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appendage in writings, acts, instruments, letters, &c., expressing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was passed or signed; together with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the same was done. The word is formed from the Latin datum, "given," the participle of do, "I give." Our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deeds had no dates, but only the month and year, to signify that they were not made in haste, or in the space of a day, but upon longer and more mature deliberation. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s grants began with these words, Presentibus et futuris, &c., but the grants of private persons with Omnibus, presentes literas inspcturis, &c. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> is good, though it mentions no date or hath a false date; or even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it hath an impossible date, as the 30th of February: provided the real day of its being dated or given, that is, delivered, can be proved. Blackst. Com. vol. ii. p. 304.

DATI

Pages 106-106

CARLO, professor of polite learning at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. His native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> became very famous, as well on account of his works, as of the eulogies which have been bestowed on him by learned men. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to which Dati applied himself, was Della Pittria Antica, on which he published an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> in the year 1667. He died in 1675, much lamented, as well for his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and amiable manners as for his parts and learning.

DATISCA

Pages 106-106

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dicoccia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 54th order, Miscellanea.

DATISI

Pages 106-106

in Logic, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of syllogisms in the third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> is an universal affirmative, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> and conclusion particular affirmative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>. For example, DA- All who serve God are kings; TI- Some who serve God are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; SI- Therefore some who are poor are kings.

DATIVE

Pages 106-106

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in the declension of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>: expressing the state <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> relation of a thing to whose profit or loss some other thing is referred. See Grammar. It is called dative, because usually governed by a verb, implying something to be given to some person. As, commodare Socrati, "to lend to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>;" utilis republicae, "useful to the commonwealth;" perniciosus ecclesiae, "pernicious to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>." In English, where we have properly no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, this relation is expressed by the sign to or for.

DATUM

Pages 106-106
or DATUS, in Ancient Geography, a town of Thrace, situated between Neapolis and the river Nestus: A colony of Thracians, according to Eustathius; who places it on the sea-coast, near the Strymon, in a rich and fruitful soil, famous for ship-building and mines of gold; hence the proverb Δάλις Αγαθόν, denoting property and plenty. (Strabo.) Apian describes it as seated on a steep eminence, the whole of which it covered. It was taken by Philip of Macedon, who changed its name to Philippi, being originally called Crenides on account of its springs. It was afterwards famous for the defeat of Brutus and Cassius, by Augustus and Antony.

DATURA

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">THORN</a>-APPLE: a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 28th order, Lurida. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DAUBENTON

Pages 106-107
LOUIS JEAN MARIE, a distinguished naturalist, was born at Montbier, in the department of the Côte d'Or, in France, on the 29th of May 1716. His father, Jean Daubenton, was a notary in that place, and his mother's name was Marie Piche-not. In his youth he distinguished himself by the sweetness of his temper, and by his diligent application The Jesuits of Dijon, under whose tuition he was first placed, noticed him in a peculiar manner. Having gone through a course of what was called philosophy, under the Dominicans of Dijon, his father, who destined him for the church, and who had made him assume the ecclesiastical dress at the age of twelve, sent him to Paris to study theology. But his predilection for href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural history induced him privately to study medicine. Accordingly he attended the lectures of Baron Martineng, and Col de Villars, and likewise those of Winslow, Humault, and Antoine de Jussieu in the botanic garden. The death of his father in 1736 enabled him to follow his inclination without constraint. Accordingly he took a degree at Rheims in 1741, and returned to his own country with the intention of following the practice of medicine. But fortune destined him for a more brilliant career. Montbier had given birth, about the same time, to another man of a very different character, who, though possessed of an independent fortune, a robust constitution, and actuated by a violent passion for pleasure, had determined notwithstanding to devote himself to the cultivation of the sciences. This man was Buffon. Hesitating for some time what branch of physics he should make his peculiar study, he tried by turns geometry, mechanical philosophy, and agriculture. At last his friend Dufay, who during his short superintendence had raised the botanic garden from that state of neglect in which former naturalists had left it, and who had procured for Buffon the reversion of his office, dying, and leaving him his place, Buffon's choice was fixed on natural history, and he saw before him that wide field which he afterwards traversed with so much reputation. Natural history was at that time little else than a dry catalogue of names, destitute of that methodical arrangement, of that precision, of those interesting details which have since distinguished it. It occupied a very low station among the sciences, and instead of being a fashionable study, was degraded into the drudge of medicine and surgery. Buffon formed the bold plan of giving life to this dry and apparently sterile mass, of painting nature as she is, always young, always active; of pointing out the harmony of all her parts, and the laws by which they are combined into one system, and of giving his picture all the glow, all the freshness, all the charms of nature herself. But to secure success it was necessary to make truth the basis of his system. Every thing must be collected, revised, and examined. The forms and dimensions of animals must be compared, and their internal structure ascertained. The ardent and impatient spirit of Buffon could ill brook a task so tedious and painful, and the imperfection of his sight rendered him unqualified for it. He looked about, therefore, for a man possessed of sufficient judgment, patience, and neatness of hand for his purpose, and at the same time modest enough to submit willingly to act a secondary part. He found such a man in Daubenton, the companion of his infancy. The character of these two philosophers was almost opposite in every respect. Buffon was violent, impatient, rash; Daubenton was all gentleness, patience, and caution: Buffon wished to divine the truth rather than to discover it: Daubenton believed nothing which Daubenton had not himself seen and ascertained. Buffon suffered his imagination to lead him from nature; Daubenton, on the contrary, discarded from his writings every expression which was calculated to mislead. They were thus happily fitted to correct each other's faults. Accordingly the history of quadrupeds, which appeared while they laboured together, is the most exempt from error of any of the divisions which constitute Buffon's natural history. Buffon drew Daubenton to Paris about 1742: procured for him the place of demonstrator of the cabinet of natural history, at first with a salary of only 500 francs, but which was gradually increased to 2000. He furnished him likewise with a lodging, and neglected nothing to secure his comfort and convenience. Daubenton on his side devoted himself to second the views of his benefactor. The cabinet of natural history, which was arranged, and in a great measure collected by his means, was of immense service. In the history of quadrupeds, he gave the description and dissection of 182 species of quadrupeds. These details contained a vast number of new facts, and arranged in such a manner that the most curious results are often obtained merely by comparing them together. This work procured for Daubenton a very high reputation, and drew upon him the envy of Reaumur, who at that time considered himself at the head of natural history. But the credit and reputation of Buffon was sufficient to prevent his friend from falling a victim to the attack of this formidable antagonist. In the subsequent parts of his natural history, Buffon was persuaded to separate himself from Daubenton. This injured the precision and value of these parts excessively; while it deprived Daubenton of 12,000 francs a year. Afterwards the intimacy between them revived, and continued till the death of Buffon. The number of dissertations on natural history which Daubenton published in the Memoirs of the French Academy, is so great, that even a list of them would be too long for this place. Descriptions of different animals, dissections, comparisons between the forms of different animals, anatomical examinations of fossil bones, to determine the animals to which they had belonged, the physiology of vegetables, and different parts of mineralogy, successively occupied him; not to mention his experiments on agriculture and rural economy, which, however, were of more service to him afterwards than all the rest of his labours, on account of the reputation among the populace which they had procured him. In the year 1794, when the dregs of the people were masters of France, Daubenton was under the necessity of applying to the section of Sans-culottes for a certificate of civism, to enable him to retain his place in the garden of plants, which he had filled with honour for 52 years. A professor and academician would scarcely have obtained it; but it was readily granted to Shepherd Daubenton, under which title it had been fortunately presented. The following is a translation of this certificate:

DAUGHTER

Pages 108-108

(filia), a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> child. See the article Children. Daughters, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, were more frequently exposed than sons, as requiring greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to educate and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> them in the world. See Exposure of Children. Those who had no legitimate sons were obliged, by the Athenian laws, to leave their estates to their daughters, who were confined to marry their nearest relations, otherwise to forfeit their inheritance; as we find to have been practised likewise among the Jews, many of whose laws seem to have been transcribed by Solon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> an heiress happened to be married before her father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, this did not hinder the nearest relation to claim the inheritance, and even to take the woman from her husband; which is said to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>.

DAUPHIN

Pages 109-110

is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> which was given to the eldest son of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family of France, and presumptive heir of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Dauphiné, which in 1343 was given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> de Valois, on this condition, by Humbert dauphin of the Viennois. The dauphin, in his letters patent, styled himself, By the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of God, eldest son of France, and dauphin of Viennois. Dauphin was anciently the title <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appellation of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Viennois in France. Most authors who have sought the origin of the name Dauphin and Dauphine, seem to have given too much loose to conjecture. Du Chesne is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it was the grandson of Guy the Fat who first bore the name of dauphin. Chorier observes, that William, canon of Notre Dame at Grenoble, who has written the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Margaret, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Stephen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, married with Guy, son of Guy the Fat, calls the latter simply Guy the Old, and the former always <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Dauphin; and adds, that no record or monument ever attributes the title of dauphin to Guy the Fat, or any of his predecessors: so that it must necessarily have taken its rise in his son, all whose successors so constantly assumed it, that it became the proper name of the family. He died in 1142, in the flower of his youth; so that it must be about the year 1120 that the title commenced; and without doubt, adds he, on some illustrious occasion. He observes farther, that this prince was of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> disposition, and delighted in nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>: and again, that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the cavaliers to deck their casques, coats of arms, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSING">housing</a> of their horses, with some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or device peculiar to themselves, whereby they were distinguished from all others engaged in the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a>. From all these circumstances he conjectures that this Guy chose the dolphin for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a>; that this was the crest of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>; and that he bore it on his coat in some notable tournament or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, wherein he distinguished himself. And this, Chorier makes no doubt, is the real origin of the appellation. Nothing was more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in those times than to make proper names become the names of families or dignities. Witness the Ademars, Arthands, Aynards, Attomans, Berengers, and many others; who all owe their names to some one of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, from whom it has been transmitted throughout the family. The seigneurs or lords of Auvergne have likewise borne the appellation of dauphin; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUPHINS">dauphins</a> of Auvergne had it not till a good while after those of the Viennois, and even received it from them. The manner was this: Guy VIII., dauphin of Viennois, had by his wife Margaret, daughter of Stephen earl of Burgundy, a son and two daughters. The son was Guy IX., his successor. Béatrix, one of the daughters, was married to the count d'Auvergne, who, according to Blondel, was William V. or rather, as Chorier and others hold, Robert VI., father of William V. This prince lost the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Auvergne, which was taken from him by his uncle William, assisted by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> the Young: and was only left <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> whereof Vodable is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. He had a son whom he called Dauphin, on account of Guy, or Guignes, his uncle by the mother's side. From his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his successors, holding the same petty canton of Auvergne, styled themselves dauphins of Auvergne, and bore a dolphin for their arms. Dauphins, or Delphines, in literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given to the commentators on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin authors, who were employed by Louis XIV. of France for the benefit of the prince, under the care and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of M. de Montausier his governor, and Bossuet and Huet his preceptors. They were 39 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

DAUPHINY

Pages 110-110

a late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Rhone and Savoy, on the south by Provence, and on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>; and now forming the departments of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DROME">Drome</a>, Isere, and Upper Alps. In some places it is very fertile; and produces corn, wine, olives, wood, copperas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, crystal, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. But the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the province is barren, and the inhabitants are obliged to go into other countries for subsistence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> abound in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> of all sorts; and here are fir-trees proper for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are, the Rhone, the Durance, the Isere, and the Drome. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; and Grenoble is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

DAURAT

Pages 110-110

JOHN, an eminent French poet, born in 1507. In the reign of Henry II., he was preceptor to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX., who took <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> delight in his conversation, honoured him with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his poet; but his generosity and want of management placed him in that class of learned men who have been very near starving. Conformable to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he had so much skill in making anagrams, that several illustrious persons gave him their names to anagrammatize; he also undertook to explain the Centuries of Nostradamus. Making verses was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> in him: for no book was printed, nor did any person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> die, but Daurat made some verses on the occasion; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been poet ordinary, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his muse had been a hired mourner to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Scaliger tells us, that he spent the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in endeavouring to find all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. He died in 1588.

DAVENANT

Pages 108-108

Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, an eminent civilian and writer, eldest son of the preceding, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>: he wrote several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> tracts, and likewise plays. He was (1685) empowered, with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the revels, to inspect the plays designed for the stage, that no immoralities might be presented. His Essays on Trade are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem, and were reprinted in 5 vols 8vo, in 1771. Dr Davenant was inspector-general of exports and imports; and died in 1712.

DAVENTRY

Pages 108-108
or DAINTRY, a handsome town of Northamptonshire in England, situated on the side of a hill, on the great road to Chester and Carlisle. W. Long. 1. 15. N. Lat. 52. 12.

DAVID

Pages 108-108
king of Israel, and Hebrew poet, was born at Bethlehem 1085, and died 1014 years B.C. His history is particularly recorded in the sacred writings. [Merged from ST DAVID'S, p.108] a town and fort of Asia, in the peninsula on this side the Ganges, and on the coast of Coromandel, 80 miles south of Fort St George. E. Long. 79. 55. N. Lat. 11. 30. On the taking of Madras by the French in 1746, the presidency of all the English settlements on the Coromandel coast was removed to Fort St David, and continued there till about the year 1752, when it was removed back to Madras. In June 1758, the fort was taken and demolished by the French, and has never been rebuilt since.

DAVIDISTS

Pages 108-108

Davidici, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>-Georgians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics, the adherents of David George, a native of Delft, who, in 1525, began to preach a new doctrine; publishing himself to be the true Messiah; and

DAVILA

Pages 108-109

HENRY CATHARINE, a celebrated historian, was the youngest son of Antonio Davila, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of Cyprus, who on the taking of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> by the Turks in 1570, had been obliged to retire into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, whence this family supposed they had derived their name and origin. From Spain Antonio repaired to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France, and settled his son <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> and two daughters under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Catherine of Medicis; whose name he afterwards gave to the young historian, born 1576, at an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle in the territories of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, though generally called a native of Cyprus. The little Davila was brought early into France; and at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 18 he signalized himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> scenes of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His last exploit there was at the siege of Amiens, where he fought under Henry IV, and received a wound in the knee, as he relates himself in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. After peace was established in France, he withdrew into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the Venetians. Davila, while he was at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, wrote his admirable history of the civil wars in France, which contains every thing worth notice that passed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Henry II. in 1539, to the peace of Vervins in 1598. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to serve the republic of Venice with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation, till a most unfortunate adventure put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in 1631. Passing through <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> with his wife and family on his way to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREMA">Crema</a>, which he was appointed to defend, and demanding, according to the usual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of persons in his station, a supply of horses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> for his retinue, a brutal Veronese, called Il Turco, entered the room where he and his family were at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, and being mildly reprimanded for his intrusion by Davila, discharged a pistol at the historian, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> him dead on the instant. His accomplices also killed the chaplain of Davila, and wounded most of his attendants. But his eldest son Antonio, a youth of 18, revenged the death of his father, by killing the murderer on the spot. All the confederates were secured next morning, and publicly executed at Verona. It is very remarkable, that Davila passed no censure on the massacre of St Bartholomew. Davila's character of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>-mother has that partiality, which it was <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for him to show to the patroness of his family; but his general veracity is confirmed by the great authority of the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Epernon, who (to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the words of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bolingbroke) "had been an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> actor too, in many of the scenes that Davila recites." Girard, secretary to the duke, and no contemptible biographer, relates that this history came <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> resided in Gascony, a little before his death; that he read it to him; that the duke confirmed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of it; and seemed only surprised by what means the author could be so well informed of the most secret councils and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of those times.

DAVIS

Pages 109-109

Sir John, an eminent lawyer and poet, born about the year 1570. He first distinguished himself by his poem Nosce Teipsum, on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">Immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>. He became <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, and speaker of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; and afterwards was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a> in England, but died before his installation, in 1626. He published many <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> tracts; but was esteemed more as a scholar and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> than as a lawyer. Davis, John, a famous navigator in the 16th century, was born at Sandridge, near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>; and distinguished himself by making three voyages to the most northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in order to discover a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west passage to the East Indies; in which he discovered the straits which bear his name. He afterwards performed five voyages to the East Indies; in the last of which he was slain in a desperate fight with some Javanese, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, on the 27th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1625. He wrote an account of his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> voyage for the discovery of the north-west passage; a voyage to the East Indies; and other tracts. DAVIS'S Straits. See <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NEW_BRITAIN">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

DAVIT

Pages 109-109

in a ship, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> beam of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, represented by a, a, Plate CLXIX, and used as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRANE">crane</a> whereby to hoist the flukes of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> to the top of the bow, without injuring the sides of the ship as it ascends; an operation which, by mariners, is called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> the anchor. The anchors being situated on both the bows, the davit may be occasionally shifted so as to project over either side of the ship, according to the position of that anchor on which it is employed. The inner end of the davit is secured by being thrust into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> b, which is bolted to the deck, and forelocked under the beams. This ring, which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a>-shackle, exhibited at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> by fig. 9, is fixed exactly in the middle of the deck, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> behind the foremast. Upon the outer end of the davit is hung a large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> c, through which a strong rope traverses, called the fish-pendant, d; to whose foremost end is fitted a large iron hook e, and to its after-end a tackle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> complication of pulleys, f; the former of which is called the fish-hook, and the latter the fish-tackle. The davit, therefore, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> phrase, is employed to fish the anchor; which being previously cutted, the fish-hook is fastened upon its flukes; and the efforts of the tackle being transmitted to the hook, by means of the fish-pendant, draws up that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the anchor sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> upon the bow to fasten it,

DAY

Pages 110-111

according to the most <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and obvious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, signifies that space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> during which it continues to be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; in contradistinction to night, which is that portion of time wherein it is dark: but the space of time in which it is light, being somewhat vague and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a>, the time between the rising and the setting of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is usually looked on as the day; and the time which lapses from its setting to its rising again, the night. The word day is often taken in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sense, so as to include the night also; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to denote the time of a whole apparent revolution of the sun round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; in which sense it is called by some a natural day, and by others an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> one: but, to avoid confusion, it is usual to call it in the former sense simply the day, and in the latter a nycthemeron: by which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> that acceptation of it is aptly denoted, as it implies both day and night. The nycthemeron is divided into twenty-four parts, called hours; which are of two sorts, equal, and unequal or temporary. See the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">Hour</a>. Different nations begin their day at a different hour. Thus the Egyptians begin their day at midnight; from whom <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> introduced that way of reckoning into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and Copernicus and others have followed him; but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of astronomers reckon the day to begin at noon, and so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> twenty-four hours, till the noon of the next day; and not twice twelve, according to the vulgar computation. The method of beginning the day at midnight prevails in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and most parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The Babylonians began their day at sunrise; reckoning the hour immediately before its rising again, the twenty-fourth hour of the day; from whence the hours reckoned in this way are called the Babylonian. In several parts of Germany, they begin their day at sunsetting, and reckon on till it sets next day, calling that the twenty-fourth hour; these are generally termed Italian hours. The Jews also began their nycthemeron at sunsetting; but then they divided it into twice twelve hours as we do; reckoning twelve for the day, be it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> or short, and twelve for the night; so that their hours continually varying with the day and night, the hours of the day were longer than those of the night for one half year, and the contrary the other; from whence their hours are called temporary: those at the time of the equinoxes became equal, because then those of the day and night are so. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> also reckoned their hours after this manner, as do the Turks at this day. This kind of hours is called planetary, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> were anciently looked upon as presiding over the affairs of the world, and to take it by turns each of these hours, according to the following order; <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> first, then <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, the Sun, Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and last of all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>: hence they denominated each day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> from that planet whose turn it was to preside the first hour of the nycthemeron. Thus, assigning the first hour of Saturday to Saturn, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to Jupiter, the third to Mars, and so the twenty-second of the same nycthemeron will fall to Saturn again, and therefore the twenty-third to Jupiter, and the last to Mars: so that on the first hour of the next day, it will fall to the sun to preside; and by the like manner of reckoning, the first hour of the next will fall to the Moon; of the next to Mars; of the next to Mercury; of the next to Jupiter; and of the next to Venus: hence the days of the week came to be distinguished by the Latin names of Dies Saturni, Solis, Lunae, Martis, Mercurii, Jovis, and Veneris; and among us, by the names of Saturday, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, Monday, &c. Day-Coal, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by the miners of England, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people who live in coal countries, to that seam or stratum of the coal which lies uppermost in the earth. The same vein or stratum of coal usually runs a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and dips and rises in the earth at different places; so that this upper stratum, or day-coal, is in the various parts of the same stratum, sometimes near the surface, and sometimes many fathoms deep. The subterranean fires found in some of our coal countries feed principally on this coal; and are nearer to or farther from the surface as it rises or sinks. Day-Fly. See Ephemeris, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Day-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">Net</a>, among fowlers. See Net. Days of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>, are those granted by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> of the defendant or plaintiff, in whose delay it is. Days of Grace, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, are a customary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of days allowed for the payment of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, &c., after the same becomes due. Three days of grace are allowed in Britain; ten in France and Danzig; eight at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; six at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; four at Frankfurt; five at Leipzig; twelve at Hamburgh; six in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; 14 in Spain; 30 in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, &c. In Britain the days of grace are given and taken as a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of course, the bill being only paid on the last day; but in other countries, where the time is much longer, it would be reckoned dishonourable for a merchant to take advantage of it; bills are therefore paid on the very day they fall due. Day's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, an arbitrator or person chosen to determine an affair in dispute. Intercalary Days. See Intercalary Days. Day's-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">Work</a>, among seamen, the reckoning or account of the ship's course during 24 hours, or between noon and noon, according to the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>. See Dead-Reckoning.

DAZE

Pages 111-111

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by our miners to a glittering sort of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which often occurs in their works; and, as it is an unprofitable substance, is one of those things they call weeds. The word does takes in, with them, every stone that is hard and glittering; and therefore it comprehends the whole genus of the talia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stony nodules, which have the flakes of tale in their substance; these according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the stony <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> they are bedded in, and their own colour, give the names of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> daze, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> daze, to these <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>.

DE WIT

Pages 208-209

JOHN, the famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a>, was born in 1625, at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>; where he prosecuted his studies so diligently, that, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 23, he published Elementa Curvarum Linearum, one of the profoundest books in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. After taking his degrees, and travelling, he, in 1650, became pensionary of Dort, and distinguished himself very early in the management of public affairs. He opposed with all his power the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the English and the Dutch; and when the event justified his predictions, he was unanimously chosen pensionary of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. In this capacity he laboured to procure a peace with Cromwell; in which peace a secret article was introduced by one side <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other, for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. In the war with England after the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s restoration, when it was thought expedient, on Opdam's defeat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, that some of their own deputies should command the fleet, he was one of the three put in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>; and wrote an accurate relation of all that happened during the expedition he was engaged in, for which, at his return, he received the solemn thanks of the States General. In 1667, he established the perpetual edict for abolishing the office of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">Stadtholder</a>, to fix the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the republic, as it was hoped, on a firm basis; which produced seditions and tumults, that restored the office, on pretence that the De Wits were enemies to the house of Orange, and plundered the state. The pensionary begged dismission from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>; which was granted, with thanks for his faithful services. But the invasion of the French, and the internal divisions among the Hollander themselves, spread everywhere terror and confusion; which the Orange party heightened to ruin the De Wits. Cornelius, the pensionary's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, was imprisoned and condemned to exile; and a report being raised that he would be rescued, the mob armed, and surrounded the prison where the two brothers then were together, dragged them out, barbarously murdered them, hung the bodies on the gallows, and cut them to pieces, which many of them even broiled and ate with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> fury. Such was the end of one of the greatest geniuses of his age; of whom Sir William Temple, who was well acquainted with him, writes with the greatest esteem and admiration. He observes, that when he was at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, he differed nothing in his manner of living from from an ordinary citizen. His office, for the first ten years, brought him in little more than £300l. and in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, not above £200l. per annum. He refused a gift of £10,000l. from the states-general, because he thought it a bad precedent in the government. With <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reason, therefore, Sir William Temple, speaking of his death, observes, "He was a person that deserved another fate, and a better return from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, after 18 years spent in their ministry, without any care of his entertainments or ease, and little of his fortune. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of unwearied industry, inflexible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, clear, and deep understanding, and untainted integrity; so that whenever he was blinded, it was by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> he had for that which he esteemed the good and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the state. This testimony is justly due to him from all that were well acquainted with him; and is the more willingly paid, since there can be as little interest to flatter, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to reproach, the dead." Besides the works already mentioned, he wrote a book containing those maxims of government upon which he acted; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be a never-fading monument to his immortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. A translation of it from the original Dutch, entitled The true interest and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> maxims of the republic of Holland, has been printed in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; to the last edition of which, in 1746, are prefixed historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the illustrious brothers Cornelius and John de <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">Wit</a>, by John Campbell, Esq.

DEACON

Pages 111-112

(Diaconus), a person in the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of holy orders, whose business is to baptize, read in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and assist at the celebration of the eucharist. The word is formed from the Latin Diaconus, of the Greek διάκονος, minister, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>. Deacons were instituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, by the apostles, Acts chap. vi., which number was retained a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in several churches. Their office was to serve in the Agape, and to distribute the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine to the communicants. Another <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the office of deacons was to be a sort of monitors and directors to the people in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their public devotions in the church; for which purpose they made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of certain known forms of words, to give notice when each part of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> began. Whence they are sometimes called cirkerukers, "the holy cryers of the church."
