Deacons had, by license and authority from the bishop, a power to preach, to reconcile penitents and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a>, and to represent their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> in general councils. Their office out of the church was to take care of the necessitous, such as orphans, widows, prisoners, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and sick who had any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to be maintained out of the revenues of the church; to inquire into the morals and conversation of the people, and to make their report thereof to the bishop. Whence, on account of the variety of business, it was usual to have several deacons in the same church. In the Romish church it is the deacon's office to incense the officiating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prelate; to lay the corporal on the altar; to receive the paten or cup from the subdeacon, and present them to the person officiating; to incense the choir; to receive the pix from the officiating prelate, and carry it to the subdeacon; and at the pontifical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, when the bishop gives the blessing, to put the mitre on his head, and to take off the archbishop's pall and lay it on the altar. In England, the form of ordaining deacons, declares that it is their office to assist the priest in the distribution of the holy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>: in which, agreeably to the practice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church, they are confined to the administering the wine to the communicants. A deacon in England is not capable of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> promotion; yet he may be a chaplain to a family, curate to a beneficed clergyman, or lecturer to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-church. He may be ordained at 23 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, anno currente; but it is expressly provided, that the bishop shall not ordain the same person a priest and deacon in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Deacons, according to St Paul, should be chaste, sincere, and blameless; neither <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> drinkers, nor given to filthy lucre: they should hold the mystery of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in a pure <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>; and should be well approved before they are admitted to the ministry. In the church of Scotland, the deacon's office is only to take care of the poor.

DEACONESS

Pages 112-112

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> deacon; an order of women who had their distinct offices and services in the primitive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. This office appears as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as the apostolical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>: for St Paul calls Phoebe a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the church of Cenchrea. The original word is διάκονος, answerable to the Latin word ministra. Tertullian calls them viduæ, "widows," because they were <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> chosen out of the widows of the church; and, for the same reason, Epiphanius, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Laodicea, call them ἀρχαίαι γυναῖκες, elderly women, because none but such were ordinarily taken into this office. For, indeed, by some ancient laws, these four qualifications are required in every one that was to be admitted into this order. 1. That she should be a widow. 2. That she should be a widow that had born children. 3. A widow that was but once married. 4. One of a considerable age, 40, 50, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 60 years old. Though all these rules admitted of exceptions. Concerning their ordination, whether it was always performed by imposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the learned are much divided in their sentiments. Baronius and Valesius think they were not, and made no other account of them than as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> lay persons. But the author of the constitutions, speaking of their ordination, requires the bishop to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> imposition of hands, with the form of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> which is there recited. We are not, however, to imagine, that this ordination gave them any power to execute any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sacerdotal office. They were only to perform some inferior services of the church, and those chiefly relating to the women for whose sakes they were ordained. One part of their office was to assist the minister at the baptizing of women, to undress them for immersion, and to dress them again, that the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> might be performed with all the decency becoming so sacred an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Another part of their office was to be private catechists to the women-catechumens who were preparing for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. They were likewise to attend the women that were sick and in distress; to minister to martyrs and confessors in prison; to attend the women's gate in the church; and lastly, to assign all women their places in the church, regulate their behaviour, and preside over the rest of the widows; whence in some canons they are styled στρατηγίσσαι, "governesses." This order, which since the 10th or 12th century has been wholly laid aside, was not abolished everywhere at once, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the Greek church longer than in the Latin, and in some of the Latin churches longer than in others.

DEACONRY

Pages 112-112

(Diaconia,) is also a name still reserved to the chapels and oratories in Rome, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the several deacons, in their respective regions <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. To the deaconries were annexed a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> or boards for the distribution of alms, governed by the regionary deacons, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> deacons, of whom there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, answering to the seven regions, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> being called the archdeacon. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the deaconry had an administrator for the temporal concerns, called the father of the deaconry, who was sometimes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and sometimes a layman. At present there are fourteen of these deaconries or hospitals at Rome, which are reserved to the cardinals. Du Cange gives us their names: as, the deaconry of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">Broad</a>-way, the deaconry of St Eustachio near the Pantheon, &c. DEAD LANGUAGES. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOLOGY">PHILOLOGY</a>, chap. ii. Preservation of Dead Bodies. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBALMING">EMBALMING</a>. Feast of the Dead. See FEAST OF THE DEAD.

DEAD RECKONING

Pages 112-112

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, the judgment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> estimation which is made of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where a ship is situated, without any observation of the heavenly bodies. It is discovered by keeping an account of the distance she has run by the log, and of her course steered by the compass; and by rectifying these <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a> by the usual allowance for drift, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-way, &c., according to the ship's known <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a>. This reckoning, however, is always to be corrected, as often as any good observation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> can be obtained.

DEAD-LIGHTS

Pages 112-112

certain wooden ports which are made to fasten into the cabin windows, to prevent the waves from gushing into the ship in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. As they are made exactly to fit the windows, and are strong enough to resist the waves, they are always fixed in on the approach of a storm, and the glass lights taken out, which must otherwise be shattered to pieces by the surges, and suffer <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to enter the vessel.

DEAD-MENS-EYES

Pages 112-112

in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a kind of blocks, with many holes in them, but no shevers, whereby the shrouds are fastened to the chains: the crow-feet reeve also through these holes; and, in some ships, the main-stays are set tight in them: but then they have only one hole, through which the lanyards are passed several times. See Plate CLXIX. DEAD'S <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">PART</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">LAW</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

DEAD-SEA

Pages 112-112

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a lake of Judea, into which the river Jordan discharges itself; being about 70 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPHALTITES">ASPHALTITES</a>.

DEAD-TOPS

Pages 112-113

DEAD-TOPS, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> incident to young trees, and cured by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the dead parts <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the next good twig <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shoot, and claying them over as in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a>.

DEAD-WATER

Pages 113-113

at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, the eddy-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> astern of a ship; so called because it does not <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> away so swift as the water running by her sides does. They say that a ship makes much dead-water when she has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eddy following her stern. DEADLY-CARROT. See THATIA. DEADLY-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEUD">Feud</a>, in English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, a profession of irreconcilable enmity, till a person is revenged by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his enemy. The word feud is derived from the German Feud; which, as Hottoman observes, signifies modo bellum, modo capitales intimicatus*. Such enmity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> were allowed by law in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Saxons, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was killed, and a pecuniary satisfaction was not made to the kindred, it was lawful for them to take up arms and revenge themselves on the murderer; which was called deadly feud. And this probably was the original of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">APPEAL</a>.

DEAFNESS

Pages 113-113

the state of a person who wants the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of hearing; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, which prevents its due reception of sounds. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Deafness generally arises either from an obstruction or a compression of the auditory nerve; or from some collection of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in the cavities of the inner ear; or from the auditory passage being stopped up by some hardened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>; or, lastly, from some excrescence, a swelling of the glands, or some foreign body introduced within it. Those born deaf are also dumb, as not being able to learn any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, at least in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way. However, as the eyes, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> serve them for ears, they may understand what is said by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the lips, tongue, &c. of the speaker; and even accustom themselves to move their own, as they see other people do, and by this means learn to speak.—Thus it was that Dr Wallis taught two young gentlemen born deaf to know what was said to them, and to return pertinent answers. Digby gives us another instance of the same within his own knowledge; and there was a Swiss physician in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, one John <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMMAN">Amman</a>, who reduced the thing to a fixed art or method, which he published in his Surdus Loquens, Amstelod. 1692, and de Loquela, ibid. 1700. See an account of methods employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of this class of persons, in the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEAF_AND_DUMB">DEAF and DUMB</a>, in the Supplement. In the Phil. Trans. No. 312. we have an account by Mr Waller, R. S. Secr. of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and his sister, each about 50 years old, born in the same town with Mr Waller, who had neither of them the least sense of hearing; yet both of them knew, by the motion of the lips only, whatever was said to them, and would answer pertinently to the question proposed. It seems they could both hear and speak when children, but lost their hearing afterwards: whence they retained their speech, which, though uncooth, was yet intelligible. Such another instance is that of Mr Goddy's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, minister of St Gervais in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, related by Bishop Burnet. "At two years old they perceived she had lost her hearing; and ever since, though she hears <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> noises, yet hears nothing of what is said to her. Deafness. But by observing the motions of the mouth and lips of others, she acquired so many words, that out of these she has formed a sort of jargon, in which she can hold conversation whole days with those that can speak her language. She knows nothing that is said to her, unless she see the motion of their mouths that speak to her, so that in the night they are obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> candles to speak to her. One thing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear the strangest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>: she has a sister, with whom she has practised her language more than with any body else; and in the night, by laying her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> on her sister's mouth, she can perceive by that what she says, and so can discourse with her in the dark." Burnet. Let. IV. p. 248. It is observable, that deaf persons, and several others thereto the thick of hearing, hear better and more easily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a loud noise be raised at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when you speak to them; which is owing, no doubt, to the greater tension of the ear-drum on that occasion. Dr Wallis mentions a deaf woman, who, if a drum were <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> in the room could hear any thing very clearly; so that her husband hired a drummer for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, that by this means he might hold conversation with his wife. The same author mentions another, who, living near a steeple, could always hear very well if there was a ringing of three or four bells, but never else.

DEAL

Pages 113-113

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England, lying between <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 20' N. Lat. 51° 16'. is supposed to be the Dola of Nennius, and is situated on a flat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. This town, according to Dr Campbell, justifies an observation he had made in favour of situations of this kind, viz. that they are less liable than others to be injured by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The town of Deal, as far as we are able to judge, except it may be the sea's sinking a little from it, is in much the same condition in which it ever was, even from the earliest accounts. The learned Dr Halley has proved, Miscellanea Curiosa, vol. iii. p. 426. that Julius Caesar landed here, August 26th, the year before the coming of Christ 55.—The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> convenience of landing has been of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: so that it is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous, divided into the upper and lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and is in effect the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> place in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 3420 in 1811.

DEALS

Pages 113-113

a thin kind of fir-planks, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>. They are formed by sawing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree into a great many longitudinal divisions, of more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less thickness according to the purposes they are intended to serve. A very good method of seasoning planks of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> and fir is to throw them into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> as soon as they are sawed, and keep them there three or four days, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> them: in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be rendered much harder, by drying afterwards in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>: but neither this, nor any other method yet known, will prevent them from shrinking. Rods of deal expand gradually, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the grain, in moist <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> again in dry; and thence have been found to make an useful hygrometer.

DEAN

Pages 113-115

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> and collegiate churches, and head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>. Rural-Dean, called also <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">Arch</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">Presbyter</a>, originally exercised jurisdiction over ten churches in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and afterwards became only the bishop's substitute, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> grant letters of administration, probate of wills, &c.; to convocate the clergy; and to signify to them sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and to give induction to the archdeacon. Their office is not lost in that of the archdeacons and chancellors. Dean of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">Monastery</a>, was a superior established under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, to ease him in taking care of ten monks; whence he was called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECANUS">decanus</a>. Dean and Chapter, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the bishop, to assist him with their advice in affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and also in the temporal concerns of his see. When the rest of the clergy were settled in the several parishes of each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, these were reserved for the celebration of divine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the bishop's own cathedral; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of them, who presided over the rest, obtained the name of decanus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dean, being probably at first appointed to superintend ten canons or prebendaries. All <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deans are elected by the chapter by conge d'etre from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and letters missive of recommendation, in the same manner as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>: but in those chapters that were founded by Henry VIII. out of the spoils of the dissolved monasteries, the deanery is donative, and the installation merely by the king's letters patent. The chapter, consisting of canons or prebendaries, are sometimes appointed by the king, sometimes by the bishop, and sometimes elected by each other. The dean and chapter are the nominal electors of a bishop. The bishop is their ordinary and immediate superior; and has, generally speaking, the power of visiting them, and correcting their excesses and enormities. They had also a check on the bishop at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>; for till the statute 32 Hen. VIII. c. 28. his grant or lease would not have bound his successors, unless confirmed by the dean and chapter. Dean of Guild. See Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Deanery, the office of a dean.—Deaneries and prebends may become void like a bishopric, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by deprivation, or by resignation either to the king or bishop. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a dean, prebendary, or other spiritual person, be made a bishop, all the preferments of which he was before possessed are void: and the king may present to them in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>. But they are not void by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, but only by the consecration. Death, is generally considered as the separation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> from the body; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which consists in the union thereof. Physicians usually define death by a total stoppage of the circulation of the blood, and a cessation of the animal and vital functions consequent thereon; as respiration, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, &c. An animal body, by the actions inseparable from life, undergoes a continual change. Its smallest fibres become rigid; its minute vessels grow into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> fibres no longer pervious to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>; its greater vessels grow hard and narrow; and every thing becomes contracted, closed, and bound up; whence the dryness, immobility, and extenuation, observed in old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. By such means the offices of the minuter vessels are destroyed; the humours stagnate, harden, and at length coalesce with the solids. Thus are the subtlest fluids in the body intercepted and lost, the concoction weakened, and the reparation prevented; only the coarser juices continue to run slowly through the greater vessels, to the preservation of life, after the animal functions are destroyed. At length, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of these changes, death itself becomes inevitable, as the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of life. But it is rare that life is thus <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> protracted, or that death succeeds merely from the decays and impairments of old age. Diseases, a long and horrid train, cut the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> short. The signs of death are in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> very uncertain. If we consult what Winslow or Bruchier have said on this subject, we shall be convinced, that between life and death the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> is so very undistinguishable, that even all the powers of art can scarcely determine where the one ends and the other begins. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the visage, the warmth of the body, and suppleness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, are but uncertain signs of life still subsisting; while, on the contrary, the paleness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, the coldness of the body, the stiffness of the extremities, the cessation of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and the total insensibility of the parts, are but uncertain marks of death begun. In the same manner also, with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> and breathing; these motions are so often kept under, that it is impossible to perceive them. By bringing a looking-glass near to the mouth of the person supposed to be dead, people often expect to find whether he breathes or not. But this is a very uncertain experiment; the glass is frequently sullied by the vapour of the dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s body; and often the person is still alive, though the glass is no way tarnished. In the same manner, neither <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> nor scaring, neither noises in the ears nor pungent spirits applied to the nostrils, give certain signs of the discontinuance of life; and there are many instances of persons who have endured them all, and afterwards recovered without any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> assistance, to the astonishment of the spectators. This ought to be a caution against hasty burials, especially in cases of sudden death, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DROWNING">drowning</a>, &c. Death, in Law. In law, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> death and civil death: natural, where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> itself expires; civil, where a person is not actually dead, but adjudged so by law. Thus, if any person, for whose life an estate is granted, remains beyond <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or is otherwise absent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, and no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> made of his being alive, he shall be accounted naturally dead. Brothers of Death, a denomination usually given to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of the order of St Paul, the first hermit. They are called brothers of death, fratres à morte, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a death's head which they were always to have with them, in order to keep perpetually before them the thoughts of death. This order, by its constitutions made in 1622, does not seem to have been established long before Pope Paul V. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. in 1621, permitted them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in France. The order was probably suppressed by Pope Urban VIII. Law of Death-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">Bed</a>. See Law Index. Death-Watch, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a little insect famous for a ticking noise, like the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> of a watch, which the vulgar have long taken for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESAGE">presage</a> of death in the family where it is heard: whence it is also called pediculus fatidicus, mortisaga, pulsatorius, &c. There are two kinds of death-watches. Of the first we have a good account in the Phil. Trans. by Mr Allen. It is a small beetle, 5-16ths of an inch long, of a dark <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour, spotted; having pellucid wings under under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> on the head, and two antennae proceeding from beneath the eyes, and doing the office of proboscides. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> it beats withal, he observed, was the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, which he chooses to call the upper-lip, the mouth being protracted by this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> part, and lying underneath out of view. This account is confirmed by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that instead of ticking with the upper lip, he observed the insect to draw back its mouth, and beat with its forehead. That author had two death-watches, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, which he kept alive in a box several months; and could bring one of them to beat whenever he pleased, by imitating its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a>. By this ticking noise he could frequently invite the male to get up upon the other in the way of coition. When the male found he got up in vain, he would get off again, beat very eagerly, and then up again: Whence the ingenious author concludes those pulsations to be the way whereby these insects woo one another, and find out and invite each other to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPULATION">copulation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind of death-watch is an insect in appearance quite different from the first. The former only beats seven or eight strokes at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and quicker; the latter will beat some hours together without intermission; and his strokes are more leisurely, and like the beat of a watch. This latter is a small grayish insect, much like a louse when viewed with the naked eye. It is very common in all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months: it is very nimble in running to shelter, and shy of beating when disturbed; but will beat very freely before you, and also answer the beating, if you can view it without giving it disturbance, or shaking the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it lies, &c. The author cannot say whether they beat in any other thing, but he never heard their noise except in or near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. As to their noise, the same person is in doubt whether it be made by their heads, or rather snouts, against the paper; or whether it be not made after some such manner as grasshoppers and crickets make their noise. He inclines to the former <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. The reason of his doubt is, that he observed the animal's body to shake and give a jerk at every beat, but could scarce perceive any part of its body to touch the paper. But its body is so small and near the paper, and its motion in ticking so quick, that he thinks it might be, yet he not perceive it. The ticking, as in the other, he judges to be a wooing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>; as having observed another, after much beating, come and make offers to the beating insect, who, after some offers, left off beating, and got upon the back of the other. When they were joined, he left off again; and they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some hours joined tail to tail, like dog and bitch in coition. Whether this insect changes its shape, and becomes another animal or not, he cannot say; though he has some cause to suspect that it becomes a sort of fly. It is at first a minute <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, much smaller than the nits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>; though the insect is near as big as a louse. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> it is hatched, and creeps about with its shell on. When it first leaves its shell, it is even smaller than its egg; though that be scarcely discernible without a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. In this state it is perfectly like the mites in cheese. From the mite state they grow gradually to their mature perfect state. When they become like the old ones, they are at first very small, but run about much more swiftly than before.

DEBENTURE

Pages 115-115

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of trade used at the customhouse for a kind of certificate signed by the officers of the customs, which entitles a merchant exporting goods to the receipt of a bounty <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> draw-back. All merchandises that are designed to be taken on board for that voyage being entered and shipped, and the ship being regularly cleared out, and sailed out of port on her intended voyage, debentures may be made out from the exporter's entries, in order to obtain the draw-backs, allowances, bounties, or premiums; which debentures for foreign goods are to be paid within one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after demand. And in making out these debentures, it must be observed, that every piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, containing any debenture for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> back customs or duties, must, before <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, be stamped, and pay a duty of 8d. The forms of debentures vary according to the merchandise exported. In the execution of debentures for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, it must be particularly observed, 1. That debentures for the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> may be made on one or more parchments. 2. That the exporter's oath must be printed, specifying whether he acts for himself or on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> exported to any other foreign ports than <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, the word Ireland must be added to the oath after <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. 4. That no tobacco may be consumed on board of ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> but what has paid full duties, and been manufactured in Great Britain, no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a> is to be allowed for tobacco exported in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of war. 5. That the eight pounds per hogshead of 350 pounds, or more, allowed for draught at importation, must not be deducted on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. 6. That debentures for tobacco exported to Ireland must not be paid till a certificate be produced, testifying the landing thereof. 7. That no persons may swear to the exportation but such as are permitted to swear to debentures for other goods. In debentures for all other foreign goods, no person may be admitted to swear to the exportation but the true exporter, either as a proprietor, or who, being employer by commission, is concerned in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the voyage. All kinds of debentures, before delivered or paid to the exporters, are entered into a separate book kept for that purpose by the collector and comptroller of the customs. DEBITA <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDI">FUNDI</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DEBITA Fructuum. See Law Index.

DEBILITY

Pages 115-115

among physicians, a relaxation of the solids, occasioning oftentimes weaknesses and faintings.

DEBIR

Pages 115-115

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a sacerdotal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEBRON">Hebron</a>; but neither distance, nor point of the compass on which it lies, can be determined. It was anciently called Kariath-sepher <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Kirjath-sepher, and Kirjath-sannah (Joshua).—Another Debir in the tribe of Gad, beyond Jordan.

DEBRECHEN

Pages 115-115

a town of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, about 77 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUDA">Buda</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21° 10' N. Lat. 47° 45'.

DEBRUIZED

Pages 115-115

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> peculiar to the English, by which is intimated the grievous restraint of any animal, debarred of its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> freedom, by any of the ordinances being laid over it.

DEBTOR

Pages 116-116

a person who owes anything to another; in contradistinction to creditor, which is he to whom the debt is owing.

DECADE

Pages 116-116

a word used by some old writers for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> ten, and decades for an enumeration by tens. The word is formed from the Latin decus, which is derived from a Greek word of the same import. The word has been more peculiarly appropriated to the number of books, q. d. decades, into which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Titus Livius is divided. Hence also came decadal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, the Decameron of Boccaccio, &c.

DECAGON

Pages 116-116

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a plain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> with ten sides and ten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>.

DECAGYNYA

Pages 116-116

the name of an order, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> secondary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, in the class decandria, of the sexual method, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> whose <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are furnished with ten stamens and the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of styles; which last are considered by Linnaeus and the sexualists as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in plants. Neurada and American nightshade furnish examples.

DECALOGUE

Pages 116-116

the ten precepts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> commandments delivered by God to Moses, after engraving them on two tables of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The Jews, by way of excellence, call these commandments the ten words, from whence they had afterwards the name of decalogue: but it is to be observed, that they joined the first and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> into one, and divided the last into two. They understand that against stealing to relate to the stealing of men, or kidnapping; alleging, that the stealing one another's goods or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> is forbidden in the last commandment. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian objected to the decalogue, that the precepts it contained (those only excepted which concern the worship of false gods, and the observation of the sabbath) were already so familiar to all nations, and so universally received, that they were unworthy, for that very reason, to be delivered by so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, to so peculiar a people. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome has struck the second commandment quite out of the decalogue; and to make their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> complete, hath split the tenth into two: the reason of which may be easily conceived.

DECAN

Pages 116-116

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges, bounded on the south by the kingdom of Bisnagar, on the west by the ocean, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Mogulistan, and on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which separate it from Golconda.

DECANDRIA

Pages 116-116

(ἀκή, ten, and ἀγελα, a husband), Linnaeus's tenth class, comprehending those hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which bear <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> with ten stamens. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DECANTATION

Pages 116-116

among chemists, &c. the gently pouring off a liquor from its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEES">lees</a>, by inclining the lip <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> canthus of the vessel; whence the name.

DECANUS

Pages 116-116

in Roman antiquity, an officer who presided over the other ten officers, and was head of the contubernium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILE">file</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>.

DECAPOLIS

Pages 116-116

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district Decapolis beyond Jordan, almost all of it belonging to the half tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>; before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, called Beth-decomer-sam; but after occupied by the heathen, who could not be driven out. It comprised, as the name denotes, ten <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities on the other side the Jordan, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except Scythopolis, which stood on this side, but its territory on the other.

DECAPROTI

Pages 116-116

DECENPRIMI, in Roman antiquity, officers for gathering the tributes and taxes. The decaproti were also obliged to pay for the dead, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to answer to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> for the quota parts of such as died, out of their own estates.

DECASPERMUM

Pages 116-116

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the icosaandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DECASTYLE

Pages 116-116

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> with an ordinance of ten columns in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, as the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Olympius was.

DECEIT

Pages 116-116

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a subtile trick <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> device, to which may be added all manner of craft and collusion, or underhand practice, used to defraud another, by any means whatever.

DECEMBER

Pages 116-116

the last <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> enters the tropic of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPRICORN">Capricorn</a>, and makes the winter solstice. In <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>'s year, December was the 10th month, whence the name, viz. from decem, "ten:" for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> began their year in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. The month of December was under the protection of Vesta. Romulus assigned it 30 days, Numa reduced it to 29, which Julius Caesar increased to 31. Under the reign of Commodus, this month was called, by way of flattery, Amazonius, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a courtezan whom that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> passionately loved, and had got painted like an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMAZON">Amazon</a>: but it only kept the name during that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. At the latter end of this month they had the juxtae miles tudi; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people kept the feast of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Vacuna in the fields, having then gathered in their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and sown their corn; whence seems to be derived our popular festival called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-home.

DECEMPAGI

Pages 116-116

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>: Now Dience, in Lorrain, on the rivulet Scille <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Selna, near the lake Lindre, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> German miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANCY">Nancy</a>.

DECEMPEDA

Pages 116-116
Amazons, ten-feet rod, an instrument used by the ancients in measuring. The decempeda was a rule or rod divided into ten feet; whence its name, from decem, "ten," and pes, pedis, "foot." The foot was subdivided into twelve inches, and each inch into ten digits. The decempeda was used both in measuring of land, like the chain among us; and by architects to give the proper dimensions and proportions to the parts of their buildings, which use it still retains. Horace, lib. ii. od. i5, blaming the magnificence and delicacy of the buildings of his time, observes, that it was otherwise in the times of Romulus and Cato; that in the houses of private persons there were not then known any porticoes measured out with the decempeda, nor turned to the north to take the cool air.

DECEMVIRI

Pages 116-117

ten magistrates of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The privileges of the patricians raised dissatisfaction among the plebeians; who, though freed from the power of the Tarquins, still <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> depended upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> and caprice of their superiors, without any written statute to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them, and convince them that they were governed with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> and impartiality. The tribunes complained to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and demanded that a code of laws might be framed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and benefit of the Roman people. The petition was complied with; and three ambassadors were sent to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and all the other Grecian states, to collect the laws of Solon and of all the other celebrated legislators of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Upon the return of the commissioners it was universally agreed, that ten new magistrates called Decemviri should be elected from the senate to put the project into execution. Their power was absolute, all other offices ceased after their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, and they presided over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> with regal authority. They were invested with the badges of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, in the enjoyment of which they succeeded by turns, and only one was preceded by the fasces, and had the power of assembling the senate and confirming decrees. The first decemvirs were Appius Claudius, T. Genutius, P. Sextus, Sp. Veturius, C. Julius, A. Manlius, Ser. Sulpius, Pluricius, T. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, Sp. Posthumius, in the year of Rome 302. Under them the laws, which had been exposed to public view, that every citizen might speak his sentiments, were publicly approved of as constitutional, and ratified by the priests and augurs in the most solemn and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> manner. They were ten in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and were engraved on tables of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; two were afterwards added, and they were called the laws of the twelve tables, leges duodecim tabularum, and leges decemvirales. The decemviral power, which was beheld by all ranks of people with the greatest satisfaction, was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>; but in the third year after their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> the decemvirs became odious on account of their tyranny; and the attempt of Ap. Claudius to ravish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> totally abolished that office. The people were so exasperated against them, that they demanded them from the senate to burn them alive. Consuls were again appointed, and tranquillity re-established in the state. There were other officers in Rome called decemvirs, who were originally appointed in the absence of the praetor to administer justice. Their appointment became afterwards necessary, and they generally assisted at sales, called subastaiones, because a spear, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HASTA">hasta</a>, was fixed at the door of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the goods were exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. They were called decemviri lictibus judicandis. The officers whom Tarquinius appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the Sibylline books were also called decemviri. They were originally two in number, called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUUMVIRI">duumviri</a>, till the year of Rome 388, when their number was increased to ten, five of which were chosen from the plebeians and five from the patricians. Sylla increased their number to fifteen, called quindecemviri.

DECENNALIA

Pages 117-117
ancient Roman festivals, celebrated by the emperors every tenth year of their reign, with sacrifices, games, and largesses for the people. The emperor Augustus first instituted these solemnities, in which he was imitated by his successors. At the same time the people offered up vows for the emperor, and for the perpetuity of the empire; which were therefore called vota decennalia. Augustus's view in establishing the decennalia was to preserve the empire and the sovereign power without offence or restraint to the people. For during the celebration of this feast, that Decennalia prince used to surrender up all his authority into the hands of the people; who filled with joy, and charmed with the goodness of Augustus, immediately delivered it him back again.

DECHALES

Pages 117-117

CLAUDIUS FRANCES MILLIET, an excellent mathematician, mechanic, and astronomer, descended from a noble family, and born at Chambery in 1611. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> performances are an edition of Euclid's Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, in which the unseemly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> are rejected, and the uses of those retained annexed; a discourse on fortification; and another on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. These with others have been collected, first in 3 vols folio, and afterwards in 4, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Mundus Mathematicus: being indeed a complete course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. He died in 1673, professor of mathematics in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>.

DECIATES

Pages 117-117
or Deciati, in Ancient Geography, a people of Galia Narbonensis, next the borders of Italy, on the Mediterranean. Now the diocese of Grasse and Antibes. Deciatum oppidum, was a town situated between Antibes and Nice.

DECIDUOUS

Pages 117-117

an appellation chiefly used in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>: thus, the calyx <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cup of a flower is said to be deciduous, when it falls along with the flower-petals; and, on the contrary, it is called permanent, when it remains after they are fallen. Again, deciduous leaves are those which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in autumn; in contradistinction to those of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, which remain all the winter. See DEFOILATION.

DECIL

Pages 117-117

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an aspect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> position of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, when they are distant from each other a tenth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

DECIMATION

Pages 117-118

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, on such <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> as quitted their posts, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> behaved themselves cowardly in the field. The names of the guilty were put into an urn or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, and as many were drawn out as made the tenth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and those were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and the others saved. This was called decimare; a word of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, who, to punish whole legions when they had failed in their duty, made every tenth soldier draw lots, and put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for an example to the others. As the Romans had their decimatio, they had also the vicissimatio, and even centesimatio, when only the 20th or 100th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> suffered by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>.

DECIPHERING

Pages 118-118

the art of finding the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> of a cipher. For the art both of Ciphering and Deciphering, see the article Cipher. DECIUS Mus, a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, who, after many glorious exploits, devoted himself to the gods manco for the safety of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against the Latins, about 340 years before the Augustan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His son Decius imitated his example, and devoted himself in like manner in his fourth consulship, when fighting against the Gauls and Samnites. His grandson also did the same in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against Pyrrhus and the Tarentines. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of devoting one's self was of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the state. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were animated by the example, and induced to follow with intrepidity a commander who, arrayed in an unusual dress, and addressing himself to the gods with solemn invocation, rushed into the thickest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the enemy to meet his fate.

DECIUS

Pages 118-118

Cn. Metius, Q. Trojanus, a native of Pannonia, sent by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> to appease a sedition in Moesia. Instead of obeying his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s command, he assumed the imperial purple, and soon after marched against him, and at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> became the only emperor. He signalized himself against the Persians; and, when he marched against the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, he pushed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> into a deep marsh, from which he could not extricate himself, and he perished with all his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> by the darts of the barbarians, A.D. 251, after a reign of two years. DECK of a Ship (from decken, Dan. to cover); the planked floors of a ship, which connect the sides together, and serve as different platforms to support the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and lodge the men, as also to preserve the cargo from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in merchant vessels. As all ships are broader on the lower deck than on the next above it, and as the cannon thereof are always heaviest, it is necessary that the frame of it should be much stronger than that of the others; and for the same reason the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> middle deck ought to be stronger than the upper deck or forecastle. Ships of the first and second <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> are furnished with three whole decks, reaching from the stem to the stern, besides a forecastle and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-deck, which extends from the stern to the mainmast; between which and the forecastle a vacancy is left in the middle, opening to the upper deck, and forming what is called the waist. There is yet another deck above the hinder or aftmost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the quarter-deck, called the poop, which also serves as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>'s cabin or couch. The inferior ships of the line of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> are equipped with two decks and a half; and frigates, sloops, &c., with one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-deck and a half, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>-deck below to lodge the crew. The decks are formed and sustained by the beams, the clamps, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-ways, the carlings, the ledges, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and two rows of small pillars called stanchions, &c. See those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. That the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the deck, with its corresponding parts, may be more clearly understood, we have exhibited a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the lower-deck of a 74 gun ship in Plate CLXIX. And as both sides of the deck are exactly similar, the pieces by which it is supported appear on one side, and on the other side the planks of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of which it is composed, as laid upon those upper pieces. A, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> or main <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a>-way. B, the stern-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>. C, the stern. D, the beams, composed of three pieces, as exhibited by D, in one of which the dotted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> show the arrangement of one of the beams under the other side of the deck. E, part of the vertical or hanging knees. F, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> or lodging knees, which fasten the beams to the sides. G, the carlings, ranging fore and aft from one beam to another. H, the gun-ports. I, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>-dales, being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> wooden tubes, which return the water from the pumps into the sea. K, the spurs of the beams, being curved pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> serving as half-beams to support the decks, where a whole beam cannot be placed on account of the hatchways. L, the wing-transom, which is bolted by the middle to the stern-post, and whose ends rest upon the fashion-pieces. M, the bulk-head or partition which incloses the manger, and prevents the water which enters at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAWSE">hawse</a>-holes from running aft between decks.

DECLAMATION

Pages 119-121

a speech made in public, in the tone and manner of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, uniting the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> to the propriety of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, in order to give the sentiment its full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon the mind. According to the manners and customs of the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, public harangues are made only, 1. In the pulpit. 2. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other public <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. 3. By public professors. 4. On the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. I. With regard to the declamation of the pulpit, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and sanctity of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the importance of the subject, require the preacher to exert the utmost powers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> to produce a pronunciation that is perfectly distinct and harmonious, and that he observe a deportment and action which is expressive and graceful. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, therefore, who is destitute of a voice, should ascend the pulpit, and there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a pantomime before his audience. The preacher should not, however, roar like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> crier, and rend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> with a voice of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>; for such kind of declamation is not only without meaning and without persuasion, but highly incongruous with the meek and gentle expressions of the gospel. He should likewise take particular care to avoid a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a>; his voice should rise from the beginning, as it were by degrees, and its greatest strength should be exerted in the application. Each inflection of the voice should be adapted to the phrase, and to the meaning of the words; and each remarkable expression should have its peculiar inflexion. The dogmatic requires a plain, uniform tone of voice only; and the menaces of the gospel demand a greater force than do its promises and rewards; but the latter should not be pronounced in the soft tone of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, nor the former with the loud <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>. The voice should still retain its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tone in all its various inflexions. Happy is that preacher, to whom <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has given a voice that is at once strong, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, and harmonious. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of complacency and benevolence, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, should be constantly visible in the countenance of the preacher. But every appearance of affectation must be carefully avoided; for nothing is so disgustful to an audience as even the semblance of dissimulation. Eyes constantly rolling, turned towards heaven, and streaming with tears, rather denote a hypocrite, than a man possessed of the real spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and that feels the true import of what he preaches. An air of affected devotion infallibly destroys the efficacy of all that the preacher can say, however <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and important it may be. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he must avoid every appearance of mirth or raillery, or of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> unfeeling manner which is so apt to freeze the hearts of his hearers. The body should be in general erect, and in a natural and easy attitude. The perpetual movement or contortion of the body has a ridiculous effect in the pulpit, and makes the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a preacher and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARLEQUIN">harlequin</a> much too similar. But, on the other hand, he ought not to remain constantly upright and motionless like a speaking statue. The motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> give a strong expression to a discourse; but they should be constantly decent, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, noble, and expressive. The preacher who is incessantly in action, who is perpetually clasping his hands, or who menaces with a clenched fist, or counts his arguments on his fingers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> only excite mirth among his auditory. In a word, declamation is an art that the sacred orator should <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> with the utmost assiduity. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of a sermon is to convince, to affect, and to persuade. The voice, the countenance, and the action, which are to produce this triple effect, are therefore the objects to which the preacher should particularly apply himself. II. The declamation of a minister or statesman in the senate, in council, or other public assembly, is of a more unconfined nature. To persuade, to move the passions, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> an ascendency in a public assembly, the orator should himself feel the force of what he says, and the declamation should only express that internal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. But nothing should be carried to excess. A suavity in the tone of voice, a dignity of deportment, a graceful action, and a certain tranquillity of countenance, should constantly accompany the statesman when he speaks in public, even when he is most earnestly engaged in debate, or when he is addressing his sovereign in person. A pleasing tone of voice and a distinct pronunciation, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the hearers greatly in the speaker's favour. A young man may improve these to a surprising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, who had a natural impediment in his speech, was accustomed to go to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shore, and partly filling his mouth with pebbles, he declaimed with a loud voice. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> by degrees gave a volubility to his tongue, and the roaring of the waves reconciled him insensibly to the noise of the multitude. III. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of a public professor is the instruction of the studious youth; for which purpose he is to convince and persuade. Every tone of voice, every expression of the countenance, or action of the body, which can produce this effect by enforcing the words, should therefore be employed by those who are Declaiming to teach the science. There is, moreover, one very essential reflection which every professor ought to make, and which is, that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> from which he hangs is surrounded by young students, naturally possessed with vivacity, not unfrequently ludicrous; and for the most part previously instructed in the preparatory sciences. They are therefore constantly inclined to criticise, to jest, and to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; for which reason, the professor should endeavour to inspire them with respect and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, by a grave, commanding, and venerable countenance, and carefully avoid all appearance of grimace in his action, and every kind of affectation in his discourse, that he may not afford the least opportunity of pleasantry. IV. We now come to theatric declamation. This was very different among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> from what it is, and ought to be, with us, from the nature of the thing itself, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of circumstances. Numberless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in Quintilian, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians, critics, grammarians, and commentators, evidently prove, that the ancient dramatic declamation was subservient to the rules of the musical rhythmus; and by this, according to Aristides*, their action, as well as recital, was regulated. But to explain this seeming <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>, it will be necessary to make here some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> remarks. The ancients gave a much more extensive signification than we do to the word music (musica), which they derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, or at least from some of them. It is for this reason that the same Aristides and Quintilian defined it to be "An art that teaches all that relates to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the voice, and the manner of performing all the motions of the body with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>:" Ars decoris in vocibus et motibus. Therefore <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, declamation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, pantomimes, and many other gestures and exercises, were subservient to this art. 2. That part of general music which taught the art of declamation and gesture according to the rules of an established method (and which we perform by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, or at most by the aid of common <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>), was distinguished by the name hypocritic music; and this musical art was called by the Greeks orchesis, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> salutio. It was, however, so far from being an advantage to the ancients to have had this art, which we have not, that it was, on the contrary, a mark of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> imperfection. For, in the first place, it was an instance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> absurdity to represent a tragedy, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, before an audience of twenty thousand people, the far greatest part of whom could neither hear nor see what passed to any good purpose, unless they were possessed of organs which we have not. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> may conveniently contain about a thousand persons; and that is found sufficient in the most populous cities, where there are several places of entertainment on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and where the people are reasonable enough to succeed each other in their diversions. As the features of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> could not be distinguished at so great a distance, and still less the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of countenance; in order to represent the different passions, they were obliged to have recourse to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a>, a wretched childish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, that destroyed all the strength and variety of expression.
