Their action became extravagant, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> subservient to a regular mechanism; which prevented all the refinement, and all the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of surprise, in the performance, and must have had an effect horribly disagreeable to those who were placed near the stage. 3. The egregious imperfection of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> likewise, which consisted of syllables <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> was determined by a set <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of time, and their manner of tuning these syllables, after the method of the orchesis of the Greeks, was another disadvantage. For by this means they determined by notes or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> placed after the long and short syllables, not only the nature, but the duration, of each action. Now, nothing could be more affected, more constrained and disgustful, than such a method of declaiming. How far superior in this respect are the moderns, who consult nature alone in their theatric declamation; who can make the audience hear each sigh; who can accompany it with a proper attitude; who can incessantly vary their action; who can <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the lucky moment, and make the countenance fully express the sensations of the mind! Nature does all here; and art, infinitely inferior to nature, did all among the ancients. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> declamation cannot be subservient to a musical rhythmus, seeing we speak rapidly, and without affectation. Our <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> learn their art without art, from nature itself, assisted by reflection; and they arrive at a degree of excellence infinitely greater than that of the ancients, by a method far more simple, and by efforts incomparably more easy. 4. We do not, moreover, precisely know what the theatric declamation of the ancients was; nor what were the musical instruments which accompanied that declamation. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the Eunuch of Terence says, for example, "that Flaccus, the freedman of Claudius, made the music of that piece, in which he employed the two flutes, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and the left." These flutes, it is likely, gave the tone to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, which must have had a very odd effect on the audience. Most of the ancient pieces have similar titles. They who would be particularly informed of the art of declaiming among the Greeks and Romans, may read to advantage the Critical Reflections on Poetry and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a> by the Abbé du <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>. The third part of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> consists entirely of learned researches and ingenious reflections on this silly practice of the ancients. But as this art has happily no place in modern declamation, and can at best serve only to make a parade of erudition, we shall say no more of it, but <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to matters of real utility. 5. We think there is good reason to believe, moreover, that the most polished nations of modern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> do not accompany their discourses in general with so many gesticulations, as did the Greeks, the Romans, and other inhabitants of warm climates. They appear to have found the method of animating a discourse, and giving it an expression, by the simple inflections of the voice, and by the features of the countenance; which is far more decent, more just and rational, than all those contortions which perpetually derange the natural attitude of the body and its members, and give the speaker the air of a harlequin. 6. Expression, therefore, forms at once the essence and the end of declamation: and the means of producing it consists, in a pronunciation that is sonorous, distinct, and pleasing, supported by an action that is decent and proper to the subject. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the best dramatic poet has need of a good declaimer or actor to make his his writings produce their proper effect, the actor has likewise need of a good poet to enable him to please and affect by the action; for it is to little purpose that he endeavours to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> his auditory by uniting with nature, all the powers of art, if the poet has not furnished him with sentiments that are rational and affecting. 7. The actor, in studying his part before a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> mirror, where he can see his whole figure, in order to determine the most proper expressions for every thought, should consult nature, and endeavour to imitate her. But in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, he should take care not to make too servile a copy. He has this to observe, in common with his colleagues, the masters in all the polite arts: The theatre is intended to exhibit an imitation of nature, and not nature itself. Tragedy and comedy form pictures of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but these pictures are also pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, which require strokes somewhat stronger than nature, that they may be discerned at a distance. The actor is elevated to a considerable height from the ground; he is surrounded by scenery, he is separated from the audience by the orchestra, and he speaks in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; all this is not natural; but the spectator is to accede to this necessary illusion, in order to promote his own pleasure, which would not be so great as it were all these matters otherwise disposed. Declamation, therefore, should somewhat exceed, but never lose sight of, nature. 8. The tone of the actor's voice should be natural, but regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the theatre; sufficiently loud to be heard by all the audience, but not so violent as to rend their ears. A pure and graceful pronunciation, without any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a>, is likewise a great merit in an actor; and he should also habituate himself to speak in a manner perfectly distinct. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> point in pronouncing of verse, not to separate the two hemistichs, by resting too long on the caesura in the middle, or dwelling on the end of each hemistich: for, by so doing, the actor falls into a monotony, an insufferable uniformity of cadence, in a piece that consists of some thousand verses. The gradations of the voice demand also a very judicious observance. The speaker, who begins in a high tone, will find it very difficult to sustain it through the whole piece; and he, who clamours incessantly, will find his lungs fail him in those parts where the vehemence of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> requires the strongest efforts. If we may be allowed the expression, the strongest touches, the boldest figures, will not there stand out from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in a striking manner. 9. The deportment of an actor should be constantly graceful, decent, and proper to the character he represents. An old man has a different position of body from a young petit-maitre; an aged <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> from a young princess; a noble gallant from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre. A rational observance of nature, and an imitation of the best actors, are here the surest guides. The same may be said of the action of the hands, the theatric step, &c. An inanimated figure, a body in the position of a statue, and hands immovable, are as displeasing in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, as a player whose incessant gesticulation resembles the action of a puppet. 10. Every actor who aspires to make his art something more than merely <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>, will begin by enabling himself readily to repeat his part, that the defect of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> may not embarrass his action. When he is so far a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it, he will make it the subject of serious reflection in his closet; endeavour to seize the true sense of the author; and to find out that expression of each sentiment and passion, which is the most natural, the most striking, and best adapted to the stage; and which he will cultivate by repeated essays, till he is able to render it in its full force. DECLARATORY ACTION. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">LAW</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DECLINATION

Pages 121-121

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the distance of any celestial object from the equinoctial, either northward <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> southward. It is either true or apparent, according as the real or apparent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the object is considered. See ASTRONOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DECLINATION of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Compass or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>, is its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from the true meridian of any place. DECLINATION of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">Plane</a> or Wall, in Dialing, is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> contained between the plane and the prime vertical circle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you reckon from east to west; or between the meridian and the plane, reckoning from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south. Many ways are used for finding this declination: but the most easy and practicable is by a declinator. See DECLINATOR.

DECLINATOR

Pages 121-121
or DECLINATORY, an instrument chiefly used in practical dialing, for taking the declinations, inclinations, or reclinations of the planes on which the dials are to be delineated. See DIALING, No. 24, 25. DECLINATION of Judges. See LAW Index.

DECOCTION

Pages 121-122

usually signifies either the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> a substance in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the water itself in which the substance has been boiled. It is only applicable to matters containing some principles soluble in water: such particularly are animal and vegetable matters. Decoction ought not to be used with such substances as contain any volatile principles, as they would be dissipated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. But it may be safely used, nay even becomes necessary, when the matters to be treated are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture; because then the water could not extract its principles without a boiling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Most soft animal matters, as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, skin, tendons, may be conveniently boiled in water; because they contain no principle volatile with a boiling heat. Water extracts from them nothing but a gelatinous substance, and some oily parts which float on the surface of the water. All vegetable matters which are inodorous, and particularly those which are hard, as roots, barks, &c. are generally boiled, when an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of their principles by water is required.—To this rule, however, there are some exceptions. Peruvian bark, for instance, gives its strength to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water better than to such as is boiling hot. Many other vegetables also have the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of yielding less to boiling than to cold water. And therefore a general rule may be established, that decoction ought not to be employed but when absolutely necessary; that is, when the same principles, or the same quantities of those principles, cannot be obtained by an infusion, and that without heat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it can be so done, considering that the proximate principles Decoys of vegetables are generally so delicate, and so susceptible of change and decomposition, that frequently the most gentle heat changes much their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and properties.

DECOLLATION

Pages 122-122

BEHEADING**, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> seldom used but in the phrase *decollation* of St John Baptist: which denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, wherein is represented the Baptist's head struck off from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the feast held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>.

DECOMPOSITION

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, usually signifies the disunion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> separation of the constituent parts of bodies.—It differs from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; for when a body is chemically decomposed, the parts into which it is resolved are essentially different from the body itself: and though a mechanical force be applied to it ever so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, or with ever so much violence, the minutest particles into which the body may be reduced still retain their original <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>.—Thus, for example, though we suppose nitre, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, to be reduced to ever so fine powder, each particle retains the nature of nitre, as much as the largest unpounded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> sulphuric acid be applied, a decomposition takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and one of the component parts of the nitre, namely the nitric acid, rises in the form of fumes, which lay hid in the mild neutral salt. See DECOMPOSITION, CHEMICAL, SUPPLEMENT.

DECORATION

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, any thing that adorns and enriches a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, either without side or within. The orders of architecture contribute greatly to the decoration; but then the several parts of those orders must have their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> proportions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and ornaments; otherwise the finest order <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring confusion rather than richness. See ARCHITECTURE. Decorations in churches are paintings, vases, festoons, &c. occasionally applied to the walls; and with so much conduct and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, as not to take off anything from the form of the architecture: as is much practised in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> at the solemn feasts. **DECORATION** is more particularly applied to the scenes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>. In operas, and other theatrical performances, the decorations must be frequently changed conformably to the subject. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had two kinds of decorations for their theatres: the first, called *versatiles*, having three sides, or faces, which were turned successively to the spectators: the other called *ductiles*, showing a new decoration by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> or sliding another before it. This latter sort is still used, and apparently with much greater success than among the ancients, who were obliged to draw a curtain whenever they made a change in the decorations; whereas on our stage the change is made in a moment, and almost without being perceived.

DECORUM

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is the suitableness of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and the several parts and ornaments thereof, to the station and occasion.

DECOUPLE

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the same as uncoupled; thus a chevron decouple is a chevron wanting so much of it towards the point, that the two ends stand at a distance from one another, being parted and uncoupled.

DECOY

Pages 122-122

among fowlers, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> made for catching wild-fowl. A decoy is generally made where there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pond surrounded by a wood, and beyond that a marshy and uncultivated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is not thus surrounded, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be attended with the noise and other accidents which may be expected to frighten the wild-fowl from a quiet haunt, where they <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in security. If these noises <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disturbances are wilful, it hath been held that an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> will <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> against the disturber.—As soon as the evening sets in, the decoy rises (as they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> it), and the wild fowl feed during the night. If the evening is still, the noise of their wings, during their flight, is heard at a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance, and is a pleasing though rather melancholy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. This rising of the decoy in the evening, is in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> called *raddling*. The decoy-ducks are fed with hempseed, which is thrown over the skreens in small quantities, to bring them forwards into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, and to allure the wild fowl to follow, as this seed is so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> as to float. There are several pipes, as they are called, which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> up a narrow ditch that closes at last with a funnel-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>. Over these pipes (which grow narrower from their first entrance) is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of netting suspended on hoops. It is necessary to have a pipe or ditch for almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> that can blow, as upon this circumstance it depends which pipe the fowl will take to; and the decoy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> always keeps on the leeward side of the ducks, to prevent his effluvia reaching their sagacious nostrils. All along each pipe, at certain intervals, are placed skreens made of reeds, which are so situated, that it is impossible the wild-fowl should see the decoy-man, before they have passed on towards the end of the pipe, where the purse-net is placed. The inducement to the wild-fowl to go up one of these pipes is, because the decoy-ducks trained to this lead the way, either after hearing the whistle of the decoy-man, or enticed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>-seed; the latter will dive under water whilst the wild-fowl fly on, and are taken in the purse. It often happens, however, that the wild-fowl are in such a state of sleepiness and dozing, that they will not follow the decoy-ducks. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">Use</a> is then generally made

DECREMENT

Pages 122-123

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, signifies the wane of Decrement; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> from the full to the new. The moon in this state is called moon decrecent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in decours; and when borne in coat armour, faces to the left side of the escutcheon, as she does to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side when in the increment.

DECREPIDITUDE

Pages 123-123

in Medicine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the infirmities of old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; which by degrees leads to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. See Death.

DECREPITATION

Pages 123-123

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, signifies the quick separation of the parts of a body, occasioned by a strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and accompanied with a crackling noise. This effect is most frequently produced by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> contained betwixt the parts of the decrepitating body, when these parts have a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> together. This water being quickly reduced into vapour by the heat suddenly applied to it, rarefies and bursts with noise the parts which compress it. The bodies most subject to decrepitation are certain salts, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, sulphate of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, nitrate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, &c., the decrepitation of all which proceeds from the water of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>. Clays which are not perfectly dry, and flints, are also subject to decrepitation.

DECRETAL

Pages 123-123

in the canon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of a pope, determining some point <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> question in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> law. The decretals compose the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the canon law. The first genuine one, acknowledged by all the learned as such, is a letter of Pope Siricius, written in the year 385, to Himerus bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARRAGONA">Tarragona</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, concerning some disorders which had crept into the churches of Spain. Gratian published a collection of decretals, containing all the ordinances made by the popes till the year 1150. Gregory IX, in 1227, following the example of Theodosius and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, formed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of his own, collecting into one body all the decisions and all the causes which served to advance the papal power; which collection of decretals was called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">pentateuch</a>, because it contains five books.

DECUMARIA

Pages 123-123

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dodecanidia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under those of which the order is doubtful.

DECUMATES AGRI

Pages 123-123

tithed fields, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> granted on a tithe, as appears from Tacitus, to that rabble of Gauls who succeeded the Marcomanni, that had till then proved a check to the Roman conquests up the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; and hence probably their name, people living on the marches or limits of the empire. In Cicero we have <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AGER">Ager</a> Decumans, which is of the same import with the Ager Decumanus of Tacitus.

DECURIO

Pages 123-123

a subaltern officer in the Roman armies. He commanded a decuria, which consisted of ten men, and was the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a turma, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the 30th part of a legio of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, which was composed of 580 men. There were certain magistrates in the provinces, called decuriones municipales, who formed a body to represent the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> in free and corporate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. They consisted of ten, whence the name; and their duty extended to watch over the interests of their fellow citizens, and to increase the revenues of the commonwealth. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> was called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURIA">curia</a> decurionum and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> senatus; and their decrees, called decreta decurionum, were marked with two D. D. at the top. They generally styled themselves civitatum patres curiae.

DEDICATION

Pages 123-124

in literature, is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> prefixed to a book, soliciting <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> testifying respect for the person to whom it is made. The dedication of the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mr Edwards's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Birds, is curious: To God! the one eternal! the incomprehensible, the omnipresent, omniscient, and almighty Creator of all things that exist! from orbs immeasurably <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, to the minutest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>!—this Atom is dedicated and devoted, with all possible <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a>, and worship, and the highest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> both of body and mind, by his most resigned, low, and humble creature, G. E.

DEE

Pages 124-125

JOHN, a famous mathematician and astrologer, was born (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1527) in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where his father was a wealthy vintner. In 1542, he was sent to St John's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. After five years <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> application to mathematical studies, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in order to visit several eminent mathematicians on the continent. Having <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> abroad near a year, he returned to Cambridge, and was there elected one of the fellows of Trinity college, then first erected by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. In 1548, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; and, in the same year, left England a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; his stay at home being rendered uneasy to him, by the suspicions that were entertained of his being a conjuror; arising partly from his application to astronomy, but especially on account of a piece of machinery in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, which he exhibited to the university, and in which he represented the scarabaeus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> up to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of victuals on its back. These suspicions he could never after shake off; nor did his subsequent conduct, as we shall see, tend to clear him of the imputation; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he was not actually a conjuror, it was not for want of endeavours. Upon leaving England, he went to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>; where he was much esteemed, and visited by several persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. Here he resided about two years, and then set out for France; where, in the college of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, he read lectures of Euclid's elements with vast applause. In 1551, he returned to England, and was introduced by the secretary Cecil to King Edward, who assigned him a pension of 100 crowns, which he afterwards relinquished for the rectory of Upton upon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>: but soon after the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, having some correspondence with the lady <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s servants, he was accused of practising against the queen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by enchantment. On this account he suffered a tedious confinement, and was several times examined; till, in the year 1555, he obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> by an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. When Queen Elizabeth ascended the throne, our astrological Dee was consulted by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, concerning a propitious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> for her majesty's coronation. He was on this occasion introduced to the queen, who made him <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> promises, which were never performed, though she condescended to receive his instructions relative to the mystical interpretation of some of his unintelligible writings, which he published about this time. In 1564, he made another voyage to the continent; in order to present a book which he had dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian. He returned to England in the same year: but in 1571, we find him in Lorraine, where, being dangerously ill, the queen sent over two physicians. physicians to his relief. Having once more returned to his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he settled at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTLAKE">Mortlake</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, where he continued his studies with unremitting ardour, and collected a considerable library of curious books and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and a variety of instruments; most of which were afterwards destroyed by the mob, as belonging to one who dealt with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. In 1578, the queen being much indisposed, Mr Dee was sent abroad to consult with German physicians and philosophers (astrologers no doubt) on the occasion. We now behold him again in England, where he was soon after employed in a more rational <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Her majesty, desirous to be informed concerning her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to those countries which had been discovered by her subjects, commanded Mr Dee to consult the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> records, and furnish her with proper geographical descriptions. Accordingly, in a short time he presented to the queen, in the gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rolls, in which the discovered countries were geographically described and historically illustrated. These rolls are preserved in the Cotton library, Augustus I. His next employment was the reformation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, on which subject he wrote a rational and learned treatise, preserved in the Ashmolean library at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Hitherto the extravagancies of our eccentric <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> seem to have been counterpoised by a tolerable proportion of reason and science; but henceforward we consider him as a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> necromancer and credulous alchemist. In the year 1581, he became acquainted with one Edward Kelly, by whose assistance he performed diverse incantations, and maintained a frequent imaginary intercourse with spirits. He was particularly intimate, it seems, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> Raphael and Gabriel. One of them made him a present of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> speculum, in which his angels and demons appeared as often as he had occasion for them; they answered his questions, and Kelly's business was to record their dictates: Kelly did all his feats upon The devil's looking-glass, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. HUDIB. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANTO">Canto</a> iii. 631. In 1583, they were both introduced to a certain Polish nobleman, then in England, named Albert Laski, palatine of Siradia, a person equally addicted to the same ridiculous pursuits. He was so charmed with Dee and his companions, that he persuaded them to accompany him to his native country. They embarked for Holland in Sept. 1583; and travelling over <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, arrived at the town of Laski in February following. Their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, however, finding himself abused by their idle pretensions, persuaded them to pay a visit to Rudolph king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>; who, though a credulous man, was soon disgusted with their nonsense. They were afterwards introduced to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, but with no better success. Soon after this, they were invited by a rich Bohemian nobleman to his castle of Trebona, where they continued for some time in great affluence: owing, as they asserted, to their art of transmutation by means of a certain powder in the possession of Kelly. Dee, now quarrelling with his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in iniquity, quitted Bohemia, and returned to England, where he was once more graciously received by the queen; who, in 1595, made him warden of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> college, in which town he resided several years. In 1604, he returned to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Mortlake, where he died in the year 1628, aged 81; leaving a large family, and many works behind him.—The black stone into which Dee used to call his spirits, was in the collection of the earls of Peterborough, whence it came to Lady Elizabeth Germaine. It was next the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle, and is now Mr Walpole's. It appears upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> to be nothing but a polished piece of cannel coal.—That Dee was a man of considerable acquirements, is beyond a doubt; his mathematical knowledge is generally allowed; but, unless we suppose him a wicked impostor, which is by no means improbable, we must transmit him to posterity as one of the most foolish superstitious necromancers of his time. Nevertheless, the celebrated Dr Hook, many years after Dee's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, took it into his head to prove that his journal, published by Casaubon, was entirely cryptographical, concealing his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> transactions, and that he was employed by Queen Elizabeth as a spy.

DEEMSTERS

Pages 125-125
or DEMSTERS (from the Saxon dema, judge or umpire). All controversies in the isle of Man are decided without process, writings, or any charges, by certain judges, chosen yearly from among themselves, called deemsters; there being two of them for each division of the island: they sit judges in all courts, either for life or property; and with the advice of 24 keys, declare what is law in uncommon emergencies.

DEEPING

Pages 125-125

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England, seated in a fenny ground, on the river Weland, six miles east from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 20. N. Lat. 52. 35.

DEER

Pages 125-125

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>. See CERVUS.—The method of hunting deer in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon is very particular. The huntsmen go out in the night, and only two usually go together; the one of these carries upon his head an earthen vessel, in which there is some fire <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> and flaming; the ingredients are generally small sticks cut into pieces, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rosin. Of this the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> carries a supply about him to replenish the pot when it grows low. The person who has the fire upon his head, carries in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, on which there are fixed eight bells; and the larger these are, the better. This man goes first into the woods, and the other follows <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> behind with a spear in his hand. As soon as the deer hears the noise of the bells, he turns towards the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> whence the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> comes; and seeing the fire, he eagerly runs up to it, and stands gazing at a small distance: the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> man

DEFENDANT

Pages 125-126

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the person sued in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> personal; as tenant is he who is sued in an action real. See ACTION. DEFENDER of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a> (Fidei Defensor), a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England; as Catholicus to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and Christianissimus to the king of France, &c. These titles were given by the popes of Rome. That of Fidei Defensor was first conferred by Leo X. on King Henry VIII. for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> against Martin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>; and the bull for it bears <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> quinto idus Octob. 1521. It was afterwards confirmed by Clement VII. But the pope, on Henry's suppressing the houses of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Reformation, not only deprived him of his title, but deposed him from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> also: though in the 35th year of his reign, his title, &c. was confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and hath <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be used by all succeeding kings to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Chamberlayne says, the title belonged to the king of England before that time; and for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> hereof appeals to several charters granted to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. So that Pope Leo's bull was only a renovation of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>.

DEFENDERS

Pages 126-126

were anciently notable dignitaries both in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state, whose business was to look to the preservation of the public weal, to protect the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and helpless, and to maintain the interests and causes of churches and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses. See PROTECTOR. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>, can. 2, calls the defender of a church Exclusus Codin, de officio curiae Const. makes mention of defenders of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. There were also a defender of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, defensor regni; defenders of cities, defensores civitatis; defenders of the people, defensores plebis; of the poor, fatherless, widows, &c. About the year 420, each patriarchal church began to have its defender; which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was afterwards introduced into other churches, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to later days under other names; as those of Advocate and Advocate. In the year 407, we find the council of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> asked the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, for defenders, of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Scholastici, i.e. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> who were in office; and that it might be allowed them to enter and search the cabinets and papers of the judges and other civil magistrates, whenever it should be found necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the church.

DEFERENS

Pages 126-126
or Deferent, in the ancient astronomy, an imaginary circle, which, as it were, carries about the body of a planet, and is the same with the eccentric; being invented to account for the eccentricity, perigee, and apogee of the planets.

DEFILE

Pages 126-126

in Fortification, a straight narrow passage, through which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foot can <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> only in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILE">file</a>, by making a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>.

DEFINITE

Pages 126-126

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is applied to an article that has a precise determinate signification; such as the article the in English, le and la in French, &c. which fix and ascertain the noun they belong to, to some particular; as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, le roy: whereas, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of king, de roy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of and, de mark nothing precise, and are therefore indefinite.

DEFINITIVE

Pages 127-127

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to whatever terminates a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, question, &c., in opposition to provisional and interlocutory.

DEFLAGRATION

Pages 127-127

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the kindling <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> setting fire to a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> or mineral, &c., either alone, or mixed for that purpose with a sulphureous one, in order to purify it. This short <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> has been often recommended to the world as of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in trying the strength of brandies and other vinous spirits, and has been greatly improved in this respect by Mr Geoffroy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of trying spirits by deflagration, is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> out any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of it, then to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> it, and set it on fire. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, after it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> no longer burn, the remainder is half as much as the quantity measured out for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> was, then the spirit tried is found to consist of half <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and half totally inflammable spirit; that is, it is somewhat below what we understand by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> perfect <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>.—This method is much more certain than that by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of bubbles which arises upon shaking the spirit in a phial. Mons. Geoffroy's method is this: Take a cylindric vessel two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and as much in diameter, consisting of thin plate silver, that metal being much less liable to rust than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; this vessel must be fitted with a little rectangular gage exactly graduated into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, half lines, &c., then the vessel being set <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> upon a copper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> made to contain it, a parcel of the brandy to be examined is poured in, to the height of 16 lines. This height is to be exactly <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> by pouring in more than enough at first, and then sucking out the overplus with a very small tube. Then the vessel being heated a little, so as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> to make the liquor fume, it is to be set on fire and left to go out of itself; at the instant when the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> expires, the gage is plunged perpendicularly into the vessel, and the lines and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> exactly noted which the liquor wants of its former height: this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> gives the precise quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a> or pure spirit contained in the liquor. Thus, if eight lines of phlegm are found remaining, this being the half of the 16 lines of the original filling, it is plain that the liquor contained one half spirit, or was something below proof. If only four lines remained, it was nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> proof, or of a middle <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> betwixt alcohol and common proof-spirit.

DEFLECTION

Pages 127-127

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> any thing aside from its former course by some adventitious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> cause. The word is often applied to the tendency of a ship from her true course by reason of currents, &c., which turn her out of her <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> way. It is likewise applied by astronomers to the tendency of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> from the line of their projection, or the tangent of their orbit. DEFLECTION of the Rays of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which Dr Hook observed in 1675, and read an account of before the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 18th the same year. He says he found it different both from reflection and refraction, and that it was made towards the surface of the opaque body, perpendicularly. This is the same property which Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton calls inflection.

DEFLORATION

Pages 127-127
or DEFLOWERING, the act of violating or taking away a woman's virginity. See Deformation VIRGINITY.—Death or marriage are decreed by the civil law in case of defloration. The ancients had so much respect for virgins, that they would not put them to death till they had first procured them to be deflowered. It is said, the natives of the coast of Malabar pay strangers to come and deflower their brides. In Scotland and the northern parts of England, it was a privilege of the lords of the manor, granted them by King Ewen, that they should have the first night's lodging with their tenants wives. King Malcolm III. allowed the tenants to redeem this service at a certain rate, called marcheta, consisting of a certain number of cows: Buchanan says it was redeemed with half a mark of silver. The same custom had place in Wales, Flanders, Friesland, and some parts of Germany.

DEFLUXION

Pages 127-127

in Medicine, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the humours from a superior to an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body.

DEFOE

Pages 127-127

DANIEL, a writer famous for politics and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, was bred a hosier; which profession however he soon forsook, and became one of the most enterprising authors that any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> produced. When dissents ran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> at the Revolution, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William was obliged to dismiss his Dutch guards, Defoe, who had true notions of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, ridiculed the enemies of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in his well-known poem, called the True-Born Englishman, which had a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The next satire he wrote was entitled Reformation of Manners; aimed at some persons of high <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, who rendered themselves a disgrace to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> in power breathed too much of a spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, Defoe wrote a tract called the Shortest Way with the Dissenters: for which he was called to account, and explained himself with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> firmness. He was afterwards sentenced to the pillory for attacking some public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>; which so little intimidated him, that, in defiance of their usage, he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">Hymn</a> to the Pillory. It would be endless to enumerate all his publications; but the following are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">Plague</a> in 1665; a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> entitled the History of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Jack; a new Voyage round the World by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a>, printed for Bettesworth, 1725; the History of Roxana; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of a Cavalier; the History of Moll <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; a book entitled <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a> Courtship, which has undergone upwards of 22 editions; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, an admirable performance of which there have been editions without <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, but concerning which there is an anecdote that does the author of it no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> as to the better <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a writer's character, honesty. When <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Woodes Rogers touched at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Juan Fernandez, in the South <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, he brought away Alexander Selkirk, a Scotch sailor, who had been left ashore there, and had lived on that desolate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> above four years. When Selkirk came back to England, he wrote a narrative of his adventures, and put the papers into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Defoe, to digest for publication; who ungenerously converted the materials into the History of Robinson Crusoe, and returned Selkirk his papers again! A fraud for which, in a humane view, the distinguished merit of that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> can never atone. Daniel Defoe died at Islington, in 1731. All his productions of the romantic...

DEFOLIATION

Pages 127-129

(from de, and folium "a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>"); the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the leaves. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> opposed to fronde-scentia, the annual renovation of the leaves, produced by the unfolding of the buds in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. See FRONDE-SCENTIA. Most <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and temperate climates shed their leaves every year; this happens in autumn, and is generally announced by the flowering of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> saffron. The term is only applied to trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; for herbs perish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the roots every year, losing stem, leaves, and all. All plants do not drop their leaves at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Among <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees, the ash and walnut, although latest in unfolding, are soonest divested of them: the latter seldom carries its leaves above five months. On the oak and hornbeam, the leaves die and wither as soon as the colds commence; but remain attached to the branches till they are pushed off by the new ones, which unfold themselves the following spring. These trees are doubtless a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>: the leaves are probably destroyed only by cold; and perhaps would continue longer on the plant, but for the force of the spring sap, joined to the moisture. In mild and dry seasons, the lilac, privet, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> jasmine of the woods, and maple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, preserve their leaves green until spring, and do not drop them till the new leaves are beginning to appear. The fig-tree, and many other trees that grow between the tropics, are of this particular class of evergreens. The trees in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, says <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Hasselquist, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> their leaves in the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> and beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, having young leaves ready before all the old ones are fallen off; and, to forward this operation of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, few of the trees have buds; the sycamore and willow, indeed, have some, but with few and quite loose stipulae <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scales. Nature did not imagine buds so necessary in the southern as in the northern countries: this occasions a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them. Lastly, some trees and shrubs preserve their leaves constantly through the whole year; and are not in the least influenced by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> or inclemency of seasons. Such are the firs, juniper, yew, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, cypress, and many other trees, hence denominated evergreens. These preserve their old leaves a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time after the formation of the new, and do not drop them at any determinate time. In general, the leaves of evergreens are harder, and less succulent, than those which are renewed annually. The trees are generally natives of warm climates; as the alaternuses of France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the evergreen oak of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> and Suabia. Some herbaceous perennials, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-leeks and navel-worts, enjoy the same privilege with the evergreen trees, and resist the severities of winter: some even can dispense with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> for some time; being replete with juices, which the leaves imbibe from the humidity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and which, in such plants, are of themselves sufficient for effecting the purposes of vegetation. It is for this reason, that, unless in excessive hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, gardeners are seldom wont to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fat succulent plants, as the aloes, which rot when they are moistened, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> does not quickly dry them up. The leaves of all the evergreen shrubs and trees have a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> skin or cover over their surface; as is easily discovered by macerating them in water, in order to separate the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENCHYMA">parenchyma</a>, or pulp, from the vessels of the leaves; which cannot be effected in any of these evergreens till a thin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>-like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is taken off. These trees and shrubs are found by experiment to perspire but little, when compared with others which shed their leaves; and it is, perhaps, principally owing to this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> covering, as also to the small proportion of moisture contained in their vessels, that they retain their verdure, and continue through the winter on the trees. The nutritive juices of these plants always abound, more or less, with an oily <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, which secures them from being injured by severe frosts; so that many of these evergreen trees are adapted to grow in the coldest parts of the habitable world. With respect to deciduous trees, the falling off of the leaves seems principally to depend on the temperature of the atmosphere, which likewise serves to hasten or retard the appearance in question. An ardent sun contributes to hasten the dropping of the leaves. Hence in hot and dry summers the leaves of the lime-tree and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chesnut turn yellow about the first of September; whilst in other years, the yellowness does not appear till the beginning of October. Nothing, however, contributes more to hasten the fall of the leaves than immoderate cold or moist weather in autumn; moderate droughts, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, serve to retard it. As a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this position, Mr Adamson relates, that in the year 1759, the leaves of the elm-tree, which generally fall off about the 25th of November, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in verdure and vigour at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where the autumn was remarkably dry, till the 10th of the following <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> times in which different trees shed their leaves is founded upon observation. | Tree <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">Type</a> | Generally quit their leaves about | |------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------| | Gooseberry-tree and bladder-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, Walnut and ash, Almond-tree, horse-chesnut, and lime-tree, Maple, hazel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> poplar, and aspen-tree, Birch, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>-tree, mountain-oak, false <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, and apple-tree, Vine, mulberry, fig, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMACH">sumach</a>, and angelica-tree, Elm-tree and willow, Apricot and elder-trees | October 1st. 15th. 20th. 25th. November 1st. 10th. 15th. 20th. | It deserves to be remarked, that an evergreen tree grafted upon a deciduous, determines the latter to retain its leaves. This observation is confirmed by repeated experiments, particularly by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a> the laurel, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">Deformity</a> or cherry-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, an evergreen, on the common cherry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ILEX">ilex</a>, or evergreen oak, on the oak.

DEFORCEMENT

Pages 129-129

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the opposing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resisting of the officers of the law in the execution of their office. See Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DEFORMITY

Pages 129-134

the want of that uniformity necessary to constitute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of an object. See Beauty. Deformity is either <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> moral. These are both referred by Mr Hutcheson to an internal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and our perceptions, of them as he supposes, arise from an original arbitrary structure of our own minds, by which certain objects, when observed, are rendered the occasions of certain sensations and affections. That many objects give no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to our sense is obvious. Many are certainly void of beauty; but then, says this author, there is no form which seems necessarily disagreeable of itself, when we dread no other evil from it, and compare it with nothing better of the kind. Many objects are naturally displeasing and distasteful to our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, as well as others pleasing and agreeable; as smells, tastes, and some separate sounds; but with regard to our sense of beauty, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of objects which give not unpleasant simple <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, seems positively unpleasant or painful of itself, had we never observed anything better of the same kind. Had there been a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the form which we now denominate ugly or deformed, and had we never seen or expected greater beauty, we should have received no disgust from it; though the pleasure would not have been so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> in this form as in those we now admire. Our sense of beauty seems designed to give us positive pleasure; but not positive pain or disgust, any farther than what arises from disappointment. There are indeed many faces which at first view are apt to raise dislike. But this is generally not from any positive deformity; but either from want of expected beauty, or from the carrying some natural indications of morally bad dispositions, which we all acquire a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of discerning in countenances, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, and gestures. That this is not occasioned by any form positively disgusting, appears hence, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, upon <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> acquaintance, we are sure of finding sweetness of temper, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and cheerfulness, though the bodily form continues, it shall give us no disgust. There are horrors raised by some objects, which are only the effects of fear for ourselves, or compassion towards others, when either reason, or some foolish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of ideas, makes us apprehend danger; and not the effect of any thing in the form itself. For we find, that most of these objects which excite horror at first, when <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> or reason has removed the fear, may become the occasion of pleasure. The casual conjunction of ideas gives us disgust, when there is nothing disagreeable in the form itself. And this, in effect, is the cause of most of our fantastic aversions to the figures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> animals, &c. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> of all kinds, and many insects, really beautiful enough, are beheld with aversion by many people, who have got some accidental ideas of mischief associated to them. A similar reasoning is applied to our perception of moral beauty and deformity. Deformity. Inquiry into the Original of our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue, passim. But it is more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> to distinguish between the sentiments of delight or disgust, excited in us by beautiful or deformed objects, which are effects of some cause, and the natural and real qualities of the perceived objects by which they are produced. There are objects, says an excellent writer, which have a natural aptitude to please or offend, or between which and the contemplating mind there is a necessary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGRUITY">congruity</a> or incongruity; and though the actual perception of the understanding, and consequent feeling of the heart, in contemplating the actions and affections of moral agents, may exist in very different degrees, on account of the incidental obstructions arising from bodily indisposition, mental prejudices and biases, and the association of ideas; yet, in every rational mind properly disposed, morally good actions must for ever be acceptable, and can never of themselves offend; and morally evil actions must for ever be disagreeable, and can never of themselves please. What is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in actions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> is beautiful and amiable, and gives pleasure; what is wrong is deformed and odious, and excites disgust; right and pleasure, wrong and pain, are as distinct as cause and effect. It is no less absurd to maintain, that the perception of virtue is nothing distinct from the perception of the pleasure resulting from it, than to infer, with some metaphysicians, that solidity, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, are only particular modes of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, because attended, whenever they are perceived, with some sensations of sight or touch. Thus does the author show, that moral beauty and deformity are real qualities of certain actions; in which consists their aptitude to please or disgust. With respect to natural beauty, he observes, that uniformity amidst variety pleases, because of the natures of variety and uniformity, which are such, that whenever united, they are adapted to please every unbiassed mind that discerns them. He accounts for the pleasure they afford, without referring them to an arbitrary internal sense, by the following circumstances that attend them. They are more easily comprehended by the mind; order and symmetry give things their stability and strength, and subserviency to any valuable purpose; regularity and order <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> art and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. Disorder and confusion, whence deformity arises, denote only the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a> of regularity and order; or any arrangement and disposition of things, which are not according to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, rule, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and prove not design. These are not positively displeasing; except where we previously expected order, or where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a> or want of skill appear, and the contriver has either failed of his design or executed it ill. In a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Fugitive Pieces, is preserved an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on Bodily Deformity, by William Hay, Esq. who was himself what he describes, and who, while he rallies his own figure with great pleasantry, discusses the general subject in a manner equally instructive and agreeable. He considers, 1. The natural consequences of bodily deformity; 2. How it affects the outward circumstances; and, 3. What turn it gives to the mind. 1. It is certain, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frame, being warped and disproportional, is lessened in strength and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, Deformity, and rendered less fit for its functions. Scarron had invented an engine to take off his hat; "and I wish (says our author) I could invent one to buckle my <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, or to take up a thing from the ground, which I can scarce do without kneeling, for I can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> my body no farther than it is bent by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. For this reason, when ladies drop a fan or glove, I am not the first to take it up; and often restrain my inclination to perform these little services, rather than expose my spiderlike shape. And I hope it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be construed as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, if I do not always rise from my seat when I ought: for if it is low, I find some trouble in it; and my centre of gravity is so ill placed, that I am often like to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> back. Things hanging within the reach of others are out of mine; and what they can execute with ease, I want strength to perform. I am in danger of being trampled upon or stifled in a crowd, where my back is a convenient lodgment for the elbow of any tall person that is near. I can see nothing, and my whole employment is to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> my person. I have forborne to attend his majesty in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> since I was like to be squeezed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> there against the wall. I would willingly come thither when his majesty commands, but he is too gracious to expect impossibilities. Besides, when I get in, I can never have the pleasure of seeing on the throne one of the best princes who ever sat on it. These, and many others, are the inconveniences continually attending a figure like mine. They may appear grievous to persons not used to them, but they grow easier by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and though they may a little disturb, they are not sufficient to destroy the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; of which, at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, I have enjoyed as great a share as most men. And perhaps one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of it may be my <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> this essay; not intended as a complaint against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> for my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, but as an innocent amusement to myself and others. As to what effect deformity may have on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, it appears natural to imagine, that as the inward parts of the body must in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> comply with the outward mould, so the form of the latter being <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, the first cannot be so well placed and disposed to perform their functions; and that generally deformed persons would not be healthy or long lived.
