But this is a question best determined by facts; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the instances are too few or unobserved, to draw a general conclusion from them: and health is more than is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> thought in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s own power, and the reward of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> more than the effect of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; which makes it more difficult to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a judgment. Aesop could not be young when he died; and might have lived longer if he had not been murdered at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> scarce passed the meridian of life, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Luxemburg died about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 67. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Burleigh lived to 78; but his son the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, who died about 15 years after him, could not reach near that age. It is said that Mr Pope's father was deformed, and he lived to 75; whereas the son died in middle age, if he may be said to die whose works are immortal. "My father (adds our author) was not deformed, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and my mother a celebrated beauty; and I, that am so unlike them, have lived to a greater age, and daily see my acquaintance of a stronger frame quitting the stage before me." But whether deformity, abstractedly considered, be really prejudicial to health, in its consequences it appears to be most commonly an advantage. Deformed persons have a less share of strength than others, and therefore should naturally be more careful to preserve it; and as temperance is the great preservative of health, it may incline them to be more temperate. Another great preservative of health is moderate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, which few deformed persons can want strength to perform. As a deformed person is not formed for violent exercise, he is less liable to such disorders as are the natural consequences of it. He will also escape many accidents, to which men of athletic make, and who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in their strength, are always <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> themselves to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> and proof of it. If he cannot carry an ox, like Milo, he will not like Milo be handcuffed in the oak by attempting to rend it. He will not be the man that shall ride from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, or to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, for a wager; or that shall be perpetually performing surprising long journeys in a surprising short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, for no earthly business but the pleasure of relating them. Conscious of his own weakness, he will be cautious of running into places or occasions of danger. Nature, too, warns deformed persons to be careful not to offer such affronts as may call them forth into the field of false <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, where they cannot acquit themselves well for want of strength and agility; and they are secure from such affronts themselves, since others will consider the little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> they will <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by compelling them to appear on that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. On the whole, therefore, it may be concluded, that deformity is a protection to a man's health and person; which (strange as it may appear) are better defended by feebleness than strength. 2. The influence of bodily deformity on a man's fortune may next be considered. Among the lower class, he is cut off from many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> and employments. He cannot be a soldier; he is under standard; he cannot be a sailor, he wants activity to climb the rigging; he cannot be a chairman or porter, he wants strength to bear the burden. In higher life, he is ill qualified for a lawyer, he can scarce be seen over the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; for a divine, he may drop from his hassock out of sight in his pulpit. The improvement of his mind is his proper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and his business only such as depends on ingenuity. If he cannot be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to adjust the heels, he may be a schoolmaster to instruct the head; he cannot be a graceful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> on the stage; but he may produce a good play; he would appear ill as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>; but may pass as a merchant on the change; he cannot undergo the fatigue of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>; but he may advise the operations of it: he is designed by nature rather to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, than to descend on the plains of Eolis; he cannot be crowned at the Olympic games; but may be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a> to celebrate them; he can acquire no glory by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but he may by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, and may grow famous by only relating those exploits which are beyond his power to imitate. Lord <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> (that extensive and penetrating genius who pointed out every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of nature for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>), in his Essay on Deformity, says, "that in their superiors it quencheth jealousy towards them, as persons that they think they may at pleasure despise; and it layeth their competitors and emulators asleep, as never believing..." Deformity, believing they should be in a possibility of advancement till they see them in possession." But it is much to be doubted whether this is not more than counterbalanced by the contempt of the world, which it requires no <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> parts to conquer; for if (as has been said) a good person is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of recommendation, deformity must be an obstruction in the way to favour. In this respect, therefore, deformed persons set out in the world to a disadvantage; and they must first surmount the prejudices of mankind before they can be upon a par with others, and most obtain by a course of behaviour that regard which is paid to beauty at first sight. When this point is once gained, the tables are turned, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> goes in their favour: for others, sensible of their injustice to them, no sooner find them better than they expected, than they believe them better than they are; whereas in the beautiful person they sometimes find themselves imposed upon, and are angry that they have worshipped only a painted idol. For (again take Lord Bacon's words) "neither is it almost seen, that very beautiful persons are otherwise of great virtue: they prove accomplished, but not of great spirit; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> rather behaviour than virtue. Whereas deformed persons, if they be of spirit, will free themselves from scorn, which must be either by virtue or malice; and therefore let it not be marvelled if they sometimes prove excellent persons, as was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGESILAUS">Agesilaus</a>, Zanger the son of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, Æsop, Gascu <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> may likewise go amongst them, with others." Nay, he says, "in a great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> deformity is an advantage to rising;" and in another part of his works, "that they who by accident have some inevitable and indelible mark on their persons or fortunes, as deformed people, bastards, &c. if they want not virtue, generally prove fortunate." Osborn, in his Historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, informs us, that "she chose the goodliest persons for her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> servants: but in her counsellors did not put by sufficiency, though accompanied with a crooked person; as it chanced in a father and a son of the Cecils, both incomparable for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>." It is well known the queen would make the father (Burleigh) sit in her presence; telling him that she did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> him for his legs but his head. But the son (afterwards lord treasurer and earl of Salisbury) was not so civilly treated by the populace; and is an instance, not only that envy pursues a great man, but that the highest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> cannot redeem a deformed one from contempt: it attends him like his shadow, and like that too is ever reminding him of his ill figure, which is often objected for want of real crimes. For the same writer says of the same great man, "that the misfortunes accompanying him from his birth, did not a little add to that cloud of detraction that fell upon all that he said or did; a mulet in nature, like an optic spectacle, multiplying much in the sight of the people the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a> of ill." Nor was this contempt buried with him: it trampled on his ashes, and insulted his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>; as appears by an epitaph, which Osborn cites, as void of wit as it is full of scurrility; in one line of Deformity, which there is an epithet, not so elegant as descriptive of his person, viz. "Little Bossive Robin that was so great." Such contempt in general, joined with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of the vulgar, is another certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of bodily deformity; for men naturally despise what appears less beautiful or useful, and their pride is gratified when they see such foils to their own persons. It is this sense of superiority which is testified by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> in the lower sort; while their betters, who know how little any man whatsoever hath to boast of, are restrained by good sense and good breeding from such an insult. But it is not easy to say why one species of deformity should be more ridiculous than another, or why the mob should be more merry with a crooked man, than with one that is deaf, lame, squinting, or paralysed. It is a back in alto relievo that bears all the ridicule; though one would think a prominent belly a more reasonable object of it, since the last is generally the effect of intemperance, and of a man's own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Socrates was ugly, but not contemned; and Philopsemen (A) of very mean appearance, and though contemned on that account not ridiculed: for Montaigne says, "Ill features are but a superficial ugliness, and of little certainty in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of men; but a deformity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> is more substantial, and strikes deeper in." As it is more uncommon, it is more remarkable; and that perhaps is the true reason why it is more ridiculed by the vulgar. 5. The last consideration on this subject relates to those passions and affectations which most naturally result from deformity. Lord Bacon observes, that "deformed persons are commonly even with nature; for as nature hath done ill by them, so do they by nature, being for the most part (as the scripture saith) void of natural affection." But (says Mr Hay) "I can neither find out this passage in scripture, nor the reason of it; nor can I give my assent or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> to a proposition, till I am well acquainted with the terms of it. If by natural affection is here meant universal benevolence, and deformity necessarily implies a want of it, a deformed person must then be a complete monster. But however <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> the case may be, my own sensations inform me that it is not universally true. If by natural affection is meant a partial regard for individuals, I believe the remark is judicious, and founded in human nature. Deformed persons are despised, ridiculed, and ill-treated by others; are seldom favourites, and commonly most neglected by parents, guardians, and relations; and therefore, as they are not indebted for much fondness, it is no wonder if they repay but little. It is the command of scripture, Not to set our affections on things below; and it is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of reason not to overvalue what we must soon part with; therefore, to be so fond of others as not to be able to bear their absence, or to survive them, is neither a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> nor moral duty, but a childish and womanish weakness; and I must congratulate deformed persons, who, by example, (A) Coming to an inn, where he was expected, before his attendants, the mistress of the house seeing a plain person of very mean aspect, ordered him to assist in getting things ready for Philopsemen. His attendants finding him so employed, he told them he was then paying the tribute of his ugliness. Plutarch. Vol. VII. Part I. Deformity, ample, are early taught another lesson. And I will now lay open my own heart to the reader, that he may judge if Lord Bacon's position is verified in me. "I hope it proceeds not from a malignity of heart; but I never am much affected with the common accidents of life, whether they befall myself or others. I am little moved when I hear of death, loss, or misfortune; I think the case is common. Tritus, et medio fortunae ductus acervo; Juv. Sat. xiii. And as it is always likely to happen, I am not surprised when it does. If I see a person cry or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> on any such occasion, I cannot bear him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; but am not a Demetrius to laugh at his folly. I read of battles and fields covered with slain; of cities destroyed by sword, famine, pestilence, and earthquake; I do not shed a tear: I suppose it is because they are the usual storms, to which the human species are exposed, proceeding from the just judgments of God, or the mistaken and false principles of rulers. I read of persecutions, tortures, murders, massacres; my compassion for the sufferers is great, but my tears are stopped by resentment and indignation against the contrivers and perpetrators of such horrid actions. But there are many things that bring tears into my eyes whether I will or no; and when I reflect, I am often at a loss in searching out the secret source from whence they flow. What makes me weep (for weep I do) when I read of virtue or innocence in distress; of a good man helpless and forsaken, unmoved by the greatest insults and cruelties, or courageously supporting himself against oppression in the article of death? I suppose it is to see vice triumphant, and virtue so ill rewarded in this life. May I judge by myself, I should imagine that few sincere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> could read the sufferings of their Saviour, or Englishmen those of a Cranmer, Ridley, or Latimer, without tears; the first dying to establish his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, the last to rescue it from corruption. When I read of Regulus returning to torment, and John of France to imprisonment, against the persuasion of friends, to keep <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> with their enemies, I weep to think there is scarce another instance of such exalted virtue. Those who often hear me read, know that my voice changes, and my eyes are full, when I meet with a generous and heroic saying, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, or character, especially of persons whose example or command may influence mankind. I weep when I hear a Titus say, that he had lost the day in which he did no good; when Adrian tells his enemy, that he had escaped by his being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. that he is not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the affront of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. These are the first instances that happen to occur to me: I might recollect many, too many to insert in this essay; yet all are but few, compared to instances of cruelty and revenge: perhaps I am concerned that they are so rare; perhaps too I inwardly grieve that I am not in a situation to do the like. I am entertained, but not moved, when I read Voltaire's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. but I melt into tears on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> Hanway's character of his antagonist <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great. The first is a story of a madman; the other of a father, friend, and benefactor of his people; whose character (as the author observes in the conclusion of it) will command the admiration of all succeeding generations; and I suppose I lament, that God is pleased to advance to royalty so few such instruments of good to mankind. Again: "I am uneasy when I see a dog, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, or any other animal, ill treated: for I consider them as endowed with quick sense, and no contemptible share of reason; and that God gave man dominion over them, not to play the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, but to be a good prince, and promote the happiness of his subjects. But I am much more uneasy at any cruelty to my own species; and heartily wish Procrustes disciplined in his own <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. A man bruised all over in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOXING">boxing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, or cut to pieces in fighting a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, is a shocking spectacle; and I think I could with less horror see a thousand fall in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, than human nature thus depreciated and disgraced. Violence, when exerted in wantonness or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, is brutality; and can be termed bravery only when it is sanctioned by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. "I have been in a situation to see not a little of the pomp and vanity, as well as of the necessity and misery, of mankind: but the last only affect me; and if, as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, I am ever guilty of partiality, it is in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. When I am at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> among my poor but honest neighbours in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and see them serious in performing the ceremonies prescribed, tears sometimes steal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> my cheek, on reflecting, that they are doing and hearing many things they do not understand, while those who understand them better neglect them; that they, who labour and live hard, are more thankful to heaven than those who fare luxuriously on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their labour; and are keeping and repeating the fourth commandment at the very instant the others are breaking it. "These are some of the sensations I feel; which I have freely and fairly disclosed, that the reader may judge how far I am an instance of a deformed person wanting natural affection. And I am a good subject of speculation; because all in me is nature: for to own the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, I have taken but little pains (though I ought to have taken a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>) to correct my natural defects. "Lord Bacon's next position is, 'That deformed persons are extremely bold: first in their own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, as being exposed to scorn; but in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time by a general habit.' This probably is so among the inferior sort, who are in the way of continual insults; for a return of abuse is a natural weapon of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-defence</a>, and in some measure justified by the law of retaliation: To upbraid a man with a personal defect, which he cannot help, is also an immoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>; and he who does it, has reason to expect no better <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> than to hear of faults, which it was in his own power not to commit. But I find this observation far from being verified in myself: an unbecoming bashfulness has been the consequence of my ill figure, and of the worse management of me in my childhood. I am always uneasy when any one looks stedfastly on so bad a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>; and cannot look with a proper confidence in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of another. I have ever reproached myself with this weakness, but am not able to correct it. And it may be a disadvantage to a man in the opinion of those he converses with; for though true <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> is amiable, the false is liable to misconstruction: and when a man is out of countenance for no reason, it may be imagined that he has some bad reason for being so. In Deformity, point of assurance, I am indeed a perfect riddle to myself; for I, who feel a reluctance in crossing a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>-room, or in opening my mouth in private company before persons with whom I am not well acquainted, find little in delivering my sentiments in public, and exposing my discourse, often as trifling as my person, to the ears of a thousand. From what cause this proceeds, I know not: it may be partly from hopes of wiping off any ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> from my person by my discourse, partly from a sense of doing my duty, and partly from a security in public assemblies from any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> personal reflection. Lord Bacon compares the case of deformed persons to that of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>; "in whom kings were wont to put great trust as good spies and whisperers; for they that are envious towards all, are more obsequious and officious towards one." But, with submission to so good a judge of human nature, I own I can discover no uncommon qualification in them for spies; and very few motives to envy peculiar to themselves. Spies submit to that base and ungenerous office, either for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> or power: if for interest, it is to gratify their covetousness; if for power, their ambition or revenge; which passions are not confined to the eunuch or deformed, but indiscriminately <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> all classes of men. Envy too may prompt a man to mean actions, in order to bring down the person envied to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>; but if it is on account of superiority of fortune it will operate alike on men of all shapes. Eunuchs have but one peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to envy: but that (as Lord Bacon expresses it) makes them envious towards all; because it is for a pleasure which all but themselves may enjoy. Deformed persons are deprived only of beauty and strength, and therefore those alone are to be deemed the extraordinary motives to their envy; for they can no more be beautiful or strong than eunuchs be successful lovers. As to myself, whatever sparks of envy might be in my constitution, they are now entirely extinguished; for, by frequent and serious reflections, I have long been convinced of the small value of most things which men value the most. There is another passion to which deformed persons seem to be more exposed than to envy; which is jealousy: for being conscious that they are less amiable than others, they may naturally suspect that they are less beloved. I have the happiness to speak this from conjecture, and not from experience; for it was my lot, many years ago, to marry a young lady, very piously educated, and of a very distinguished family, and whose virtues are an honour to her family and her <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>: so that I had never any trial of my temper, and can only guess at it by emotions I have felt in my younger days; when ladies have been more liberal of their smiles to those whom I thought, in every respect deformity, but person, my inferiors." The most useful inference from all this to a deformed person is, to be upon his guard against those frailties to which he is more particularly exposed; and to be careful, that the outward frame do not distort the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. Orandum est (says Juvenal), ut sit mens <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANA">sana</a> in corpore sano, "Let us pray for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> mind in a healthy body:" and every deformed person should add this petition, ut sit mens recta in corpore curvo, for "an upright mind in a crooked one." And let him frequently apply to himself this article of self-examination, Lenior et melior fit, accedente senecta? "As age approaches, do your temper and morals improve?" It is a duty peculiarly incumbent; for if beauty adds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> to virtue itself, vice must be doubly hideous in deformity. Ridicule and contempt are a certain consequence of deformity; and therefore what a person cannot avoid, he should learn not to regard. He should bear it like a man; forgive it as a Christian; and consider it as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. And his triumph will be complete, if he can exceed others in pleasantry on himself. Wit will give over when it sees itself outdone: and so will malice when it finds it has no effect: and if a man's behaviour afford no cause of contempt, it will fall upon those who condemn him without cause. Instead of repining, therefore, a deformed person ought to be thankful to Providence for giving him such a guard to his virtue and repose. Thousands are daily ruined by a handsome person; for beauty is a flower that every one wants to gather in its bloom, and spares no pains or stratagem to reach it. All the poetical stories concerning it have their moral. A Helen occasions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and confusion; the Hyacinths and Ganymedes are seized on for catamites; the Endymions and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADONIS">Adonis</a> for gallants; Narcissus can admire nobody but himself, and grows old before he is cured of that passion. Who is a stranger to the story of Lucretia killing herself for her violated chastity? or of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> killed by her father to preserve it? In those circumstances says Juvenal, she might wish to change persons with Rutula, the only lady we know among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> celebrated for a hump-back. The handsomest men are chosen for eunuchs and gallants; and when they are caught in exercising the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, both (b) Horace and Juvenal inform you of the penalties and indignities they undergo. Silius (c) was converted by the insatiable Messalina into a husband; and Sporus, by the monster Nero, into a wife. The last-mentioned poet shows that praying for beauty is praying for a curse; and (d) Persius refuses to join in such a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; and has not the deformed person reason to thank his stars, which have placed him --- (b) Hic se præcipitem tecto dedit: ille flagellis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">Ad</a> mortem cessus: fugiens hic decidit acrem Praedonum in turbam: dedit hic pro corpore nummos: Hunc permixxerunt calones: quin etiam illud Accidit, ut cuidam testes caudamque salacem Demeteret ferrum. —— Hor. Sat. ii. lib. i. Quosdam moechos et mugillis intrat. —— Juv. ib. (c) —— Optimum hic et formosissimus idem Gentis Patriciae rapitor <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISER">miser</a> extinguendus Messalinae oculis. —— Juv. Sat. x. (d) Hunc optent generum Rex et <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">Regina</a>: puellae Hunc rapiant: quicquid calcaverit hic, rosa fiat: Ast ego nutrici non mando vota; negato. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> hoc illi —— Pers. Sat. ii. Deformity, more out of danger than even virtue could? for that could not guard a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, an (x) Hippolytus, a Bellerophon, and others, against the revenge of slighted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. Another great advantage of deformity is, that it tends to the improvement of the mind. A man that cannot shine in his person, will have recourse to his understanding; and attempt to adorn that part of him, which alone is capable of ornament. When his ambition prompts him to begin, with Cowley, to ask himself this question, What shall I do to be for ever known, And make the age to come my own? on looking about him, he will find many avenues to the temple of fame barred against him; but some are still open through that of virtue; and those, if he has a right ambition, he will most probably attempt to pass. The more a man is inactive in his person, the more his mind will be at work; and the time which others spend in action, he will pass in study and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>: by these he may acquire <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; and by wisdom, fame. The name of Socrates is as much sounded as those of Alexander and Caesar; and is recorded in much fairer characters. He gained renown by wisdom and goodness; they by tyranny and oppression; he by instructing, they by destroying, mankind: and happy it is, that their evil deeds were confined to their lives; while he continues to instruct us to this day. A deformed person will naturally consider where his strength and his foible <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a>: and as he is well acquainted with the last, he will easily find out the first; and must know, that (if it is anywhere) it is not like Samson's, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; but must be in the lining of the head. He will say to himself, "I am weak in person; unable to serve my country in the field, I can acquire no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> glory; but I may, like Socrates, acquire reputation by wisdom and probity: let me therefore be wise and honest. My figure is very bad; and I should appear but ill as an orator either in the pulpit or at the bar: let me therefore pass my time in my study, either in reading what may improve myself, or in writing what may entertain or instruct others. I have not the strength of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, nor can I rid the world of so many monsters: but perhaps I may get rid of some that infest myself. If I cannot draw out Cacus from his den, I may pluck the villain from my own breast. I cannot cleanse the stable of Augeas: but I may cleanse my own heart from filth and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>: I may demolish the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">hydra</a> of vices within me; and should be careful too, that while I lop off one, I do not suffer more to grow up in its stead. Let me be serviceable in any way that I can: and if I am so, it may, in some measure, be owing to my deformity; which at least should be a restraint on my conduct, lest my conduct make me more deformed." Few persons have a house entirely to their mind; or the apartments in it disposed as they could wish. And there is no deformed person, who does not wish that his soul had a better habitation; which is sometimes not lodged according to its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Lord Clarendon says of Sir Charles Cavendish (<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>), that he was a man of the noblest and largest mind, though of the least and most inconvenient body that lived. And every body knows, that the late prince of Orange had many amiable qualities. Therefore, in justice to such persons, we must suppose that they did not repine that their tenements were not in a more regular style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. And let every deformed person comfort himself with reflecting, that though his soul hath not the most convenient and beautiful apartment, yet that it is habitable; that the accommodation will serve as an inn upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>; that he is but tenant for life, or (more properly) at will; and that, while he remains in it, he is in a state to be envied by the deaf, the dumb, the lame, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>.

DEFOSSION

Pages 134-134

the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of burying alive, inflicted among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> on vestal virgins guilty of incontinency. It is also a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> among the Hungarians to inflict this punishment on women convicted of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>. Heretics were also punished in this manner. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a>-Alive.

DEGENERATION

Pages 134-134
or DEGENERATING, in general, denotes the growing worse, or losing some valuable qualities whereof a thing was formerly possessed. Some naturalists have been of opinion, that things are capable of degenerating into quite a distinct species; but this is a mere chimera. All that happens in the degeneration of a plant, for instance, is the losing its usual beauty, colour, smell, &c., a circumstance entirely owing to its being planted in an improper soil, climate, &c.

DEGRADATION

Pages 134-135

in our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books called disgradation and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of depriving <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stripping a person for ever of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and taking away the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, badge, and privileges thereof. The degradation of a peer, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, an officer, &c. are performed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> ceremonies. That which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> obtained in degrading a person from his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> is very curious. It was practised in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Francis I. upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Fangel, who had in a cowardly manner given up Fontarabia, whereof he was governor. On this occasion, 20 or 30 cavaliers, without blemish or reproach, were assembled; before whom the gentleman was accused of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>-at-arms. Two scaffolds were erected; the one for the judges, heralds, and pursuivants; and the other for the guilty cavalier, who was armed at all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and his shield placed on a stake before him, reversed with the point upwards. On one side assisted 12 priests in surplices, who sung the vigils of the dead. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of each psalm they made a pause, during which the officers of arms --- (1.) Quid profuit olim Hippolyto <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> propositum? Quid Bellerophonti Erubuit nempe hæc, seu fastidia repusa: Nec Sthenobœa minus quam Cressa excanduit, et se Concussere ambo. — Juvenal Sat. x. arms stripped the condemned of some piece of his armour, beginning with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, and proceeding thus till he was quite disarmed; which done, they broke his shield in three pieces with a hammer. Then the king-at-arms emptied a basin of hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on the criminal's head; and the judges, putting on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> habits, went to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. This done, the degraded was drawn from off the scaffold with a rope tied under his arm-pits, laid on a bier, and covered with mortuary clothes; the priest singing some of the prayers for the dead; and then he was delivered to the civil judge and the executioner of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. For a more <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> instance: Sir Andrew Harcla, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Carlisle, being attainted and convicted of treason, 18 Edw. II. coron regis; after judgment was pronounced on him, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> was broken over his head, and his spurs hewn off his heels; Sir Anthony Lucy the judge, saying to him, "Andrew, now thou art no knight but a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a>." By stat. 13 Car. II. William <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Monson, Sir Henry Mildmay, and others, were degraded from all titles of honour, dignities, and pre-eminences, and prohibited to bear or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the title of lord, knight, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESQUIRE">esquire</a>, or gentleman, or any coat of arms, for ever afterwards. It has been maintained that the king may degrade a peer; but it appears from late authorities, that he cannot be degraded but by act of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. As to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, we have an instance of degradation before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in the eighth century, at Constantinople. It is in the person of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> Constantine, whom Constantine Copronymus caused to be executed. He was made to ascend the ambo; and the patriarch Nicetas sent some of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> to strip him of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALLIUM">pallium</a>, and anathematized him; then they made him go out of the church backwards. But we have a much later instance in our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>: When Cranmer, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was degraded by order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, they dressed him in episcopal robes, made only of canvas, put the mitre on his head, and the pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and in this attire showed him to the people. Which done, they stripped him again piece by piece. At present they do not stand so much on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of degradation in order to the putting a priest to death; by reason of the delays and difficulties that it would occasion. Pope Boniface pronounced that six bishops were required to degrade a priest; but the difficulty of assembling so many bishops rendered the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> frequently impracticable. In England, a priest, after having been delivered to his ordinary, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he cannot purge himself of the crime with which he is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> and other robes are stripped over his ears by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hangman; by which he is declared divested of his orders. It is decided, however, that degradation does not efface the priestly character. Degradation only seems to differ from deposition in a few ignominious ceremonies which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has added thereto. Accordingly, in the business of Arnoul archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, sentenced in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> in 991, it was deliberated what form they should follow in the deposition; whether that of the canons, that is, simple deposition; or that of custom, viz. degradation. And it was declared, that he should surrender the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, pastoral staff, and pallium, but that his robes should not be torn off. In effect, the canons prescribe no more than a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. It is the rest, therefore, added thereto by custom, viz. the stripping off the ornaments, and the tearing the pontifical vestments, that properly constitute degradation. Degradation, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, expresses the lessening the appearance of distant objects in a landscape, in the same manner as they would appear to an eye placed at that distance from them. Degree, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a circle, including a three hundred and sixtieth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of its circumference. Degree of Latitude. See Latitude. Degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">Longitude</a>. See Longitude. A degree of the meridian on the surface of the globe is variously determined by various observers. Mr Picart measured a degree in the latitude of 49° 21', and found it equal to 57,062 French toises. But the French mathematicians, who have lately examined Mr Picart's operations, assure us, that the degree in that latitude is 57,183 toises. Our countryman, Mr Norwood, measured the distance between <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and found it 925,751 English feet; and finding the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of latitudes 2° 28', determined the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of one degree to be 367,196 English feet, or 69 English miles and 288 yards. Mr Maupertuis measured a degree in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, in the latitude of 66° 20', and found it 57,438 toises. A degree was likewise measured at the equator by other French mathematicians, and found to contain 56,767-8 toises. Whence it appears, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is not a sphere, but an oblate spheroid. Degree, in the civil and canon law, denotes an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> in kinship, by which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> and remoteness of blood are computed. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">Consanguinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">Descent</a>. Degrees, in Music, are the little intervals whereof the concords or harmonical intervals are composed. Degree, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> conferred on the students or members thereof, as a testimony of their proficiency in the arts or sciences, and entitling them to certain privileges. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEJANIRA">Dejanira</a>, in fabulous history, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Oeneus king of Ætolia, and wife to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. The centaur Nessus endeavouring to ravish her, was slain by Hercules with a poisoned <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>. Nessus, when dying, gave his bloody shirt to Dejanira; assuring her, that it was a sovereign remedy to cure her husband if ever he proved unfaithful. Some time after Dejanira thinking she had reason to suspect his fidelity, sent him the shirt; which he had no sooner put on, than he was seized with the most excruciating torments. Being unable to support his pains, he retired to Mount Oeta, and erecting a pile of wood, set fire to it, and threw himself into the flames; upon which Dejanira killed herself in despair. Dejection, in Medicine, the act of voiding the excrements by the anus. See Anatomy, No. 93. Dejection, in Astrology, is applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> when in their detriment, as astrologers speak, i.e. when they have lost their force or influence, as is pretended, by reason of their being in opposition to some others which check and counteract them. Or it is used when a planet is in a sign opposite to that in which it has its greatest effect or influence, which is called its

DEIPHON

Pages 136-136

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Triptolemus, son of Celeus and Metanira. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> travelled over the world, she stopped at his father's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and undertook to nurse him and bring him up. To reward the hospitality of Celeus, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> began to make his son immortal, and every evening she placed him on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals to purify him from whatever mortal particles he still possessed. The uncommon growth of Deiphon astonished Metanira, who wished to see what Ceres did to make him so vigorous. She was frightened to see her son on burning coals; and the shrieks that she uttered disturbed the mysterious operations of the goddess, and Deiphon perished in the flames.

DEISCAL

Pages 136-136

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> British customs, the name of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> originally used in the druidical worship, and retained in many places <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a very late <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, as a civil ceremony towards persons of particular distinction. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of the ancient Britons were all circular; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a>, in performing the public offices of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, never neglected to make three turns round the altar, accompanied by all the worshippers. This practice was so habitual to the ancient Britons, that it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in some places many ages after the druids and their religion were both destroyed. In the Scottish isles, the vulgar never come to the ancient sacrificing and fire-hallowing cairns, but they walk three times round them, from east to west, according to the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. This sanctified tour, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> round by the south, is called deiscal, from deas or des, "the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>," and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> or sul, "the sun;" the right hand being ever next the heap or cairn. In the same isles it is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> and fashion of the people to testify their respect for their chieftains, the proprietors of their several isles, and other persons of distinction, by performing the deiscal round them in the same manner. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> giving an account of his reception in one of the Western <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, of which he was proprietor, describes the ceremony of the deiscal in this manner: "One of the natives would needs express his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem for my person, by making a turn round about me, sun-ways, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> blessing me, and wishing me all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. But I bid him let alone that piece of homage, telling him I was sensible of his good meaning towards me. But this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was very much disappointed, as were also his neighbours; for they doubted not but this ancient ceremony would have been very acceptable to me; and one of them told me, that this was a thing due to my character from them, as to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>; and that they could not, and would not, fail to perform it."

DEISM

Pages 136-136

the doctrine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the deists. Deism, from θεός God, may properly be used to denote <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, as comprehending those truths which have a real foundation in reason and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is so far from being opposite to Christianity, that it is one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the gospel to illustrate and enforce it. Thus some of the deistical writers have affected to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it. But deism more precisely signifies that system of religion, relating both to doctrine and practice, which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is to discover for himself by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> force of natural reason, independent of all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, and exclusive of it; and this religion Dr Tindal and others pretend is so perfect, as to be incapable of receiving any addition or improvement even from divine revelation.

DEISTS

Pages 136-136

a class of people known also under the denomination of Free-thinkers, whose distinguishing character it is, not to profess any particular form <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> system of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; but only to acknowledge the existence of a god, and to follow the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, rejecting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, and opposing Christianity. This name seems to have been first assumed as the denomination of a party about the middle of the 16th century, by some gentlemen in France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, who were desirous of thus disguising their opposition to Christianity by a more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> appellation than that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">atheists</a>. Vivot, an eminent reformer, mentions certain persons, in his epistle dedicatory prefixed to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> tome of his Instruction Chretienne, published in 1563, who called themselves by a new name, that of Deists. These, he tells us, professed to believe in God, but showed no regard to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and considered the doctrine of the apostles and evangelists as fables and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>. He adds, that they laughed at all religion, though they outwardly conformed to the religion of those with whom they lived, or whom they wished to please, or feared to offend. Some, he observes, professed to believe the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; others denied both this doctrine and that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>. Many of them were considered as persons of acute and subtle genius, and took pains in disseminating their notions. The deists hold, that, considering the multiplicity of religions, the numerous pretences to revelation, and the precarious arguments generally advanced in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> thereof, the best and surest way is to return to the simplicity of nature and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of one God; which is the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> agreed to by all nations. They complain, that the freedom of thinking and reasoning is oppressed under the yoke of religion; and that the minds of men are ridden and tyrannized by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> imposed on them of believing inconceivable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>; and contend that nothing should be required to be assented to or believed but what their reason clearly conceives. The distinguishing character of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> deists is, that they reject all revealed religion, and discard all pretences to it as the effects of imposture or enthusiasm. They profess a regard for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> religion, though they are far from being agreed in their notions concerning it. They are classed by some of their own writers into mortal and immortal deists: the latter acknowledging a future state; and the former denying it, or representing it as very uncertain. Dr Clarke distinguishes four sorts of deists. 1. Those who pretend to believe the existence of an eternal, infinite, independent, intelligible Being, who made the world, without concerning himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of it. 2. Those who believe the being and natural providence of God, but deny the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of actions, as morally good or evil, resolving it into the arbitrary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> laws; and therefore they suppose that God takes no notice of them. With respect to both these classes, he observes that their opinions can consistently terminate in nothing but downright atheism.

DEITY

Pages 136-137

Godhead; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> appellation given to God; and also by the poets to the heathen gods and goddesses.

DELAWARE

Pages 137-139

a state of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated on a river of the same name. The Dutch, under the pretended purchase made by Henry Hudson, took possession of the lands on both Delaware sides the river Delaware; and as early as the year 1623 built a fort at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which has since been called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>. In 1627, by the influence of William Ussing, a respectable merchant in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, a colony of Swedes and Finns came over, furnished with all the necessaries for beginning a new settlement, and landed at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Henlopen; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Dutch had wholly quitted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Dutch, however, returned in 1630, and built a fort at Lewistown, by them named Hoarkill. The following year the Swedes built a fort near Wilmington, which they called Christiania <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Christiana. Here also they laid out a small town, which was afterwards demolished by the Dutch. The same year they erected a fort higher up the river, upon Tenerum <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which they called New Gottenburgh; they also about the same time built forts at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, Elsinburgh, and other places. John Prinz then governed the Swedes, who, in 1654, deputed his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, John Pappoia, and returned to Sweden. Pappoia soon followed his father-in-law to his native country, and John Rysing succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In 1655, the Dutch, under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Stuyvesant, arrived in Delaware river, from New <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>), in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> vessels, with 6 or 700 men. They dispossessed the Swedes of their forts on the river, and carried the officers and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants prisoners to New Amsterdam, and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people submitted to the conquerors, and remained in the country. On the first of October 1664, Sir Robert Carr obtained the submission of the Swedes on Delaware river. Four years after, Col. Nicolls, governor of New York, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, on the 21st of April, appointed a scout and five other persons to assist Capt. Carr in the government of the country. In 1672, the town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> was incorporated by the government of New York, to be governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> and six assistants; after the first year, the four oldest were to leave their office, and four others to be chosen. The bailiff was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> vote; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> was chosen by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. They had power to try causes not exceeding 10l. without <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>. The office of scout was converted into that of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, who had jurisdiction in the corporation and along the river, and was annually chosen. They were to have a free trade, without being obliged to make entry at New York, as had formerly been the practice. Wampum was at this time the principal currency of the country. Governor Lovelace of New York, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, ordered that four <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> grains and three <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> ones should <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for the value of a stiver or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>. This proclamation was published at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>, Esopus, Delaware, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> Island, and the parts adjacent. In 1674 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> patent, dated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 29th, granted to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of York all that country called by the Dutch New <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, of which the three counties of Newcastle, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, were a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. In 1683, the duke of York, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> dated Aug. 24th, sold to William Penn the town of Newcastle, with the district of 12 miles round the same; and by another deed of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, granted to him the remainder of the territory, which till the revolution was called the Three Lower Counties. These three counties were considered as a part of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> in matters of government. Delaware. The same governor presided over both; but the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> and courts of judicature were different; different as to their constituent members, but in form nearly the same. At the late revolution they became a distinct territory, called The Delaware State. This state is bounded on the north by Pennsylvania; on the east by Delaware river and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>; on the south, by a due east and west line, from Cape Henlopen, in lat. 38° 30' to the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>; and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>. It is the smallest state in the Union except Rhode, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> being only 2200 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is generally low and flat, which occasions the waters to stagnate, and subjects the inhabitants to intermittent fevers. The Delaware state is divided into three counties, viz. Newcastle, Kent, Sussex: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of which are, Wilmington and Newcastle, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILFORD">Milford</a>, and Lewiston. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the whole state in 1810 was 72,674, including 4177 slaves. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of free blacks was 13,136. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THREE_RIVERS">Three <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the Choptank, Nanticoke, and Pocomoke, having their sources in this state, and are navigable for vessels of 50 or 60 tons, 20 or 30 miles into the country. They all run a westerly course into Chesapeake bay. The fourth part of the state is a low flat country, and a considerable portion of it lies in forest. What is under cultivation is chiefly barren, except in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, of which it produces fine crops. In some places rye and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> may be raised, but wheat is a foreigner in these parts. Where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is deficient in one resource, she is generally bountiful in another. This is verified in the tall thick forests of pines which are manufactured into boards, and exported in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities into every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port in the three adjoining states. As you proceed north, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is more fertile, and produces wheat in large quantities, which is the staple commodity of the state. They raise all the other kinds of grain common to Pennsylvania. The state has no mountain in it, except <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a> Hill, in the western part of Newcastle <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and is generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, except some small parts, which are stony and uneven. The trade of this state is carried on almost entirely in the chief town, Wilmington, which had 9,591 tons of shipping in 1815, and contained about 5000 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> exported are principally wheat, corn, and lumber. No preference is given by law to any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of worship. In 1814 the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a> had 24 churches; the Episcopalians 14; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> 8; the Baptists 7; the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a> several. A considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> is appropriated by the state for the support of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. The expense of instruction varies from 10 to 32 dollars per annum. The value of lands and houses in this state in 1799, was 6,233,413 dollars, and in 1814 it was 13,449,370 dollars. The value of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> in this state in 1810 was 970,701 dollars; and the exports in 1817 amounted to 44,854 dollars. The state taxes in 1811 were stated to be 72,163 dollars. Under the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, the legislature is divided into two distinct branches, which together are styled The General Assembly of Delaware. One branch, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Assembly, consists of seven representatives from each of the three counties, chosen annually by the freeholders. The other branch, called the Council, consists of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> members, three for a county, Delaware who must be more than 25 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, chosen likewise by the freeholders. A <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of members is established by displacing one member for a county at the end of every year. All <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> bills must originate in the house of assembly, but they may be altered, amended, or rejected by the legislative council. A president or chief <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> is chosen by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> ballot of both houses, and continues in office three years; at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he is ineligible the three succeeding years. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this office becomes vacant during the recess of the legislature, or he is unable to attend to business, the speaker of the legislative council is vice-president for the time; and in his absence the powers of the president devolve upon the speaker of the assembly. A <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, consisting of four members, two from each house, chosen by ballot, is constituted to assist the chief magistrate in the administration of the government. The three justices of the supreme <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, a judge of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, and four justices of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a> and orphan courts, are appointed by the joint ballot of the president and general assembly, and commissioned by the president to hold their offices during good behaviour. The president and privy council appoint the secretary, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, registers for the produce of wills, registrars in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, clerks of the common pleas and orphan courts, and the clerks of the peace, who hold their offices during five years, unless sooner removed for mal-conduct. The house of assembly name 24 persons in each county for justices of peace, from which number the president, with the advice of his council, appoints and commissions twelve, who serve for seven years, unless sooner dismissed for mal-administration. The members of the legislative and privy councils are justices of the peace for the whole state.—The courts of common pleas and orphan courts have power to hold chancery courts in certain <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. The clerk of the supreme court is appointed by the chief <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and the recorders of deeds by the justices of the common pleas, for five years, unless sooner dismissed. All the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and marine officers are appointed by the general assembly. The court of appeals consists of seven persons: the president, who is a member, and presides by virtue of his office, and six others, three to be chosen by the legislative council, and three by the house of assembly. To this court appeals <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> from the supreme court, in all matters of law and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>. The judges hold their office during good behaviour. The justices of the several courts, the members of the privy council, secretary, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of the loan office, clerks of the common pleas, and all persons concerned in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> contracts, are ineligible to either house of assembly. Every member, before taking his seat, must take the oath of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and subscribe a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> test, declaring his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in God the Father, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and the Holy Ghost; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> of the Scriptures. The house of assembly have the privilege of impeaching delinquent officers of government; and impeachments are to be prosecuted by the attorney-general, or other persons appointed by the assembly, and tried before the legislative council. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> may extend to temporal or perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a> to hold Though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> exists in this state, the number of slaves was found to have diminished greatly between 1800 and 1810. The habits and character of the people greatly resemble those of the Pennsylvanians.

DELEGATES

Pages 139-139

commissioners appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, to hear and determine appeals from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Court of DELEGATES, the great court of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> in all ecclesiastical causes. These delegates are appointed by the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> under his great seal, and issuing out of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, to represent his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> person, and hear all appeals to him made by virtue of the statute 25 Henry VIII. c. 19. This commission is usually filled with lords spiritual and temporal, judges of the courts at Westminster, and doctors of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Appeals to Rome were always looked upon by the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, even in the times of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, with an evil eye, as being contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the subject, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and the independence of the whole realm; and were first introduced, in very turbulent times, in the 16th year of King Stephen (A.D. 1151), at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> (Sir Henry Spelman observes) that the civil and canon laws were first imported into England. But in a few years after, to obviate this growing practice, the constitutions made at Clarendon, 11 Hen. II. on account of the disturbances raised by Archbishop Becket and other zealots of the holy see, expressly declare, that appeals in causes ecclesiastical ought to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> from the archdeacon to the diocesan; from the diocesan to the archbishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>; and from the archbishop to the king; and are not to proceed any farther without special license from the crown. But the unhappy advantage that was given in the reign of King John, and his son Hen. III., to the encroaching power of the Pope, who was ever vigilant to improve all opportunities of extending his jurisdiction to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, at length rivetted the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of appealing to Rome in causes ecclesiastical so strongly, that it never could be thoroughly broken off till the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> rupture happened in the reign of Hen.
