VIII. when all the jurisdiction usurped by the pope in matters ecclesiastical was restored to the crown, to which it originally belonged; so that the statute 25 Hen. VIII. was but declaratory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law of the realm. But in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the king himself be party in any of these suits, the appeal does not then lie to him in chancery, which would be absurd; but, by the 24 Henry VIII. c. 12, to all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the realm, assembled in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>.

DELEGATION

Pages 139-139

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> extraordinary given by a judge to take cognisance of, and determine, some cause which ordinarily does not come before him.

DELEN

Pages 139-139

DIRK VAN, an eminent painter of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEUSDEN">Heusden</a>, but in what year is not known. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Francis Hals, in whose school he practised to paint those particular subjects which were most esteemed by that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, such as portraits and conversations; and by that means he acquired the skill to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> figures with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of spirit and correctness. But his predominant inclination directed him to paint architecture and perspective; and these he studied with so much care, as to make his works admired and coveted through the Low Countries. His subjects were the insides of churches, filled with figures; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; magnificent saloons and galleries, with people assembled at concerts of music, feasting, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>. Those subjects he finished highly; his architecture was in a noble <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and the figures were well designed, as well as grouped with a great deal of judgment. Several authors mention the performances of this master with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> commendation, for the goodness of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and neatness of his handling.

DELETERIOUS

Pages 139-139

an appellation given to things of a destructive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">POISON</a>.

DELFT

Pages 139-140

a town of the United Provinces, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Delftland in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, very clean and well built, with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> in the streets, planted on each side with trees. The public buildings, especially the town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, are very magnificent. Here are two churches; in one is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, who was assassinated; and in the other, that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Tromp. It has a fine arsenal, well furnished; is about two miles in circumference, and is defended against inundations by three dams <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dikes. Here is made a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fine earthen-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> called delft-ware; but the trade is on the decline since extensive potteries were established in England and Germany. It is pleasantly situated among the meadows on the river Shie, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 13. N. Lat. 52. 6. Delft-Ware, a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a> of baked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, covered with an enamel or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> glazing, which gives it the appearance and neatness of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>. Some kinds of this enamelled pottery differ much from others, either in their sustaining sudden <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> without breaking, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and regularity of their forms, of their enamel, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> with which they are ornamented. In general, the fine and beautiful enamelled potteries, which approach the nearest to porcelain in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, are, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, those which least resist a brisk fire. Again, those which sustain a sudden heat, are coarse, and resemble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pottery. The basis of this pottery is clay, which is to be mixed, when too fat, with such a quantity of sand, that the earth shall preserve enough of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a> to be worked, moulded, and turned easily; and yet that its fatness shall be sufficiently taken from it, that it may not crack or shrink too much in drying or in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>. Vessels formed of this earth must be dried very gently to avoid cracking. They are then to be placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> to receive a slight baking, which is only meant to give them a certain consistence or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>. And, lastly, they are to be covered with an enamel or glazing, which is done, by patting upon the vessels thus prepared the enamel, which has been ground very fine, and diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. As vessels on which the enamel is applied are but slightly baked, they readily imbibe the water in which the enamel is suspended, and a layer of the enamel adheres to their surface; these vessels may then be painted with colours composed of metallic calces, mixed and ground with a fusible glass. When they are become perfectly dry, they are to be placed in the furnace, included in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of baked earth called teggars, and exposed Delft-ware, posed to a heat capable of fusing uniformly the enamel which covers them. This heat given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> the enamel being much stronger than that which was applied at first to give some consistence to the ware, is also the heat necessary to complete the baking of it. The furnace and colours used for painting this ware, are the same as those employed for porcelain. The glazing, which is nothing but white enamel, ought to be so opaque as not to show the ware under it. There are many receipts for making these enamels; but all of them are composed of sand or flints, vitrifying salts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and calx of tin; and the sand must be perfectly vitrified, so as to form a glass considerably fusible. Somewhat less than an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, or twice its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of calx of lead, is requisite to effect such vitrifications of sand. The calx of tin is not intended to be vitrified, but to give a white opaque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; and one part of it is to be added to three or four parts of all the other ingredients taken together. From these general principles various enamels may be made to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the different kinds of earths. To make the enamel, lead and tin are calcined together with a strong fire; and the sand is also to be made into a frit with the salt or ashes. The whole is then to be well mixed and ground together. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is then to be placed under the furnace, where it is melted and vitrified during the baking of the ware. It is next to be ground in a mill, and applied as above directed. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the white enamel is a very essential article in making delft-ware, and one in which many artists fail. M. Bosc. d'Antic, in a memoir concerning this kind of ware, published in the Mem. des Savans Etrangers, tom. vi. recommends the following proportions. A hundred pounds of calx of lead are to be mixed with about a seventh part of that quantity of calx of tin for common delft-ware, or a fourth part of calx of tin for the finest kind; a hundred, or a hundred and ten pounds of fine sand; and about twenty or thirty pounds of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-salt. Concerning the earth of which the ware is made, he observes, that pure clay is not a proper material when used alone. Different kinds of earth mixed together are found to succeed better. Pieces of ware made of clay alone are found to require too much time to dry; and they crack, and lose their form, unless they are made exceedingly thick. An addition of marle diminishes the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the clay; renders its less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>; and allows the water to escape, without altering the form of the ware in drying. It affords also a better ground for the enamel; which appears more glossy and white than when laid on clay alone. The kinds of clay which are chiefly used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of delft-ware, are the blue and green. A mixture of blue clay and marle would not be sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and would be apt to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, unless it were exposed to a fire more intense than what is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of delft-ware. To give a greater solidity, some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> clay is added; which, on account of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> matter, possesses the requisite binding <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The proportions of these ingredients vary in different works, according to the different qualities of the earths employed. Three parts of blue clay, two parts of red clay, and five parts of marle, form the composition used in several manufactories. M. d'Antic thinks that the best delft-ware might be made of equal parts of pure clay and pure Delft-ware calcareous earth; but this composition would require that the fire should be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> twice as long as it generally is.

DELIAC

Pages 140-140

(Deliacus), among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, denoted a poulterer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a person who sold fowls, fatted capons, &c. The traders in this way were called Deliaci; the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Delos first practised this occupation. They also sold eggs, as appears from Cicero, in his Academic Questions, lib. iv. Pliny, lib. x. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 30. and Columella, lib. viii. cap. 8. likewise mention the Deliaci.

DELIACAL PROBLEM

Pages 140-140

a celebrated problem among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, concerning the duplication of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a>.

DELIAS

Pages 140-140

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, because she was born in Delos.

DELIBAMENTA

Pages 140-140

in antiquity, a libation to the infernal gods, always offered by pouring downwards. See Libation. JUS DELIBERANDI. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DELIBERATIVE

Pages 140-142

an appellation given to a kind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branch of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, employed in proving a thing, or convincing an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> thereof, in order to persuade them to put it in execution. To have a deliberative <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the assembly, is when a person has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to give his advice and his vote therein. In councils, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> have deliberative Delict, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies such small offenses or breaches of the peace as are punishable only by fine or short imprisonment. Delille, Jacques, an eminent French poet. See Supplement. Delinquent, a guilty person, or one who has committed some fault or offence for which he is punishable. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, No. 97. Deliquescence, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which certain bodies have of attracting moisture from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and becoming liquid thereby. This property is never found but in saline substances, or matters containing them. It is caused by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> which these substances have for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The more simple they are, according to Mr Macquer, the more they incline to deliquescence. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, which are the most simple, are also the most deliquescent salts. Mineral acids are so deliquescent, that they strongly imbibe moisture from the air, even though they are already mixed with a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water to be fluid. For this purpose, it is sufficient that they be concentrated only to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>.—Many neutral salts are deliquescent, chiefly those whose bases are not saline substances. Salts formed by the vitriolic acid, with fixed or volatile alkalies, earths, or most metallic substances, are not deliquescent; although this acid is the strongest of all, and, when disengaged, attracts the moisture of the air most powerfully. Though the immediate cause of deliquescence is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of the moisture of the air, as we have already observed; yet it remains to be shown why some salts attract this moisture powerfully, and others, though seemingly equally simple, do not attract it at all. The vegetable alkali, for instance, attracts moisture powerfully; the mineral alkali, though to appearance equally simple, does not attract it at all. The acid of tartar by itself does not attract the moisture of the air; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, which has a little attraction for moisture, the mixture is exceedingly deliquescent.—Some theories have been suggested, in order to account for these and other similar facts; but we are as yet too little acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> to form certain conclusions on the subject. Deliquium, or Deliquium Animi (from delinquo, "I swoon"), a swooning or fainting away: called also syncope, lipothymia, lipopygeia, eclysis, and astyphxia. Deliquium (from deliquesco, "to be dissolved"), in Chemistry, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> or melting of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> by suspending it in a moist cellar. Salt of tartar, or any fixed alkali, set in a cellar or other cool moist <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and in an open vessel, resolves or runs into a kind of liquor called by the older chemists <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of tartar per deliquium. Delirium (from deliro, "to rave or talk idly"). When the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> excited in the mind do not correspond to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects, but are produced by the change induced on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sensory, the patient is said to be delirious. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Delivery, or Child-Birth. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>. Delli, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in Hindostan. The city was once the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> between it and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, the other capital, is that famous alley or walk planted with trees by Jehin Ghir, and 150 leagues in length. Each half <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> is marked with a kind of turret; and at every stage there are little sarays or caravanserais for the benefit of travellers. The road, though pretty good, has many inconveniences. It is not only frequented by wild beasts, but by robbers. The latter are so dexterous at casting a noose about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s neck, that they never fail, if within reach, to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> and strangle him. They <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> their point likewise by means of handsome women; who, feigning great distress, and being taken up behind the unwary traveller, choke him with the same snare.—The capital consists of three cities, built near one another. The first, now quite destroyed, is said to have had 52 gates; and to have been the residence of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Porus, conquered by Alexander the Great. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, which is also in ruins, was demolished by Shah Jehan, to build <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JEHANABAD">Jehanabad</a> with the materials. This makes the third city, and joins the ruins of the second. This city stands in an open plain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on the river Jamuna, which rises in this province. It is encompassed with walls, except towards the river. These are of brick, flanked with round towers; but without a ditch, and terraced behind, four or five feet thick. The circumference of the walls may be about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles. The fortress, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circuit, has good walls and round towers, and ditches full of water, faced with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. It is surrounded with fine gardens, and in it is the Mogul's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. See Indostan. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 77. 25. N. Lat. 28. 20. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELMENHORST">Delmenhorst</a>, a strong town of Germany, in Westphalia, and now united to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Osnburg, seated on the river Delm, near the Weser. E. Long. 8. 37. N. Lat. 53. 10. Delos, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, very famous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Originally it is said to have been a floating island, but afterwards it became fixed and immovable. It was held sacred on account of its being the birth-place of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>.—Anciently this island was governed by its own kings. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> mentions one Anius reigning here in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He was, according to that poet, both king and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Apollo, and entertained Æneas with great kindness. The Persians allowed the Delians to enjoy their ancient liberties, after they had reduced the rest of the Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. In after ages, the Athenians made themselves masters of it; and held it till they were driven out by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> the Great, who plundered the rich temple of Apollo, and obliged the Delians to side with him. Mithridates was in his turn driven out by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who granted the inhabitants many privileges, and exempted them from all sorts of taxes. At present it is quite abandoned; the lands being covered with ruins and rubbish in such a manner as to be quite incapable of cultivation. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYCONE">Mycone</a> hold it now, and pay but ten crowns <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax to the Grand Signior for an island which was once one of the richest in the world.—Strabo and Callimachus tells us that the island of Delos was watered by the river Inapu: but Pliny calls it only a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>: and adds, that its waters swelled and abated at the same time with those of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. At present there is no river in the island, but one of the noblest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. Delos springs in the world; being twelve paces in diameter, and inclosed partly by rocks, and partly by a wall. Mount Cynthus, whence Apollo had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Cynthus, is by Strabo placed near the city, and said to be so high, that the whole island was covered by its shadow; but our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> travellers speak of it as a hill of a very moderate height. It is but one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> of the ordinary sort, cut on that side which faced the city into regular steps, and inclosed on both sides by a wall. On the top of the mountain are still to be seen the remains of a stately <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, with a mosaic pavement, many broken pillars, and other valuable monuments of antiquity. From an inscription discovered there some time ago, and which mention a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> made to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERAPIS">Serapis</a>, Isis, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANUBIS">Anubis</a>, some have conjectured, that on this hill stood a temple dedicated to these Egyptian deities, though nowhere mentioned in history.—The city of Delos, as is manifest from the magnificent ruins still extant, took up that spacious plain reaching from one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> to the other. It was well peopled, and the richest city in the Archipelago, especially after the destruction of Corinth; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> flocking thither from all parts, both in regard of the immunity they enjoyed there, and of the convenient situation of the place between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Strabo calls it one of the most frequented empories in the world; and Pliny tells us, that all the commodities of Europe and Asia were sold, purchased, or exchanged, there. It contained many noble and stately buildings; as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of Apollo, Diana, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>; the porticoes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon, and Dionysius Eutyches; a gymnasium; an oval basin made at an immense expense, for the representation of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-fights; and a most magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. The temple of Apollo was, according to Plutarch, begun by Ergasilothus the son of Cecrops; but afterwards enlarged and embellished at the common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of all the states of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Plutarch tells us, that it was one of the most stately buildings in the universe; and speaks of an altar in it, which, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, deserved a place among the wonders of the world. It was built with the horns of various animals, so artificially adapted to one another that they hanged together without any cement. This altar is said to have been a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a>; and the doubling it was a famous mathematical problem among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. This went under the name of Problems Deliacum; and is said to have been proposed by the oracle, for the purpose of freeing the country from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>. The distemper was to cease when the problem was solved.—The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the famous statue of Apollo, mentioned by Strabo and Pliny, is still an object of great admiration to travellers. It is without head, feet, arms, or legs; but from the parts that are yet remaining, it plainly appears, that the ancients did not exaggerate when they commended it as a wonder of art. It was of gigantic size, though cut out of a single block of marble; the shoulders being six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and the thighs nine feet round. At a small distance from this statue lies, amongst confused heaps of broken columns, architraves, bases, chapters, &c., a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> piece of marble 15 feet long, ten feet nine inches broad, and two feet three inches thick: which undoubtedly served as a pedestal for this colossus. It bears in very fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> this inscription in Greek, "The Naxians to Apollo." Plutarch tells us, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Nicias, that he caused to be set up, near the temple of Delos, an huge palm-tree of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, which he consecrated to Apollo; and adds, that a violent storm of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> threw <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> this tree on a colossal statue raised by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAXOS">Naxos</a>. Round the temple were magnificent porticoes built at the charge of various princes, as appears from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> which are still very plain. The names of Philip king of Macedon, Dionysius Eutyches, Mithridates Euergetes, Mithridates Eupator, kings of Pontus, and Nicomedes king of Bithynia, are found on several pedestals.—To this temple the inhabitants of the neighbouring islands sent yearly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of virgins to celebrate, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, the festival of Apollo and his sister Diana, and to make offerings in the name of their respective cities. So very sacred was the island of Delos held by the ancients, that no hostilities were practised here, even by the nations that were at war with one another, when they happened to meet in this place. Of this Livy gives an instance. He tells us, that some Roman deputies being obliged to put in at Delos, in their voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, found the galleys of Perseus king of Macedon, and those of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, anchored in the same harbour, though these two princes were then making war upon one another.—Hence this island was a general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, and the protection extended to all kinds of living creatures; for this reason it abounded with hares, no dogs being suffered to enter it. No dead body was suffered to be buried in it, nor was any woman suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in there; all dying persons, and women ready to be delivered, were carried over to the neighbouring island of Rhenea.

DELPHI

Pages 142-144

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, situated on the south-west extremity of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>. It was famous for a temple and oracle of that god, of which the following was said to be the origin: A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of goats that were feeding on Mount Parnassus, came near a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which had a deep and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> perforation. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> which issued from the hole seemed to inspire the goats, and they played and frisked about in such an uncommon manner, that the goat-herd was tempted to lean on the hole, and see what <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> the place contained. He was immediately seized with a fit of enthusiasm, his expressions were wild and extravagant, and passed for prophecies. This circumstance was soon known about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and many experienced the same enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. The place was revered; a temple was soon after erected in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> built, which became the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and most illustrious in Phocis. The influence of its god has controled the councils of states, directed the course of armies, and decided the fate of kingdoms. The ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> is full of his energy, and an early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of his authority. The circumjacent cities were the stewards and guardians of the god. Their deputies composed the famous Amphictyonic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, which once guided Greece. The temple of Apollo, it is related, was at first a kind of cottage covered with boughs of laurel; but he was early provided with a better habitation. An edifice of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was erected by Trophonius and Agamedes, which subsisted about 700 years, and was burned in the year 636 after the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and 548 before Christ. It is mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Apollo ascribed Delphi, ascribed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. An opulent and illustrious family, called Alcmæonidae, which fled from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Hippias, contracted with the deputies for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of a new temple, and exceeded their agreement. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> was raised with Parian marble, instead of the stone called Poros; which resembled it in whiteness, but was not so heavy. A Corinthian was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>. The pediments were adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, and Apollo, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>; the setting of Phebus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and the women called Thyiades. The architraves were decorated with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> armour; bucklers suspended by the Athenians after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a>, and shields taken from the Gauls under Brennus. In the portico were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the celebrated maxims of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sages of Greece. There was an image of Homer, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a> was an altar of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the Fates, and of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Apollo, who were surnamed Leaders of the Fates. Near the hearth, before the altar at which Neoptolemus the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> was slain by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, stood the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. In the sanctuary was an image of Apollo gilded. The inclosure was of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and filled with treasures, in which many cities had consecrated tenths of spoil taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and with the public donations of renowned states in various ages. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> repository of ancient Greece, in which the labours of the sculptor and statuary, gods, heroes, and illustrious persons, were seen collected and arranged; the inequalities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of acclivity contributing to a full display of the noble assemblage. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> were delivered by a priestess called Pythia, who received the prophetic influence in the following manner. A lofty tripod, decked with laurel, was placed over the aperture, whence the sacred vapour issued. The priestess, after washing her body and especially her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of Castalia, mounted on it, to receive the divine effluvia. She wore a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of laurel, and shook a sacred tree, which grew by. Sometimes she chewed the leaves; and the frenzy which followed may with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> be attributed to this usage, and the gentler or more violent symptoms to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> taken. In one instance the paroxysm was so terrible, that the priests and supplicants ran away, and left her alone to expire; it was believed, of the god. Her <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> was unpleasant; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she declined acting, they dragged her by force to the tripod. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of her order was that of virgins. The rules enjoined <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and chastity, and prohibited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> in apparel. The season of inquiry was in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, during the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> called Bulsius; after which Apollo was supposed to visit the altars of the Hyperboreans. The city of Delphi arose in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, upon the winding declivity of Parnassus, whose fantastic tops overshadowed it, like a canopy, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, while two immense rocks rendered it inaccessible on the east and west, and the rugged and shapeless Mount Cirphis defended it on the south. The foot of the last named mountain was washed by the rapid Plistus, which discharged itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at the distance of only a few leagues from the sacred city. This inaccessible and romantic situation, from which the place derived the name of Delphi (signifying, as explained in the glossaries, solitary, alone), was rendered still more striking, by the innumerable echoes which multiplied every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and increased the ignorant veneration of visitants for the god of the oracle. The artful ministers of Apollo gradually collected such objects in the groves and temple as were fitted to astonish the senses of the admiring multitude. The splendour of marble, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, the invaluable statues of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, represented (to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of antiquity) not the resemblance of an earthly habitation, but rather expressed the image of Olympus, adorned and enlightened by the actual presence of the gods. The protection and superintendence of this precious depository of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> belonged to the Amphictyons, as already noticed. But the inhabitants of Delphi, who, if we may use the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, were the original proprietors of the oracles, always <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, and to conduct the important business of prophecy. It was their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> alone to determine at what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and on what occasion, the Pythia should mount the sacred tripod, to receive the prophetic steams by which she communicated with Apollo. When overflowing with the heavenly inspiration, she uttered the confused words, or rather frantic sounds, irregularly suggested by the impulse of the god; the Delphians collected these sounds, reduced them into order, animated them with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and adorned them with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. The Pythia, appointed and dismissed at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, was a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of those artful ministers, whose character became so venerable and sacred, that they were finally regarded, not merely as attendants and worshippers, but as the peculiar family of the god. Their number was considerable, and never exactly ascertained, since all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants of Delphi, claiming an immediate relation to Apollo, were entitled to officiate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of his sanctuary; and even the inferior ranks belonging to that sacred city were continually employed in dances, festivals, processions, and in displaying all the gay pageantry of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> and elegant superstition. Delphi was conveniently situated for the conflux of votaries, lying in the centre of Greece, and, as was then imagined, of the universe. It was customary for those who consulted the oracle to make rich presents to the god; his servants and priests feasted on the numerous victims which were sacrificed to him; and the rich magnificence of his temple had become proverbial even in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Homer. In aftertimes, Croesus, the wealthiest of monarchs, was particularly munificent in his donations. This sacred repository of opulence was therefore often the object of plunder. Neoptolemus was slain, while sacrificing, on suspicion of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of that kind. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> divided his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at Panopens and proceeded with the main body through <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, while a party keeping Parnassus on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, advanced along Schiste to Delphi; but was taken with a panic when near Ilium, and fled. This monarch, it is related, was as well apprised of the contents of the temple, and the sumptuous offerings of Halyattes and Croesus, as of the effects which he had left behind in his own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. The divine board was seized by the Phocessians under Philomelus, and dissipated in a long war with the Amphictyons. The Gauls experienced a reception like that of the Persians, and mani- fested similar dismay and superstition. Sylla, wanting <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to pay his army, sent to borrow from the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and when his messenger would have frightened him, by reporting a prodigy, that the sound of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> had been heard from within the sanctuary, replied, it was a sign that the god was happy to oblige him. The trade of Apollo, after it had flourished for a long <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, was affected by the mal-practices of some concerned in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a>, who were convicted of bribery and corruption, and ruined the character of their principal. The temple in the time of Strabo was reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> poverty; but the offerings which remained were very numerous. Apollo was silent, except some efforts at intervals to regain his lost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. Nero attempted to drive him, as it were, by violence, from the cavern; killing men at the mouth, and polluting it with blood; but he lingered on, and would not entirely forsake it. Answers were reported as given by him afterwards, but not without suspicion of forgery. An oracle of Apollo at another place informed the consultors, that he should no more recover utterance at Delphi, but enjoined the continuance of the accustomed offerings. The city of Delphi was free under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. In the time of Pausanias, who has particularly described it, there still remained an invaluable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of the offerings within the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the temple. The number, variety, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of these were prodigious. The store appeared inexhaustible; and the robbery of Nero, who removed five hundred brazen images, was rather regretted than perceived. The holy treasuries, though empty, served as memorials of the piety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the cities which erected them. The Athenian portico preserved the beaks of ships and the brazen shields; trophies won in the Peloponnesian war. And a multitude of curiosities remained untouched. Constantine the Great, however, proved a more fatal enemy to Apollo and Delphi than either Sylla or Nero. He removed the sacred tripods to adorn the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPODROME">hippodrome</a> of his new city; where these, with the Apollo, the statues of the Heliconian muses, and the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>, dedicated by the Greek cities, after the war with the Medes, were extant when Sozomen wrote his history. Afterwards Julian sent Oribasius to restore the temple; but he was admonished by an oracle to represent to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> the deplorable condition of the place. 'Tell him the well-built court is fallen to the ground. Phoebus has not a cottage, nor the prophetic laurel, nor the speaking fountain Cassotis; and even the beautiful water is extinct.'

DELPHINIUM

Pages 144-144

DOLPHIN-FLOWER, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> LARKSPUR; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 26th order, Multisiliqua. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DELPHINUS

Pages 144-144
or DOLPHIN, a genus of fishes Delphini, belonging to the order of Cete. See CETOLOGY. Delphinus Index. Delphinus, in Astronomy, a constellation of the northern hemisphere; whose stars in Ptolemy's catalogue are 10; in Tycho's the same number; in Hevelius's 14; and in Flamsteed's 18.

DELPHOS

Pages 144-144

a town, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather village, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Libadus; occupying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the site of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>. See DELPHI. A late traveller informs us, that some vestiges of Chand-temple are visible; and above them in the mountain's Tronside, are sepulchres, niches, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> cavities for vels in the body, some covered with slabs. Farther on is a niche cut in the rock with a seat, intended, it seems, for the accommodation of travellers wearied with the rugged track and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ascent. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> is on the site of the gymnasium. Strong terrace walls and other traces of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> edifice remain. The village is at a distance. Castalia is on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> as you ascend to it, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> coming from on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and crossing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>; a steep precipice, above which the mountain still rises immensely, continuing on in that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The village consists of a few <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> cottages of Albanians covering the site of the temple and oracle. Beneath it to the south is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Elias, with areas, terrace-walls, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, and vestiges of the buildings once within the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The concavity of the rock in this part gave to the site the resemblance of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">Turning</a> to the left hand, as it were toward the extremity of one of the wings, you come again to sepulchres hewn in the rock, and to a semicircular recess or niche with a seat as on the other side. Higher up than the village, is the hollow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, in which were some seats and scattered fragments. Higher up, within the village, is a piece of ancient wall, concealed from view by a shed, which it supports. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, rough, and ordinary, probably that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>. On the south side are many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, with wide gaps between the letters, which are negligently and faintly cut; all nearly of the same tenor, and very difficult to copy. They <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> the purchase of slaves who had entrusted the price of their freedom to the god; containing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and their owners, witnessed by his priests and by some of the archons. This remnant seems to be part of the wall before Cassotis; as above it is still a fountain, which supplies the village with excellent water. The water of Castalia in the neighbourhood, from which the Pythia, and the poets who versified her answers, were believed to deprive a large share of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, descends through a cleft of Parnassus; the rock on each side high and steep, ending in two summits; of which one was called Hyampetra, and had beneath it the sacred portion of Autonous, a local <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> as distinguished as Phylacus. From this precipice the Delphians threw <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the famous Æsop. By the stream within the cleft, are seen small broken stairs leading to a cavity in which is water, and once perhaps up to the top. Grooves have been cut, and the marks of tools are visible on the rock; but the current, instead of supplying a fountain, now passes over its native <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and hastens down a course, deep-worn to join the Plistus. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> by, at the foot of the eastern precipice,

DELTA

Pages 144-145

is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, which takes up a considerable space of ground between the branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> and the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Delta, because it is in the shape of a triangle, like the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of that name. It is about 130 miles along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> from Damietta to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and 70 on the sides from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the Nile begins to divide itself. It is the most plentiful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in all Egypt, and it rains more there than in other parts, but the fertility is chiefly owing to the inundation of the river Nile. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the coast are Damietta, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROSETTA">Rosetta</a>, and Alexandria; but, within <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, Menousia, and Maala <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Elmaa.

DELUGE

Pages 145-165

an inundation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> overflowing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, either wholly or in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. We have several deluges recorded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; as that of Oggyes, which overflowed almost all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>; and that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, which drowned all Thessaly in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; but the most memorable was that called the Universal Deluge, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">Flood</a>, which overflowed and destroyed the whole earth; and from which only Noah, and those with him in the ark, escaped. This flood makes one of the most considerable epochs in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>. Its history is given by Moses, Gen. ch. vi. and vii. Its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is fixed, by the best chronologers, to the year from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> 1656, answering to the year before Christ 2293. From this flood, the state of the world is divided into diluvian and antediluvian. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTEDILUVIANS">ANTEDILUVIANS</a>. Among the many testimonies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this part of the Mosaic history, we may account the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of mankind at all times, and in all parts of the world. The objections of the free-thinkers have indeed principally turned upon three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, viz. 1. The want of any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> history of that event by the profane writers of antiquity; 2. The apparent impossibility of accounting for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water necessary to overflow the whole earth to such a depth as it is said to have been; and, 3. There appearing no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for an universal deluge, as the same might have been accomplished by a partial one. I. The former of these objections has given rise to several very elaborate treatises, though all that has yet been done in this way has scarcely been able to silence the objectors. Mr Bryant, in his system of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, has with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning and considerable success endeavoured to show, that the deluge was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the only foundation of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> worship; that the first of their deities was Noah; that all nations of the world look up to him as their founder; and that he, his sons, and the first patriarchs, are alluded to in most if not all of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, not only of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> but of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> heathens. In short, according to this author, the deluge, so far from being forgot, or obscurely mentioned by the heathen world, is in reality conspicuous throughout every one of their acts of religious worship. The Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, according to him, was the same with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">Ham</a> the son of Noah, though the name was sometimes bestowed on Noah himself. That this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, is evident, he thinks, from its being said that he was exposed in the ark, and afterwards restored to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>: that he planted the vine, taught mankind <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, the ancient and inculcated upon them the maxims of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and heroes' <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Something of the same kind is related of Perseus. He is represented by some ancient historians as a great astronomer, and well versed in other sciences. After being conceived in a shower of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, he was exposed in an ark upon the waters, and is said to have had a renewal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.—The history of Myrina the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMAZON">Amazon</a> affords a kind of abridgement and mixture of the histories of Osiris and Perseus. Similar to these is the history of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> himself. But our author observes, that under the titles of Osiris, Perseus, Myrina, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> spoke of the exploits of a whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, who were no other than the Cuthites or Cushites, the descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSH">Cush</a> the son of Ham and father of Nimrod. These people spread themselves into the most remote corners of the globe; and hence the heroes whom they represented are always set forth as conquering the whole world.—According to Diodorus Siculus, the Egyptian Osiris was the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIONYSUS">Dionysus</a> of the Greeks. He is said to have been twice born, and to have had two fathers and two mothers; to have been wonderfully preserved in an ark; to have travelled all over the earth; taught the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the vine, to build, plant, &c. The Indians claim him as a native of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, though some allow that he came from the west. Of Cronus and Astarte, it is said that they went over the whole earth, disposing of the countries as they pleased, and doing good wherever they came. The same is related of Ouranus, Themis, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, &c. though all their exploits are said to have been the effects of conquest, and their benevolence enforced by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. In a similar manner he explains the histories of other heroes of antiquity; and having thus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and history of the most celebrated personages, found traces of the history of Noah and his family, our author proceeds to inquire into the memorials of the deluge itself, to be met with in the history or religious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the different nations of antiquity. "We may reasonably suppose (says he), that the particulars of this extraordinary event would be gratefully commemorated by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> himself, and deluge to be met with in every branch of his family; that they were made the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>, where with in the history was often renewed, and ever attended with authors' reverential awe and horror, especially in those who had been witnesses to the calamity, and had experienced the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> in their favour. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, when there was a falling off from the truth, we might farther expect, that a person of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> a character as Noah, so particularly distinguished by the Deity, could not fail of being reverenced by his posterity; and when idolatry prevailed, that he would be one of the first among the sons of men to whom divine honours would be paid. Lastly, we might conclude, that these memorials would be interwoven in the mythology of the Gentile world; and that there would be continual allusions to these ancient occurrences in the rites and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> as they were practised by the nations of the earth. In conformity to these... these suppositions, I shall endeavour to shew that these things did happen; that the history of the deluge was religiously preserved in the first ages; that every circumstance of it is to be met with among the historians and mythologists of different countries; and traces of it are to be found, particularly in the sacred rites of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and of Greece. "It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear from many circumstances in the more ancient writers, that the great patriarch was highly reverenced by his posterity. They looked up to him as a person highly favoured by heaven; and honoured him with many titles, each of which had a reference to some particular part of his history. They styled him <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMETHEUS">Prometheus</a>, Deucalion, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, Thoth, Zeth, Xuthus, Inochus, Osiris. When there began to be a tendency towards idolatry, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> was introduced by the posterity of Ham, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Helius, among others, was conferred upon him. They called him also <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. When colonies went abroad, many took to themselves the title of Minyae and Minyas from him; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as others were denominated Achaeans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, Heliades, from the sun. People of the former name are to be found in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> and in other parts of the world. The natives at Orchomenos were styled Minyae, as were some of the inhabitants of Thessaly. Noah was the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZEUS">Zeus</a> and Dios. He was the planter of the vine, and inventor of fermented liquors; whence he was denominated Zeth, which signifies ferment, rendered Zeus by the Greeks. He was also called Dionysos, interpreted by the Latins <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, but very improperly. Bacchus was Chus, the grandson of Noah; as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a> may in general be esteemed Ham, so much reverenced by the Egyptians. "Among the people of the east, the true name of the patriarch was preserved; they called him Noas, Naus, and sometimes contracted Nos; and many places of sanctity, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, were denominated from him. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a> of Clazomene had obtained some knowledge of him in Egypt. By him the patriarch was denominated Noas or Nous; and both he and his disciples were sensible that this was a foreign appellation; notwithstanding which, he has acted as if it had been a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Eusebius informs us, that the disciples of Anaxagoras say, 'that Nous is, by interpretation, the deity <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">Dis</a> or Dios; and they likewise esteem Nous the same as Prometheus, because he was the renewer of mankind, and was said to have fashioned them again,' after they had been in a manner extinct. After this, however, he gives a solution of the story, upon the supposition that Nous is the same with the Greek word νοῦς, the mind: that 'the mind was Prometheia; and Prometheus was said to renew mankind, from new forming their minds, and leading them, by cultivation, from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>.' "Guidas has preserved, from some ancient author, a curious memorial of this wonderful personage, whom he affects to distinguish from Deucalion, and styles Nannacus. According to him, this Nannacus was a person of great antiquity, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the time of Deucalion. He is said to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, who foreseeing the approaching deluge, collected everybody together, and led them to a temple, where he offered up his prayers for them, accompanied with many tears. There is likewise a proverbial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> about Nannacus applied to people of great antiquity. "Stephanus gives great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to this history, and supplies many deficiencies. 'The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> is (says he), that there was one formerly named Nannacus, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of whose life was above 300 years. The people who were of his neighbourhood and acquaintance had inquired of an oracle how <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> he was to live; and there was an answer given, that when Nannacus died, all mankind would be destroyed. The Phrygians, upon this account, made great lamentations, from whence arose the proverb ἐν Ἀνακού τὸ κλαίειν, the lamentation of Nannacus, made use of for people in circumstances highly calamitous. When the flood of Deucalion came, all mankind were destroyed, according as the oracle had foretold. Afterwards, when the surface of the earth began to be again dry, Zeus ordered Prometheus and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> to make images of clay in the form of men; and, when they were finished, he called the winds, and made them breathe into each, and render them vital.' "From these histories Mr Bryant concludes as follows: 'However the story may have been varied, the principal outlines plainly point out the person who is alluded to in these histories. It is, I think, manifest, that Annacus, and Nannacus, and even Inachus, relate to Noahus or Noah. And not only these, but the histories of Deucalion and Prometheus have a like reference to the patriarch; in the 600th year, these, and not the 300th, of whose life the waters prevailed upon the earth. He was the father of mankind, who were renewed in him. Hence he is represented by another author, under the character of Prometheus, as a great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, by whom men were formed anew, and were instructed in all that was good. "Noah was the original Cronus and Zeus; though the latter is a title conferred sometimes upon his son Ham. There is a very particular expression recorded by Clemens of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who is said to have called the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> the tear of Cronus; and there was a farther tradition concerning this person, that he drank, or swallowed up all his children. The tears of Isis are represented as very mysterious. They are said to have flowed whenever the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> began to rise, and to flood the country.—The overflowing of that river was the great source of affluence to the people, and they looked upon it as their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> blessing; yet it was ever attended with mystical tears and lamentations. This was particularly observed at Coptos, where the principal deity was Isis. An ancient writer imagines that the tears and lamentations of the people were to implore an inundation; and the tears of Isis were supposed to make the river swell. But all this was certainly said and done in memorial of a former flood, of which they made the overflowing of the Nile a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a>. "As the patriarch was by some represented as a king called Nauchus or Nauchus; so by others he was styled Inachus, and supposed to have reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>. Hence Inachus was made a king of Greece; and Phereus and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> brought in succession after him. But Inachus was not a name of Grecian original; it is mentioned by Eusebius, in his account of the first ages, ages, that there reigned in Egypt Telemon a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, who was the son of Ones the shepherd, and the seventh in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from Inachus. And in the same author we read, that a colony went forth from that country into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, where they founded the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Antioch; and that they were conducted by Casus and Belos, who were sons of Inachus. By Inachus is certainly meant Noah; and the history relates to some of the more early descendants of the patriarch. His name has been rendered very unlike itself, by having been lengthened with terminations, and likewise fashioned according to the idiom of different languages. But the circumstances of the history are so precise and particular, that we cannot miss of the truth. He seems in the east to have been called Noas, Noasius, Nuxus, and Nus; and by the Greeks his name was compounded Dionysus. The Ammonians, wherever they came, founded cities to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; hence places called Nuxi will often occur; and indeed a great many of them are mentioned by ancient authors. These, though widely distant, being situated in countries far removed, yet retained the same original histories; and were generally famous for the plantation of the vine. Misled by this similarity of traditions, people in after times imagined that Dionysus must necessarily have been where his history occurred; and as it was the turn of the Greeks to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> every thing to the account of conquest, they made him a great conqueror, who went over the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the whole earth, and taught mankind the plantation of the vine. We are informed, that Dionysus went with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> over the face of the whole earth, and taught mankind, as he passed along, the method of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the vine, and how to press out the juice, and receive it in proper vessels. Though the patriarch is represented under various titles, and even these not always uniformly appropriated; yet there will continually occur such peculiar circumstances of his history as will plainly point out the person referred to. The person preserved is always mentioned as preserved in an ark. He is described as being in a state of darkness, which is represented allegorically as a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He then obtained a new life, which is called a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> birth; and is said to have his youth renewed. He is, on this account, looked upon as the first-born of mankind; and both his antediluvian and postdiluvian states are commemorated, and sometimes the intermediate state is also spoken of. Diodorus calls him Deucalion; but describes the deluge as in a manner universal. 'In the deluge which happened in the time of Deucalion, almost all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> died.' <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a> having mentioned Deucalion as λαγκανιστης, consigned to the ark, takes notice upon his quitting it, of his offering up an immediate sacrifice to the God who delivered him. As he was the father of all mankind, the ancients have made him a person of very extensive rule; and supposed him to have been a king. Sometimes he is described as a monarch of the whole earth; at other times he is reduced to a petty king of Thessaly. He is mentioned by Heliades in this latter capacity; who speaks of the deluge in his time, and of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> altars to the gods. Apollonius Rhodius supposes him to have been a native of Greece, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> notions; but notwithstanding his prejudices he gives so particular a character of him, that the true history cannot be mistaken. He makes him indeed the son of Prometheus, the son of Japetus; but in these ancient mythological accounts all genealogy must be entirely disregarded. Though this character be not precisely true, yet we may learn that the person represented was the first of men, through whom religious rites were renewed, cities built, and civil polity established in the world; none of which circumstances are applicable to any king of Greece. We are assured by Philo, that Deucalion was Noah; and the Chaldeans likewise mentioned him by the name of Xisuthrus, as we are informed by Cedrenus. That Deucalion was unduly adjudged by the people of Thessaly to their country solely, may be proved from his name occurring in different parts of the world, and always accompanied with some history of the deluge. The natives of Syria laid the same claim to him. He was supposed to have founded the temple at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERAPOLIS">Hierapolis</a>, where was a chasm through which the waters after the deluge were said to have retreated. He was likewise reported to have built the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; where there was a cavity of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and a like tradition, that the waters of the flood passed off through this aperture. However groundless the notions may be of the waters having retreated through these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, yet they show what impressions of this event were retained by the Ammonians, who introduced some history of it wherever they came. As different nations succeeded one another in these parts, and time produced a mixture of generations, they varied the history, and modelled it according to their notions and traditions; yet the ground-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was always true, and the event for a long time universally commemorated. Josephus, who seems to have been a person of extensive knowledge, and versed in the histories of nations, says, that this great occurrence was to be met with in the writings of all persons who treated of the first ages.
