DEVEREUX

Pages 202-204

ROBERT, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, the son of Walter Devereux, Viscount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, was born at Netherwood in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, in the year 1567. He succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl of Essex at ten years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and about two years after was sent by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Burleigh, to Trinity-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in 1582; and soon after retired to his seat at Lampsie in South <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. He did not however continue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in this retreat; for we find him, in his seventeenth year, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, who immediately honoured him with singular marks of her favour. Authors seem very unnecessarily perplexed to account for this young earl's gracious reception at the court of Elizabeth. The reasons are obvious; he was her relation, the son of one of her most faithful servants, the son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of her favourite <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, and a very handsome and accomplished youth. Towards the end of the following year, 1585, he attended the earl of Leicester to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and gave signal proofs of his personal courage during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of 1586, particularly at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, where the gallant Sidney was mortally wounded. On this occasion the earl of Leicester conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> banneret. In the year 1587, Leicester being appointed lord <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, Essex succeeded him in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> of master of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; and the year following, when the queen assembled an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TILBURY">Tilbury</a> to oppose the Spanish invasion, Essex was made general of the horse. From this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was considered as the happy favourite of the queen. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there was any mark yet wanting to fix the people's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in that respect, it was shown by the queen's conferring on him the honour of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>. We need not wonder that so quick an elevation, and so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a height, should affect so young a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> as the earl of Essex; who showed from henceforwards a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> spirit, and often behaved petulantly enough to the queen herself, who yet did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to be controlled by her subjects. His eagerness about this time to dispute her favour with Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Blunt, afterwards Lord Mountjoy and earl of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, cost him some blood; for Sir Charles, thinking himself affronted by the earl, challenged him, and after a short dispute wounded him in the knee. The queen, so far from being displeased with it, is said to have sworn a good round oath, that it was fit somebody should take him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, otherwise there would be no ruling him. However, she reconciled the rivals; who, to their honour, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> good friends as long as they lived. The gallant Essex, however, was not so entirely captivated with his situation as to become insensible to the allurements of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. In 1589, Sir John Norris and Sir Francis Drake having sailed on an expedition against <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, our young favourite, without the permission <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> knowledge of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> mistress, followed the fleet; which he joined as they were sailing towards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, and acted with great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> in the repulse of the Spanish garrison of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The queen wrote him a very severe <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> on the occasion; but she was, after his return, soon appeased. Yet it was not long before he again incurred her displeasure, by marrying the widow of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Sidney. In 1591, he was sent to France with the command of 4000 men to the assistance of Henry IV. In 1596, he was joined with the lord high <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> Howard in the command of the famous expedition against <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, the success of which is universally known. In 1597 he was ap- pointed master of the ordnance; and the same year commanded another expedition against Spain, called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> voyage, the particulars of which are also well known. Soon after his return, he was created earl marshal of England; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the great Lord Burleigh, in 1598, elected <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the university of Cambridge. This is reckoned one of the last instances of this great man's felicity, who was now advanced too high to sit at ease; and those who longed for his honours and employments, very closely applied themselves to bring about his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The first great shock he received in regard to the queen's favour, arose from a warm dispute between her majesty and himself, about the choice of some fit and able person to superintend the affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. The affair is related by Camden; who tells us, that nobody was present but the lord admiral, Sir Robert Cecil secretary, and Windebank clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. The queen looked upon Sir William Knolls, uncle to Essex, as the most proper person for that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>: Essex contended, that Sir George Carew was a much fitter man for it. When the queen could not be persuaded to approve his choice, he so far forgot himself and his duty, as to turn his back upon her in a contemptuous manner; which insolence her majesty not being able to bear, gave him a box on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and bid him go and be hanged. Essex, like a blockhead, put his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and swore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. Where was his gallantry on this occasion? Could a stroke from an angry woman tinge the honour of a gallant soldier? This violent storm, however, soon subsided; and they were again reconciled, at least apparently. The total <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Ireland being brought upon the tapis soon after, the earl was pitched upon as the only man from whom it could be expected. This was an artful contrivance of his enemies, who hoped by this means to ruin him. Nor were their expectations disappointed. He declined this fatal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> as long as he could; but perceiving that he should have no quiet at home, he accepted; and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> for lord <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> passed the great seal on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1598. His enemies now began to insinuate that he had sought this command, for the sake of greater things which he then was meditating; but there is a letter of his to the queen, preserved in the Harleian collections, which shows, that he was so far from entering upon it with alacrity, that he looked upon it rather as a banishment, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> assigned him for a retreat from his sovereign's displeasure, than a potent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> bestowed upon him by her favour. "To the Queen." "From a mind delighting in sorrow; from spirits wasted with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; from a heart torn in pieces with care, grief, and travail; from a man that hath himself and all things else that keep him alive; what <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> can your majesty expect, since any service past deserves no more than banishment and proscription to the cursedest of all <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>? It is your rebels <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and succession must give me leave to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> myself out of this hateful prison, out of my loathed body; which if it happen so, your majesty shall have no cause to mislike the fashion of my death, since the course of my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> could never please you. "Happy he could finish forth his fate, "In some unhaunted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> most obscure "From all <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, from love and hate "Of worldly folk; then should he <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> secure. "Then wake again, and yield God ever praise, "Content with hips and haws, and brambleberry; "In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> passing out his days, "And change of holy thoughts to make him merry. "Who when he dies, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> may be a bush "Where harmless robin dwells with gentle thrush. "Your majesty's exiled <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, "ROBERT ESSEX." The earl met with nothing in Ireland but ill success and crosses: in the midst of which, an army was suddenly raised in England, under the command of the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>; nobody well knowing why, but in reality from the suggestions of the earl's enemies to the queen, that he rather meditated an invasion on his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, than the reduction of the Irish rebels. This and other considerations made him resolve to quit his post, and come over to England; which he accordingly did without leave. He burst into her majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber as she was rising, and she received him with a mixture of tenderness and severity: but she soon after thought fit to deprive him of all his employments, except that of master of the horse. He was committed to the custody of the lord-keeper, with whom he continued six months. No sooner had he regained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, than he was guilty of many extravagancies; to which he was instigated by knaves and fools, but perhaps more powerfully by his own passions. He first determined to obtain an audience of the queen by force. He refused to attend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> when summoned. When the queen sent the lord-keeper, the lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and two others, to know his grievances, he confined them; and then marched with his friends into the city, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> that the people would rise in his favour; but in that he was disappointed. He was at last besieged and taken in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Essex-street; committed to the Tower; tried by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, condemned, and executed. Thus did this brave man, this favourite of the queen, this idol of the people, fall a sacrifice to his want of that dissimulation, that cunning, that court-policy, by which his enemies were enabled to effect his ruin. He was a polite scholar, and a generous friend to literature. To those who have not taken the trouble to consult and compare the several authors who have related the story of this unfortunate earl, it must appear wonderful, if, as hath been suggested, he was really beloved by Queen Elizabeth, that she should consent to his execution. Now that she had conceived a tender passion for him, is proved beyond a doubt by Mr Walpole in his very entertaining and instructive Catalogue of Noble Authors:—"I am aware (says that author) that it is become a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> to treat the queen's passion for him as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>. Voltaire laughs at it; and observes, that when her struggle about him must have been the greatest (the time of his death), she was sixty-eight.—Had he been sixty-eight, it is probable she would not have been in love with him."—Whenever Essex acted a fit of sickness, not a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> passed without the queen's sending often to see him; and once went so far as to sit Devereux, long by him, and order his brothers and things. It is recorded by a diligent observer of that court, that in one of his sick moods, he took the liberty of going up to the queen in his night-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>. In the height of these fretful fooleries, there was a mask at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Friars on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Lord Herbert and Mrs Russel. Eight lady maskers chose eight more to dance the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. Mrs Fitton, who led them, went to the queen, and wooed her to dance. Her majesty asked what she was? Affection, she said. Affection! said the queen; Affection is false. Were not these the murmurs of a heart ill at ease? Yet her majesty rose, and danced. She was then sixty-eight. Sure it was as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for her to be in love. Mr Walpole farther observes, that her court and contemporaries had an uniform opinion of her passion for Essex, and quotes several instances from a letter written by Sir Francis <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> to the earl; in which, among other things, he advises him to consult her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in his very apparel and gestures, and to give way to any other inclination she may have. Sir Francis advised the queen herself, knowing her inclination, to keep the earl about her for society. What Henry IV. of France thought of the queen's affection for Essex, is evident from what he said to her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>—"Que sa majesté ne laisscroit jamais son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> d'Essex éloigner de son cotillon."—After his confinement, on hearing he was ill, she sent him word, with tears in her eyes, that if she might with her honour, she would visit him. "If (says Mr Walpole) these instances are problematic, are the following so? In one of the curious letters of Rowland <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, he says, the queen hath of late used the fair Mrs Bridges with words and blows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>. In a subsequent letter, he says, the earl is again fallen in love with his fairest B. It cannot choose but come to the queen's ear, and then he is undone."—Essex himself says, that her fond parting with him when he set out for Ireland, pierced his very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. Probably the reader has now very little doubt as to Queen Elizabeth's affection for the unfortunate Essex; but, in proportion to our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the existence of the affection, her motives for consenting to his execution became more inexplicable. Queen Elizabeth had a very high opinion of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and personal attractions, and probably expected more entire <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> than the earl's passion for variety would suffer him to pay. Towards the latter end of her life, she was certainly an object of disgust. He had too much honest simplicity in his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to feign a passion which he did not feel. She foolishly gave <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the stories of his ambitious projects incompatible with her safety; and was informed that he had once inadvertently said, that she grew old and cankered, and that her mind was become as crooked as her carcass. If this be true, where is the woman that would not sacrifice such a lover to her resentment? It is said, however, that, concerning his execution, her majesty was irresolute to the last, and sent orders to countermand it: but, considering his obstinacy in refusing to ask her <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, afterwards directed that he should die. It is reported that the queen, in the height of her passion for the earl of Essex, had given him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, ordering him to keep it, and that whatever crime he should commit, she would pardon him when he should return that pledge. The earl, upon his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>, applied to Admiral Howard's lady, his relation, desiring her, by a person whom she could trust, to return it into the queen's own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; but her husband, who was one of the earl's greatest enemies, and to whom she had imprudently told the circumstance, would not suffer her to acquit herself of the commission; so that the queen consented to the earl's death, being full of indignation against so proud and haughty a spirit, who chose rather to die than implore her mercy. Some time after, the admiral's lady fell sick, and being near her death, she sent word to the queen that she had something of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to communicate before she died. The queen came to her bedside, and having ordered all her attendants to withdraw, the lady returned, but too late, the ring, desiring to be excused that she did not return it sooner: on which, it is said, the queen immediately retired, overwhelmed with grief. The earl of Essex died in the thirty-fourth year of his age; leaving by his lady one son and two daughters.

DEVIL

Pages 204-204

an evil angel, one of those celestial spirits <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven for pretending to equal himself with God. The Ethiopians paint the devil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, to be even with the Europeans who paint him <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. There is no mention of the word devil in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, but only of the word Satan and Belial: nor do we meet with it in any heathen authors, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is taken among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, that is, as a creature revolted from God. Their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> went no farther than to evil genii <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> demons. Some of the American idolaters have a notion of two collateral independent beings, one of whom is good and the other evil: which last they imagine has the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> and superintendence of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, for which reason they chiefly worship him: whence those that give us an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of these savages give out with some impropriety, that they worship the devil. The Chaldeans, in like manner, believed both a good principle and an evil one; which last they imagined was an enemy to mankind. Isaiah, speaking, according to some commentators, of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the devil, calls him Lucifer, from his former elevation and state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>: but others explain this passage of Isaiah in reference to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, who had been precipitated from his throne and glory. The Arabians call Lucifer, Eblis; which some think is only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> or corruption of the word Diabolus. DEFI on the Neck, a tormenting engine made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, straitening and wincing the neck of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, with his legs together, in a horrible manner; so that the more he stirreth in it, the strainer it presseth him; formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the persecuting papists.

DEVINATION

Pages 204-204

in antiquity, was used to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> incantation to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the affection of a person beloved. It was done by tying knots; and is thus described by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> in his eighth Eclogue: Necete tribus nodis ternos, Amarylli, colores: Necete, Amarylli, modo; et Veneris, die, vincula neco.

DEVISE

Pages 205-205

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby a person bequeathes his lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements to another by his last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>.

DEVOLUTION

Pages 205-205

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> acquired by succession from one to another.

DEVOLVED

Pages 205-205

something acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOLUTION">devolution</a>. Such a right is devolved to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; such an estate devolved on M—— by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of N——. The word is also used for a right, acquired by a superior, of conferring a benefice, when the inferior and ordinary collator has neglected to confer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> has conferred it on an unqualified person. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person neglects to present to a benefice in six months, the presentation lapses or devolves upon the bishop, from thence to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>, and from thence to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>.

DEVONSHERING

Pages 205-205

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the farmers to express the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> by way of manure: the method is to cut off the turf about four inches thick, and burn it in heaps, and then spread the ashes upon the land. The name is probably derived from its having been earliest practised in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>.

DEVONSHIRE

Pages 205-205

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the south by the English channel, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> channel, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and on the west by Cornwall. It is about 72 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 71 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is various; in the western parts of the county it is coarse and moorish, bad for sheep, but proper for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. In the northern parts, the dry soil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> are well adapted to sheep, with numerous flocks of which they are well covered. Tolerable crops of corn are also produced there when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is well manured. The soil of the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rich and fertile both in corn and pasture, yielding also in some places plenty of marle for manuring it. In other places they pare off and burn the surface, making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the ashes as a manure. It has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and silver, in which it formerly exceeded Cornwall, though now it is greatly inferior. On the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> also they have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and pilchard <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>. Devonshire sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to the noble family of Cavendish. It contains 464 parishes; and in 1811 the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted to 383,308. See DEVONSHIRE, SUFFLENT.

DEVOTION

Pages 205-208

(Devotio), a sincere ardent worship of the Deity. Devotion, as defined by Jurieu, is a softening and yielding of the heart, with an internal consolation, which the souls of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> feel in the practice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of piety. By devotion is also understood certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> practices, which a person makes it a rule to discharge regularly; and with reason, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the exactitude be founded on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> piety, otherwise it is vanity or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. That devotion is vain and trifling, which would accommodate itself both to God and to the world. Trevoux. The character of devotion has frequently suffered from the forbidding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> which has been thrown over it, by the narrowness of bigotry on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or the gloom of superstition on the other. When freer and more cheerful minds have not had occasion to see it accompanied with those feelings of delight and benevolence which naturally attend it, they are apt to be prejudiced against piety at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, by mistaking this ungracious appearance for its genuine form. Nor has the rant of vulgar enthusiasts contributed a little to beget or strengthen the same aversion, in persons of a cool and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> temper; who have happened to meet with such images and phrases among religionists of a certain strain, as ill <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the rational, pure, and spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of true devotion. It may likewise be remarked, on the other side, that people of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> have not seldom been disgusted with the insipid style too often employed on such subjects, by those who possess neither, or who purposely avoid everything of that kind, from an aim at simplicity misunderstood, or perhaps from a fear of being thought too warm, in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fashionable indifference and false refinement. Wherever the vital and unadulterated spirit of Christian devotion prevails, its immediate object <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be to please him whom we were made to please, by adoring his perfections; by admiring his works and ways; by entertaining with reverence and complacence the various intimations of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, especially those contained in holy writ; by acknowledging our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> dependence, and infinite obligations; by confessing and lamenting the disorders of our nature and the transgressions of our lives; by imploring his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and mercy through <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; by interceding for our brethren of mankind; by praying for the propagation and embellishment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, righteousness, and peace on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; in fine, by longing for a more entire conformity to the will of God, and breathing after the everlasting enjoyment of his friendship. The effects of such a spirit habitually cherished, and feelingly expressed before him, with conceptions more or less enlarged and elevated, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> more or less emphatical and accurate, sententious or diffuse, must surely be important and happy. Among these effects may be reckoned, a profound humility in the sight of God, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> veneration for his presence and attributes, an ardent zeal for his worship and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, an affectionate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in the Saviour of the world, a constant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of his divine example, a diffusive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> for men of all denominations. Devotion, denominations, a generous and unwearied self-denial for the sake of virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, a total resignation to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, an increasing esteem for the gospel, with clearer and firmer hopes of that immortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> which it has brought to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Devotion, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a kind of sacrifice or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, whereby they consecrated themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of some person. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had a notion, that the life of one might be ransomed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of another; whence those devotions became frequent for the lives of the emperors. Devotion to any particular person was unknown among the Romans till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Augustus. The very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Augustus had been conferred upon Octavius, Pacuvius, a tribune of the people, publicly declared, that he would devote himself to Augustus, and obey him at the expense of his life (as was the practice among barbarous nations), if he was commanded. His example was immediately followed by all the rest; till at length it became an established <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> never to go to salute the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, without declaring that they were devoted to him. Before this, the practice of the Romans was that of devoting themselves to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. See Decius. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUTEROCANONICAL">Deuterocanonical</a>, in the school <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, an appellation given to certain books of holy Scripture, which were added to the canon after the rest; either by reason they were not wrote till after the compilation of the canon, or by reason of some dispute as to their canonicity. The word is Greek, being compounded of δεύτερος, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and κανόνις, canonical. The Jews, it is certain, acknowledged several books in their canon, which were put there later than the rest. They say, that under Esdras, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of their doctors, which they call by way of eminence the great synagogue, made the collection of the sacred books which we now have in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. And they agree that they put books therein which had not been so before the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>; such are those of Daniel, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, Haggai, &c., and those of Esdras and Nehemiah. And the Romish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has since added others to the canon, that were not, and could not be, in the canon of the Jews, by reason some of them were not composed till after. Such is the book of Ecclesiasticus, with several of the apocryphal books, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a>, &c. Others were added still later, by reason their canonicity had not been yet examined; and till such examen and judgment they might be set aside at pleasure.—But since that church has pronounced as to the canonicity of these books, there is no more room now for her members to doubt of them, than there was for the Jews to doubt of those of the canon of Esdras. And the deuterocanonical books are with them as canonical as the protocanonical; the only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them consisting in this, that the canonicity of the one was not generally known, examined, and settled, so soon as that of the others. The deuterocanonical books in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> canon, are the book of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>, either the whole, or at least the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> last chapters thereof; the Epistle to the Hebrews; that of James; and that of Jude; the second of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>; the second and third of St John; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. The deuterocanonical parts of books are in Daniel, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> of the three children; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> of Azariah; the histories of Susannah, of Bel canonic and the Dragon; the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of St Mark; the bloody sweat, and the appearance of the angel, related in St Luke, chap. xxii.; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the adulterous woman in St John, chap. viii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUTERONOMY">Deuteronomy</a>, one of the sacred books of the Old Testament; being the last of those written by Moses; (see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>). The word is Greek, compounded of δεύτερος, second, and νόμος, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Deuteronomy was written in the 40th year after the delivery from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the country of the Moabites, beyond Jordan; Moses being then in the 120th year of his age. It contains, in Hebrew, 11 parashes; though only 10 in the edition of the rabbins at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; 20 chapters, and 955 verses. In the Greek, Latin, and other versions, it contains 34 chapters. The last is not of Moses. Some say, it was added by Joshua immediately after Moses's death; which is the most probable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Others will have it added by Esdras. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUTEROPOTMI">Deuteropotmi</a>, in Grecian antiquity, a designation given to such of the Athenians as had been thought dead, and, after the celebration of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">funeral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, unexpectedly recovered. It was unlawful for the deuteropotmi to enter into the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUMENIDES">Eumenides</a>, or to be admitted to the holy rites, till after they were purified, by being let through the lap of a woman's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, that they might seem to be new born. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUTEROSIS">Deuterosis</a>, the Greek name by which the Jews called their Mischnah or second law. See Misnah. Deutzia, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the deciduous class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">Dew</a>, a dense, moist vapour, found on the earth in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> mornings, in form of a misting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, being collected there chiefly while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is below the horizon. It hath been disputed whether the dew is formed from the vapours ascending from the earth during the night time, or from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of such as have been already raised through the day. The most remarkable experiments adduced in favour of the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> are those of Dr Dufay of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He supposed, that if the dew ascended it must wet a body placed low <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> sooner than one placed in a higher situation; and if a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bodies were placed in this manner, the lowermost would be wetted first; and the rest in like manner, gradually up to the top. To determine this, he placed two ladders against one another, meeting at their tops, spreading wide asunder at the bottom, and so tall as to reach 32 feet high. To the several steps of these he fastened large squares of glass like the panes of windows, placing them in such a manner that they should not overshade one another. On the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> it appeared exactly as Dr Dufay had apprehended. The lower surface of the lowest piece of glass was first wetted, then the upper, then the lower surface of the pane next above it; and so on, till all the pieces were wetted to the top. Hence it appeared plain to him, that the dew consisted of the vapours ascending from the earth during the nighttime; which, being condensed by the coldness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, atmosphere, are prevented from being dissipated as in the day-time by the sun's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. He afterwards tried a similar experiment with pieces of cloth instead of panes of glass, and the result was quite conformable to his expectations. He weighed all the pieces of cloth next morning, in order to know what <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> each had imbibed, and found those that had been placed lowermost considerably heavier than such as had been placed at the top; though he owns that this experiment did not succeed so perfectly as the former. M. Muschenbroek, who embraced the contrary opi- nion, thought he had invalidated all Dr Dufay's proofs, by repeating his experiments, with the same success, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> covered with sheet-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. But to this Dr Dufay replied, that there was no occasion for suppo- sing the vapour to rise through the lead, nor from that very spot; but that as it arose from the adjoining open ground, the continual fluctuation of the air could not but spread it abroad, and carry it thither in its ascent. But though this experiment of M. Muschenbroek's is not sufficient to overthrow those of Dr Dufay, it must still remain dubious whether the dew rises or falls. One thing which seems to favour the hypothesis of its descent is, that in cloudy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> there is little or no dew to be observed. From this M. de Luc brings an argument in favour of the hypothesis <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now men- tioned. He accounts for it in the following manner: When there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> in the air, the heat of the inferior air and that which rises from the earth dissi- pates itself into the superior regions; and then the va- pours which are dispersed throughout the air condense, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down in dew: But, when the clouds continue, they separate the inferior from the superior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the atmosphere, and thus prevent the dissipation of the heat, by which means the vapours remain suspended. When the sky grows cloudy, some hours after sunset, although the heat has been sensibly diminished, it is again increased; because continuing to rise out of the earth, it is accumulated in the inferior air. But nei- ther can this be reckoned a positive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the de- scent of the dew; since we may as well suppose the heat of the atmosphere to be great enough to dissipate it in its ascent, as to keep it suspended after its ascent through the day. On the other hand, its being found in greater quan- tities on bodies placed low down than on such as are high up, is no proof of the ascent of the dew; because the same thing is observed of rain. A body placed low down receives more rain than one placed in an elevated situation; and yet the rain certainly descends from the atmosphere. The reason why the dew appears first on the lower parts of bodies may be, that, in the evening, the lower part of the atmosphere is first cooled, and consequently most disposed to part with its vapours. It is also certain, that part of the water contained in the air may be condensed at any time on the sides of a glass, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, so as to run down its sides in small drops like dew. It seems therefore, that this subject is not sufficiently determined by such experi- ments as have yet been made; nor indeed does it ap- <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a> easy to make such experiments as shall be perfect- ly decisive on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Several substances exposed to the same dew receive and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> themselves with it in a very different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>- ner; some more, others less, and some even not at all. The drops seem to make a sort of choice of what bo- dies they shall affix themselves to; glass and crystals are those to which they adhere in the most ready man- ner, and in the largest quantity; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> of all kinds never receive them at all, nor do the drops ever adhere to them. The reason of this is, probably, because me- tals promote <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> more than glass does. Thus, if a piece of metal and a piece of glass are both made equally moist, the former will be found to dry in much less time than the latter. Hence it would seem, that there is between metals and water some kind of re- pulsion; and this may be sufficient to keep off the very small quantity that falls in dew; for whatever tends to make water evaporate after it is actually in contact with any substance, also tends to keep the water from ever coming into contact with it. On this subject several curious particulars are mentioned by Dr Per- cival relative to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> and repulsion between dew and glass or metallic vessels. The experiments were made by M. Dufay, who, in order to determine with certainty whether the difference between vitrified substances and metals was the same in all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, set a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a> saucer in the middle of a silver plate, and on one side, adjoining to it, was placed a china plate, with a silver <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISH">dish</a> very much resembling the saucer in the middle. In this experiment the china saucer was cov- ered with dew, but the plate, though extending four inches round it, was not moistened in the least. The china plate also had become quite moist, while the silver vessel in the middle had not received the smallest drop. M. Dufay next endeavoured to ascertain whether a china saucer set upon a plate of metal, as already descri- <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, did not receive more dew than it would have done if exposed alone. To accomplish this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, he took two watch crystals of equal dimensions, and placed the one upon a plate of silver, the other upon a plate of china, each with its concavity uppermost. That which was upon the silver plate he surrounded with a ferrel of the same metal, well polished, that no watery par- ticles might attach themselves to the convex surface of the glass. In this situation he exposed the crystals for several days successively, and always found five or six times more dew in that which was on the china plate than on the other placed on the silver. The repulsion between the dew and silver is further confirmed by the following experiment of M. Dufay, with regard to the crystal on the silver plate. He informs us, that the small quantity of dew on the side near the centre, was in minute drops; and that round the border there was a space of five or six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> perfectly dry; towards which the drops regularly decreased in magnitude, as if the silver ferrel had driven away the dew from that part of the glass which was contiguous to it. These experi- ments were repeated thirty times with invariable suc- cess. M. Dufay's experiments have received a re- markable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, from some lately made by Dr Watson, now bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LLANDAFF">Llandaff</a>, with a view to de- termine the quantity of vapour that ascends from a given surface of earth. "By means of a little bees- wax (says he), I fastened a half-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> very near, but not quite contiguous, to the side of the glass; and, setting the glass with its mouth downward on the grass, it presently became covered with vapour, except that part of it which was next the half-crown. Not only the- the half-crown itself was free from vapour, but it had hindered any from settling on the glass which was near it; for there was a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of glass surrounding the half-crown, to the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch, which was quite dry, as well as that part of the glass which was immediately under the half-crown; it seemed as if the silver had repelled the water to that distance. A large <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wafer had the same effect as the half-crown; it was neither wetted itself, nor was the ring of glass contiguous to it wetted. A circle of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> produced the same effect, so did several other substances, which it would be too tedious to enumerate." Substances of a very different kind from the usual dew are said to have sometimes fallen from the atmosphere. In the Phil. Trans. we are told, that in the year 1695 there fell in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, for a considerable part of the winter and spring, a fatty substance resembling <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, instead of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> dew. It was of a clammy texture, and dark-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and was, from its great resemblance, generally called dew-butter by the country people. It always fell in the night, and chiefly in the moorish low grounds; and was found hanging on the tops of the grass, and on the thatch of the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people. It was seldom observed to fall twice in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and usually, wherever it fell, it lay a fortnight upon the ground before it changed colour; but after that it gradually dried up, and became <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. The cattle fed in the fields where it lay as well as in others, and received no harm by it. It fell in pieces of the bigness of one's finger-end; but they were dispersed scatteringly about, and it had an offensive smell like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>. There were in the same places very stinking fogs during the winter, and some people supposed this no other than a sediment from the fog. It would not keep very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but never bred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. See DEW, SUPPLEMENT. May-Dew whitens <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and wax; the dew of autumn is converted into a white <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. Out of dew purified by the sun, arise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> insects, which change shape from one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> into another; what remains is converted into a fine white <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> like those of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, after a number of evaporations, calcinations, and fixations. There is a spirit drawn from May-dew, which has wonderful virtues attributed to it. The method of collecting and preparing it, is described by Hanneman, physician at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KIEL">Kiel</a>. It is to be gathered in clean linen cloths; exposed to the sun in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vials; then distilled, and the spirit thrown upon the caput mortuum; this is to be repeated till the earth unites with the spirit, and become liquid; which happens about the seventh or eighth cohabitation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. By such means you <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a very red, odoriferous spirit. Stolterfoht, a physician of Labee, thinks May-dew may be gathered in glass-plates, especially in still weather, and before sunrise; and Etmuller is of the same sentiment. It might likewise be collected with a glass funnel, exposed to the air, having a crooked neck to bring the dew into a vial in a chamber. See Phil. Trans. No. 3. Hoffman, and others. It is apparently from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of this dew, that the brothers of the Rosy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a> took their denomination. See ROSICRUCIANS. Dew-Born, in country affairs, a distemper in cattle, being swelled in the body, as much as the skin can hold, so that some beasts are in danger of bursting. This distemper proceeds from the greediness of a beast to feed, when put into a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> pasture, but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> when the grass is full of water. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the beast should be stirred up and down, and made to purge well; but the proper cure is bleeding in the tail; then take a grated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>, with an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and breaking the top of the shell, put out so much of the white as you may have room to slip the nutmeg into the shell; mix them together, and then let shell and all be put down the beast's throat; that done, walk him up and down, and he will soon mend. DEW-Worm. See LUMBRICUS, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> Index.

DEWAN

Pages 208-208

in the Mogul <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, is the receiver-general and civil governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. In private affairs the same word signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>.

DEXTANS

Pages 209-209

in Roman antiquity, ten ounces, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ⅔ of their libra. See LIBRA.

DEXTER

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, an appellation given to whatever belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of a shield <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coat of arms; thus we say, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>-dexter, dexter-point, &c.

DEXTROCHERE

Pages 209-209
or DESTROCHERE, in Heraldry, is applied to the right arm painted in a shield, sometimes naked, sometimes clothed, or adorned with a bracelet; and sometimes armed, or holding some moveable member used in the arms.

DEY

Pages 209-209

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the sovereign of Algiers, under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior. A <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> under this title was appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, at the request of the Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, in the year 1710. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> dey in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies an uncle by the mother's side; and the reason of the denomination is this: that the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> consider the grand signior as their father; the republic as their mother, by which they are nourished and maintained; and the dey as the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the republic, and consequently the uncle of all who are under his dominion. Besides the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and valour, which are necessary qualifications of a person to be elected, he must also be a native Turk, and have made the voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. He has no guards <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> considerable retinue. He presides at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVAN">divan</a>, and is most distinguished by the respect and submission which are paid him.

DIA DIA

Pages 209-210

[194] DIA Diæresis to have been; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> certain <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are dilated beyond their ordinary dimensions, so that the humours which ought to have been contained in the vessels extravasate or run out. DIÆRESIS, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> into two, which is usually noted by two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> over a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, as aulai, instead of aula, dissolvienda for dissolvenda. DIÆTETÆ, in Grecian antiquity, a kind of judges, of which there were two sorts, the cleroti and diallacterii. The former were public arbitrators, chosen by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to determine all causes exceeding ten drachms, within their own tribe, and from their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lay to the superior courts. The diallacterii, on the contrary, were private arbitrators, from whose sentence there lay no appeal, and accordingly they always took an oath to administer <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> without partiality.

DIABETES

Pages 209-209

in Physic, a supernatural discharge of urine, which has changed its properties, and exceeds the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of liquids drank. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DIABOLUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">DEVIL</a>. DIABOLUS Marinus. See RAJA, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. DIABOLUS Metallorum, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given by chemists to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tin: because, when incorporated with other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, it renders them incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a>, or at least very difficult to undergo that operation. DIACAUSTIC curve, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the caustic curves formed by refraction.

DIACHYLON

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, an emollient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, composed of mucilages <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> viscid juices drawn from certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See PHARMACY.

DIACODIUM

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a syrup prepared from poppy heads. It is also called the syrupus de melconio. See PHARMACY.

DIACOUSTICS

Pages 209-209

called also DIAPHONICS, the consideration of the properties of refracted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, as it passes through different mediums. The word is formed from the Greek δια, peri, "through," which intimates a passage, and ακοή, "I hear;" q. d. the consideration of the passage of the sounds we hear. See Acoustics.

DIACRII

Pages 209-209

in antiquity, was the name of a party <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>.—That <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, we read, was divided into two parties; the one favourers of an oligarchy, who would only have a few persons employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; the other consisted of such as were for a democratical or popular government, wherein the whole people should have a share. The first were called diacrii; and the latter pediuci; the latter inhabiting the lower, and the former the ἀρχή, or upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city.—The laws of Solon imported, that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a> should be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the diacrii; though the scholiast on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> The Wasps, affirms, that Pandon distributed the quarter of the diacrii among his sons, and put Lycus at their head.

DIADELPHIA

Pages 209-209

the 17th class in the sexual system, comprehending those <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which bear hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> with two sets of united stamina; but this circumstance must not be absolutely depended on. They are the papilionaceae of Tournefort, the irregularae tetrapetalii of Rivinus, and the leguminosae of Ray. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIADEM

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is applied to certain circles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rims serving to inclose the crowns of sovereign princes, and to bear the globe and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, or the fleur de lis, for their crest. The crowns of sovereigns are bound, some with a greater and some with a less <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of diadems.—The bandage about the heads of Moors on shields is also called diadems in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a>.

DIAGLYPHICE

Pages 210-210

the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> engraving figures on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, such as seals, intaglios, matrices of letters, &c., or coins for medals. See ENGRAVING.

DIAGNOSIS

Pages 210-210

(from ἰατροῦσιν, to discern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distinguish), the diagnostics or the signs of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. They are of two kinds, viz. the adjunct and the pathognomonic: the first are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to several diseases, and serve only to point out the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between diseases of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the latter are those which always attend the disease, and distinguish it from all others.

DIAGNOSTIC

Pages 210-210

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> given to those signs which indicate the present state of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and cause.

DIAGONAL

Pages 210-210

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line drawn across a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRILATERAL">quadrilateral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, from one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> to another; by some called the diameter, and by others the diameter, of the figure. See GEOMETRY.

DIAGORAS

Pages 210-210

surnamed the Atheist, lived in the 91st Olympiad. He was not a native of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, but he philosophised there. He delighted in making verses, and had composed a poem which a certain poet stole from him. He sued the thief, who swore it was his own, and got <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> by it. This tempted Diagoras to deny a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. The Athenians summoned him to give an account of his doctrine. He fled, and they set a price upon his head, promising a reward to any who should kill him; but he took shipping, and was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away.

DIAGRAM

Pages 210-210

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> musicians, the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. See SCALE.

DIAH

Pages 210-210

DIAT, a name given by the Arabs to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of retaliation. By the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the next relation of a murdered person, ought to take <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> against the murderer, and demand his blood in reparation for that which he has shed. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Mahomet, the Arabs had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of putting a freeman of their prisoners to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in lieu of every slave they lost in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> for every woman that was killed. But Mahomet regulated the laws of reprisal; directing in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a>, by the diat, that a freeman should be required for a freeman, and a slave for a slave. The Turks, probably in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this law, formerly massacred almost all their prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, but they now content themselves with enslaving and selling them.

DIAHEXAPLA

Pages 210-210
or DIAHEXAPTE, among farriers, a compound medicine, so called from its containing six ingredients, viz. birthwort and gentian roots, juniper-berries, bay-berries, myrrh, and ivory shavings. It is commended for colds, consumptions, puriness, and many other disorders in horses.

DIAL

Pages 210-210

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, serving to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> effected by the aid of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, is called a sundial. The word is from the Latin dies, "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>," because indicating the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the day. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> also called it sciotherium, from its effect by the shadow. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALLING">DIALLING</a>.

DIALECT

Pages 210-210

an appellation given to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in so far as it differs from that of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, however, is more particularly used in speaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek, whereof there were four dialects, the Attic, Ionic, Æolic, and Doric; each of which was a perfect language in its kind, that took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in certain countries, and had peculiar beauties. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, besides, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> diversity of English and Scotch, almost every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> has a dialect of its own, all differing considerably in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a>, and tone, although one and the same language.

DIALECTICS

Pages 210-211

by dividing, defining, and bringing things to the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; where being arrived, and stopped there a little, it applies itself to explain sensible things, but with a view to return to the first truth, where alone it can rest. Such is the idea of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>. The fourth is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s dialectics; containing the doctrine of simple words, delivered in his book of Predicaments; the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, in his book De Interpretatione; and that of the several kinds of syllogism, in his books of Analytics, Topics, and Elenchuses. The fifth is the dialectics of the Stoics; which they call a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and divide into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and dialectic; to which some add the definitive, whereby things are justly defined; comprehending likewise the canons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> criterions of truth. The Stoics, before they come to treat of syllogisms, have two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places; the one about the signification of words, the other about the things signified. On occasion of the first, they consider abundance of things belonging to the grammarian's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>: what, and how many letters; what is a word, diction, speech, &c. On occasion of the latter, they consider things themselves, not as without the mind, but as in it, received in it by means of the senses. Accordingly, they first teach, that nil sit in intellectu, quod non prius fuerit in sensu; "whatever is in the mind came thither by the senses;" and that aut inversione sui, as Plato, who meets the sight; aut similitudine, as Caesar by his effigy; aut proportione, either by enlarging as a giant, or by diminishing as a pigmy; aut translatione, as a Cyclops; aut compositione, as a Centaur; aut contrario, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; aut privazione, as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The sixth is Epicurus's dialectics; for though he seems to have despised dialectic, he cultivated it with vigour. He was only averse to that of the Stoics; Dialectics who he thought attributed too much to it, as pronouncing him alone wise who was well versed in dialectics. For this reason, Epicurus, seeming to set aside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> dialectics, had recourse to another way, viz. to certain canons which he substituted in their stead, the collection whereof he called canonica; and as all questions in philosophy are either de re or de voce, he gave separate rules for each. See EPICUREANS.

DIALITHA

Pages 211-211

in the writings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a word used to express the elegant ornaments of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, composed of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and gems. They also called these lithocola, "cemented <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gems;" the gold being in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> as a cement to hold the stones together. They wore bracelets and other ornamental things about their habits thus made; and their cups and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-furniture, for magnificent treats, were of this kind. The green stones were found to succeed best of all in these things; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a> and greenish topaz, or, as we call it, chrysolite, were most in esteem for this purpose. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the stones explains what Pliny very often says of them in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>: Nihil jucundius aurum decet, "Nothing becomes gold better;" this he says of the green topaz or chrysolite; and this and many other like <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> have greatly perplexed the critics, who did not <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon this explication.
