Till his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it had been called φύλλον, from a notion that an inflammation of this part produced phrenzy; which is not more warranted by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> than ano- ther <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that a transverse <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the diaphragm with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> causes the patient to die laughing.

DIARBECK

Pages 243-244

DIARBECK, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> DIARBEKR, an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Eastern Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; comprehending, in its latest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, Diarbekr, properly so called, Irack or Chaldea, and Curdistan, which were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> countries of Mesopotamia, Chaldea, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. It is called Diarbeck, Diarbecker, or Diarbekr, as signifying the "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>," from the word dhyar "a duke," and bekr, "country." It extends along the banks of the Tigris and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-north-west to south-east, that is, from Mount Taurus, which divides it from Turcomania on the north, to the inmost recess of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> on the south, about 600 miles; and from east to west, that is, from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> on the east to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deserta on the west, in some places 200, and in others about 300 miles, but in the southern or lower parts not above 150. As extending also from the 30th to the 38th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, it lies under <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fifth and sixth climates, whose longest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> is about 14 hours and a half, and so in proportion, and consequently enjoys a good temperature of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as well as, in the greater part of it, a rich and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. There are indeed, as in all hot countries, some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> deserts in it, which produce no sustenance for men or cattle, nor have any inhabitants. Being a considerable frontier towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Persia, it is very well guarded and fortified; but as for those many cities once so renowned for their greatness and opulence, they are at present almost dwindled into heaps of ruins. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, Moussul, Caramed, and a few more, indeed continue to be populous and wealthy; but the rest can scarce be called by any other name than that of sorry places. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Euphrates and Tigris have almost their whole course through this country. Diarbeck Proper is bounded on the north by Turcomania, on the west by Syria, on the south by part of Arabia Deserta, and Irack Proper, and on the east by Curdistan. It was named by Moses Padan-Aram; the latter being the general name of Syria; and the former signifying fruitful, a proper epithet for this country, which is really so to a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree, especially on the northern side, where it yields corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and all necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance. Formerly it was the residence of many famed patriarchs, yet was overrun with the grossest idolatry, not only in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>'s coming out of it, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>'s sojourning in it, but likewise during the time it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of the Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, Persians, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It received indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the gospel soon after our Saviour's ascension, from St Thaddaeus, who is said to have been sent thither by St Thomas, at the request of Abgarus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Edessa. This account, together with that monarch's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, we have from Eusebius, who took it from the archives of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and the whole had passed current and uncontradicted for many ages, till more enlightened moderns found reasons to condemn it; but whether <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or wrong, it plainly appears that Christianity flourished here in a most eminent manner, till its purity was assailed about the beginning of the sixth century by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> of the Jacobites, whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> still resides here, with a jurisdiction over all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the Turkish dominions. Diarbeck Proper is a beglerbegate, under which are reckoned twelve sangias; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in it are, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a> or Caramed, Rika, Moussul, Orsa Diarbek or Edessa, Elbir, Nisibis, Gezir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERDIN">Merdin</a>, Zibin, Ur of the Chaldees, Amad, and Carasara; but all now of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> excepting Diarbekir and Moussul.

DIARBEKIR

Pages 244-245

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above district, is situated on a delightful plain, on the banks and near the head of the Tigris, about 155 miles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 15 caravan days journey <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, in latitude 37° 35', east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 40° 50'. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> over the said river is said to have been built by the order of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. It is one of the richest and most mercantile cities in all Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; and is well fortified, being encompassed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall, the outermost of which is flanked with 72 towers, said to have been raised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of our Saviour's 72 disciples. It has several stately piazzas or marketplaces, well stored with all kinds of rich merchandise, and 12 magnificent mosques, said to have been formerly Christian churches. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacture is the dressing, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>, and dying of goats skins, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Turkey <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, of which the vent is almost incredible in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; besides this, there is another of dyed fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and cotton cloths, which are nearly in the same request. The waters of the Tigris are reckoned extraordinary for those two branches of trade, and give <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> leather a finer grain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> than any other. There is a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and convenient inns on both sides of the river, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> that go to and from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> near the town is a chapel with a cupola, where <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> is said to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> buried. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is much frequented by pilgrims of all nations and religions, and a Turkish hermit has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it. The fair <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, who, in most other parts of the Turkish empire, are kept quite immured, and considered as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> slaves, enjoy here an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and are commonly seen on the public walks of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the Christian women, and live in great friendship and familiarity with them. The same is said of the men, who are polite, affable, and courteous, and very different from what they affect to be, especially the Turks, in other cities of this empire. The city is under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a basha, who has great power and very large dominions. He has commonly a body of 22,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> under him, for repelling the frequent incursions of the Curdes and Tartars, who always go on horseback to rob the caravans. The adjacent territory is very rich and beautiful; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> are excellent, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> exquisite, and the pigeons better and larger than any in Europe. Mr Ives, who passed through this city in 1758, informs us, that "about two years ago it was very populous, its inhabitants amounting to 400,000 souls; but in the last year, 300,000 died either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or famine. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> residing in the city before this calamity were reckoned to amount to 26,000, of whom 20,000 died. This account he had from one of the French missionaries, a Capuchin, who also said, that before the famine the city contained 62,000 fighting men, but that now they are not able to muster 10,000. He assures us, that the houses and streets, nay the very mosques, were filled with dead; that every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city exhibited a dreadful image of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and that the surviving inhabitants not only greedily greedily devoured all kinds of beasts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, and reptiles, but also were obliged to feed on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies. Yet, in the midst of this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of horror, the grandees of the city had every thing in plenty; for they had taken care to monopolize vast quantities of corn, which they sold out to the other inhabitants at most extravagant prices, and thereby acquired for themselves immense fortunes. Corn rose from two piastres a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to 50, 60, and even 70, in the space of six months. The father added, that the very severe winter of 1736, and the locusts in 1737, were the causes of this dreadful visitation; for by reason of the former, there were but few acres of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> sown with corn; and by the latter, the small crop they had was in a great measure destroyed. He spoke of the severity of that winter in terms almost incredible: that it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to see the people <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> dead in the streets; that he himself once on quitting a warm room, and going into the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, fell down motionless; and that his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, in attempting to assist him, met with the same fate. This account of the effects of cold in the city of Diarbekir, which lies only in about 38° north, seems at first very surprising; but considering that the place stands on a rising ground in the midst of an extensive plain, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> Curdistan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> lie to the south and east of it, and the Armenian or Turcomanian to the north, whose heads are always covered with snow, and even now in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> supply the city with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>; it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not appear at all improbable, that in a very severe winter, such as that was in 1736, the inhabitants of this city should so severely feel the effects of it. This account of the missionary is most probably exaggerated in many particulars. General Gardanne reckons the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> at 80,000, and Mr McDonald Kinneir at no more than 38,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> probably lies between these statements.

DIARRHOEA

Pages 245-245
or LOOSENESS, in Medicine, is a frequent and copious evacuation of liquid excrement by stool. See MEDICINE Index.

DIARTHROSION

Pages 245-245

in Anatomy, a kind of articulation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; which being pretty lax affords room for a manifest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. The word comes from ἀρθρον, and ἀσφαλεία, juncture, assemblage. It is opposed to synarthrosis, wherein the articulation is so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> that there is no sensible motion at all. See ANATOMY, No. 2.

DIARY

Pages 245-245

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes used for a journal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-book, containing an account of every day's proceedings. Thus we say, diaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, &c. Diary Fever, is a fever of one day. See EPHEMERA.

DIASCISM

Pages 245-245

among musicians, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMA">comma</a> and enharmonic diesis, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the lesser comma.

DIASCORDIUM

Pages 245-245

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, so called from scordium, one of its ingredients. See PHARMACY.

DIASTOLE

Pages 245-245

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in prosody whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> naturally short is made <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Such is the first syllable of Priamides in the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>: Atque hic Priamides! nihil e tibi, amice, reliquum.

DIASYRMUS

Pages 245-245

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a kind of hyperbole, being an exaggeration of some low, ridiculous thing.

DIATESSARON

Pages 245-245

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> musicians, a concord <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> harmonical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, composed of a greater tone, a less tone, and one greater semitone; its proportion in numbers is as 4 : 3.

DIATONICK

Pages 245-245

in Music, (compounded of two Greek words, viz. the preposition δια, signifying a transition from one thing to another, and the substantive τονις, importing a given <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tension <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>), is indifferently applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> or gamut, to intervals of a certain kind, or to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of music, whether in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, composed of these intervals. Thus we say the diatonick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, a diatonick <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, diatonick melody or harmony. As the diatonick scale forms the system of diatonick music, and consists of diatonick intervals, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be necessary, for understanding the former, that we should explain the latter. See INTERVAL.

DIATRAGACANTH

Pages 245-245

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a name applied to certain powders, of which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> tragacanth is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ingredient.

DIBBLE

Pages 245-245
or DIBBER, a simple but useful instrument in gardening, used for planting out all sorts of young plants, &c. DIBBLING WHEAT. See AGRICULTURE Index.

DIBIO

Pages 245-245
or DIVIO, in Ancient Geography, the Divionense Castrum and the Dicionum of the lower age: a town of the Lingones, in Gallia Belgica: Dibionenses the people. Now Dijon the capital of Burgundy. E. Long. 5. 5. N. Lat. 47. 15.

DICAMMUS

Pages 246-246
WHITE DITTANY, or Fraxinella; a genus of plants belonging to the decandria class; and in the natural method ranking under the 26th order, Multiflora. See Botany Index.

DICCHONDRA

Pages 245-245

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the order Companaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DICE

Pages 245-245

among gamesters, certain cubical pieces of bone <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, marked with dots on each of their faces, from one to six, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of faces. Sharpers have several ways of falsifying dice. 1. By sticking a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s bristle in them, so as to make them run <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or low as they please. 2. By drilling and loading them with quicksilver; which cheat is found out by holding them gently by two diagonal corners: for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> false, the heavy sides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn always <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. 3. By filing and rounding them. But all these ways <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> far short of the art of the dice-makers; some of whom are so dexterous this way, that your sharpening gamester will give any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for them. Dice formerly paid 5s. every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> imported, with an additional duty of 4s. 9½d. for every 20s. value upon each; but are now prohibited to be imported. DICÆARCHUS, a scholar of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, composed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of books which were much esteemed. Cicero and his friend Pomponius Atticus valued him highly. He wrote a book to prove, that men suffer more mischief from one another than from all evils beside. And the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he composed concerning the republic of Lacedemon was extremely honoured, and read every year before the youth in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the ephori. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> was one of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> studies, on which science there is a fragment of a treatise of his still extant, and preserved among the Veteris geographicæ scriptores minores.

DICHTOMY

Pages 246-246

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by astronomers for that phasis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appearance of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, wherein she is bisected, or shows <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> half her disk. In this situation the moon is said to be in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> aspect, or to be in her quadrature.

DICKER

Pages 246-246

in old writers, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ten <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> of skins whereof 20 made a last; also 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of gloves, ten bars of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and the like, are sometimes expressed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> dicker.

DICKINSON

Pages 246-246

EDMUND, a celebrated English physician and chemist, was born in 1624. He studied and took his degrees at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and in 1659 published his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> Phonicierianae, &c., in which he attempted to prove, that the Greeks borrowed the story of the Pythian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and all that rendered the oracle at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a> famous, from the Holy Scriptures, and the book of Joshua in particular; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that procured him <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation both at home and abroad. He practised physic first at Oxford; but removing to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1684, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> in recovering the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Arlington from a dangerous sickness, procured his promotion to be physician in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. As that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> understood and loved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, Mr Dickinson grew into great favour at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in his appointments under James II. After the abdication, he retired from practice, and died in 1707. He published many other things, particularly Physica vetus et vera, &c., containing a system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, chiefly framed on principles collected from the Mosaic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>.

DICRANUM

Pages 246-246

a genus of mosses, including various <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, brought together from the Mnium, and Bryum, chiefly, and partly from the Hypnum of Linnaeus. See Smith's Flora Britannica.

DICTATOR

Pages 246-246

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> at Rome invested with regal authority. This officer was first chosen during the Roman wars against the Latins. The consuls being unable to raise forces for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the state, because the plebeians refused to enlist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were not discharged of all the debts they had contracted with the patricians, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> found it necessary to elect a new magistrate with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and uncontrollable power to take care of the state. The dictator remained in office for six months, after which he was again elected if the affairs of the state seemed to be desperate; but if tranquillity was re-established, he generally laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his power before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was expired. He knew no superior in the republic, and even the laws were subjected to him. He was called dictator, because dictus, named by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quoniam dictis ejus parebat populus, because the people implicitly obeyed his command. He was named by the consul in the night viva voce, and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> was confirmed by the augurs. As his power was absolute, he could proclaim <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, levy forces, conduct them against an enemy, and disband them at his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He punished as he pleased, and from his decision there lay no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, at least till latter times. He was preceded by 24 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LICTORS">lictors</a> with the fasces; during his administration, all other officers, except the tribunes of the people, were suspended, and he was the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the republic. But amidst all this Dictator independence, he was not permitted to go beyond the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; he was always obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> Dictator on foot in his expeditions; he never could ride in difficult and laborious marches without previously obtaining a formal leave from the people. He was chosen only when the state was in imminent danger from foreign enemies or inward seditions. In the time of a pestilence, a dictator was sometimes elected, as also to hold the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> or to celebrate the public festivals, or drive a nail into the capitol, by which superstitious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> believed that a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> could be averted or the progress of an enemy stopped. This office, so respectable and illustrious in the first ages of the republic, became odious by the perpetual usurpations of Sylla and Julius Caesar; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the latter, the Roman senate passed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> which for ever after forbade a dictator to exist in Rome. The dictator, as soon as elected, chose a subordinate officer called his master of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, magister equitum. This officer was respectable; but he was totally subservient to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the dictator, and could do nothing without his express order. This subordination, however, was some time after removed; and during the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic war the master of the horse was invested with a power equal to that of the dictator. A second dictator was also chosen for the election of magistrates at Rome after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae. The dictatorship was originally confined to the patricians; but the plebeians were afterwards admitted to share it. Titus Lartius Flavus was the first dictator in the year of Rome, 253.

DICTION

Pages 246-246

the phrase, elocution <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> style, of a writer or speaker. See Oratory, No 99-122.

DICTIONARY

Pages 246-250

in its original acceptation, is the arranging all the words of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> according to the order of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, and annexing a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> explanation to each word. When arts and sciences began to be improved and extended, the multiplicity of technical terms rendered it necessary to compile dictionaries, either of science in general, or of particular sciences, according to the views of the compiler. Dictionary of the English Language. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of every dictionary of language is to explain, in the most accurate manner, the meaning of every word; and to show the various ways in which it can be combined with others, in as far as this tends to alter its meaning. The dictionary which does this in the most accurate manner is the most complete. Therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of a lexicographer ought to be, to discover a method which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be best adapted for that purpose. Dr Johnson, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> labour, has collected the various meanings of every word, and quoted the authorities: but, would it not have been an improvement <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had given an accurate definition of the precise meaning of every word; pointed out the way in which it ought to be employed with the greatest propriety; showed the various deviations from that original meaning, which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> had so far established as to render allowable; and fixed the precise limits beyond which it could not be employed without becoming a vicious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>? With this view, it would have been necessary to exhibit the nice distinctions that take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between words which are nearly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>. Without this, many words can IMMEDIATELY. adv. of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. 1. Instantly, without delay. Always employed to denote future time, and never past. Thus, we may say, *I will come immediately;* but not *I am immediately come from such a place.* See PRESENTLY. 2. Without the intervention of any cause or event; as opposed to immediately. PRESENTLY. adv. of time. 1. Instantly, without delay. Exactly synonymous with immediately; being never with propriety employed to denote any thing but future time. 2. Formerly it was employed to express present time. Thus, *The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> presently possessed by such a one,* was often used; but this is now become a vicious expression; and we ought to say, *The house possessed at present.* It differs from immediately in this, that even in the most corrupt phrases it never can denote past time. FORM. subst. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance of any object, when considered only with respect to shape or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> therefore, in the literal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, can only be applied to the objects of the sight and touch; and is nearly synonymous with figure; but they differ in some respects. Form may be employed to denote more rude and unfinished shapes; figure, those which are more perfect and regular. Form can never be employed without denoting <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; whereas figure may be employed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>; thus, we say a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> or a triangular figure; but not a square or triangular form. And in the same manner we say, the figure of a house; but we must denote the substance which forms that figure, if we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word form; as, a cloud of the form of a house, &c. See Figure. 2. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to irregularity or confusion. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> cannot exist without order, it is by a figure of speech employed to denote beauty, order, &c. 3. As form respects only the external appearance of bodies, without regard to their internal qualities, it is, by a figure of speech, employed in contrast to these qualities, to denote empty show, without essential qualities. In this sense it is often taken when applied to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, &c. 4. As form is employed to denote the external appearance of bodies; so, in a figurative sense, it is applied to reasoning, denoting the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> or manner in which this is conducted; as, the form of a syllogism, &c. 5. In the same manner it is employed to denote the particular mode of procedure established in courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>; as, the forms of law, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, &c. 6. Form is sometimes, although improperly, used to denote the different circumstances of the same body; as, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in a fluid or a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form. But as this phrase regards the internal qualities rather than the external figure, it is improper; and Dictionary ought to be; water in a fluid or a solid state. 7. But when bodies of different kinds are compared with one another, this term may be employed to denote other circumstances than shape or figure: for we may say, *a juice exuding from a tree in the form of wax or resin;* although, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the consistence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, &c. and not the external arrangement of parts, constitutes the resemblance. 8. From the regular appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons arranged in one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> seat, such persons so arranged are sometimes called a form; as, a form of students, &c. And, 9. By an easy transition, the seat itself has also acquired that name. GREAT. adj. A relative word, denoting largeness of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, number, &c. serving to augment the value of those terms with which it is combined, and opposed to small or little. The principal circumstances in which this word can be employed are the following: 1. When merely inanimate objects are considered with regard to quantity, great is with propriety employed, to denote that the quantity is considerable; as, a great mountain, great house, &c. and it is here contrasted with small. When great is thus employed, we have no other word that is exactly synonymous. 2. When inanimate objects are considered with regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, this term is sometimes employed, although with less propriety; as, a great plain, a great field, &c. And in this sense it is nearly synonymous with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; and they were often used indiscriminately, but with some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of meaning: for, as large is a term chiefly employed to denote extent of superficies, and as great more particularly regards the quantity of matter; therefore, when large is applied to any object which is not merely superficial, it denotes that it is the extent of surface that is there meant to be considered, without regard to the other dimensions: whereas when the term great is employed, it has reference to the whole contents. If, therefore, we say, a large house, or a large river, we express that the house, the river, have a surface of great extent, without having any necessary connexion with the size in other respects. But if we say, a great house, or a great river, it at once denotes that they have not only a large surface, but are also of great size in every respect. 3. Great, when applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, never denotes the size or largeness of body, but is applied solely to the qualities of the mind. Thus, when we say that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> was a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, we do not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that he was a man of great size, but that he was a man who excelled in the endowments of the mind. The terms which denote largeness of size in the human body, are big, bulky, huge, &c. 4. Great is sometimes applied to the human species, as denoting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. In this case it is oftener used in the plural number than otherwise. Thus, we say simply the great, meaning the whole body of of men in high station, as opposed to mean. It should seldom be employed in this sense, as it tends to confound <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of rank with elevation of mind. 5. As this is a general term of augmentation, it may be joined with all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> which denote quantity, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, number, excellence, or defects; or such as imply praise, blame, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, contempt, or any other affection of the mind. 6. It is employed to denote every step of ascending or descending <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>; as great-grandfather, great-grandson, &c. HIGH. adj. Exalted in a perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> at a distance from the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Opposed to low. 1. High is a term altogether indefinite, and is employed to express the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of elevation of any inanimate body. Thus, we say a high mountain, a high house, steeple, tower, pillar, &c. Nor is there any other word that can here be considered as synonymous; lofty being employed only to denote a very eminent degree of elevation. 2. To express the perpendicular elevation of vegetables either high or tall may be employed, as being in this case nearly synonymous. We may therefore say, a high or tall tree, a high or tall mast, &c. but with this difference between these two expressions, that tall can be more properly applied to those that are much elevated and of small dimensions; and high, to such as are more bulky, and of greater size. 3. The perpendicular height of man can never be expressed by the word high; tall being here the proper expression. And although high is sometimes used to express the height of other animals, yet it seems to be an improper expression. See TALL. 4. High, when applied to the human species, always refers to the mind; and denotes haughtiness, stateliness, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, &c. and, when combined with the expressions of any energy of the mind, it denotes that in a higher degree. In this sense, it is opposed to meanness, abjectness, and humility. 5. As this is an indefinite term, tending to denote any thing that is elevated above us, it may be combined with almost every noun which admits of this elevation. And as objects high above us are always out of our reach, it is in a metaphorical sense used to denote any thing that seems to be above the ordinary condition of mankind; or those qualities or endowments of mind that are not easily acquired; as, dignity or elevation of sentiment; dignity of rank; acuteness in reasoning on difficult subjects; pride, haughtiness, or any other quality which seems beyond the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of mankind; clearness of price, &c. 6. In the same manner we apply this term to time; which having a metaphorical resemblance to a river flowing on with an unceasing current through all successive ages, any thing of remote antiquity is denoted by the term high. 7. Likewise those degrees of latitudes far removed from the line, where the pole becomes more elevated. 8. And to some particular crimes, as being attended with peculiar degrees of guilt; as, high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. TALL. adj. Something elevated to a considerable degree in a perpendicular direction. Opposed to low. 1. This term is chiefly employed to express the height of man and other animals; and is applied to denote the height of the body only, without having any reference to the mind. When applied to man, no other word can be substituted in its stead; when applied to other animals, high is sometimes considered as nearly synonymous. See HIGH. 2. It is likewise employed to denote the perpendicular height of vegetables; and in this case, it is nearly synonymous with high. See HIGH. 3. It can in no case be employed to express the height of merely inanimate objects; as we can never say a tall steeple, tower, or pillar, but a high steeple, &c. For the distinctions in these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, see HIGH. LONG. adj. A relative term, denoting the distance between the extremes of any body, which is extended more in one of its geometrical dimensions than another. Opposed to short. 1. This term may be applied to all inanimate objects, of whatever kind, whose dimensions in one way exceed the other, and when not in an erect posture, whatever be the other circumstances attending them; whether it relates to superficies alone, or to solid bodies; whether these be bounded or open, straight or crooked, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> or rigid, or in any other circumstances whatever; thus we say, a long or short line, a long or short ridge, street, ditch, rope, chain, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, &c. But it is to be observed, that although long is in the strict sense only opposed to short; yet as it expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of matter in one of its geometrical proportions, it is often contrasted by those words which express the other proportions when we mean only to describe the several proportions; as, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> long and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. And as these several dimensions are expressed by different words, according to the various forms, modifications, and circumstances, in which bodies are found, therefore it is in this sense contrasted by a great diversity of terms: as, a long and broad or wide, narrow or strait, street or lane; a long and thick, or small rope, chain, staff. For the distinctions in these cases, see BROAD, WIDE, &c. 2. Objects necessarily fixed in an erect position can never have this term applied to them; and therefore we cannot say a long, but a high, tower or steeple. And for the same reason, while trees are growing and fixed in an erect position, we cannot apply this term to them; but when they are felled and laid upon the ground, it is quite proper and necessary. Thus, we do not say a long, but a tall or high tree, while it is growing; but we say a long, not a tall log of wood; and in the same manner we say a tall mast, when it is fixed in the ship; but a long mast, while it lies upon the beach. See TALL and HIGH. 3. Those vegetables which are of a tender pliant <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, ture, or so weak as not to be able to retain a fixt position, being considered as of a middle nature between erect and prostrate bodies, admit of either the terms long, tall, or high; as a long or tall rush or willow wand, or a long, tall, or high stalk of corn. See HIGH and TALL. 4. The parts of vegetables, when considered as distinct from the whole, even when growing and erect, assume the term long: for we do not say a tall, but a long shoot of a tree; and a tree with a long stem, in preference to a tree with a high stem. 5. For the same reason, a staff, and pole, even when fixed in a perpendicular direction, assume the word long, in preference to tall or high. 6. With regard to animals, the general rule is applied, without any exceptions: tall, and not long, being employed to denote the height of the human body, when in an erect posture; and long, and not tall, to denote its length when in an incumbent situation. Long applied to all other animals which do not walk erect, always denotes their greatest length in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position from head to tail. 7. In a figurative sense, it denotes, with regard to time, any thing at a great distance from us. 8. As also, any thing that takes up much time before it is finished; as a long discourse, a protracted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in music, &c. BROAD. adj. The distance between the two nearest sides of any body, whose geometrical dimensions are larger in one direction than in another; and has a reference to superficies only, and never to the solid contents. Opposed to narrow. 1. Broad, in the strictest acceptation, is applied to denote those bodies only whose sides are altogether open and unconfined; as a broad table, a broad wheel, &c., and in these cases it is invariably contrasted by the word narrow; nor is there any other word which in these cases can be considered as synonymous with it, or used in its stead. 2. When any object is in some sort bounded on the sides, although not quite closed up, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, street, ditch, &c., either broad or wide may be employed, but with some difference of signification; broad being most properly used for those that are more open, and wide for those which are more confined: nor can this term be ever applied to such objects as are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> bounded all around, as a house, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, &c., wide being here employed. For the more accurate distinctions in these cases, see the article WIDE. WIDE. adj. A term employed to denote relative extent in certain circumstances. Opposed to narrow and strait. 1. This term is in its proper sense applied only to denote the space contained within any body closed all round on every side; as a house, gate, &c.; and differs from broad in this, that it never relates to the superficies of solid objects, but is employed to express the capaciousness of any body which containeth vacant space; nor can capaciousness in this sense be expressed by any other word but wide. 2. As many bodies may be considered either with respect to the capaciousness or superficial extent; in all these cases, either the term broad or wide may be used; as a broad or wide street or ditch, &c., but with a greater or less degree of propriety, according to the circumstances of the object, or the idea we wish to convey. In a street where the houses are low and the boundaries open, or in a ditch of small depth and large superficies, as this largeness of superficies bears the principal proportion, broad would be more proper; but if the houses are of great height, or the ditch of great depth, and capaciousness is the principal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> that affects the mind, we would naturally say a wide street or ditch; and the same may be said of all similar cases. But there are some cases in which both these terms are applied, with a greater difference of meaning; thus we say a broad or a wide gate: But as the gate is employed to denote either the aperture in the wall, or the matter which closes that aperture, these terms are each of them used to denote that particular quality to which they are generally applied: and as the opening itself can never be considered as a superficies, the term wide, in this case, denotes the distance between the sides of the aperture; while on the contrary, broad denotes the extent of matter fitted to close that aperture; nor can these two terms in any case be substituted for one another. 3. As a figurative expression, it is used as a cant phrase for a mistake: as, you are wide of the mark; that is, not near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. NARROW. adj. A relative term, denoting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> smallness of distance between the sides of the superficies of plain bodies. Opposed to broad. 1. As this is only applied to superficies, it is exactly contrasted by broad, and is applied in all cases where the term broad can be used, (see BROAD); and in no other case but as a contrast to it, except the following. 2. It sometimes is employed to describe the smallness of space circumscribed between certain boundaries, as opposed to wide, and nearly synonymous with straight; as we say a wide or a narrow house, church, &c. For the necessary distinctions here, see the article STRAIT. 3. In a figurative sense it denotes parsimony, poverty, confined sentiments, &c. STRAIT. adj. A relative term, denoting the extent of space in certain circumstances. Opposed to wide; see WIDE. 1. This term is employed, in its proper sense, to denote only space, as contained between surrounding bodies in such circumstances as to denote some degree of confinement; and is exactly opposed to wide; as a wide or a strait gate, &c. See WIDE. 2. So necessary is it that the idea of confinement should be connected with this word, that in all those cases where the space contained is large, as in a church, or house, we cannot express a smaller proportional width by this term. And as we have no other word to express space in these circumstances, cumstances; we have been obliged to force the word narrow from its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> signification, and make it express this. See NARROW. 3. In some particular cases, narrow or strait may be applied to the same object; as, a narrow or a strait line; but here strait is never employed but where an idea of confinement is suggested, and where it is exactly contrasted to wide; nor can narrow be employed but in such circumstances where broad would be a perfect contrast to it. Therefore these two terms may be always used in the same circumstances as those which contrast them may be. For an account of which see WIDE. 4. The term strait is likewise in a peculiar manner used to denote the smallness of the internal diameter of those small bodies which are fitted to receive or contain others, as any kind of bag, tube, body clothes, mortoises, and others of the same kind; and in all these cases this term may be employed to denote the smallness of their lesser diameter, and never the term narrow. But in certain circumstances the word tight may be substituted for it. See TIGHT. 5. Strait, in a figurative sense, denotes any sort of confinement of sentiment or disposition.

DICTYMNIA

Pages 251-251
or **Dictynnia**, in Mythology, were feasts celebrated at Lacedaemon and in Crete, in honour of Diana Dictynnia or Dictynnia, or of a nymph taken for her, who, having plunged herself into the sea, to escape the passion of Minos, was caught in a fisherman's net or *λάστρον*, whence the name.

DICTYS CRETENSIS

Pages 251-251

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historian, who serving under Idomeneus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> in the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, wrote the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that expedition in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> books; and Tzetzes tells us, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> formed his Iliad upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of that history. It is however maintained, that the Latin history of Dictys which we have at present is spurious.

DIDACTIC

Pages 251-252

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, signifies the manner of speaking <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, adapted to teach or explain the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of things. The word is formed from the Greek διδάσκω, *doceo*, "I teach." There are many words which are only used in the didactic and dogmatic way; and there are many works, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, both in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, written after Didactic after this method: such are the Georgics of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Lucretius's poem De Rerum Natura, and Pope's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Criticism and on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, &c., &c. DIDAPPER. See COLOMBUS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIDELPHIS

Pages 252-252
or Opossum, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of fere. See MAMMALIA Index.

DIDEROT

Pages 252-253

DENYS, an eminent French writer, was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANGRES">Langres</a> in the year 1713. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> among the Jesuits, and being destined for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> by one of his uncles, who had a canonry to bestow upon him, he had received the tonsure. But he discovered so little inclination for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> profession, that his father sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to prosecute his studies, and afterwards placed him with an attorney. It soon appeared, however, that he was more attached to different departments of literature and science, than disposed to submit to the drudgeries of the profession to which his father had destined him; and having thus neglected his business, his allowance was withheld, which obliged him to make provision for himself. The studies to which Diderot devoted his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> were extremely various. Physics, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and belles lettres, were at different times the objects of his pursuit. He even indulged in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and works of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; but attached himself chiefly to more serious studies. He possessed a ready flow and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in conversation; and these qualities, with a decisive tone and manner, procured for him partizans and protectors. One of the first of his publications was a translation of "Stanyan's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>." In the year 1745 he published "Principles of Moral Philosophy," 12mo, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> by which he obtained some reputation. But the year following, when he published a piece entitled Pensées Philosophiques, he acquired considerable celebrity. This work was highly commended by the partizans of the new philosophy, among whom he had now enlisted himself, and became one of its most zealous disciples. The same work was afterwards reprinted under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Étrennes aux Esprits Forts. It was greatly read, and it is supposed contributed much to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of those free opinions which had now become so prevalent in France. Soon after this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, in conjunction with his friend D'Alembert, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the vast undertaking, the Dictionnaire Encyclopédique, was laid. The professed object of this work was to become a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for every branch of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> knowledge: but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it has been alleged that it was also intended by the authors and editors as the great engine by means of which the established opinions, whether of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which they supposed had their origin in fraud and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, should be subverted. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of this work which was entrusted to Diderot was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Arts and Trades, (Arts et Métiers). But, besides, he contributed many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in various departments of science. His writings in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> have been considered as extremely verbose and diffuse; and in all of them he is too fond of metaphysical subtleties and the pompous parade of scientific language. The first edition of the Dictionary was completed between the years 1751 and 1767; and although Diderot was occupied in this laborious undertaking for a period of nearly 20 years, the recompense which he obtained is said to have been extremely small. During this time he composed various other works. Among these he published, "A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">Blind</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of those who see." This work made a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of noise, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of some of the sentiments which it contained, had given offence to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, for which the author was kept in confinement for six months at Vincennes. This piece was soon followed by another, entitled "A letter on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEAF_AND_DUMB">Deaf and Dumb</a>, for the use of those who hear and speak," 2 vols. 12mo, 1751. "The sixth <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">Sense</a>," published in 1752; "Thoughts on the interpretation of Nature," 1754; "The Code of Nature," 1755, are similar works, and may be ranked in the same class. His moral character was considerably affected by the publication of Bijoux Indiscrets, 2 vols. 12mo; which is a collection of licentious tales; for this indeed he made some kind of compensation, when he published two prose comedies, Le Fils Naturel, 1757; and Le Pere de Famille, 1758; which are not only interesting as dramatic pieces, but exhibit a pure and correct morality. The latter is considered as one of the best comedies of the sentimental kind which has appeared on the French stage. It has indeed received universal admiration. He published afterwards a pamphlet, "On Public Education," which contains undoubtedly some useful hints; but at the same time it proposes many things which are impracticable. To the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his works now mentioned we may add, "An Eulogy on Richardson," which is full of warmth and enthusiasm; and "An <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> and Writings of Seneca the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">Philosopher</a>." This was his last work, and was published in 1779. Among some observations on this work by the Monthly Reviewers, the author of it is thus characterized: "The works of M. Diderot, says the writer, have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> since disgusted the modest votaries of true philosophy, by the tone of arrogance and self-sufficiency, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> and fumes of a declamatory eloquence, that form their essential and distinctive character." "It contains, it is farther added, like the other writings of that author, a glaring mixture of good and bad; of brilliant thoughts and obscure reasonings; of sentences that dart from the imagination with the energy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and cloudy periods of metaphysical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, that convey either no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, or false ones." The character of Diderot suffered considerably from some defamatory attacks which he made on his former friend Rousseau, who had quarrelled with the French philosophers and had separated himself from their school. From the "Confessions" of the Genevan philosopher, it would appear that they expected some anecdotes which would not have been much to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. In one of his letters Rousseau thus speaks of Diderot. His words are remarkable, as they are equally applicable to his own character. "Although born with a good heart and an open disposition, he had an unfortunate propensity to misinterpret the words and actions of his friends; and the most ingenious explanations only supplied his subtle imagination with new interpretations against them." Diderot was married and had a family; and although he possessed some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a> of temper, he was a kind husband and a tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. At the conclusion of the Dictionary, the state of his affairs rendered Diderot, it was purchased by the empress of Russia, who, with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, was at that time the great encourager and promoter of literature and literary men. These sovereigns were also considered as disciples of the French school. The price which Diderot received for his library was 50,000 livres; and he was to have the use of it during his life. Some of his biographers, with what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> we pretend not to say, have not hesitated to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> him with disposing of it a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time; and when some person commissioned by the empress wished to see it, the philosopher declined the visit by excuses till he had time to fill it with books borrowed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, it is obvious, must have been extremely superficial, otherwise the truth would have been at once detected. Diderot had been admitted a member of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>. He died suddenly, as he rose from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 31st, 1784. His literary and philosophical works have been collected and published in 6 vols 8vo.

DIDO

Pages 253-253

called also ELISA, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Belus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, who married Sichaeus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Sicharbas her uncle, who was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. Pygmalion, who succeeded to the throne of Tyre after Belus, murdered Sichaeus to get possession of the immense <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> which he had; and Dido, disconsolate for the loss of her husband, whom she tenderly loved, and by whom she was equally esteemed, set sail in quest of a settlement with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Tyrians, to whom the cruelty of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> became odious. According to some accounts, she threw into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> the riches of her husband which Pygmalion so greedily desired, and by that artifice compelled the ships to fly with her that had come by order of the tyrant to obtain the riches of Sichaeus. During her voyage, Dido visited the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Cyprus; where she carried away 50 women who prostituted themselves on the sea-shore, and gave them as wives to her Tyrian followers. A storm drove her fleet on the African coast, and she bought of the inhabitants as much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> as could be covered by a bull's hide cut into thongs. Upon this piece of land she built a citadel called Byrsa; and the increase of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and the rising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> among her subjects, soon obliged her to enlarge her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and the boundaries of her dominions. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> as well as the fame of her enterprise, gained her many admirers; and her subjects wished to compel her to marry Jarbas king of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, who threatened them with a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Dido begged three months to give her decisive answer; and during that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> she erected a funeral pile, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> wishing by a solemn sacrifice to appease the manes of Sichaeus, to whom she had promised eternal fidelity. When all was prepared, she stabbed herself on the pile in presence of her people; and by this uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> obtained the name of Dido, "valiant woman," instead of Elisa. According to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> and Ovid, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dido was caused by the sudden departure of Æneas; of whom she was deeply enamoured, and whom she could not obtain as a husband. This poetical fiction represents Æneas as living in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Dido, and introduces an anachronism of near 300 years. Dido left Phoenicia 247 years after the Trojan war or the age of Æneas, that is, about 953 years before Christ. This chronological <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> proceeds not from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the poets, but it is supported by the authority of Horace. Aut famam sequere, aut sibi convenientia finge. While Virgil describes, in a beautiful episode, the desperate <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of Dido, and the submission of Æneas to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the gods, he at the same time gives an explanation of the hatred which existed between the republics of Rome and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>; and informs his reader, that their mutual enmity originated in their very first foundation, and was apparently kindled by a more remote cause than the jealousy and rivalry of two flourishing empires. Dido after her death was honoured as a deity by her subjects.

DIDUS

Pages 253-253
or DODO, a genus of birds belonging to the order of gallinace. See ORNITHOLOGY Index. DIDYMUS of Alexandria, an ecclesiastical writer of the fourth century; who, though he is said to have lost his eyes at five years of age, when he had scarcely learned to read, yet applied so earnestly to study, that he attained all the philosophic arts in a high degree, and was thought worthy to fill the chair in the famous divinity school at Alexandria. He was the author of a great number of works: but all we have now remaining are, a Latin translation of his book upon the Holy Spirit, in the works of St Jerome, who was the translator; short strictures on the Canonical Epistles; and a book against the Manichæes.

DIDYNAMIA

Pages 253-253

(from δις, twice, and δύναμις, power), the name of the 14th class in Linnaeus's sexual method, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> with hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which have four stamens <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs, two of which are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two short. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIEMEN'S LAND

Pages 253-253

formerly supposed to be the southern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> point of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, but now found to be an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, as it is separated from New Holland by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">Bass</a>'s strait, which was discovered by Mr Bass and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Flinders in the end of the year 1798. The northern coast is in S. Lat. 40° 55', and between 146° 45' and 148° 15' E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. This coast was discovered in November 1642, by Tasman, who gave it the name of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VAN_DIEMEN_S_LAND">Van Diemen's <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Furneaux touched at it in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1773, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> has since been further explored by other navigators. Here is a very safe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, named by Captain Cook <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ADVENTURE_BAY">Adventure <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>. Two other harbours or bays were discovered or explored by Messrs Bass and Flinders, viz. Port Dalrymple and Frederick Henry bay, and two considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which have been called Port Dalrymple and Derwent rivers. The parts adjoining to Adventure bay are mostly hilly, and form an entire forest of tall trees, rendered almost impassable by brakes of fern, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on the flat land, and on the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the hills, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, or consists of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and in some parts of a reddish clay; but further up the hills it is of a gray rough <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. The forest trees are all of one kind, generally quite straight, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> clusters of small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> observed were wood-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, milkwort, cudweed, bellflower, gladiolus, samphire, and several kinds of fern. The only quadruped seen distinctly was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of opossum, about twice the size of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">rat</a>. The kangaroo, found farther northward in New Holland, may also be supposed to inhabit here, as some of the inhabitants had

DIEPPE

Pages 253-254

a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of France, in Upper Normandy, in the department of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, with a good harbour, an old castle, and two handsome moles. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St James is an elegant structure; and there is a tower from which, in fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of England may be seen. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounts to 20,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade consists in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, toys, and laces. It was bombarded by the English in 1694, and it is not now so considerable as it was formerly. It is seated at the mouth of the river Bethune, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 4. N. Lat. 47° 5'.

DIERESIS

Pages 209-209

in Medicine, is the consuming of the vessels of an animal body, when, from some corroding cause, certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are made which naturally ought not

DIES MARCHII

Pages 254-254

was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> meeting of the English and Scots, annually appointed to be held on the marches or borders, in order to adjust all differences between them. DIESIS in Music, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a tone less than a semitone; or an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> consisting of a less or imperfect semitone. Diesis is the smallest and softest change or inflexion of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> imaginable; it is called a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, expressed thus X, by a St Andrew's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> or salter.

DIESPITER

Pages 254-254

in antiquity, a name given to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; and signifying diei pater, "father of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>." St Augustin derives the name from dies, "day," and partus, "production, bringing forth;" it being Jupiter that brings forth the day.
