To relieve his mind under this loss, he voluntarily offered his assistance to the physicians and surgeons in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with it till after the surrender of Carlisle to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s forces, when he received the duke's thanks, and returned to Hertford. In 1746 he married <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Illes, a relation of his first wife, Dindymus, and by her fortune, and that which he acquired by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the widow of Sir John Dimsdale of Hertford, he retired from practice; but his family becoming numerous, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of his ten children being living, he resumed it, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine, in 1761. Having fully satisfied himself about the new method of treating persons under inoculation for the small-pox, he published his treatise on it in 1776, which was soon circulated all over the continent, and translated into all its languages, not omitting the Russian. He concludes with saying that, "although the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> may have some share in the success, it, in my <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, consists chiefly in the method of inoculating with recent fluid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and the management of the patients at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of eruption." This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his professional knowledge occasioned his being invited to inoculate the empress Catherine and her son, in 1768, of which he gives a particular account in his Tracts on Inoculation, 1781. His reward for this was an appointment of actual counsellor of state and physician to her imperial majesty, with an annuity of 500l. the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a baron of the Russian empire, to be borne by his eldest lawful descendant in succession, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> wing of the Russian eagle in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> shield in the middle of his arms, with the customary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, adorned with the baron's coronet, over the shield; to receive immediately 10,000l. and 2000l. for travelling charges, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> pictures of the empress and her son, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to his son, to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke gave a gold snuff-box, richly set with diamonds. The baron inoculated numbers of people at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>; and, resisting the empress's invitation to reside as her physician in Russia, he and his son were admitted to a private audience of Frederic II., king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, at Sans Souci, and thence returned to England. In 1779, he lost his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife, who left him seven children. He afterwards married <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> daughter of William Dimsdale, of Bishop's-Stortford, who survived him. He was elected representative of the borough of Hertford in 1783; and declined all practice, except for the relief of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. He went to Russia once more, in 1781, to inoculate the late <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Constantine, sons of the grand duke; and, as he passed through <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, the late emperor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> received him in private, and wrote in his presence a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, which he was to convey to the empress of Russia. In 1790, his son, Baron Nathanael, was elected for the borough of Hertford, on his resignation and retirement to Bath, for several winters; but at last he fixed altogether at Hertford, and died, aged 89, Dec. 30, 1800, after an illness of about three weeks. About 17 years before his death he felt the sight of one eye declining, having before lost that of the other, but recovered both by the operation of the cataract, by Wenzel.

DINDYMA

Pages 262-263

-ORUM, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>,) from Dindymus, -i; a mountain allotted by many to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. Strabo has two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of this name; one in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a> near Cyzicus; the other in Gallogrecia near Pessinus; and none in Phrygia. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> extends this ridge from the borders of Troas, through Phrygia, to Gallogrecia; though therefore there were two mountains called Dindymus in particular, both sacred to the mother of the gods, and none of them in Phrygia <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>; yet there here might be several hills and eminences in it, on which this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> was worshipped, and therefore called Dindyma in general. Hence Cybele is surnamed Dindymane, (Horace.)

DINGWALL

Pages 263-263

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough of Scotland in the shire of Ross, seated on the frith of Cromarty, 15 miles west of the town of Cromarty. Near it runs the river Conel, famous for producing pearls. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 15'. N. Lat. 57° 45'. Dingwall was a Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> in the person of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his lady, but forfeited in 1715. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 800.

DINNER

Pages 263-263

the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> taken about the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>.—The word is derived from the French dinner, which Du Cange derives from the barbarous Latin disnare. Henry Stephens derives it from the Greek ἀναστάναι and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it wrote dinner. Menage deduces it from the Italian desinare, "to dine;" and that from the Latin desinere, "to leave off <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>." It is generally agreed to be the most salutary to make a plentiful dinner, and to eat sparingly at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. This is the general practice among us. The French, however, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, defer their good cheer to the evening; and Bernardinus Paternus, an eminent Italian physician, maintains it to be the most wholesome method, in a treatise expressly on the subject. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> Tartar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, after he has dined, makes publication by his heralds, that he gives leave for all the other kings and potentates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to go to dinner; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they waited for his leave.

DINOCRATES

Pages 263-263

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, who rebuilt the temple of Ephesus, when burnt by Erostratus, with much more magnificence than before. Vitruvius informs us that Dinocrates proposed to Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> to convert Mount <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOS">Athos</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> should contain a walled <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of the mount flow into his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and from thence into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>! He also conceived a scheme for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> of the temple of Arsinoe at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, of loadstone; that should by its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> uphold her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> image in the centre, suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>! Projects which at least showed a vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of imagination.

DIO CHRYSOSTOM

Pages 263-263

that is, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Mouth, a celebrated orator and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, in the first century, was born at Prusa in Bithynia. He attempted to persuade Vespasian to quit the empire: was hated by Domitian; but acquired the esteem of Trajan. This last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> took <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in conversing with him, and made him ride with him in his triumphal chariot. There are still extant 80 of Dio's orations, and some other of his works; the best edition of which is that of Hermann Samuel Raimarus, in 1750, in folio.

DIOCESE

Pages 263-263
or Diocese, the circuit or extent of the jurisdiction of a Bishop. The word is formed from the Greek διοικητής, government, administration; formed of διοικέω, which the ancient glossaries render administro, moderator, ordino; hence διοικήσις τῆς πόλεως, the administration or government of a city. Diocese is also used in ancient authors, &c., for the province of a Metropolitan. Diocesis (διοικήσις), was originally a civil government, or prefecture, composed of divers provinces. The first division of the empire into dioceses is ordinarily ascribed to Constantine; who distributed the whole Roman state into four, viz. the diocese of Italy, the diocese of Illyria, that of the East, and that of Africa. And yet long before Constantine, Strabo, who wrote under Tiberius, takes notice, lib. iii. p. 432, that the Romans had divided Asia into dioceses; and complains of the confusion such a division occasioned in geography, Asia being no longer divided by people, but by dioceses, each whereof had a tribunal or court, where justice was administered. Constantine then was only the institutor of those large dioceses, which comprehended several metropoles and governments; the former dioceses only comprehending one jurisdiction or district, or the country that had resort to one judge, as appears from this passage in Strabo, and (before Strabo) from Cicero himself, lib. iii. epist. ad familia. 9. and lib. xiii. ep. 67. Thus, at first a province included divers dioceses; and afterwards a diocese came to comprise divers provinces. In after times the Roman empire became divided into 13 dioceses or prefectures; though, including Rome, and the suburban regions, there were 14. These 14 dioceses comprehended 120 provinces; each province had a proconsul, who resided in the capital or metropolis; and each diocese of the empire had a consul, who presided in the principal city of the district. On this civil constitution the ecclesiastical one was afterwards regulated: each diocese had an ecclesiastical vicar or primate, who judged finally of all the concerns of the church within his territory. At present there is some further alteration: for diocese does not now signify an assemblage of divers provinces; but is limited to a single province under a metropolitan, or more commonly to the single jurisdiction of a bishop. Gul. Brito affirms diocese to be properly the territory and extent of a baptismal or parochial church; whence divers authors use the word to signify a simple parish. See Parish.

DIOCLEIA

Pages 263-263

(Διοκλεία), in antiquity, a solemnity kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, who died in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the youth he loved.

DIOCLESIANUS

Pages 263-265
CAIUS VALERIUS JOVIVS, a celebrated Roman emperor, born of an obscure family in Dalmatia in 245. He was first a common soldier, and by merit and success he gradually rose to the office of a general; and at the death of Numerian in 284, he was invested with imperial power. In this high station he rewarded the virtues and fidelity of Maximian, who had shared with him all the subordinate offices in the army, by making him his colleague on the throne. He created two subordinate emperors, Constantius and Galerius, whom he called Caesars, whilst he claimed for himself and his colleague the superior title of Augustus. Dioclesian has been celebrated for his military virtues; and though he was naturally unpolished by education and study, yet he was the friend and patron of learning and true genius. He was bold and resolute, active and diligent, and well acquainted with the arts, which will endear a sovereign to his people, and make him respectable even in the eyes of his enemies. His cruelty, however, against the followers of Christianity, has been deservedly branded with infamy. After he had reigned 22 years in the greatest prosperity, he publicly ab- Dioclesian dicated the crown at Nicomedia in 305, and retired to a private station at Salona. Maximian his colleague followed his example, but not from voluntary choice; and when he some time after endeavoured to rouse the ambition of Dioclesian, and persuade him to reassume the imperial purple, he received for answer, that Dioclesian took now more delight in cultivating his little garden than he formerly enjoyed in a palace, when his power was extended over all the earth. He lived nine years after his abdication in the greatest security and enjoyment at Salona, and died in 314, in the 68th year of his age. Dioclesian is the first sovereign who voluntarily resigned his power. His bloody persecution of the Christians forms a chronological era, called the era of Dioclesian, or of the martyrs. It was for a long time in use in theological writings, and is still followed by the Copts and Abyssinians. It commenced August 29, 284. Diodati, John, a famous minister, and professor of theology at Geneva, was born at Locca in 1579, and died at Geneva in 1652. He is distinguished by translations, 1. Of the Bible into Italian, with notes, Geneva, 1607, 4to. The best edition at Geneva in 1621, folio. This is said to be more a paraphrase than a translation, and the notes rather divine meditations than critical reflections. 2. Of the Bible into French, Geneva, 1644. 3. Of Father Paul's History of the Council of Trent into French. Diodia, a genus of plants belonging to the te-trandria class, and in the natural method ranking under the 47th order, Stellate. See Botany Index. Diodon, or Sun-fish, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of amphibia nantes. See Ichthyology Index. Diodorus, an historian, surnamed Siculus because he was born at Argyra in Sicily. He wrote a history of Egypt, Persia, Syria, Media, Greece, Rome, and Carthage; and it is said that he visited all the places of which he has made mention in his history. It was the labour of 30 years. He is, however, too credulous in some of his narrations; and often wanders far from the truth. He often dwells too long upon fabulous reports and trifling incidents; while events of the greatest importance to history are treated with brevity, and sometimes passed over in silence. He lived in the age of Julius Caesar and Augustus; and spent much time at Rome to procure information, and authenticate his historical narrations. This important work, which he composed in Greek, contained 40 books, of which there are only 15 remaining. The style is clear and neat, and very suitable to history. The best edition is that of Amsterdam, 1743, in 2 vols folio. Dioecia, (from διεκτον, twice, and οίκος, a house or habitation) two houses; the name of the 22d class in Linnæus's sexual method, consisting of plants which having no hermaphrodite flowers, produce male and female flowers on separate roots. These latter only ripen seeds; but require for that purpose, according to the sexualists, the vicinity of a male plant; or the aspersion, that is, sprinkling of the male dust. From the seeds of the female flowers are raised both male and female plants. The plants then in the class dioecia are all male and female; not hermaphrodite, as in the greater number of classes; nor with male and female flowers upon one root, as in the class monocœcia of the same author. See Botany Index. Diogenes of Apollonia, in the island of Crete, held a considerable rank among the philosophers who taught in Ionia before Socrates appeared at Athens. He was the scholar and successor of Anaximenes, and in some measure rectified his master's opinion concerning air being the cause of all things. It is said, that he was the first who observed that air was capable of condensation and rarefaction. He passed for an excellent philosopher, and died about the 450th year before the Christian era. Diogenes the Cynic, a famous philosopher, was the son of a banker of Sinope in Pontus. Being banished with his father for coining false money, he retired to Athens, where he studied philosophy under Antisthenes. He added new degrees of austerity to the sect of the Cynics, and never did any philosopher carry so far a contempt for the conveniences of life. He was one of those extraordinary men who run every thing to extremity, without excepting even reason itself; and who confirm the saying, that "there is no great genius without a tincture of madness." He lodged in a tub; and had no other moveables besides his staff, wallet and wooden bowl, which last he threw away on seeing a boy drink out of the hollow of his hand. He used to call himself a vagabond, who had neither house nor country; was obliged to beg, was ill clothed, and lived from hand to mouth; and yet, says Ælian, he took as much pride in these things as Alexander could in the conquest of the world. He was not indeed a jot more humble than those who are clothed in rich apparel, and fare sumptuously every day. He looked down on all the world with scorn; he magisterially censured all mankind, and thought himself unquestionably superior to all other philosophers. Alexander one day paid him a visit, and made him an offer of riches or anything else; but all that the philosopher requested of him was, to stand from betwixt the sun and him. As if he had said, "Do not deprive me of the benefits of nature, and I leave to you those of fortune." The conqueror was so affected with the vigour and elevation of his soul, as to declare, that, "if he was not Alexander, he would choose to be Diogenes;" that is, if he was not in possession of all that was pompous and splendid in life, he would, like Diogenes, heroically despise it. Diogenes had great presence of mind, as appears from his smart sayings and quick repartees; and Plato seems to have hit off his true character when he called him a Socrates run mad. He spent a great part of his life at Corinth, and the reason of his living there was as follows: as he was going over to the island Ægina, he was taken by pirates, who carried him into Crete, and there exposed him to sale. He answered the crier who asked him what he could do, that "he knew how to command men;" and perceiving a Corinthian who was going by, he shewed him to the crier, and said "Sell me to that gentleman, for he wants a master." Xeniares, for that was the Corinthian's name, bought Diogenes, and carried him with him to Corinth. He appointed him tutor to his children, and intrusted him also with the management of his house. Diogenes's friends being desirous to redeem him, "You are fools (said he); the lions are not the slaves of those who feed them, but they are the servants of the lions." He therefore therefore plainly told Xeniaes, that he ought to obey him, as people obey their governors and physicians. Some say, that Diogenes spent the remainder of his life in Xeniaes's family; but Dion Chrysostom asserts that he passed the winter at Athens, and the summer at Corinth. He died at Corinth when he was about 90 years old; but authors are not agreed either as to the time or manner of his death. The following account, Jerome says, is the true one. As he was going to the Olympic games, a fever seized him in the way; upon which he lay down under a tree, and refused the assistance of those who accompanied him, and who offered him either a horse or a chariot. "Go you to the games (says he), and leave me to contend with my illness. If I conquer, I will follow you; if I am conquered, I shall go to the shades below." He despatched himself that very night; saying, that "he did not so properly die, as get rid of his fever." He had for his disciples Onesicritus, Phocion, Stilpo of Megara, and several other great men. His works are lost. DIogenes Laertius, so called from Laerta in Cilicia where he was born, an ancient Greek author, who wrote ten books of the Lives of the Philosophers, still extant. In what year he flourished, is not easy to determine. The oldest writers who mention him are Sopater Alexandrinus, who lived in the time of Constantine the Great, and Hesychius Milesius, who lived under Justinian. Diogenes often speaks in terms of approbation of Plutarch and Phavorinus; and therefore, as Plutarch lived under Trajan, and Phavorinus under Hadrian, it is certain that he could not flourish before the reigns of those emperors. Menage has fixed him to the time of Severus; that is, about the year of Christ 200. From certain expressions in him, some have fancied him to have been a Christian; but, as Menage observes, the immoderate praises he bestows upon Epicurus will not suffer us to believe this, but incline us rather to suppose that he was an Epicurean. He divided his Lives into books, and inscribed them to a learned lady of the Platonic school, as he himself intimates in his life of Plato. Montaigne was so fond of this author, that instead of one Laertius he wishes we had a dozen; and Vossius says, that his work is as precious as gold. Without doubt we are greatly obliged to him for what we know of the ancient philosophers: and if he had been as exact in the writing part as he was judicious in the choice of his subject, we had been more obliged to him still. Bishop Burnet, in the preface to his Life of Sir Matthew Hale, speaks of him in the following proper manner: "There is no book the ancients have left us (says he), which might have informed us more than Diogenes Laertius's Lives of the Philosophers, if he had had the art of writing equal to that great subject which he undertook: for if he had given the world such an account of them as Gassendus has done of Peirce, how great a stock of knowledge might we have had, which by his unskilfulness is in a great measure lost! since we must now depend only on him, because we have no other and better author who has written on that argument." There have been several editions of his Lives of the Philosophers; but the best is that printed in two volumes 4to, at Amsterdam, 1693. This contains the advantages of all the former, besides some peculiar to itself: the Greek text and the Latin version corrected and amended by Meibomius; the entire notes of Henry Stephens, both the Caesarian, and of Menage; 24 copperplates of philosophers elegantly engraved: to which is added The History of the Female Philosophers, written by Menage, and dedicated to Madame Dacier. Besides this, Laertius wrote a book of Epigrams upon illustrious Men, called Pammetrus, from its various kinds of metre; but this is not extant.

DIOMEDES

Pages 265-265

son of Tydeus and Deiphyle, was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ætolia, and one of the bravest of the Grecian chiefs in the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He often engaged Hector and Æneas, and obtained much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. He went with Ulysses to steal the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALLADIUM">Palladium</a> from the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; and assisted in murdering Ilæus, king of Thrace, and carrying away his horses. At his return from the siege of Troy, he lost his way in the darkness of night, and landed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, where his companions plundered the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and lost the Trojan Palladium. During his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> absence, his wife Ægiale forgot her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> vows, and prostituted herself to Comites one of her servants. This lasciviousness of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> was attributed by some to the resentment of Venus, whom Diomedes had severely wounded in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> before Troy. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> of Ægiale was highly displeasing to Diomedes. He resolved to abandon his native country which was the seat of his disgrace; and the attempts of his wife to take away his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, according to some accounts, did not a little contribute to hasten his departure. He came to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which has been called Magna Graecia, where he built a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which he called Argyrippa, and married the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Danus the king of the country. He died there in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> according to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, he perished by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was greatly lamented by his companions, who in the excess of their grief were changed into birds resembling swans. These birds took flight into a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Adriatic, and became remarkable for the tameness with which they approached the Greeks, and for the horror with which they shunned all other nations. They are called the birds of Diomedes. Altars were raised to Diomedes as to a god, one of which Strabo mentions at Tivavus.

DIOMEDIA

Pages 265-265

a genus of birds belonging to the order of anseres. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DION

Pages 265-266

a Syracusan, son of Hipparinus, famous for his power and abilities. He was related to Dionysius, and often advised him, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, who at his request had come to reside at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to lay aside the supreme power. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> popularity rendered him odious in the eyes of the tyrant, who banished him to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. There he collected a numerous force, and resolved to free his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from tyranny. This he easily effected on account of his uncommon popularity. He entered the port of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> only in two ships; and in three days reduced under his power an empire which had already subsisted for 50 years, and which was guarded by 500 ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and above 100,000 troops. The tyrant fled to Corinth, and Dion kept the power in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, fearful of the aspiring ambition of some of the friends of Dionysius; but he was shamefully betrayed Dion Cassius, a native of Nicaea in Bithynia. His father's name was Apronianus. He was raised to the greatest offices of state in the Roman empire by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERTINAX">Pertinax</a>, and his three successors. He was naturally fond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and he improved himself by unwearied application. He was ten years in collecting materials for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Rome, which he made public in 80 books, after a laborious employment of 12 years in composing it. This valuable history began with the arrival of Æneas in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Alexander Severus. The first 34 books are totally lost, the 20 following, that is, from the 35th to the 54th, remain entire, the six following are mutilated, and fragments is all that we possess of the last 20. In the compilation of this extensive history, Dion proposed to himself <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, but he is not perfectly happy in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. His style is pure and elegant, and his narrations are judiciously managed, and his reflections learned; but upon the whole, he is credulous, and the bigoted slave of partiality, satire, and flattery. He inveighs against the republican principles of Brutus and Cicero, and extols the cause of Caesar. Seneca is the object of his satire, and he represents him as debauched and licentious in his morals. Dionis, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, a distinguished French surgeon, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV, he was appointed anatomical and chirurgical demonstrator in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> garden, and he was the first who held that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. He was surgeon in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Theresa of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of France, and to two dauphinesses and the royal children. He was the author of several works, both on anatomical and surgical subjects. One of the first of his publications is entitled Anatomie de l'Homme, suivant la Circulation du Sang, 8vo, which appeared in 1690, and has been frequently reprinted, and translated into different languages. It was translated into the Tartarian dialect by a Jesuit for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the emperor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been considered as a useful compendium of anatomy. In another work which he published in 1698, entitled Dissertation Historique et Physique sur la <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a> de l'Homme, he supports the ovarian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>. In 1707 he published a work on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, entitled Cours d'Operations de Chirurgie, 8vo, which was several times reprinted; and latterly it was edited with notes by La Faye in 2 vols. This treatise was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> received as a standard book on the subject. It contains many useful and pertinent observations detailed in plain, unaffected <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Dionis is the author of two other works; the first, Sur la Mort subite, et sur la Catalepsie, published in 1709, and the other Traité générale des Accouchements, in 1718. But the last is little else than an abridgement of Mauricéan's work on the same subject. Dionis died at Paris in 1718. Dionaea, Venus's Fly-trap, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIONYSIA">Dionysia</a>, in Grecian antiquity, solemnities in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, sometimes called by the general name of Orgia; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Bacchanalia, and Liberalia. See Bacchanalia and Bacchus. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIONYSIAC">Dionysiac</a>, in antiquity, was a designation given to plays and all manner of sports acted on the stage; because playhouses were dedicated to Dionysius, i.e. Bacchus, and Venus, as being the deities of sports and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. DIONYSIAN <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">PERIOD</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, No. 31. Dionysius I. from a private secretary became general and tyrant of Syracuse and all <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. He was likewise a poet; and having, by bribes, gained the tragedy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, he indulged himself so immoderately at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> from excess of joy, that he died of the debauch, 386 B.C.; but some authors relate that he was poisoned by his physicians. Dionysius II. (his son and successor) was a greater tyrant than his father; his subjects were obliged to apply to the Corinthians for succour; and Timoleon their general having conquered the tyrant, he fled to Athens, where he was obliged to keep a school for subsistence. He died 343 B.C. Dionysius Halicarnassensis, a celebrated historian, and one of the most judicious critics of antiquity, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>; and went to Rome after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>, where he staid 22 years under the reign of Augustus. He there composed in Greek his History of the Roman Antiquities, in 20 books, of which the first 11 only are now remaining. There are also still extant several of his critical works. The best edition of the works of this author is that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in 1704, in Greek and Latin, by Dr Hudson. Dionysius, a learned geographer, to whom is attributed a Periegesis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Survey of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, in Greek <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. Some suppose that he lived in the time of Augustus; but Scaliger and Saumasius place him under the reign of Severus, or Marcus Aurelius. He wrote many other works, but his Periegesis is the only one we have remaining; the best and most useful edition of which is that improved with notes and illustrations by Hill. Dionysius Areopagitae, was born at Athens, and educated there. He went afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; where, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe some writers of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that wonderful eclipse which happened at our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and was urged by some extraordinary impulse to cry out, Aut Deus patitur, aut cum patiente dolet; "either God himself suffers, or consoles with him who does." At his return to Athens he was elected into the court of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a>, from whence he derived his name of Areopagitae. About the year 50 he embraced Christianity; and, as some say, was appointed first bishop of Athens by St Paul. Of his conversion we have an account in the 17th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Acts of the Apostles.—He is supposed to have suffered martyrdom; but whether under Domitian, Trajan, or Adrian, is not certain. We have nothing remaining under his name, but what there is the greatest reason to believe spurious. Dionysius the Lesser, a Scythian, became <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> at Rome; he was the first who computed time from the birth of Dionysius to Christ, and fixed that great event, according to the vulgar era. He was also a learned canon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> writer, and died about the year 540.

DIOPHANTINE PROBLEMS

Pages 266-267

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, certain questions relating to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> numbers, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-angled triangles, &c., the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which was determined by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOPHANTUS">Diophantus</a>, a mathematician of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, who is believed to have lived about the third century. We have his works, which were published with notes at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 1621, by Bachet de Meziriac; and another edition in 1679, with observations on every question by M. Fermat. In these questions it is endeavoured to find commensurable numbers to answer <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> problems; which bring out an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of incommensurable quantities. For example, it is proposed to find a right-angled triangle, whose sides, \(x, y, z\), are expressed by commensurable numbers; it is known that \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\), \(z\) being the supposed hypotenuse. But it is possible to assume \(x\) and \(y\), so that \(z\) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be incommensurable; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> \(x = 1\), and \(y = 2\), \(z = \sqrt{5}\). The art of resolving such problems consists in so managing the unknown <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities in such a manner, that the square or higher power may vanish out of the equation, and then by means of the unknown quantity in its first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a>, the equation may be resolved without having recourse to incommensurables; e.g., let it be supposed to find \(x, y, z\), the sides of a right-angled triangle, such as will give \(x^2 + y^2 = z^2\). Suppose \(z = x + u\), then \(x^2 + y^2 = x^2 + 2xu + u^2\); out of which equation \(x^2\) vanishes, and \(x = \frac{y^2 - u^2}{2u}\); then assuming \(y\) and \(u\) equal to any numbers at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, the sides of the triangle will be \(y, \frac{y^2 \times u^2}{2u}\), and the hypotenuse \(x + u = \frac{y^2 \times u^2}{2u}\); if \(y = 3\), and \(u = 1\), then \(\frac{y^2 - u^2}{2u} = 4\).

DIOPTER

Pages 267-267
or DIOPTRA, the same with the index or alidade of an astrolabe, or other such instrument. Dioptra was an instrument invented by Hipparchus, which served for several uses; as, to level water-courses; to take the height of towers, or places at a distance; to determine the places, magnitudes, and distances of the planets, &c.

DIOPTRICS

Pages 267-267

THAT <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a> which treats of the laws of refraction, and the effects which the refraction of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> has in vision. The word is originally Greek, formed of ὁράω, "to see," and ἀπόλημα, "I see." As this and the other branches of Optics are fully treated under the collective name, we shall here, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> give a summary of the general principles of the branch, in a few plain aphorisms, with some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> definitions; and, 2. Present our readers with a set of entertaining experiments, illustrative of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dependent upon, those principles.

DIOSCOREA

Pages 274-277

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the Dioscia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th order, Sarmentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The only remarkable and useful <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the bulbifer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> yam. The roots of it are eaten by the inhabitants of both the Indies; and are particularly serviceable in the West <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, where they make the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> food. The plant is supposed to have been brought from the East to the West Indies; for it has never been observed to grow wild in any part of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; but in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon, and on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, it grows in the woods, and there are in those places a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of sorts. It is propagated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the root in pieces, observing to preserve an eye in each, as is practised in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> potatoes. One plant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce three or four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> roots. The skin of these roots is pretty thick, rough, unequal, covered with many stringy fibres or filaments, and of a violet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> approaching to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. The inside is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and of the consistence of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> beet. It resembles the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a> in its mealliness, but is of a closer texture. When raw, the yams are viscous and clammy; when roasted or boiled, they afford very nourishing food; and are often preferred to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> by the inhabitants of the West Indies, on account of their lightness and facility of digestion. When first dug out of the ground, the roots are placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to dry; after which they are either put into sand, dry garrets, or casks; where, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> kept from moisture, they may be preserved whole years, without being spoiled or diminished in their goodness. The root <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> weighs two or three pounds; though some yams have been found upwards of 20 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>.

DIOSCORIDES

Pages 277-277

a physician of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, who lived, as some suppose, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Nero. He was originally a soldier; but afterwards he applied himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and wrote a book upon medicinal herbs.

DIOSCURA

Pages 277-277

in antiquity, a festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Dioscours, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, who were reputed to be the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. It was observed by the Cyreneans, but more especially by the Spartans, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was honoured by the birth of these heroes. The solemnity was full of mirth, being a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wherein they shared plentifully of the gifts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and diverted themselves with sports, of which wrestling matches always made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>.

DIOSMA

Pages 277-277

AFRICAN SPURGE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIOSPOLIS

Pages 277-277

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Delta, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; to the south of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUSIRIS">Busiris</a> branch, before it divides into two.—Another of Bithynia, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERACLEA">Heraclea</a>.—A third, called Magma, denoting Thebes of the Higher Egypt.—A fourth, Diospolis Parva, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Nomos Diospolites of the Higher Egypt.—A fifth Diospolis, of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, the same with Lydda.—A sixth Diospolis, the ancient name of Laodicea of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, on the Lycus.

DIOSPOLITES NOMOS

Pages 277-277

(<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>,) a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Thebais <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, to distinguish it from another of the Lower Egypt or the Delta; to the south of the Nomos Thinites, on the west side of the Diospolites <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>.

DIOSPYROS

Pages 277-277

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">INDIAN</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">DATE</a> PLUM; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polygamy class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 18th order, Bicones. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIPHTHONG

Pages 277-277

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> vowel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the mixture of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a> pronounced together, so as to make one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>. The Latins pronounced the two vowels in their diphthongs ae or oe, oe or oe, much as we do; only that the one was heard much weaker than the other, though the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> was made with all the delicacy imaginable. Diphthongs, with regard to the eyes, are distinguished from those with regard to the ears: in the former either the particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of each vowel is heard in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>; or the sound of one of them is drowned; or, lastly, a new sound, different from either, results from both; the first of these only are real diphthongs, as being such both to the eye and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. Diphthongs with regard to the ear are either formed of two vowels meeting in the same syllable, or whose sounds are severally heard; or of three vowels in the same syllable, which only afford two sounds in the pronunciation. English diphthongs, with regard to the eye and ear, are ai, au, ea, ee, ei, oo, ou. Improper English diphthongs, with regard to the eye only, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">aa</a>, ae, eo, eu, ie, er, oe, ue, ui.

DIPLOE

Pages 277-279

in Anatomy, the soft meditullium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> medullary substance which lies between the two laminae of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the cranium. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DIPLOMA. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPLOMATICS">Diplomatics</a>. In a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it is used for an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> or license given by colleges, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, &c. to a clergyman to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the ministerial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, or to a physician to practise the profession, &c. after passing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, or admitting him to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Diplomatics, the science of diplomas, or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> literary monuments, public documents, &c. It does not, however, nor can it, absolutely extend its researches to antiquity; but is chiefly confined to the middle <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and the first centuries of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. For though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were accustomed to reduce their contracts and treaties into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; yet they graven them on tables, or covered them over with wax, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or wood, &c. And all that in the first ages were not traced on brass or marble, has perished by the length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of destructive events. 1. The word diploma signifies properly a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> or epistle, that is folded in the middle, and that is not open. But, in more modern times, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> has been given to all ancient epistles, letters, literary monuments, and public documents, and to all those pieces of writing which the ancients called Syngraphia Chirographa, Codicilli, &c. In the middle age, and in the diplomas themselves, these writings are called Litterae, Praecipia, Placita, Chartae indiculae, Sagilla, and Bulla; as also Pancharta, Pantocharta, Tractoriae, Descriptiones, &c. The originals of these pieces are named Exemplaria, or Autographa, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a> authenticae, Originatia, &c. and the copies, Apographa, Copiae, Particular, and so forth. Diplomatics. The collections that have been made of them are called Chartaria and Chartulae. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where these papers and documents were kept, the ancients named Scripia, Tabularium, or Ararium, words that were derived from the tables of brass, and, according to the Greek idiom, Archivum or Archivum. 2. In order to understand the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of these ancient papers, diplomas, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and to distinguish the authentic from the counterfeit, it is necessary to know that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> of the ancients came from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and was formed of thin leaves or membranes, taken from the branches of a tree named <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPYRUS">Papyrus</a>, or Biblium Aegyptiacum, and which were pasted one over the other with the slime of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, and were pressed and polished with a pumice stone. This paper was very scarce; and it was of various qualities, forms, and prices, which they distinguished by the name of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a> hieratica, lura, augusta, amphitheatrica, sofitica, tanirica, emperatrici, &c. They cut this paper into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> leaves, which they pasted one to the other, in order to make rolls of them: from whence an entire book was called volumen, from volvendo; and the leaves of which it consisted, paginae. Sometimes, also, they pasted the leaves all together by one of their extremities, as is now practised in binding; by this method they formed the back of a book, and these the learned called codices. They rolled the volume round a stick, which they named umbilicus; and the two ends that came out beyond the paper, cornua. The title, wrote on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, in purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, was joined to the last sheet, and served it as a cover. They made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all sorts of strings or ribbands, and even sometimes of locks, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the book; and sometimes also it was put into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. But there is not now to be found, in any library or cabinet whatever, any one of these volumes. We have been assured, however, by a traveller, that he had seen several of them in the ruins of Herculaneum; but so damaged, the paper so stiff and brittle, by the length of time, that it was impossible to unroll them, and consequently to make use of any of them; for on the first touch they fell into shatters. 3. We are ignorant of the precise time when our modern paper was invented; and when they began to make use of pens in writing, instead of the stalks of reeds. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> that the ancients used, was not made of vitriol and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, like the modern, but of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOOT">soot</a>. Sometimes also they wrote with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> ink made of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>; or in letters of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, on purple or violet parchment. It is not difficult for those who apply themselves to this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, to distinguish the parchment of the ancients from that of the moderns, as well as their ink and various exterior characters: but that which best distinguishes the original from the counterfeit is, the writing or character itself; which is so distinctly different from one century to another, that we may tell with certainty, within about 40 or 50 years, when any diploma was written. There are two works which furnish the clearest lights on this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and which may serve as sure guides in the judgments we may have occasion to make on what are called ancient diplomas. The one is the celebrated treatise on the Diplomatic, by F. Mabillon; and the other, the first volume of the Chronicon Gotvicense. We there find specimens of all the characters, the flourishes, and different methods of writing, of every age. For these matters, therefore, we must refer our readers to those authors; and shall here only add, that, 4. All the diplomas are written in Latin, and consequently the letters and characters have a resemblance to each other: but there are certain strokes of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> which distinguish not only the ages, but also the different nations; as the writings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, French, Saxons, &c. The letters in the diplomas are also usually longer, and not so strong as those of manuscripts. There has been also introduced a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, of a very disproportionate length, and the letters of which are called Exiles litterae crispe, ac protractiores. The first line of the diploma, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> of the sovereign, that of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, notary, &c. are usually wrote in this character. 5. The signature of a diploma consists either of the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, or of a monogram or cipher, composed of the letters of the names of those who subscribed it. The initial letters of the name, and sometimes also the titles, were placed about this cross. By degrees the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> changed, and they invented other marks, as, for example, the sign of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> was thus: ``` R K A S V L ``` They sometimes also added the dates and epoch of the signature, the feasts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the days of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDAR">kalendar</a>, and other like matters. The successive corruption of the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the style and orthography of each age, as well as their different titles and forms; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a>, accentuation, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCTUATION">punctuation</a>, and the various methods of writing the diphthongs; all these matters united, form so many characters and marks by which the authenticity of a diploma is to be known. 6. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> annexed to a diploma was anciently of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wax, and artfully imprinted on the parchment itself. It was afterwards pendant from the paper, and inclosed in a box or case, which they called bulla. There are some also that are stamped on metal, and even on pure gold. When a diploma bears all the characters that are requisite to the time and place where it is supposed to be written, its authenticity is not to be doubted: but at the same time we cannot examine them too scrupulously, seeing that the monks and priests of former ages have been very adroit in making of counterfeits, and the more as they enjoyed the confidence of princes and statesmen, and were even sometimes in possession of their rings or seals. 7. With regard to manuscripts that were wrote before the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, it is necessary (1.) to know their nature, their essential qualities, and matter; (2.) to be able to read them freely, and without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>; (3.) to judge of their antiquity by those characters which we have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned with regard to the diplomas; and (4.) to render them of use in the sciences. As there are scarce any of the ancient codes now remaining (see par. 2.), wrote on the Egyptian paper, or on wood, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, &c. we have only to consider those that are written on parchment or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a> (membranæ), and such as are wrote on our paper (chartæcos). The former former of these are in most esteem. With regard to the character, these codes are written either in square and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> letters, or in half square, or round and small letters. Those of the first kind are the most ancient. There are no intervals between the words, no letters different from the others at the beginning of any word, no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, nor any other distinction. The codes which are wrote in letters that are half square, resemble those we have in Gothic characters, as well for the age as the form of the letters. Such as are wrote in round let- ters are not so ancient as the former, and do not go higher than the ninth or tenth century. These have spaces between the words, and some punctuation. They are likewise not so well wrote as the preceding, and are frequently disfigured with comments. The codes are divided, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, into Lombard, Italian, Gaulic, Franco-Gaulic, Saxon, Anglo-Saxon, &c. 8. In the ancient Greek books, they frequently ter- minated the periods of a discourse, instead of all other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; and these divisions were called, in Latin, versus, from vertendo: for which reason these lines are still more properly named versus than lineae. At the end of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, they put <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the number of verses of which it consisted, that the copies might be more easily collated: and it is in this sense we are to understand Trebonius, when he says, that the Pandects contain 150,000 versus. These codes were like- wise vel probae vel deterioris notae, more or less perfect, not only with regard to the calligraphy or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the character, but to the correction of the text also. 9. It is likewise necessary to observe, in ancient codes, the abbreviations, as they have been used in dif- ferent centuries. Thus, for example, A.C.D. signi- fies Aulus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Decimus; Ap.Cn.Appius Cænius; Aug.Imp.Augustus Imperator. The characters that are called notae, are such as are not to be found in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; but which, notwithstanding, signify certain words. All these matters are explained in a copious manner by Vossius, and in the Chronicon Gotvicense. Lastly, The learned divide all the ancient codes into codices minus raros, rariores, editos, et anecdotos. The critical art is here indispensably necessary: its re- searches, moreover, have no bounds; and the more, as the use of it augments every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, by the discoveries that are made in languages, and by the increase of erudition.

DIPONDIUS

Pages 279-279

in the scripture <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is used by St Luke to signify a certain <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a> which was of very little value. Our translation of the passage is, "Are not two sparrows sold for two farthings?" In St Mat- thew, who relates the same thing, we read "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing?" The Greek reads assarion instead of as. Now assarion, as some say, was worth half an as, that is to say, four French deniers and ½ th; and, according to others, two deniers and ½ ths. Dipondius seems rather to signify half an as. Calmet, Diction. Bibl. Luke xii. 6. Matt. x. 29. Dr Arbuthnot differs in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> from the author last quoted. He says, that this coin was at first libralis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and even when diminished, it re- tained the name of libella. So that dipondius denotes two asses.

DIPPING

Pages 279-280

among miners, signifies the interrup- tion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> breaking off the veins of ore; an accident that gives them a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of trouble before they can <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- cover the ore again. A great deal of the skill of the miners consists in the understanding this dipping of the veins, and knowing how to manage in it. In Corn- wall they have this general rule to guide them in this respect: most of their tin-leads, which run from east to west, constantly dip towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Sometimes they underlie; that is, they slope <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> towards the north three feet in height perpendicular. This must carefully be observed by the miners, that they may exactly know where to make their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-shafts when occa- <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a> requires; yet, in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Dart- moor, there are some considerable leads, which run north and south; these always underlie toward the east. Four or five leads may run nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other in the same hill; and yet, which is rare, they may meet altogether in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a>, as it were a knot, which well ties the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and so separate again, and keep their former distances. Dipping <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used for observing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of inclination towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, assumed by any needle or other body after it has acquired the magnetic virtue. This was first observed by one Ro- bert Norman, an Englishman, and maker of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> for mariners, in the end of the 16th century; who finding that he was always obliged to counterbalance that end which turns to the north by a bit of wax or such other substance, though the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> had been ever so exact before, published an account of his dis- covery as a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of importance. The subject was instantly attended to; and instruments were not only contrived for ascertaining the quantity of the dip, but various speculations formed concerning the cause of such a surprising phenomenon. The general phenomena of the dipping needle are: that about the equatorial parts of the earth it remains in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, but depresses one end as we recede from these; the north end, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we go towards the north, and the south end if we proceed towards the south pole. The farther north or south that we go, the inclination becomes the greater; but there is no place of the globe hitherto discovered where it <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> directly downwards, though it is supposed that it would do so in some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> very near the pole. Its inclination is likewise found to vary very considerably at different times in different places of the earth, and by some changes of situation, in such a manner as must appear at first sight very unaccountable. Of all those who have attempted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of this obscure sub- ject, none have been more successful than M. Cavallo, who in his Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a> has given particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to all the phenomena, and accounted for them upon plain and rational principles, in the following manner: The dip of the magnetical needle in general may be understood from the following easy experiment:— Lay an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> magnet horizontally upon a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and over it suspend another smaller magnet (a sewing needle to which the magnetic virtue has been communicated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer the purpose), in such a manner as to re- main in a horizontal position when not disturbed by another magnet. Now, if this last small magnet or sewing needle, suspended by the middle, be brought <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> over the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one, it will turn itself in such a manner that the south pole of the small mag- <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> Dipping needle will point towards the north pole of the large one; and if at an equal distance from both, will remain in a horizontal position. But if we move it nearer to one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> than the other, it will readily be understood that the corresponding end of the needle will be attracted by the pole to which it approaches, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> inclined downwards; the contrary end being proportionably elevated. It is likewise evident, that this inclination will be greater or less according to the distance at which the small magnet is placed from the pole of the large one; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of the nearest pole having always the greatest effect upon it. And it is equally plain, that when brought directly over one of the poles of the large magnet, it will turn its own contrary one directly towards it, and thus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> exactly in the axis of the large one. The application of this experiment to the phenomena of the dipping needle is obvious, as nothing more is requisite for solving the whole mystery than to suppose the earth itself to be the large magnet, and the magnetic needle or any other magnetic body the small magnet in the experiment; for admitting that the north pole of the earth possesses a south magnetism, and that the opposite pole is possessed of a north magnetical polarity; it appears, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> is confirmed by experiment, that when a magnet is suspended properly in the equatorial parts of the world, it must remain in a horizontal position; but when removed nearer to one of the poles, it must decline one of its extremities, viz. that which is possessed of the contrary magnetic polarity, and that this inclination must increase in proportion as the magnet or magnetic needle recedes from the equator of the earth; and, lastly, when brought exactly upon either of the poles of the earth it must stand perpendicular to the ground, or in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> with the axis of the earth. The only difficulty in this explanation arises from the attributing a south magnetism to the north pole of the earth: but by this our author means only that its magnetism is contrary to that end of the magnetic needle which turns towards it; and in the same manner it must be understood, that the south pole of the earth has a north magnetic polarity. If the extremities of the axis of the earth, or the poles about which it performs its diurnal revolution, coincided with its magnetic poles, or even if the magnetic poles were always at a certain distance from them, the inclination of the needle would be always the same at equal distances from the equator, and might be very useful for determining the latitudes. But it would seem, that these poles are perpetually shifting their place, since both the inclination and horizontal direction of the needle are continually varying even in the same place, so that its quantity of inclination cannot be exactly calculated. Two general remarks may be made upon this subject. 1. That the inclination of the needle does not alter regularly in going from north to south, or from south to north, in any meridian.—2. That its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the same place, and at different times, is but small. Thus, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, about the year 1576, the dip was 71° 50' below the horizon, and in 1775 it stood at 72° 3'; the alteration in near 200 years scarce amounting to three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; which may be attributed to the errors of the instruments; as these were at first exceedingly erroneous and even yet are far from being arrived at perfection. The general method of constructing dipping <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> is, to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> an axis quite through the needle itself, and to let the extremities of the axis rest upon two supports, like the beam of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scales, that the needle may move vertically round; and hence, when placed in the magnetic meridian, it will naturally assume that position which is called the magnetic line, viz. the two ends nearly north and south, and one of them inclined considerably to the horizon. The degrees of the inclination are shown upon a graduated circle; and when the instrument is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, it has a stand, but at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> is necessary to suspend it. When furnished with a stand, it has also a spirit-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>; and the stand has three screws, by which the whole is adjusted in such a manner as to let the centre of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in the needle, and the mark of 90° on the lower part of the divided circle, be exactly in the same line perpendicular to the horizon. The greatest imperfections attending this instrument are the balancing of the needle itself, and the difficulty of knowing whether, after being made magnetic, it be properly balanced or not. The inaccuracy here indeed can be but very small, as arising only from dust or moisture. The method recommended by Mr Cavallo to obviate these inconveniences, is first to observe the dip of the needle; then to reverse its magnetism by the application of magnets, so that the end of it which before was elevated above the horizon may now be below it; and, lastly, to observe its dip again; for a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of the two observations will be pretty near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, though the needle may not be perfectly balanced. See Magnetism and Magnetical Needle.

DIPSACUS

Pages 280-280
