Teazel; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, Aggregatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIPSAS

Pages 280-280

a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, the bite of which produces such a thirst as proves mortal; whence its name dipsas, which signifies thirsty. In Latin it is called situla, "a pail." Moses speaks of it in Deut. viii. 15.

DIPTERA

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, an order of insects, which have only two wings, and under each wing a style, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> body, terminated by a protuberance or head, and called a balancer. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIPTOTES

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, are such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> as have only two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, as suppletice, suppletices, &c.

DIPTYCHA

Pages 280-281

in antiquity, a public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, wherein were written the names of the consuls, and other magistrates, among the heathens; and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and defunct as well as surviving brethren, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. The word is formed from the Greek διπτυχα, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> διπτυξ, and that from διπτυξ, a masculine noun derived from διπτυξ, I fold on plain. From its future, διπτυξ is formed διπτυξ, a fold or plait, to which adding δες, twice, we have διπτυξ, in the genitive διπτυξ, whence the nominative <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a> διπτυξ, q. d. a book folded in two leaves; though there were some in three, and others in four or five leaves. An ingenious author imagines this name to have been first given them, to distinguish them from the books that were rolled, called volumina. It is certain there were profane diptycha in the Greek empire, as well as sacred ones in the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The former were the matricula, or registers, wherein the names of the magistrates were entered; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> diptycha is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> in the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. Sacred Diptycha. The word is plural; diptycha being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> catalogue, in one whereof were written the names of the living, and in the other those of the dead, which were to be rehearsed during the office. We meet with something not unlike the sacred diptycha of the Greeks, in the canon of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> according to the Latin usage; where the people are enjoined to pray once for the living, and once for the dead; several saints are invoked in different times, &c. In these diptycha were entered the names of bishops, who had governed their flock aright; and these were never expunged out of the same, unless they were convicted of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> crime. In the diptycha were likewise entered the names of such as had done any signal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the church, whether they were living or dead, and mention was made of them in the celebration of the liturgy. Casaubon, in his observations on Athenaeos, lib. vi. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 14, supposes the Christians to have borrowed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> names in a book, and rehearsing them at mass, from the heathens, who entered the names of persons they would do any signal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to, in the verses of the Salii; as was done to Germanicus and Verus, sons of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Marcus Aurelius, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before, during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the republic, to Mamercus Veturius, and Lucia Volumnia, as we are told by Tacitus, lib. ii. Spartan, Ovid, Festus, Plutarch, &c. But Fa. Rosweyd does not approve this notion of Casaubon. The pretended St. Dionysius, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> author, says the contrary, and asserts the first establishment of this usage to have been founded on Scripture, 2 Tim. ii. 19. PsaL cxvi. 15. Rosweyd adds Ecclesiastic, xlv. i. and takes these to have been the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> the ancient church had a view to, rather than the Salian verses. The profane diptycha were frequently sent as presents to princes, &c., on which occasions they were finely gilt, and embellished; as appears from Symmachus, lib. ii. ep. 81. Those presented were usually of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, De Expens. Lodo. C. Theod. forbids all magistrates below consuls to make presents of diptycha of ivory in the public ceremonies. DIRÆ, the general name of the three furies in the Pagan system of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. They were so called, as being quasi Deorum iræ, the ministers of divine vengeance in punishing guilty souls after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. They were the daughters of Night and Acheron. See Furies.

DIRCA

Pages 281-281

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 21st order, Vepriculae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIRECT

Pages 281-281

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, is when the proportion of any terms, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities, is in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or direct order in which they stand, being the opposite to inverse, which considers the proportion in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> order of the terms. So, $3 : 4 :: 6 : 8$ directly; or $3 : 4 :: 8 : 6$ inversely.

DIRECTION

Pages 281-281

in Astrology, is a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a>, by which it is pretended to find the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in which any notable accident shall befall the person whose horoscope is drawn.

DIRECTOR

Pages 281-281

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a grooved probe, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scissors in opening sinuses or fistulae, that by this means the adjacent vessels, nerves, and tendons, may remain unhurt. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DIRIBITORES

Pages 281-281

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, officers appointed to distribute tablets to the people at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>. See Comitia.

DIRIGENT

Pages 281-281
or Directrix, a term in geometry, signifying the line of motion, along which the described line or surface is carried in the genesis of any plane or solid figure.

DIS

Pages 281-281

an inseparable article prefixed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> words; the effect whereof is either to give them a signification contrary to what the simple words have, as disobliges, disobey, &c.; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to signify a separation, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a>, &c., as disposing, distributing. Dis, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, seated on the river Waveney, on the side of a hill. It is a neat flourishing town, with one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a Presbyterian and a Quaker meeting. It has about 600 good houses; the streets are well paved, pretty wide, and always clean. At the west end of the town is a large meer or lake; but so muddy, that the inhabitants can make no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it but in catching of eels. In the town are carried on manufactories of sail-cloth, hose, and the making of stays. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 16. N. Lat. 52. 25. Dis, a god of the Gauls, the same as Pluto the god of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> supposed themselves descended from that deity.

DISABILITY

Pages 281-282

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is disabled, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> made incapable to inherit any lands, or take that benefit which otherwise he might have done; and this may happen four ways; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of an ancestor, or of the party himself, by the act of God, or of the law. 1. Disability by the act of the ancestor, is where the ancestor is attainted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, &c., which corrupts the blood of his children, so that they may not inherit his estate. 2. Disability by the act of the party, Disability party; is where a man binds himself by obligation, that, upon surrender of a lease, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> a new estate to a lessee; and afterwards he grants over the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> to another, which puts it out of his power to perform it. 3. Disability by the act of God, is where a man is non sane memoriae, whereby he is incapable to make any grant, &c. So that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he passeth an estate out of him, it may after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> be made void; but it is a maxim in law, "That a man of full <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> shall never be received to disable his own person." 4. Disability by the act of the law, is where a man by the law, without anything by him done, is rendered incapable of the benefit of the law; as an alien born, &c.

DISANDRIA

Pages 282-282

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the heptandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DISCERNING

Pages 282-282
or DISCERNMENT, a faculty of the mind whereby it distinguishes between ideas. See METAPHYSICS.

DISCIPLE

Pages 282-282

one who learns anything from another; thus, the followers of any teacher, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, &c. are called disciples. In the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, they were followers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, in general; but in a more restrained sense, the disciples denote those alone who were the immediate followers and attendants on his person, of which there were 70 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 72. The names disciples and apostles are often synonymously used in the gospel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; but sometimes the apostles are distinguished from disciples, or persons selected out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples, to be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ministers of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>: of these there were only 12. The Latins kept the festival of the 70 or 72 disciples on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 15th, and the Greeks on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 4th.

DISCIPLINE

Pages 282-282

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes instruction and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> discipline, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> discipline, &c. Ecclesiastical discipline consists in putting those laws in execution by which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is governed, and inflicting the penalties enjoined by them against the several sorts of offenders that profess the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>. The primitive church never pretended to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> discipline upon any but such as are within her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, in the largest sense, by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of their own profession; and even upon these she never pretended to exercise her discipline so far as to cancel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disannul their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>: all that she pretended to was to deprive men of the benefits of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, such as public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, receiving the eucharist, and other acts of divine worship. The church discipline was only confined to the admonition of the party, and to the lesser and greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>. As to the objects of ecclesiastical discipline, they were all such delinquents as fell into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and scandalous crimes after baptism. Discipline, in a more peculiar sense, is used for the chastisements or bodily punishments inflicted on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of the Romish church who has been found a delinquent; or even for that which the religious voluntarily undergo or inflict on themselves by way of mortification. Book of Discipline, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the church of Scotland, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> order, drawn up by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of ministers in 1650, for the reformation and uniformity to be observed in the discipline and policy of the church. In this book the government of the church by prelates is set aside, church sessions are established, the superstitions observation of fast days and saints days is condemned, and other regulations for the government of the church are determined. This book was approved by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and is called the First Book of Discipline.

DISCORD

Pages 282-284

in general, signifies disagreement, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> opposition between different persons or things. Discord, in Music, every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> which, joined with another, forms an assemblage disagreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>; or rather, every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> whose extremes do not coalesce. Now, as there are no other concords or consonances, except those which form amongst themselves, and with their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> sound, perfect chords, it follows, that every interval must be a real dissonance or discord: even the third and sixth were reckoned such among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who excluded them from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of consonant chords. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> dissonance, which is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with discord, is compounded of two words, the inseparable position <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a> and the verb sonare; which, both in a literal and metaphorical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies disagreement or disunion. In reality, that which renders dissonances grating, is, that the sounds which form them, far from uniting in the ear, seem to repel each other, and are heard each by itself as two distinct sounds, though produced at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. This repulsion or violent oscillation of sounds is heard more or less, as the vibrations which produce it are more or less frequently coincident. When two vocal strings are gradually tuned, till they approach a consonant interval, the pulsations become slower as the chord grows more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, till at last they are scarcely heard, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> heard at all; from whence it appears certain, that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> produced in us by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> results from the more or less exact and frequent coincidence or vibration; though the reason why this coincidence should give pleasure, more than any other modification or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of sounds, appears to us inscrutable. The agreeable effects of dissonance in harmony, are no objection to this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>; since it is allowed, that the sensations excited by discord are not in themselves immediately and necessarily pleasing, but only please by auricular deception. The ear is surprised with the shock it receives, without being able to imagine how it should have happened; and in proportion as it is harsh and grating, we feel the pleasure of returning harmony enhanced, and the disappointment of being artfully and insensibly extricated more agreeable. The name of dissonance is given sometimes to the interval, and sometimes to each of the two sounds which form it. But though two sounds equally form a dissonance between themselves, the name is most frequently given to that sound in particular which is most extraneous to the chord. The number of possible dissonances is indefinite; but as in music we exclude all intervals which are not found in the system received, the number of dissonances is reduced to a very few: besides, in practice, we can only select from those few such as are agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> in which we compose; and from this last number we must exclude such as cannot be used consistently with the rules prescribed. But what are these rules? Have they any foundation in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, or are they merely arbitrary? This is what Rousseau, whom in this article we have followed or abandoned as his observations appeared useful or frivolous, purposes to investigate as its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object. But where does his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCRUTINY">scrutiny</a> terminate? Not in the abolition of the rules prescribed. These have still subsisted, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> still subsist, while the frame of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and the nature of music, remain what they are. If then the rules be permanent and universal, the principle upon which they are founded may be latent or ambiguous; but the rules themselves can never be purely arbitrary. How else could it happen, that Rameau, D'Alembert, and Rousseau, should admit the force and effect of these rules, whilst each of those masters exerts his whole genius to give a different account of their cause and origin? Rousseau himself, as we have seen in a former article, inculcates the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of dissonances for the completion of harmony; (see CHORD). Now, if this be true, the easiest methods of introducing and dismissing these discords must be the most eligible, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> the rules for using them must be established. It is not then upon the subsistence or demolition of any particular theory that they depend. Should we attend to the particular objections which may be urged against any system whatever; where is the theory which will be found <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against the efforts of skepticism? After all, the objections of Rousseau against Rameau's theory, as applied by D'Alembert to the origin of consonances, (see MUSIC, art.94, 95, 96, 97, 98, 99.), appear to be much more frivolous than the analogies from which he pretends this origin to be deduced. It appears from D'Alembert's exposition to this theory, that, if not for all, it affords a solution for the most material and essential phenomena in harmony; which is sufficient for its establishment, till another can be found, which gives a rational and consistent account of the whole: a discovery which has not yet been made. But whilst we acknowledge the futility of Rousseau's objections against D'Alembert's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">Discretion</a>, explication of dissonances, we must at the same time admire the ingenuity with which he has deduced them from principles purely <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>, without departing from the system of M. Rameau. This mechanical explication will be found in his Musical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, under the article Dissonance. Discord (the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of), in Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. She is represented by Aristides with fiery eyes, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> countenance, livid lips, and wearing a dagger in her bosom. It was she who at the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a> and Thetis threw in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> apple, whereon was written "To the fairest:" which occasioned a contention between the goddesses Juno, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and Venus; each pretending a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the apple. She was likewise called Ate and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ERIS">Eris</a>. Discovery, in dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a manner of unravelling a plot or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> in tragedies, comedies, and romances; wherein, by some unforeseen accident, a discovery is made of the name, fortune, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, &c. of a principal person, which were before unknown. See Catastrophe. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">Discount</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a term among traders, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>. It is used by the two former on occasion of their buying commodities on the usual time of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, with a condition that the seller shall allow the buyer a certain discount at the rate of so much per cent. per annum, for the time for which the credit is generally given, upon condition that the buyer pays ready <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for such commodities, instead of taking the time of credit. Traders and merchants also frequently taking promissory notes for moneys due payable to them or order at a certain time, and sometimes having occasion for money before the time is elapsed, procure these notes to be discounted by bankers before the time of payment. Bills of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> are also discounted by bankers; and in this consists one article of the profits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKING">banking</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">Bank</a>. Discrete, or Disjunct, Proportion, is when the ratio of two or more pairs of numbers or quantities is the same, but there is not the same proportion between all the four numbers. Thus, if the numbers $3 : 6 :: 8 : 16$ be considered, the ratio between $3 : 6$ is the same, as that between $8 : 16$, and therefore the numbers are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a>: but it is only discretely or disjunctly, for $3$ is not to $6$ as $6$ to $8$; that is, the proportion is broken off between $8$ and $3$, and is not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> as in the following continual proportions, $3 : 6 :: 12 : 24$. Discrete <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">Quantity</a>, is such as is not continued and joined together. Such, for instance, is any number. Discretion; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, or knowledge to govern one's self. There are many more shining qualities in the mind of man, but there is none so useful as discretion; it is this indeed that gives a value to all the rest, which sets them at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in their proper times and places; and turns them to the advantage of the person who is possessed of them. Without it learning is pedantry, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> impertinence; virtue itself looks like weakness; the best parts only qualify a man to be more sprightly in errors, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> to his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. Nor does discretion only make a man <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of his own Discretion own parts, but of other men's. The discreet man finds out the talents of those he converses with, and knows how to apply them to proper uses. Accordingly, if we look into particular communities and divisions of men, we may observe that it is the discreet man, not the witty, nor the learned, nor the brave, who guides the conversation, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. A man with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> talents, but void of discretion, is like <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLYPHEMUS">Polyphemus</a> in the fable, strong and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, endowed with an irresistible force, which for want of sight is of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to him. Though a man has all other perfections, and wants discretion, he will be of no great consequence in the world; but if he has this single <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> in perfection, and but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> share of others, he may do what he pleases in his particular station of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. It is proper, however, to distinguish between discretion and cunning, the latter being the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> only of little <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, ungenerous minds. Discretion <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out the noblest ends to us, and pursues the most proper and laudable methods of attaining them; cunning has only private selfish aims, and sticks at nothing which may make them succeed. Discretion has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and extensive views, and, like a well-formed eye, commands a whole horizon: cunning is a kind of short-sightedness, that discovers the minutest objects which are near at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, but is not able to discern things at a distance. Discretion, the more it is discovered, gives the greater authority to the person who possesses it; cunning, when it is once detected, loses its force, and makes a man incapable of bringing about even those events which he might have done, had he passed only for a plain man. Discretion is the perfection of reason, and a guide to us in all the duties of life; cunning is a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, that only looks out after our immediate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and welfare. Discretion is only found in men of strong sense and good understanding: cunning is often to be met with in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> themselves, and in persons who are but the fewest removes from them. In short, cunning is only the mimic of discretion, and may <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> upon weak men, in the same manner as vivacity is often mistaken for wit, and gravity for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>.

DISCUS

Pages 284-284

in antiquity. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISC">DISC</a>. Discus, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the middle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a radiated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> flower, generally consisting of small florets, with a hollow regular petal. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> surrounded by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, plain, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flat, tongue-shaped petals, in the circumference or margin; as in daisy, groundsel, and leopard's-bane; sometimes the circumference is naked, as in cotton-weed and some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of coltsfoot. DISCUS Foliis, the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>.

DISCUSSION

Pages 284-284

in matters of literature, signifies the clear treating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> handling of any particular point, or problem, so as to shake off the difficulties with which it is embarrassed: thus we say, such a point was well discussed, when it was well treated and cleared up. [Merged from FREEDOM OF DISCUSSION, p.566] m of discussion means the power of presenting all opinions, equally, relative to the subject of discussion; and of recommending them by any medium of persuasion which the author may think proper to employ. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any obstruction is given to the delivering of one sort of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, not given to the delivering of another; if any advantage is attached to the delivering of one sort of opinion, not attached to the delivery of another, so far equality of treatment is destroyed, and so far the freedom of discussion is infringed;—so far <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is not left to the support of her own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, and so far, if the advantages are attached to the side of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, truth is deprived of her chance of prevailing. To attach advantage to the delivering of one set of opinions, disadvantages to the delivering of another, is to make a choice. But we have already seen, that it is not safe for the people to let any body choose opinions for them. If it be said, that the people themselves might be the authors of this preference, what is this but to say, that the people can choose better before discussion than after; before they have obtained information than after it? No, if the people choose before discussion, before information, they cannot choose for themselves. They must follow blindly the impulse of certain individuals, who, therefore, choose for them. This is, therefore, a pretence, for the purpose of disguising the truth, and cheating the people of that choice, upon which all their security for good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> depends. If these deductions are as clear and incontrovertible as to us they appear to be, the inquiry respecting the principles which ought to regulate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the press is drawn pretty nearly to its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. We have shown, that as far as regards the violation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of individuals in respect to both persons and things, no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> on account of the press is required. We have shown in what manner the rights of individuals, in regard to reputation, should be defined by the civil code, and the violation of them prevented by the penal. We next proceeded to what may be considered as the main branch of the inquiry, namely, the use of the press in speaking of the institutions and functionaries of government. We have found, that in this respect the freedom of the press is of such importance, that there is no security for good government without it. We have also found, that the use of it, in respect to these subjects, admits but of two useful restrictions,—that of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> exhortation to obstruct any of the operations of government in detail, and that of imputing to a functionary of government a criminal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, which there was no ground, nor even any appearance of ground, to impute to him. These restrictions, of course, it would be very easy to define in the criminal code, and to find appropriate motives to sanction. In all other respects, we have seen that the press ought to be free; that if there is any limit to the power of delivering unfavourable opinions, either of the functionaries or the institutions of government, and of recommending those opinions by any media, with the single exception of false facts, under the circumstances mentioned above, the benefits which may be derived from the freedom of the press are so greatly infringed, that hardly any security for good government can remain. In the administration of English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or rather of what is called law, upon this subject, without being any thing better than the arbitrary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the judges, it is said, that though discussion should be free, it should be "decent;" and that all "indecency" in discussion should be punished as a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a>. It is not our object in this discourse to give an exposition of the manifold deformities of the English law of libel. If we have been successful in developing the true principles which ought to regulate the freedom of the press, every reader may, by an application of those principles, determine what he ought to think of the several particulars which may there attract his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. We shall confine ourselves to a short notice of those dicta, or doctrines, which seem most likely to be pleaded in opposition to the principles which we have endeavoured to establish. The question is, whether indecent discussion should be prohibited? To answer this question, we must, of course, inquire what is meant by indecent. In English libel law, where this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> holds so distinguished a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>,—is it not defined? English legislators have not hitherto been good at defining; and English lawyers have always vehemently condemned, and grossly abused it. The word "indecent," therefore, has always been a term under which it was not difficult, on each occasion, for the judge to include whatever he did not like. "Decent," and "what the judge likes," have, therefore, been pretty nearly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>. Indecency of discussion cannot <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the delivery either of true or of false opinions, because discussion implies both. In all discussion there is supposed at least two parties, one who affirms, and one who denies. One of them must be in the wrong. The delivery, though not of all true opinions, yet of some, may be said to be indecent. All opinions are either favourable or unfavourable. True opinions that are favourable to government and its functionaries will not be said to be indecent; nor will all opinions that are true and unfavourable be marked out for prohibition under that name. Opinions unfavourable may either be greatly unfavourable or slightly unfavourable. If any unfavourable opinions are exempted from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of indecency, it must be those which are slightly so. But observe, what would be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of prohibiting, as indecent, those which are greatly unfavourable. A true opinion, greatly unfavourable to a functionary, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of government, is greatly hurtful to the people. You would permit the slight evil to be spoken of, and hence removed; you would not permit the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> evil to be spoken of. If no true opinion can be regarded as indecent, meaning by indecent, requiring <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, we must inquire if any false opinion on matters of government ought to be treated as such. If all false opinions are indecent, all discussion is indecent. All false opinions, therefore, are not indecent. The English libel law does not treat any favourable opinions, how much soever false, as indecent. If all opinions that are false and unfavourable are said to be indecent, who is to judge if they are false? It has been already proved, that the people can confide the power of determining what opinions are true, what are false, to none but themselves. Nothing can resist this argument. Either the people do know, or they do not know, that an opinion is false. If they do not know, they can permit nobody to judge for them, and must leave discussion its free course. If they do know, all infliction of evil for the delivery of an opinion which then can do no harm, would be purely mischievous and utterly absurd. If all opinions, true and false, must be allowed to be delivered, so must all the media of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. We need not examine minutely the truth of this deduction, because it will probably be allowed. It will be said, however, that though all opinions may be delivered, and the grounds of them stated, it must be done in calm and gentle <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Vehement expressions, all words and phrases calculated to inflame, may justly be regarded as indecent, because they have a tendency rather to pervert than rectify the judgment. To examine this proposition, it must be taken out of that state of vagueness in which so many things are left by the English law, and made, if possible, to speak a language, the meaning of which may be precisely ascertained. We have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> decided, as appeared, on very substantial grounds, that the statement of no opinion, favourable or unfavourable, true or false, with its media of proof, ought to be forbidden. No language, necessary for that purpose, can be indecent, meaning here, as before, nothing by that term, as nothing can be meant, but simply punishable, or proper for punishment. But the only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between delivering an opinion one way and another way is, that in the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is simply delivered, in the other it is delivered with indications of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The meaning of the phrase in question then must be, that an opinion must not be delivered with indications of passion. What! not even a favourable one? "Oh, yes! a favourable one. Merited praise ought to be delivered with warmth." Here, then, is inequality, and therefore mischief at once. An opinion, meaning here a true opinion, if it is favourable, you allow—if unfavourable, you do not allow—to be delivered in a certain way. Why? Because in that way, you say, it is calculated to make an undue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. Opinions favourable, then, you wish to make an undue impression, and by that confess the wickedness of your intention. You desire that the people should think better of the institutions and functionaries of their government than they deserve; in other words, you wish the government to be bad. If opinions, to what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> soever unfavourable, may be freely and fully delivered, there are two conclusive reasons why the terms in which they are delivered should not be liable to punishment. In the first place, the difference between one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of delivery and another is of little consequence. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> place, you cannot forbid the delivery in one set of terms, without giving a power of preventing it in almost all. 1. The difference is of little consequence. If I say barely that such a functionary of government, or such an institution of government, is the cause of great injury and suffering to the people, all that I can do more by any language is, to give intimation, that the conduct of such functionary, or the existence of such institution, excites in me great contempt, or great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, or great hatred, and ought to excite them in others. But if I put this in the way of a direct proposition, I may do so, because then it will be a naked statement with regard to a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact, and cannot be forbidden, without overthrowing the whole of the doctrine which we have already established. If, then, I give indication of certain sentiments of mine, and of my opinion of what ought or be the sentiments of others explicitly, I ought, you say, to be held innocent; if implicitly, guilty. Implicitly, or explicitly, that is the difference, and the whole of the difference. If I say, that such a judge, on such an occasion, took a bribe, and pronounced an unjust decision, which ruined a meritorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and his family, this is a simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of opinion, and ought not, according to the doctrine already established, to meet with the smallest obstruction. If I also state the matter of fact with regard to myself, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> has excited in me great compassion for the injured family, and great anger and hatred against the author of their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WRONGS">wrongs</a>, this must be fully allowed. I must further be allowed to express freely my opinion, that this action ought to excite similar sentiments in other members of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, and that the judge ought to receive an appropriate punishment. Much of all this, however, I may say in another manner. I may say it much more shortly by implication.—Here, I may cry, is an act for the indignation of mankind! Here is a villain, who, invested with the most sacred of trusts, has prostituted it to the vilest of purposes! Why is he not an object of public execration? Why are not the vials of wrath already poured forth upon his odious head?—All this means nothing, but that he has committed the act; that I hate him for it, and commiserate the sufferers; that I think he ought to be punished; and that other people should feel as I do. It cannot be pretended, that between these two modes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> the difference, in point of real and ultimate effect, can be considerable. For a momentary warmth, the passionate language may have considerable power. The permanent opinion formed of the character of the man, as well as the punishment which, under a tolerable administration of law, he can sustain, must depend wholly upon the real state of the facts; any peculiarity in the language in which they may have been originally announced soon loses its effects. If that language has expressed no more indignation than what was really due, it has done nothing more than what the knowledge of the facts themselves would have done. If it has expressed more indignation than what was due, the knowledge of the facts operates immediately to extinguish it, and, what is more, to excite an unfavourable opinion of him who had thus displayed his intemperance. No evil then is produced; or none but what is very slight and momentary. If there should be a short-lived excess of unfavourable feeling, we have next to consider what is the proper remedy. Punishment should never be applied, when the end can be attained by more desirable means. To destroy any excess of unfavourable feeling, all that is necessary is, to show the precise state of the facts, and the real amount of the evil which they import. All excess of feeling arises from imputing to the facts a greater efficacy in the way of evil than belongs to them. Correct this opinion, and the remedy is complete. 2. You cannot forbid the use of passionate language, without giving a power of obstructing the use of censorial language altogether. The reason exists in the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of language. You cannot speak of moral acts in language which does not imply approbation and disapprobation. All such language may be termed passionate language. How can you point out a line when passionate language begins, impassionate ends? The effect of words upon the mind depends upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> which we have with them. But no two men have the same associations with the same words. A word which may excite trains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, will excite none in another. A word may appear to one man a passionate word, which does not appear so to another. Suppose the legislature were to say, that all censure, conveyed in passionate language, shall be punished, hardly could the vices either of the functionaries or institutions of government be spoken of in any language which the judges might not condemn as passionate language, and which they would not have an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with other functionaries, to prohibit by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>. The evil, therefore, which must of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> be incurred by a power to punish language to which the name of passionate could be applied, would be immense. The evil which is incurred by leaving it exempt from punishment is too insignificant to allow that almost anything should be risked for preventing it. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, in some of its shapes, has, in most countries, been placed on the footing of an institution of the state. Ought the freedom of the press to be as complete, in regard to this, as we have seen that it ought to be, in regard to all other institutions of the state? If any one says that it ought not, it is incumbent upon him to show wherein the principles which are applicable to the other institutions fail in their application to this. We have seen, that, in regard to all other institutions, it is unsafe for the people to permit any but themselves to choose opinions for them. Nothing can be more certain, than that it is unsafe for them to permit any but themselves to choose for them in religion. If they <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with the power of choosing their own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> opinions, they part with every power. It is well known with what ease religious opinions can be made to embrace every thing upon which the unlimited power of rulers, and the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of the people, depend. The doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> obedience and non-resistance was a religious doctrine. Permit any man, or any set of men, to say what shall and what shall not be religious opinions, you make them despotic immediately. This is so obvious, that it requires neither illustration nor proof. But if the people here, too, must choose opinions for themselves, discussion must have its free course; and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> which we have proved to be true in regard to other institutions, are true in regard to this. (F.F.) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">LIFE</a> PRESERVERS. See PRESERVERS.

or BISDIAPASON, in Music, a compound concord, described by F. Parrau, in the quadruple ratio of $4 : 1$, or $8 : 2$. DISDIAPASON Diapente, a concord in a sextuple ratio of $1 : 6$. DISEASE

Pages 284-285

has been variously defined by physicians, almost every founder of a new system having given a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of disease, differing in some respects from his predecessors. For a particular account of these definitions, see MEDICINE. Of all animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is subject to the most diseases; and of men, the studious and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> are most exposed thereto. Other animals have their diseases; but they are in smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: nor are <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, without them; though their maladies scarce exceed half a score. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> deified their diseases. Some diseases only impair the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> immediately affected; as the ophthalmia, gout, &c. Others destroy it entirely; as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUTTA">gutta</a> serena, palsy, &c. Some affect the whole body; as the fever, apoplexy, epilepsy, &c. Others only impair a part; as the asthma, colic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>, &c. Some only affect the body; as the gout: others disturb the mind; as melancholy, delirium, &c. Lastly, others affect both the body and mind; as the mania, phrensy, &c. The colder the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in general, the fewer and the less violent are the diseases. Scheffer tells us that the Laplanders know no such thing as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fevers of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> kind, nor are subject to half the distempers we are. They are robust and strong, and live to $80$, $90$, and many of them to more than $100$ years; and at this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> they are not feeble and decrepid as with us; but a man of $90$ is able to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> or travel as well as a man of $60$ with us. They are subject, however, to some diseases more than other nations; thus they have often distempers of the eyes, which is owing to their living in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or being blinded by the snow. Pleurises and inflammations of the lungs are also very frequent among them; and the small-pox often rages with great violence. They have one general remedy against these and all other internal diseases: this is the root of that sort of moss, as Scheffer expresses it, which they call jertth. They make a decoction of this root in the whey of rein-deer <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and drink very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> doses of it warm, to keep up a breathing sweat; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they cannot get this, they use the stalks of angelica boiled in the same manner: they have not so great an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of this as of the other remedy: but the keeping in a sweat, and drinking plentifully of diluting liquors, may go a great way in the cure of their diseases, whether either the one or the other of the drugs have any virtue or not. They cure pleurises by this method in a very few days; and get so well through the small-pox with it, that very few die of it. It has been always observed, that people of particular places were peculiarly subject to particular diseases, which which are owing to their manner of living, or to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and effluvia of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Hoffman has made some curious observations on diseases of this kind. He observes, that swellings of the throat have always been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the inhabitants of mountainous countries; and the old Roman authors say, Who wonders at a swelled throat in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>? The people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, Carinthia, Stiria, the Hartz forest, Transylvania, and the inhabitants of Croustadt, he observes, are all subject to this disease from the same cause. The French are peculiarly troubled with fevers, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and with hydroceles and sarcoceles; and all these disorders seem to be owing originally to their eating very large quantities of chestnuts. The people of our own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> are peculiarly afflicted with hoarsenesses, catarrhs, coughs, dysenteries, consumptions, and the scurvy; and the women with the fluor albus or whites; and children with a disease scarce known elsewhere, which we call the rickets. In different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> different diseases reign. At <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> the venereal disease is more common than in any other part of the world. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, people are peculiarly subject to the bleeding piles. At Rome, tertian agues and lethargic distempers are most common. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> the epilepsy or falling sickness. And in Apulia they are most subject to burning fevers, pleuritis, and to that sort of madness which is attributed to the bite of the tarantula, and which, it is said, is only to be cured by music. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> apoplexies are common, as also melancholy, hypocondriacal complaints, and bleeding piles. The Dutch are peculiarly subject to the scurvy, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the kidneys. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, Pomerania, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, are all terribly afflicted with the scurvy; and it is remarkable, that in Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, fevers are very common; but in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, there is scarce ever such a disease met with; though peripneumonies are very common in these places, as also diseases of the eyes and violent pains of the head. The Russians and Tartars are afflicted with ulcers, made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of what we call chilblains, but greatly worse; and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> and Lithuania there reigns a peculiar disease, called the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLICA_POLONICA">plica polonica</a>, so terribly painful and offensive, that scarce any thing can be thought of worse. The people of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> are very subject to the gout and rheumatism: they are more infested also with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> and fleas than any other people in the world, and they have a peculiar disease which they call cremor. The Germans, in different parts of the empire, are subject to different reigning diseases. In Westphalia, they are peculiarly troubled with peripneumonies and the itch. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, Franconia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and other places thereabout, they are very liable to fevers of the burning kind, to bleedings at the nose, and other hemorrhages; and to the gout, inflammations, and consumptions. In Misnia they have purple fevers; and the children are peculiarly infested with worms. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, and Thrace, there are very few diseases; and what they have are principally burning fevers and frenzies. At Constantinople the plague often rages; and in the West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, malignant fevers, and the most terrible colics. These diseases are called endemic. Diseases of Horses. See Farriery. Diseases of Dogs. See Dogs. Diseases of Plants. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DISEMBOGUE. When a ship passes out of the mouth of some great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, they call it disemboguing. They say also of a river, that at such a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or after it has run so many leagues, it disembogues itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

DISFRANCHIZING

Pages 285-285

among civilians, signifies the depriving a person of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges of a free citizen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subject.

DISGUISE

Pages 285-285

a counterfeit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. Persons doing unlawful acts in disguise are by our statutes sometimes subjected to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> penalties, and even declared felons. Thus, by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> act, persons appearing disguised and armed in a forest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> grounds enclosed, or hunting deer, or robbing a warren or a fish-pond, are declared felons.

DISH

Pages 285-285

in mining, is a trough made of wood, about 28 inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, four inches deep, and six inches wide; by which all miners <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> their ore. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any be taken selling their ore, not first measuring it by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s dish, and paying the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s duty, the seller forfeits his ore, and the buyer forfeits for every such offence 40s. to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the field <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>.

DISJUNCTIVE

Pages 285-285

something that separates <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disjoins. Thus, or, neither, &c. which in connecting a discourse, yet separate the parts of it, are called disjunctive conjunctions. DISK. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISC">Disc</a>.

DISLOCATION

Pages 285-285

the putting a bone out of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> by some violence, usually called by the physicians luxation. DISMISSION of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">BILL</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the plaintiff does not attend on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> fixed for the hearing, his bill is dismissed with costs. It may be also dismissed for want of prosecution, which is in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a non-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, if he suffers three terms to elapse without moving forward in the cause.

DISMOUNTING

Pages 285-285

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of unhorsing. Thus, to dismount the cavalry, the dragoons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, is to make them alight. To dismount the cannon, is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, and axletrees, so as to render them unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Horses are also dismounted when they are rendered unfit for service.

DISPARAGEMENT

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used for the matching an heir, &c. in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, below his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> or condition, or against the rules of decency. The word is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the privative particle <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>, and por, "equal."

DISPART

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, is the setting a mark upon the muzzle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thereabouts, of a piece of ordnance, so that a sight line taken upon the top of the base ring against the touch-hole, by the mark set on or near the muzzle, may be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the axis of the concave <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of doing this, is to take the two diameters of the base ring, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the dispart is to stand, and divide the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them into two equal parts, one of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the length of the dispart which is set on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> with wax or pitch, or fastened there with a piece of twine or marlin. By means of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> it may be done with all possible nicety.

DISPATCH

Pages 285-286

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> on some affair of state, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other business of importance, sent with care and expedition, by a courier express. The business of dispatches patches lies on the secretaries of state and their clerks. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> gives directions to his ministers abroad by dispatches. The word is also used for the packet or mail containing such letters. The French, during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV had a conseil des depeches, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of dispatches," held in the king's presence, at which the dauphin, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and four secretaries of state, assisted. DISPAUPER. A person suing in forma pauperis is said to be dispaupered, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> is ended, he has any lands or other estate fallen to him, or if he has any thing to make him lose his privilege. See the article Forma Pauperis.

DISPENSARY

Pages 286-286
or Dispensatory, denotes a book containing the method of preparing the various kinds of medicines used in pharmacy. Such are those of Bau- deron, Quercetan, Zwelfer, Charas, Bate, Mesue, Salmon, Lemery, Quincy, &c.; but the latest and most esteemed, besides the London and Edinburgh pharmacopoeias, is the Edinburgh New Dispensatory, being an improvement upon that of Dr Lewis's. Dispensary, or Dispensatory, is likewise a magazine or office for selling medicines at prime cost to the poor. The College of Physicians maintain three of these in London; one at the college itself in Warwick-lane; another in St Peter's alley, Cornhill; and a third in St Martin's lane. Dispensaries have also been established in several of the principal towns in Scotland and England; particularly in Edinburgh, Dundee, and Kelso; as also at Newcastle upon Tyne.

DISPENSATION

Pages 286-286

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the granting a license of doing some certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> that otherwise is not permitted.

DISPERSSION

Pages 286-287

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, is the same with the divergency of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Point of Disperession, in Dioptries, the point from which refracted rays begin to diverge, where their refraction renders them divergent. Disperession of Inflammation, in Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, is the removing the inflammation, and restoring the inflamed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> to its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state. Disperession of Mankind, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the world, was occasioned by the confusion of tongues, and took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the overthrow of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a> at the birth of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELEG">Peleg</a>; whence he derived his name: and it appears by the account given of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, Gen. chap. xi. 10—16. to have happened in the 101st year after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, and by the Samaritan computation in the 401st. However, various difficulties have been suggested by chronologers concerning the true era of this event. Sir John Marsham and others, in order to reconcile the Hebrew and Egyptian chronologies, maintain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of mankind before the birth of Peleg. Others, unable to find numbers sufficient for the plantation of colonies in the space of 101 years, according to the Hebrew computation, fix the dispersion towards the end of Peleg's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, thus following the computation of the Jews. Petavius assigns the 153d year after the flood; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> the 180th; and Usher, though he generally refers it to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Peleg's birth, in one place assigns the 131st after the flood for this event. Mr Shuckford supposes the dispersion to have been gradual, and to have commenced with the separation of mankind of some companies at the birth of Peleg, and to have been completed 31 years after. According to the calculation of Petavius, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> at the birth of Peleg amounted to 32,768: Cumberland makes them 30,000; Mr Mede states them at 7000 men, besides women and children: and Mr Whiston, who supposes that mankind now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> themselves in 400 years, and that they doubled themselves between the deluge and the time of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> in 60 years at a medium, when their lives were six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as they have been since, by his computation produces about 2389; a number much too inconsiderable for the purposes of separating and forming distinct nations. This difficulty induced Mr Whiston to reject the Hebrew and to adopt the Samaritan chronology, as many others have done; which, by allowing an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of 401 years between the flood and the birth of Peleg, furnishes, by the last-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of computation, more than 240,000 persons. As to the manner of the dispersion of the posterity of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> from the plain of Shinar, it was undoubtedly conducted with the utmost regularity and order. The sacred historian informs us, that they were divided in their lands, every one according to his tongue, according to his family, and according to his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, Gen. x. 5, 20, 31; and thus, as Mr Mede observes, they were ranged according to their nations, and every nation was ranged by their families; so that each nation had a separate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, and each family in every nation. The following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve to give a general idea of their respective settlements: Japbet, Noah's eldest son, had seven sons; viz. Gomer, whose descendants inhabited those parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> upon the Ægean <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and Hellespont northward, containing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, Pontus, Bithynia, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>. The Galatians, according to Josephus, were called Gomerai; and the Cimmerii, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, occupied this tract of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and from these Gomerians, Cimmerii, for Celts, Mr Camden derives our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons, who still retain the name Cymro or Cymru. Magog, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Japhet, was probably the father of the Scythians on the east and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the Euxine sea. Madai planted Media, though Mr Mede assigns <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> to his share. Javan was the father of the Grecians about <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, whose country lies along upon the Mediterranean sea; the radicles of Javan and Ionia being the same, viz. To Tubal and Mescech belonged Cappadocia and the country which lies on the borders of the Euxine sea; and from them, migrating over <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, it is supposed the Russians and Muscovites are descended. And Tiras occupied Thrace. The sons of Shem were five: Elam, whose country lay between the Medes and Mesopotamians, and was called by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> writers Elemais; and Josephus calls the Elamites the founders of the Persians: Ashur, who was driven out of Shinar by Nimrod, afterwards settled in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and there built <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a>, and other cities; Arphaxad, who gave name to the country which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> calls Arraphacitis, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Assyria, though Josephus makes him the father of the Chaldees; Lud who inhabited and gave name to the country of Lydia about Dispersion about the river Meander, remarkable for its windings, mankind in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; and Aram, the father of the Syrians. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>, the youngest son of Noah, had four sons; viz., <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSH">Cush</a>, whose posterity spread into the several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> over the borders of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Edom, into Arabia Felix, up to Midian and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIZRAIM">Mizraim</a>, the father of them who inhabited Egypt and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; Phut, to whom Bochart assigns the remaining part of Africa, from the lake of Tritonides to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, called Ligya; and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, to whom belonged the land of Canaan, whence the Phenicians derived their origin. Dr Bryant has advanced a new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> on this subject, and supported it with his usual acuteness and learning. He maintains, that the dispersion as well as the confusion of tongues was local, and limited to the inhabitants of the province of Babel; that the separation and distribution recorded to have taken place in the days of Peleg, Gen. x. 25, 31, 32, which was the result of divine appointment, occasioned a general <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a>; and that all the families among the sons of men were concerned in it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Shem, from which the Messiah was to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, was particularly regarded in this distribution: the portion of his children was near the place of separation; they in general had Asia to their lot; as Japhet had <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and Ham the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> continent of Africa. But the sons of Chus would not submit to the divine dispensation: they went off under the conduct of Nimrod, and seem to have been for a long time in a roving state. However, at last they arrived at the plains of Shinar; and having ejected Ashur and his sons, who were placed there by divine appointment, seized his dominions, and laid there the foundation of a great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>.
