in Fortification, called also foss and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>, a trench dug round the rampart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wall of a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCARP">scarp</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTERSCARP">counterscarp</a>. See FOR-

DITHYRAMBUS

Pages 300-300

DITHYRAMBUS, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, full of transport and poetical rage. This poetry owes its birth to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and to the transports of wine; and yet art is not quite exploded, but delicately applied to guide and restrain the dithyrambic impetuosity, which is indulged only in pleasing flights. Horace and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> tell us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> gave the name of dithyrambus to those verses wherein none of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rules <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> were observed. As we have now no remains of the dithyrambus of the ancients, we cannot say exactly what their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> was.

DITONE

Pages 300-300

in Music, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> comprehending two tones. The proportion of the sounds that form the ditone is $4:5$, and that of the semitone is $5:6$.

DITRIHEDRIA

Pages 300-300

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> expressive of crystals with twice three sides, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six planes; being formed of two trigonal pyramids joined base to base, without any intermediate prism. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ditrihedria are distinguished by the different figures of these pyramids. DITTANDER. See LEPIDIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DITTANY. See DICTAMNUS, BOTANY Index.

DITTO

Pages 300-300

in books of accounts, usually written D°, signifies the afore-mentioned. The word is corrupted from the Italian detto, "the said: as in our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-phrase, "the said premises," meaning the same as were afore- mentioned.

DITTON

Pages 300-301

HUMPHRY, an eminent mathematician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, May 29, 1675. Being an only son, and his father observing in him an extraordinary good capacity, determined to cultivate it with a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. For this purpose he placed him in a reputable private academy; upon quitting of which he at the desire of his father, though against his own inclination, engaged in the profession of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and began to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to preach some years; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he married a lady of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. But a weak <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, induced Mr Ditton to quit that profession. And at the persuasion of Dr Harris and Mr Whiston, both eminent mathematicians, he engaged in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; a science to which he had always a strong inclination. In the prosecution of this science, he was much encouraged by the success and applause he received: being greatly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> professors of it, and particularly by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, by whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and recommendation he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the new mathematical school in Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>; where he continued till his death, which happened in 1715, in the 40th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, much regretted by the philosophical world, who expected many useful and ingenious discoveries from his assiduity, learning, and penetrating genius. Mr Ditton published several mathematical and other tracts, as below.—1. Of the Tangents of Curves, &c. Phil. Trans. vol. xxiii. 2. A Treatise on Spherical Catoptries, published in the Philos. Trans. for 1705; from whence it was copied and reprinted in the Acta Eruditorum 1707, and also in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. 3. General Laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a>; 8vo, 1705. Wolfius mentions this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and says that it illustrates and renders easy the writings of Galileo, Huygens, and the Principia of Newton. It is also noticed by La Roche, in the Memoires de Literature, vol. viii. page 46. 4. An <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>, containing the first Principles, Operations, and Applications, of that admirable method, as invented by Sir Isaac Newton, 8vo, 1706. This work, with additions and alterations, was again published by Mr John Clarke, in the year 1726. 5. In 1709 he published the Synopsis Algebraica of John Alexander, with many additions and corrections. 6. His Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">Perspective</a> was published in 1712. In this work he explained the principles of that art mathematically; and besides teaching the methods then generally practised, gave the first hints of the new method afterwards enlarged upon and improved by Dr Brook Taylor; and which was published in the year 1715. 7. In 1714, Mr Ditton published several pieces both theological and mathematical; particularly his Discourse on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">Resurrection</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; and The New <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a Discourse concerning the Ascent of Liquids, in exact Geometrical Figures, between two nearly contiguous Surfaces. To this was annexed a tract, to demonstrate the impossibility of thinking or perception being the result of any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and motion: a subject much agitated about that time. To this work also was added an advertisement from him and Mr Whiston, concerning a method for discovering the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, which it seems they had published about half a year before. This attempt probably cost our author his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; for although it was approved and countenanced by Sir Isaac Newton, before it was presented to the Board of Longitude, and the method has been successfully put in practice, in finding the longitude between Paris and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>; yet that board then determined against it; so that the disappointment, together with some public <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> (particularly in a poem written by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Swift), affected his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> so that he died the ensuing year, 1715. In an account of Mr Ditton, prefixed to the German translation of his Discourse on the Resurrection, it is said that he had published, in his own name only, another method for finding the longitude; but which Mr Whiston denied. However, Raphael Levi, a learned Jew, who had studied under Leibnitz, informed the German editor, that he well knew that Ditton and Leibnitz had corresponded upon the subject; and that DIV Ditton had sent to Leibnitz a delineation of a machine he had invented for that purpose; which was a piece of mechanism constructed with many <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> like a clock, and which Leibnitz highly approved of for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but doubted whether it would answer on ship board, on account of the motion of the ship.

DIUM

Pages 311-311

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a town of Chalcidice in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, near Mount <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOS">Athos</a>. Also a promontory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>.—A third Diium, a promontory of Euboea; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a town of that name in Euboea, near the promontory Cnemum, on the north-west side of the island, called also Dia.—A fourth Diium in Pieria of Macedonia, on the west side of the Sinus Thermaicus. Strabo and Livy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it on the borders of Pieria to the south, at the foot of Mount Olympus towards Thessaly. That it was a splendid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, appears from Polybius; who relates, that its gymnasium and wall were overthrown by the Aetolians. From which overthrow, however, it again recovered, Alexander adding new splendour to it, by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYSIPPUS">Lysippus</a>, and erected there in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the slain at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANICUS">Granicus</a>: an ornament which was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; who made it a colony, called Dionis.—A fifth Diium beyond Jordan, near Pella in the Piræa.

DIURNAL

Pages 312-312

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, something relating to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; in opposition to nocturnal, which regards the night.

DIVAL

Pages 301-301

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> nightshade, used by such as blazon by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and herbs instead of colours and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, for sable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>.

DIVALIA

Pages 301-301

in antiquity, a feast held among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, on the 21st <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Angeronia; whence it is also called Angeronalia.—On the day of this feast, the pontifices performed sacrifice in the temple of Voluptia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the goddess of joy and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; who, some say, was the same with Angeronia, and supposed to drive away all the sorrows and chagrins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

DIVAN

Pages 301-301

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> chamber <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> among the eastern nations, particularly the Turks.—The word is Arabic, and signifies the same with sofa in the Turkish dialect. There are two sorts of divans; that of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior, called the council of state, which consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers of the empire; and that of the grand vizir, composed of six other vizirs or counsellors of state, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and secretaries of state, for the distribution of justice. The word is also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in the private houses of the orientals. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> does not allow the receiving of visits in the inner parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, but only at the entry, in a divan contrived on purpose for ceremonies. Travellers relate wonders of the silence and expedition of the divans of the east. Divan-Beghi, the superintendant of justice in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is the last of the six ministers of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, who are all under the athemadouler or first minister. To this tribunal of the divan-beghi <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> appeals from sentences passed by the governors. He has a fixed stipend of 50,000 crowns for administering justice. All the sergeants, ushers, &c., of the court are in his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He takes cognizance of the criminal causes of the chams, governors, and other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords of Persia, when accused of any fault. There are divan-beghis not only at court and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, but also in the provinces and other cities of the empire. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a> is the sole rule of his administration of justice, which also he interprets at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He takes no cognizance of civil causes; but all differences arising between the officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> and between foreign ministers are determined by him.

DIVANDUROW

Pages 301-301

the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Maldives, and 24 from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, almost opposite to Cananor. DIVER. See Colymbus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DIVERGENT <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> DIVERGING <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">LINES</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, are those which constantly recede from each other. DIVERGENT Rays, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, are those which, going from a point of the visible object, are dispersed, and continually depart one from another in proportion as they are removed from the object: in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is opposed to convergent. See Optics.

DIVERSIFYING

Pages 301-301

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, is of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the orator; it is an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> essential to his character, and may fitly be called the subject of all his tropes and figures. Vossius lays <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> six ways of diversifying a subject. 1. By enlarging on what was briefly mentioned before. 2. By a concise enumeration of what had been insisted on at length. 3. By adding something new to what is repeated. 4. By repeating only the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> heads of what had been said. 5. By transposing the words and periods. 6. By imitating them.

DIVERSION

Pages 301-301

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, is when an enemy is attacked in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they are weak and unprovided, in order to draw off their forces from another place where they have made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> intend to make an irruption. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had no other way in their power of driving <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> out of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, but by making a diversion in attacking <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>.

DIVESTING

Pages 301-301

properly signifies undressing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stripping off one's garment; in contradistinction from investing. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, it is used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of surrendering or relinquishing one's effects. By a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of donation or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, the donor or seller is said to be disseised and divested of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in such a commodity, and the donee or purchaser becomes invested therewith. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">INVESTITURE</a>. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> is a general divestiture which the fathers and mothers make of all their effects in favour of their children.

DIVIDEND

Pages 301-301

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> proposed to be divided into equal parts. See ARITHMETIC, No. 14. DIVIDEND of Stocks is a share <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proportion of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of stocks erected on the public funds, as the South <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, &c., divided among and paid to the adventurers half yearly.

DIVINATION

Pages 301-302

the knowledge of things obscure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> future, which cannot be attained by any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> means. It was a received <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among the heathens, that the gods were wont to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> familiarly with some men, whom they endowed with extraordinary powers, and admitted to the knowledge of their councils and designs. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, Plutarch, Cicero, and others, divide divination into two sorts or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. natural and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>. The former was so called, because not attained by any rules or precepts of art, but infused or inspired into the diviner, without his taking any further care about it than to purify and prepare himself for the reception of the divine afflatus. Of this kind were all those who delivered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>, and foretold future events by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, without observing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> signs or accidents. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> species of divination was called artificial, because it was not obtained by immediate inspiration, but proceeded upon certain experiments and observations arbitrarily instituted, and mostly superstitious. Of this sort there were various kinds, as by sacrifices, entrails, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, cakes, flour, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, birds, lots, verses, omens, &c. In holy Scripture we find mention made of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> different kinds of divination. The first performed by the inspection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, stars, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>: it is supposed to be the practisers of this whom Moses calls pyn meonem, of pyn anan, "cloud," Deuter. chap. xviii. ver. 10. 2. Those whom the prophet calls in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Divination. which the Vulgate and generality of interpreters render augur. 3. Those who in the same place are called mecaesheph, which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and Vulgate translate "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> given to ill practices." 4. Such others whom Moses in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, ver. 11, calls hohober. 5. Those who consult the spirits called Python; or, as Moses expresses it in the same book, "those who ask questions of Python." 6. Witches or magicians, whom Moses calls judeoni. 7. Those who consult the dead, necromancers. 8. The prophet Hosea, chap. iv. ver. 12, mentions such as consult staves, which kind of divination may be called rhadomancy. 9. The last kind of divination mentioned in Scripture is hepatascopy, or the consideration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. Divination of all kinds was necessarily made an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> science, which naturally remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the priests and priestesses, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">magi</a>, the soothsayers, the augurs, the visionaries, the priests of the oracles, the false prophets, and other like professors, till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the coming of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the gospel, it is true, has dissipated much of this darkness; but it is more difficult than is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> conceived, to eradicate from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, a deep-rooted <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, even though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> be set in the strongest light, especially when the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> has been believed almost from the origin of the world; so we still find existing among us the remains of this Pagan superstition, in the following chimeras, which enthusiastic and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> men have formed into arts and sciences; though it must be owned, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the 18th century, that the pure doctrines of Christianity, and the spirit of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which become every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> more diffused, equally concur in banishing these visionary opinions. The vogue for these pretended sciences and arts, moreover, is past, and they can no longer be named without exciting <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> in all sensible people. By relating them here, therefore, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> them from their obscurity, we only <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to show their futility, and to mark those rocks against which the human mind, without the assistance of a pilot, might easily run. For the attaining of these supernatural qualifications, there are still existing in the world the remains of, 1. Astrology: a conjectural science which teaches to judge of the effects and influences of the stars; and to predict future events by the situation of the planets and their different aspects. It is divided into natural astrology, or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">meteorology</a>; which is confined to the foretelling of natural effects, as the winds, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, and snow, frosts and tempests. In this consists one branch of the art of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALMANACK">almanack</a>-makers; and by merely confronting these predictions in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> each day produces, every man of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> see what regard is to be paid to this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of astrology. The other part, which is called judicial astrology, is still far more illusive and rash than the former; and having been at first the wonderful art of visionaries, it afterwards became that of impostors; a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fate with all those chimerical sciences, of which we shall here speak. This art pretends to teach the method of predicting all sorts of events that shall happen upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, as well such as relate to the public as to private persons; and that by the same inspection of the stars and planets and their different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>.

DIVINE

Pages 303-303

something relating to God. The word is also used, figuratively, for any thing that is excellent, extraordinary, and that seems to go beyond the power of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and the capacity of mankind. In which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the compass, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a>, clocks, &c. are said to be divine inventions: <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> is called the divine author, the divine Plato; and the same appellation is given to Seneca: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> is called, "the divine old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>," divinus senex, &c.

DIVING

Pages 303-309

the art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of descending under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to considerable depths, and abiding there a competent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The uses of diving are very considerable, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> for pearls, corals, sponges, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a>-Fishing, &c. There have been various methods proposed, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> contrived, to render the business of diving more safe and easy. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> point is to furnish the diver with fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; without which, he must either make a short stay or perish. Those who dive for sponges in the Mediterranean, help themselves by carrying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> sponges dipt in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> in their mouths. But considering the small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of air that can be contained in the pores of a sponge, and how much that little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be contracted by the pressure of the incumbent water, such a supply cannot <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> subsist the diver. For it is found by experiment, that a gallon of air included in a bladder, and by a pipe reciprocally inspired and expired by the lungs, becomes unfit for respiration in little more than one minute of time. For though its elasticity be but little altered in passing the lungs, yet it loses its vivifying spirit, and is rendered effete. In effect, a naked diver, Dr Halley assures us, without a sponge, cannot remain above a couple of minutes enclosed in water, nor much longer with one, without suffocating; nor, without long practice, near so long; ordinary persons beginning to stifle in about half a minute. Besides, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the depth be considerable, the pressure of the water on the vessels makes the eyes blood-shotten, and frequently occasions a spitting of blood. Hence, where there has been occasion to continue long at the bottom, some have contrived <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, to circulate air down into a cavity, enclosing the diver as with armour, both to furnish air and to bear off the pressure of the water, and give leave to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to dilate upon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; the fresh air being forced down one of the pipes with bellows, and returning by the other of them, not unlike to an artery and vein. But this method is impracticable when the depth surpasses three fathoms; the water embracing the bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> so closely as to obstruct the circulation of the blood in them; and withal pressing so strongly on all the junctures where the armour is made tight with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, that, if there be the least defect in any of them, the water rushes in, and instantly fills the whole engine, to the great danger of the diver's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. It is certain, however, that people, by being accustomed to the water from their infancy, will at length be enabled, not only to stay much longer under water than the time above mentioned, but put on a kind of amphibious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, so that they seem to have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all their faculties as well when their bodies are immersed in water as when they are on dry <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nations are remarkable for this. According to the accounts of our late voyagers, the inhabitants of the South <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> are such expert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, that when a nail or any piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> was thrown overboard, they would instantly jump into the sea after it, and never failed to recover it, notwithstanding the quick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the metal. Even among civilized nations, many persons have been found capable of continuing an incredible length of time below water. The most remarkable instance of this kind is the famous Sicilian diver Nicola Pesce. The authenticity of the account, indeed, depends entirely on the authority of F. Kircher. He assures us that he had it from the archives of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>: but, notwithstanding this assertion, the whole hath so much of the marvellous in it, that we believe there are few who will not look upon it to have been exaggerated. "In the times of Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sicily (says Kircher), there lived a celebrated diver, whose name was Nicholas, and who, from his amazing skill in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, and his perseverance underwater, was surnamed the fish. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had from his infancy been used to the sea; and earned his scanty subsistence by diving for corals and oysters, which he sold to the villagers on shore. His long acquaintance with the sea, at last, brought it to be almost his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> element. He was frequently known to spend five days in the midst of the waves, without any other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> than the fish which he caught there, and ate raw. He often swam over from Sicily into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, a tempestuous and dangerous passage, carrying letters from the king. He was frequently known to swim among the gulls of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIPARI_ISLANDS">Lipari islands</a>, noway apprehensive of danger. "Some mariners out at sea, one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> observed something at some distance from them, which they regarded as a sea monster; but upon its approach it was known to be Nicholas, whom they took into their ship. When they asked him whither he was going in so stormy and rough a sea, and at such a distance from land, he showed them a packet of letters, which he was carrying to one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, exactly done up in a leather bag, in such a manner as that they could not be wetted by the sea. He kept them thus <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> for some time in their voyage, conversing, and asking questions; and after eating a hearty <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> with them, he took his leave, and, jumping into the sea, pursued his voyage alone. "In order to aid these powers of enduring in the deep, nature seemed to have assisted him in a very extraordinary manner: for the spaces between his fingers and toes were webbed, as in a goose; and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> became so very capacious, that he could take in, at one inspiration, as much breath as would serve him for a whole day. "The account of so extraordinary a person did not fail to reach the king himself; who commanded Nicholas to be brought before him. It was no easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to find Nicholas, who generally spent his time in the solitudes of the deep; but, at last, after much searching, Diving, searching, he was found, and brought before his majesty. The curiosity of this monarch had been long excited by the accounts he had heard of the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Charybdis; he now therefore conceived, that it would be a proper opportunity to have more certain information. He therefore commanded our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> diver to examine the bottom of this dreadful whirlpool; and as an incitement to his obedience, he ordered a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> cup to be flung into it. Nicholas was not insensible of the danger to which he was exposed; dangers best known only to himself; and therefore he presumed to remonstrate: but the hopes of the reward, the desire of pleasing the king, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of showing his skill, at last prevailed. He instantly jumped into the gulf, and was as instantly swallowed up in its bosom. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> below; during which time the king and his attendants remained on shore, anxious for his fate; but he at last appeared, holding the cup in triumph in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and making his way good among the waves with the other. It may be supposed he was received with applause when he came on shore: the cup was made the reward of his adventure; the king ordered him to be taken proper care of; and, as he was somewhat fatigued and debilitated by his labour, after a hearty meal he was put to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and permitted to refresh himself by sleeping. "When his spirits were thus restored, he was again brought to satisfy the king's curiosity with a narrative of the wonders he had seen; and his account was to the following effect. He would never, he said, have obeyed the king's commands, had he been apprised of half the dangers that were before him. There were four things, he said, which rendered the gulf dreadful, not only to men, but to fishes themselves. 1. The force of the water bursting up from the bottom, which required great strength to resist. 2. The abruptness of the rocks that on every side threatened destruction. 3. The force of the whirlpool dashing against those rocks. And, 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and magnitude of the polyous fish, some of which appeared as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a man; and which everywhere sticking against the rocks, projected their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> arms to entangle him. Being asked how he was able so readily to find the cup that had been thrown in, he replied, that it happened to be flung by the waves into the cavity of a rock against which he himself was urged in his descent. This account, however, did not satisfy the king's curiosity. Being requested to venture once more into the gulf for further discoveries, he at first refused: but the king, desirous of having the most exact information possible of all things to be found in the gulf, repeated his solicitations; and, to give them still greater <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, produced a larger cup than the former, and added also a purse of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. Upon these considerations the unfortunate diver once again plunged into the whirlpool, and was never heard of more." To obviate the inconveniences of diving to those who have not the extraordinary powers of the diver above mentioned, different instruments have been contrived. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of these is the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol8.html#article-DIVING_BELL">diving-<a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>; which is most conveniently made in form of a truncated cone, the smaller base being closed, and the larger open. It is to be poised with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>; and so suspended, that the vessel may sink full of air, with its open basis downward, and as near as may be in a situation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, so as to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> with the surface of the water all at once. Under this covercle the diver sitting, sinks down with the included air to the depth desired: and if the cavity of the vessel contain a ton of water, a single man may remain a full hour, without much inconvenience, at five or six fathoms deep. But the lower you go, still the included air contracts itself according to the weight of the water which compresses it: so that at 33 feet deep the bell becomes half full of water, the pressure of the incumbent water being then equal to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; and at all other depths the space occupied by the compressed air in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bell will be to the under part of its capacity filled with water, as 33 feet to the surface of the water in the bell below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> surface thereof. And this condensed air being taken in with the breath soon insinuates itself into all the cavities of the body, and has no ill effect, provided the bell be permitted to descend so slowly as to allow time for that purpose. One inconvenience that attends it, is found in the ears, within which there are cavities which open only outwards, and that by pores so small as not to give admission even to the air itself, unless they be dilated and distended by a considerable force. Hence, on the first descent of the bell, a pressure begins to be felt on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>; which, by degrees, grows painful, till the force overcoming the obstacle, what constrains these pores yields to the pressure, and letting some condensed air slip in, presently ease ensues. The bell descending lower, the pain is renewed, and again eased in the same manner. But the greatest inconvenience of this engine is, that the water entering it, contracts the bulk of air into a small compass, it soon heats and becomes unfit for respiration; so that there is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for its being drawn up and renewed. "The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of this bell, (says Professor Beckmann,) is generally assigned to the 16th century; and I am of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it was little known before that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. We read, however, that in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> divers used a kind of kettle, to enable them to continue longer under the water; but the manner in which it was employed is not clearly described. The oldest information which we have of the use of the diving-bell in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, is that of John Taisnier, who was born in Hainault in 1509, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. whom he attended on his voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. He relates in what manner he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and several thousand spectators, two Greeks let themselves down under water, in a large <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> kettle, with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and rise up again without being wet. It appears that this art was then new to the emperor and the Spaniards, and that the Greeks were caused to make the experiment in order to prove the possibility of it." "When the English in 1588, dispersed the Spanish fleet, called the Invincible Armada, part of the ships went to the bottom, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, on the western <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Scotland; and some of these, according to the account of the Spanish prisoners, contained great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. This information excited, from time to time, the avarice of speculators, and gave rise to several attempts..." tempts to procure part of the lost <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. In the year 1665, a person was so fortunate as to bring up some cannon, which, however, were not sufficient to defray the expenses. Of these attempts, and the kind of diving-bell used in them, the reader will find an account in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> printed at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> in 1669, and entitled *G. Sinelari Ars nova et magna gravitatis et levitatis*. In the year 1680, William Phipps, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, formed a project for searching and unloading a rich Spanish ship sunk on the coast of Hispaniola; and represented his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> in such a plausible manner, that King Charles II. gave him a ship, and furnished him with every thing necessary for the undertaking. He set sail in the year 1683; but being unsuccessful, returned again in great poverty, though with a firm conviction of the possibility of his scheme. By a subscriptions promoted chiefly by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>, the son of the celebrated Monk, Phipps was enabled, in 1687, to try his fortune once more, having previously engaged to divide the profit according to the twenty shares of which the subscription consisted. At first all his labour proved fruitless; but at last, when his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> was almost entirely exhausted, he was so lucky as to bring up, from the depth of six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> fathoms, so much treasure, that he returned to England with the value of two hundred thousand pounds <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Of this sum he himself got about sixteen, others say twenty thousand, and the duke ninety thousand pounds. After he came back, some persons endeavoured to persuade the king to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> both the ship and the cargo, under a pretence, that Phipps, when he solicited for his majesty's permission, had not given accurate information respecting the business. But the king answered, with much greatness of mind, that he knew Phipps to be an honest man, and that he and his friends should share the whole among them had he returned with double the value. His majesty even conferred upon him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, to show how much he was satisfied with his conduct. We know not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of Phipps's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>: but of the old figures of a diving-machine, that which approaches nearest to the diving-bell is in a book on fortification by Lorini; who describes a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> box bound round with iron, which is furnished with windows, and has a stool affixed to it for the diver. This ingenious contrivance appears, however, to be older than that Italian; at least he does not pretend to be the inventor of it. "In the year 1617, Francis Kessler gave a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of his water-armour, intended also for diving, but which cannot really be used for that purpose. In the year 1671, Witsen taught, in a better manner than any of his predecessors, the construction and use of the diving-bell; but he is much mistaken when he says that it was invented at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. In 1679 appeared, for the first time, Borelli's well known work *de motu animalium*; in which he not only described the diving-bell, but also proposed another, the impracticability of which was shewn by James Bernoulli. When Sturm published his *Collegium curiosum* in 1678, he proposed some hints for the improvement of this machine, on which remarks were made in the *Journal des Savans*." To obviate the difficulties of the diving-bell, Dr Halley contrived some further apparatus, whereby not only to recruit and refresh the air from time to time, but also to keep the water wholly out of it at any depth. The manner in which this was effected, he relates in the following words: "The bell I made use of was of wood, containing about 60 cubic feet in its concavity; and was of the form of a truncated cone, whose diameter at the top was three feet, and at the bottom five. This I coated with lead so heavy that it would sink empty; and I distributed the weight so about its bottom, that it would go down in a perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and no other. In the top I fixed a strong but clear glass, as a window, to let in the light from above; and likewise a cock to let out the hot air that had been breathed; and below, about a yard under the bell, I placed a stage which hung by three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, each of which was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with about one hundred weight to keep it steady. This machine I suspended from the mast of a ship by a sprit, which was sufficiently secured by stays to the mast head, and was directed by braces to carry it overboard clear of the ship's side, and to bring it again within board as occasion required. "To supply air to this bell when under water, I caused a couple of barrels of about 36 gallons each to be cased with lead, so as to sink empty; each of them having a bung-hole in its lowest parts to let in the water, as the air in them condensed on their descent; and to let it out again when they were drawn up full from below. And to a hole in the uppermost part of these barrels, I fixed a leathern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> or hose well liquored with bees wax and oil, and long enough to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> below the bung-hole, being kept down by a weight appended: so that the air in the upper part of the barrels could not escape, unless the lower ends of these hose were first lifted up. "The air-barrels being thus prepared, I fitted them with tackle proper to make them rise and fall alternately, after the manner of two buckets in a well; which was done with so much ease, that two men, with less than half their strength, could perform all the labour required; and in their descent they were directed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> fastened to the under edge of the bell, the which passed through rings on both sides the leathern hose in each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>; so that, sliding down by these lines, they came readily to the hand of a man who stood on the stage on purpose to receive them, and to take up the ends of the hose into the bell. Through these hose, as soon as their ends came above the surface of the water in the barrels, all the air that was included in the upper parts of them was blown with great force into the bell, whilst the water entered at the bung holes below, and filled them; and as soon as the air of one barrel had been thus received, upon a signal given, that was drawn up, and at the same time the other descended; and by an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> succession, furnished air so quick, and in so great plenty, that I myself have been one of five who have been together at the bottom in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten fathom water, for above an hour and a half at a time, without any sort of ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; and I might have continued there as long as I pleased, for any thing that appeared to the contrary. Besides, the whole cavity of the bell was kept entirely free from water, so that I sat on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> which was diametrically placed near the bottom, wholly dressed, with all my clothes on. I only observed, that it was necessary to be let down gradually at first, as about 12 feet at a time; and then..." Diving then to stop and drive out the air that entered, by receiving three or four barrels of fresh air before I descended further. But, being arrived at the depth designed, I then let out as much of the hot air that had been breathed, as each barrel would replenish with cool, by means of the cock at the top of the bell; through whose aperture, though very small, the air would rush with so much violence, as to make the surface of the sea boil, and to cover it with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> foam, notwithstanding the weight of the water over us. Thus I found that I could do anything that required to be done <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> under us; and that, by taking off the stage, I could, for a space as wide as the circuit of the bell lay the bottom of the sea so far dry, as not to be overshoes thereon. And, by the glass window, so much light was transmitted, that when the sea was clear, and especially when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> shone, I could see perfectly well to write or read; much more to fasten or lay hold on any thing under us that was to be taken up. And, by the return of the air-barrels, I often sent up orders written with an iron <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, on small plates of lead, directing how to move us from place to place as occasion required. At other times, when the water was troubled and thick, it would be as dark as night below; but in such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> I have been able to keep a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> burning in the bell as long as I pleased, notwithstanding the great expense of air necessary to maintain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>.—By an additional contrivance, I have found it not impracticable, for a diver to go out of an engine to a good distance from it, the air being conveyed to him with a continued stream, by small flexible pipes; which pipes may serve as a clue, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> him back again when he would return to the bell." Plate CLXXVI. fig. 1 shows Dr Halley's diving-bell, with the divers at work. DBLKIRIMP represents the body of the bell. D, the glass which serves as a window. B, the cock for letting out the air which has been breathed. LM the seats. C, one of the air-barrels. P, H, two of the divers. F, another diver at a distance from the bell, and breathing through the flexible tube K.—This diver is supposed to have a head-piece of lead, made to fit quite close about his shoulders; this head-piece was capable of containing as much air as would supply him for a minute or two. When he had occasion for more air, he turned a cock at F, by which means a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> was opened with the air in the bell, and thus he could receive a new supply at pleasure. Since the invention of this diving machine, there has been one contrived by Mr Triewald, F. R. S. and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, which for a single person, is in some respects thought to be more eligible than Dr Halley's, and is constructed as follows: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> is the bell, which is sunk by lead weights DD hung to its bottom. This bell is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and tinned all over in the inside, which is illuminated by three strong convex lenses, G, G, G, with copper lids H, H, H, to defend them. The iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> or plate E serves the diver to stand on when he is at work; and is suspended at such a distance from the bottom of the bell by the chains F, F, F, that when the diver stands upright, his head is just above the water in the bell, where the air is much better than higher up, because it is colder, and consequently more fit for respiration. But as the diver must always be within the bell, and his head of course in the upper part, the inventor has contrived, that even there, when he has breathed the hot air as well as he can, he may, by means of a spiral copper tube, b c, placed close to the inside of the bell, draw the cooler and fresher air from the lowermost parts; for which purpose, a flexible leather tube, about two feet long, is fixed to the upper end of the copper tube at b; and to the other end of this tube is fixed an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> mouth-piece, by which the diver draws in the air. The greatest improvement, however, which the diving-bell ever received, or probably can receive, was from the late Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALDING">Spalding</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of his improved diving bell is represented in fig. 3. This construction is designed to remedy some inconveniences of Dr Halley's, which are very evident, and of very dangerous tendency. These are, 1. By Dr Halley's construction, the sinking or rising of the bell depends entirely on the people who are at the surface of the water; and as the bell even when in the water has a very considerable weight, the raising it not only requires a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of labour, but there is a possibility of the rope breaking by which it is raised, and thus every person in the bell would inevitably perish. 2. As there are, in many places of the sea, rocks which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at a considerable depth, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of which cannot possibly be perceived from above, there is danger that some of their rugged prominences may catch hold of one of the edges of the bell in its descent, and thus overset it before any signal can be given to those above, which would infallibly be attended with the destruction of the people in the bell; and as it must always be unknown, before <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, what kind of a bottom the sea has in any place, it is plain, that without some contrivance to obviate this last danger, the descent in Dr Halley's diving-bell is not at all eligible. How these inconveniences are remedied by Mr Spalding's new construction will be easily understood from the following description.—ABCD represents a section of the bell, which is made of wood; e, e, are iron hooks, by means of which it is suspended by ropes Q B F e, and Q A E R e, and Q S, as expressed in the figure; c, c, are iron hooks, to which are appended lead weights, that keep the mouth of the bell always parallel to the surface of the water, whether the machine taken altogether is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> or heavier than an equal bulk of water. By these weights alone, however, the bell would not sink; another is therefore added, represented at L; and which can be raised or lowered at pleasure, by means of a rope passing over the pulley a, and fastened to one of the sides of the bell at M. As the bell descends, this weight, called by Mr Spalding the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>-weight, hangs down considerably way below the mouth of the bell. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the edge of the bell is caught by any obstacle, the balance-weight is immediately lowered down so that it may rest upon the bottom. By this means the bell is lightened, so that all danger of oversetting is removed; for being lighter without the balance-weight, than an equal bulk of water, it is evident that the bell will rise, as well as the length of the rope affixed to the balance weight will allow it. This weight, therefore, will serve as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> to keep the bell at any particular depth which the divers may think necessary; or by pulling it quite up, the descent may be continued to the very bottom. By another very ingenious contrivance, Mr Spalding rendered it possible for the divers to raise the bell, with all the weights appended to it, even to the surface, or to stop at any particular depth, as they think proper; and thus they could still be safe, even though the rope designed for pulling up the bell was broke. For this purpose the bell is divided into two cavities, both of which are made as tight as possible. Just above the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> bottom EF, are small slits in the sides of the bell; through which the water entering as the bell descends, displaces the air originally contained in this cavity, which flies out at the upper orifice of the cock GH. When this is done, the divers turn the handle G, which stops the cock; so that if any more air was to get into the cavity AEFD, it could not longer be discharged through the orifice H as before. When this cavity is full of water, the bell sinks; but, when a considerable quantity of air is admitted, it rises. If, therefore, the divers have a mind to raise themselves, they turn the small cock g, by which a communication is made between the upper and under cavities of the bell. The consequence of this is, that a quantity of air immediately enters the upper cavity, forces out a quantity of the water contained in it, and thus renders the bell lighter by the whole weight of the water which is displaced. Thus, if a certain quantity of air is admitted into the upper cavity, the bell will descend very slowly; if a greater quantity, it will neither ascend nor descend, but remain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>; and if a larger quantity of air is still admitted, it will arise to the top. It is to be observed, however, that the air which is thus let out into the upper cavity must be immediately replaced from the air-barrel; and the air is to be let out very slowly, or the bell will rise to the top with so great velocity that the divers will be in danger of being shaken out of their seats. But, by following these directions, every possible accident may be prevented, and people may descend to great depths without the least <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of danger. The bell also becomes so easily manageable in the water, that it may be conducted from one place to another by a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> with the greatest ease, and with perfect safety to those who are in it. Instead of wooden seats used by Dr Halley, Mr Spalding made use of ropes suspended by hooks b b b; and on these ropes the divers may sit without any inconvenience. I and K are two windows made of thick strong glass, for admitting light to the divers. N represents an air-cask with its tackle, and OCP the flexible pipe through which the air is admitted to the bell. In the ascent and descent of this cask the pipe is kept down by a small weight appended, as in Dr Halley's machine. R is a small cock by which the hot air is discharged as often as it becomes troublesome. Fig. 4. is a representation of the whole diving apparatus, which it is hoped will be readily understood without any further explanation. Two air-barrels are represented in this figure; but Mr Spalding was of opinion, that one capable of containing 30 gallons is sufficient for an ordinary machine. We are told of another method put in practice by a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. He has contrived a large case of strong leather, perfectly water-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, which may hold about half a hogshead of air. This is so contrived, that when he shuts himself up in this case, he may walk at the bottom of the sea, and go into any part of a wrecked vessel, and deliver out the goods.—This method, we are told, he has practised for many years and has thus acquired a large fortune. It would be a considerable improvement on this machine to condense the air in it as much as possible before the diver descended; as he would thus be furnished with an atmosphere endowed with elasticity sufficient to resist the weight of the water, which otherwise would squeeze his case into much less room than it originally took up. The condensed air also would serve for respiration a much longer time than that which is in its ordinary state. See the article Diving, in the Supplement. Diving-Bladder, a machine invented by Borelli, and by him preferred, though without any good reason, to the diving-bell. It is a globular vessel of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or copper, about two feet in diameter, which contains the diver's head. It is fixed to a goat's skin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> exactly fitted to his person. Within the vessel are pipes; by means of which a circulation of air is contrived; and the person carries an air-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> by his side by which he can make himself heavier or lighter, as fishes do by contracting or dilating their air-bladder. By this means he thought all the objections to which other diving machines are liable were entirely obviated, and particularly that of want of air; the air which had been breathed, being, as he imagined, deprived of its noxious qualities by circulating through the pipes. These advantages, however, it is evident, are only imaginary. The diver's limbs, being defended from the pressure of the water only by a goat's skin, would infallibly be crushed, if he descended to any considerable depth; and from the discoveries now made by Dr Priestley and others, it is abundantly evident, that air, which is once rendered foul by breathing, cannot in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> be restored by circulation through pipes. Concerning the use of copper machines in general, Mr Spalding favoured us with the following curious observation, namely, That when a person has breathed in them a few minutes, he feels in his mouth a very disagreeable brassy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, which continues all the time he remains in the vessel; so that, on this account, copper seems by no means an eligible material. This taste most probably arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the alkaline effluvia of the body upon the copper; for volatile alkali is a strong <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLVENT">dissolvent</a> of this metal; but how these effluvia volatilize the copper in such a manner as to make the taste of it sensible in the mouth, it is not easy to say.

DIVINITY

Pages 309-309

properly signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and essence of God. DIVINITY is also used in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>.

DIVISIBILITY

Pages 309-310

that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> by which the particles of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in all bodies are capable of a separation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disunion from each other. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> and Cartesians hold divisibility to be an affection of all matter. The Epicureans, again, allow it to agree to every physical continuum; but they deny that this affection agrees to all bodies, for the primary corpuscles or atoms they maintain to be perfectly inseparable and indivisible. As it is evident that body is extended, so it is no less evident that it is divisible; for since no two particles of matter can exist in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it follows, that they are really distinct from each other; which is all that is meant by being divisible. In this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the least conceivable particle must still be divisible, since it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> consist of parts which will be really distinct. To illustrate this by a familiar instance. Let the least imaginable piece of matter be conceived lying on a smooth plain surface, it is evident the surface will not touch it everywhere; those parts, therefore, which it does not touch may be supposed separable from the others, and so on as far as we please; and this is all that is meant when we say matter is infinitely divisible. The infinite divisibility of mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is demonstrated thus geometrically. Suppose the line AC perpendicular to BF; and another, as GH, at a small distance from it, also perpendicular to the same line; with the centres CCC, &c. describe circles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the line GH in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> eee, &c. Now the greater the radius AC is, the less is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> eH. But the radius may be augmented in infinitum; so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, therefore, the part eH may be divided into still less portions; consequently it may be divided in infinitum. All that is supposed in strict <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> (says Mr Maclaurin) concerning the divisibility of magnitude, amounts to no more than that a given magnitude may be conceived to be divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parts equal to any given or proposed number. It is true, that the number of parts into which a given magnitude may be conceived to be divided, is not to be fixed or limited, because no given number is so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> but a greater may be conceived and assigned; but there is not, therefore, any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of supposing the number of parts actually infinite; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> some have drawn very abstruse consequences from such a supposition, yet geometry ought not to be loaded with them. How far matter may actually be divided, may in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be conceived from hence, that a piece of wire gilt with so small a quantity as eight grains of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, may be drawn out to a length of 13,000 feet, the whole surface of it still remaining covered with gold. We have also a surprising instance of the minuteness of some parts of matter from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and vision. Let a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> be lighted, and placed in an open plain, it will then be visible two miles round; and consequently, was it placed two miles above the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, it would fill with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> particles a sphere whose diameter was four miles, and that before it had lost any sensible part of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. A quantity of vitriol being dissolved, and mixed with 9000 times as much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, will tinge the whole; consequently will be divided into as many parts as there are visible portions of matter in that quantity of water. There are perfumes, which, without a sensible diminution of their quantity, shall fill a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> space with their odoriferous particles; which must therefore be of an inconceivable smallness, since there will be a sufficient number in every part of that space sensibly to affect the organ of smelling. Dr Keill demonstrates, that any particle of matter, how small soever, and any finite space, how large soever, being given, it is possible for that small particle of matter to be diffused through all that space, and to fill it in such a manner, as that there shall be no pore in it whose diameter shall exceed any given line. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> objections against the divisibility of matter in infinitum are, That an infinite cannot be contained by a finite; and that it follows from a divisibility in infinitum, either that all bodies are equal, or that one infinite is greater than another. But the answer to these is easy; for the properties of a determined quantity are not to be attributed to an infinite considered in a general sense; and who has ever proved that there could not be an infinite number of infinitely small parts in a finite quantity, or that all infinities are equal? The contrary is demonstrated by mathematicians in innumerable instances. See the article INFINITY, and 'S Gravesande Elem. Mathem. l. i. c. 4.

DIVISION

Pages 311-311

in *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>*. See *ARITHMETIC*, No. 11. **Divisions of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">Army</a>**, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, the several brigades and squadrons into which it is cantoned. **Divisions of a Battalion**, are the several platoons into which it is divided in marching <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> firing, each of which is commanded by an officer. **Division**, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> affairs, a select <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ships in a fleet or squadron of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, distinguished by a particular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> or pendant, and usually commanded by a general officer. A squadron is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ranged into three divisions, the commanding officer of which is always stationed in the centre. When a fleet consists of 60 sail of the line, that is, of ships having at least 60 cannon each, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> divides it into three squadrons, each of which has its divisions and commanding officers. Each squadron has its proper colours, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the admiral who commands it, and every division its proper mast. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flag denotes the first division of France; the white and blue the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; and the third is characterized by the blue. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the first admiral, or the admiral of the fleet, displays the union flag at the main-topmast head; next follows the white flag with St George's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>; and afterwards the blue. The private ships carry pendants of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> with their respective squadrons at the mast of their particular divisions; so that the last ship in the division of the blue squadron carries a blue pendant at her mizen-topmast head. [Merged from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">MECHANICAL</a> DIVISION, p.310] l Division signifies that separation which is occasioned in the parts of a body by help of mechanical instruments.—The mechanical division of bodies does indeed separate them into smaller, homogeneous, similar parts; but this separation cannot extend to the primary integrant molecules of any body; and consequently is incapable of breaking what is properly called their aggregation; also, no union is formed betwixt the divided and dividing bodies, in which respect division essentially differs from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>. Division is not properly a chemical operation. It is only employed preparatorily to facilitate other operations, and particularly solution.
