For this purpose it is very useful, as it increases the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of surface, and consequently the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of contact of any body.—Different methods are used to divide bodies according to their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Those which are tenacious and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, as horns and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, require to be cut, rasped, or filed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">Metals</a>, because of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a>, require the same treatment: but as they are also fusible, they may be quickly and conveniently reduced into grains small enough for most operations, by pouring them, when melted, into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. All brittle bodies may be reduced conveniently into fine parts by being bruised in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> with a pestle. Very hard bodies, such as glass, crystals, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, particularly those of the vitrifiable kind, before they are pounded, ought to be plunged when <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot into water, by which they are split and cracked, and rendered more easily pulverable. Bodies of this kind may also be bruised or ground by means of a hard and flat <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, upon which the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is to be put, and bruised by another hard stone so small as to be held and moved upon the larger stone with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The larger stone is called a porphyry, from its being generally of that kind of stone; and the operation is called porphyritzation. Instead of porphyritzation, a mill may be used, composed of a hard grit millstone, moving round upon another stone of the same kind, which must be fixed: in the upper stone is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> or channel, through which the matter to be ground passes. By this method a substance may be more quickly reduced to a fine powder than by porphyritzation. But these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> can be only employed for considerable quantities of matter. These methods of mechanically dividing bodies are attended attended with some practical inconveniences; the most considerable of which is, that some parts of the dividing instruments are always struck off, and mixed with the matter to be divided. This may greatly affect the operations. For instance, instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> furnish metallic colouring particles, and copper is very prejudicial to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Porphyry is coloured by a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> matter, which injures the colour of crystal glasses, enamels, and porcelains made with matters ground upon this stone. These matters therefore must be cleansed after their porphyritization, or else no instruments capable of injuring the intended operations ought to be employed. Thus, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of all medicines to be taken internally, no copper instruments, as mortars, pestles, &c. ought to be used; those made of iron are preferable; and, instead of porphyries, mortars, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> stones and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a> made of hard and white stones, ought to be employed for substances which are to enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of enamels, crystal glass, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, the whiteness of which is a most necessary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>.

DIVODURUM

Pages 311-311

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a town of the Mediomatrici, in Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>; situated on the Moselle, on the spot where now <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a> stands; now a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lorraine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6°. N. Lat. 49°. 16'.

DIVORCE

Pages 311-312

a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the bond of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. See *MARRIAGE*, and *<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">LAW</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>*. Divorce is of two kinds: the one à vinculo matrimoni, which alone is properly divorce; the other, à mensa et thoro, "a separation from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> and board." The woman divorced à vinculo matrimoni receives all again that she brought with her: the other has a suitable separate maintenance allowed her out of her husband's effects. The first only happens through some essential impediment, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> within the degrees forbidden, pre-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, impotency, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, &c. of which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a> the canon law allows 14, comprehended in these verses: ``` <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">Error</a>, conditio, volum, cognatio, crimen, Cultus, disparitas, vis, ordo, ligamen, honestas, Si sis affinis, si forte core nequibus, Si parochi et duplicis deict presentia testis, Raptave sit <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULIER">mulier</a>, nec parti reddita tua. ``` Divorce is a spiritual judgment, and therefore is passed in the spiritual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Under the old law, the woman divorced was to have of her husband a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, as St Jerome and Josephus testify, to this effect: I <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, that hereafter I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> lay no claim to thee; which was called a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of divorce. Divorce was allowed of in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> latitude both among the Pagans and Jews. At Rome, barrenness, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, madness, and banishment, were the ordinary causes of divorce. Spurius Carvilius, between 500 and 600 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of Rome, under the consulship of M. Attius and P. Valerius, was the first who put away his wife because she was barren; though Plutarch, in his Roman Questions, maintains, that Domitian was the first who permitted divorce. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> afterwards added <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of chastity, and the profession of a monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as valid reasons of divorce. The Roman lawyers distinguish between *repudium* and *divortium*; making the former to be the breaking of a contract or espousal, and the latter separation after matrimony. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> enacted a severe law, which suffered not a wife to leave her husband, but gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> off his wife, either upon poisoning her children, counterfeiting his private keys, or for the crime of adultery; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the husband on any other occasion put her away, he ordered one moiety of his estate for the wife, and the other to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>: besides an atonement to the gods of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. However, in later times, the women as well as the men might sue a divorce. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of divorcing was by sending a bill to the woman, containing the reasons of separation, and the tender of all her goods which she brought with her; and this was called repudium mittens; or else it was performed in her presence, and before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> witnesses, and accompanied with the formalities of tearing the writings, refunding the portion, taking away the keys, and turning the woman out of doors. The Grecian laws concerning divorces were different: The Cretans allowed divorce to any man that was afraid of having too many children. The Spartans seldom divorced their wives; and it was extremely scandalous for a woman to depart from her husband. The Athenians allowed divorce on very small grounds, by a bill, containing the reason of the divorce, and approved, if the party appealed, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; and women also were allowed to leave their husbands on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> occasions. Persons divorcing their wives were obliged to return their portions; otherwise, the Athenian laws obliged them to pay <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> oboli a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> for alimony. The terms expressing the separation of men and women from each other were different; the men were said ἀποτρίβειν or ἀπολύειν, to dismiss their wives; but wives, ἀπολύειν, to leave their husbands. "The law of Moses (Mr Paley observes), for reasons of local expediency, permitted the Jewish husband to put away his wife; but whether for every cause, or for what cause, appears to have been controverted amongst the interpreters of those times. Christ, the precepts of whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> were calculated for more general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and observation, revokes this permission, as given to the Jews 'for their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of heart,' and promulgates a law which was thenceforward to confine divorces to the single cause of adultery in the wife: 'Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery; and whoso marrieth her which is put away, doth commit adultery,' Mat. xix. 9. "Inferior causes may justify the separation of husband and wife, although they will not authorize such a dissolution of the marriage contract as would leave either at liberty to marry again: for it is that liberty in which the danger and mischief of divorces generally consist. The law of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in conformity to our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>, confines the dissolution of the marriage contract to the single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of adultery in the wife; and a divorce even in that case can only be brought about by the operation of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, founded upon a previous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> in the spiritual court, and a verdict against the adulterer at common law: which proceedings taken together compose as complete an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the complaint as a cause can receive. It has lately been proposed to the legislature to annex a clause to these acts, restraining the offending party from marrying with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of her crime, who by the course of proceeding is always known and convicted; for there is reason to fear, that adulterous connections are often formed with the prospect of bringing them to this conclusion; at least, when the seducer has once captivated the affection of a married woman, he may avail himself of this tempting argument to subdue her scruples, and complete his victory; and the legislature, as the business is managed at present, assists by its interposition the criminal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the offenders, and confers a privilege where it ought to inflict a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. The proposal deserved an experiment; but something more penal, it is apprehended, will be found necessary to check the progress of this alarming depravity. Whether a law might not be framed, directing the fortune of the adulteress to descend as in case of her <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; reserving, however, a certain proportion of the produce of it, by way of annuity, for her subsistence (such annuity in no case to exceed a certain sum); and also so far suspending the estate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the heir, as to preserve the inheritance to any children she might bear to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriage, in case there was none to succeed in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their mother by the first: whether such a law would not render <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> virtue in higher life less vincible, as well as the seducers of that virtue less urgent in their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, I would recommend to the deliberation of those who are willing to attempt the reformation of this important but most incorrigible class of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for splendour, for expensive amusements and distinctions, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> found in that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of women who would become the subject of such a law, not less inordinate than their other appetites. A severity of the kind proposed applies immediately to that passion. And there is no room for any complaint of injustice, since the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> above stated, with others which might be contrived, confine the punishment, so far as it is possible, to the person of the offender; suffering the estate to remain to the heir, or within the family of the ancestor from whom it came, or to attend the appointments of his will. "Sentences of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> courts, which release the parties à vinculo matrimoni, by reason of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>, frigidity, consanguinity within the prohibited degrees, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> marriage, or want of the requisite consent of parents or guardians, are not dissolutions of the marriage contract, but judicial declarations that there never was any marriage; such impediment subsisting at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as rendered the celebration of the marriage rite a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> nullity. And the rite itself contains an exception of these impediments. The man and woman to be married are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>, 'if they know any impediment why they may not be lawfully joined together, to confess it:' and assured, 'that so many as are coupled together, otherwise than God's word doth allow, are not joined together by God, neither is their matrimony lawful:' all which is intended by way of solemn notice to the parties, that the vow they are about to make will bind their consciences and authorize their cohabitation only upon the supposition that no legal impediment exist." DIURETICS (from dux, by, and ura, urine,) medicines which provoke a discharge by urine. Such is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> drank plentifully; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine drank in a morning; alkaline salts of all kinds; <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, sal gemmæ, nitre, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, tartar, sal ammoniac, whey, sour <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, lemon juice, &c. Aqueous liquors are generally diuretic, especially if mixed with salt, and drank <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. Fermented liquors are the least diuretic of all; and the less so, as they are the fatter. Sharp thin sour wines, Rhenish, &c. as also acid spirits of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, salt, sulphur, alum, vitriol, &c. asparagus, bitter almonds, smallage, eryngium, eupatorium, sassafras, &c. are all diuretics.

DIVUS

Pages 312-313

DIVA, in antiquity, appellations given to men men and women who had been deified, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the gods. See Deification, &c. Hence it is, that on medals struck for the consecration of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> or empress, they give them the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of divus or diva: for example, DIVUS JULIUS. DIVO ANTONINO PIO. DIVO PIO. DIVO CLAUDIO. DIVA FAUSTINA AUG. &c.

DOBSON

Pages 313-313

WILLIAM, an eminent English <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> painter, born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1610. He served an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> with one Peck a stationer and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>-dealer; and owed his improvement to the copying some pictures of Titian and Van Dyck, whose manner he always retained. He had farther obligations to the latter of these artists; for it is said, that a picture of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> being exposed at a shop on Snow-hill, Van Dyck passing by was struck with it exceedingly; and inquiring after the author, found him at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> garret. Van Dyck had the generosity to equip him in a manner suitable to his merit. He presented him to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I, who took him under his protection, kept him with him at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his majesty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and not only sat to him several times for his picture, but caused the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, Prince Rupert, and most of the lords of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> to do so too. Mr Dobson, however, being somewhat loose and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> in his way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, was far from improving the many opportunities he had of making his fortune; and died very poor in 1647, at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in St Martin's Lane.

DOBUNI

Pages 313-313
or Boduni; an ancient people of Britain, who possessed the territory which now forms the counties of Oxford and Gloucester. Both the names of this British nation seem to have been derived from the low situation of a great part of the country which they inhabited: for both Duun and Bodun signify "profound" or "low," in the ancient language of Gaul and Britain. The Dobuni are not mentioned among the British nations who resisted the Romans under Julius Cæsar, which was probably owing to the distance of their country from the scene of action; and before the next invasion under Claudius, they had been so much oppressed by their ambitious neighbours the Cattivellani, that they submitted with pleasure to the Romans, in order to be delivered from that oppression. Cogidunus, who was at that time (as his name imports) prince of the Dobuni, recommended himself so effectually to the favour of the emperor Claudius, by his ready submission, and other means, that he was not only continued in the government of his own territories, but had some other states put under his authority. This prince lived so long, and remained so steadily a friend and ally to the Romans, that his subjects, being habituated to their obedience in his time, never revolted, nor stood in need of many forts or forces to keep them in subjection. This is certainly the reason that we meet with so few Roman towns and stations in the country anciently inhabited by the Dobuni. The Durocornovium of Antoninus, and the Corinium of Ptolemy, are believed by antiquaries to have been the same place, the capital of the Dobuni, and situated at Cirencester in Gloucestershire, where there are many marks of a Roman station. Clevum or Clevum, in the thirteenth iter of Antoninus, stood where the city of Gloucester now stands; and Abone, in the fourteenth iter, was probably situated at Avinton on the Severn. The country of the Dobuni was comprehended in the Roman province Britannia Prima. DOCETÆ (from δοκεῖν, to appear), in ecclesiastical history, the followers of Julius Cassianus, one of the Valentinian sect, towards the close of the second century, who revived a notion that had been adopted by a branch of the Gnostics, against whom St John, Ignatius, and Polycarp, had asserted the truth of the incarnation. They believed and taught, as their name imports, that the actions and sufferings of Jesus Christ were not in reality, but only in appearance.

DOCIMASIA

Pages 313-313

in Greek antiquity, a probation of the magistrates and persons employed in public business at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. It was performed publicly in the forum, where they were obliged to give account of themselves and their past <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> before certain judges. Among several questions proposed to them, we find the following: Whether they had been dutiful to their parents, had served in the wars, and had a competent estate?

DOCIMASTIC ART

Pages 313-313

a name given to the art of essaying, by operations in small, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of metallic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other matters which may be obtained from mineral or other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> bodies. See Refining and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>.

DOCIMENUM MARMOR

Pages 313-313

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of marble of a bright and clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, much used in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and sumptuous buildings, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and the like. It had its name from Docimenes, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, afterwards called Synna; near which it was dug, and from whence it was sent to Rome. It was accounted little inferior to the Parian in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, but not capable of so elegant a polish; whence it was less used by the statuaries, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in other smaller works. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian is said to have used this marble in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; and many of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> are constructed of the same materials.

DOCK

Pages 313-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Rumex, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Dock, in the manege, is used for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the dock of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s tail, which serves it for a cover. The French call the dock trosssequene. It is made fast by straps to the crupper, and has leathern thongs that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between his thighs, and along his flanks to the saddle straps, in order to keep the tail tight, and to hinder it from whisking about. Dock, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and deep trench formed on the side of a harbour, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> on the banks of a river; and commodiously fitted either to build ships or receive them to be repaired and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAM">bream</a>'d therein. These sort of docks have generally strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>-gates to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of the tide from entering the dock while the ship is under repair.—There are likewise docks of another kind, called wet docks, where a ship can only be cleaned during the recess of the tide, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the tide left her dry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when it again reaches her by the return of the flood. Docks of the latter kind are not furnished with the usual flood-gates. See the article Dock, Supplement. Dock-Yards, certain magazines containing all sorts of Dockyards of naval stores and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. In England, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> dock-yards are at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOLWICH">Woolwich</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a>. His majesty's ships and vessels of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> are generally moored at these ports during the time of peace; and such as want repairing are taken into the docks, examined, and refitted for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> dock-yards are governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>, resident at the port; who superintends all the masters of the officers, artificers, and labourers, employed in the dock-yard and ordinary. He also controls their payments therein; examines their accounts; contracts, and draw bills on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>-office to supply the deficiency of stores; and, finally, regulates whatever belongs to the dock-yard, maintaining due order in the respective offices. These yards are generally supplied from the northern crowns with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, pitch, tar, rosin, canvas, oak plank, and several other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. See the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> and fitting up of a dock-yard. See the article Dockyards in the Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>, a person who has passed all the degrees of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, and is empowered to teach or practise the same: thus we say, doctor in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, doctor in physic, doctor of laws. The establishment of the doctorate, such as now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among us, is ordinarily attributed to Inerius, who himself drew up the formulary. The first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of this kind was performed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, in the person of Bulgarus, who began to profess the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and on that occasion was solemnly promoted to the doctorat, i.e. installed juris utriusque doctor. But the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was soon transferred from the faculty of law to that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; the first instance whereof was given in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Lombard and Gilbert de la <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTREE">Portree</a>, the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> divines of those days, were created doctors in theology, sacrae theologiae doctor. Spelman takes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of doctor not to have commenced till after the publication of Lombard's sentences, about the year 1140; and affirms, that such as explained that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to their scholars were the first that had the appellation of doctors. Others go much higher, and hold Bede to have been the first doctor at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and John de <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEVERLEY">Beverley</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, which latter died in the year 721. But Spelman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not allow doctor to have been the name of any title or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in England till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John, about the year 1207. To pass doctor in divinity at Oxford, it is necessary the candidate have been four years bachelor of divinity. For doctor of laws, he must have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in the university to commence bachelor of law; five years after which he may be admitted doctor of laws. Otherwise, in three years after taking the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, he may take the degree of bachelor in law; and in four years more, that of L.L.D. which same method and time are likewise required to pass the degree of doctor in physic. At Cambridge, to take the degree of doctor in divinity, it is required the candidate have been seven years bachelor of divinity: Though in several of the colleges the taking of the bachelor of divinity's degree is dispensed with, and they may go out per saltum. To commence doctor in laws, the candidate must have been five years bachelor of law, or seven years master of arts. To pass doctor in physic, he must have been bachelor in physic five years, or seven years master of arts. A doctor of the civil law may <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> jurisdiction, though a layman, stat. 37 Hen. VII. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 17, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 4. Doctor of the Law, a title of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> among the Jews. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may so say, of this order, was performed by putting a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> book, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; which is what some authors imagine our Saviour had in view, Luke xi. 52, when, speaking of the doctors of the law, he says, "Wo unto you, doctors of the law, for you have taken away the key of knowledge: you entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering you hindered." Doctor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, a title given to certain of the fathers whose doctrines and opinions have been the most generally followed and authorized. We usually reckon four doctors of the Greek church, and three of the Latin. The first are, St Athanasius, St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, St Gregory Nazianzen, and St Chrysostom. The latter are St Jerome, St Augustine, and Gregory the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. In the Roman breviary there is a particular office for the doctors. It only differs from that of the confessors, by the anthem of the Magnificat, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>. Doctor, is also an appellation adjoined to several specific epithets, expressing the merit of some of the schoolmen: thus, Alexander Hales is called the irrefragable doctor; Thomas Aquinas, the angelic doctor; St Bonaventure, the seraphic doctor; John Duns Scotus, the subtile doctor; Raimond Lully, the illuminated doctor; Roger <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, the admirable doctor, &c. Doctor, (διδάσκαλος), in the Greek church, is a particular officer, appointed to interpret <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the scriptures. He who interprets the gospels, is called doctor of the Gospel; he who interprets St Paul's Epistles, doctor of the Apostles; he who interprets the Psalms, doctor of the Psalter. Doctors Commons. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Civilians. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCUMENT">Document</a>, in Law, some written monument produced in any thing asserted. Dodartia, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Personatae. See Botany Index. Dodd, Dr William, an unfortunate English divine, eldest son of the Rev. William Dodd, many years <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURNE">Bourne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, was born May 29, 1729. He was sent, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16, to the university of Cambridge; and admitted in the year 1745 a sizer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>. In 1749-50 he took the degree of B.A. with great honour, being upon that occasion in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of wranglers. Leaving the university, he imprudently married a Miss <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Perkins in 1751, was ordained a deacon the same year, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in 1753, and soon became a celebrated and popular preacher. His first preferment was the lectureship of West-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>. In 1754 he also was chosen lecturer of St Olave's, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HART">Hart</a>-street; and in 1757 took the degree of M.A. at Cambridge. On the foundation of the Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a> in 1758, he was a strenuous supporter of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, and soon after became preacher at the chapel of it. By the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Bishop Squire, he in 1763 obtained a prebend of Brecon, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> friends procured himself to be appointed one of of the king's chaplains; soon after which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Chesterfield committed to his care. In 1766 he went to Cambridge and took the degree of LL.D. At this period, the estimation in which he was held by the world was sufficient to give him the expectations of preferment, and hopes of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and honours; and these he might probably have acquired had he possessed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> portion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. But, impatient of his situation, and eager for advancement, he rashly fell upon means which in the end were the occasion of his ruin. On the living of St George, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>, becoming vacant, he wrote an anonymous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>'s lady, offering 3000 guineas, if by her assistance he was promoted to it. This being traced to him, complaint was immediately made to the king, and Dr Dodd was dismissed with disgrace from his office of chaplain. From this period he lived neglected, if not despised; and his extravagance still continuing, he became involved in difficulties, which tempted him to forge a bond from his late pupil <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Chesterfield, Feb. 4, 1777, for 4200l. which he actually received: but being detected, he was tried at the Old Bailey, found guilty, and received <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and in spite of every application for mercy, was executed at Tyburn, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 27, 1777. Dr Dodd was a voluminous writer, and possessed considerable abilities, with little judgment and much vanity. An accurate list of his various writings is prefixed to his "Thoughts in Prison," edit. 1781. DODDER. See CUSCUTA, Botany Index.

DODDRIDGE

Pages 315-315
PHILIP, D.D., an eminent Presbyterian minister, was the son of Daniel Doddridge an oilman in London, where he was born on the 26th of June 1702; and having completed the study of the classics in several schools, was in 1719 placed under the tuition of the reverend Mr John Jennings, who kept an academy at Kilworth in Leicestershire. He was first settled as a minister at Kilworth, where he preached to a small congregation in an obscure village; but, on Mr Jennings's death, succeeded to the care of his academy; and soon after was chosen minister of a large congregation of Dissenters at Northampton, to which he removed his academy, and where the number of his pupils increased. He instructed his pupils with the freedom and tenderness of a father; and never expected nor desired that they should blindly follow his sentiments, but encouraged them to judge for themselves. He checked any appearance of bigotry and uncharitableness, and endeavoured to cure them by showing what might be said in defence of those principles they disliked. He died at Lisbon, whither he went for the recovery of his health; and his remains were interred in the burying-ground belonging to the British factory there, and a handsome monument was erected to his memory in the meeting-house at Northampton, at the expense of the congregation, on which is an epitaph written by Gilbert West, Esq. He wrote, 1. Free Thoughts on the most probable means of reviving the Dissenting Interest. 2. The Life of Colonel James Gardiner. 3. Sermons on the Education of Children. 4. The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul. 5. The Family Expositor, in 6 vols. 8vo. &c. And since the author's death, a volume of his hymns has been published, and his Theological Lectures. Several of his works have been translated into Dutch, German, Doddridge and French.

DODECAGON

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a regular polygon consisting of twelve equal sides and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>.

DODECAHEDRON

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">platonic</a> bodies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> regular solids, contained under twelve equal and regular pentagons.

DODECANDRIA

Pages 315-315

(from δωδεκα, twelve, and ἄνθος, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>); the name of the eleventh class in Linnaeus's sexual system, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> with hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, that, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, have twelve stamens <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs. This class, however, is not limited with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stamens. Many genera have sixteen, eighteen, and even nineteen, stamens; the essential character seems to be, that in the class in question, the stamens, however numerous, are inserted into the receptacle; whereas in the next class, icosandra, which is as little determined in point of number as the present, they are attached to the inside of the calyx or flower-cup. The orders of this class, which are six, are founded upon the number of the styles, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> organs. A-sarabaceae, mangostan, storax, purple loosestrife, wild Syrian rue, and purslain, have only one style; agrimony and heliocarpus have two; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> thorny plant, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> rocket, three; glinus, five; illicium, eight; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEEK">leek</a>, twelve.

DODECAS

Pages 315-315

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dodecandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DODECATHEON

Pages 315-315

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 21st order, Preciae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DODO. See Didus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index.

DODONA

Pages 315-316

a town of Thesprotia in Epirus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> (according to others) in Thessaly. There was in its neighbourhood a celebrated oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. The town and temple of the god were first built by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, after the universal deluge. It was supposed to be the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> oracle of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and according to the traditions of the Egyptians mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, it was founded by a dove. Two <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> doves, as he relates, took their flight from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; one of which flew to the temple of Jupiter <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, and the other to Dodona, where with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> they acquainted the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that Jupiter had consecrated the ground, which in future would give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>. The extensive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> which surrounded Jupiter's temple was endowed with the gift of prophecy; and oracles were frequently delivered by the sacred oaks and the doves which inhabited the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. This fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the oracular power of the doves is explained by Herodotus, who observes that some Phoenicians carried away two priestesses from Egypt, one of which went to fix her residence at Dodona, where the oracle was established. It may farther be observed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> might have been founded upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> meaning of the word ἀπάτη, which signifies doves in most parts of Greece, while in the dialect of the Epirots it implies old women. In ancient times the oracles were delivered by the murmuring of a neighbouring fountain; but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was afterwards changed. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">Large</a> kettles were suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> near a brazen statue, which held a lash in its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blew strong, the status DODONÆA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DODONIAN

Pages 316-316

(Dodonæus), in antiquity, an epithet given to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, because he was worshipped in a temple built in the forest of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>, where was the most famous, and (it is said) the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> oracle of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. See DODONA.

DODONIDES

Pages 316-316

the priestesses who gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>. According to some traditions the temple was originally inhabited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> daughters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, who nursed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. Their names were Ambrosia, Eudora, Pasithoe, Pytho, Pleixaure, Coronis, Tythe <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tyche. In the latter ages the oracles were always delivered by three old women; which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was first established when Jupiter enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of Dione, whom he permitted to receive divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> in his temple at Dodona. The Boeotians were the only people of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> who received their oracles at Dodona from men, for reasons which Strabo, l. 9. fully explains.

DODRANS

Pages 316-316

in antiquity, three-fourths of the as. See the article As.

DODSLEY

Pages 316-316

ROBERT, an eminent bookseller, and ingenious writer, born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, in the year 1703. He was not indebted to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> for his literary fame, being originally a very <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>; but his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> genius, and early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, soon elevated him to a superior station. He wrote an elegant little satirical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> called The Toyzshop, which was acted with applause in 1735, and which recommended him to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Mr Pope. The following year he produced the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> and Miller of Mansfield. The profits of these two farces enabled him to commence bookseller, and his own merit procured him eminence in that profession. He wrote some other dramatic pieces, and published a collection of his works in one vol. 8vo, under the modest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Trifles; which was followed by Public Virtue, a poem in 4to. Mr Dodsley was the author of the Economy of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which acquired considerable celebrity; but for this, it is supposed to have been indebted to the mistaken <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> prevailed of its being the production of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Chesterfield.

DODWELL

Pages 316-316

HENRY, a very learned controversial writer, born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, but of English <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, in 1641. He wrote an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of tracts; but his services were so little acknowledged, that Bishop Burnet and others accuse him of doing more hurt than good to the cause of Christianity, by his indiscreet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of paradoxes and novelties, and thus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> himself to the scoffs of unbelievers. His pamphlet on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> gave rise to the well known controversy between Mr Collins and Dr Clark on that subject. He died in 1711.

DOESBURG

Pages 316-316

a town of the United Provinces, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guelderland. It is small, but well peopled, and very strong both by art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, having the river Yssel on one side, and a morass on the other, and is only to be approached by a narrow neck of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 55'. N. Lat. 52° 3'.

DOG

Pages 316-319

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, an animal remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> docility, fidelity, and affection for his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; which qualities mankind are careful to improve for their own advantage. These useful creatures <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> our houses, gardens, and cattle, with spirit and vigilance. By their help we are enabled to take not only beasts, but birds; and to pursue <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> both over <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and through the waters. In some northern countries, they serve to draw sledges, and are also employed to carry burdens. In several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and by the West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, dogs are eaten, and accounted excellent food. Nay, we have the testimony of Mr Forster, that dogs <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, exactly resembles mutton*. They were also used as food by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before them by the Greeks, as we learn from several treatises of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>. In the present times, their skins, dressed with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on, are used in muffs, made into a kind of buskins for persons in the gout, and for other purposes. Prepared in another way, they are used for ladies gloves, and the linings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a>, being thought to make the skin peculiarly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and smooth. The French import many of these skins from Scotland, under a small duty. Here, when tanned, they serve for upper leathers for neat pumps. Dogs skins dressed are exported under a small, and imported under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> duty. The French import from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of dogs hair, both white and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. The last is esteemed the best, and is worked up in the black <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of a particular kind of woollen cloth; but is not used, as many have supposed, in making of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, being entirely unfit for this purpose. With regard to the qualities of dogs, those bred in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> are justly reckoned superior to the dogs bred in any other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The swiftness of the greyhound is amazing; as are also the steadiness and perseverance of other hounds and beagles; the boldness of terriers in unearthing foxes, &c.; the sagacity of pointers and setting dogs, who are taught a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> by signs as intelligible to sportsmen as speech; and the invincible spirit of a bull dog, which can be quelled only by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.—All the nations in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> not only do <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to the superior qualities of the British dogs, but adopt our terms and names, and thankfully receive the creatures creatures as presents.—It is remarkable, however, that almost every kind of British dogs degenerates in foreign countries; nor is it possible to prevent this degeneracy by any art whatever. For the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the dog, see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANIS">Canis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Choosing of Dogs.—In order to choose a dog and bitch for good whelps, take care that the bitch come of a generous kind, be well proportioned, having large ribs and flanks; and likewise that the dog be of a good breed and young, for a young dog and an old bitch breed excellent whelps. The best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for hounds nitches, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bratches, to be lined in, are the months of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, February, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. The bitch should be used to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENNEL">kennel</a>, that she may like it after her whelping, and she ought to be kept warm. Let the whelps be weaned after two months old; and though it be some difficulty to choose a whelp under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> prove the best of the litter, yet some approve that which is last, and account him to be the best. Others remove the whelps from the kennel, and lay them severally and apart one from the other; then they watch which of them the bitch first takes and carries into her kennel again, and that they suppose to be the best. Others again imagine that which weighs least when it sucks to be the best: this is certain, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> whelp will prove the swifter. As soon as the bitches have littered, it is proper to choose them you intend to preserve, and drown the rest: keep the black, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, or of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; for the spotted are not much to be esteemed, though of hounds the spotted are to be valued. Hounds for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> are to be chosen by their colours. The white, with black ears, and a black spot at the setting on of the tail, are the most <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> to compose a kennel of, and of good scent and condition. The black <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HOUND">hound</a>, or the black tanned, or the all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>-coloured or all white: the true talbots are the best of the stronger line; the grizzled, whether mixed or unmixed, so they be shag-haired, are the best verminers, and a couple of these are proper for a kennel.—In short, take these marks of a good hound: That his head be a middle proportion, rather long than round; his nostrils wide, his ears large, his back bowed; his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, his hunches large, thighs well trussed, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">ham</a> strait, tail big near the reins, the rest slender; the leg big, the sole of the foot dry, and in the form of that of a fox, with large claws. Keeping Dogs in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>.—As pointers and spaniels, when good of their kinds and well broken, are very valuable to a sportsman, it is worth while to take some care to preserve them in health. This very much depends on their diet and lodging: frequent cleaning their kennels, and giving them fresh straw to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on, is very necessary; or, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> time, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> shavings, or sand, instead of straw, will check the breeding of fleas. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you rub your dog with chalk, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> and comb him once or twice a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, he will thrive much the better; the chalk will clear his skin from all greasiness, and he will be the less liable to be mangy. A dog is of a very hot <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: he should therefore never be without clean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> by him, that he may drink when he is thirsty. In regard to their food, carrion is by no means proper for them; it must hurt their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of smelling, on which the excellence of these dogs greatly depends. Barley <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, the dross of wheat flour, or both mixed together, with broth or skimmed <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, is very proper food. For change, a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of grease from which the tallow is pressed by the chandlers, mixed with flour, or sheep's feet well baked or boiled, are a very good diet: and when you indulge them with flesh, it should always be boiled. In the season of hunting your dogs, it is proper to feed them in the evening before, and give them nothing in the morning you intend to take them out except a little milk. If you stop for your own refreshment in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, you should also refresh your dogs with a little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and milk. It has been already observed that dogs are of a hot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; the greatest relief to them in the summer is twitch-grass or dog-grass, which is the same thing. You should therefore plant some of it in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where you can turn them into every morning: they will feed freely on it to be cured of the sickness they are subject to, and cured of any extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of blood: but unless the grass be of this sort, it will have no effect. Diseases of Dogs.—1. Bites and Stings. If dogs are bitten by any venomous creatures, as snakes, adders, &c., squeeze out the blood, and wash the place with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and urine; then lay a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> to it made of calamin, pounded in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, with turpentine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> wax, till it come to a salve. If you give your dog some of the juice of calamin to drink in milk, it will be good; or an ounce of treacle dissolved in some sweet wine. 2. Mange.—Dogs are subject to the mange from being fed too high, and allowed no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> or an opportunity of refreshing themselves with dog-grass; or by being starved at home, which will cause them to eat the vilest stuff abroad, such as carrion, or even <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>; or by want of water, and sometimes by not being kept clean in their kennel, or by foundering and melting in their grease. Either of these will heat the blood to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, which will have a tendency to make them mangy. The cure may be effected by giving <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> brimstone powdered fine, either in milk or mixed up with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and rubbing them well every day for a week with an ointment made of some of the brimstone and pork <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, to which add a small quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of turpentine. Or, boil four ounces of quicksilver in two quarts of water to half the quantity; bathe them every day with this water, and let them have some of it to lick till the cure is perfected. Or, a small quantity of trooper's ointment rubbed on the parts on its first appearance will cure it. It will also free lousy puppies from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>. Or, take two ounces of euphorbium; flour of sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> oil of bays, and soft <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, each four ounces. Anoint and rub your dog with it every other day; give him warm milk, and no water. The cure will be performed in about a week. The following receipt is also said to be efficacious. Take two handfuls of wild creases, and as much elecampane, and also of the leaves and roots of roerb and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, and two pounds of the roots of fourel; boil all these well together in lye and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>; strain the decoction, and put into it two pounds of gray soap, and when it is melted, rub the dog with it four or five days successively, and it will cure him. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">Poison</a>.—If you suspect your dog to be poisoned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUX_VOMICA">nux vomica</a> (the poison usually employed by the warreners, which causes convulsive fits and soon kills), the most effectual remedy, if immediately applied, is to give him a good deal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salt; to administer which, you may open his mouth, and put a stick across to prevent the shutting it, whilst you cram his throat full of salt, at the same time holding his mouth upwards; and it will dissolve so that a sufficient quantity will be swallowed to purge and vomit him. When his stomach is sufficiently cleared by a free passage obtained by stool, give him some warm broth frequently, to prevent his expiring from faintness; and he will recover. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>.—Dogs are very frequently troubled with worms; but more particularly whilst they are young. Anything bitter is so nauseous to these worms, that they are very often voided by taking two or three purges of aloes; or (which is the same thing) Scots pills, four or five being a dose for a large dog: this is to be repeated two or three times in a week. If this do not succeed, you may give him an ounce of powder of tin mixed up with butter, in three doses; which seldom fails to cure. Or, of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> savin, dried and rubbed to powder, give about as much as will lie on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> for a dose; which will entirely destroy worms and their seed. 5. Sore Feet.—A pointer ought not to be hunted oftener than two or three days in a week; and unless you take care of his feet, and give him good lodging as well as proper food, he will not be able to perform that through the season. You should therefore, after a hard day's hunting, wash his feet with warm water and salt; and when dry, wash them with warm broth, or beer and butter, which will heal their soreness, and prevent a settled stiffness from fixing. 6. Strains, Blows, or Small Wounds.—If your dog has received any little wounds by forcing through hedges, or gets any lameness from a blow or strain; bathe the wound or grieved <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with salt and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> vinegar (for warming it only evaporates the fine spirit); and when dry, if a wound, you may pour in a little friar's balsam, which will perform the cure sooner than any method hitherto experienced. 7. Coughs and Colds.—Dogs are very subject to a cough, with an extraordinary choking, which is thought to arise generally from a cold or some inward disorder; and probably it is often occasioned by their eating of fish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. To guard against it, order your servants to throw all such fish bones where the dogs cannot get at them. But if the disorder be from a cold, let bleeding be repeated in small quantities if necessary; but if it be what is called the distemper in dogs, and they appear to be very low in spirits, the bleeding is better omitted. Let meat broth, or milk broth warmed, be the principal part of his diet, using at the same time the following medicine. Take flour of sulphur, cold drawn linseed oil, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, of each an ounce; divide it into four doses, giving him one dose every other day, and let him have plenty of clean straw to lie on; or one spoonful of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> daily. Dog-Madness.—Of this there are no less than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sorts common among dogs. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> causes are, high feeding, want of exercise, fulness of blood, and costiveness. As for the two first, you must observe when you hunt them, that they should be better fed than when they rest; and let them be neither too fat nor too lean; but, of the two, rather fat than lean; by which means they will not only be preserved from madness, but also from the mange and scab: which diseases they will be subject to for want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, water, or exercise: but if you have but the knowledge to keep them in an even temper, they may live long and continue <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. As for water, they should be left to their own <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; but for exercise and diet, it must be ordered according to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, observing a medium. Give them once a week, especially in the heat of the year, five or six spoonfuls of salad oil, which will cleanse them: at other times, the quantity of a hazel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> of mithridate is an excellent thing to prevent diseases. It is also very good to bleed them under the tongue, and behind the ears. The symptoms of madness are many and easily discerned. When any dog separates himself contrary to his former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, becomes melancholy or droops his head, forbears eating, and as he runs snatches at everything; if he often looks upwards, and his stern at his setting on be a little erect, and the rest hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; if his eyes be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, his breath strong, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> hoarse, and he drivels and foams at the mouth; you may be assured he has this distemper. The seven sorts of madness are as follows; of which the two first are incurable. 1. The hot <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> madness. 2. The running madness. The animals labouring under these are peculiarly dangerous; for all things they bite and draw blood from will have the same temper; and they generally <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> on all they meet with, but chiefly on dogs. Their pain is so great it soon kills them.—The five curable madnesses are, 3. Sleeping Madness, so called from the dog's great drowsiness, and almost continual sleeping. This is caused by the little worms that breed in the mouth of the stomach, from corrupt humours, vapours, and fumes which ascend to the head; for cure of which, take six ounces of the juice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a>, two ounces of the powder of hartshorn burnt, and two drams of agaric; mix all these together in a little white wine, and give it the dog to drink in a drenching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. 4. Dumb Madness, lies also in the blood, and causes the dog not to feed, but to hold his mouth always wide open, frequently putting his feet to his mouth, as if he had a bone in his throat; to cure this, take the juice of black hellebore, the juice of spatula putrida, and of true, of each four ounces; strain them well, and put thereto two drachms of unprepared scammony, and being mixed well together, put it down the dog's throat with a drenching horn, keeping his head up for some time, lest he <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> it out again; then bleed him in the mouth, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> two or three veins in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>. It is said, that about eight drachms of the juice of an herb called hartshorn or dog's tooth, being given to the dog, cures all sorts of madness. 5. Lank Madness, is so called by reason of the dog's leanness and pining away. For cure, give them a purge as before directed, and also bleed them; but some say there is no cure for it. 6. Rheumatic or slavering madness, occasions the dog's head to swell, his eyes to look yellow, and he will be always slavering and drivelling at the mouth. To cure which, take four ounces of the powder of the roots of polipody of the oak, six ounces of the juice of fennel roots, roots; with the like quantity of the roots of mistletoe, and four ounces of the juice of ivy; boil all these together in white wine, and give it to the dog as hot as he can take it, in a drenching horn. 7. Falling madness, is so termed because it lies in the dog's head, and makes him reel as he goes, and to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down. For the cure, take four ounces of the juice of bryony, and the same quantity of the juice of peony, with four drachms of stavesacre pulverized; mix these together, and give it the dog in a drenching horn; also let him blood in the ears, and in the two veins that come down his shoulders; and indeed bleeding is necessary for all sorts of madness in dogs. When a dog happens to be bit by a mad one, there is nothing better than their licking the place with their own tongues, if they can reach it; if not, then let it be washed with butter and vinegar, made lukewarm, and let it afterwards be anointed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> turpentine; but, above all, take the juice of the stalks of strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> boiled in water, and bathe the place therewith; also wash him in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> water, or water artificially made salt; give him likewise a little mithridate inwardly in two or three spoonfuls of sack; and so keep him apart; and if you find him after some time still to droop, the best way is to hang him. Some have asserted their having cured several creatures that have been bit by mad dogs, with only giving them the middle yellow bark of buckthorn; which must be boiled in ale for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or cow, and in milk for a dog; but that it must be boiled till it is as bitter as you can take it. As to the preventive of worming dogs, see Worming. DOG-Dogs. See Canicula. DOG-Fish. See Squalus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. DOG-Bane. See Afoxynum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. DOG-Wood-Tree. See Piscidia, Botany Index.

DOGGER

Pages 319-319

a Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> vessel navigated in the German ocean. It is generally employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> fishery; being equipped with two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, viz. a mainmast and a mizen-mast, and somewhat resembling a ketch. See the Plates at the article Ship.

DOGMA

Pages 319-319

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> maxim, tenet, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> settled <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, particularly with regard to matters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>.

DOGMATICAL

Pages 319-319

something belonging to a doctrine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. A dogmatical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> is one who asserts things positively; in opposition to a sceptic, who doubts of every thing.

DOGMATISTS

Pages 319-320
