a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians, of which Dogmatists which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> was the first author. They are also called logici, "logicians," from their using the rules of logic in subjects of their profession. They laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> definitions and divisions; reducing diseases to certain genera, and those genera to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and furnishing remedies for them all; supposing principles, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> conclusions, and applying those principles and conclusions to particular diseases under consideration; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the dogmatists stand contradistinguished from empirics and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">methodists</a>. They reject all medicinal virtues, that they think not reducible to manifest qualities; but Galen hath <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago observed of such men, that they must either deny plain <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> assign but very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> reasons and causes of many effects they pretend to explain.

DOGTERS

Pages 319-319

in the English <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> works, a name given by the workmen to a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> found in the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> with the true alum rock, and containing some alum, though not near so much as the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> kind. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, which abounds greatly with the true alum rock, affords also a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of these doggers; and in some places they approach so much to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the true rock, that they are wrought to advantage.

DOLCE

Pages 320-320

CARLO, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> CARLINO, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1616, and was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Vignali. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was particularly fond of representing pious subjects, though he sometimes painted portraits; and his works are easily distinguished by the peculiar delicacy with which he perfected all his compositions, by a pleasing tint of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and by a judicious management of the chiaroscuro. His performance was remarkably slow; and it is reported that his brain was fatally affected by seeing Luca Jordana despatch more business in four or five hours than he could have done in as many months. He died in 1686.

DOLICHOS

Pages 320-320

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DOLLAR

Pages 320-320
or DALLER, a silver coin nearly of the value of the Spanish piece of eight, or French crown. Dollars are coined in different parts of Germany and Holland; and have their diminutions, as semi-dollars, quarter-dollars, &c. See Money Table.

DOLOMIEU

Pages 320-320

D. G. S. T. a late eminent French mineralogist and geologist. See Supplement. DOLPHIN. See Delphinus, Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Dolphin of the Mast, a peculiar kind of wreath, formed of plaited cordage, to be fastened occasionally round the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, as a support to the puddening, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the fore and main yards, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the rigging <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chains by which those yards are suspended should be <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> away in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; a circumstance which might render their sails useless at a season when their assistance is extremely necessary. See the article Puddening.

DOMAIN

Pages 320-320

the inheritance, estate, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> possession of any one. See Demesne.

DOMAR

Pages 320-320

JOHN, a celebrated French lawyer, born in 1625, who observing the confused state of the laws, digested them in 4 vols. 4to, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The Civil Laws in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order: for which undertaking, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. settled on him a pension of 2000 livres. Domar was intimate with the famous Pascal, who left him his private papers at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: he himself died in 1696.

DOMENICHINO

Pages 320-320

a famous Italian painter, born of a good family at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in 1581. He was at first a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Calvart the Fleming, but soon quitted his school for that of the Caracci. He always applied himself to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and thoughtfulness; and never offered to touch his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> but when he found a proper kind of enthusiasm upon him. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> also procured him the appointment of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> of the apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> from Pope Gregory XV.; nor was he without a theoretical knowledge in music. He died in 1641.

DOMESDAY

Pages 320-321
or Doomsday Book, a most ancient record, made in the time of William I. surnamed the Conqueror, and containing a survey of all the lands of England. It consists of two volumes, a greater and a less. The first is a large folio, written on 382 double pages of vellum, in a small but plain character; each page having a double column. Some of the capital letters and principal passages are touched with red ink; and some have strokes of red ink run across them, as if scratched out. This volume contains the description of 31 counties. The other volume is in quarto, written upon 450 double pages of vellum, but in a single column, and in a large but very fair character. It contains the counties of Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, part of the county of Rutland, included in that of Northampton. This work, according to the red book in the exchequer, was begun by order of William the Conqueror, with the advice of his parliament, in the year of our Lord 1085, and completed in the year 1086. The reason given for taking this survey, as assigned by several ancient records and historians, was, that very man should be satisfied with his own right, and not usurp with impunity what belonged to another. But, besides this, it is said by others, that now all those who possessed landed estates became vassals to the king, and paid him so much money by way of fee or homage in proportion to the lands they held. This appears very probable, as there was at that time extant a general survey of the whole kingdom, made by order of King Alfred. For the execution of the survey recorded in domesday book, commissioners were sent into every county and shire; and juries summoned in each hundred, out of all orders of freemen, from barons down to the lowest farmers. These commissioners were to be informed by the inhabitants, upon oath, of the name of each manor, and that of its owner; also by whom it was held in the time of Edward the Confessor; the number of hides; the quantity of wood, of pasture, and of meadow land; how many ploughs were in the demesne, and how many in the tenanted part of it; how many mills; how many fish-ponds or fisheries belonged to it; with the value of the whole together in the time of King Edward, as well as when granted by King William, and at the time of this survey; also whether it was capable of improvement or of being advanced in its value; they were likewise directed to return the tenants of every degree, the quantity of lands then and formerly held by each of them, what was the number of villains or slaves, and also the number and kinds of their cattle and live stock. These inquisitions being first methodized in the county, were afterwards sent up to the king's exchequer. This survey, at the time it was made, gave great offence to the people; and occasioned a jealousy that it was intended for some new imposition. But notwithstanding all the precaution taken by the conqueror to have this survey faithfully and impartially executed, it appears from indisputable authority, that a false return was given in by some of the commissioners; and that, as it is said, out of a pious motive. This was particularly the case with the abbey of Croyland in Lincolnshire, the possessions of which were greatly underrated both with regard to quantity and value. Perhaps more of these pious frauds were discovered, as it is said Ralph Flambard, minister to William Rufus, proposed the making a fresh and more rigorous inquisition; but this was never executed. Notwithstanding this proof of its falsehood in some instances, which must throw a suspicion on all others, the authority of domesday book was never permitted to be called in question; and always, when it hath been necessary to distinguish whether lands were held in ancient demesne, or in any other manner, recourse was had to domesday book, and to that only, to determine the doubt. From this definitive authority, from which, as from the sentence pronounced at domesday or the day of judgment, there could be no appeal, the name of the book is said to have been derived. But Stowe assigns another reason for this appellation; namely, that domesday book is a corruption of domus Dei book; a title given it because heretofore deposited in the king's treasury, in a place of the church of Westminster or Winchester, called domus Dei. From the great care formerly taken for the preservation of this survey, we may learn the estimation in which its importance was held. The dialogue de Sacraritis says, "Liber ille (domesday) sigilli regis comes est individuus in thesaurus." Until lately it has been kept under three different locks and keys; one in custody of the treasurer, and the others in that of the two chamberlains of the exchequer. It is now deposited in the chapterhouse at Westminster, where it may be consulted on paying to the proper officers a fee of 6s. 8d. for a search, and fourpence per line for a transcript. Besides the two volumes above mentioned, there is also a third made by order of the same king; and which differs from the others in form more than matter. There is also a fourth called domesday, which is kept in the exchequer; which, though a very large volume, is only an abridgement of the others. In the remembrancers office in the exchequer is kept a fifth book, likewise called domesday, which is the same with the fourth book already mentioned. King Alfred had a roll which he called domesday; and the domesday book made by William the Conqueror referred to the time of Edward the Confessor, as that of King Alfred did to the time of Ethelred. The fourth book of domesday having many pictures and gilt letters in the beginning relating to the time of King Edward the Confessor, this had led some into a false opinion that domesday book was composed in the reign of King Edward.

DOMESTIC

Pages 321-323

adj. is sometimes opposed to foreign. Thus "domestic occurrences" signify those events which happen in our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in contradistinction to those of which we receive intelligence from abroad. In its more usual acceptation, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> implies something peculiar to home <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. Thus we speak of domestic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> or pleasures: meaning the pleasures enjoyed in the bosom of one's family; in opposition to those found in the bustle of public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, or delusively sought in the haunts of dissipation. The solace of domestic enjoyment has been coveted by the wisest and greatest of men. Senators and heroes have shut out the acclamations of an applauding world, to enjoy the prattling of their little ones, and to partake the endearments of family conversation. They knew that even their best friends, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> intercourse of life, were in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> actuated by interested motives in displaying their affection; that many of their followers applauded them in hopes of reward; and that the giddy multitude, however zealous, were not always judicious in their approbation. But the attentions paid them at their fireside, the smiles which exhilarated Domestic exhilarated their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, were the genuine result of undisssembled <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. To pursue the observations of an elegant essayist: "The nursery has often alleviated the fatigues of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Nothing contributes more to raise the gently pleasing emotions, than the view of infant innocence, enjoying the raptures of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> at play. All the sentiments of uncontrolled <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> display themselves to the view, and furnish <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for agreeable reflection to the mind of the philosophical observer. To partake with children in their little pleasures, is by no means unmanly. It is one of the purest sources of mirth. It has an influence in amending the heart, which necessarily takes a tincture from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> that surrounds us. Innocence as well as guilt is communicated and increased by the contagion of example. And the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Author of evangelical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> has taught us to emulate the simplicity of the infantine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He seems indeed himself to have been delighted with young children, and found in them, what he in vain sought among those who judged themselves their superiors, unpolluted purity of heart. Among the great variety of pictures which the vivid imagination of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> has displayed throughout the Iliad, there is not one more pleasing than the family piece, which represents the parting interview between Hector and Andromache. It deeply interests the heart, while it delights the imagination. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> ceases to be terrible, that he may become amiable. We admire him while he stands completely armed in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; but we love him more while he is taking off his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, that he may not frighten his little boy with its nodding plumes. We are refreshed with the tender <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of domestic love, while all around breathes rage and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>. We are pleased to see the arm, which is shortly to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> and destruction among an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> of foes, employed in caressing an infant son with the embraces of paternal love. A professed critic would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the pleasing effect entirely to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>; but the heart has declared, previously to the inquiries of criticism, that it is chiefly derived from the satisfaction which we naturally take in beholding great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> engaged in tender and amiable employments. But after all that is said of the purity and the solidity of domestic pleasures, they unfortunately appear to a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind, insipid, unmanly, and capable of satisfying none but the weak, the spiritless, the inexperienced, and the effeminate. The pretenders to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> philosophy are often found to renounce the received opinions of prudential conduct; and, while they affect a superior liberality, to regulate their lives by the most selfish principles. Whatever appears to have little tendency to promote personal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and advantage, they leave to be performed by those simple individuals, who are dull enough, as they say, to pursue the journey of life by the straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of common <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. It is true, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow, that the world must be replenished by a perpetual succession; and it is no less true, that an offspring, once introduced into the world, requires all the care of painful <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. But let the task be reserved for meaner spirits. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the passions can be gratified without the painful consequences of supporting a family, they eagerly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. But the toil of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> they leave to those whom they deem fools enough to take a pleasure in it. There will always be a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, say they, whose folly will <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them, for the sake of a silly <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> called virtuous love, to engage in a life of perpetual anxiety. The fool's paradise, they add with derision, will never be deserted. Presumptuous as are all such pretenders to newly invented systems of life and conduct, it is not to be supposed they will think themselves superior to Cicero. Yet Cicero, with all his liberality of mind, felt the tenderness of conjugal and parental <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, and acknowledged that, at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he received no satisfaction in any company but that of his wife, his little <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his own epithet, his HONIED young Cicero. The great Sir Thomas More, whom nobody will suspect of narrowness of mind, who by a very singular treatise evinced that he was capable of thinking and of choosing for himself, has left it on record that he devoted a great share of his time, from the united motives of duty and delight, to the amusement of his children. It will be objected by those who pretend to have formed their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of life from actual observation, that domestic happiness, however pleasing in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, like many a poetic dream, is but an alluring <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, designed by a good heart, and painted in glowing colours by a lively fancy. The constant company, they urge, even of those we love, occasions an insipidity. Insipidity grows into disgust. Disgust, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, sours the temper. Peevishness is the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The domestic circle becomes the scene of dispute. Mutual antipathy is ingenious in devising mutual torment. Sullen silence or malignant remarks fill up every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, till the arrival of a stranger causes a temporary restraint, and excites that good humour which ought to be displayed among those whom the bonds of affection and blood have already united. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a>, indeed, proves that these remarks are sometimes verified. But that there is much domestic misery is no argument that there is no domestic happiness, or that the evil may not be removed. Natural stupidity, natural ill temper, acquired ill habits, want of education, illiberal manners, and a neglect of the common rules of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, will render every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of intercourse disagreeable. When those are united by connubial ties who were separated by natural and inherent diversity, no wonder if that degree of happiness which can only result from a proper union, is unknown. In the forced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, which the poet of Venusium mentions, of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> with the dove, of the tyger with the lamb, there can be no love. When we expatiate on the happiness of the domestic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a>, we presuppose that all who compose it are originally assimilated by affection, and are still kept in union by discreet friendship. When this is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the censure must <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the discordant disposition of the parties, and not on the essential nature of family intercourse. To form, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and by the impulse of virtuous love, an early conjugal attachment, is one of the best securities of virtue, as well as the most probable means of happiness. The duties, which are powerfully called forth by the relations of husband... husband and father, are of that tender kind which inspires goodness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. He who beholds a woman whom he loves, and a helpless infant, looking up to him for support, will not easily be induced to indulge in unbecoming extravagance, or devote himself to indolence. He who has a rising family to introduce into a vicious world, will be cautious of setting a bad example, the contagion of which, when it proceeds from parental authority, must be irresistibly malignant. Thus many who, in their individual and unconnected state, would probably have spent a life not only useless to others, but profligate and careless in itself, have become valuable members of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, and have arrived at a degree of moral improvement, to which they would not otherwise have attained. "The contempt in which domestic pleasures have in modern times been held, is a mark of profligacy. It is also a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of a prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of real enjoyment. It argues a defect in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and judgment as well as in morals. For the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the experienced has in all ages declared, that the truest happiness is to be found at home."

DOMICILE

Pages 323-323

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the dwelling <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where a person lives with an intention to remain.

DOMIFYING

Pages 323-323

in Astrology, the dividing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distributing the heavens into 12 houses, in order to erect a theme, or horoscope, by means of six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circles, called circles of position. There are various ways of domifying: that of Regiomontanus, which is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, makes the circles of position <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the intersections of the meridian and the horizon; others make them pass through the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

DOMINANT

Pages 323-323

among musicians, is used either as an adjective <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> substantive; but these different acceptations are far from being indiscriminate. In both senses it is explained by Rousseau as follows: The dominant or sensible chord is that which is practised upon the dominant of the tone, and which introduces a perfect cadence. Every perfect <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> chord becomes a dominant chord, as soon as the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> is added to it. DOMINANT (subst.). Of the three notes essential to the tone, it is that which is a fifth from the tonick.—The tonick and the dominant fix the tone: in it they are each of them the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of a particular chord; whereas the mediant, which constitutes the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, has no chord peculiar to itself, and only makes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the chord of the tonick. Mr Rameau gives the name of dominant in general to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> which carries a chord of the seventh, and distinguishes that which carries the sensible chord by the name of a tonick dominant; but, on account of the length of the word, this addition to the name has not been adopted by artists: they continue simply to call that note a dominant which is a fifth from the tonick; and they do not call the other notes which carry a chord of the seventh dominants, but fundamentals; which is sufficient to render their meaning plain, and prevents confusion. A dominant, in that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> music which is called plain-chant, is that note which is most frequently repeated or beaten, in whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> it may be from the tonick. In this species of music there are dominants and tonicks, but no mediant.

DOMINATION

Pages 323-323
or Dominion, in Theology, the fourth order of angels or blessed spirits in the hierarchy, reckoning from the seraphim. See Angel.

DOMINGO

Pages 323-323
or St Domingo, the capital of the island of Hispaniola in the West Indies, is seated in that part belonging to the Spaniards on the south side of the island, and has a commodious harbour. The town is built in the Spanish manner, with a great square in the middle of it; about which are the cathedral and other public buildings. From this square run the principal streets, in a direct line, they being crossed by others at right angles, so that the form of the town is almost square. The country on the north and east side is pleasant and fruitful; and there is a large navigable river on the west, with the ocean on the south. It is the see of an archbishop, an ancient royal audience, and the seat of the governor. It has several fine churches and monasteries; and is so well fortified, that a fleet and army sent by Oliver Cromwell in 1654 could not take it. The inhabitants are Spaniards, Negroes, Mulattoes, Mestices, and Albatraces; of whom about a sixth part may be Spaniards. From this town the whole island has generally been named St Domingo. See Domingo, St Supplement. The river on which it is seated is called Osama. W. Long, 69. 30. N. Lat. 18. 25. DOMINIC de Gusman, founder of the Dominican order of monks, was born at Calaroga in Old Castile, 1170. He preached with great fury against the Albigenzes, when Pope Innocent III. made a croiseade against that unhappy people; and was inquisitor in Languedoc, where he founded his order, and got it confirmed by the Lateran council in 1215. He died at Bologna in 1221, and was afterwards canonized. The Dominican order has produced many illustrious men. See Dominicans.

DOMINICA

Pages 323-324

one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, in the West Indies, about 29 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 16 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, situated between 61° and 62° W. Long, and between 15° and 16° of N. Lat. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> formerly belonged to the French, but was ceded to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> in 1763. It contains many fertile valleys interspersed among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, some of which are volcanic. It abounds in forests, and has several hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. The value of its imports in 1809 was 161,201l. and of its imports 315,584l. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1805 consisted of 1,594 whites, 2,822 free persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and 22,083 slaves. This island was reduced, in the year 1778, by the French, under the marquis de Bouille, governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a>. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the island, though very well fortified, had been unaccountably neglected by the British <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, in such a manner as to be almost entirely destitute of a garrison. The French commander, therefore, who made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> with 2,000 men, found only 100 regular forces and a few companies of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> to oppose him. All resistance therefore being vain, the only thing the garrison could do was to procure as favourable terms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> as possible. These were granted with such readiness as did <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the character of this officer; the inhabitants experiencing no kind of change except that of transferring their obedience from Britain to France, being left unmolested in the enjoyment of all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>. DOMINICA both civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. The capitulation was strictly observed by the marquis; no plunder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> irregularity being allowed, and a pecuniary gratification being distributed among the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and volunteers who accompanied him in the expedition. An hundred and sixty-four pieces of excellent cannon, and twenty-four <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> mortars, besides a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores, were found in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; insomuch that the French themselves expressed their surprise at finding so few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them. The marquis, however, took care to supply this defect, by leaving a garrison of 1500 of the best men he had with him. It was restored to Britain at the conclusion of the peace in 1783. La Dominica, one of the Marquesas islands in the South <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

DOMINICAL

Pages 324-324

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUXERRE">Auxerre</a>, held in 578, decrees, that women communicate with their dominical. Some authors contend, that this dominical was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, wherein they received the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; as not being allowed to receive them in the bare <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it a kind of veil, wherewith they covered the head. The most probable account is, that it was a sort of linen cloth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> handkerchief wherein they received and preserved the eucharist in times of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, to be taken on occasion at home. This appears to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> by the practice of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and by Tertullian's book <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">Ad</a> Uxorium.

DOMINICAL LETTER

Pages 324-324

popularly called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> letters A B C D E F G, used in almanacks, ephemerides, &c., to denote the Sundays throughout the year. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">CHRONOLOGY</a>, No. 32. The word is formed from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICA">dominica</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dominicus dies, "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, Sunday." The dominical letters were introduced in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> by the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in lieu of the NUNDINAL letters in the Roman calendar.

DOMINICANS

Pages 324-324

an order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, called in some places Jacobins; and in others Predicants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Preaching Friars. The Dominicans take their name from their founder Dominic de Guzman, a Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, born in 1170, at Calaroga in Old Castile. He was first canon and archdeacon of Ossuna; and afterwards preached with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> zeal and vehemence against the Albigenses in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, where he laid the first foundation of his order. It was approved of in 1215 by Innocent III. and confirmed in 1216 by a bull of Honorius III. under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of St Augustine; to which Dominic added several austere precepts and observances, obliging the brethren to take a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> poverty, and to abandon entirely all their revenues and possessions; and also the title of Preaching Friars, because public instruction was the main end of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. The first convent was founded at Thoulouse by the bishop thereof and Simon de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>. Two years afterwards they had another at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, near the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after a third in the rue St Jacques, (St James's street), whence the denomination of Jacobins. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, Dominic sent Gilbert de Fresney, with twelve of the brethren, into England, where they founded their first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in the year 1221, and soon after another at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In the year 1276 the mayor and aldermen of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London gave them two whole streets by the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, where they erected a very commodious convent, whence that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is still called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Friars, from the name by which the Dominicans were called in England. St Dominic, at first, only took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the regular canons; that is, a black casock and rochet; but this he quitted in 1219, for that which they now wear, which it is pretended was shown by the blessed Virgin herself to the beatified Renaud d'<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. This order is diffused throughout the whole known world. It has forty-five provinces under the general, who resides at Rome; and 12 particular congregations or reforms, governed by 12 vicars general. They reckon three popes of this order, above sixty cardinals, several patriarchs, a hundred and fifty archbishops, and about eight hundred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>; beside masters of the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, whose office has been constantly discharged by a religious of this order, ever since St Dominic, who held it under Honorius III. in 1213. Of all the monastic orders, none enjoyed a higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of power and authority than the Dominican friars, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> was great, and their influence universal. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> they used in order to maintain and extend their authority were so pernicious and cruel, that their influence began to decline towards the beginning of the sixteenth century. The tragic story of Jetzer, conducted at Bern in 1509, for determining an uninteresting dispute between them and the Franciscans, relating to the immaculate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> reflect indelible infamy on this order. See an account of it in Burnet's Travels through France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, p. 31. or Mosheim's Ecc. Hist. vol. iii. p. 294. 8vo. They were indeed perpetually employed in stigmatizing with the opprobrious name of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> numbers of learned and pious men; in encroaching upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and properties of others, to augment their possessions; and in laying the most iniquitous snares and stratagems for the destruction of their adversaries. They were the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> counsellors, by whose instigation and advice Leo X. was determined to the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>. The papal see never had more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and useful abettors than this order, and that of the Jesuits. The dogmata of the Dominicans are usually opposite to those of the Franciscans. There are also nuns or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> of this order, called in some places Preaching Sisters. These are even more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> than the friars; St Dominic having founded a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of religious maids at Prouilles some years before the institution of his order of men; viz. in 1206. There is also a third order of Dominicans, both for men and women.

DOMINION

Pages 324-324

(Dominium) in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies the power to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dispose of a thing as we please.

DOMINIS

Pages 324-325

Mark Antony de, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 15th and beginning of the 16th centuries, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose sicknessness in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> proved his ruin. His preferment, instead of attaching him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, rendered him disaffected to it. Becoming acquainted with our Bishop Bedell, while chaplain to Sir Henry Wotton, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from James I. at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, he communicated his books *De Republica Ecclesiastica* to him; which were afterwards published at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, with Bedell's corrections. He came to England with Bedell; where he was received with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect, and preached and wrote against the Romish religion. He is said to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in publishing Father Paul's *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>*, at London, which was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to James in 1619. But on the promotion of Pope Gregory XIV. who had been his schoolfellow and old acquaintance, he was deluded by Gondomar the Spanish ambassador into the hopes of procuring a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>'s hat, by which he fancied he should prove an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of great reformation to the church. Accordingly he returned to Rome in 1622, recanted his errors, and was at first well received; but he afterwards wrote letters to England, repenting his recantation; which being intercepted, he was imprisoned by Pope Urban VIII. and died in 1625. He was also the author of the first philosophical explanation of the rainbow, which before his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was regarded as a prodigy.

DOMINIUM EMINENS

Pages 325-325

in *Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>*, that power which the state <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sovereign has over private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and by which the proprietor may be compelled to sell it for an adequate price where public utility requires. See *Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*. **DOMINIUM Directum**, in *Scots Law*, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> which a superior retains in his lands, notwithstanding the feudal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to his vassal. See *Law Index*. **DOMINIUM Utile**, in *Scots Law*, the right which the vassal acquires in the lands by the feudal grant from his superior. See *Law Index*.

DOMINUS

Pages 325-325

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> prefixed to a name, usually to denote the person either a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a clergyman. See *Vice Dominus*. The title was sometimes also given to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> not dubbed; especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>. See *Dom*, *Gentleman*, and *Sire*. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> the title *dominus* is still retained, to distinguish a minister of the reformed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.

DOMITIAN

Pages 325-325

the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, son to Vespasian, was the last of the 12 Caesars. See (*<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of*) *Rome*.

DON

Pages 325-325
or *Tanaïs*, a river of Russia, which takes its rise from the small lake of St John, near Tula, in the government of Moscow, and passing through part of the province of Voronetz, a small portion of the Ukraina-Slobodskia, and the whole province of Azof, divides itself near Tcherkask into three streams, and falls in these separate branches into the sea of Azof. This river has so many windings, is in many parts so shallow, and abounds with such numerous shoals, as to be scarcely navigable, excepting in the spring, upon the melting of the snows; and its mouth is also so choked up with sand, that only flat-bottomed vessels, excepting in the same season, can pass into the sea of Azof. The banks of the Don, and the rivulets which fall into it, are clothed with large tracts of forest, whose timber is floated down the stream to St Demetri and Rostof, where the frigates for the sea of Azof are chiefly constructed. The navigation of the Don, Mr Coxe observes, may possibly hereafter be rendered highly valuable, by conveying to the "xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black sea, the iron of Siberia, the Chinese goods, and the Persian merchant **Don** disc: which latter commodities, as well as the products of India, formerly found their way into Europe through this same channel. Don is also the name of a river in Scotland, noticed under the article *Aberdeen*; the Old Town being situated near its mouth. See *Aberdeen*. **Don Martin de Mayorea**, the name given by the Spaniards to a cluster of islands in the South sea, which were discovered in 1781 by Don F. A. Maurelle. According to the description given of these islands, they abound with tropical fruits and roots, are in a tolerable state of cultivation, and the inhabitants have made some progress in civilization. Their government, manners, and dress, resemble in most points those of the natives of the other South sea islands. In thieving, whether in disposition or dexterity, they seemed inferior to none. In one of these islands Don Maurelle found a good harbour, which he places in 18° 36' S. Lat. and in 177° 48' W. Long.

DONARIA

Pages 325-325

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in its primary signification, was taken for the places where the oblations offered to the gods were kept; but afterwards was used to denote the offerings themselves; and sometimes, though improperly, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>.

DONATIA

Pages 325-325

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra class. See *<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*.

DONATION

Pages 325-325

(*Donativus*), an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> transfers to another either the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the whole or a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his effects as a free gift. A donation, to be valid and complete, supposes a capacity both in the donor and the donee; and requires consent, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>, and delivery; and by the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> registry also. **DONATION Mortis Causa**, in *Law*, a disposition of property made by a person in his last sickness, who apprehending his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> near, delivers, or causes to be delivered to another, the possession of any personal goods, to keep in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of his decease. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the donor dies, this gift needs not the consent of his executor; but it shall not prevail against creditors; and it is accompanied with this implied trust, that, if the donor lives, the property shall revert to himself, being only given in prospect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, or *mortis causa*. This method of donation seems to have been conveyed to us from the civil lawyers, who borrowed it from the Greeks.

DONATISTS

Pages 325-326
ancient schismatics in Africa, so denominated from their leader Donatus. This sect arose in the year 311, when, in the room of Mensurius, who died in that year on his return to Rome, Cæcilian was elected bishop of Carthage, and consecrated by the African bishops alone, without the concurrence of those of Numidia. The people refused to acknowledge him, and set up Majorinus in opposition; who, accordingly, was ordained by Donatus bishop of Casse Nigrae. The Donatists were condemned, in a council held at Rome, two years after their separation; and afterwards in another at Arles, the year following; and again at Milan, before Constantine the Great, in 316, who deprived them of their churches, sent their seditious bishops into banishment, and even punished some of them with death. Their cause was espoused by another Donatus, called the great, the principal bishop of that sect, who, with numbers of his followers, was exiled by order of Constantine. Many of them were punished with great severity. See *Circumcelliones*. However, after the accession Donatists, accession of Julian to the throne in 362, they were permitted to return, and restored to their former liberty. Gratian published several edicts against them; and in 377 deprived them of their churches, and prohibited all their assemblies. But notwithstanding the severities they suffered, it appears that they had a very considerable number of churches towards the close of this century; but at this time they began to decline, on account of a schism among themselves, occasioned by the election of two bishops, in the room of Parmenian, the successor of Donatus; one party elected Primian, and were called Primianists, and another Maximian, and were called Maximianists. Their decline was also precipitated by the zealous opposition of St Augustine, and by the violent measures which were pursued against them, by order of the emperor Honorius, at the solicitation of two councils held at Carthage; the one in 404, and the other in 411. Many of them were fined, the bishops were banished, and some put to death. This sect revived and multiplied under the protection of the Vandals, who invaded Africa in 427, and took possession of this province; but it sunk again under new severities, when their empire was overturned in 534. Nevertheless, they remained in a separate body till the close of this century, when Gregory, the Roman pontiff, used various methods for suppressing them; his zeal succeeded, and there are few traces to be found of the Donatists after this period. They were distinguished by other appellations; as Circumcellionists, Montenses or Mountainers, Campites, Rupestres, &c. They held three councils, or conciliabules; one at Cirta in Numidia, and two at Carthage. The errors of the Donatists, besides their schism, were, 1. That baptism conferred out of the church, that is, out of their sect, was null; and accordingly they rebaptized those who joined their party from other churches, and re-ordained their ministers. 2. That theirs was the only true, pure, and holy church; all the rest of the churches they held as prostitute and fallen. Donatus seems likewise to have given into the doctrine of the Arians, with whom he was closely allied; and accordingly, St Epiphanius, Theodoret, and some others, accused the Donatists of Arianism; and it is probable that the charge was well founded, because they were patronized by the Vandals, who held that doctrine. But St Augustine, Ep. 185, to Count Boniface, & Haer. 69, affirms, that the Donatists, in this point, kept clear of the errors of their leader.

DONATIVE

Pages 326-326

in the canon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a benefice given, and collated to a person, by the founder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>; without either presentation, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, or induction by the ordinary. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> chapels founded by laymen be not approved by the diocesan, and, as it is called, spiritualized, they are not accounted proper benefices, neither can they be conferred by the bishop but remain to the pious disposition of the founders; so that the founders, and their heirs, may give such chapels without the bishop. Gwin observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> might of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> found a free chapel, and exempt it from the jurisdiction of the diocesan; so may be, by letters patent, give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> person to found such a chapel, and make it donative, not presentable; and the chaplain, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BENEFICIARY">beneficiary</a>, shall be deprivable by the founder or his heir, and not by the bishop. And this seems to be the original of donatives in England. Donatives are within the statute against simony; and if they have cure of souls, within that against pluralities. If the patron of a donative doth not nominate a clerk, there can be no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> thereof, unless it be specially provided for in the foundation; but the bishop may compel him to do it by spiritual censures. But if it be augmented by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s bounty, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> lapse like other presentative livings. 1 Geo. I. stat. 2. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 10. The ordinary cannot visit a donative, and therefore it is free from procuration, and the incumbent is exempted from attendance at visitations. All bishoprics in ancient times were donative by the king. Again, where a bishop has the gift of a benefice, it is properly called a donative, because he cannot present to himself.

DONATORY

Pages 326-326

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, that person to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> bestows his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to any forfeiture that has fallen to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.

DONATUS

Pages 326-326

Elius, a famous grammarian, lived at Rome in 354. He was one of St Jerome's masters; and composed commentaries on Terence and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>.

DONAWERT

Pages 326-326

a strong town of Germany. It is situated on the left <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Danube, at the influx of the Wernitz. It was formerly an imperial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but is now subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 32. N. Lat. 48. 32.

DONAX

Pages 326-326

a genus of shells belonging to the bivalves. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">CONCHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DONCASTER

Pages 326-326

a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, 37 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. It has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> noted for the manufacture of stockings, knitted waistcoats and gloves. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was erected here in 1795. It contained 6935 inhabitants in 1811. W. Long. 1. 12. N. Lat. 53. 33.

DONEGAL

Pages 326-326

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on one side, and the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRONE">Tyrone</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a> on the other. Its greatest length is 90 miles, and breadth 45, and it contains 1,100,000 English acres. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is moist, and it abounds in bogs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Barley is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> grain crop, but a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the agricultural labour is performed

DONNE

Pages 326-327

Dr John, an excellent poet and divine of the 17th century. His parents were of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and used their utmost efforts to keep him firm to it; but his early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the controversy between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, at last determined him to adhere to the latter. He travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; where he made many useful observations, and learned their languages to perfection. Soon after his return to England, Sir Thomas Egerton, keeper of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, appointed him his secretary; in which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> five years. He marrying privately <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir George Moore then <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>, and niece to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> keeper's lady, was dismissed from his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and thrown into prison. But he was reconciled to Sir George by the good offices of Sir Francis Wolley. In 1612, he accompanied Sir Robert Drury to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. During this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> solicited the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> employment for him. But his majesty, who took <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in his conversation, had engaged him in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his *Pseudo <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>*, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1610; and he was so highly pleased with that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, that in 1614 he prevailed with him to enter into holy orders; appointed him one of his chaplains, and procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> from the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In 1619, he attended the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DONCASTER">Doncaster</a> in his embassy into Germany. In 1621, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Paul's; and the vicarage of St Dunstan in the West, in London, soon after fell to him. He wrote, besides the above, 1. Devotions upon emergent occasions. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, translated from the Greek of Aristaeus, quarto. 3. Three volumes of sermons, folio. 4. A considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of poems; and other works. His writings show him to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of incomparable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and learning; but his greatest excellence was satire. He had a prodigious richness of fancy, but his thoughts were much debased by his versification.

DONOR

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the person who gives lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements to another in tail, &c.; as he to whom such lands, &c., are given, is the donee. DOOMSDAY book. See DOMESDAY Book.

DORADO

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a southern constellation, not visible in our latitude; it is also called *siphias*. The stars of this constellation, in Sharp's Catalogue, are six.

DORCHESTER

Pages 327-327

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, situated on the river Frome, on a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Weymouth. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 45. N. Lat. 50. 40. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and is a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. The inhabitants amounted to 2546 in 1811.

DORIA

Pages 327-327

ANDREW, a gallant Genoese <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> officer, born in 1466. He entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Francis I. of France; but preserved that spirit of independence so <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to a sailor and a republican. When the French attempted to render <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVONA">Savona</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> the object of jealousy of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, its rival in trade, Doria demonstrated against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tone; which bold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, represented by the malice of his courtiers in the most odious <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, irritated Francis to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he ordered his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> Barbesieux to sail to Genoa, then in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the French troops, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> Doria, and to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> his galleys. This rash order Doria got timely hints of; retired with all his galleys to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of safety; and, while his resentment was thus raised, he closed with the offers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. returned his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> with the collar of St Michael to Francis, and hoisted the Imperial colours. To deliver his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, weary alike of the French and Imperial yoke, from the dominion of foreigners, was now Doria's highest ambition; and the favourable moment offered. Genoa was afflicted with the pestilence, the French garrison was greatly reduced and ill paid, and the inhabitants were sufficiently disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> his views. He sailed to the harbour with 13 galleys, landed 500 men, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the gates and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> with very little resistance. The French governor with his feeble garrison retired to the citadel, but was quickly forced to capitulate; when the people ran together, and levelled the citadel with the ground. It was now in Doria's power to have rendered himself the sovereign of his country; but with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> of which there are few examples, he assembled the people in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> before the palace, disclaimed all pre-eminence, and recommended to them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> that form of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> they chose to establish. The people animated by his spirit, forgot their factions, and fixed that form of government which has subsisted ever since with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>. This event happened in 1528. Doria lived to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, respected and beloved as a private citizen; and is still celebrated in Genoa by the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> of all appellations, "The father of his country, and the restorer of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>."

DORIC

Pages 327-328

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of the five orders; being that between the Tuscan and Ionic. It is usually placed upon the Attic base, though originally it had no base. See ARCHITECTURE, No 43. At its first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> it was more simple than at present; and when in after times it was more adorned and enriched, the appellation Doric was restrained to this richer manner, and the primitive simple manner was called by a new name, the Tuscan order, which was chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; as the former being more <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and delicate, was for porticoes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> is, that Dorus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Achaia, having first built a temple of this order at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, which he dedicated to Juno, occasioned it to be called Doric; though others derive its name from its being invented <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> used by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a>. The moderns, on account of its solidity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> strong buildings; as in the gates of cities and citadels, the outside of churches, and other massy works, where delicacy of ornament would be unsuitable. The gate of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Piccadilly is of the Doric order. The most considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments of this order, are the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of Marcellus at Rome, wherein the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, the height of the frieze, and its projection, are much smaller than in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> architecture; and the Parthenon, or temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, in which the short and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> columns bear upon the pavement without a base; and the capital is a simple torus, with its cincture, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, plain, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABACUS">abacus</a>. Doric Cymatium. See Cyma. Doric Dialect, one of the five dialects, or manners of speaking, which obtained among the Greeks. It was first used by the Lacedemonians, and particularly those of Argos; thence it passed into Epirus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. In this dialect, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a> wrote, who were both of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>; as likewise <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. In strictness, however, we should rather define Doric, the manner of speaking peculiar to the Dorians, after their recess near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a> and Asopus; and which afterwards came to obtain among the Lacedemonians, &c. Some even distinguish between the Lacedemonian and Doric; but in reality, they were the same; setting aside a few particularities in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Lacedemonians; as is shown by Rulandus, in his excellent treatise De Lingua Graeca ejusque Dialectis, lib. v. Beside the authors already mentioned to have written in the Doric dialect, we might add Archytas of Tarentum, Bion, Callinus, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHYLIDES">Bacchylides</a>, Cypselas, Alcman, and Sophron. Most of the medals of the cities of Graecia Magna, and Sicily, savour of the Doric dialect in their inscription: witness, ΑΜΒΡΑΚΙΩΝΤΑΝ, ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΙΑΤΑΝ, ΑΧΕΟΠΟΝΤΑΝ, ΑΧΥΡΙΤΑΝ, ΗΡΑΧΑΕΩΤΑΝ, ΤΡΑΞΙΝΙΩΝ, ΘΕΡΙΤΑΝ, ΚΑΤΑΝΙΑΤΑΝ, ΚΟΙΠΙΑΤΑΝ, ΤΑΥΡΟΜΕΝΙΤΑΝ, &c. Which shows the countries wherein the Doric dialect was used. The general rules of this dialect are thus given by the Port Royalists. Dit Hva d'w <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>, d't d'a et d'u l'a fait le Dore. D'u fait vra; d'u, u; et d'u av fait encore. Oste i de l'infini; et pour le singulier Se sert au feminin du nombre plurier. But they are much better explained in the fourth book of Rulandus; where he even notes the minuter differences of the dialects of Sicily, Crete, Tarentum, Rhodes, Lacedemon, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, and Thessaly. The a abounds everywhere in the Doric; but this dialect bears so near a conformity to the Æolic, that many reckon them but one. Doric <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">Mode</a>, in Music, the first of the authentic modes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Its character is to be severe, tempered with gravity and joy; and is proper upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> occasions, as also to be used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It begins D, la, sol, re. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> admires the music of the Doric mode, and judges it proper to preserve good manners as being masculine; and on this account allows it in his commonwealth. The ancients had likewise their subdoric or hypodoric mode, which was one of the plagal modes. Its character was to be very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and solemn; it begins with re, a fourth lower than the Doric.

DORING

Pages 328-328
or DARING, among sportsmen, a term used to express a method of taking larks, by means of a clap-net and a looking-glass. For this sport there must be provided four sticks very straight and light, about the bigness of a pike; two of these are to be four feet nine inches long, and all notched at the edges or the ends. At one end of each of these sticks there is to be fastened another of about a foot long on one side; and on the other side a small wooden peg about three inches long. Then four or more sticks are to be prepared, each of one foot length; and each of these must have a chord of nine feet long fastened to it at the end. Every one should have a buckle for the commodious fastening on to the respective sticks when the net is to be spread.—A cord must also be provided, which must have two branches. The one must be nine feet and a half, and the other ten feet long, with a buckle at the end of each; the rest, or body of the cord, must be 24 yards long. All these cords, as well the long ones as those about the sticks, must be well twisted and of the bigness of one's little finger. The next thing to be provided is a staff of four feet long, pointed at one end, and with a ball of wood at the other, for carrying these conveniences in a sack or wallet.—There should also be carried on this occasion, a spade to level the ground where there may be any little irregularities; and two small rods, each eighteen inches long, and having a small rod fixed with a pack-thread at the larger end of the other. To these are to be tied some pack-thread loops, which are to fasten in the legs of some larks: and there are to be reels to these, that the birds may fly a little way up and down. When all this is done, the looking-glass is to be prepared in the following manner: Take a piece of wood about an inch and a half thick, and cut it in form of a bow, so that there may be about nine inches space between the two ends; and let it have its full thickness at the bottom; that it may receive into it a false piece; in the five corners of which there are to be set in five pieces of looking-glass. These are so fixed, that they may dart their light upwards; and the whole machine is to be supported on a moveable pin, with the end of a long line fixed to it, and made in the manner of the children's plaything of an apple and a plumbstone; so that the other end of the cord being carried through a hedge, the barely pulling it may set the whole machine of the glass a turning.
