To **DOUSE**, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is to lower suddenly, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a>; and it is applied to a sail in a squall of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, an extended <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAWSER">hawser</a>, &c.

DOUW

Pages 335-336

GERHARD, a celebrated painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1613; and received his first instructions in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> from Bartholomew Dolendo an engraver, and also from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Kouwhoorn a painter on glass; but at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fifteen he became a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Rembrandt. In that famous school he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for three years; and then found himself qualified to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, the most unerring <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>. From Rembrandt he learned the true principles of colouring, and obtained a complete knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIARO_SCURO">chiaro-scuro</a>: but to that knowledge he added a delicacy of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> in working up his colours to the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of neatness, superior to any other <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He therefore was more pleased with those pictures of Rembrandt which were painted in his youth than those by which he was distinguished in his more advanced age; because the first seemed finished with more care and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, the latter with more boldness, freedom, and negligence, which was quite opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of Douw. But although his manner appears so different from that of his master, yet it was to Rembrandt alone that he owed all that excellence in colouring by which he triumphed over all the artists of his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His pictures are usually of a small size, with figures so exquisitely touched, so transparent, so wonderfully delicate, as to excite astonishment as well as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He designed every object after nature, and with an exactness so singular, that each object appears as perfect as nature itself, in respect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, freshness and force. His general manner of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> portraits, was by the aid of a concave mirror, and sometimes by looking at the object through a frame with many exact squares of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. But the latter <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is disused, as the eye of a good <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> seems a more competent rule, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the former is still practised by painters in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>. It is almost incredible what vast sums have been given and are given at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> for the pictures of Douw, even in his own country; as also in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and every polite polite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; for he was exceedingly curious in finishing them, and patiently assiduous beyond example. Of that patience Sandrart gives a strong <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> in a circumstance which he mentions relative to this artist. He says, that having once, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Bamboccio, visited Gerhard Douw, they could not forbear to admire the prodigious neatness of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> which he was then painting, in which they took particular notice of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>; and expressing their surprise at the excessive neatness of the finishing that minute object, Douw told them he should spend three days more in working on that broom before he should account it entirely complete. In a family picture of Mrs Spiering, the same author observes, that the lady sat five days for the finishing one of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> that leaned on an arm <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>. For that reason not many would sit to him for their portraits; and he therefore indulged himself mostly in works of fancy, in which he could introduce objects of still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and employ as much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on them as suited his own inclination. Houbraken testifies, that his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Mr Spiering allowed him a thousand guilders a-year, and paid beside whatever he demanded for his pictures, and purchased some of them for their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in silver; but Sandrart, with more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, assures us, that the thousand guilders a-year were paid to Gerhard, on no other consideration than that the artist should give his benefactor the option of every picture he painted, for which he was immediately to receive the utmost of his demand. This great master died in 1674, aged 61. Douw appears incontestably to be the most wonderful in his finishing of all the Flemish masters. Everything that came from his pencil is precious, and his colouring hath exactly the true and the lovely tints of nature; nor do his colours appear tortured, nor is their vigour lessened by his patient pencil; for whatever pains he may have taken, there is no look of labour <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stiffness; and his pictures are remarkable, not only for retaining their original lustre, but for having the same beautiful effect at a proper distance as they have when brought to the nearest view. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> are several pictures by Gerhard Douw, wonderfully beautiful; especially one, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> attending a sick woman, and surveying an animal. The execution of that painting is astonishingly fine, and although the shadows appear a little too dark, the whole has an inexplicable effect. In the gallery at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> there is a night-piece by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, which is exquisitely finished; and in the same apartment, a mountebank attended by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of figures, which it seems impossible either sufficiently to commend or to describe.

DOVER

Pages 334-335

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in the Delaware state, and is the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. It stands on Jones's creek, a few miles from the Delaware river, and consists of about 100 houses, principally of brick. Four streets intersect each other at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, in the centre. centre of the town, whose incidencies form a spacious parade, on the east side of which is an elegant state-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of brick. The town has a lively appearance, and drives on a considerable trade with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>. Wheat is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> article of export. The landing is five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six miles from the town of Dover.

DOWAGER

Pages 336-336

Dotisca (q.d. a widow endowed, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that has a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a>), a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, or addition, applied to the widows of princes, dukes, earls, and persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> only. **<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">QUEEN</a> Dowager**, is the widow of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and as such enjoys most of the privileges belonging to her as queen consort: but it is not high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> to violate her chastity or conspire her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, because the succession is not endangered thereby; but no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can marry her without special license from the king, on pain of forfeiting his lands and goods. See **Queen**.

DOWER

Pages 336-336

(Dotarium, Doarium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dos), a portion of lands or tenements which a widow enjoys for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> from her husband, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> she survives him; and which, at her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, descends to their children. But she must have been the wife of the party at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his decease; or not divorced à vinculo matrimoni; nor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she has eloped from her husband, and lives with an adulterer, shall she be entitled to dower, unless her husband be voluntarily reconciled to her. The widows of traitors are also barred of their dower by 5 and 6 Edw. VI. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. ii., but not the widows of felons. An alien cannot be endowed, unless she be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> consort. And if a woman levies a fine with her husband, or if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> be had with the husband and wife of the husband's lands, she is barred of her dower. A widow, clear of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a>, is by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> entitled to be endowed of all lands and tenements, of which her husband was seised in fee-simple or fee-tail at any time during the coverture; and of which any issue she might have had might by possibility have been heir. See **<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">Jointure</a>**.

DOWN

Pages 336-337

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster; bounded on the east and south by St George's channel; on the west by the county of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the county of Antrim. It lies opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>; and the north <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it fronts the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> in Scotland, and is about 44 miles from it. It is about 44 miles in length and 30 in breadth, and contains about 558,000 English acres. The county of Down contains 60 parishes, and in 1813 the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted to 204,500 souls. This county is rough and full of hills; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate and healthy. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> naturally produces wood, unless constantly kept open and ploughed; and the low grounds degenerate into bogs and moss, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> are neglected. But by the industry of the inhabitants it produces good crops of corn, particularly oats; and, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> is found, barley. This last is exported from Killogh to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. The staple commodity of this county is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture. See **Down, Supplement**. **Down**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **Down-Patrick**, a town of Ireland, in the county of Down, is one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is a market town and a bishopric, said to be erected in the fifth century by St Patrick, but is now united to the see of Connor. Within 200 paces of the town, on the ascent of a hill, are the ruins of an old <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of St Patrick the founder, in which they say the bodies of St Bridget and St Columb are also laid. The town, which is seated on the south corner of Lough <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">Coin</a>, now called the lake of Strongford, is adorned with several handsome public buildings. Among the hills, and in many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, are flights of swans and other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fowl; and the lough abounds with salmon, mullets, lets, and other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fish. About a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from this town is St Patrick's well, which many people frequent to drink at some seasons of the year, and others to perform a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> enjoined them by the Popish priests. The linen manufacture is carried on here, as it is in several places in this county. The population is about 5000. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 50'. N. Lat. 54° 23'. Down, the fine feathers from the breasts of several birds, particularly of the duck kind.—That of the elder duck is the most valuable. These birds pluck it from their breasts and line their nests with it. We are told that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of down found in one nest more than filled the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of a hat, yet weighed no more than three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an ounce. Br. Zool. —Three pounds of this down may be compressed into a space scarce bigger than one's fist; yet it is afterwards so dilatable as to fill a quilt five feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. Salern. Orn. p. 416.—That found in the nests is most valued, and termed live down; it is infinitely more <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> than that plucked from the dead <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, which is little esteemed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>. The best sort is sold at 45 fish per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> when cleansed, and at 16 when not cleansed. There are generally exported every year, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>'s account, fifteen hundred or two thousand pounds of both sorts, exclusively of what is privately exported by foreigners. In 1759 the Iceland company sold as much in quantity of this article as amounted to three thousand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hundred and forty-five banco dollars, besides what was sent directly to Glückstadt.—Von Troil, p. 146. Down, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See Hair.

DOWNETON

Pages 337-337

a borough town of Wiltshire, five miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. It contained 2624 inhabitants in 1811, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

DOWNHAM

Pages 337-337

a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, 10 miles south of Lynn, famous for its good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; there being 1000, and sometimes 2000, firkins bought here every Monday, and sent up the river Ouse to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and thence to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1771 in 1811.

DOWNS

Pages 337-337

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> elevation of sand, which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> gathers and forms along its shores; and which serves it as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>. The word is formed from the French dune, of the Celtic dum, a "mountain." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> de Visch, in his Compend. Chronolog. Exord. et Progress, Abbat. Clariss. B. Marier, de Duni, says, Vallem repertit arenarum colibus (quos incolae Duyuen vocant) univale cinetum. DOWNS is particularly used for a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for ships, along the eastern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Foreland; where both the outward and homeward bound ships frequently make some stay; and squadrons of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> rendezvous in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war. It affords excellent anchorage; and is defended by the castles of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">Deal</a>, Dover, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>.

DOWRY

Pages 337-337

the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fortune which the wife brings her husband in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; it is otherwise called maritagium, marriage goods, and differs from dower. See Dower.

DOXOLOGY

Pages 337-337

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> used in praise of the Almighty, distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of greater and lesser. The lesser doxology was anciently only a single <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, without response, running in these words; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a> be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost, world without end, Amen. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the latter clause, As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, was inserted some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. Some read this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> hymn, Glory be to the Father, and to the Son with the Holy Ghost. Others, Glory be to the Father in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the Son, and by the Holy Ghost. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> occasioned no dispute in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, till the rise of the Arian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; but when the followers of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a> began to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the latter as a distinguishing character of their party, it was entirely laid aside by the Catholics, and the use of it was enough to bring any one under suspicion of heterodoxy. The doxology was used at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of every solemn office. The western church repeated it at the end of every psalm, and the eastern church at the end of the last psalm. Many of their prayers were also concluded with it, particularly the solemn thanksgiving or consecration <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> at the eucharist. It was also the ordinary conclusion of their sermons. The greater doxology, or angelic hymn, was likewise of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the ancient church. It began with these words, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> sung at our Saviour's birth, Glory be to God on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, &c. It was chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and in men's private devotions. Both the doxologies have a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the church of England, the former being repeated after every psalm, and the latter used in the communion service.

DRABA

Pages 337-337

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetradynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 39th order, Siliqueae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DRABLER

Pages 337-337

in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a small sail in a ship, which is the same to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a> as a bonnet is to a course, and is only used when the course and bonnet are too shoal to clothe the mast. See Bonnet and Course.

DRABLING

Pages 337-337

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLING">Angling</a>, is a method of catching barbels. Take a strong line of six yards; which, before you fasten it to your rod, must be put through a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the fish bite, it may slip to and fro, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> may something move it on the ground; bait with a lob worm well secured, and so by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> the barbel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be enticed into the danger without suspicion. The best places are in running water near piles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> under wooden bridges, supported with oaks floated and slimy.

DRABS

Pages 337-337

in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> works, a kind of wooden boxes for holding the salt when taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>; the bottoms of which are made shelving <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inclining forwards, that the briny moisture of the salt may drain off.

DRAC

Pages 337-338

an imaginary being, much dreaded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people in many parts of France. The dracs are supposed to be malicious, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least tricksome demons; but, which is very rare, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one of them happens to take a fancy to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or woman, they are sure to be the better for it. They are still said to lay <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> cups and rings on the surface over pits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, as baits to draw women and children in; though their usual dwelling is some old empty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, whence they make excursions in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form, visible or invisible as best suits their purpose. The country folks shudder at the very name of the drac. Some are positive that they have seen seen him; for happy indeed is that village in which there is not a house execrated as the lurking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of this tremendous drac. **DRACÆNA**, Dragon-tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DRACHM

Pages 338-338

a Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, of the value of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pence three farthings. Drachm is also a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> used by our physicians; containing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> sixty grains, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three scruples, or the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an ounce.

DRACO

Pages 338-338

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the northern hemisphere; whose stars, according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, are 81; according to Tycho, 32; according to Hevelius, 49; according to Bayer, 33; and according to Mr Flamstead, &c. See Astronomy, No. 406.

DRACOCEPHALUM

Pages 338-338

Dragon's Head; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DRACONARIUS

Pages 338-338

in antiquity, Dragon-bearer. Several nations, as the Persians, Parthians, Scythians, &c., bore dragons on their standards; whence the standards themselves were called *dracones*, "dragons." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> borrowed the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> from the Parthians; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as Casaubon has it, from the Daci; or, as Codin, from the Assyrians. The Roman dracones were figures of dragons painted in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> on the flags, as appears from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a>; but among the Persians and Parthians they were, like the Roman eagle, figures in full relievo; so that the Romans were frequently deceived, and took them for real dragons. The soldier who bore the dragon or standard was called by the Romans *draconarius*; and by the Greeks *δρακοντιάς* and *δρακοντιάς*; for the emperors carried the custom with them to Constantinople.

DRACONTIC MONTH

Pages 338-338

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the revolution of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> from her ascending node, called *caput draconis*, to her return thither.

DRACONTIUM

Pages 338-338

Dragons; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the first order, Palmae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DRACUNCULI

Pages 338-338

in Medicine, a peculiar eruption, which was supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> in the muscular parts of the arms and legs, called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> worms. These worms were removed by the point of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>; and to prevent their forming again, the usual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is to wash the parts with wine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, nitre, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, or with a strong lixivium of oak ashes, and afterwards anoint them with an ointment of the common kind used for scorbutic eruptions, with a small mixture of quicksilver. **DRACUNCULUS**. See Arum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DRAFF

Pages 338-338

a name given in some places to the wash given to hogs, and the grain given to cows.

DRAGOMAN

Pages 338-338
or **DROGMAN**, a term of general use through the east for an interpreter, whose office is to facilitate commerce between the orientals and occidentals. These are kept by the ambassadors of Christian nations residing at the Porte for this purpose. The word is formed from the Arabic *targeman* or *targiman*, of the verb *targem*, "he has interpreted." From *dragoman* the Italians formed *dragomano* and, with a nearer relation to its Arabic etymology, *turciniano*; whence the French and our trucheman, as well as *dragoman* and *drogman*.

DRAGON

Pages 338-340

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a>. **Dragon's Head and Tail** (*caput et cauda draconis*), are the nodes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> wherein the ecliptic is intersected by the orbits of the planets and particularly that of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; making with it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of five degrees and eighteen minutes. One of these points looks northward; the moon beginning then to have <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and the other southward, where she commences south. Thus her deviation from the ecliptic seems (according to the fancy of some) to make a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> like that of a dragon, whose belly is where she has the greatest latitude; the intersection representing the head and tail, from which resemblance the denomination arises. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, that these points abide not always in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of their own in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, and retrograde-wise, 3 minutes 11 seconds per <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; completing their circle in 18 years 225 days; so that the moon can be but twice in the ecliptic during her monthly <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, but at all other times she <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have a latitude or declination from the ecliptic. It is about these points of intersection that all eclipses happen. They are usually denoted by these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, Ω dragon's head, Ψ dragon's tail. **Dragon**, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>. See Draco. **Dragon's Blood**, a gummi-resinous substance brought from the East Indies, either in oval drops wrapped up in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> leaves, or in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses composed of smaller tears. It is said to be obtained from the palmijuncus draco, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALAMUS">calamus</a> rotang, the dracaena draco, the pterocarpus draco, and several other vegetables. The writers on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a> in general give the preference to the former, though the others are not unfrequently of equal goodness. The fine dragon's blood of either sort breaks smooth, free from any visible impurities, of a dark <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which changes upon being powdered into an elegant bright crimson. Several <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> compositions, coloured with the true dragon's blood, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> wood, are sometimes sold in the room of this commodity. Some of these dissolve like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; others crackle in the fire without proving inflammable; whilst the genuine sanguis draconis readily melts and catches <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and is not acted on by watery liquors. It totally dissolves in pure spirit, and tinges a large <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the menstruum of a deep red colour. It is likewise soluble in expressed oils, and gives them a red hue, less beautiful than that communicated by anchusa. This drug in substance has no sensible smell or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; when dissolved, it discovers some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of warmth and pungency. It is usually, but without foundation, looked upon as a gentle astringent; and sometimes directed as such in contemporaneous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> against seminal gleets, the fluor albus, and other fluxes. In these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it is supposed to produce the general effects of resinous bodies, lightly incrassating the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and somewhat strengthening the solids. But in the present practice it is very little used either externally or internally. A solution of dragon's blood in spirit of wine is used for staining marble, to which it gives a red tinge, which penetrates more or less deeply according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the marble during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of application. But as it spreads at the same time that it sinks deep, for fine designs the marble should be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. M. Dufay says, that by adding pitch to this solution the colour may be rendered deeper. **Dragon Fish**, or Dragonet. See Callionymus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Dragon Fly.** See Libellula, Entomology Index. **Dragon Shell**, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by some to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of concamerated patella or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMPET">limpet</a>. This has a top very much bent; and is of an ash colour on the outside, but of an elegant and bright <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-colour within. This has been found sticking on the back of a tortoise, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> limpets do on the sides of rocks; and some have been found affixed to large shells of the pinna marina brought from the East Indies at different times. **Dragons.** See Dracontium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. **Dragonet**, or **Dragon Fish.** See Callionymus, Ichthyology Index. **Dragonne'e**, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. A lion dragonée is where the upper half resembles a lion, the other half going off like the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a dragon. The same may be said of any other beast as well as a lion. **Dragoon**, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, a musqueteer mounted on horseback, who sometimes fights or marches on foot, as occasion requires. Menage derives the word dragoon from the Latin dracoarius, which in Vespasius is used to signify soldier. But it is more probably derived from the German tragen or dragen, which signifies to carry; as being infantry carried on horseback. Dragoons are divided into brigades as the cavalry; and each regiment into troops; each troop having a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, cornet, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, two sergeants, three corporals, and two drums. Some regiments have hautboys. They are very useful on any expedition that requires despatch; for they can keep pace with the cavalry, and do the duty of infantry; they encamp generally on the wings of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, or at the passes leading to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and sometimes they are brought to cover the general's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>: they <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and rear of the army. The first regiment of dragoons raised in England was in 1681, and called the regiment of dragoons of North <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> or attacks they generally fight <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> after the first fire. Their arms are, a sword, firelock, and bayonet. In the French <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, when the dragoons march on foot, their officers bear the pike and the sergeants the halbert, neither of which are used in the English service. **Dragooning**, one of the methods used by Papists for converting refractory heretics, and bringing them within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> of the true <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The following method of dragooning the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, after the revocation of the edict of Nantz, under <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. is taken from a French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> translated in 1686. "The troopers, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and dragoons, went into the Protestant houses, where they marred and defaced their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> stuff, broke their looking glasses, and other utensils and ornaments, let their wine run about their cellars, and threw about their corn and spoiled it. And as to those things which they could not destroy in this manner, such as furniture of beds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, wearing apparel, plate, &c. they carried them to the market place, and sold them to the Jesuits and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. By these means the Protestants in Montaubon alone were, in four or five days, stripped of above a million of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. But this was not the worst. "They turned the dining rooms of gentlemen into stables for their horses; and treated the owners of the houses where they quartered with the highest indignity and cruelty, lashing them about from one to another, day and night, without intermission, not suffering them to eat or drink; and when they began to sink under the fatigue and pains they had undergone, they laid them on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and when they thought them somewhat recovered, made them rise, and repeated the same tortures. When they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the blood and sweat run <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their faces and other parts of their bodies, they sluiced them with water, and putting over their heads kettle drums, turned upside down, they made a continual din upon them till these unhappy creatures lost their senses. When one party of these tormentors..." Dragoon-mentors were weary, they were relieved by another, who practised the same cruelties with fresh vigour. "At Negreplise, a town near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTAUBAN">Montauban</a>, they hung up <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Favin, a Protestant citizen of that place, by his armpits, and tormented him a whole night by pinching and tearing off his flesh with pincers. They made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fire round a boy of about 12 years old, who with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and eyes lifted up to heaven cried out 'My God, help me!' And when they found the youth resolved to die rather than renounce his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, they snatched him from the fire <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as he was on the point of being burnt. "In several places the soldiers applied red-hot irons to the hands and feet of men and breasts of women. At Nantz they hung up several women and maids by their feet, and others by their armpits, and thus exposed them to public view stark naked. They bound to posts mothers that gave suck, and let their sucking <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> languishing in their sight for several days and nights, crying, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, and gasping for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Some they bound before a great fire, and being half roasted, let them go: a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> worse than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Amidst a thousand hideous cries and a thousand blasphemies, they hung up men and women by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and some by their feet, on hooks in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>, and smoked them with wisps of wet hay till they were suffocated. They tied some under the arms with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, and plunged them again and again into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>; they bound others like criminals, put them to the torture, and with a funnel filled them with wine till the fumes of it took away their reason, when they made them say, they consented to be Catholics. They stripped them naked, and after a thousand indignities, stuck them with pins and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> from head to foot. They cut and slashed them with knives; and sometimes with red-hot pincers took hold of them by the nose and other parts of the body, and dragged them about the rooms till they made them <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to be Catholics, or till the cries of these miserable wretches, calling upon God for help, forced them to let them go. They <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> them with staves, and thus bruised, and with broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, dragged them to church, where their forced presence was taken for an abjuration. In some places they tied fathers and husbands to their bed-posts, and before their eyes ravished their wives and daughters with impunity. They blew up men and women with bellows till they burst them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any to escape these barbarities endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> themselves by flight, they pursued them into the fields and woods, where they <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> at them like wild beasts, and prohibited them from departing the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> (a cruelty never practised by Nero or Diocletian) upon pain of confiscation of effects, the galleys, the lash, and perpetual imprisonment; insomuch that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> of the seaport <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> were crammed with men, women, and children, who endeavoured to save themselves by flight from their dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. With these scenes of desolation and horror, the Popish clergy feasted their eyes, and made them only a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> and sport. "Though my heart aches (says the writer of the piece from which we are transcribing) whilst I am relating these barbarities, yet for a perpetual memorial of the infernal cruelty practised by these monsters I beg the reader's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> to lay before him two other instances, which, if he hath a heart like mine, he will not be able to read without watering these sheets with his tears. "The first is of a young woman, who being brought before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, upon refusing to abjure her religion, was ordered to prison. There they shaved her head, singed off the hair from other parts of her body; and having stripped her stark naked, led her through the streets of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, where many a blow was given her, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> flung at her; then they set her up to the neck in a tub full of water, where, after she had been for a while, they took her out, and put on her a shift dipt in wine, which, as it dried and stuck to her sore and bruised body, they snatched off again, and then had another ready dipt in wine to clap on her. This they repeated six times, thereby making her body exceeding raw and sore. When all these cruelties could not shake her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, they fastened her by her feet in a kind of gibbet, and let her hang in that posture, with her head downward, till she expired. "The other is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> were quartered some of these missionary dragoons. One day, having drank plentifully of his wine, and broken their glasses at every <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, they filled the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> with the fragments, and by often walking over them reduced them to very small pieces. This done, in the insolence of their mirth, they resolved on a dance, and told their Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> that he must be one of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; but as he would not be of their religion, he must dance quite barefoot; and thus barefoot they drove him about the room, treading on the sharp points of the broken glasses. When he was no longer able to stand, they laid him on a bed, and, in a short time, stripped him stark naked, and rolled him from one end of the room to the other, till every part of his body was full of the fragments of glass. After this they dragged him to his bed, and having sent for a surgeon, obliged him to cut out the pieces of glass with his instruments, thereby putting him to the most exquisite and horrible pains that can possibly be conceived. "These, fellow Protestants, were the methods used by the most Christian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s apostolic dragoons to convert his heretical subjects to the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>! These, and many other of the like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, were the torments to which Louis XIV. delivered them over to bring them to his own church: and as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> is unchangeably the same, these are the tortures prepared for you, if ever that religion should be permitted to become settled amongst you; the consideration of which made <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> say of it, what every man that knows anything of Christianity must agree with him in, 'If you had no other reason to go out of the Roman church, this alone would suffice, that you see and hear, how contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of God, they shed innocent blood. This single circumstance shall, God willing, ever separate me from the Papacy. And if I was now subject to it, and could blame nothing in any of their doctrines; yet for this crime of cruelty, I would fly from her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, as from a den of thieves and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>.'

DRAGS

Pages 340-341

in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are whatever hangs over the ship in the sea, as shirts, coats, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like; and boats, when towed, or whatever else that after this manner may hinder the ship's way when she sails, are called drags.

DRAIN

Pages 341-341

a cut <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ditch for carrying off <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, to improve it for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. In the fen countries of England <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> are 20, 30, and sometimes 40 feet wide, carried through the marshy ground to some river or other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> capable of discharging the water which they carry out of the fen lands. DRAINING. For the different methods, see Agriculture <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DRAKE

Pages 341-342

the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> of the duck kind. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Drake, Sir Francis, a celebrated English <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, was the son of Edmund Drake a sailor, and born near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAVISTOCK">Tavistock</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, in the year 1545. He was brought up at the expense, and under the care of Sir John Hawkins, who was his kinsman; and, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 18, was purser of a ship trading to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>. At 20, he made a voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; and, at 22, had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the Judith. In that capacity he was in the harbour of St John de Ulloa, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, where he behaved most gallantly in the glorious actions under Sir John Hawkins, and returned with him to England with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation, though not worth a great. Upon this he projected a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> against the Spaniards in the West Indies; which he no sooner published, than he had volunteers enough ready to accompany him. In 1570, he made his first expedition with two ships; and the next year with only one, in which he returned safe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not with such advantages, as he expected. He made another expedition in 1572, wherein he did the Spaniards some mischief, and gained considerable booties. In these expeditions he was much assisted by a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of Indians, who then were, and have been ever since, engaged in perpetual wars with the Spaniards. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of these people was named Pedro; to whom Drake presented a fine cutlass from his side, which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> greatly admired. Pedro, in return, gave him four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> wedges of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; which Drake threw into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stock, saying, That he thought it but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> that such as bore the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of so uncertain a voyage on his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, should share the utmost advantage that voyage produced. Then, embarking his men with all the wealth he had obtained, which was very considerable, he bore away for England, where he arrived in August 1573. His success in this expedition, joined to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> behaviour towards his owners, gained him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> he made of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, a still greater. For, fitting out three stout frigates at his own expense, he sailed with them to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; where, under Walter <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, the father of the famous unfortunate earl, he served as a volunteer, and did many glorious actions. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his noble <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, he returned to England; where Sir Christopher Hatton introduced him to her majesty, and procured him countenance and protection at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. By this means he acquired a capacity of undertaking that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> expedition which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> render his name immortal. The first thing he proposed was a voyage into the South seas through the straits of Magellan; which was what hitherto no Englishman had ever attempted. This project was well received at court; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> furnished him with means; and his own fame quickly drew together a sufficient force. The fleet with which he sailed on this extraordinary undertaking, consisted only of five vessels, small when compared with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> ships, and no more than 162 able men. He sailed on the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1577; on the 25th fell in with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Barbary, and on the 29th with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Verd. On the 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> he passed the equinoctial, made the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> on the 5th of April, and entered the river de la Plata, where he lost the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of two of his ships; but meeting them again, and taking out their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, he turned them adrift. On the 29th of May he entered the port of St Julian's, where he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> two months for the sake of laying in provisions; on the 20th of August he entered the straits of Magellan, and on the 25th of September passed them, having then only his own ship. On the 25th of November he came to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACAO">Macao</a>, which he had appointed for a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of rendezvous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> his ships separated; but Captain Winter his vice admiral having repassed the straits, was returned to England. Thence he continued his voyage along the coast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, taking all opportunities of seizing Spanish ships, and attacking them on shore, till his men were sated with plunder; and then, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> to the height of 48 degrees, he endeavoured to find a passage that way back into our seas, but could not. However he landed, and called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> New <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a>, taking possession of it in the name and for the use of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; and having careened his ship, set sail from thence on the 29th September 1579, for the Moluccas. He is supposed to have chosen this passage round, partly to avoid being attacked by the Spaniards at a disadvantage, and partly from the lateness of the season, whence dangerous storms and hurricanes were apprehended. On the 13th of October he fell in with certain <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> inhabited by the most barbarous people he had met with in all his voyage: on the 4th of November he had sight of the Moluccas; and, coming to Ternate, was extremely well received by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> thereof, who appears from the most authentic relations of this voyage to have been a wise and politic prince. On the 10th of December he made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>; where his ship unfortunately ran upon a rock, the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> following; from which, beyond all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, and in a manner miraculously, they got off, and continued their course. On the 16th of March he arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>; and from thence he intended to have directed his course to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>; but found himself obliged to alter his purpose, and to think of returning home. On the 25th of March 1580, he put this design in execution; and on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> he doubled the Cape of Good Hope, having then on board 57 men, and but three casks of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. On the 12th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> he passed the line, reached the coast of Guinea on the 16th, and there watered. On the 11th of September he made the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Tercras; and on the 3d of November entered the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>. This voyage round the world was performed in two years and about ten months. Shortly after his arrival, the queen going to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> went on board his ship; where, after dinner, she conferred on him the order of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, and declared her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> approbation of all he had done. She likewise gave directions for the preservation of his ship, that it might remain a monument of his own and his country's Drake's country's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. This celebrated ship, which had been contemplated many years at Deptford, at length decaying, it was broke up, and a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, made out of the planks, was presented to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; upon which the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Cowley made the following verses: To this great ship, which round the world has run, And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATCH">match</a>'d in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> the chariot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>: This Pythagorean ship (for it may claim Without presumption, so deserved a name, By knowledge once, and transformation now) In her new shape this sacred port allow. Drake and his ship could not have wished, from fate, A happier station, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more blest estate: For lo! a seat of endless rest is given, To her in Oxford, and to him in heaven. Works, Vol. II. In the year 1585, he sailed with a fleet to the West Indies, and took the cities of St Jago, St Domingo, Cartagena, and St Augustine. In 1587, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> with a fleet of 30 sail; and having intelligence of a great fleet assembled in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, which was to have made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the armada, he with great courage entered that port, and burnt there upwards of 10,000 tons of shipping: which he afterwards merrily called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the king of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. In 1588, when the armada from Spain was approaching our coasts, Sir Francis Drake was appointed vice-admiral under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Howard of Effingham, high admiral of England, where fortune favoured him as remarkably as ever: for he made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of a very large galleon, commanded by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Pedro de Valdez, who was reputed the projector of this invasion. This affair happened in the following manner: On the 22d of July, Sir Francis observing a great Spanish ship floating at a distance from both fleets, sent his pinnace to summon the commander to yield. Valdez replied, with much Spanish solemnity, that they were 450 strong; that he himself was Don Pedro, and stood much upon his honour; and thereupon propounded several conditions, upon which he was willing to yield. But the vice-admiral replied, that he had no leisure to parley; but if he thought fit instantly to yield, he might; if not, he should soon find that Drake was no coward. Pedro, hearing the name of Drake, immediately yielded, and with 46 of his attendants came on board Drake's ship. This Don Pedro remained about two years Sir Francis Drake's prisoner in England; and when he was released, paid him for his own and his captain's liberties a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of 350l. Drake's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were well recompensed with the plunder of this ship; for they found in it 55,000 ducats of gold, which were divided among them. A little before this formidable Spanish armament put to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> of his Catholic majesty had the confidence to propound to Queen Elizabeth, in Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, the terms upon which she might hope for peace; which, with an English translation by Dr Fuller, we will insert in this place, because Drake's expedition to the West Indies makes a part of this message. The verses are these: Te voto ne pergas bello defendere Belgas; Quae Dracus eripuit nunc restituantur oportet: Quas pater evertit jubeto te condere cellas: Religio Papae fac restituantur <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> unguem. These to you are our commands, Send no help to th' <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>: Of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> took by Drake, Restitution you must make: And those abbeys build anew, Which your father overthrew: If for any peace you hope, In all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> restore the pope. The queen's extempore return: Ad Graecas, bone rex, fiant mandata kalendas. Worthy king, know this you will At Latter Lammas we'll fulfil. In the year 1559, Sir Francis Drake commanded as admiral the fleet sent to restore Don Antonio, king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces being given to Sir John Norris: but they were hardly got to sea, before the commanders differed, and so the attempt proved abortive. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Spain continuing, a more effectual expedition was undertaken by Sir John Hawkins and Sir Francis Drake, against their settlements in the West Indies, than had hitherto been made during the whole course of it: but the commanders here again not agreeing about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, this also did not turn out so successfully as was expected. All difficulties, before these two last expeditions, had given way to the skill and fortune of Sir Francis Drake; which probably was the reason why he did not bear these disappointments so well as he otherwise would have done. A strong <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of them is supposed to have thrown him into a melancholy, which occasioned a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>; and of this he died on board his own ship, near the town of Nombre de Dios in the West Indies, on the 28th of January 1595-6. His death was lamented by the whole nation, and particularly by his countrymen; who had great reason to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> him from the circumstance of his private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as well as to esteem him in his public character. He was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> for the town of Bossiny, alias Tintagal, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cornwall, in the 27th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Queen Elizabeth; and for Plymouth in Devonshire, in the 35th of the same reign. This town had very particular obligations to him: for, in the year 1587, he undertook to bring water into it, through the want of which, till then, it had been grievously distressed; and he performed it by conducting thither a stream from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> at eight miles distance, that is to say, in a straight line: for in the manner he brought it, the course of it runs upwards of 20 miles.

DRAKENBORCH

Pages 342-343

ARNOLD, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws. This celebrated literary character was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, and was born on the 1st of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1684, and in which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> he was afterwards professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Gravinus and Burmann taught him the belles lettres, and Cornelius Van Eck was his preceptor while he devoted his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. He succeeded Professor Burmann in the year 1716, and terminated his mortal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> in 1748, in the 64th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was an author of very considerable eminence, as the following publications sufficiently evince. His dissertation entitled, Disputatio Philologica Hist. Hist. de praefectis urbis, in 4to, proves him to have been an able philologist; and gave flattering indications of future eminence. Its intrinsic merit caused it to be reprinted at Frankfort-on-the-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, in 1750, by Professor Uhl, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of its learned author. His next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled Disputatio de officio praefectorum praetorio, was published in the year 1757; and ten years after his C. Sili Italicus Punicorum, in 17 books, to render which perfect and complete, nothing was omitted by this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; many historical subjects being engraved for the purpose of elucidating the text, to which his own copious and learned annotations most powerfully contributed. His splendid edition of Livy, with a life of that eminent historian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> render his name immortal. It is entitled T. Livii Patavinii historiarum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> urbe condita libri, qui supervent, omnes. Lugd. Batav. 1738 and 1746; 7 tom. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to this work is very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and replete with erudition, giving a particular account of all the literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> who have at different periods commented on the works of Livy. He took the edition of Gronovius for his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, as being in his estimation the most correct; but he made many important alterations on the authority of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> which it is probable Gronovius had either never seen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not taken the pains to consult. Upon the whole, this edition of Livy is at once the most elaborate, interesting, and instructive, ever given to the world, since into it he has introduced the criticisms of Duchier, Gronovius, Perizonius, and Signonius; in addition to his own, which are certainly fraught with much literature and deep discernment.

DRAMA

Pages 343-343

a poem containing some certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and representing a true <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, for the delight and improvement of mankind. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the drama are two, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> and tragedy. See the subject fully considered in a historical view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> dramas, in the article DRAMA, Supplement.

DRAMATIC
