an epithet given to pieces written for the stage. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">POETRY</a>.

DRAN

Pages 343-343

Henry Francis Le, a French surgeon of distinguished eminence, was born in the year 1685. His father followed the same profession at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and was highly celebrated for his treatment of cancers. Dran had much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> as well as abilities, although his anatomical knowledge was rather circumscribed, and his acquaintance with books was far from being extensive. In 1730, he published in 8vo a valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled Parallele des différentes Manières de tirer la Pierre hors de la Vessie. In this work he takes a comparative view of the different modes of performing the hazardous operation of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITHOTOMY">lithotomy</a>, preferring the lateral method which was practised by Cheselden. In the year 1731, he published his Observations de Chirurgie, avec des Reflections, in 2 vols 12mo, which is justly considered as a valuable performance for men who are employed in the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>. In 1757, appeared his Traité ou Reflections tirées de la Pratique sur les Plages d’Armes à Feu; in which he gives the results of his own practice while in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, with efficacious methods for the cure of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> wounds. Gataker translated into English his Traité des Operations de Chirurgie, to which many interesting observations were added by Cheselden. In 1765, were published his Consultations sur la plupart des Maladies qui sont du Ressort de la Chirurgie; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of which is admirably calculated for the instruction of young practitioners. As at least one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the merit of Dran’s works, translations of them have been made into various languages. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> his judgment was penetrating, he was equally famed for his successful operations. He died at Paris in the year 1775, in the 85th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

DRANK

Pages 343-343

among farmers, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote wild oats, which never fail to infest worn-out lands; so that, when ploughed lands run to these weeds and thistles, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> knows it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to fallow them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> else to sow them with hay seed, and make pasture of them.

DRAPERY

Pages 343-343

in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, signifies the representation of the clothing of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> figures, and also hangings, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, curtains, and most other things that are not carnations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> landscapes. See PAINTING, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CRAYON">CRAYON</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">DRAWING</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">MINIATURE</a>.

DRASTIC

Pages 343-343

in Physic, an epithet bestowed on such medicines as are of present efficacy, and potent in operation; and is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> applied to emetics and cathartics.

DRAUGHT

Pages 343-344

body of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> whose depth is equal to 12 feet, to float <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWBACK">Drawback</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUOY">buoy</a> up a ship on its surface, she is said to draw 12 feet water; and that this draught may be more readily known, the feet are marked on the stem and stern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>, regularly from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> upwards. DRAUGHT-Hooks, are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hooks of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, fixed on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> of a cannon carriage, two on each side, one near the trunnion-hole, and the other at the train, distinguished by the name of fore and hind draught hooks. Large guns have draught hooks near the middle transom, to which are fixed the chains that serve to keep the shafts of the limbers on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>. The fore and hind hooks are used for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> backwards or forwards, by men with strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, called draught-ropes, fixed to these hooks. DRAUGHT-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>, in farming, a sort of coarse-made horse, destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CART">cart</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>.

DRAVE

Pages 343-343

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> navigable river, which, taking its rise in the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>, in Germany, runs south-east through Stiria; and continuing its course, divides <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> from Slavonia, and falls into the Danube at Esseck.

DRAWBACK

Pages 344-344

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, certain duties, either of the customs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, allowed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of some of our own <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, or upon certain foreign merchandises, that have paid duty on importation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> importing and exporting are required to obtain the drawback on foreign goods, affirming the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the officers certificate on the entry, and the due payment of the duties: and these may be made by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> or husband of any corporation or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; or by the known <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of any merchant usually employed in making his entries, and paying his customs. In regard to foreign goods entered outward, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or value be fraudulently shipped out than what is expressed in the exporter's certificate, the goods therein mentioned, or their value, are forfeited, and no drawback to be allowed for the same. Foreign goods exported by certificate in order to obtain the drawback, not shipped or exported, or relanded in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, unless in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of distress to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> them from perishing, are to lose the benefit of the drawback, and are forfeited, or their value, with the vessel, horses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, &c. employed in the relanding thereof; and the persons employed in the relanding them, or by whose privity they are relanded, or into whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> they shall knowingly come, are to forfeit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the amount of the drawback. Officers of the customs conniving at, or assisting in any fraud relating to certificate goods, besides other penalties, are to forfeit their office, and suffer six months imprisonment without bail or mainprise; as are also masters, or persons belonging to the ships employed therein. Bonds given for the exportation of certificate goods to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> must not be delivered up, nor drawback allowed for any goods, till a certificate under the hands and seals of the collector or comptroller, &c. of the customs be produced, testifying the landing. Draw-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>, a bridge made after the manner of a float, to draw up or let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, as occasions serve, before the gate of a town or castle. See Bridge. A draw-bridge may be made after several different ways; but the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> are made with plyers, twice the length of the gate, and a foot in diameter. The inner <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is traversed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, which serves for a counterpoise; and the chains which hang from the extremities of the plyers to lift up or let down the bridge are of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. In navigable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> it is sometimes necessary to make the middle <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of bridges with two moveable platforms, to be raised occasionally, in order to let the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> and rigging of ships <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through. This kind of draw-bridge is represented in Plate CLXVIII., where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> is the width of the middle arch; AL and BL, the two piers that support the draw-bridge NO, one of the platforms of which is raised, and the other let down, having the beam PQ for its plyer. To NO are suspended two moveable braces EH, EH; which resting on the support E, press against the bracket M, and thereby strengthen the draw-bridge. These braces are conducted to the rest by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> S, pulling the chain SLF. Draw-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">Net</a>, a kind of net for taking the larger sort of wildfowl, which ought to be made of the best sort of packthread, with wide meshes; they should be about two fathoms deep and six <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, verged on each side with a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, and stretched at each end on long <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. It should be spread smooth and flat upon the ground; and strewed over with grass, sedge, or the like, to hide it from the fowl; and the sportsman is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself in some shelter of grass, fern, or some such thing.

DRAWING

Pages 344-352

THE art of representing the appearances of objects upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> surface, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, shades, and shadows, formed with certain materials adapted to the purpose. § 1. Of the proper Materials for Drawing, and the manner of using them. The first thing necessary for a beginner is to furnish himself with proper materials, such as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> pencils, crayons of black, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> chalk, crow-quill pens, a rule and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>, camel's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> pencils, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>. He must accustom himself to hold the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> farther from the point than one does a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> give him a better command of it, and contribute to render the strokes more free and bold. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the pencil is to draw the first sketches or outlines of the piece, as any stroke or line that is amiss may in this be more easily rubbed out than in any other thing; and when he has made the sketch as correct as he can with the pencil, he may then draw carefully the best outline he has got, with his crow-quill pen and ink (A); after which he may discharge the pencil lines, by rubbing the piece gently with the crumb of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> or Indian-rubber. Having thus got the outline clear, his next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> the piece properly, either by drawing fine strokes with his pen where it requires to be shaded, or by washing it with his pencil and the Indian ink. As to his rule and compasses, they are never, or very rarely to be used, except in measuring the proportions of figures after he has drawn them, to prove whether they are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or not; or in houses, fortifications, and other pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. § 2. Of Drawing Lines, Squares, Circles, and other regular and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> Figures. Having got all these implements in readiness, the first practice must be to draw straight and curve lines, with ease and freedom, upwards and downwards, side-wise to the right or left, or in any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> whatsoever. He must also learn to draw, by command of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, squares, circles, ovals, and other geometrical figures: for, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, or a knowledge of the letters, is an introduction to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>; so is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> to drawing. The practice of drawing these simple figures till he is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of them, will enable him to imitate, with greater ease and accuracy, many things both in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art. And here it is proper to admonish him, never to be in a hurry: but to make himself perfectly master of one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> before he proceeds to another: the advantage, and even <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, of this, will appear as he proceeds. Two observations more may be added: 1. That he accustom himself to draw all his figures very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, which is the only way of acquiring a free bold manner of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>. 2. That he practise drawing till he has gained a tolerable mastery of his pencil, before he attempts to shadow any figure or object of any kind whatever. § 3. Of Drawing Eyes, Ears, Legs, Arms, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">Hands</a>, Feet, &c. As to the drawing of eyes and ears, legs and arms, the learner will have very little more to do than to copy carefully the examples given in Plate CLXXVII. and CLXXVIII. taken from Sebastian le Clerc's drawing book. But the actions and postures of the hands are so many and various, that no certain rules can be giving for drawing them, that will universally hold good. Yet as the hands and feet are difficult members to draw, it is very necessary, and well worth while, to bestow some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and pains about them, carefully imitating their various postures and actions, so as not only to avoid all lameness and imperfection, but also to give them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and spirit. To arrive at this, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and practice, are requisite; particularly in imitating the best <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> or drawings that can be got of hands and feet (some good examples of which are given in Plate CLXXVIII.) for, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> rules of drawing them by lines and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, they are not only perplexed and difficult, but also contrary to the practice of the best masters. One general rule, however, may be given (which is universally to be observed in all subjects), and that is, Not to finish perfectly at first any single <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, but to sketch out faintly, and with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> strokes of the pencil, the shape and proportion of the whole hand, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and turn of it; and after considering carefully whether this first sketch be perfect, and altering it wherever it is amiss, you may then proceed to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, the knuckles, the veins, and other small particulars, which, when the learner has got the whole shape and proportion of the hand or foot, will not only be more easily but also more perfectly designed. § 4. Of Drawing Faces. The head is usually divided into four equal parts, (1.) From the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the head to the top of the forehead. (2.) From the top of the forehead to the eyebrows. (3.) From the eyebrows to the bottom of the nose. (4.) From thence to the bottom of the chin. But this proportion is not constant; those features in different men being often very different as to length and shape. In a well-proportioned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, however, they are nearly right. To <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the learner therefore in forming a perfect face, his first business is to draw an oval, or rather the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; in the middle of which, from the top to the bottom, draw a perpendicular line. Through the centre or middle of this line draw a diameter line, directly across from one side to the other of your oval. On these two lines all the features of your face are to be placed as follows: Divide your perpendicular line into four equal parts; the first must be allotted to the hair of the head; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is from the top of the forehead to the top of the nose between the eyebrows; the third is from thence to the bottom of the nose; and the fourth includes the lips and chin. Your diameter line, or the breadth of the face, is always supposed to be the length of five eyes; you must therefore divide it into five equal parts, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the eyes upon it so as to leave exactly the length of one eye betwixt them. This is to be understood only of a full <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> face, Plate CLXXVII. fig. a; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it turn to either side, then the distances are to be lessened on that side which turns from you, less or more in proportion to its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> (fig. b b b). The top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> is to rise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the eyebrows, at the end of the diameter line; and the bottom of it must be equal to the bottom of the nose. The nostrils ought not to come out farther than the corner of the eye in any face; and the middle of the mouth must always be placed upon the perpendicular line. § 5. Of Drawing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Figures. When the learner is tolerably perfect in drawing faces, heads, hands, and feet, he may next attempt to draw the human figure at length. In order to which, let him first sketch the head; then draw a perpendicular (A) The ink made use of for this purpose must not be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> but Indian ink; which is much softer than the other, and does not run; by mixing it with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it may be made to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of strength, and used in a pen like common ink. lar line from the bottom of the head <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times its length (for the length of the head is about one-eighth part of the length of the figure). The best proportioned figures of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are 7½ heads in height. If, therefore, the figure stands upright, (as fig. a, Plate CLXXIX.) draw a perpendicular line from the top of the head to the heel, which must be divided into two equal parts. The bottom of the belly is exactly the centre. Divide the lower part into two equal parts again, the middle of which is the middle of the knee. For the upper part of the figure, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> must be varied. Take off with your compasses the length of the face (which is three parts in four of the length of the head; from the throat pit to the pit of the stomach is one face, from thence to the navel is another, and from thence to the lower rim of the belly is a third. The line must be divided into seven equal parts. Against the end of the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, place the breasts; the second comes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the navel; the third to the privities; the fourth to the middle of the thigh; the fifth to the lower part of the knee; the sixth to the lower part of the calf; and the seventh to the bottom of the heel, the heel of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> leg being always exactly under the pit of the throat. But as the essence of all drawing consists in making at first a good sketch, the learner must in this particular be very careful and accurate; he ought to draw no one part perfect or exact till he see whether the whole draught be good; and when he has altered that to his mind, he may then finish one part after another as perfectly as he can. There are some who, having a statue to copy, begin with the head, which they finish, and then proceed in the same manner to the other parts of the body, finishing as they go; but this method generally succeeds ill; for if the head be made in the least too big or too little, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is a disproportion between all the parts, occasioned by their not having sketched the whole proportionably at first. Let the learner remember, therefore, in whatever he intends to draw, first to sketch its several parts, measuring the distances and proportions between each with his finger or pencil, without using the compasses; and then judge of them by the eye, which by degrees will be able to judge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and proportion, and will become his best and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> guide. And let him observe, as a general rule, always to begin with the right side of the piece he is copying: for by that means he will always have what he has done before his eyes; and the rest will follow more naturally, and with greater ease; whereas if he begin with the left side, his hand and arm will cover what he does first, and deprive him of the sight of it; by which means he will not be able to proceed with so much ease, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, or certainty. As to the order and manner of proceeding in drawing the human body, he must first sketch the head; then the shoulders in the exact breadth; then draw the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the body, beginning with the armpits (leaving the arms till afterwards), and so draw down to the hips on both sides; and be sure he observe the exact breadth of the waist. When he has done this, let him then draw that leg which the body stands upon; and afterwards the other which stands loose; then the arms; and last of all the hands. He must take notice also of the bowings and bendings that are in the body; making the part which is opposite to that which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> correspond to it in bending with it. For instance: If one side of the body <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> in, the other must stand out answerable to it; if the back bend in, the belly must stick out; if the knee bend out, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">ham</a> must <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in; and so of any other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of the body. Finally, he must endeavor to form all parts of the figure with truth, and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> proportion; not one arm or one leg bigger or less than the other; not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> Herculean shoulders, with a thin and slender waist; nor raw and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> arms, with thick and gouty legs: but let there be a kind of harmonious agreement amongst the members, and a beautiful symmetry throughout the whole figure. Proportions and Measures of the Human Body. The centre or middle part, between the two extremes of the head and feet of a new born child, is in the navel, but that of an adult is in the os <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-PUBIS">pubis</a>; and the practice of dividing the measures of children into four, five, or six parts, whereof the head is one, is made use of by painters and sculptors. A child of two years old has about five heads in its whole length, but one of four or five years old has near six; about the fifteenth or sixteenth year, seven heads are the proportion or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, and the centre inclines to the upper part of the pubis. Hence it appears, as the growth of the body advances, there is a gradual approach to the proportion of an adult of near eight heads in the whole length, of which, as mentioned above, the head makes one. Agreeable to these principles, the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> is constructed, exhibiting the proportions of the parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and of a woman, as they were fixed by the ancients, and measured by M. Audran from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> Pythius (Plate CLXXX.) in the garden of the Vatican at Rome, and the Venus Aphrodites (Plate CLXXXI.) belonging to the family of the Medicis. Supposing the figures to stand upright and duly poised on both legs, the whole height of the former is divided into $3\frac{1}{2}$ parts, being 7 heads 3 parts and 6 minutes; and that of the latter other most admired antique <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> differ a little from these proportions, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAOCOON">Laocoon</a> measuring 7 h. 2 p. 3 m. the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> 7 h. 3 p. 7 m. the Pyramus 7 h. 2 p. the Antinous 7 h. 2 p. the Grecian shepherdess 7 h. 3 p. 6 m. and the Mirmillo 8 h. But all their other proportions are allowed to be harmonious and agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the figures they represent. The most remarkable differences of the symmetry or proportions of a man and of a woman to be observed from the Table are: First, The shoulders of a man are broader, measuring two heads, and the haunches narrower, measuring 1 h. 1 p. 5 m. whereas the shoulders of a woman measure only 1 h. 3 p. 8 m. and the haunches measure 1 h. 2 p. 3 m. The sternum or breast-bone of a man is longer, measuring 3 p. 8 m. and the sternum of the woman only 3 p. 3 m. On the contrary, the pelvis of a man is less, measuring from the top to bottom only 4 p. whereas the pelvis of a woman measures from the top to the bottom 4 p. 3 m. It is a leading principle, in which every person conversant in designing has agreed, that without a perfect knowledge of the proportions, nothing can be produced but monstrous and extravagant figures; and it is also universally admitted, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek and Roman sculptors attained the highest success in producing the most perfect models. The greatest of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> artists who have examined their figures with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> admit, that several of the ancient sculptors in some degree have excelled nature, they never having found any man so perfect in all his parts as some of their figures are. Their opportunities indeed were great; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> abounded with beauties; and Rome being mistress of the world, every thing that was curious and beautiful was brought to it from all parts. Their motives were also powerful; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. They considered it as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship to give the figures of their gods so much nobleness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> as to be able to attract the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and veneration of the people. Their own glory was also concerned, particular honours being bestowed on those who succeeded; and for their fortune they had no further care to take when they once arrived at a certain degree of merit. Attitudes and Action of the Muscles. If a strong person is to be represented in a vigorous action, such as Hercules, &c. after a suitable proportion to such a figure and the action is designed, the parts or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> employed in the chiefest force of the action ought to be considered. If the figure is standing, the foot must be placed in a right line, or perpendicular to the trunk or bulk of the body, where the centre of gravity may be placed in equilibrio. This centre is determined by the heel: or, if the figure is upon tiptoe, then the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of the great toe is in the centre. The muscles of the leg which supports the body ought to be swollen, and their tendons drawn more to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> than those of the other leg, which is only placed so as to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the body towards that way to which the action inclines it. For example, suppose Hercules with a club striking at any thing before him towards the left side: Then let his right leg be placed so as to receive the whole weight of the body, and the left loosely touching the ground with his toes. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> muscles of the right leg ought to be expressed very strong; but those of the left scarcely appearing more than if it were in some sedentary posture, except in the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. The foot being extended, the muscles which compose the calf of the leg are in action and appear very strong; though it is not meant that all the muscles of the right leg, which supports the weight of the body, ought to be expressed very strong or equally swelled, but those most tumefied which are chiefly concerned in the action or posture that the leg is then in. For example, if the leg or tibia is extended, then the extending muscles placed on the thigh are most swollen; if it is bended, then the bending muscles and their tendons appear most. The like may be observed of the whole body in general when it is put into vigorous action. The Laocoön formerly in the Vatican garden at Rome, now in the Louvre at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, furnishes an example of this muscular appearance through the whole; but in the Antinous, Apollo, also in the Louvre, and other figures of the ancients, in postures where no considerable actions are designed, we see their muscles expressed but faintly, or scarcely appearing. The clavicles or collar-bones, and muscles in general, do not appear in women as in men; nor will any action in which a woman uses her utmost strength occasion such swellings or risings of the muscles to appear as they do in men, since the great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fat placed under the skin of women so clothes their muscles, &c., as to prevent any such appearance. Effects of the Exertion of the Muscles. The following are the most obvious effects of the exertion of several of the muscles; of those, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, which chiefly demand the attention of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. If either of the mastoid muscles (Plate CLXXXII. 1. 1.) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, the head is turned to the contrary side, and the muscle which performs that action appears very plain under the skin. If the arms are lifted up, the deltoid muscles placed on the shoulders, which perform that action, swell, and make the extremities of the spines of the shoulder-blades (Plate CLXXXIII. 3. 3.), called the tops of the shoulders, appear indented or hollow. The shoulder-blades following the elevation of the arms, their bases (Plate CLXXXIII. 4. 4.) incline at that time obliquely downward. If the arms are drawn down, put forwards, or pulled backwards, the shoulder-blades necessarily vary their positions accordingly. All these particulars are to be learned by consulting the life only; when being well acquainted with what then appears in every action, the artist will be able to form an adequate idea how it ought to be expressed. These circumstances are little known; hence seldom attended to in designing. When the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> or fore-arm is bended, the biceps (Plate CLXXXII. 5. 5.) has its belly very much raised, as appears in the left arm. The like may be observed of the triceps (Plate CLXXXIII. 6. 6.) when the arm is extended as observed in the right arm. The straight muscles of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> (Plate CLXXXII. 7. 7.) appear very strong when rising from a decumbent posture. The parts of the great serratus muscle (ib. 8. 8.) which are received in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> or beginnings of the oblique descending muscle immediately below, are very much swelled when the shoulder on the same side is brought forwards; that serratus muscle then being in action in drawing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCAPULAR">scapular</a> forwards. The long extending muscles of the trunk (Plate CLXXXIII. 9. 9.) act alternately in walking, after this manner: If the right leg bears the weight of the body, and the left is in translation as on tiptoe, the last-mentioned muscles of the back on the left side may be observed to be tumefied on the other side about the region of the loins, and so on the other side. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROCHANTERS">trochanters</a>, or outward and uppermost heads of the thigh-bones (Plate CLXXXIII. 10. 10.), vary in their positions in such a manner as no precise observation can explain their several appearances; but the study after the life ought to be carefully attended to. If the thigh is extended, as when the whole weight of the body rests on that side, the gluteus or buttock muscle (Plate CLXXXIII. 11. 11.) makes a very different appearance from what offers at another time; but if the thigh is drawn backwards, that muscle appears still more and more tumefied. When the whole leg is drawn upwards forwards, and at the same time the foot is inclined inwards, the upper part of the sartorius muscle (Plate CLXXXII. 12. 12.) appears rising very strong; in other positions of the thigh, that muscle makes a furrowing appearance in its whole progress. If a man is upon tiptoe, the extending muscles of the leg placed on the fore part of the thigh (Plate CLXXXII. 13. 13. 13.), and those of the foot that compose the calf of the leg (Plate CLXXXIII. 14. 14.) appear very strong, and the long peroneous (Plate CLXXXII. 15.) makes a considerable indentation or furrowing at that time in its progress on the outside of the leg. Many other remarks might here be offered: but a due attention to nature will soon discover them. § 6. Of Light and Shade. After the learner has made himself in some measure perfect in drawing outlines, his next endeavour must be to shade them properly. It is this which gives an appearance of substance, shape, distance, and distinction, to whatever body he endeavours to represent, whether animate or inanimate. The best rule for doing this is, to consider from what point, and in what direction, the light falls upon the objects which he is delineating, and to let all his lights and shades be placed according to that direction throughout the whole work. That part of the object must be lightest which hath the light most directly opposite to it; if the light falls sideways on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, he must make that side which is opposite to it lightest, and that side which is farthest from it darkest. If he is drawing the figure of a man, and the light be placed above the head, then the top of the head must be made lightest, the shoulders next lightest, and the lower parts darker by degrees. That part of the object, whether in naked figures or drapery, or buildings, that stands farthest out, must be made the lightest, because it comes nearest to the light; and the light loseth so much of its brightness, by how much any part of the body bends inward, because those parts that stick out hinder the lustre and full brightness of the light from striking on those parts that fall in. Titian used to say, that he knew no better rule for the distribution of lights and shadows than his observations drawn from a bunch of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>. Satins and silks, and all other shining stuffs, have certain glancing reflections, exceeding bright where the light falls strongest. The like is seen in armour, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> pots, or any other glittering metal, where you see a sudden brightness in the middle or centre of the light, which discovers the shining nature of such things. Observe also, that a strong light requires a strong shade; a fainter light a fainter shade; and that an equal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> be preserved throughout the piece between the lights and shades. Those parts which must appear round require but one stroke in shading, and that sometimes but very faint; such parts as should appear steep or hollow, require two strokes across each other, or sometimes three, which is sufficient for the deepest shade. Care must be also taken to make the outlines faint and small in such parts as receive the light; but where the shades fall, the outline must be strong and bold. The learner must begin his shadings from the top, and proceed downward, and use his utmost endeavours both by practice and observation to learn how to vary the shadings properly; for in this consists a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of the beauty and elegance of drawing. Another thing to be observed is, that as the human sight is weakened by distances, so objects must seem more or less confused or clear according to the places they hold in the piece: Those that are very distant,—weak, faint, and confused; those that are near and on the foremost ground,—clear, strong, and accurately finished. § 7. Of Drapery. In the art of clothing the figures, or casting the drapery properly and elegantly upon them, many things are to be observed. 1. The eye must never be in doubt of its object; but the shape and proportion of the part or limb, which the drapery is supposed to cover, must appear; at least so far as art and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> will permit: and this is so material a consideration, that many artists draw first the naked figure, and afterwards put the draperies upon it. 2. The drapery must not sit too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the parts of the body: but let it seem to flow round, and as it were to embrace them; yet so as that the figure may be easy, and have a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. 3. The draperies which cover those parts that are exposed to great light must not be so deeply shaded as to seem to pierce them; nor should those members be crossed by folds that are too strong, lest by the too great darkness of the shades the members look as if they were broken. 4. The great folds must be drawn first, and then stroked into lesser ones: and great care must be taken that they do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> one another improperly. 5. Folds in general should be large, and as few as possible. However, they must be greater or less according to the quantity and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the stuffs of which the drapery is supposed to be made. The quality of the person is also to be considered in the drapery. If they are magistrates, their draperies ought to be large and ample: if <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> clowns or slaves, they ought to be coarse and short; if ladies or nymphs, light and soft. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">Suit</a> the garments to the body, and make them bend with it, according as it stands in or out, straight or crooked; or as it bends one way or another; and the closer the garment sits to the body, the narrower and smaller must be the folds. 7. Folds well imagined give much spirit to any kind of action; because their motion implies a motion in the acting member, which seems to draw them forcibly, and makes them more or less stirring as the action is more or less violent. 8. An artful complication of folds in a circular manner greatly helps the effect of foreshortenings. 9. All folds consist of two shades, and na more; which you may turn with the garment at pleasure, shadowing the inner side deeper, and the outer more faintly. 10. The shades in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> are very thick and small, requiring little folds and a light shadow. 11. Observe the motion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, in order to draw the loose apparel all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> one way; and draw that part of the garment that adheres closest to the body before you draw the looser part that flies off from it; lest, by drawing the loose part of the garment first, you should mistake the position of the figure, and place it awry. 12. Rich ornaments, when judiciously and sparingly used, may sometimes contribute to the beauty of draperies. But such ornaments are far below the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> or heavenly figures; the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of whose draperies ought rather to consist in the boldness and nobleness of the folds, than in the quality of the stuff or the glitter of ornaments. 13. Light and flying draperies are proper only to figures in great motion, or in the wind: but when in a calm place, and free from violent action, their draperies should be large and flowing; that by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> and the fall of the folds, they may appear with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and dignity. Thus much for draperies; an example or two of which are given in Plate CLXXXIX. But see farther the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CRAYON">CRAYON</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">PAINTING</a>. § 8. On the Passions. The passions, says M. le Brun, are motions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, either upon her pursuing what she judges to be for her good, or shunning what she thinks hurtful to her; and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a>, whatever causes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> in the soul, creates also some action in the body. It is therefore necessary for a painter to know which are the different actions in the body that express the several passions of the soul, and how to delineate them. M. le Brun has been extremely happy in expressing many of the passions, and the learner cannot study anything better than the examples which he has left us of them. However, as M. de Piles justly observes, it is absurd as well as impossible to pretend to give such particular demonstrations of them as to fix their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> to certain strokes, which the painter should be obliged to make use of as essential and invariable rules. This (says he) would be depriving the art of that excellent variety of expression which has no other principle than diversity of imagination, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of which is infinite. The same passion may be finely expressed several ways, each yielding more or less pleasure in proportion to the painter's understanding and the spectator's discernment. Though every part of the face contributes towards expressing the sentiments of the heart, yet the eyebrow, according to M. le Brun, is the principal seat of expression, and where the passions best make themselves known. It is certain, says he, that the pupil of the eye, by its fire and motion, very well shows the agitation of the soul, but then it does not express the kind or nature of such an agitation; whereas the motion of the eyebrow differs according as the passions change their nature. To express a simple passion, the motion is simple; to express a mixed passion, the motion is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>: if the passion be gentle, the motion is gentle; and if it be violent, the motion is so too. We may observe farther, says he, that there are two two kinds of elevation in the eyebrows. One, in which the eyebrows rise up in the middle; this elevation expresses agreeable sensations, and it is to be observed that then the mouth rises at the corners: Another, in which the eyebrows rise up at the ends, and fall in the middle; this motion denotes bodily pain, and then the mouth falls at the corners. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>, all the parts agree; for the eyebrows, which fall toward the middle of the forehead, make the nose, the mouth, and the eyes, follow the same motion. In weeping, the motions are compound and contrary; for the eyebrows fall toward the nose and over the eyes, and the mouth rises that way. It is to be observed also, that the mouth is the part of the face which more particularly expresses the emotions of the heart: for when the heart complains, the mouth falls at the corners; when it is at ease, the corners of the mouth are elevated; and when it has an aversion, the mouth shoots forward, and rises in the middle. "The head (says M. de Piles) contributes more to the expression of the passions than all the other parts of the body put together. Those separately can only show some few passions, but the head expresses them all. Some, however, are more particularly expressed by it than others: as humility, by hanging it down; arrogance, by lifting it up; languishment, by inclining it to one side; and obstinacy, when with a stiff and resolute air it stands upright, fixed, and stiff between the two shoulders. The head also best shows our supplications, threats, mildness, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, love, hatred, joy, and grief. The whole face, and every feature, contributes something: especially the eyes; which, as Cicero says, are the windows of the soul. The passions they more particularly discover are, pleasure, languishing, scorn, severity, mildness, admiration, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>; to which one might add joy and grief, if they did not proceed more particularly from the eyebrows and mouth; but when those two passions fall in also with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the eyes, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> will be wonderful. But though the passions of the soul are more visible in the lines and features of the face, they often require the assistance also of the other parts of the body. Without the hands, for instance, all action is weak and imperfect; their motions, which are almost infinite, create numberless expressions: it is by them that we desire, hope, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, call, send back; they are the instruments of threatening, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, horror, and praise; by them we approve, condemn, refuse, admit, fear, ask; express our joy and grief, our doubts, regrets, pain, and admiration. In a word, it may be said, as they are the language of the dumb, that they contribute not a little to speak a language common to all nations, which is the language of painting. But to say how these parts must be disposed for expressing the various passions, is impossible; nor can any exact rules be given for it, both because the task would be infinite, and because every one must be guided in this by his own genius and the particular turn of his own studies." See the article PASSIONS, and the Plate there referred to. § 9. Of drawing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">Fruits</a>, Birds, Beasts, &c. The learner may proceed now to make some attempts at drawing flowers, fruits, birds, beasts, and the like; not only as it will be a more pleasing employment, but as it is an easier task, than the drawing of hands and feet, and other parts of the human body, which require not only more care, but greater exactness and nicer judgment. Very few rules or instructions are requisite upon this head: the best thing the learner can do is, to furnish himself with good prints or drawings by way of examples, and with great care and exactness to copy them. If it is the figure of a beast, begin with the forehead, and draw the nose, the upper and under jaw, and stop at the throat. Then go to the top of the head, and form the ears, neck, back, and continue the line till you have given the full shape of the buttock. Then form the breast, and mark out the legs and feet, and all the smaller parts. And, last of all, finish it with the proper shadows. It is not amiss, by way of ornament, to give a small sketch of landscape; and let it be suitable and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the place or country of the beast you draw. Much the same may be said with regard to birds. Of these, as well as beasts and other objects, the learner will find many examples among the plates given in this work. § 10. Of drawing Landscapes, Buildings, &c. Of all the parts of drawing, this is the most useful and necessary, and it is what every man may have occasion for at one time or another. To be able, on the spot, to take the sketch of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, or a beautiful prospect; of any curious production of art, or uncommon appearance in nature; is not only a very desirable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a>, but a very agreeable amusement. Rocks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, fields, woods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, catacombs, cities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, castles, houses, fortifications, ruins, or whatsoever else may present itself to view on our journeys or travels in our own or foreign countries, may be thus brought home, and preserved for our future use either in business or conversation. On this part, therefore, more than ordinary pains should be bestowed. All drawing consists in nicely measuring the distances of each part of the piece by the eye. In order to facilitate this, let the learner imagine in his own mind, that the piece he copies is divided into squares. For example: Suppose or imagine a perpendicular and a horizontal line crossing each other in the centre of the picture you are drawing from; then suppose also two such lines crossing your own copy. Observe in the original, what parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> those lines intersect, and let them fall on the same parts of the supposed lines in the copy: We say, the supposed lines; because though engravers, and others who copy with great exactness, divide both the copy and original into many squares, as below; yet this is a method not to be recommended, as it will be apt to deceive the learner, who will fancy himself a tolerable proficient, till he comes to draw after nature, where these helps are not to be had, when he will find himself miserably defective and utterly at a loss. If he is to draw a landscape from nature, let him take take his station on a rising ground, where he will have a large horizon; and mark his tablet into three divisions, downwards from the top to the bottom; and divide in his own mind the landscape he is to take, into three divisions also. Then let him turn his face directly opposite to the midst of the horizon, keeping his body fixed, and draw what is directly before his eyes upon the middle division of the tablet; then turn his head, but not his body, to the left hand, and delineate what he views there, joining it properly to what he had done before; and, lastly, do the same by what is to be seen upon his right hand, laying down every thing exactly both with respect to distance and proportion. One example is given on Plate CLXXIX. The best artists, in drawing their landscapes, make them shoot away one part lower than another. Those who make their landscapes mount up higher and higher, as if they stood at the bottom of a hill to take the prospect, commit a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>: the best way is to get upon a rising ground, make the nearest objects in the piece the highest, and those that are farther off to shoot away lower and lower till they come almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the line of the horizon, lessening every thing proportionally to its distance, and observing also to make the objects fainter and less distinct the farther they are removed from the eye. He must make all his lights and shades fall one way, and let every thing have its proper motion: as trees shaken by the wind, the small boughs bending more, and the large ones less: water agitated by the wind, and dashing against ships or boats, or falling from a precipice upon rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and spitting up again into the air, and sprinkling all about: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> also in the air; now gathered with the winds; now violently condensed into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and the like: Always remembering, that whatever motions are caused by the wind must be made all to move the same way, because the wind can blow but one way at once. Finally, It must be observed, that in order to attain any considerable proficiency in drawing, a knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">Perspective</a> is absolutely necessary: see that article. ---

DRAYTON

Pages 352-352

MICHAEL, an eminent English poet, was born in 1563, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>. His propensity to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was extremely strong, even from his infancy; and we find the most of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> poems published, and himself highly distinguished as a poet, by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was about 30 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.—It appears from his poem of Moses's Birth and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>, that he was a spectator at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> of the famous Spanish armada, and it is not improbable that he was engaged in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> employment there. It is certain, that not only for his merit as a writer but his valuable qualities as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, he was held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation, and strongly patronized by several personages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; particularly by Sir Henry Goodere, Sir Walter Aston, and the countess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>; to the first of whom he owns himself indebted for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> he was for many years supported. His poems are very numerous; and so elegant, that his manner has been copied by many <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers of eminence since. Among these the most celebrated one is the Poly-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a>, a chorographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of England, with its commodities, antiquities, and curiosities, in metre of 12 syllables; which he dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry, by whose encouragement it was written: and whatever may be thought of the poetry, his descriptions are allowed to be exact. He was styled poet laureat in his time: which, as Ben Johnson was then in that office, is to be understood in a loose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of approbation as an excellent poet; and was bestowed on others as well as Drayton, without being confined strictly to the office known by that appellation. He died in 1631; and was buried in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> among the poets, where his bust is to be seen, with an epitaph penned by Ben Johnson.

DREAMS

Pages 352-367

are all those thoughts which people feel passing through their minds, and those imaginary transactions in which they often fancy themselves engaged, when in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. Scarce any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is less open to our observation than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind in this state. The dreamer himself cannot well observe the manner in which dreams arise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disappear to him. When he awakes, he cannot recollect the circumstances of his dreams with sufficient accuracy. Were we to watch over him with the most vigilant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, we could not perceive with certainty what emotions are excited in his mind, or what thoughts <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it, during his sleep. But though we could ascertain these phenomena, many other difficulties would still remain. What parts of a human being are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, what dormant, when he dreams? Why does not he always dream while asleep? Or why dreams he at all? Do any circumstances in our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, situation, and peculiar character, determine the nature of our dreams? We may lay before our readers such facts as have been ascertained concerning dreaming, and the most plausible conjectures that have been offered to explain those particulars, about which we can only conjecture, or have at least hitherto obtained nothing more certain than conjecture. 1. In dreaming, we are not conscious of being asleep. This is well known from a thousand circumstances. When awake, we often recollect our dreams; and we remember on such occasions, that while those dreams were passing through our minds, it never occurred to us that we were separated by sleep from the active world. We are often observed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> and talk in dreaming as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we were busily engaged in the intercourse of social <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. 2. In dreaming, we do not consider ourselves as witnessing witnessing or hearing a part in a fictitious <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>: we seem not to be in a similar situation with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> in a dramatic performance, or the spectators before whom they exhibit, but engaged in the business of real life. All the varieties of thought that pass through our minds when awake may also occur in dreams; all the images which imagination presents in the former state, she is also able to call up in the latter; all the same emotions may be excited, and we are often actuated by equal violence of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; none of the transactions in which we are capable of engaging while awake is impossible in dreams: in short, our range of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and observation is equally wide in the one state as in the other; and while dreaming, we are not sensible of any distinction between our dreams and the events and transactions in which we are actually concerned in our intercourse with the world. 3. It is said that all men are not liable to dream. Dr Beattie, in a very pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on this subject, relates, that he knew a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who never dreamed except when his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was in a disordered state; and Locke mentions that a certain person of his acquaintance was almost a stranger to dreaming till the 26th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and then began to dream in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of having a fever. These instances, however, are too few, and we have not been able to obtain more; and, besides, it does not appear that those persons had always attended, with the care of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> making an experiment, to the circumstances of their sleep. They might dream, but not recollect their dreams on awaking; and they might both dream and recollect their dreams immediately upon awaking, yet afterwards suffer the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of them to slip out of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. We do not advance this, therefore, as a certain fact concerning dreaming; we are rather inclined to think it a mistake.

DREDGING

Pages 370-370

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for removing mud and other deposited matters from the beds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, &c. See Supplement.

DRELLINCOURT

Pages 370-370
CHARLES, minister of the reformed church at Paris, was born at Sedan in 1593, where his father enjoyed a considerable post. He had all the qualifications that compose a respectable clergyman; and though he defended the Protestant cause against the Romish religion, was much esteemed even among the Catholics. He is best known in England by his Consolations against the Fears of Death, which work was translated, and is often printed. He married the daughter of a rich merchant at Paris, by whom he had 16 children. His third son, professor of physic at Leyden, was physician to the prince and princess of Orange before their accession to the crown of England. Bayle has given him a high character. Mr Drelincourt died in 1665.

DRENCH

Pages 370-370

among farriers, a physical potion for horses. The ingredients for this purpose are to be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> coarsely, and either mingled with a decoction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with wine. Then let all infuse about a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and give it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> after he has been tied up two hours to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a>.

DREPANE

Pages 370-370

(Drepanum) in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Bithynia, situated between the Sinus Astacus and the Bosphorus Thraciæ; called Helenopolis by Constantine, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his mother. (Nicephorus Callistus).

DREPANUM

Pages 370-370

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the promontory Rhium in Achæa; so called because bent in the manner of a sickle. Another Drepanum on the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, on the side of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. A third on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYDONIA">Cydonia</a> and the Sinus Amphimallus. A fourth on the west side of Cyprus. A fifth, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, on the Mediterranean. DREPANUM,-i; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Drepana,-orum; a town and port on the west side of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and to the west of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERYX">Eryx</a>; Drepanitani the people. Now Trepano, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and port town on the westmost point of Sicily. F. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 8. N. Lat. 38. 0.

DRESDEN

Pages 370-371

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> in Germany. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, which divides it into two parts. One <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is called Old Dresden, and the other the New Town, in the German <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> Neustadt. They are joined together by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, supported by 19 piers, and 630 paces in length. As this bridge was too narrow for the crowds of people that were continually passing and repassing, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Augustus in 1730, caused two walks for foot passengers to be built, one on each side, in a very wonderful manner; the one for those that go into the city, and the other for those that return back. These are bordered with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> pallisadoes of curious workmanship. This noble bridge was much injured by the French in 1813. Dresden is surrounded by fortifications; and was said to contain 45,000 inhabitants in 1811. All the buildings of this city are constructed with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> freestone, and are almost all of the same height. They have stone from the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIRNA">Pirna</a>, about ten miles from this city, which is readily brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Elbe. In general the houses are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and strong; the streets wide, straight, well paved, clean, and well illuminated in the night; and there are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> squares, disposed in such a manner, that Dresden may <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for one of the handsomest cities in the world. The king's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is a magnificent structure, and abounds in many valuable curiosities both of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art. The collection of pictures is reckoned one of the finest that exists, and is valued at 500,000l. Above 700 men are here constantly employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> manufacture, the annual expense of which is estimated at no more than 80,000 crowns; and the manufacture yields to the king 200,000 crowns yearly, besides besides the magnificent presents which he occasionally makes, and the large <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> reserved for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. The other most considerable article of trade is silver, of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> near Erfurig produce every 15 days near the value of 20,000 dollars. The metal is brought into the city in ingots, where it is immediately coined and delivered to the proprietors. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Dresden is one of the most remarkable in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> for splendour and profusion. Six thousand five hundred ducats are yearly allowed for consorts and similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, which is near twice as much as the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> allows for the whole expense of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. The revenues of the king of Saxony are estimated at about 900,000; which arise from the taxes on lands, and a capitation on all males as soon as they commence an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> begin to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. People of a higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are taxed according to their class, and are liable to be called to account <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they assume not an exterior appearance correspondent to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their fortune. Every foreigner pays capitation after residing six months in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Jews are taxed at 50, their wives at 30, and their children at 20 dollars. There is also an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> on all eatables and liquors; and 10 per cent. is levied out of the incomes of the people. Though this city lies in a low situation, yet it hath agreeable prospects. It is supplied with a prodigious quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, not only out of the neighbourhood, but from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, which are brought every market <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, which is once a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 34. N. Lat. 51. 12. DRESSING of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">Hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">Flax</a>. See Flax-Dressing. DRESSING of Meats, the preparing them for food by means of culinary fire. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of dressing is to loosen the compages or texture of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and dispose it for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> and digestion in the stomach. Flesh not being a proper food without dressing, is alleged as an argument that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was not intended by nature for a carnivorous animal. The usual operations are roasting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, and stewing.—In roasting, it is observed, meat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear a much greater and longer <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> than either in boiling or stewing; and in boiling, greater and longer than in stewing. The reason is, that roasting being performed in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as the parts begin externally to warm, they extend and dilate, and so gradually let out part of the rarefied included air, by which means the internal succussions, on which the dissolution depends, are much weakened and abated. Boiling being performed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the pressure is greater, and consequently the succussions to lift up the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> are proportionably strong, by which means the cotion is hastened; and even in this way there are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> differences; for the greater the weight of water, the sooner is the business done. In stewing, though the heat be infinitely short of what is employed in the other ways, the operation is much more quick, because performed in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vessel, and full; by which means the succussions are oftener repeated, and more strongly reverberated. Hence the force of Papin's digester; and hence an illustration of the operation of digestion. Boiling, Dr Cheyne observes, draws more of the rank strong juices from meat, and leaves it less nutritive, more diluted, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, and easier of digestion; roasting, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, leaves it fuller of the strong nutritive juices, harder to digest, and needing more dilution. Strong, grown, and adult animal food, therefore, should be boiled, and the younger and tenderer roasted.

DRESSING

Pages 371-371

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the treatment of a wound, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any disordered <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of dressing consists of dressings, tents, plasters, compresses, bandages, bands, ligatures, and strings. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DREUX

Pages 371-371

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, remarkable for its antiquities; and for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> which was fought in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1562 between the Papists and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, in which the latter were defeated. Some think it took its name from the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>, in the times of Paganism. It consists of two parishes, St Stephen's, and Notre Dame, called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which is pretty well built.
