From thence he returned to Friesland, where he was admitted <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> professor in the university of Franeker; the functions of which he discharged with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1616. His works show him to have been well skilled in Hebrew; and the states-general employed him in 1600 to write notes on the most difficult <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, with a pension of 400 florins a-year: but being frequently disturbed in this undertaking, it was not published till after his death. He held a vast correspondence with the learned; for besides letters in Hebrew, Greek, and other languages, there were found 2300 Latin letters among his papers. He had a son John, who died in England at 21, and was a prodigy for his early acquisition of learning.

DRYADES

Pages 401-401

in the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a sort of deities, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> nymphs, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> thought inhabited groves and woods. They differed from the Hamadryades; these latter being attached to some particular tree, with which they were born, and with which they died; whereas the Dryades were goddesses of trees and woods in general. See HAMADRYADES.

DRYAS

Pages 401-401

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the icosandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 35th order, Senticose. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

Pages 404-404

See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DUBLIN

Pages 404-411

the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in his majesty's dominions, and esteemed the fifth for magnitude in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, is situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Dublin, at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>. The river Liffey, which here falls into the ocean, divides the town into two nearly equal parts. Formerly the city of Dublin was confined to the south side of the river. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, who flourished in the reign of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, about the year 140, says, it was anciently called Aschelod. In 155, Alpinus, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Auliana was drowned in the Liffey, changed the name from Aschelod to Auliana. It was afterwards named Dublana, and Ptolemy calls it Eblana. Dublana, whence comes Dublimum and Dublin, is evidently derived from Dub-leana, "the place of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> harbour <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lake," or rather "the lake of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>," the bay of Dublin being frequently so called. This city has had a variety of names. The Irish call it Drum-choll-eoil, "the brow of a hazel wood;" and in 181, Eogan <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> being on a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> tour, paid a visit to this place, which was then called Atha Cliath Dubh-Line, "the passage of the ford of hurdles over the black pool:" the harbour of Dublin was likewise known by the name of Lean-Cliath, or Lean-Cliath, from Lean or Lean, "a harbour;" and from Cliath or Cliabb, which literally signifies "a hurdle or any thing made of wicker <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>;" it also signified certain weirs formed with hurdles, and placed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and bays by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Irish for the purpose of taking fish: whence any river, or bay, wherein these weirs were fixed had the name of Cliath or Cliab, annexed to it, to signify the establishment of a fishery. Dublin, therefore, being originally built on or near one of these harbours, harbours, was anciently called Bally-leon-Cliath, that is, "the town on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> harbour." It is described at the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> by the appellations of Ath-Cliath, "the ford of hurdles," and Ballyath-Cliath, "the town of the ford of hurdles," the inhabitants having formerly had access to the river by hurdles laid on the low marshy grounds adjoining the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and this name was also extended to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river, from a temporary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of hurdles thrown over the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> Liffey, a corruption of Auin Louirfe, or "the swift river," so termed from the rapidity of the mountain floods. This side was enlarged by Mac Turkill the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who, notwithstanding, fixed his habitation on the south side, and abandoned the northern town; which, from the original <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the invaders, was called Eastmantown, since corrupted to Oxmantown. King Edgar, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> dated 964, mentions Ireland with its most noble city (nobilissima civitas) of Dublin. By the Fingalians it is called Divelin, and by the Welsh Dinas Dulyn, or the city of Dulyn. In 448, Alpin Mac Fachardh, king of Dublin, and all his subjects, were converted to Christianity by St Patrick. In the year 498, the Ostmen or Danes having entered the Liffey with a fleet of 60 sail, made themselves masters of Dublin and the adjacent country, and soon after environed the city with walls. About 1170 Dermot Mac Murrough, king of Leinster, having quarrelled with the other princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, a confederacy was formed against him by Roderick O'Connor, monarch of Ireland. Dermot applied to Henry II., king of England, who sent over a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of English adventurers, by whose assistance he was reinstated in his dominions; and in the year 1171, the descendants of the Danes still continuing to hold possession of Dublin, it was besieged and taken by a powerful party of the English under Raymond le Gros. Mac Turkill the Danish king escaped to his shipping; he returned, however, soon after with a strong fleet to recover the city, but was killed in the attempt, and in him ended the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of easterling princes in Ireland. In 1172, Henry II. landed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>, and obtained from Richard <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Strongbow (who married the daughter of Dermot Mac Murrough, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> was his successor) a surrender of the city of Dublin, where he built a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> of wicker work near St Andrew's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, then situated where Castlemarket lately stood, and there entertained several Irish princes, who voluntarily submitted to him on condition of being governed by the same laws as the people of England. Henry also held a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> here. In 1173 he granted his first charter to Dublin, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> privileges encouraged a colony from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> here. In 1210, upwards of 20 Irish princes swore <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to King John at Dublin; engaging to establish the English laws and customs in the kingdom; and in the same year courts of judicature were instituted. In 1216, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a> was granted to the Irish by Henry III., an entry of which was made in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> book of the exchequer at Dublin. In 1217, the city was granted to the citizens in fee-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> at 200 marks per annum; and in 1227 the above monarch ordained that the charter granted by King John should be kept inviolably. In 1404, the statutes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a> and Dublin were confirmed in a parliament held at this city under the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>. The charter of the city of Dublin was renewed in 1609 by James I. The civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the city was anciently under the management of a provost and bailiffs; in 1308, John le Decer was appointed the first provost, and Richard de St Olave and John Stakebold bailiffs. In 1409, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> was changed to that of mayor, when Thomas Cusack was appointed to the office, Richard Bove and Thomas Shortall being bailiffs; the office of bailiffs was changed to sheriffs in 1547. In 1660, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. gave a collar of SS. and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of foot guards to the mayor; and in 1665, this monarch conferred the title of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor on the chief magistrate, to whom he also granted 500l. per annum in lieu of the foot company. Sir Daniel Bellingham was the first lord mayor of Dublin; Charles Lovet and John Quelsh were sheriffs the same year. In 1672, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> earl of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> introduced new rules for the better government of the city; and in 1683 the Tholsel was built for the purpose of the magistrates meeting to hold their courts, assemblies, &c. In the 10th century, after the fortifications of Dublin were repaired by the Ostmen, the walls of the city, including those of the castle, did not occupy more than an Irish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; they extended from Winetavern gate to Audeon's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, and were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from thence to where Newgate formerly stood; and from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> published by John Speed in 1610, it appears that they were continued to Ormond's gate, or, as it has been since called, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">Wormwood</a> gate; from thence to the old bridge, and along the banks of the river to a very large portal called Newman's tower, nearly in the present site of the south entrance of Essex bridge; and from Newman's tower in an angular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to Dame's gate, at the west end of Dame's street. From the gate at the southwest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the castle the wall ran to Nicholas gate, and was continued from thence to Newgate. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets without the walls were, on the west, New row, Francis street, Thomas street, and James's street; on the south were Patrick street, Bridge street, and Ship street; and on the east, Dame street, George's lane, and Stephen street. That space of ground now occupied by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRANE">Crane</a> lane, Temple <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, Fleet street, Lazar's hill, or as it is now called South Townsend street, Crampton, Aston's, George's, and Sir John Rogerson's quays, &c., was then overflowed by the Liffey. On the north side of the river there were only Church street, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s lane, Hammond lane, and Pill lane, then built but on one side as far as Mary's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, which terminated the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town to the eastward; Grange Gorman, Stoney-batter, now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">Manor</a> street, and Glassmanogue, were then villages at some distance from the city; and at the latter the sheriffs have held their courts in times of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, as being remote from the stage of infection. In 1664, the inhabitants being numbered amounted to 2565 men and 2986 women, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>; and 1202 men and 1406 women, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>; making in the whole 8159. By comparing this account of the ancient state and boundaries of the metropolis with the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of its present extent, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and magnitude, nificence, an idea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be readily formed of the amazing increase and improvement it has experienced within the course of a century. Dublin is seated in view of the sea on the east, and a fine country which swells into gently-rising eminences on the north and west, while it towers boldly up in lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that bound the horizon on the south. The city itself cannot be seen to full advantage on entering the harbour; but the approach to it from thence exhibits a fine prospect of the country for improvement and cultivation, interspersed with numerous villas, that have a most agreeable effect to enliven this delightful <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, which, beginning at the water's edge, is continued all over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> to the northward of the bay as far as the eye can reach, and is finely contrasted by a distant view of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WICKLOW">Wicklow</a> mountains to the south, where the conical hills, called the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> Loaves, contribute not a little, by the singularity of their appearance, to embellish the landscape, so extensive and picturesque as not to be equalled by any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> scenery in Europe, but the entrance of the bay of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, to which it bears a very striking resemblance. The form of Dublin is nearly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that includes the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> proportioned to its circumference. From the royal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at Kilmainham, at the western extremity of the town, to the east end of Townsend street, the length is two miles and a half, and its greatest breadth is computed to be of the same extent: hence the city is about 10 miles in circumference. Its increase within the last thirty years has been amazing. It contains 16,458 houses, and 187,939 inhabitants. Dublin, with respect to its streets, bears a near resemblance to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Some of the old streets were formerly narrow; but this defect is now in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> remedied by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, passed in 1774, for opening the public avenues, taking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> sign posts, palisades, pent-houses, &c. new <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> the streets, and flagging the foot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>: and, in 1785, another act passed for the better paving, cleansing, and lighting the city. Still greater improvements have been made in the essential <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of paving, lighting, and cleansing, since 1806. Those necessary improvements contribute exceedingly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and convenience of the metropolis: the new streets are wide and commodious, the houses lofty, uniform, and elegant; nor are several of the old streets totally deficient in these respects; Sackville street, or the Mall, which, though built many years ago, has been included in the number of our new streets by the late geographers (a self-evident <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that these writers had not even seen the city), is a noble avenue, with a gravel walk in the centre, enclosed by a wall of about three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; this walk is 36 feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and the distance between it and the palisades fronting the houses, on either side, is 42 feet and a half. The new customhouse, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> universally admired for its beauty, has rendered this a most desirable situation for wholesale <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, not only on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to that building, but its great depth in the rear. Some years ago, it was esteemed one of the finest public avenues in Europe: many of the new streets, however, in this city are now much superior to it in the magnificence and uniformity of the houses. Among these, on the north side of the river, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> with Sackville street, are Gardiner's row, North Great George's street, Cranby row, Cavendish row, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">Palace</a> row: the last three form a superb square, having the garden of the lying-in hospital in the centre: the old wall that encompassed the garden has been taken down: there is now a full view of this delightful spot surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> palisades, and upwards of 100 globes with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> burners disposed at equal distances, which added to the globes from the surrounding houses, have a most brilliant effect. This square, which for its size, is not perhaps to be equalled, has received the name of Rutland square, in compliment to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Rutland, who contributed munificently towards the improvements in the enclosure of the new garden, and the erecting an elegant edifice for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> rooms, situated to the east of the hospital. In Sackville street is Nelson's pillar, a fluted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> 130 feet high. Among the new streets and buildings on the south side of the river, those wherein persons of distinction reside, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> chiefly to the eastward of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> and Stephen's green; which last, though it does not <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> with the new buildings, possesses much <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and elegance, being one of the largest squares in Europe: it is an English mile in circumference, surrounded by a gravel walk planted on each side with trees; within this walk is a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, having in the centre an equestrian statue of the late king: there are several fine edifices, though almost all differing in the style of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; this variety, however, is esteemed by many rather a beauty than a defect: but, besides the other streets and buildings in this quarter, there is a new square nearly as extensive as Stephen's green, called Merrion square; it was laid out some years ago by the late Lord Fitzwilliam: the houses on the north side are uniform and lofty; most of them being carried up with hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> to the first story, gives the whole an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of strength, beauty, and magnificence. At the south-west angle of Stephen's green, a new street has been also opened, called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARCOURT">Harcourt</a> street, in which are several elegant structures that merit notice, particularly the town residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Lord Earlsford. A variety of other public buildings have been erected since the union. The Dublin <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a>, begun in 1813, cost 40,000l.; the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a> lunatic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, finished in 1815, cost 28,000l.; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST_OFFICE"><a class="x</a>ref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>-office, begun in 1815, and which was estimated to cost 50,000l. The principal entrance to the walks of Stephen's green is on the west side opposite the end of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>-street (which may properly be classed among the new streets), as all the old houses have been pulled down and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> buildings erected in their room. Those parts of the city inhabited by merchants and traders begin to wear a new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>; and amongst this number the new buildings of Dame street on the south side, exhibit an extensive, uniform, and beautiful range of houses all of an equal height; the shop doors and windows are formed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, exactly similar in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and ornaments, which are simply elegant. When the other side of this street shall be rebuilt, it may be justly pronounced one of the first trading streets in Europe; and Parliament street, which was built some years ago, is now nearly equal to any trading street in London. The river Liffey, being banked in through the whole length of the town, exhibits spacious and beautiful quays, where vessels below the bridges load and unload before the merchants' doors and warehouses; it is navigable as far as a bridge near the west end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. This bridge, which is a very elegant structure, was built since the year 1790. Essex bridge was first built in 1687, and took its name from the unfortunate earl of Essex, then viceroy of Ireland. It was taken down in 1753, and rebuilt in an elegant form, after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of Westminster bridge, but much better proportioned, and on a more secure foundation. It has five arches, the buttresses between which support semicircular niches that project from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>; there are balustrades between these niches, and continued to the ends of the bridge, which is commodiously flagged for foot passengers; the whole constructed with hewn stone in a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. There are five bridges besides the two already mentioned; three of which have nothing to recommend them, further than the antiquity of the Old bridge, which was erected in this city at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, when it had the name of Dublin Bridge; it was rebuilt in 1428, since which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it received its present title. Bloody bridge, built in 1671, was originally constructed with wood, and derives its present harsh appellation from an attempt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> it down, wherein four persons were killed. Ormond bridge was built in 1684, during the Ormond administration. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a> bridge, now called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s bridge, was erected in the same year; but, being destroyed by the floods in 1763, was rebuilt of hewn stone, and finished in 1768. It consists of three arches, with flagged foot passages, stone balustrades and ornamental decorations, in a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> style, which has been much admired. Richmond bridge, which was begun in 1813, was opened to the public in 1816. It is 52 feet broad, and 220 <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and cost £25,800. Between this bridge and Essex bridge, an iron bridge for foot passengers was opened in 1816. It is 140 feet long, 12 feet broad, and cost £3000. The foundation of Whitworth bridge was laid in 1816, in place of the one formerly known under the names of the Old bridge, Dublin bridge, and Ormond bridge, which was carried away in 1802. This city has 2 cathedrals, 19 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches, several chapels of ease, 26 Roman Catholic chapels, 6 meeting houses for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, 1 for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, 4 for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, 2 for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, a church for French Calvinists, a Danish and a Dutch church, and a Jewish synagogue. Christ church, or the Holy Trinity, built in 1338 by Donat bishop of Dublin, to whom Sitricus the son of Amlave king of the Ostmen of Dublin granted the site for that purpose, stands on the summit of the rising ground at the head of Winetavern street. It is a venerable Gothic pile; and its present appearance evinces its antiquity. St Patrick's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, first built by Archbishop Comyn in 1190, and decorated by Archbishop Minot in 1370 with a steeple, on which a lofty spire was erected in 1750, is also a fine Gothic structure; it stands on the east side of Patrick's street; the monuments here are more numerous than in Christ church; and the steeple is the highest in the city. St Werburgh's church was originally built in a very early <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In 1301, when a great part of the city was consumed by an accidental fire, this church suffered in the conflagration; it was burnt a second time in 1754, and repaired in its present beautiful form in 1759. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and steeple are admired for their elegance, lightness, and symmetry: the spire is a fine octagon supported by eight pillars; and a gilt ball terminates the whole, being 160 feet from the ground. Catherine's church, first built in 1105, and re-edified in its present form in 1769, is situated on the south side of Thomas's street. St Thomas's church is the latest foundation of the kind in this city, having been begun in the year 1758, and finished and consecrated in 1762. It is situated on the west side of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> street, opposite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> street, to which it forms an elegant termination. The other churches in this city are; on the north side of the river, Mary's, Michan's, and Paul's; on the south side, James's, Luke's, Kevin's, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">Bride</a>'s, Nicholas within, Auden's, Michael's, Mark's, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s, John's, and Andrew's: this last is called also the Round church, from its form being exactly circular: most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all the others were built in an early age: many, however, have been since re-edified, and assumed a more modern form; some of these are not totally devoid of elegance, particularly Anne's. St John's in Fishamble street was rebuilt in 1773, and has now a handsome front of hewn stone decorated with columns supporting a pediment. Besides these churches, Dublin is adorned with several other public buildings; the most remarkable of which are the following: The castle, the residence of the chief governor, built in 1213 by Henry de Londres, was formerly moated and flanked with towers; but the ditch has been long since filled up, and the old buildings razed, the chapel and wardrobe tower excepted, which still remain: <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> tower was rebuilt in 1777, and is now called Harcourt tower. The castle at present consists of two courts, the principal of which is an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> square formed by four ranges of building: within a few years, in the middle of the south range, a handsome edifice called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> tower has been erected; the front is decorated with a small arcade of three arches, over which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a> supporting a pediment, from whence rises an octagon steeple crowned with a small cupola and gilt ball in a light pleasing style. This tower, which fronts the entrance to the viceroy's apartments, is connected with the buildings on each side by two fine gates; over that on the right <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is a statue of Fortitude; and over the left gate, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> portal to the upper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, is the statue of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a>. In the lower court are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> and other offices, with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores, an arsenal and armory for 40,000 men, and a barrack in which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of infantry are stationed. Between this barrack and the arsenal is the castle garden; opposite to which, at the rear of the lord <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>'s apartments, is a range of building called the Garden front, erected about the year 1740, finished in mountain stone, ornamented by semicolonnades of the Ionic order, and the windows embellished with cornices and architraves, in a fine taste. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> room is now titled St Patrick's Hall. The viceroy's body <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> consists of a captain, two subalterns, and sixty private men, with a subaltern's guard of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. The parliament ment house, a most superb structure, is situated on the north side of College green; it was begun in 1729, finished in 10 years, and cost £40,000. It is built with Portland stone, and the front formed by a grand portico of Ionic columns in the most finished style of architectural elegance; the internal parts correspond with its outward magnificence; and the manner in which the inside is lighted is universally admired. The house of commons is an octagon, covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> supported by columns of the Ionic order, that rise from an amphitheatrical gallery balustraded with iron scroll-work; this room is admirably well adapted to its purpose. The house of lords is an oblong room, spacious and lofty, and ornamented in a superb manner; it is also judiciously adapted for the reception of the august <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> which formerly met there; among other decorations are two very fine pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a> and siege of Derry. Since the union of Ireland with Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, this building being no longer necessary as a place of meeting for the Irish legislative body, has been converted into apartments for the national <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. The college founded by Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> in 1591 is situated at the east end of College green. It is a most beautiful structure, consisting of two spacious squares, the first of which contains the refectory, the old hall and chapel, and the new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> for lectures and examinations; the front of this last building is finely decorated with Corinthian columns supporting a pediment; and over the front of the old hall, on the east side of this square, a handsome steeple rises crowned with a cupola. In the other square, which consists partly of brick buildings for the students, there is a superb library, extending through its whole length on the south side: behind this square there is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>. The west side of the first square, which is built with Portland stone, forms the grand front, upwards of 300 feet in length, ornamented with Corinthian pillars and other decorations in a very fine taste. At a small distance to the south side of this front is an elegant edifice in which the provost resides. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> office is a neat handsome structure on the north side of the park; and opposite to it is the anatomy house, in which are to be seen the celebrated wax models of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> figure, executed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> by M. Douane, purchased by the right honourable the earl of Shelburne, and presented to this university. The college of Dublin is an university in itself, consisting of a provost, vice provost, 7 senior and 15 junior fellows, and 17 scholars of the house; the number of students in 1817 was 1230: it has also professors in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, physic, Greek, modern languages, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, oriental tongues, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and oratory, modern history, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, anatomy and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. To accommodate the increasing number of students at the university, it has been found necessary to erect a new and extensive range of apartments, on the south side of the New Square, which had not before been completed. This wing forms a new front to the college, 270 feet in length. The Royal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">Exchange</a>, situated on Cork hill, was begun in 1769, and opened for business in 1779; the expense, amounting to £40,000, being defrayed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a> schemes, conducted by the merchants of Dublin with an integrity that did them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. The building is nearly a square, having three fronts of Portland stone in the Corinthian order, and crowned in the midst with a fine dome, which is supported on the inside by 12 Composite fluted pillars that form a circular walk in the centre of the ambulatory: above these pillars are 12 circular windows, and the ceiling of the dome, which is ornamented with stucco, in the mosaic style, has also a large window in the middle that illuminates most of the building. Opposite the north entrance, in the circular walk, is a statue of his late majesty George III. in a Roman military <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; it is executed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> by Van Nost, and elevated on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble pedestal. In a niche on the staircase leading to the coffee room is a white marble statue of the late Dr Charles Lucas, executed by Smith. The north front, which commands a fine view of Parliament street and Essex bridge, is embellished by a range of six columns and their correspondent pilasters, supporting a grand pediment with a balustrade on each side: a flight of stone steps leads from the street to the entrance, which is by three fine iron-railed gates: the west front varies but little from the north, except in the want of a pediment, and having only three steps ascending to the entrance, the ground on that side being nearly on a level; this front is opposite the east end of Castle street, near the principal entrance to the castle. The hospital for lying-in women, founded by Dr Bartholomew Mosse, and opened in 1757, stands on the north side of Great-Britain street. The building is extremely light and elegant; a beautiful steeple rises in the centre, and the wings are formed by simicircular colonnades on each side. Adjoining the east colonnade is the Rotunda, where balls and assemblies are held, and concerts performed, for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it are erected the grand <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of apartments before mentioned. The garden at the rear of the hospital is laid out in a good taste. The Blue-coat hospital was founded on the west side of Queen street by Charles II. in 1670, for educating the children of reduced freemen of the city: but the original building being greatly decayed, was taken down, and the new Blue-coat hospital, situated in Oxmantown green, was begun in 1773. The front is enriched by four Ionic columns, supporting a pediment in the centre, over which the steeple rises, embellished with Corinthian and Composite columns in an admired taste. Connected with the front by circular walls ornamented with balustrades and niches, are the school on one side and the church on the other: these form two well-proportioned wings; they are of a similar construction; and each is crowned with a small steeple or turret, corresponding with the rest in uniform <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and beauty. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">Barracks</a>, the foundation of which was laid in 1704, are esteemed the largest and most commodious in Europe. They consist of four squares, situated at the west end of the town, on the north side of the river. The royal square in the centre, with the horse barrack and the little square on each side, form a spacious and extensive front to the south: the palatine, now called the new square, is opposite to Oxmantown green; it has been lately rebuilt with hewn stone in a very elegant manner. The royal hospital at Kilmainham for the support of invalids of the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was founded by King Charles II. on a plan similar to that of Chelsea in England. The building was completed in 1683, and cost upwards of £23,500. It is situated at the west end of the town, on a rising ground near the south side of the river, from whence there is an easy ascent to it through several rows of tall trees. This edifice is of a quadrangular form, enclosing a spacious area handsomely laid out in grass plots and gravelled walks: an arcade is carried along the lower story in each square to the entrance of the hall and chapel, which are both curiously decorated; in the former are several whole-length portraits of royal personages and other distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. Dr Stevens's Hospital, the foundation of which was laid in 1720, is a neat quadrangular building, pleasantly situated on the banks of the river near the west end of James's street, from whence a gravelled walk leads by a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to the entrance of the hospital, and is continued thence to the water's edge. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">Linen</a> Hall, at the north end of Linen Hall street, which was opened at the public expense in 1728, for the reception of linen cloths brought to the Dublin market, is a handsome building, lately enlarged with treble its number of former rooms, which furnish a new proof of commercial prosperity. The New Prison in Green street, the first stone of which was laid in 1773, is a large quadrangular structure, designed and executed under the direction of the late Mr Cooley. The east front consists of a centre break of mountain stone rusticated and crowned by a pediment, with a plain façade of black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> on each side; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the building are four round towers. There are many other public edifices in this city and its environs which merit particular notice. The Hospital for Lunatics in West Bow lane, founded by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Swift, and opened in 1757; the Hibernian school in the Phoenix Park, and the Marine School on Sir John Rogerson's Quay, the first for educating the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> children of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and the other for bringing up to the sea <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> the sons of deceased or disabled seamen; the Hospital for Incurables in South Townsend street; Mercer's Hospital in Stephen street; the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a> Hospital on the Coombe; and Simpson's Hospital in Great-Britain street, the last of which was established for the reception of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> and gouty men; are all handsome edifices constructed of hewn stone in the modern style. To these public buildings may be added St Nicholas's Hospital in Francis street; the Infirmary for sick and wounded soldiers of the army, and the Foundling Hospital in James's street; the Magdalen Asylum in Leeson street; and the House of Industry in Channel row; the halls for corporations (particularly the Weavers Hall on the Coombe, over the entrance of which is a statue of his late majesty George II.); the Tholsel; the old Four Courts; the old Customhouse; and several others. The Charitable Infirmary, which was first opened in 1728 and rebuilt in 1741, stood on the Inn's Quay, but has lately been pulled down, together with most of the houses on that quay, where the new courts of justice are to be erected; and the benefits of this humane <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> are now dispensed to the public at a house taken for that purpose in Jervis street. The new courts of justice, on the north side of the river, form a principal ornament to the metropolis, and are from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Mr Gandon's, as well as the new customhouse on the north wall. The front of the latter extends 375 feet, enriched with arcades and columns of the Doric order, crowned with an entablature: the centre has a portico finished with a pediment, in which is a bas relief of emblematical figures alluding to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>: over the pediment is an attic story; and a magnificent dome finishes the centre, wherein is a pedestal supporting a statue of Commerce; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> over the entrances and in the centre of the pavilions are decorated with emblematical heads representing the produce of the principal rivers of Ireland; the south or front to the river, with the arms of Ireland over each pavilion, is of Portland stone: the whole, being formed of large and striking parts, adds much to the picturesque scene of the river, and will remain a lasting monument of reputation to the several artists employed in this superb building. The playhouses, considered as public buildings, have nothing to recommend them to notice. One only, viz. the old house, now the theatre-royal, in Smock-alley, is kept open by Mr Daly; who, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> passed in the Irish parliament for the regulation of the stage, enjoys the exclusive privilege of managing and directing the theatrical exhibitions in this metropolis. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a> in Crow street, which formerly possessed the distinction of theatre-royal, has been shut up these several years past. But a minute description of every public edifice would occupy more room than this publication admits, not to mention the several private houses justly admired for their elegance. Among these are, Leinster House, the town residence of his grace the duke of Leinster. The entrance to this princely mansion is from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a> street, through a grand gateway of rustic stone work, into a spacious court which forms a segment of a circle before the principal front. The inside of this magnificent structure is equal to its exterior appearance; the hall is lofty and noble; and the apartments, which are decorated and furnished in a splendid taste, are enriched with several very valuable paintings. The garden front, plain yet bold, possesses a pleasing simplicity; the garden is spacious and elegant, with a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> in the centre. The whole of this building is inferior to few private edifices in the British dominions. The earl of Charlemont's house is finely situated in the middle of Palace row, on an eminence exactly fronting the centre of the garden at the rear of the lying-in hospital. The front is built with hewn stone brought from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARKLOW">Arklow</a>, superior to that of Portland. The inside of this house is superb and convenient: the hall ceiling is supported by columns; some of the apartments are decorated with a select but choice collection of paintings of the best masters; among which are one of Rembrandt's finest pictures, representing Judas repenting and casting the silver pieces on the ground; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of Cesar Borgia, by Titian; and the Lady's Last Stake by Hogarth, &c. &c. The library is esteemed one of the finest apartments in Dublin, and contains a very valuable collection of the best authors. At one end of it is an antichamber, with a fine statue in white marble of the Venus de Medicis, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a>; Dublin, which is the seat of government and of the chief courts of justice, has received many charters and ample privileges from the kings of England since the reign of Henry II., who introduced the English laws into this kingdom. Richard II. erected it into a marquisate in favour of Robert de Vere earl of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, whom he also created duke of Ireland. It is an archiepiscopal see, and returns with the university and the county six members to parliament. The civil government of Dublin is executed by a lord mayor, recorder, two sheriffs, twenty-four aldermen, and a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> formed of representatives from the twenty-five corporations. Every third year the lord mayor, in conformity with an old charter, perambulates the bounds of the city and its liberties; and formerly the freemen of the several corporations, armed and mounted on horseback, were accustomed to attend the chief magistrate on this occasion, which was titled riding the franchises: but as this custom was productive of idleness, intoxication, and riots, among the lower orders of the people, it has been of late years very properly laid aside. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, and worsted <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> carried on in that quarter of the suburbs called the Earl of Meath's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>, and which have been considerably improved within these few years, other branches of useful manufactures are establishing in different parts of the metropolis; and though the trade of Dublin has heretofore consisted chiefly in the importation of foreign commodities, yet, now that the restrictions on their woollens and most of their other goods are removed, it is hoped the daily enlargement of their export trade will cause a proportionable increase of national opulence. Dublin would have had a commodious station for shipping, were it not that the harbour is choked up with two banks of sand, called the North and South Bulls, which prevent vessels of large burden from coming over the bar. This, however, is in some measure remedied by a prodigious work of stone, and piles of wood extending some miles into the bay on the south side, at the end of which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>, beautifully constructed, after a design of the late Mr Smith's. But the port of Dublin is capable of much greater improvement; particularly by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the course of the river Dodder, building a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> from the north wall to Ringsend, and clearing the harbour so as to form a grand basin on the south side for the reception of vessels of all burthens. This work is to be immediately carried into execution, and will no doubt meet every possible encouragement, from that spirit for promoting the national welfare which now prevails throughout this kingdom, and is remarkably conspicuous in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, where, among others, are the following public institutions. The Board of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">Trustees</a> for promoting the linen and hempen manufactures, established by act of parliament. The Dublin <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, incorporated by charter in the year 1749, for improving husbandry and other useful arts. The Royal College of Physicians, established in the year 1679 for promoting medical knowledge. The Royal College of Surgeons, instituted in the year 1785. The Royal Irish Academy, for the advancement of science, polite literature, and antiquities, incorporated by letters patent the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1786: His majesty is <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and the chief governor for the time being his visitor. The Hibernian Society, for maintaining, educating, and apprenticing, the orphans and children of soldiers in Ireland. The Hibernian Marine Society, for maintaining, educating, and apprenticing, the orphans and children of decayed seamen in his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> and the merchants service; also incorporated by royal charter. But among these public institutions, that of the Bank of Ireland must not be omitted: it was established by act of parliament in 1783; and by facilitating the circulation of specie, gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and vigour to manufactures and commerce. It is conducted under the management of a governor, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-governor, and fifteen directors, chosen annually from among the subscribers; with this restriction, that five new directors at least must be chosen every year. This bank is kept in the late parliament house of Ireland. There are four other great banks in the city under the following firms, viz. Right Honourable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> La Touche and Co. and Sir William Glendow Newcomen, Bart. and Co. both in Castle street; John Dawson Coats, Esq. Thomas street; and John Finlay and Co. Upper Ormond quay. The houses in which the first three are kept are structures worthy of notice, particularly that of Sir William Glendow Newcomen's, which has been rebuilt with hewn stone, in a good taste, after a design of the late Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">Ivory</a>'s. To these public institutions may be added the General Post Office of Ireland, established by act of parliament in 1784, previous to which time the post office of this kingdom was only considered a branch of the English one. The building erected for this purpose was begun in 1815. It is 223 feet in front and 150 in depth, and consists of three stories. In the centre is a grand portico 80 feet in length, consisting of a pediment supported by six pillars, and surmounted by three beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. There are two postmasters-general, a secretary, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, accountant-general, resident surveyor, and comptroller. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-post under the direction of the same officers, established for the conveyance of letters to all parts throughout the city and its environs. Dublin is remarkably well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, fowl, and fish, the latter in much greater perfection than any other capital in Europe. It is supplied with coals chiefly from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> and Scotland; and water is conveyed to the city on the north side from the river Liffey, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> curiously constructed for the purpose, at an outlet called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> bridge; the south side is supplied with that necessary article from a fine reservoir or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASON">bason</a>, surrounded with a wall and a handsome grass walk enclosed on each side by a thick-set hedge and trees planted at equal distances. From one end of it there is a view of the canal for the convenience of inland water carriage, now completed as far as Monastercaven, between which and the canal harbour in James's street, passage boats ply daily; they are well appointed and accommodated with all necessary refreshments. At a small distance from the bason there is a bridge of a single arch thrown over the canal, the elegance and architecture of which are much admired: the sides of the canal for some miles into the country are planted with elm trees, which renders its banks in fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> a delightful place of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> for the citizens; who also <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for recreation to his majesty's Phoenix park, a fine extensive inclosure at the west end of the town, and on the side of the river opposite to the canal, diversified with woodland, champaign, and rising ground, and well stocked with deer. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in circuit; and besides the Hibernian school, is adorned with the viceroy's beautiful villa and some handsome lodges belonging to the rangers: in this park are also a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for powder and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> that commands the city. In 1747, a fluted pillar 30 feet high, with a phoenix on the top, was erected in the centre of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> in this park by the celebrated earl of Chesterfield when lord lieutenant of Ireland. The circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> which surrounds the city, beginning on one side of the river, at the east end of the town, and terminating on the opposite shore, is carried through the park. This road forms a very agreeable ride, and is much frequented. It is the boundary of the jurisdiction of the new <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, instituted for the better preservation of the peace and good order of the city and the personal security of its inhabitants. This institution, established by act of parliament, is under the direction of a chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>, assistant commissioners, and divisional justices, who are all aldermen of the city; which is therefore properly termed the district of the metropolis, and divided into four wards. The police guard consists of horsemen and foot, well armed, and in regular uniform: they are taught military <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and stationed at night time in the several watchhouses; from whence parties are constantly patrolling the streets, and centinels are placed at different stands. This institution is found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to be a much more effectual prevention of robberies, riots, and nocturnal outrages, than the parish watches; and to this security which the well-disposed working manufacturers enjoy, may in a great measure be attributed that increasing spirit of industry and peaceable behaviour now so prevalent among this useful class of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. See the recent improvements of Dublin more particularly described in the article DUBLIN, in the Supplement.

DUBOS

Pages 411-411

JOHN BAPTIST, a learned and ingenious French author, born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a> in 1670. He finished his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and at length was intrusted with the management of several important affairs in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, England, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. At his return to Paris, he had a prebendary given him; afterwards he had a pension of two thousand livres, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Notre Dame at Ressons, near Beauvais. He died at Paris, when perpetual secretary of the French academy, on the 23d of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1742. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Critical Reflections on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, in three volumes duodecimo. 2. A Critical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">Monarchy</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, two volumes 4to.

DUBRIS

Pages 411-411

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; now <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, from Doveria of the lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. A port town in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, opposite to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>.

DUCAL

Pages 411-411

in general, something belonging to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>. See Duke. The letters patent granted by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> are called ducal: so also are the letters wrote, in the name of the senate, to foreign princes. The denomi- <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of ducal is derived hence; that, at the beginning of such patents, the name of the duke <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> doge is wrote in capitals, thus, N— Det Gratia Dux Venetiorum, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of ducals is usually in Latin, but the body is in Italian. A courier was despatched with a ducal to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, returning him thanks for renewing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> in 1716, against the Turks, with the republic of Venice.

DUCAS

Pages 411-411

a learned Greek, who wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of what passed under the last emperors of Constantinople, till the ruin of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is esteemed, was printed at the Louvre in 1649, with the Latin translation and notes of Boiuard.

DUCAT

Pages 411-411

a foreign <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, either of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver, struck in the dominions of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>; being about the same value with a Spanish piece of eight, or a French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; or four shillings and sixpence <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> when of silver, and twice as much when of gold. See Coin. The origin of ducats is referred to one Longinus, governor of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; who revolting against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Justin the Younger, made himself duke of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, and called himself Exarcha, i.e. without <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> or ruler; and to show his independence, struck pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of very pure gold in his own name, and with his own stamp, which were called ducati, ducats; as Procopius relates the story. After him, the first who struck ducats were the Venetians, who called them Zecchini or sequins, from Zecca, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they first were struck. This was about the year 1280, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of John Danduli; but we have pretty good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, that Roger <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> had coined ducats as early as 1240. And Du Cange scruples not to affirm, that the first ducats were struck in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Apulia in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> gold ducats now current are, the single and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> ducats of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>. The heaviest of them weighs 5 pennyweights 17 grains, and the lightest 5 pennyweights 10 grains; which is to be understood of the double ducats, and of the single in proportion. The Spaniards have no ducats of gold; but, in lieu thereof, they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the silver one; which, with them, is no real <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, but only a money of account like our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 11 rials. See RIAL. The silver ducats of Florence serve there for crowns.

DUCATOON

Pages 411-411

a silver <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, struck chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and Parma; though there are also Dutch and Flemish ducatoons. They are all nearly on the same footing; and being a little both finer and heavier than the piece of eight, are valued at twopence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> threepence more; viz. at about four shillings and eightpence <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> ducatoon struck and current chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>: it is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to twenty florins, on the footing of one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> and elevenpence halfpenny the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIN">florin</a>.

DUCENARIUS

Pages 411-412

in antiquity, an officer in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, who had the command of 2000 men. The emperors had also ducenarii among their procurators <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> intendants, called procuratores ducenarii. Some DUCE Ducen- say, that these were such whose salary was two hundred sesterces; as in the games of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, horses hired for two hundred sesterces were called *ducenarii*. Others hold, that *ducenarii* were those who levied the two hundredth <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, the officers appointed to inspect the raising of that tribute. In the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a>, the word *ducenarius*, in Greek δυσκεναριος, occurs very often.

DUCENTESIMA

Pages 412-412

in antiquity, a tax of the two hundredth <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, exacted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>.

DUCHAL

Pages 412-414

JAMES, D.D.** A late pious and learned dissenting minister, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and finished his studies at the university of Glasgow; which afterwards, from a regard to his merit, conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He resided 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 11 years at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, as the pastor of a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> there; where he enjoyed his beloved retirement, the advantage of books and of learned conversation, which he improved with the greatest diligence. On Mr Abernethy's removal from Antrim, he succeeded him there; and on that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he succeeded him as minister of a dissenting meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Wood-street, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. In this situation he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his death, which happened on the 4th of May 1761, when he had completed his 64th year. He published a volume of excellent discourses on the presumptive arguments in favour of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and many occasional tracts; and after his death was published a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his sermons, in three volumes 8vo. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">DUCHY</a>,** in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an appellation given to the dominions of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>. **Duchy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a>,** a court where all matters belonging to the duchy or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> palatine of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> are decided by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of that court. The origin of this court was in Henry IV's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, who obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of Richard II, and having the duchy of Lancaster by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his mother, became seized thereof as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, not as duke: So that all the liberties, franchises, and jurisdictions of the said county passed from the king by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, and not by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> or attornment, as the earldom of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and other possessions, which descended to him by other <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> than the king's did. Henry IV, by authority of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> severed the possessions, liberties, &c., of the said duchy from the crown; but Edward IV restored them to their former <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The officers belonging to this court are, a chancellor, attorney general, receiver general, clerk of the court, and messenger; beside the assistants, as an attorney in the exchequer, another in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, and four counsellors. **DUCK.** See *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>*, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This fowl is furnished with a peculiar structure of vessels about the heart, which enables it to live a considerable time under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as is necessary for it in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVING">diving</a>. This made Mr Boyle think it a more proper subject for experiments with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, than any other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. A full-grown duck, being put into the receiver of an air-pump, of which she filled one-third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and the air exhausted, the creature seemed to bear it better for the first moments than a hen or other such fowl; but after about a minute, she showed great signs of uneasiness, and in less than two minutes her head fell <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and she appeared dying, till revived by the admission of the air. Thus, whatever facility of diving this and other water fowl may have, it does not appear that they can subsist, without air for respiration, any longer than other animals. A young callow duck was afterwards tried in the same manner, and with the same success, being reduced very near death in less than two minutes. But it is observable, that both birds swelled very much in pumping out the air, so that they appeared greatly larger to the spectators, especially about the crop. It not being intended that any water-fowl should live in an exceeding rarefied air, but only be able to continue occasionally some time under water, Nature, though she has provided them with the means of this, hath done nothing for them in regard to the other. The strongest instance of these creatures being calculated to live almost in any situation, we have in the accounts of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> ducks in the Zirchnitzer lake in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>. It is supposed that this lake communicates with another lake under ground in the mountain Savornic, and fills or empties itself according to the fulness or emptiness of that lake; the water of the upper lake running off, and that in vast quantities, by holes in the bottom. The ducks which are here always in great numbers, are often carried down along with the water, and forced into the subterraneous lake to which it retires. In this unnatural habitation many of these creatures undoubtedly perish, but some remain alive. These become blind, and lose all their feathers; and in the next filling of the lake, both they and vast numbers of fish are thrown up with the water. At this time they are fat, but make a strange appearance in their naked state, and are easily caught, by reason of their want of sight. In about a fortnight they recover their sight and feathers: and are then of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wild duck, but of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spot on their forehead. When opened, on being taken at their first coming up in their blind state, their stomachs are found full of small fishes, and somewhat resembling weeds. From this it seems that they cannot be absolutely blind: but that the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to which they have been accustomed in their subterraneous habitation, is sufficient to enable them to procure food for themselves: and their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLINDNESS">blindness</a>, on coming again to open <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> light, is no other than that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the dark, on having in an instant a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> blaze of candles set under his eyes. **Duck, Stephen,** originally a thrasher in a barn, was born about the beginning of the 18th century. By his poetical talents, he first attracted the notice of some gentlemen at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and being recommended to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Caroline, he, under her <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, took orders, and was preferred to the living of Byfleet in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>.
