His abilities were, however, much more conspicuous in his primitive station than in his advancement: though, it is said, he was not disliked as a preacher. Falling at length into a low-spirited melancholy way, probably owing to his change of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and cessation from his usual labour, he in a fit of lunacy flung himself into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, in 1756. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCKING">Ducking</a>,** plunging in water, a diversion anciently practised among the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> by way of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>; but among the Celtæ, Franks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans, it was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for persons of scandalous lives.—At <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a> their men and wo- Ducking, a sort of marine punishment, inflicted by the French, on those who have been convicted of desertion, blasphemy, or exciting sedition. It is performed as follows: The criminal is placed astride of a short thick batten, fastened at the end of a rope, which passes through a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> hanging at one of the yard-arms. Thus fixed, he is hoisted suddenly up to the yard, and the rope being slackened at once, he is plunged into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This chastisement is repeated several times conformable to the purport of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> pronounced against the culprit, who has at that time several cannon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> fastened to his feet during the punishment; which is rendered public by the firing of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, to advertise the other ships of the fleet thereof, that their crews may become spectators. Ducking is also a penalty which veteran sailors pretend to inflict on those who, for the first time, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the tropic of Cancer, the equator, or the straits of Gibraltar, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their refusal or incapacity to pay the usual fine levied on this occasion. Ducking-Stool. See Castigator. Duckup, at sea, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the steersman, when the main-sail, fore-sail, or sprit-sail, hinders his seeing to steer by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-mark: upon which he calls out, Duck up the clew-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of these sails; that is, haul the sails out of the way. Duclos, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Pineau, a French miscellaneous writer. See Supplement. Duct, in general, denotes any tube or canal. It is a term much used by anatomists. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCTILITY">Ductility</a>, in Physics, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> possessed by certain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies, which consists in their yielding to percussion or pressure, and in receiving different forms without breaking. Some bodies are ductile both when they are hot and when they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and in all circumstances. Such are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver. Other bodies are ductile only when heated to a sufficient degree; such as wax and other substances of that kind, and glass. Other bodies, particularly some kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, called by the workmen <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> short, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and some other metallic mixtures, are ductile only when cold, and brittle when hot. The degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> requisite to produce ductility in bodies of the first kind, vary according to their different natures. In general, the heat of the body must be such as is sufficient to reduce it to a middle state, betwixt solidity and perfect fusion. As wax, for instance, is fusible with a very small heat, it may be rendered ductile by a still smaller one; and glass, which requires a most violent heat for its perfect fusion, cannot acquire its greatest ductility until it is made perfectly red hot, and almost ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a>. Lastly, Some bodies are made ductile by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of a fluid. Such are certain earths, particularly clay. When these earths have absorbed a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water to bring them into a middle state betwixt solidity and fluidity, that is, to the consistence of a considerable firm paste, they have then acquired their greatest ductility. Water has precisely the same effect upon them in this respect that fire has upon the bodies above mentioned. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, Edmund, an eminent lawyer and able statesman in the reign of Henry VII.; who with Sir Richard Empson, another lawyer of the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, assisted in filling that rapacious monarch's coffers by arbitrary prosecutions of the people on old penal statutes. They were beheaded on the accession of Henry VIII. to pacify the clamours of the people for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Dudley, John, duke of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, son of the above, a statesman; memorable in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for his unsuccessful attempt to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the crown on the head of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, Lady Jane Grey, who fell a victim to his ambition; was born in 1502, and beheaded in 1553. See (History of) England. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> his eldest son was a brave general and able statesman under Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; and received the appellation of the good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>. Henry, the duke's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son, was killed at the siege of St Quintin. Robert, the third son, a man of bad character, was created earl of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>; and was one of Queen Elizabeth's favourites. His fourth son was the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUILDFORD">Guildford</a> Dudley, whose only crime was his being the husband of Lady Jane Grey, for which he was beheaded in 1554. Dudley, Sir Robert, as he was called in England, and, as he was styled abroad, earl of Warwick and duke of Northumberland, was the son of Robert above mentioned, by the lady Douglas <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>; and was born at Sheen in Surrey in 1573, where he was carefully concealed, to prevent the queen's knowledge of the earl's engagement with his mother. He studied at Oxford; when his father dying, left him the bulk of his estate. He was at this time one of the finest gentlemen in England; and having a particular turn to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, fitted out a small squadron at his own expense, with which he sailed to the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORINOCO">Orinoco</a>, and took and destroyed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> sail of Spanish ships. In 1595, he attended the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, and the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of England, in their expedition against the Spaniards; when, for his gallant behaviour at the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, he received the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. He now endeavoured to prove the legitimacy of his birth, in order to be entitled to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> honours. But being overpowered by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the countess dowager of Leicester, he applied for a license to travel; and being well received at the court of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, resolved to continue there, notwithstanding his receiving a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of recall; on which his whole estate was seized by King James I. and vested in the crown. He discovered at the court of Cosmo II. great duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, those great abilities for which he had been admired in England, and was at length made chamberlain to his serene highness's consort. He there contrived several methods of improving shipping; introduced new <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; and by other services obtained so high a reputation, that at the desire of the archduchess, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand, in 1620, created him a duke of the holy Roman empire. He afterwards drained a vast tract of morass between <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> and the sea; and raised <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, which was then a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, pitiful place, into a large and beautiful town, improving the haven by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>, which rendered it both safe and commodious; and having engaged his highness to declare it a free port, he by his influence and correspondence, drew many English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> and set up houses there, which was of very great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as well as to the Spaniards. He was also the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learned men, and held a high place himself in the republic of letters. His most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is his *Del Arcano del Mare*, in two volumes folio.

DUEL

Pages 414-414

a single <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> appointed, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a challenge. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> came originally from the northern nations, among whom it was usual to decide all their controversies by arms. Both the accuser and accused gave pledges to the judges on their respective behalf; and the custom prevailed so far amongst the Germans, Danes and Franks, that none were excused from it but women, sick people, cripples, and such as were under 21 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> above 60. Even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, priests, and monks, were obliged to find champions to fight in their stead. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the vanquished was either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by hanging or beheading; or mutilation of members, according to the circumstances of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Duels were at first admitted not only on criminal occasions, but on some civil ones for the maintenance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> to estates, and the like? in latter times, however, before they were entirely abolished, they were restrained to these four <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. 1. That the crime should be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. 2. That it should be certain the crime was perpetrated. 3. The accused must by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fame be supposed guilty. And, 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> not capable of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> by witnesses. Duel, at present, is used for single combat on some private quarrel; and must be premeditated, otherwise it is called a rencontre. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person is killed in a duel, both the principals and seconds are guilty, whether the seconds engage or not. (See the article <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">MURDER</a>). It is also a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> offence to challenge a person either by word or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, or to be the messenger of a challenge. (See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">LAW</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.) The general practice of duelling, in this last <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, took its rise in the year 1527, at the breaking up of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. and Francis I. The former desired Francis's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> to acquaint his sovereign, that he would henceforth consider him not only as a base violator of public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, but as a stranger to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and integrity becoming a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. Francis, too high-spirited to bear such an imputation, had recourse to an uncommon expedient to vindicate his character. He instantly sent back the herald with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTEL">cartel</a> of defiance, in which he gave the emperor the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in form, challenged him to single combat, requiring him to name the time and place of the encounter, and the weapons with which he chose to fight. Charles, as he was not inferior to his rival in spirit or bravery, readily accepted the challenge; but after several messages concerning the arrangement of all the circumstances relative to the combat, accompanied with mutual reproaches bordering on the most indecent scurrility, all thoughts of this duel, more becoming the heroes of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> than the two greatest monarchs of their age, were entirely laid aside. The example of two personages so illustrious, drew such general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and carried with it so much authority, that it had considerable influence in introducing an important change in manners all over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Duels, as has already been observed, had been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> permitted by the laws of all the European nations; and, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, were authorized by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> on many occasions, as the most proper method of terminating questions with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, or of deciding in those which regarded crimes. But single combats being considered as solemn appeals to the omniscience and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the Supreme Being, they were allowed only in public causes, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> of law, and carried on in a judicial form. Men accustomed to this manner of decision in courts of justice, were naturally led to apply it to personal and private quarrels. Duels, which at first could be appointed by the civil judge alone, were sought without the interposition of his authority, and in cases to which the laws did not extend. The transactions between Charles and Francis strongly countenanced this practice. Upon every affront or injury which seemed to touch his honour, a gentleman thought himself entitled to draw his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and to call on his adversary to make reparation. Such an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, introduced among men of fierce courage, of high spirit, and of rude manners, where offence was often given, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> was always prompt, produced most fatal consequences. Much of the best blood in Christendom was shed; many useful lives were lost; and, at some periods, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> itself had hardly been more destructive than these contests of honour. So powerful, however, is the dominion of fashion, that neither the terror of penal laws, nor reverence for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, have been able entirely to abolish a practice unknown among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and not justifiable by any principle of reason: though at the same time we must ascribe to it, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that extraordinary gentleness and complaisance of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> manners, and that respectful attention of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to another, which at present render the social intercourses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> far more agreeable and decent than among the most civilized nations of antiquity. Public opinion is not easily controlled by civil institutions; for which reason it may be questioned whether any regulations can be contrived of sufficient force to suppress or change the rule of honour which stigmatizes all scruples about duelling with the reproach of cowardice. The inadequate redress which the law of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> affords for those injuries which chiefly affect a man in his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> and reputation, tempts many to redress themselves. Prosecutions for such offences, by the trifling damages that are recovered, serve only to make the sufferer more ridiculous.—This ought to be remedied. For the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, where the point of honour is cultivated with exquisite attention and refinement, there might be established a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of honour, with a power of awarding those submissions and acknowledgements which it is generally the object of a challenge to obtain; and it might grow into a fashion with persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> to refer their quarrels to the same tribunal. Duelling, as the law now stands, can seldom be overtaken by legal punishment. The challenge, appointment, and other previous circumstances, which indicate the intention with which the combatants meet, being suppressed,

DUKE

Pages 414-418

(Dux), a sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, without the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. Such are the dukes of Lorraine, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, of Savoy, of Parma, &c. The word is borrowed from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Greeks, who call *doucos* what the Latins call *dux*. There are also two sovereigns who bear the title of *<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke*: as the grand duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and the grand duke of Muscovy, now called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Russia. The title of *<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> duke* belongs to the apparent heir of Russia; and the title of *archduke* is given to all the sons of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, as that of archduchess to all the daughters. Duke, (Dux), is also a title of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, the next below princes. The dukedom or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of duke is a Roman dignity, denominated *a ducento*, "leading" or "commanding." Accordingly, the first dukes, *duces*, were the *ductores exercitum*, "commanders of armies." Under the later emperors, the governors of provinces in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> were entitled *duces*. In after times the same denomination was also given to the governors of provinces in time of peace. The first governor under the name of *duke* was a duke of the Marchia Rhaetica, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a>, whereof mention is made in Cassiodorus; and there were afterwards thirteen dukes in the eastern empire, and twelve in the western. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> and Vandals, upon their overrunning the provinces of the western empire, abolished the Roman dignities wherever they settled. But the Franks, &c., to please the Gauls, who had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been used to that form of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, made it a point of politics not to change anything therein; and accordingly they divided all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> into duchies and counties; and gave the names sometimes of dukes, and sometimes of counts, *comites*, to the governors thereof. In England, during the Saxon times, Camden observes, the officers and commanders of armies were called dukes, *duces*, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman manner, without any addition. After the Conqueror came in, the title lay dormant till the reign of Edward III., who created his son Edward, called the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Prince, first duke of Cornwall; which hath ever since been the peculiar inheritance of the king's eldest son during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of his father; so that he is *dux natus, non creatus*. After whom there were more made, in such a manner as that their titles descended to their posterity. They were created with much solemnity, *per cincturam gladii, coppeque, et circuli aurei in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a> impositionem*. However, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, A.D. 1572, the whole order became utterly extinct; but it was revived about 50 years afterwards by her successor, in the person of George Villiers duke of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>. Though the French retained the names and forms of the ducal government, yet under their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of kings there were scarce any such thing as dukes: but all the great lords were called *counts*, *<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>*, or *barons*; excepting, however, the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> and Aquitain; and the duke of France, which was a dignity Hugh Capet himself held, corresponding to the modern dignity of maire de palais, or the king's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>. By the weakness of the kings, the dukes or governors sometimes made themselves sovereigns of the provinces trusted to their administration. This change happened chiefly about the time of Hugh Capet; when the great lords began to dismember the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, so that that prince found more competitors among them than subjects. It was even with a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of difficulty they could be brought to own him their superior, or to hold of him by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and homage. By degrees, what with force, and what by marriages, these provinces, both duchies and counties, which had been rent from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, were again united to it. But the title *duke* was no longer given to the governors of provinces. From that time duke became a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> title of dignity, annexed to a person and his heirs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>, without giving him any domain, territory, or jurisdiction over the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> whereof he was duke. All the advantages thereof now consist in the name, and the precedence it gives. The dukes of our days retain nothing of their ancient splendour but the coronet on their escutcheon, which is the only mark of their departed sovereignty. They are created by patent, cincture of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, mantle of state, imposition of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> and coronet of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> on the head, and a verge or rod of gold in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The eldest sons of dukes are by the courtesy of England styled marquises, though they are usually distinguished by their father's second title, whether it be that of marquis or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a>; and the younger sons lords, with the addition of their Christian name, as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> James, Lord Thomas, &c., and they take place of viscounts, though not so privileged by the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. A duke has the title of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; and being writ to, he is styled, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, potent, and noble prince. Dukes of the blood <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> are styled most high, most mighty, and illustrious princes. Duke, among <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> grammarians, is an appellation given to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of accents answering to our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMA">comma</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCENT">Accent</a>. Duke—Duke, a quality given in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANDEE">grandee</a> of the house of Sylva, on account of his having several duchies from the uniting of two considerable houses in his person. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Rodrigo de Sylva, eldest son of Don Ruy Gomez de Sylva, and heir of his duchies and principalities, having married the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the duke de l'Infantado, the duke de Pastrana, who is descended therefrom, added to his other great titles that of duke-duke, to distinguish himself from the other dukes; some whereof may enjoy several duchies, but none so considerable ones. Dulcifying, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, is the sweetening any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> impregnated with salts, by frequently washing it in pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Dull, in the manege. The marks of a dull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, called by the French marques de ladre, are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spots round the eye and on the tip of the nose, upon any general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> whatsoever. Though the vulgar take these spots for signs of stupidity, it is certain they are great marks of the goodness of a horse; and the horses that have them are very sensible and quick upon the spur. Dullart, Heiman, a Dutch painter and poet. He was a pupil to Rembrandt, for whose works the few he left are often mistaken. He died in 1684. Dumarsais, Cesar Chesnau, a French writer on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>. See Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>. See Dunbarton. Dumbness, the privation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of speech. The most general, or rather the sole cause of dumbness, is the want of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of hearing. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of language is originally acquired by imitating articulate sounds. From this source of intelligence, deaf people are entirely excluded: they cannot acquire articulate sounds by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>: unless, therefore, articulation be communicated to them by some other medium, these unhappy people must for ever be deprived of the use of language; and as language is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> source of knowledge, whoever has the misfortune to want the sense of hearing, must remain in a state little superior to that of the brute <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Deafness has in all ages been considered as such a total obstruction to speech or written language, that an attempt to teach the deaf to speak or read has been uniformly regarded as impracticable, till Dr Wallis and some others have of late shown, that although deaf people cannot learn to speak or read by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the ear, there are other sources of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, by which the same effect may be produced. The organs of hearing and of speech have little or no connexion. Persons deprived of the former generally possess the latter in such perfection, that nothing further is necessary, in order to make them articulate, than to teach them how to use these organs. This indeed is no easy task; but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> shows that it is practicable. Mr Thomas Braidwood, late of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, was perhaps the first who ever brought this surprising art to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection. He began with a single pupil in 1764, and since that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> has taught great numbers of people born deaf to speak distinctly; to read, to write, to understand figures, the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and morality, &c. At the time we first conversed with him, being a few years after the commencement of his practice, he had a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of deaf pupils, some of them above 20 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, all making a rapid and amazing progress in those useful branches of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Mr Braidwood's principal difficulty, after he had discovered this art, was to make people believe in the practicability of it. He advertised in the public papers; he exhibited his pupils to many noblemen and gentlemen: still he found the generality of mankind unwilling to believe him. A remarkable instance of this incredulity occurred some years ago. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in England sent a deaf girl of his to Mr Braidwood's care. A year or two afterwards, Mr Braidwood wrote to the father, that his daughter could speak, read, and write distinctly. The father returned an answer, begging Mr Braidwood's excuse, as he could not believe it: however, he desired a friend of his, who was occasionally going to Edinburgh, to call at Mr Braidwood, and inquire into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what he had wrote him: he did so; conversed with Mr Braidwood, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the young lady, heard her read, speak, and answer any question he put to her. On his return, he told the father the surprising progress his child had made; but still the father thought the whole an imposition; the girl herself wrote to her father, but he looked upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> as a forgery. About this time the father died; and the mother sent an uncle and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> of the deaf lady's from Shrewsbury, in order to be satisfied of the truth. When they arrived, Mr Braidwood told the girl her uncle and cousin were in the parlour; and desired her to go and ask them how they did, and how her mother and other friends did. The friends were astonished, and could hardly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> their own ears and eyes. When we conversed with Mr Braidwood concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and method of teaching this wonderful art, he seemed to be very desirous of communicating and transmitting his discovery to posterity; but observed, and from the nature of the thing we believe it to be true, that he could not communicate it so fully in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> as to enable any other person to teach it. The first thing in the method is, to teach the pupil to pronounce the simple sounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>. We have even seen him performing this operation; but are unable to give a clear idea of it. He pronounces the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of a slowly, pointing out the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the letter at the same time; makes his pupil observe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of his mouth and throat; he then puts his finger into the pupil's mouth, depresses or elevates the tongue, and makes him keep the parts in that position; then he lays hold of the outside of the windpipe, and gives it some kind of squeeze, which it is impossible to describe. scribe: all the while he is pronouncing a, the pupil is anxiously imitating him, but at first seems not to understand what he would have him to do. In this manner he proceeds, till the pupil has learned to pronounce the sounds of the letters. He goes on in the same manner to join a vowel and a consonant, till at length the pupil is enabled both to speak and read. That his pupils were taught not only the mere <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, but also to understand the meaning of what they read, was easily ascertained by a conversation with any of them. Of this Mr Pennant gives a remarkable instance in a young lady of about 13 years of age, who had been some time under the care of Mr Braidwood. "She readily apprehended (says he) all I said, and returned me answers with the utmost facility. She read; she wrote well. Her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> was not by rote. She could clothe the same thoughts in a new set of words, and never vary from the original sense. I have forgot the book she took up, or the sentences she made a new version of: but the effect was as follows. "Original passage. Lord <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> has divided the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> knowledge into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; which are referred to the three powers of the mind,—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, imagination, and reason. "Version. A nobleman has parted the total or all of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> or understanding into, An account of the life, manners, religion or customs of any people or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> or metre; moral or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> knowledge: which are pointed to the three faculties of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> or spirit; the faculty of remembering what is past, thought or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> judgment." Mr Braidwood's success since he went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is universally known. Several other persons have since attempted the same art with various degrees of ability. But a new and different method, equally laborious and successful we understand, is practised by the abbé de l'Épee of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>. We are informed that he begins his instructions not by endeavouring to form the organs of speech to articulate sounds, but by communicating <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> to the mind by means of signs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>: to effect this, he writes the names of things; and, by a regular system of signs, establishes a connection between these words and the ideas to be excited by them. After he has thus furnished his pupils with ideas, and a medium of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, he teaches them to articulate and pronounce, and renders them not only grammarians but logicians. In this manner he has enabled one of his pupils to deliver a Latin <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> in public, and another to defend a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> against the objections of one of his fellow pupils in a scholastic disputation; in which the arguments of each were communicated to each other, but whether by signs or in writing is not said; for it does not appear that the abbé teaches his pupils to discern what is spoken, by observing the motion of the organs of speech, which those instructed by Messrs Braidwoods are able to do with astonishing readiness. There is perhaps no word, says the abbé, more difficult to explain by signs than the verb croire, "to believe." To do this, he writes the verb with its significations in the following manner: \[ \begin{align*} \text{Je <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a> oui par l'esprit.} & \quad \text{Je pense qui oui.} \\ \text{Je dis oui par le coeur.} & \quad \text{J'aime à penser que oui.} \\ \text{Je dis oui par la bouche.} & \\ \text{Je ne vois pas des yeux.} & \end{align*} \] After teaching these four significations, which he does by as many signs, he connects them with the verb, and adds other signs, to express the number, person, tense, and mood, in which it is used. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> to the four signs corresponding with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> above mentioned, be added that of a substantive, the pupil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> write the word for "faith;" but, if a sign, indicating a participle used substantively, be adjoined, he will express la croyance, "<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>;" to make him write croyable, "credible," the four signs of the verb must be accompanied with one that indicates an adjective terminating in able; all these signs are rapidly made, and immediately comprehended. M. Linguet, a member of the Royal Academy, having asserted that persons thus instructed could be considered as little more than automata, the abbé invited him to be present at his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>, and expressed his astonishment that M. Linguet should be so prejudiced in favour of the medium by which he had received the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of knowledge, as to conclude that they could not be imparted by any other; desiring him, at the same time to reflect, that the connexion between ideas, and the articulate sounds by which they are excited in the mind, is not less arbitrary than that between these ideas and the written characters which are made to represent them to the eye. M. Linguet complied with the invitation; and the abbé having desired him to fix on some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> which he would by signs communicate to his pupils, he chose the word unintelligibility: which, to his astonishment, was almost instantly written by one of them. The abbé informed him, that to communicate this word he had used five signs, which, though scarcely perceptible to him, were immediately and distinctly apprehended by his scholars: the first of the signs indicated an internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; the second represented the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of a mind that reads internally, or, in other words, comprehends what is proposed to it; a third signified that such a disposition is possible; those, taken together, form the word intelligible: a fourth sign transforms the adjective into the substantive; and a fifth, expressing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>, completes the word required. M. Linguet afterwards proposed this question, What do you understand by metaphysical ideas? which being committed to writing, a young lady immediately answered on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in the following terms: "I understand the ideas of things which are independent of our senses, which are beyond the reach of our senses, which make no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on our senses, which cannot be perceived by our senses." On reading this, we cannot help exclaiming with the poet, Labor omnia vincit improbus! a maxim by none more forcibly illustrated than by the abbé de l'Épee. Periodical Dumbness. In the Ephemerides of the Curious, we have an account of a periodical dumbness, which had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for more than 15 years, and had not gone off at the time the account was wrote. The person was son to an innkeeper at Jesing in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wirtemberg in Germany. He was one night taken so ill after <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, that he could neither stand nor sit. He continued, for about an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, oppressed with sickness to such a degree as to be in danger of suffocation. At the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of this time he grew better; but, during three months, he was much dejected, melancholy, and, at times, fearful. He was then suddenly struck... Dumbuck struck dumb, and became unable to pronounce the least word, or form the least sound, though he could speak very articulately before. The loss of speech was at first instantaneous, and continued only a few minutes; but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of it began to lengthen every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; so that it soon amounted to half an hour, two hours, three hours, and at last to 23 hours, yet without any order. At last the return of speech kept so constant and regular an order, that, for 14 years together, he could not speak except from noon, during the space of one entire hour, to the precise moment of one o'clock. Every time he lost his speech, he felt something rise from his stomach to his throat. Excepting this loss of speech, he was afflicted with no other disorder of any animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. Both his internal and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses continued sound: he heard always perfectly well, and answered the questions proposed to him by gestures or writing. All suspicion of deceit was removed by his keeping exactly the same hour, though he had no access to any instruments by which time can be measured.

DUMFERRMLINE

Pages 418-418

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough of Scotland, situated in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fife, 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30° 20'. N. Lat. 56° 15'. Here was formerly a magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the kings of Scotland, in which the princess <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James VI., and mother of the princess Sophia, from whom the present royal family are descended, was born. In the inn of this town, it is said, is the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of James VI. and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>: it is still entire, and used by strangers who lodge here. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is noted for a manufactory of figured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth called diaper. The town gave <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SETON">Seton</a> family, which was forfeited in the year 1695.

DUMFRIES

Pages 418-419

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in the south of Scotland, comprehending the shire of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NITHSDALE">Nithsdale</a>, the stewary of Annandale, and the lordship of Eskdale, extends in length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west to south-east about 60 miles, and is about 30 miles in breadth where broadest. It is bounded on the south-west by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KYLE">Kyle</a>; on the north-east by the counties of Roxburgh, Selkirk, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEEBLES">Peebles</a>; on the north-west by Clydesdale; and on the south-east by Solway frith and the marches between Scotland and England. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the county is mountainous and overspread with heath, well stocked with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> of all kinds: but the valleys, through which the Esk, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNAN">Annan</a>, the Nith, and other small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> run, are extremely pleasant; and some of them well cultivated, and very fertile, and produce oats, barley, and wheat in abundance, both for maintaining the inhabitants and for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>; while the mountainous parts afford pasture for innumerable flocks of sheep and herds of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, many thousands of which are annually exported to England. In the valleys are several <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> woods, and some extensive plantations of different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> called Nithsdale, are the rich <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Wanlockhead, the coal mines of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANQUHAR">Sanquhar</a> and Cairnburn, the inexhaustible lime quarries of Closeburn and Bargarg, and freestone in almost every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. Annandale has the rich lime quarries of Kellhead and Comlongan, with plenty of freestone near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Annan and Lochmaben: and in the lower part of Eskdale are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> and some coal. The following is a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this Dumfries county, with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of souls in each parish, taken at two different periods, and extracted from the Statistical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. | Parishes | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790—1798 | |---------------------------|-------------------|------------------------| | Annan | 1498 | 2500 | | Applegirth | 897 | 741 | | Caerlaverock | 784 | 955 | | Cannobie | 1733 | 2725 | | Closeburn | 999 | 1490 | | Cummermores | 631 | 1056 | | Dalton | 451 | 615 | | Dornock | 716 | 738 | | Drysdale | 1097 | 1600 | | Dumfries | 4517 | 5600 | | Dunscore | 651 | 1033 | | Durrasdeer | 1019 | 1031 | | Eskdalemuir | 675 | 619 | | <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">Ewes</a> | 392 | 320 | | Glencairn | 1794 | 1700 | | Gratney | 1051 | 1810 | | Hoddam | 1393 | 1198 | | Hollywood | 596 | 736 | | Hutton | 993 | 583 | | Johnston | 494 | 365 | | Keir | 495 | 520 | | Kirkeconnell | 899 | 1000 | | Kirkmahoe | 1098 | 1200 | | Kirkmichael | 894 | 950 | | Kirkpatrick Fleming | 1147 | 1542 | | Kirkpatrick Juxta | 794 | 617 | | Langholm | 1833 | 1282 | | Lochmaben | 1395 | 3000 | | Middlebie | 991 | 1404 | | <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOFFAT">Moffat</a> | 1612 | 1600 | | Morton | 435 | 908 | | Mousewald | 553 | 628 | | Penpont | 838 | 800 | | Ruthwell | 399 | 1061 | | St Mungo | 481 | 640 | | Sanquhar | 1998 | 2600 | | Tinwald | 795 | 850 | | Torthorwald | 584 | 660 | | Tundergarth | 625 | 510 | | Tynron | 464 | 500 | | Wamphray | 458 | 497 | | Westerkirk | 544 | 655 | Population in 1811: 62,960 See DUMFRIES-SHIRE, Supplement. Dumfries, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above mentioned county, a handsome town, situated on a ridge <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rising ground on the north-east side of the river Nith, about 10 miles above where it falls into Solway frith, in N. Lat. 55° 8'. 30". <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. W. of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a>, 3° 56'. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name, it is said by some of the Scotch historians, was Coticus; but on what authority we cannot tell. Its present name appears to have been derived partly from its situation, and partly from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Gray Friars that formerly stood near the head head of the street called the Friar cennat, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> of which is all that now remains; being only a corruption of Drum friars, or "the eminence of the friary;" and accordingly, till within these 40 or 50 years, it was always spelt Drumfries, and not Dumfries, as it is now for the sake of greater softness. Besides the pleasantness of its situation on the side of a beautiful winding river, it is surrounded on all sides with one of the finest and best cultivated sheets of dale <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that one can anywhere meet with, and the prospect from it terminated, at the distance of a few miles, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> chain of hills, forming altogether one of the grandest natural amphitheatres perhaps in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. There was anciently a strong castle at the south end of the town belonging to the Cummings, lords of Badenoch, of which there are now no remains. Another castle was afterwards built at the north-west end, which was taken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> about a century ago. On the northeast side of it, at some little distance, are the ruins of a chapel built by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Robert Bruce, and endowed for a number of priests to say <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> for the repose of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of Sir Christopher <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEATON">Seaton</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, who was taken prisoner by Edward I. at Loch Urr, and hanged at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It is now only employed as a burying place for suicides. It is not certain at what <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> Dumfries was erected into a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough; but it must have been before the middle of the eleventh century, as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was discovered some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of 1079, and mentioning the person buried under it to have been a merchant and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> of the town; and that it was a place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the beginning of the fourteenth century, is evident from this circumstance, that Edward II. called the estates of Scotland to meet there in the year 1307. In the above-mentioned monastery too, King Robert Bruce killed his rival Cumming <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Badenoch, with the assistance of James Lindsay and Roger Kirkpatrick, on the 5th of February 1305. As to the present state of the town, the houses are well built and commodious, the streets spacious, open, and neatly paved. It has two very elegant churches, an Episcopal chapel with a fine little organ, besides four meeting houses belonging to different descriptions of sectaries; a tolbooth; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> chamber; a trades <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> market; a strong prison; a correction <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; an infirmary, with apartments for insane patients; a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> over the river, said to have been built by one of the three daughters and coheresses of Alan Lord Galloway, and a handsome new bridge built in 1795. A large village, called the Bridge-end, stands on the opposite side, and is within the stewartry of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KIRKCUDBRIGHT">Kirkcudbright</a>. The assizes for the county, and for the shire of Galloway and stewartry of Kirkcudbright, are held in the town twice a-year. It is also the place for holding the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> courts, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions of the peace, and the courts of the commissioners of supply. It is governed by a provost, three bailies, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of guild, and a town council, composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and the convener and deacons of the incorporated trades, of which there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>-men, smiths, weavers, tailors, shoemakers, skinners, and butchers. The trades got from King James VI in one of his journeys to England, a small silver tube, like a pistol <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, called the silver <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, with his royal license to shoot for it every year. At that festival they all appear in arms, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> out of the town under their respective colours, to some convenient place, where they shoot at a mark; and the person that hits or shoots nearest to it, returns to town, marching at the convener's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with the silver gun tied to his hat with ribbons; after which they conclude the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with a social entertainment. The town has a weekly market on Wednesday, with two annual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, the first on the Wednesday on or next after the 13th of February, and the other on the Wednesday on or next after the 25th of September. But though well situated for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> at a cheap rate, it has only two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, one for stockings and the other for cottons; but the latter only in its infancy. Its foreign trade for many years has only consisted in timber, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> for home consumption. It gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the family of Crichton: and is the seat of a presbytery and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>. A handsome monument to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Robert Burns, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a> poet, was erected in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard in 1817. The town contained 9262 inhabitants in 1811.

DUMONT

Pages 419-419

Francis, a Frenchman, compiler of a general collection of treaties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, and peace, between the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. This collection, with Barbeyrac's, containing the treaties B.C., makes 16 vols. folio, very useful for historical writers. Dumont retired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in 1720. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is uncertain. DUMOSÆ (from dumus, "a bush"), an order of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in the Fragmenta methodi naturae of Linnæus, containing the following genera, viz. Viburnum, Tinos, Opulus, Sambucus, Rondelia, Bellonia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASSINE">Cassine</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ILEX">Ilex</a>, Tomax, &c.

DUN

Pages 419-420
or BURGH, the name of an ancient species of buildings, of a circular form, common in the Orkney and Shetland islands, the Hebrides, and northern parts of Scotland. The latter term points out the founders, who at the same time bestowed on them their natal name of borg, "a defence or castle," a Suco-Gothic word; and the Highlanders universally apply to these places the Celtic name dun, signifying a hill defended by a tower, which plainly points out their use. They are confined to the countries once subject to the crown of Norway. With few exceptions, they are built within sight of the sea, and one or more within sight of the other; so that on a signal by fire, by flag, or by trumpet, they could give notice of approaching danger, and yield a mutual succour. In the Shetland and Orkney islands, they are most frequently called wart or ward hills, which shows that they were garrisoned. They had their wardmadher, or watchman, a sort of centinel, who stood on the top, and challenged all who came in sight. The gackman was an officer of the same kind, who not only was on the watch against surprise, but was to give notice if he saw any ships in distress. He was allowed a large horn of generous liquor, which he had always by him, to keep up his spirits. Along the Orkney and Shetland shores, they almost form a chain; and by that means not only kept the natives in subjection, but were situated commodiously for covering the landing of their countrymen, who were perpetually roving on piratical expeditions. These towers were even made use of as state state prisons; for we learn from Torfeus, that after Sueno had surprised Paul, count of Caithness, he carried him into Sutherland, and confined him there in a Norwegian tower. Out of our own kingdom, no buildings similar to these are to be found, except in Scandinavia. On the mountain Swalberg in Norway is one; the Stir-biskop, at Upsal in Sweden, is another; and Umseborg, in the same kingdom, is a third. These towers vary in their inner structure; but externally are universally the same; yet some have an addition of strength on the outside. The burgh of Culswick in Shetland, notwithstanding it is built on the top of a hill, is surrounded with a dry ditch 13 feet broad; that of Snaburgh in Unst, has both a wet and a dry ditch; the first cut, with great labour, through the live rock. The burgh of Moura is surrounded by a wall, now reduced to a heap of stones, and the inside is cylindrical, not taper, as is usual with others. The burgh of Hogsetter, upon an isle in a loch of the same name, has also its addition of a wall; a peculiarity in a causeway, to join it to the main land, and a singular internal structure. Numbers of little burghs, with single cells, are scattered about these islands, in the neighbourhood of the greater; and which probably were built by the poorer sort of people, in order to enjoy their protection. A multitude of places in these islands have the addition of burgh to their names, notwithstanding there is not a vestige of a tower near them; the materials having long since been carried away, and applied to various uses.

DUNBAR

Pages 420-420

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough of Scotland, in the shire of East <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>, once remarkable for a strong castle, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of Scotland from the east, and which gave shelter to Edward II. of England in his flight from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANNOCKBURN">Bannockburn</a>, but of which scarce a vestige now remains. Here are still preserved some of the Scottish pikes, six ells <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and formed both for offence and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. This town has now a tolerable trade in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, and is remarkable for making good malt. Dunbar contained 3965 inhabitants in 1811.

DUNBARTON

Pages 420-420

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> town of Lennox <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dunbartonshire, in Scotland, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 32'. N. Lat. 56° 30'. is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, and one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Scotland. It is said to have been once the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the Britons, established in the vale of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, and to have been one of the seats of Fingal, called in the poems of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>, the tower of Balclutha. Aleluid was indeed the name of this ancient capital of the Strathclydenses; but whether it was situated on the site of the present town, or confined within the precincts of the castle, cannot be exactly ascertained. Dunbarton is built upon the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Leven, which almost encircles it. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the buildings are old, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> street has an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of decayed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. It was erected into a royal borough by Alexander II. in the year 1221, and declared to be free of all imposts and borough taxes; but notwithstanding this material advantage, and the excellent harbour it possesses, it is by no means in a flourishing state. There are here considerable glass-houses, which employ about 300 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and some idea may be conceived of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of this manufacture, from the amount of the duties to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, which, in the five years preceding 1818, averaged 97,300l. per annum. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is exceedingly well adapted for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, both on account of its situation on the Clyde, and from its being well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> at a cheap rate. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> is nearly circular, having a diameter of about two miles and a half; the surface is flat, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fertile, but shallow, inclining to gravel. The Clyde washes it on the south, and the Leven on the west, both of which contain excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a> and salmon. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the town in 1811 was 2970, of the parish 3121. The castle of Dunbarton lies at a small distance from the town, on the point of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> formed by the junction of the Clyde and Leven; it is situated on the top of a rock, which presents a picturesque object: the rock divides about the middle, and forms two summits: the sides are craggy, and the buildings upon it, though not of themselves beautiful, have a good effect, and, as Mr Gilpin observes, "serve to give it an air of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>." The fortress is entered by a gate at the bottom; and within the rampart, which defends the entrance, is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and lodgings for the officers; from hence the ascent is by a long flight of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> steps to the part where the rock divides: here is a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> for the garrison, and a reservoir always filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; above these, on the lower summit, are several batteries, which command a most extensive range. According to Pennant, the Britons, in very early times, made this rock a fortress, it being usual for them, after the departure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, to retire to the tops of craggy inaccessible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, to forests, and to rocks on the sides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, or the shores of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>, however, asserts, that it was possessed by the Caledonians long before the Britons, and that it resisted all the efforts of Agricola to reduce it. The venerable Bede informs us, that it was the strongest fortification in the kingdom in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and deemed almost impenetrable; it was reduced by famine in the year 756, by Egbert <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, and taken by escalade in the year 1551. The rock seems to have been anciently a volcano: the sides are composed of rude basaltic columns, of which huge masses have been broken off, and fallen to the bottom, by the injuries of time. Many parts of the rock are strongly magnetic, causing the compass to vary at a considerable distance: this circumstance was long since noticed by Buchanan (Scot. Hist. lib. xx. lect. 28.). As the castle of Dunbarton commands the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the Clyde, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the western Highlands, the fortifications are generally kept in repair. It is garrisoned by a governor, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor, a fort-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, subaltern officers, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of invalids. The government is said to be worth 700l. per annum.

DUNBARTONSHIRE

Pages 420-421
or, as it was anciently called, the shire of Lennox, extends in length about 40 miles, and in breadth about 23. It is bounded on the north by Argyleshire; on the east by the counties of Perth and Stirling; on the south by the river Clyde, and part of Lanarkshire; and on the west by an arm of the sea, called Loch Long. The greater part of the county is covered with heathy hills which are now assuming a more luxuriant appearance, since the introduction of sheep. Many of the mountains are elevated to a great height, Benlomond measuring 3158 feet above the level of the sea. The ridge of which Benlomond Dunbarlonmond is a part, is the beginning of that extensive ridge which crosses the country from this place to the east coast at Aberdeen, called the Grampians. The lower grounds, which lie on the banks of Loch Lomond, the river Clyde and the Leven, are not so fertile as the corresponding parts of some of the neighbouring counties; notwithstanding which, it is agreeably diversified, and well inhabited. The banks of the Leven, in particular, are covered with numerous bleachfields, printfields, and cotton-works, giving employment to thousands; while the villages erected for the accommodation of the workmen, the hamlets, and elegant seats, cannot fail to impress the mind with high ideas of the wealth, the industry, the public spirit, and the happiness of the inhabitants. Agriculture in this county was formerly rather neglected; but the public spirit has of late been roused to this most useful and important occupation; and the county of Dunbarton, which is capable of much improvement, is fast advancing in agricultural progress. The county contains altogether 230 square miles, or 147,200 acres. The farmers here, indeed, possess numerous advantages: being near a sea-port town, where every article bears the highest price, they find a ready market for their corn; and the numerous inhabitants in the immediate neighbourhood require supplies of other necessaries from the farmer. Upwards of 12,000 acres are covered with natural wood, and there are many fine lakes or lochs, of which Loch Lomond is the chief. Dunbartonshire contains one royal borough, Dunbarton, several thriving manufacturing villages; and is divided into 12 parishes, containing in all 24,189 inhabitants in 1811. Population of this County at two different periods, from Statist. DUNCANNON

Pages 421-421

a fort in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEXFORD">Wexford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, seated on the river Ross. It commands the river, insomuch that no ship can <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ross without its permission. Here are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> for three companies of foot. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 30'. N. Lat. 52° 10'.

DUNCOMBE

Pages 421-421

WILLIAM, younger, son of John Duncombe, Esq. of Stocks in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, in 1722 Duncombe published a translation of Racine's Athaliah; which was well received by the public, and has gone through three editions. In 1724 he was editor of the works of Mr Needler; in 1735, of the poems of his deceased <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Mr Hughes, 2 vols 12mo; in 1737, of the miscellanies of his younger brother Mr Jabez Hughes, for the benefit of his widow, in one volume 8vo; and in 1745, of the works of the Rev. Mr Samuel Say, in one volume 4to. In 1726 he married the only sister of John Hughes, Esq. whom he <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> survived. In 1734 his tragedy of Lucius Junius Brutus was acted at Drury Lane <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. It was published in 1735, and again in 1747. The works of Horace, in English <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, were published by him in two vols 8vo, with notes, &c. in 1757. A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition, in 4 vols 12mo, with many imitations, was published in 1762. In 1763 he collected and republished "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> sermons by Archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">Herring</a>, on public occasions, with a biographical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>." He died Feb. 26, 1769, aged 80.

DUNDALK

Pages 421-421

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUTH">Louth</a>, about 48 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and thriving town, with a wide street, near a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and a very fine market-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, near the entrance from Dublin. In the reign of Edward II. it was a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the last we read of where a monarch of all Ireland was actually crowned and resided.
