It was formerly very strong, and had many towers and small castles in it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> has good moorings at all times, in four to upwards of eight fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, with very good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-marks, either for bringing up to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making the harbour; and in crossing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water, or ordinary neap <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, there is from 15 to 18 feet water. The only cambic manufacture in Ireland is in this town. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is about 15,000.

DUNDEE

Pages 421-423

a borough town of Scotland, in the shire of Forfar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river Tay, about 12 measured miles from its mouth, 40 measured miles north of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and 22 east from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 48'. N. Lat. 56° 26'. Its situation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is very advantageous. Trading vessels of the largest burden can get into the harbour; and on the quay there are three very convenient and handsome warehouses built in 1756, as well as good room for shipbuilding, which is carried on to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The houses are built of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, generally three or four stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or high street in the middle of the town is a very spacious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, 360 feet long and 100 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; from whence branch out the four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets, which with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lesser ones are all paved in the best manner. On the south side of the market-place stands the townhouse, an elegant structure, with a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, piazzas below, and a neat spire over it 140 feet high. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> was finished in the year 1734, and contains the guildhall, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-room, a very neat mason lodge, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, vaulted repositories for the records, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> prison, which is in the upper story, and does <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of the magistrates, under whose auspices it was constructed, being well aired commodious rooms, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very strong and secure. Each prison is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">Dun</a> 20 feet by 12, and 7½ feet high, well arched above and below. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> market and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHAMBLES">shambles</a>, which were formerly on the high street, and esteemed a nuisance, were removed some years ago; and in the place of the shambles there is now erected by the incorporated trades, on the east end of the above large square, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> building, with a large and elegant cupola: in the ground flat of which is a very neat coffee room, and several merchant shops; and in the upper stories public rooms for each trade, and a common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> occasionally used as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. This hall is 50 feet long, 30 feet broad, and 25 feet high; having its front to the square decorated with Ionic columns. The opulence of the corporations, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in number, may be inferred from this, that they had, along with the kirk session, but very lately finished a most elegant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> when they set about building the hall. This church, which is called St Andrew's Church, stands on a rising ground a little north from the Cowgate street; and has an elegant spire 130 feet high, with a peal of bells much admired. There is a neat entry to the church by a broad gravel walk, with grass plots on each side; and the whole policies around it are laid out with excellent taste, and in a superb style, as complete and well executed as any in Scotland. Dundee, beside St Andrew's church, has four other churches, and five ministers on the legal establishment. The old church, in which were originally four places of worship, when entire, had been a very magnificent building, with a large square Gothic tower or steeple 186 feet high, on the west end of the church. This building was in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, erected by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Huntingdon, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to William I. of Scotland (surnamed the Lion), and was dedicated to the virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. This he did on his return from the third crusade (in which with 500 of his countrymen he had accompanied Richard I. of England) anno 1189, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for his deliverance from several imminent dangers, and particularly from shipwreck, by which he had nearly perished when in sight of this town. At the same time he changed the name of the town from Allocetum to Dei Donum, whence its present name is thought by many to be derived; while others maintain that its name was Duntony, or "the hill of Tey." The word Allocetum in the Gaelic signifies "beautiful," and harmonizes very well with the Scripture <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the hill of God. The word Duntony has the very same signification, "the Hill of God;" and both agree with the delightful situation of Dundee, and unite in giving it with propriety the name of Bonny Dundee. The hill rises on the north of the town to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, and is called The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a> of Dundee; law being a Saxon word for a round hill such as it is. On its top there is evidently the remains of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, said to have been first erected by Edward I. of England, and lastly repaired by General Monk. Where the meal market stood is now erected an elegant Episcopal meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; with handsome shops below. Dundee had an old castle which was demolished by the famous Scots governor Sir William Wallace, who was educated in this town. The castle had proved very useful to Edward I. when he put a garrison into it to awe the inhabitants; but Wallace getting possession, ordered it to be destroyed, lest it should again <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English. This treatment so exasperated Edward, that, taking the town by storm, he set fire to the churches; and a number of the inhabitants having taken sanctuary there with their most valuable effects, were all burnt along with them. At that time he burnt also a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town. The desolation he brought on the church has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ever since, till the year 1787, when a noble edifice began to be built on the site of the one that was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and is now finishing; in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Gothic of the outside is excellently united with internal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, making one of the largest and neatest churches in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and again completing the superb superstructure as erected at first by the earl of Huntingdon. This town suffered greatly last century during the troubles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and the usurpation of Oliver Cromwell; being sometimes under the command of one party, and at others in the mercy of another. In 1645 the marquis of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a> took it by storm; and in 1651, under the command of its provost <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> General Lumsden, it vigorously opposed General Monk, who carried it by storm the 1st of September, and put all in arms to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. And so great were the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of Dundee, all the neighbouring gentlemen having retired to it with their best effects as a place of safety, that every private soldier in General Monk's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> had near 60l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> to his share of the plunder; there being above 60 merchant vessels in the harbour at that time, and the like number of vessels sailed for England loaded with the spoils of the unfortunate inhabitants. By these and other invasions, the whole ancient records of the town were destroyed, except a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Mary, signed by herself, conferring the present burying ground; and some charters of the Charles's, confirming the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges as disposed by the Alexanders and other kings of Scotland. This burying-ground is the only place in Scotland we know of called The Hoff, a Dutch word <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> all the senses of the English word court, having been formerly the burying-ground of one of the many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses that were in this town previous to the Reformation. Dundee at present has 154 vessels belonging to the port, of about 16,000 tons burden, which employ 1300 seamen. Of these vessels 8 are employed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> fishery, 11 in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> trade, and the rest in the Baltic and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> trade. Between 1814 and 1818 the bonding system was extended to Dundee by various acts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The magistrates have been lately, and still are at great expense in enlarging and fitting up the harbour, so as to render it of easy access, safe, and commodious; and have now made the passage over the Tay, where there is a great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, so convenient, that travellers with their horses can get over at any time of tide, and a sufficient number of good boats properly manned are always ready. The river Tay opposite Dundee is about three miles broad; and being sheltered by high lands on both sides is a safe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for ships of the greatest burden: the piers are extensive, broad, and well adapted for the purposes of loading and discharging vessels; and when the harbour is completed on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> they are presently engaged in, there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be one superior to it in Scotland. To enable the town to repair the damage done by Cromwell's Cromwell's army, and also their harbour and other public works, Charles II. granted them a small impost of one-sixth of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> sterling, for 25 years, on the pint of ale brewed or brought into the town for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> has been frequently renewed by subsequent parliaments; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> arising therefrom is most properly bestowed by the magistrates in improving the town, and making it more convenient and healthy. For these purposes, several new streets have been made, the old ones have been widened, and a large convenient one at a considerable expense, carried down from the market place to join a fine walk, shaded very neatly with trees, that leads to the shore. This new street makes the access easy and commodious, which was formerly much confined and steep. Till the year 1745, the town had only draw <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>; but since that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it is most amply supplied from a large fine fountain of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, conveyed through the town in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, and discharged by good wells at proper distance. These, with a fine well in the town's meadows, and a stream of water that runs through the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> and the meadows (two large beautiful greens on the north of the town), make it as well watered as any town in Scotland; and these greens, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, serve all the inhabitants most commodiously for the necessary labours of washing and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>. The number of inhabitants in Dundee has increased amazingly since 1780. There was then an accurate <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of them taken, when they amounted to near 16,000; but by the census of 1801, the number was 26,084; and by the census of 1811, it was 29,616. Besides the established churches, there are three Episcopal meeting-houses, two of Seceders, one of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, two of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>, one Berean, and two <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>. One of the Independents is of the Glassite denomination. Mr John Glass, from whom they take that name, resided here; and his principles, though spread far and wide, have always had the most extensive influence in Dundee. The trade in the town has increased amazingly of late. Its staple is undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture: for which in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> 1788, they imported from the Baltic 32 cargoes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, &c. (near 3000 tons), besides several quantities from London, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a>, and other places; and on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> linen stamped for the two preceding seasons at the stamp office here amounted to above four millions of yards, in value about 115,000l. sterling. But the annual average value of the cloth stamped in Dundee for 1815, 1816, and 1817, was above 300,000l. The flax is wrought up into coarse linens, chiefly osnaburgs, sheetings, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>' shirtings, &c. which is sold partly bleached (several fine large bleachfields being well employed in the neighbourhood) and partly brown. These linens are sent principally to London, Glasgow, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, and from thence exported. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> or eight vessels are constantly employed in the trade between Dundee and London, one of which sails every ten or twelve days. The making sailcloth has been long established here, and is carried on to a good extent; and rope-works have succeeded well. The Dundee coloured threads have been long justly esteemed, and give <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> to a great number of people; indeed it was here that coloured threads first made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of trade in Scotland. Their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-house, a large undertaking, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> works, are of established reputation. There has been lately erected a large glass-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at a great expense, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLUMBERY">plumbery</a> and foundry are also now carried on to advantage. No doubt the trade of the place has been greatly promoted by the Bank; which is carried forward on the surest and most steady footing, and has always managed the business of the town and neighbourhood in such a way as to keep any other establishment of that kind from taking place. Of late the cotton manufactory has been introduced; a number of jennies being employed in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, and several looms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> it. A spirit for literature and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> has greatly prevailed of late years in Dundee: for beside the public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, which has an able rector and two good masters; the public English and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> school, where are three very proper masters; there is also lately established, and much encouraged, an academy for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, French, Italian, and the polite arts, with masters suitable for the different branches, and a large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. The salmon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> in Tay is of much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; and the town is generally well supplied with fish of various kinds, though like every other article of living much raised in price of late years. Their other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are also well supplied. An excellent nursery at the west end of the town has been much encouraged; and its neighbourhood is now adorned with many neat and elegant villas, showing the wealth and taste of the inhabitants. Dundee is the birthplace of the celebrated and learned Hector Boetius, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland has been long in much reputation with many. Dundee, with Perth, Forfar, St Andrew's, and Cupar, returns one member to the British parliament. DUNFERMLINE. See DUMFERMLINE.

DUNG

Pages 423-423

in Husbandry. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. DUNO-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>. See UPTA, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index. DUNO-Meers, in Husbandry, places where soils and dungs are mixed and digested together. These consist of pits, prepared at the bottom with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and clay, that they may hold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the moisture of the dung: and ought to be so situated, that the sinks and drips of the houses and barns may run into them. Into these pits they <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> refuse, fodder, litter, dung, weeds, &c. where they <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> and rot together, till the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> have occasion for them. DUNO-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fly worms, of a short and somewhat flat body, found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty among cow-dung in the months of September and October.

DUNGANNON

Pages 423-423

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRONE">Tyrone</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. It is seated on a hill, and is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some strength.

DUNGARVON

Pages 423-423

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, has a commodious harbour for ships, and is a walled town, with a castle. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 55'. N. Lat. 51° 57'. DUNIPACE. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARRON">CARRON</a>.

DUNKELD

Pages 423-424

a town of Scotland, in the shire of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river Tay, in a situation truly romantic, among very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and almost inaccessible crags, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> naked and part wooded. wooded. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> market town of the Highlands, and has been greatly improved with buildings by the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOL">Athol</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. It was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a>. About the dawn of Christianity, a Pictish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> made it the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, by erecting a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Culdees there; which King <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. in 1130 converted into a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and it ranked as the first in Scotland. The entire shell of the cathedral still remains, the east end serving for a kirk, on the north side of which is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> place of the dukes of Athol. The style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is simple and elegant, the pillars round. The monument of one of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> remains on the south aisle of the nave, as also that of Alexander Stuart <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, third son of Robert II., called for his cruelty The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">Wolf</a> of Badenoch, who died in 1394. The tower at the west end, with a singular crack <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> one of its sides, adds to the picturesque appearance which the whole makes among the venerable pines at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>'s garden. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>'s seat is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, with pleasant walks and plantations, and a fine cascade on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of Bran, which in its way from the western hills forms an astonishing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of 150 feet, called the Rumbling Brig, from a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> made by the fall of two rocks across the stream. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> of Rosa never formed a more horrid <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. The stream has a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> fall, which, without seeing the other, would be deemed capital. Sir James <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of requests to James VI. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., was created <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Dunkeld 1645, whose grandson James was attainted at the Revolution, and dying at the beginning of this century, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> became extinct. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1360 in 1811.

DUNKIRK

Pages 424-425

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 28. N. Lat. 51. 10. and is the most easterly harbour on the side of France which is next to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.—It was originally a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>, consisting only of a few fishermen's huts: but a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> being built there, it was from that, and from its situation, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> eminence, called Dunkirk; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">dun</a> signifying, in the old Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a hill; and kirk being the old Flemish name for church. About the year 960, Baldwin <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, thinking the situation convenient, enlarged it into a kind of town, and surrounded it with a wall. In the year 1322, Robert of Flanders, who held it as an appendage, built a castle for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; which was afterwards demolished by the revolters of Flanders. Robert of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a> erected a fortification round it, the remains of which are visible on the side next the harbour. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. who held it as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Flanders, built another castle to defend the harbour; but this was also demolished soon afterwards. In 1588, the French, under Marshal de Thermes, took Dunkirk by storm, and almost ruined the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; the Spaniards recovered it again in about a fortnight, and put all the French to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. During a peace procured for the Dunkirkers by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, they rebuilt their town with greater splendour than before, and the inhabitants for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> subsisted by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> fitted out against the Dutch; and at length, growing rich by these hostilities, they fortified their town and harbour, and fitted out no less than 15 ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> at their own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. In 1634, the Dunkirkers agreed with the inhabitants of Bergues to dig a canal, at their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> expense, for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; which was some time afterwards effected. By this time Dunkirk was become the best harbour the Spaniards possessed in Flanders, which induced many foreigners to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there; and it being necessary to enlarge the town for their accommodation, a new fortified wall was built at a considerable distance from the former. In 1646, it was besieged and taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Condé. In 1652 it was retaken by the archduke Leopold, then governor of the Netherlands. France entering into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with England in 1655, the Dunkirkers, with views of pecuniary advantage, fitted out privateers against both these powers: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that the French, assisted by Cromwell, attacked and took it; and it was put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, in consequence of a treaty between them and the French. To the English it was even then of very great importance; for during the war in which it was taken, the Dunkirkers had made prizes of no less than 250 of their ships, many of which were of great value. They therefore improved the fortifications, and built a citadel; yet they kept it only four years; for in 1662, two years after the Restoration, Charles II. sold this valuable acquisition to France, for the paltry sum of 500,000l. In consequence of this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, the town was taken possession of for the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> d'Estrades, on the 29th of November 1662. Louis having acquainted the celebrated engineer Monsieur Vauban, that he intended to make Dunkirk one of the strongest places in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, Vauban drew up a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> with that view, which was gradually executed. An arsenal was erected, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough to contain all the stores necessary for fitting out and maintaining a large fleet of men of war; the fortifications on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side were constructed in a manner that was thought to render them impregnable; and, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, the entrance of the harbour being properly formed, it was fortified by the jetties, and the two forts called Green Fort and the Fort of Good Hope at their extremities; the famous risbank was also erected on the side of the jetties, and Fort Galliard on the other, to secure the town. These works were all completed in 1683; and in 1685, the whole circumference of the basin was faced with masonry, and the keys completely formed: at the same time care was taken to build at the entrance of this basin a sluice, almost 45 feet wide, that the ships within might be constantly afloat. In 1689, the fort called the Cornichon, and some other works, were completed. But though 30 years had been now employed in improving the fortifications of Dunkirk, it was not yet in the state in which Louis intended to put it; and therefore, in 1701, he caused a new risbank to be built, called Fort Blanc. At the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, it having been made appear, that the privateers of Dunkirk had, during the war then closing, taken from the English no less than 1614 prizes valued at 1,334,373l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, it was stipulated, that the fortifications of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and port of Dunkirk should be entirely demolished, and the harbour filled up, so as never to be a harbour again. The treaty of which this demolition of Dunkirk was an article, was signed on the 28th of April 1713; but the demolition did not take place till the September following, when the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> deputed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Armstrong and Colonel Clayton to oversee the execution of the treaty as far as concerned the works and harbour of Dunkirk. Under the inspection of these gentlemen, the places of arms were broken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, the ditches filled up, and the demi-lunes, bastions, and covered way, totally destroyed; the citadel was razed, and the harbour and basin filled up; the jetties were also levelled with the strand, and all the forts which defended the entrance into the harbour were demolished. A large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bar, was also built across the mouth of the harbour between the jetties and the town, by which all communication between the harbour and the canal, which formed its entrance, was entirely cut off. The sluices were also broken up, and the materials of them broken to pieces. But this was no sooner done, than Louis XIV. ordered 30,000 men to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> incessantly upon a new canal, the canal of Mardick, which in a short time they accomplished; by which the harbour was rendered almost as commodious as ever; but in 1717 this likewise was rendered unserviceable. In the year 1720, during a great storm, the sea broke up the bar or dam, and restored to the Dunkirkers the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the harbour in a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. In the year 1740, when Great Britain was engaged in a war with Spain, Louis XV. set about improving the advantage which Dunkirk had derived from the storm in 1720, by restoring the works, and repairing the harbour; and soon afterwards he espoused the cause of Spain, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> in the war against us. But at the peace of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle in 1748, it was stipulated, that all the works towards the sea should be destroyed a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time; yet, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the American war, the place was in a good state of defence towards the sea. At the peace in 1783 Britain was not in a condition to insist on so obnoxious a stipulation, and its harbour has since been unmolested. The check which the British troops received here in 1793, was the commencement of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of disasters. DUNNING John, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Ashburton, an eminent English lawyer. See Supplement.

DUNS SCOTUS

Pages 425-425

John, a Franciscan friar, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Subtilis, was born in the year 1274; but whether in England, Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, hath <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of dispute among the learned of each <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Dempster, Mackenzie, and other Scottish writers, assert positively that he was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNSE">Dunse</a>, a town in Scotland, about 15 miles from Berwick; and, to secure him more effectually, Mackenzie makes him descended from the Dunses in the Mers. Macgaghwell, an Irish author, who wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of this Duns Scotus, proves him to have been born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster in Ireland: but Leland, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, Camden, and Pits, assure us, that he was born at Dunstone in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Emildune, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALNWICK">Alnwick</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>; and this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is rendered probable by the following conclusion of his manuscript works in the library of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>.—"Here end the writings of that subtile doctor of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, John Duns, who was born in a certain village, in the parish of Emildune, called Dunston, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Northumberland." We are told, that when a boy, he became accidentally known to two Franciscan friars; who, finding him to be a youth of very extraordinary capacity, took him to their convent at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and afterwards persuaded him to become one of their fraternity. From thence he was sent to Oxford, where he was made fellow of Merton college, and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and Mackenzie says, that not less than 30,000 students came to Oxford to hear his lectures. His fame was now become so universal, that the general of his order commanded him to go to Paris, that the students of that university might also profit from his lectures. He went to Paris in the year 1324, where he was honoured first with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor, then of doctor of divinity, and in 1327 was appointed regent of the divinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>: during his residence here, the famous controversy about the Immaculate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> arose. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBERTUS_MAGNUS">Albertus Magnus</a> maintained that she was born in original sin. Scotus advanced 200 arguments in support of the contrary opinion, and convinced the university of Paris that she was really conceived immaculate. This important nonsense, however, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be disputed till the year 1496, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, when the university of Paris made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, that no student, who did not believe the immaculate conception, should be admitted to a degree. Our author had not been above a year at Paris, when the same general of the Franciscans ordered him to remove to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>; where he was received with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pomp and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> by the magistrates and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and where he died of an apoplexy soon after his arrival, in the year 1308, in the 34th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Some writers have reported, that Scotus was buried in an epileptic fit; and that, upon removing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, he appeared to have turned himself in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>. This Doctor Subtilis was doubtless one of the first wranglers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, admirably well versed in scholastic divinity, and a most indefatigable scribbler; but the misfortune is, that all his huge volumes do not contain a single page worth the perusal of a rational being. He was the author of a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of schoolmen called Scotists; who opposed the opinions of the Thomists, so called from St Thomas Aquinas. The reader <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a more particular account of Scotus in the Franciscan <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">Martyrology</a>, published at Paris in 1658. He was a most voluminous writer; his works making 12 vols folio, as published at Lyons by Luke Wadding, 1639.

DUNSE

Pages 425-425

a market town of Scotland, in the shire of Mers, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 15. N. Lat. 55. 42. It is situated on a rising ground in the middle of the shire, and has a weekly market for cattle. It is by some reputed the birthplace of the famous John Duns Scotus. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> south of the town is a well of mineral <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> as a deobstruent and antiscorbutic, first discovered in 1747 by Dr Thomas Simpson who practised there. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 3082 in 1811.

DUNSTABLE

Pages 425-425

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, with a market on Wednesdays. It is seated on a chalky hill; and has ponds in the streets, which are never dry though only supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is remarkable for several good inns, it being a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> thoroughfare on the northern

DUNSTAN

Pages 425-427

a famous saint, and archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>: of whom the monkish historians give us the following account. He was descended from a noble family in Wessex, and educated in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Glastonbury. Here he studied so hard, that it threw him into a violent fever, which brought him to the very point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. When the whole family were standing about his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, dissolved in tears, and expecting every moment to see him expire, an angel came from heaven in a dreadful storm, and gave him a medicine which restored him to perfect <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> in a moment. Dunstan immediately started from his bed, and ran with all his speed towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to return thanks for his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> met him by the way, surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> dogs, and endeavoured to obstruct his passage. This would have frightened some boys; but it had no such effect upon Dunstan; who pronouncing a sacred name, and brandishing his stick, put the devil and all his dogs to flight. The church doors being shut, an angel took him in his arms, conveyed him through an opening in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, and set him softly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, where he performed his devotions. After his recovery, he pursued his studies with the greatest ardour, and soon became a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, music, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, working in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, &c. When he was still very young he entered into holy orders, and was introduced by his uncle Athelhelm archbishop of Canterbury to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Athelstan; who, charmed with his person and accomplishments, retained him in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and employed him in many great affairs. At leisure hours he used to entertain the king and his courtiers with playing on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>; and now and then he wrought a miracle, which gained him great admiration. His old enemy the devil was much offended at this, and prompted some envious courtiers to persuade the king that his favourite was a magician, which that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> too readily believed. Dunstan discovering by the king's countenance that he had lost his favour, and resolving to resign rather than be turned out, retired from court to another uncle, who was bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>. This good prelate prevailed upon his nephew to forsake the world and become a monk; after which he retired to a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, built against the church wall of Glastonbury. Here he slept, studied, prayed, meditated, and sometimes amused himself with forging several useful things in brass and iron. One evening, as he was working very busily at his forge, the devil, putting on the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, thrust his head in at the window of his cell, and asked him to make something or other for him. Dunstan was so intent upon his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that he made no answer; on which the devil began to swear and talk obscenely, which betrayed the lurking fiend. The holy blacksmith, putting up a secret ejaculation, pulled his tongs, which were <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot, out of the fire, seized the devil with them by the nose, and squeezed him with all his strength; which made his infernal majesty roar and scold at such a rate, that he awakened and terrified all the people for many miles around. Thus far the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a>. Ridiculous as were these fictions, they served, in those times of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, to procure Dunstan a reputation which has been confirmed by the authority of several succeeding historians. It appears that this extraordinary person was called to court by King Edmund, A.D. 941; who bestowed upon him the rich abbey of Glastonbury, which for his sake he honoured with many peculiar privileges. He enjoyed a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the favour of this prince during his short reign of six years; but he stood much higher in the favour of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and successor King Edred, to whom he was confessor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> confidant, and prime minister. He employed all his influence during this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of court favour in promoting the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the monks of the Benedictine order, to which he belonged, and of which he was a most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and zealous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>. Having the treasures of these two princes, especially of the last, very much at his command, he lavished them away in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and endowing monasteries for these monks, because almost all the old monasteries were in the possession of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> canons. Not contented with this, he persuaded Edred (who was a bigotted valetudinary) to bestow such immense treasures on the churches and monasteries by his last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> was stripped of its most valuable possessions, and left in a state of indigence. This conduct of Dunstan, while he was in power, rendered him very odious to Edwi, who succeeded his uncle Edred A.D. 955; and his rude behaviour to himself, and his beloved <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Elgiva, raised the resentment of that prince so high, that he deprived him of all his preferments, and drove him into exile*. The banishment of Dunstan, the great patron, or (as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALMSBURY">Malmsbury</a> calls him) the prince of monks, was a severe blow to that order, who were expelled from several monasteries; which were made the impure stables (according to the same author) of the married clergy. But their sufferings were not of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance. For Edgar the younger brother of Edwi, having raised a successful rebellion against his unhappy brother, and usurped all his dominions on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, recalled Dunstan, and gave him the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, A.D. 957. From this moment he was the chief confidant and prime minister of King Edgar, who became sole monarch of England A.D. 959, by the death of his elder brother Edwi. In the following year Dunstan was raised to be archbishop of Canterbury; and being thus possessed of the primacy, and assured of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> support and assistance, he prepared to execute the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> which he had long meditated, of compelling the secular canons to put away their wives and become monks; or of driving them out, and introducing Benedictine monks in their room. With this view he procured the promotion of Oswald to the see of Worcester, and of Ethelwald to that of Winchester; two prelates who were monks themselves, and animated with the most ardent zeal for the advancement of their order. And these three great champions of the order found means, by their arts and intrigues, in the course of a few years, to fill no fewer than 48 monasteries with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>. But on the death of Edgar in 975 they received a check. The DUNstan, sufferings of the persecuted canons had excited much compassion; and many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, who had been overawed by the power and zeal of the late king, now espoused their cause and promoted their restoration. Elferc <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Mercia drove the monks by force out of all the monasteries in that extensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and brought back the canons, with their wives and children; while Elswin duke of East Anglia, and Brithnot duke of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, raised their troops to protect the monks in these countries. To allay these commotions, several councils were held: in which Dunstan was so hard pushed by the secular canons and their friends, that he was obliged to practise some of his holy stratagems; and finally, by dint of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, overcame all St Dunstan died A.D. 988, in the 64th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, having held the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, together with the archbishopric of Canterbury, about 27 years. As this prelate was the great restorer and promoter of the monastic institutions, the grateful monks, who were almost the only historians of those dark ages, have loaded him with the most extravagant praises, and represented him as the greatest wonder-worker and highest favourite of heaven that ever lived. To say nothing of his many conflicts with the devil, in which he often laboured that enemy of mankind most severely, the following short story, which is told with great exultation by his biographer Osbern, will give the reader some idea of the astonishing impiety and impudence of those monks, and of the no less astonishing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLINDNESS">blindness</a> and credulity of those unhappy times. "The most admirable, the most inestimable Father Dunstan (says that author), whose perfections exceeded all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> imagination, was admitted to behold the mother of God and his own mother in eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; for before his death he was carried up into heaven, to be present at the nuptials of his own mother with the Eternal King, which were celebrated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> with the most sweet and joyous songs. When the angels reproached him for his silence on this great occasion, so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to his mother, he excused himself on account of his being unacquainted with those sweet and heavenly strains; but being a little instructed by the angels, he broke out into this melodious song, O King and Ruler of nations," &c. It is unnecessary to make any comment on this most shocking story. The violent and too successful zeal of Dunstan and his associates, in promoting the building and endowing so great a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of houses for the entertainment of useless monks and nuns, was very fatal to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: for by this means a spirit of irrational unmanly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> was diffused amongst the people, which debased their minds, and diverted them from nobler pursuits; and a very great proportion of the lands of England being put into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> who contributed nothing to its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, rendered it an easy prey, first to the insulting Danes, and afterwards to the victorious Normans.

DUNUM

Pages 427-427

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; now thought to be <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Down-Patrick, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Down. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 57'. N. Lat. 54° 23'.

DUODECIMA

Pages 427-427

in Music, is the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the fifth doubled. DUODENUM. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DUPIN

Pages 427-427
LEWIS ELLIS, a learned doctor of the Sorbonne, and one of the greatest critics of his time, especially in ecclesiastical matters, was born at Paris in 1657. When he published the first volume of his Bibliothèque Universelle des Auteurs Ecclesiastiques, in 1686, the liberty with which he treated some ecclesiastical writers gave such offence, that M. de Harlay, archbishop of Paris, obliged Dupin to retract many propositions, and suppressed the work. He was nevertheless suffered to continue it, by altering the title from Bibliothèque Universelle to Bibliothèque Nouvelle. This great undertaking, continued in several successive volumes, though sufficient to occupy the life of an ordinary man, did not hinder M. Dupin from obliging the world with several other works. He was a man of prodigious reading; and had an easy happy way of writing, with an uncommon talent at analyzing the works of an author; which makes his Ecclesiastical Bibliothèque so valuable. M. Dupin was professor of philosophy in the royal college: but was banished some time from the chair to Chatellerault, on account of the famous Cas de Conscience; but was restored, and died in 1719.

DUPLE

Pages 427-427

among mathematicians, denotes the ratio of 2 to 1. Thus the ratio of 8 to 4 is duple, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as 2 to 1. Sub-Duple Ratio, is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> the reverse of the former, or as 1 to 2. Such is 4 to 8, or 6 to 12.

DUPLICATE

Pages 427-427

among lawyers, denotes a copy of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> account. It is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> letters-patent, granted by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> wherein he had before done the same. Also a second <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written and sent to the same party and purpose as a former, for fear of the first's miscarrying, is called a Duplicate. DUPLICATE Proportion or Ratio. See Ratio.

DUPLICATION

Pages 427-427

in general, signifies the doubling of any thing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> multiplying of it by 2: also the folding of any thing back again on itself.

DUPLICATURE

Pages 427-427

among anatomists, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote the folds of any membrane <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessel: thus we say, the duplicatures of the intestines, peritoneum, &c.

DUPONDUS

Pages 427-427

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of two pounds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of the value of two asses. See AS. As the as at first weighed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> a pondo or libra, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUPONDIUS">dupondius</a> then weighed two; and hence the name. And though the weight of the as was afterwards diminished, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> that of the dupondius also, yet they still retained the denomination. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">Pound</a> and Libra.

DUPPA

Pages 427-428

BRIAN, a learned English bishop, born in DURER 1589 at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWISHAM">Lewisham</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his father was then <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. In 1634, he was instituted <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Sarum, and soon after made chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. He was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to Charles <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> James <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; was made bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>; and in 1641 translated to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, though the confusions that followed deprived him of all benefit from his promotion. Charles I. held him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem, and he is said to have assisted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> in composing the Eikon Basilike. On the Restoration he was made bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> high almoner; but died in 1662.

DURANDUS

Pages 428-428

WILLIAM, born at Paimoission in Provence, in the 13th century, was one of the most knowing lawyers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Pope Martin made him one of his nuncios, and then bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MENDE">Mende</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. His Speculum Juris gave him the name of Speculator; his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> piece was Rationale divinorum officiorum, containing eight books. He wrote several others.

DURANTA

Pages 428-428

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the didynamia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 40th order, Personatae. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DURATION

Pages 428-428

an idea we get by attending to the fleeting and perpetual perishing parts of succession. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>. Duration, as marked by certain periods and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, is what we most properly call <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. See Time. Duration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">Action</a>, according to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, is confined to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in tragedy; but the epopea, according to the same critic, has no fixed time. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>.

DURER

Pages 428-428

ALBERT, descended of an Hungarian family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> in 1471, was one of the best engravers and painters of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; and he was an intimate friend of Erasmus, who revised some of the pieces which he published. He was a man of business also, and for many years the leading <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of Nuremberg. Though not the inventor, he was one of the first improvers of the art of engraving; and he bethought himself of working also in wood, for expedition, having an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of designs. In many of those <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> which he executed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, the engraving is elegant to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">Hell</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">Scene</a> particularly, which was engraved in the year 1513, is as highly finished a print as ever was engraved, and as happily executed. In his wooden prints too we are surprised to see so much meaning in so early a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; the heads so well marked, and every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> so well executed.—This <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> seems to have understood the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, too, is often pleasing; and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> generally good. But he knows very little of the management of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and still less of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>: and yet his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> are purer and more elegant than we could have supposed from the awkward archetypes which his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> afforded. In a word, he was certainly a man of very extensive genius; and, as Vasari remarks, would have been an extraordinary artist, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had had an Italian instead of a German education. His prints are very numerous. They were much admired in his own lifetime, and eagerly bought up; which put his wife, who was a teasing woman, upon urging him to spend more time upon engraving than he was inclined to do. He was rich; and chose rather to practice his art as an amusement than as a business. He died in the year 1527.

DURESSE

Pages 428-428

HARDSHIP, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is where a person is kept in prison <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> restrained of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, contrary to order of law; or is threatened to be killed, maimed, or beaten. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a person so in prison, or in fear of such threats, make any specialty or obligation, by reason of such imprisonment or threats, such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> is void in law; and in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> brought on such specialty, the party may plead, that it was brought by duresse.

DURHAM

Pages 428-430

BISHOPRIC OF, one of the counties of England. Before the arrival of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> it was included in the British principality of the Brigantes, and after their arrival made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Maxima Caesariensis. During the Heptarchy it made part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, the 5th established, which began in 547, and ended in 827, having been governed by 31 kings. It was not mentioned by Alfred in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of counties, being at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> considered as a part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. At present it is included in the northern circuit, in the province of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> and principality under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of its own bishop, being a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> palatine, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and the richest in England. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Northumberland, on the south by Yorkshire, on the east by the North <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>. It is 39 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 35 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and 107 in circumference; containing 410,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> acres, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 758 square miles; with 177,625 inhabitants (1811), 80 parishes, 21 vicarages, one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> (Durham), and 9 market <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKTON">Stockton</a>, Sunderland, Barnard-Castle, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARLINGTON">Darlington</a>, Stanhope, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARTLEPOOL">Hartlepool</a>, Auckland, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAINDROP">Staindrop</a>, and Marwood; besides 223 villages. It is divided... divided into 4 wards, sends 4 members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, pays three portions of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax, and provides 400 of the national <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. It has 21 parks, 4 castles, and 20 bridges, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEES">Tees</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TINE">Tine</a>, Wear, Tame, Lune, Darwent, Gauntless, Skern, &c., and the Lune and Teesdale forests. Its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> products are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, coals, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, corn, mustard, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, glass, fine ale, with excellent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and salmon. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is various; the south is rich, but the western parts rocky and moorish. Durham, as already observed, is a county palatine, governed by the bishop, who had formerly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> prerogatives. He had power to create barons, appoint judges, convolve parliaments, raise taxes, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> were kept in his name; and he granted pardons for trespasses, alienations, rapes, murders, and felonies of every denomination. He erected corporations, granted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, created officers by patent, was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of the seas and waters within the county palatine; great part of the lands were held of the see in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>. In a word, he exercised all the power and jurisdiction of a sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. How and at what <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> these prerogatives were obtained, it is not easy to determine. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALMSBURY">Malmsbury</a> says, the lands were granted by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred, who likewise made the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> a sanctuary for criminals. This see was anciently called the patrimony of St Cuthbert, who had been bishop of Lindisfarne or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOLY_ISLAND">Holy <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> near Berwick. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> being transferred to Durham, were long esteemed as precious relics; and the people of the county considered themselves as Halwerk men, exempted from all other but holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, that is, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of St Cuthbert's body. Certain it is, they pretended to hold their lands by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>; and refused to serve out of the county either for the king or bishop; but King Edward I. broke through these privileges, and curtailed the prerogatives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, which were still further abridged by Henry VIII. Nevertheless, the bishop is still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sadberk, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in this county which he holds by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>. He is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> paramount, and appoints his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, who makes up his audit to him, instead of accounting to the exchequer. He has all the forfeitures upon outlawries; and he and his temporal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as justices of the peace for the county palatine, which comprehends Creke in Yorkshire, Bedlington, Northam, and Holy Island, in Northumberland; the inhabitants of these places having the benefit of the courts at Durham. The judges of assize, and all the officers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, have still their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> salaries from the bishop; and he constitutes the standing officers by his letters patent. He has the power of presiding in person in any of the courts of judicature. Even when judgment of blood is given, this prelate may sit in court in his purple robes, though the canons forbid any clergyman to be present in such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; hence the old saying, Solum Dumelmenae stola jus dicet et ense. It was not till the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. that the bishopric sent representatives to parliament. Durham, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above-mentioned county, is situated in W. Long. 1. 14. N. Lat. 54. 50. It stands on a hill almost surrounded by the river Wear; and is considerable for its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants, as well as for being the see or seat of the bishop, who is lord paramount. It stands about 280 miles north from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; being remarkable for the salubrity of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and the abundance and cheapness of its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. These circumstances have induced a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> to take up their residence at Durham, which is still further animated by the presence and court of the bishop and his clergy. The town is said to have been built about 70 years before the Roman conquest, on occasion of bringing hither the body of St Cuthbert. It was first incorporated by King Richard I., but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> extended its privileges. At length, in the year 1684, it obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, it is now governed by a mayor, 12 aldermen, 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men, with a recorder and inferior officers.
