These can hold a court leet and court baron within the city; but under the style of the bishop, who, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> palatine, appoints a judge, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, sheriffs, and other inferior magistrates. The mayor and aldermen also keep a pie poulardes court at their fairs, and pay a yearly toll to the bishop. They have a weekly market on Saturday, and three annual fairs. Durham is about half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, and has been by some compared to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a crab, the market place exhibiting the body, and the claws being represented by the streets, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> according to the course of the river, which almost surrounds one part of the city. They are, moreover, dark and narrow; and some of them steep and dangerous to wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. The number of inhabitants in 1811 was 6763. The houses are in general strong-built, but neither <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> nor elegant. The most remarkable edifices are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, with six other churches, three standing in the city, and as many in the suburbs; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; the castle, or bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; the tolbooth near St Nicholas's church; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> and conduit in the market place; with two bridges over the Wear. The cathedral was begun by Bishop Carilepho in the 11th century. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, magnificent, Gothic structure, 411 feet long, and 80 in breadth, having a cross aisle in the middle 170 feet in length, and two smaller aisles at each end. On the south side is a fine cloister; on the east, the old library, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and part of the deanery; on the west, the dormitory, under which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> and chantry; and on the west side is the new library, an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> begun by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Sudbury about 70 years ago, on the spot where stood the old refectory of the convent. The middle tower of the cathedral is 212 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The whole building is arched and supported by huge pillars. Several of the windows are curiously painted; and there is a handsome screen at the entrance into the choir. Sixteen bishops are interred in the chapter-house, which is 75 feet long, and 33 broad, arched overhead, with a magnificent seat at the upper end for the instalment of the bishops. The consistory is kept in the chapel of the west aisle called Galilee, which was built by Bishop Pusey, and had formerly 16 altars for women, as they were not allowed to advance farther than the line of marble by the side of the font; here likewise are deposited the bones of the venerable Bede, whose eulogium is written on an old <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> scroll that hangs over his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>. The long cross aisle at the extremity of the church was formerly distinguished by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> altars, four to the north, and four to the south, and the most magnificent in the middle dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> St Cuthbert. Durham, whose rich shrine was in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, formerly much frequented by pilgrims. The church is possessed of some old records relating to the affairs of Scotland, the kings of which were great benefactors to this cathedral. The ornaments here used for administering the divine offices, are said to be richer than those of any other cathedral in England. Before the Reformation, it was distinguished by the name Ecclesia sanctae Mariae et sancti Cuthberti; but it obtained the appellation of Ecclesia cathedralis Christi et beatae Mariae, in the reign of Henry VIII., who endowed the deanery with 12 prebendaries, 12 <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> canons, a deacon, subdeacon, 16 lay singing men, a schoolmaster and usher, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the choir, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> reader, eight almsmen, 18 scholars, 10 choristers, two vergers, two porters, two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COOKS">cooks</a>, two butlers, and two sacristans. On the south side of the cathedral is the college; a spacious court formed by the houses of the prebendaries, who are richly endowed and extremely well lodged. Above the college gate, at the east end, is the exchequer; and at the west, a large <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> for entertaining strangers, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> and other offices of the convent. The college school, with the master's house, stands on the north side of the cathedral. Between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> and castle is an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> called the palace green; at the west end of which stands the shire hall, where the assizes and sessions are held for the county. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> by is the library built by Bishop Cosin; together with the exchequer raised by Bishop Nevil, in which are kept the offices belonging to the county palatine court. There is an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> on the east, endowed by Bishop Cosin, and at each end of it are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> founded by Bishop <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGLEY">Langley</a>. On the north, is the castle built by William the Conqueror, and afterwards converted into the bishop's palace, the outward gate of which is at present the county gaol. The city consists of three manors; the bishop's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, containing the city liberties and the bailey, held of him by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of castle <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>; the manor of the dean and chapter, consisting of the Elvet's cross-gate, South-gate street; and the manor of Gilligate, formerly belonging to the dissolved hospital of Koppar in this neighbourhood, but granted by Edward VI. to John Cockburn, lord of Ormiston, and late in the possession of John Tempest, Esq. The bishopric of Durham is deemed the richest bishopric in the kingdom; and the prebends are frequently styled the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Prebends of Durham. The diocese contains the whole counties of Durham and Northumberland, except the jurisdiction of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEXHAM">Hexham</a> in the latter. It hath also one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in the county of Cumberland; making in the whole 135 parishes, whereof 87 are inappropriate. The see is valued in the king's books at £282l. 1s. 5½d. but is said to be worth about ten times that sum annually. The clergy's tenths amount to £385l. 9s. 6½d. It has two archdeacons, viz. of Durham and Northumberland. This see hath given to the church of Rome eight saints and one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>; and to the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> one lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> justice, five lord chancellors, three lord treasurers, one principal secretary of state, one chancellor to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and two masters of the rolls. In the neighbourhood of this city is Nevil's cross, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought in the year 1346, against <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> II. king of Scotland, who was defeated and taken prisoner.

DURIO

Pages 430-430

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyadelphia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DURNIUM

Pages 430-430
or Durnovaria, a town of the Durotriges in Britain; now Dorchester, the capital of Dorsetshire, on the Frome. DUROBRIVÆ, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Catyuenchiani in Britain. Now in ruins, which lie on the Nea, between Caster and Dornford, in Northamptonshire, on the borders of Huntingdon.

DUROBRIVE

Pages 430-430
or Durocobriva, a town of the Trinobantes, in Britain; whose ruins are situated between Flamstead and Redburn, in Hertfordshire.

DUROBRIVES

Pages 430-430

25 miles to the west of Durovernum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>; from which it appears to be <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> town: confirmed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of foundation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, in which it is called Durobrevis.

DUROCASES

Pages 430-430

DUROCASSIUM, DUROCASSÆ, and Durocasses, a town of the Carnutes in Gallia Celtica; now <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREUX">Dreux</a>. See Druidæ.

DUROCORNVIUM

Pages 430-430

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRENCESTER">Cirencester</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> (Camden), called Corinium by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>.

DUROCORTORUM

Pages 430-430
or Duriortora, a town of the Rhemi in Belgica; now Rheims in Champagne. E. Long. 4° 8'. N. Lat. 49° 20'.

DUROIA

Pages 430-430

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandra class of plants. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DUROLENUM

Pages 430-430

a town of the Cantii in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LENHAM">Lenham</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> (Camden); Charing (Talbot.)

DUROLITUM

Pages 430-430

a town of the Trinobantes; now Leiston, on the Lev, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> (Camden).

DUROTRIGES

Pages 430-430

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, seated in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which is now called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>. Their name is derived from the two British words Dur, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>," and Trigo, "to dwell;" and it is no less evident that they got their name from the situation of their country, which lies along the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. It is not very certain whether the Durotriges formed an independent state, under a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of their own, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> were united with their neighbours the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANMONII">Danmonii</a>; as they were reduced by Vespasian under the dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and with the same ease, and never revolted. The peaceable disposition of the inhabitants was probably the reason that the Romans had so few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, forts, and garrisons, in this pleasant country. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>, its present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, seems to have been a Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of some consideration, though our antiquaries are not agreed about its Roman name. It is most probable, that it was the Durnovaria in the 12th Iter of Antoninus. Many Roman names have been found at Dorchester; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> way, called Jeening-street, passed through it; and some vestiges of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall with which it was surrounded, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> with which it was adorned, are still visible. The country of the Durotriges was included in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> called Flavia Cesariensis, and governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of that province, as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the Romans kept any footing in these parts.

DURY

Pages 430-431

JOHN, a Scots divine, who travelled much, and laboured with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> zeal to reunite the Lutherans with with the Calvinists. His discouragements in this scheme started another still more impracticable; and this was to reunite all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> by means of a new explication of the Apocalypse, which he published at Frankfort in 1677. He enjoyed then a comfortable retreat in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is unknown: his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> du Moulin concerning the state of the churches of England, Scotland, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1658, by the care of du Moulin, and is esteemed to be curious.

DUSKY BAY

Pages 431-431

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> in the Southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. It is in S. Lat. 45° 47' and in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 166° 18'.

DUSSAULX

Pages 431-431

JOHN, a French writer of the last century. See Supplement.

DUSSELDORF

Pages 431-431

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>. It is situated at the confluence of the river Dussel with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 25', N. Lat. 51° 12'. It was formerly the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> palatine, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CARLSTADT">Carlstadt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the new town, is divided into six regular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> which open into an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; and forms a beautiful addition to the old city. Dusseldorf was taken by the French in 1795. The fortifications were demolished after the peace in 1801. In 1806 it became the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Berg; but in 1815 it was made over, with the rest of the duchy, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It contains, including the garrison, 18,000 inhabitants.

DUTENS

Pages 431-431
LOUIS, a French miscellaneous writer. See Supplement. DUTCHY. See Duchy.

DUTY

Pages 431-431

in general, denotes any thing that one is obliged to perform. Duty, in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. Duty, in policy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, signifies the impost laid on merchandises, at importation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the duties of customs; also the taxes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, stamp duties, &c. See Customs, Excise, &c. The principles on which all duties and customs should be laid on foreign merchandises which are imported into these kingdoms, are such as tend to cement a mutual friendship and traffic between one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> and another; and therefore due care should be taken in the laying of them, that they may answer so good an end, and be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> in both countries; they should be so laid as to make the exports of this nation at least equal to our imports from those nations wherewith we trade, to the end that no greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of our landholders and manufacturers should be deprived of their revenues arising from the product of the lands, and the labour of the people, by foreign importations, than are maintained by exportations to such countries. These are the national principles on which all our treaties of commerce with other countries ought to be grounded. Duty, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of those functions that belong to a soldier: with this distinction, that mounting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> and the like, where there is no enemy directly to be engaged, is called duty; but their marching to meet and fight an enemy is called going on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

DUUMVIRATE

Pages 431-431

the office <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUUMVIRI">duumviri</a>. See the next article. The duumvirate lasted till the year of Rome 388, when it was changed into a decemvirate.

DUUMVIRI

Pages 431-431

in Roman antiquity, a general appellation given to magistrates, commissioners, and officers, where two were joined together in the same functions. DUUMVIRI Capitales were the judges in criminal causes: from their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> it was lawful to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the people, who only had the power of condemning a citizen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. These judges were taken from the body of the decuriones; they had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power and authority, were members of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and had two <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LICTORS">lictors</a> to walk before them. DUUMVIRI Municipales, were two magistrates in some cities of the empire, answering to what the consuls were at Rome: they were chosen out of the body of the decuriones; their office lasted <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> five years, upon which account they were frequently termed quinquennales magistratus. Their jurisdiction was of great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>: they had officers who walked before them, carrying a small switch in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and some of them assumed the privilege of having lictors, carrying axes, and the fasces <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bundles of rods, before them. DUUMVIRI Navales, were the commissaries of the fleet, first created at the request of M. Decius, tribune of the people, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Samnites. The duty of their office consisted in giving orders for the fitting of ships, and giving their commissions to the marine officers, &c. DUUMVIRI Sacrorum, were magistrates created by Tarquinius Superbus, for the performance of the sacrifices, and keeping of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBYLS">sibyls</a> books. They were chosen from among the patricians, and held their office for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; they were exempted from serving in the wars, and from the offices imposed on the other citizens, and without them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> of the sibyls could not be consulted.

DUYVELAND

Pages 431-431
or DIVELAND, one of the islands of Zeeland, in the United Provinces, lying eastward of Schonen, from which it is only separated by a narrow channel.

DWARF

Pages 431-432

in general an appellation given to things greatly inferior in size to that which is usual in their several kinds: thus there are dwarfs of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, dwarf dogs, dwarf trees, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were passionately fond of dwarfs, whom they called nani <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> nanos, insomuch that they often used <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> methods to prevent the growth of boys designed for dwarfs, by enclosing them in boxes, or by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of tight bandages. Augustus's niece, Julia, was extremely fond of a dwarf called Sonopas, who was only two feet and a handbreadth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. We have many other accounts of human dwarfs, but most of them deformed in some way or other besides the smallness of their size. Many relations also concerning dwarfs we must necessarily look upon to be fabulous, as well as those concerning giants. The following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, however, which we have reason to look upon as authentic, is too remarkable not to be acceptable to the generality of our readers. Jeffery. Jeffery Hudson, the famous English dwarf, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-OAKHAM">Oakham</a>, in Rutlandshire, in 1619; and about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight, being then but 18 inches high, was retained in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, who resided at Burleigh on the Hill. Soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> being entertained at Burleigh, little Jeffery was served up to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> pie, and presented by the duchess to the queen, who kept him as her dwarf. From 7 years of age till 30, he never grew taller; but after 30, he <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> up to three feet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches, and there fixed. Jeffery became a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the entertainment of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Sir William Davenant wrote a poem called Jefferys, on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between him and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">turkey</a> cock; and in 1638, was published a very small book, called the New Year's Gift, presented at court by the lady Parvula to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Minimus (<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Little Jeffery) her majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, &c. written by Microphilus, with a little print of Jeffery prefixed. Before this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, Jeffery was employed on a negotiation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance: he was sent to France to fetch a midwife for the queen; and on his return with this gentlewoman, and her majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and many rich presents to the queen from her mother <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis, he was taken by the Dunkirkers. Jeffery, thus made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, grew to think himself really so. He had borne with little temper the teasing of the courtiers and domestics, and had many squabbles with the king's gigantic porter. At last, being provoked by Mr Crofts, a young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of family, a challenge ensued; and Mr Crofts coming to the rendezvous armed only with a squirt, the little creature was so enraged, that a real <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a> ensued; and the appointment being on horseback with pistols, to put them more on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, Jeffery, with the first fire, shot his antagonist dead. This happened in France, whither he had attended his mistress in the troubles. He was again taken prisoner by a Turkish rover, and sold into Barbary. He probably did not remain <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>; for at the beginning of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, he was made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and in 1644 attended the queen to France, where he remained till the Restoration. At last, upon suspicion of his being privy to the popish plot, he was taken up in 1682, and confined in the Gatehouse, Westminster, where he ended his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in the 63rd year of his age. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the Royal Academy of Sciences, a relation is given by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Tressau, of a dwarf called Bebe kept by the late Stanislaus, king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and who died in 1764, at the age of 23, when he measured only 32 inches. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his birth, he measured only between eight and nine inches. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">Diminutive</a> as were his dimensions, his reasoning faculties were not less scanty; appearing indeed not to have been superior to those of a well-taught pointer; but that the size and strength of the intellectual powers are not affected by the diminutiveness or tenuity of the corporeal organs, is evident from a still more striking instance of littleness, given us by the same nobleman, in the person of Monsieur Borulawski, a Polish gentleman, whom he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNEVILLE">Luneville</a>, who has since been at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and who at the age of 22 measured only 28 inches. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, considering him only as to his bodily dimensions, appears a giant with regard to his mental powers and attainments. He is described by the count as possessing all the graces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, united with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment and an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>; so that we may with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> say of M. Borulawski, in the words of Seneca, and nearly in the order in which he has used them, "Posse ingenium fortissimum ac beatissimum sub quolibet corpusculo lateri." Epist. 66. Count Borulawski was the son of a Polish nobleman attached to the fortunes of King Stanislaus, who lost his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in consequence of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, and who had six children, three dwarfs, and three well grown. What is singular enough, they were born alternately, a big one and a little one, though both parents were of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size. The little count's youngest sister was much less than him, but died at the age of 23. The count <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to grow till he was about 30, and has at present attained his 51st year, and the height of three feet two inches. He never experienced any sickness, but lived in a polite and affluent manner under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of a lady, a friend of the family, till <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> at the age of 41 intruded into his little peaceful bosom, and involved him in matrimony, care, and perplexity. The lady he chose was of his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but of French <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, and the middle size. They have three children, all girls, and none of them likely to be dwarfs. To provide for a family now became an object big with difficulty, requiring all the exertion of his powers (which could <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> but little) and his talents, of which music alone afforded any view of profit. He plays extremely well upon the guitar; and by having concerts in several of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities in Germany, he raised temporary supplies. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> he was persuaded to turn his thoughts to England, where it was believed the public curiosity might in a little time benefit him sufficiently to enable him to live independent in so cheap a country as Poland. He was furnished by very respectable friends with recommendations to several of the most distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, as the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, Rutland, &c. &c., whose kind patronage he is not backward to acknowledge. He was advised to let himself be seen as a curiosity, and the price of admission was fixed at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his visitors, of course, was not very great. After a pretty long stay in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> he went to Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>; visited <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> and some other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; whence he returned by way of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>, to London. He also visited <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Scotland. In every <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he acquired a number of friends. In reality, the ease and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> of his manners and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> please no less, than the diminutive, yet elegant, proportions of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> astonish those who visit him. His person is pleasing and graceful, and his look manly and noble. He speaks French fluently, and English tolerably. He is remarkably lively and cheerful, though fitted for the most serious and rational conversation. Such is this wonderful little man—an object of curiosity really worthy the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the man of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and the anatomist. His life has been published, written by himself.

DWINA

Pages 432-433

the name of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; one of which rises in Lithuania, and, dividing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a> from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, falls into the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> a little below <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>; the other gives name to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Dwina in Russia. DYCK. See VANDYCK.

DYER

Pages 433-433

John, the son of Robert Dyer, Esq., a Welsh solicitor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> capacity, was born in 1700. He passed through Westminster school under the care of Dr Freind, and was then called home to be instructed in his father's profession. His genius, however, led him a different way; for besides his early <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, having a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> no less strong for the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, he determined to make <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> his profession. With this view, having studied a while under his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he became, as he tells his friend, an itinerant painter, and wandered about South <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and the parts adjacent; and about 1727 printed Grongar Hill. Being probably unsatisfied with his own proficiency, he made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; where, besides the usual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the remains of antiquity, and the works of the great masters, he frequently spent whole days in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, sketching those picturesque prospects with facility and spirit. Images from hence naturally transferred themselves into his poetical compositions: the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> beauties of The Ruins of Rome are perhaps of this kind; and the various landscapes in The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">Fleece</a> have been particularly admired. On his return to England, he published The Ruins of Rome, 1740; but soon found that he could not relish a town <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, nor submit to the assiduity required in his profession. As his turn of mind was rather serious, and his conduct and behaviour always irreproachable, he was advised by his friends to enter into holy orders; and it is presumed, though his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> had not been regular, that he found no difficulty in obtaining them. He was ordained by the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> conferred on him. About the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he married a lady of Coleshill named Ensor; "whose grandmother (says he) was a Shakespeare, descended from a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of every body's Shakespeare." His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> provision was a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time but slender. His first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, Mr Harper, gave him, in 1741, Calthorp in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, of 80l. a-year, on which he lived ten years; and in April 1751 exchanged it for Belchford in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, of 75l. which was given him by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Hardwicke, on the recommendation of a friend to virtue and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>. His condition now began to mend. In 1752, Sir John Heathcote gave him Comingsby, of 140l. a-year; and in 1756, when he was LL.B. without any solicitation of his own, obtained for him from the chancellor Kirby-on-Bane, of 110l. In 1757, he published The Fleece, his greatest poetical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; of which Dr Johnson relates this ludicrous story. Dodgson the bookseller was one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> mentioning it to a critical visitor, with more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of success than the other could easily admit. In the conversation the author's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> was asked: and being represented as advanced in life, "He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> (said the critic) be buried in woollen." He did not indeed long outlive that publication, nor long enjoy the increase of his preferments; for a consumptive disorder, with which he had long struggled, carried him off at length in 1758. Mr Dyer's character as a writer has been fixed by three poems, Grongar Hill, The Ruins of Rome, and The Fleece; wherein a poetical imagination perfectly original, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> simplicity connected with and often productive of the true sublime, and the warmest sentiments of benevolence and virtue, have been universally observed and admired. These pieces were put out separately in his lifetime; but after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> they were collected and published in one volume 8vo, 1761; with a short account of himself prefixed. DYER'S-WEED. See RESEDA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">DYEING</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

DYNA DYANOMETER

Pages 547-547

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for ascertaining the relative strength of men and animals. Of an instrument of this kind, invented by Regnier, and of which a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is given in vol. ii. Jour. de l'Ecole Polytechnique, the author thus speaks. "Some important knowledge, says he, might be acquired, had we the easy means of ascertaining, in a comparative manner, our relative strengths at the different periods of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and in different states of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Buffon and Gueneau, who had some excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> on this subject, requested me to endeavour to invent a portable machine, which, by an easy and simple mechanism, might conduct to a solution of this question, on which they were then engaged. These philosophers were acquainted with that invented by Graham, and improved by Dr Desaguliers, at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but this machine, constructed of wooden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, was too bulky and heavy to be portable; and, besides, to make experiments on the different parts of the body, several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> were necessary, each suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> required to be tried. They were acquainted also with the dynanometer of Citizen Leroy of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It consisted of a metal tube 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 inches in length, placed vertically on a foot like that of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CANDLESTICK">candlestick</a>, and containing in the inside a spiral <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, having above it a graduated shank terminating in a globe. This shank, together with the spring, sunk into the tube in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> acting upon it, and thus pointed out, in degrees, the strength of the person who pressed on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. "This instrument, though ingenious, did not appear sufficient however to Buffon and Gueneau; for they wished not merely to ascertain the muscular force of a finger or hand, but to estimate that of each limb separately, and of all the parts of the body. I shall not here give an account of the attempts I made to fulfil the wishes of these two philosophers, but only observe, that in the course of my experiments I had reason to be convinced that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the instrument was not so easy as might have been expected. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> which an enlightened naturalist may make of this machine, it may be possible to apply it to many other important purposes. For example, it may be employed with advantage to determine the strength of draught cattle; and, above all, to try that of horses, and compare it with the strength of other animals. It may serve to make known how far the assistance of well-constructed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> may favour the movement of a carriage, and what is its vis inertiae in proportion to the load. We might appreciate by it, also, what resistance the slope of a mountain opposes to a carriage, and be able to judge whether a carriage is sufficiently loaded in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of horses that are to be yoked to it. In the arts, it may be applied to machines of which we wish to ascertain the resistance, and when we are desirous to calculate the moving force that ought to be adapted to them. It may serve, also, as a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> to weigh burdens. In short, nothing would be more easy than to convert it into an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANEMOMETER">anemometer</a>, to discover the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> force of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, by fitting to it a frame of a determined size filled up with wax cloth; and it would not be impossible to ascertain by this machine the recoil of fire-arms, and consequently the strength of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder. "This dynanometer, in its form and size, has a near resemblance to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPHOMETER">graphometer</a>. It consists of a spring twelve inches in length, bent into the form of an ellipse; from the middle of which arises a semicircular piece of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, having engraved upon it the different degrees that express a force of the power acting on the spring. The whole of this machine, which weighs only two pounds and a half, opposes, however, more resistance than may be necessary to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the strongest and most robust <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>." For a fuller description, see Phil. Mag. vol. i.

DYNAMICS

Pages 540-547

Such is the view of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of moving forces which we proposed to lay before our readers. Those who have heard the excellent lecture of the late Professor Robison of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably see that we have availed ourselves of his valuable instructions; and the learned reader will readily perceive that we have enriched our treatise with much important <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> by borrowing freely from the writings of the same distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>.

DYNASTY

Pages 547-547

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> succession of kings of the same line or family. Such were the dynasties of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. The word is formed from the Greek δυναστεία, of δυνάμης, to be powerful, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. The Egyptians reckon 30 dynasties within the space of 36,525 years; but the generality of chronologers look upon them as fabulous. And it is very certain, that these dynasties are not continually successive, but collateral.

DYRRACHIUM

Pages 547-548

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Illyricum, before called Epidamnum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Epidamnus, an insignificant name, changed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to Dyrrachium; a name taken from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on which it stood. Originally built by the Corcyreans. A Roman colony (Pliny). A town famous in story: its port answered to that of Brundusium, and the passage between both was very ready and expeditious. It was also a very famous mart for the people living on the Adriatic; and the free admission of strangers contributed much to its increase: A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to the conduct of the Apollonians who, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Spartans, discouraged strangers from settling among them. **DYSÆ**, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, inferior goddesses among the Saxons, being the messengers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Woden, whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to convey the souls of such as died in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to his abode, called Valhalla, i.e. the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of slaughter; where they were to drink with him and their other gods cerevisia, or a kind of malt liquor, in the skulls of their enemies. The Dysæ conveyed those who died a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to Hela, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, where they were tormented with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, thirst, and every kind of evil.

DYSCRASY

Pages 548-548

among physicians, denotes an ill <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state of the humours, as in the scurvy, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, &c.

DYSENTERY

Pages 548-548

in Medicine, a diarrhoea <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>, wherein the stools are mixed with blood, and the bowels miserably tormented with gripes. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. --- **E.** **E**, THE <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> vowel, and fifth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, bet. The letter E is most evidently derived from the old character ą in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> and Phoenician alphabets, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> by the Greeks to this position E, and not from the Hebrew He ń. From the same origin is also derived the Saxon e, which is the first letter in their alphabet that differs from the Latin one. It is formed by a narrower opening of the larynx than the letter A; but the other parts of the mouth are used nearly in the same manner as in that letter. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> in most languages. The short sound is audible in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, fret, den, and other words ending in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>: its long sound is produced by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> e, or an e at the end of words; as in glebe, here, hire, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, sphere, interfere, revere, sincere, &c. in most of which it sounds like ee; as also in some others by coming after i, as in believe, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, grief, reprove, &c. and sometimes this long sound is expressed by ee, as in bleed, beer, creed, &c. Sometimes the final e is silent, and only serves to lengthen the sound of the preceding vowel, as in rag, rage, stag, stage, hug, huge, &c. The sound of e is obscure in the following words axen, heaven, bounden, fire, massacre, mauere, &c. The Greeks have their long and short e, which they call epsilon and eta. The French have at least six kinds of e's: the Latins have likewise a long and short e; they also write e instead of a, as dicem for dicam, &c. and this is no doubt the reason why a is so often changed into e in the preter tense, as ago, egit; facti, fecit, &c. --- **DYSENTERIC FEVER.** See Medicine Index.

DYSOREXY

Pages 548-548

among physicians, denotes a want of appetite, proceeding from a weakly stomach.

DYSPNOEA

Pages 548-548

a difficulty of breathing, usually called asthma. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DYSSERT

Pages 548-548

a borough town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fife, situated on the northern shore of the frith of Forth, about eleven miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>.

DYSURY

Pages 548-548

in Medicine, a difficulty of making <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, attended with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and pain. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

DYVOUR

Pages 548-548

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>; otherwise Bare-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>: A person who, being involved in debt, and unable to pay the same,—for avoiding imprisonment and other pains, makes cessation of his effects in favour of his creditors; and does his devior and duty to them, proclaiming himself bare-man and indigent, and becoming debt bound to them of all that he has. The word is used in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKRUPT">Bankrupt</a>: see that article; and Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. --- As a numeral, E stands for 250, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, E, quoque ducentos et quinquaginta tenebit. In music it denotes the tone e-la-mi. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> it is the fifth of the dominical letters. And in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> it distinguishes all the easterly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: thus, E alone denotes East; and E. by S. and E. by N. East by South, and East by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>.

EACHARD

Pages 548-548

Laurence**, an eminent English historian of the 18th century, nearly related to Dr John Eachard. He was the son of a clergyman, who, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a good estate in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. He was educated in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, entered into holy orders, and was presented to the living of Welton and Elkington in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, where he spent above 20 years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and distinguished himself by his writings, especially his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England, which was attacked by Dr Edmund Calamy and by Mr John Oldmixon. His "General <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> History from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a> of Christ to the first Establishment of Christianity by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Laws under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>," has passed through several editions. He was installed archdeacon of

EADMERUS

Pages 548-549

an esteemed historian, was an Englishman; but his parents, and the particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, are not known. He received a learned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and very early discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, by recording every remarkable event that came to his knowledge. Being a monk in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to become the bosom friend and inseparable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of two archbishops of that see, St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a> and his successor Ralph. To the former of these he was appointed spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> by the pope; and that prelate would do nothing without his permission. In the year 1120, he was sent for by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alexander I. of Scotland, to be raised to the primacy of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and having obtained leave of King Henry and the archbishop of Canterbury, he departed for Scotland, where he was kindly received by the king; and on the third <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after his arrival, he was elected bishop of St Andrew's with much unanimity. But on the day after his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, an unfortunate dispute arose between the king and him, in a private conference about his consecration. Eadmerus having been a constant companion of the late and of the present archbishop of Canterbury, was a violent stickler for the prerogatives of that see. He therefore told the king, that he was determined to be consecrated by none but the archbishop of Canterbury, who he believed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Alexander, who was a fierce <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and supported the independency of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and kingdom with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> spirit, was so much offended, that he broke off the conference in a violent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, declaring, that the see of Canterbury had no pre-eminency over that of St Andrew's. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> between the king and the bishop-elect became daily wider, till at length Eadmerus, despairing of recovering the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> favour, sent his pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> to the king, and laid his pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altar, from whence he had taken it, and abandoning his bishopric returned to England. He was kindly received by the archbishop and clergy of Canterbury, though they disapproved of his stiffness, and thought him too hasty in forsaking the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> station to which he had been called. Nor was it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before Eadmerus became sensible of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, and desirous of correcting it. With this view he wrote a long submissive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the king of Scotland, entreating his leave to return to his bishopric, promising compliance with his royal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in every thing respecting his consecration, which was accompanied by an epistle to the same purpose from the archbishop. These letters, however, which were written A.D. 1122, did not produce the desired effect. But Eadmerus is most worthy of the grateful <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of posterity for his historical works, particularly for his excellent history of the affairs of England in his own time, from A.D. 1066 to A.D. 1122; in which he hath inserted many original papers, and preserved many important facts, that are nowhere else to be found. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> hath been highly commended, both by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers, for its authenticity, as well as for regularity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and purity of style. It is indeed more free from legendary tales than any other work of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; and it is impossible to peruse it with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, without conceiving a favourable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Eadmerus, the learning, good <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, sincerity, and candour of its author. EAGLE. See FALCO, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EAGLE

Pages 549-549

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is accounted one of the most noble bearings in armory; and, according to the learned in this science, ought to be given to none but such as greatly excel in the virtues of generosity and courage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> for having done singular services to their sovereigns; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they may be allowed a whole eagle, or an eagle naissant, or only the head or other parts thereof, as may be most agreeable to their exploits. The eagle has been borne by way of ensign or standard, by several nations. The first who seem to have assumed the eagle are the Persians; according to the testimony of Xenophon. Afterwards it was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; who, after a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of standards, at length fixed on the eagle, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year of the consulate of C. Marius: till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they used indifferently wolves, leopards, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, according to the humour of the commander. The Roman eagles, it must be observed, were not painted on a cloth or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>; but were figures in relief, of silver or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, borne on the tops of pikes; the wings being displayed, and frequently a thunderbolt in their talons. Under the eagle on the pike, were piled bucklers, and sometimes crowns. Thus much we learn from the medals. Constantine is said to have first introduced the eagle with two heads, to intimate, that though the empire seemed divided, it was yet only one body. Others say, that it was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> who resumed the eagle as the Roman ensign, and added to it a second head; but that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is destroyed, by an eagle with two heads, noted by Lipsius, on the Antonine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>; as also by the eagle's only having one head on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bull of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IV. The conjecture, therefore, of F. Menestrier appears more probable, who maintains that as the emperors of the East, when there were two on the throne at the same time, struck their coins with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a>, which each of them held in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as being the symbol of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; the like they did with the eagle in their ensigns; and instead of doubling their eagles, they joined them together, and represented them with two heads. In which they were followed by the emperors of the West. F. Papebroche wishes that this conjecture of Menestrier was confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> coins; without which, he rather inclines to think the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the eagle with two heads to be merely arbitrary; though he grants it probable, that it was first introduced on occasion of two emperors on the same throne. The eagle on medals, according to M. Spanheim, is a symbol of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>; and, according to all other antiquaries, of empire. The princes on whose medals it is most usually found, are the Ptolemies and the Seleucides of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. An eagle with the word CONSECRATIO, expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of an emperor.

EAGLES

Pages 549-553

a name found very frequently in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> histories of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and used to express a sort of base <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> that was current in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in the first first years of the reign of Edward I., that is, about the year 1272. There were, besides the eagles, lionines, rosades, and many other coins of the same sort, named according to the figures they were impressed with. The current <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the kingdom was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and silver, in a determined proportion; but these were so much worse than the standard proportion of that time, that they were not intrinsically worth quite half so much as the others. They were imported out of France and other foreign countries. When this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> had been a few years established on the throne, he set up mints in Ireland for the coining sufficient quantities of good money, and then decreed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these eagles, and other like kinds of base coins, and made it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, with confiscation of effects, to import any more of them into the kingdom. Eagle, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is a constellation of the northern hemisphere, having its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing contiguous to the equinoctial. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">Aquila</a>. There are also three several stars, particularly denominated among the Arab astronomers, nasr, i.e. "eagle." The first, nasr sahail, the "eagle of Canopus," called also sitareh jemen, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix, over which it is supposed to preside; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, nasr althair, the "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> eagle;" and the third, nasr aluteke, the "resting eagle." <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Eagle, is a Polish order of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, instituted in 1325 by Uladislaus V. on marrying his son Casimir with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lithuania. The knights of this order were distinguished by a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> chain, which they wore on the stomach, whereon hung a silver eagle crowned. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Eagle, was a like order, instituted in 1701 by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Brandenburgh, on his being crowned <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. The knights of this order wear an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured ribbon, to which is suspended a black eagle. Eagle, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> anciently used as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cognizance of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and friezes of the columns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> consecrated to that god. Eagle-flower. See Balsamine. Eagle-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, in a stone by the Greeks called cétites, and by the Italians pietra d'aguiola, as being supposed to be sometimes found in the eagle's nest. It is of famous traditionary virtue, either for forwarding or preventing the delivery of women in labour, according as it is applied above or below the womb. Matthiolus tells us, that birds of prey could never <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> their young without it, and that they go in search of it as far as the East Indies. Bausch has an express Latin treatise on the subject. See Ætites. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLET">Eaglet</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of eagle, properly signifying a young eagle. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, when there are several eagles on the same escutcheon, they are termed eaglets. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EALDERMAN">Ealderman</a>, or Ealdorman, among the Saxons, was of like import with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> among the Danes. The word was also used for an elder, senator, or statesman. Hence, at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, we call those aldermen who are associates to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> or corporate town. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">Ear</a>. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Several naturalists and physicians have held, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the ear rendered persons barren and unprolific; and this idle notion was what first occasioned the legislators to order the ears of thieves, &c. to be cut off, lest they should produce their like. The ear has its beauties, which a good painter ought by no means to disregard; where it is well formed, it would be an injury to the head to be hidden. Suetonius insists, particularly, on the beauties of Augustus's ears; and Ælian, describing the beauties of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ASPASIA">Aspasia</a>, observes, she had short ears. Martial also ranks <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ears among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of deformities. Among the Athenians, it was a mark of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> to have the ears bored or perforated. And among the Hebrews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, this was a mark of servitude. Loss of one ear is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> enacted by 3 and 6 Edw. VI. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 4, for fighting in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>; and by 2 and 3 Edw. VI. cap. 15, for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> to raise the price of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, labour, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be the third offence, beside pillory, and perpetual infamy, or a fine of 40l. By a statute of Henry VIII. maliciously cutting off the ear of a person is made a trespass, for which treble damages shall be recovered; and the offender is to pay a fine of ten pounds to the king, 37 Hen. VIII. cap. 6. § 4. In the Index to the Statutes at Large, it is said, that this offence may be punished as felony, by 22 and 23 Car. II. cap. 1. § 7. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>; but ear is not mentioned in that statute. Ear of Fishes. See Anatomy Index. Ear, in Music, denotes a kind of internal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, whereby we perceive and judge of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and musical sounds. See Music. In music we seem universally to acknowledge something like a distinct sense from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> one of hearing; and call it a good ear. And the like distinction we should, probably acknowledge in other affairs, had we got distinct names to denote these powers of perception by. Thus a greater capacity of perceiving the beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, architecture, &c. is called a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Ear is also used to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> or seeds, produced by certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; usually called by botanists spica. The flowers and seeds of wheat, rye, barley, &c. grow in ears. The same holds of the flowers of lavender, &c. We say the stem of the ear, i.e. its tube or straw; the knot of the ear; the lobes or cells wherein the grains are enclosed; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> of the ear, &c. Ear-Ach. See Medicine Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARING">Earing</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bolt rope which at the four corners of the sail is left open, in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. The two uppermost parts are put over the ends of the yard arms, and so the sail is made fast to the yard; and into the lowermost earrings, the sheets and tacks are seized or bent at the clew. Ear-Pick, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, silver, or other metal, somewhat in form of a probe, for cleansing the ear. The Chinese have a variety of these instruments, with which they are mighty fond of tickling their ears; but this practice, Sir Hans Sloane observes, must be very prejudicial to so delicate an organ, by bringing too great a flow of humours on it. **Ear-Ring.** See **PENDENT.** **Ear-Wax.** See **ANATOMY Index.** **Earwig.** See **FORNICULA, ENTOMOLOGY Index.** **Earl,** a British <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of nobility, next below a marquis, and above a viscount. The title is so ancient, that its original cannot be clearly traced out. Thus much, however, seems tolerably certain, that among the Saxons they were called *ealdormen*, quasi elder men, signifying the same with senior or senator among the Romans; and also *schiremen*, because they had each of them the civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a several <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> or shire. On the irruption of the Danes they changed their names to *corvus*, which, according to Camden, signified the same in their language. In Latin they are called *comites* (a title first used in the empire), from being the king's attendants; *a societate nomen sumpsuntur, reges enim tales sibi assentant*.
