After the Norman conquest they were for some time called *counts*, or *countesses*, from the French; but they did not long retain that name themselves, though their shires are from thence called *counties* to this day. It is now become a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> title; they having nothing to do with the government of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; which is now entirely devolved on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, the earl's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, or *vicecomes*. In writs, commissions, and other formal instruments, the king, when he mentions any peer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of an earl, usually styles him "trustly and well beloved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>;" an appellation as ancient as the reign of Henry IV.; who being either by his wife, his mother, or his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, actually related or allied to every earl in the kingdom, artfully and constantly acknowledged that connection in all his letters and other public acts; whence the usage has descended to his successors, though the reason has long ago failed. An earl is created by cincture of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, mantle of state put upon him by the king himself, a cap and a coronet put upon his head, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. **Earl Marshal.** See **MARSHAL.** **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">Earnest</a> (arrhez),** money advanced to bind the parties to the performance of a verbal bargain. By the civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he who recedes from his bargain loses his earnest, and if the person who received the earnest give back, he is to return the earnest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>. But with us, the person who gave it, is in strictness obliged to abide by his bargain; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he decline it, is not discharged upon forfeiting his earnest, but may be sued for the whole money stipulated. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>,** among ancient philosophers, one of the four elements of which the whole system of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> was thought to be composed. See **ELEMENT.** **Earths,** in **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>,** are such substances as have neither taste nor smell, are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a>, are nearly insoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and have a specific gravity under 5. Such are lime, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARYTES">barytes</a>, &c. See **CHEMISTRY Index.** **Earth,** in **Astronomy** and **<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>,** one of the primary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>; being this terraqueous globe which we inhabit. For the astronomical facts with regard to the earth, see **ASTRONOMY**; for its geographical history, see **GEOGRAPHY**; and for the opinions or theories of its formation and changes, see **<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a> Index.** **Earthquake.** See **GEOLOGY Index.** **Earthworm.** See **<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> Index.** **Easel pieces,** among painters, such small pieces, either portraits or landscapes, as are painted on the easel, i.e. the frame whereon the canvas is laid. They are thus called to distinguish them from larger pictures drawn on walls, ceilings, &c. **Easement,** in Law, a privilege or convenience which one neighbour has of another, whether by charter or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, without profit: such are, a way through his lands, a sink, or the like. These, in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, may be claimed. **Easing,** in the sea languages, signifies the slackening a rope or the like. Thus, to ease the bow line, or sheet, is to let them go slacker; to ease the helm, is to let the ship go more large, more before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, or more larboard. **East,** one of the four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the world; being that point of the horizon where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is seen to rise when in the equinoctial. The word east is Saxon. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and throughout the Mediterranean, the east wind is called the *levante*: in Greek, *εσταλια* and *εσταλιανη*, because it comes from the side of the sun, *αναστα*; in Latin *ventus*. **Easter,** a festival of the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, observed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>. The Greeks call it *pascha*, the Latins *pascha*, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word signifying passage, applied to the Jewish feast of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a>. It is called *easter* in English, from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Ostre, worshipped by the Saxons with peculiar ceremonies in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April. The Asiatic churches kept their easter upon the very same day the Jews observed their passover, and others on the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> after the first full <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in the new year. This controversy was determined in the council of Nice; when it was ordained that easter should be kept upon one and the same day, which should always be a Sunday, in all Christian churches in the world. For the method of finding easter by calculation, see **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">CHRONOLOGY</a>.** **Easter <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>,** an island in the South Sea, lying in N. Lat. 27. 5. W. Long. 109. 46. It is thought to have been first discovered in 1686 by one Davis an Englishman, who called it *Davis's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>*. It was next visited by Commodore Roggewein, a Dutchman, in 1722; who gave it the name of *Easter Island*, and published may fabulous accounts concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and its inhabitants. It was also visited by a Spanish ship in 1770, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of which gave it the name of *St Carlos*. The only authentic accounts of this island, however, which have yet appeared, are those published by Captain Cook and Mr Forster, who visited it in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1774. According to these accounts, the island is about 10 or 12 leagues in circumference, and of a triangular figure; its greatest length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west to south-east is about four leagues, and its greatest breadth two. The hills are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that they may be seen at the distance of 15 or 16 leagues. The north and east points of the island are of a considerable height; between them, on the south-east side, the shore forms an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, in which Captain Cook thinks the Dutch anchored in 1722. He himself anchored on the west side of the island, three miles north- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> from the south point. This, he says, is a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> with easterly winds; but a dangerous one when the wind blows from the contrary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, as the other on the south-east side must be with easterly winds; so that there is no good accommodation to be had for shipping round the whole island. The island itself is extremely barren; and bears evident marks not only of a volcanic origin, but of having been not very long ago entirely ruined by an eruption. As they approached the south point, Mr Forster informs us, that they observed the shore to rise perpendicularly. It consisted of broken rocks, whose cavernous appearance, and black or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, seemed to indicate that they had been thrown up by subterraneous fire. Two detached rocks <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> about a quarter of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> off this point: one of them is singular on account of its shape, and represents a huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> or obelisk; and both these rocks were inhabited by multitudes of sea fowls. On landing and walking into the country, they found the ground covered with rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of all sizes, which appeared to have been exposed to a great fire, where they seemed to have acquired a black colour and porous texture. Two or three shrivelled <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grasses grew among these stones, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> softened the desolate appearance of the country. The farther they advanced, the more ruinous the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country seemed to be. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> were intolerably rugged, and filled with heaps of volcanic stones, among which the Europeans could not make their way but with the greatest difficulty; but the natives leaped from one stone to another with surprising agility and ease. As they went northward along the island, they found the ground still of the same nature; till at last they met with a rock of large black melted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, which seemed to contain some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and on which was neither <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> nor grass, nor any mark of vegetation. Notwithstanding this general barrenness, however, there are several large tracts covered with cultivated soil, which produces potatoes of a gold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour as sweet as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARROTS">carrots</a>, plantains, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes. The soil is a dry hard clay; and the inhabitants use the grass which grows between the stones in other parts of the island as a manure, and for preserving their vegetables when young from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the sun. The most remarkable curiosity belonging to this island is a number of colossal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>; of which, however, very few remain entire. These statues are placed only on the sea <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. On the east side of the island were seen the ruins of three platforms of stone <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, on each of which had stood four of these large statues; but they were all fallen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from two of them, and one from the third: they were broken or defaced by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> measured one that had fallen, which was 15 feet in length, and six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> over the shoulders; each statue had on its head a large cylindric stone of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, wrought perfectly round. Others were found that measured near 27 feet, and upwards of eight feet over the shoulders; and a still larger one was seen standing, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of which was sufficient to shelter all the party, consisting of near 30 persons, from the rays of the sun. The workmanship is rude, but not bad, nor are the features of the face ill formed; the ears are long, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISTORTION">distortion</a> practised in the country, and the bodies have hardly anything of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> figure about them. How these islanders, wholly unacquainted with any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> power, could raise such stupendous figures, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the large cylindric stones upon their heads, is truly wonderful! The most probable conjecture seems to be, that the stone is fictitious; and that each figure was gradually erected, by forming a temporary <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> round it, and raising it as the work advanced; but they are at any rate very strong proofs of the ingenuity and perseverance of the islanders in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> when they were built, as well as that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of the present <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> had seen better days than their descendants enjoy. The water of this island is in general brackish, there being only one well that is perfectly fresh, which is at the east end of the island: and whenever the natives repair to it to slake their thirst, they wash themselves all over; and if there is a large <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, the first leaps into the middle of the hole, drinks, and washes himself without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; after which another takes his place, and so on in succession. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was much disrelished by their new friends, who stood greatly in need of this valuable article, and did not wish to have it contaminated by such ablutions. The people are of a middle size. In general they are rather thin; go entirely naked; and have punctures on their bodies, a custom common to all the inhabitants of the South Sea <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Their greatest singularity is the size of their ears, the lobe of which is stretched out so that it almost rests on their shoulder; and is pierced with a very large hole, capable of admitting four or five fingers with ease. The chief ornaments for their ears are the white down of feathers, and rings which they wear in the inside of the hole, made of the sugar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, which is very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, and for this purpose is rolled up like a watch <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Some were seen clothed in the same cloth used in the island of Otaheite, tinged of a bright orange colour with turmeric; and these our voyagers supposed to be chiefs. Their colour is a chestnut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> black, curling, and remarkably strong; and that on the head as well as the face is cut short. The women are small, and slender limbed: they have punctures on the face, resembling the patches sometimes used by European ladies; they paint their face all over with a reddish brown ruddle, and above this they lay a fine orange colour extracted from turmeric root; the whole is then variegated with streaks of white shell lime. But the most surprising circumstance of all with regard to these people, is the apparent scarcity of women among them. The nicest calculation that could be made, never brought the number of inhabitants in this island to above 700, and of these the females bore no proportion in number to the males. Either they have but few females, or else their women were restrained from appearing during the stay of the ship; notwithstanding, the men showed no signs of a jealous disposition, or the women any scruples of appearing in public; in fact, they seemed to be neither reserved nor chaste; and the large pointed cap which they wore gave them the appearance of professed wantons. But as all the women who were seen were liberal of their favours, it is more than probable that all the married and modest ones had concealed themselves from their impetuous visitants in some inscrutable parts of the island; and what further strengthens this supposition is, that heaps of stones were seen piled up into little hillocks, which had one steep perpendicular side, where a hole went under ground. The space within, says Mr Forster, could be but small; and yet it is probable that these cavities served, together with their miserable huts, to give shelter to the people at night; and they may communicate with natural caverns, which are very common in the lava currents of volcanic countries. The few women that appeared were the most lascivious of their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a> perhaps that have been ever noticed in any country; shame seemed to be entirely unknown to them.

EATON

Pages 553-553

a town of Buckinghamshire, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, and famous for its collegiate school, founded by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VI. being a seminary for King's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, the fellows of which are all from this school. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETON">ETON</a>. EAU DE CARMES. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">PHARMACY</a>. Eau de Luce, a fragrant alkaline liquor which was some years ago in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute, especially among the fair <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and of which the leading perfection is, that it shall possess and retain a milky opacity. Mr Nicholson, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his valuable Journal, tells us, that being informed by a philosophical friend, that the usual recipes for making this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> do not succeed, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of mastic in it has hitherto been kept a secret, he made the following trials to procure a good eau de luce. One dram of the rectified <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> was dissolved in four ounces of the strongest ardent spirit of the shops; its specific gravity being 840 at 60 degrees of Fahrenheit. A portion of the clear spirit was poured upon a larger <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fine powdered mastic than it was judged could be taken up. This was occasionally agitated without <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; by which means the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> resin was for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> gradually dissolved. One part of the oily solution was poured into a phial, and to this was added one part of the solution of mastic. No opacity <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other change appeared. Four parts of strong caustic volatile alkali were then poured in, and immediately shaken. The fluid was of a dense opaque <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, affording a slight ruddy tinge when the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> was seen through a thin portion of it. In a second mixture, four parts of the alkali were added to one of the solution of mastic; it appeared of a less dense and more yellowish white than the former mixture. More of the gum resinous solution was then poured in; but it still appeared less opaque than that mixture. It was ruddy by transmitted light. The last experiment was repeated with the oily solution instead of that of mastic. The white was much less dense than either of the foregoing compounds, and the requisite opacity was not given by augmenting the dose of the oily solution. No ruddiness nor other remarkable appearance was seen by transmitted light. These mixtures were left at repose for two days; no separation appeared in either of the compounds containing mastic; the compound, consisting of the oily solution and alkali, became paler by the separation of a cream at the top. It appears, therefore, that the first of these three mixtures, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the quantity of its ingredients, and the odorant additions which may be made, is a good eau de luce. In a subsequent number of the same Journal, we have the following recipe by one of the author's correspondents, who had often proved its value by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. "Digest ten or twelve grains of the whitest pieces of mastic, selected for this purpose and powdered, in two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>; and, when nearly dissolved, add twenty grains of elemi. When both the resins are dissolved, add ten or fifteen drops of rectified oil of amber, and fifteen or twenty of essence of bergamot: shake the whole well together, and let the pieces subside. The solution <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> amber colour. It is to be added in very small portions to the best <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> ammoniae pure, until it assumes a milky whiteness, shaking the phial well after each addition, as directed by Maquer. The strength and causticity of the ammoniac are of most essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, upon the addition of the first drop or two of the tincture, a dense opaque conglobated precipitate is formed, not much unlike that which appears on dropping a solution of silver into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> slightly impregnated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, it is too strong, and must be diluted with alcohol."

EAVES

Pages 553-553

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the margin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; being the lowest tiles, slates, or the like, that hang over the walls, to throw off <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to a distance from the wall. EAVES-Droppers, are such persons as stand under the eaves, or walls, and windows of a house, by night or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to hearken after news, and carry it to others, and thereby cause strife and contention in the neighbourhood. They are called evil members of the commonwealth by the stat. of West. 1. c. 33. They may be punished either in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> leet by way of presentment and fine, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> sessions by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> and binding to good behaviour. EBBING OF THE <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">TIDES</a>. See Tide.

EBDOMARIUS

Pages 553-553

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, an officer formerly appointed weekly to superintend the performance of divine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in cathedrals, and prescribe the duties of each person attending in the choir, as to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, singing, praying, &c. To this purpose the ebdomary, at the beginning of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, drew up in form a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of the respective persons, and their several offices, called tabula, and the persons there entered were styled intabulati.

EBDOME

Pages 553-553

Easium, in antiquity, a festival kept on the seventh of every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, to whom all seventh days were sacred, because one of them was his birth-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; whence he was sometimes called Ebdomagenes. For the ceremonies of this solemnity see Potter's Archael. Grac. lib. ii. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 20.

EBION

Pages 553-553

the author of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> of the EBIONITES, was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Cerinthus, and his successor. He improved upon the errors of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and added to them new opinions of his own. He began his preaching in Judea; he taught in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and even at Rome. His tenets infected the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Cyprus. St John opposed both Cerinthus and Ebion in Asia; and it is thought, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> wrote his gospel, in the year 97, particularly against this heresy.

EBIONITES

Pages 553-555
ancient heretics, who rose in the church in the first ages, and formed themselves into a sect in the second century, denying the divinity of Jesus Christ. Ebionites. Origen takes them to have been so called from the Hebrew word *ebion*, which in that language signifies poor; because, says he, they were poor in sense, and wanted understanding. Eusebius, with a view to the same etymology, is of opinion they were thus called, as having poor thoughts of Jesus Christ, taking him for no more than a mere man. It is more probable the Jews gave this appellation to the Christians in general out of contempt; because in the first times there were few but poor people that embraced the Christian religion. This opinion Origen himself seems to give into, in his book against Celsus, where he says that they called Ebionites, such among the Jews as believed that Jesus was truly the expected Messiah. It might even be urged, with some probability, that the primitive Christians assumed the name themselves, in conformity to their profession. It is certain Epiphanius observes, they valued themselves on being poor, in imitation of the apostles. The same Epiphanius, however, is of opinion, that there had been a man of the name of Ebion, the chief and founder of the sect of Ebionites, contemporary with the Nazarenes and Cerinthians. He gives a long and exact account of the origin of the Ebionites, making them to have risen after the destruction of Jerusalem, when the first Christians, called Nazarenes, went out of the same to live at Pella. The Ebionites were little else than a branch of Nazarenes: only that they altered and corrupted in many things the purity of the faith held among those first adherents to Christianity. For this reason Origen distinguishes two kinds of Ebionites, in his answer to Celsus; the one believed that Jesus Christ was born of a virgin; and the other, that he was born after the manner of other men. The first were orthodox in every thing, except that to the Christian doctrine they joined the ceremonies of the Jewish law, with the Jews, Samaritans, and Nazarenes; together with the traditions of the Pharisees. They differed from the Nazarenes, however, in several things, chiefly as to what regards the authority of the sacred writings; for the Nazarenes received all for Scripture contained in the Jewish canon; whereas the Ebionites rejected all the prophets, and held the very names of David, Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, in abhorrence. They also rejected all St Paul's epistles, whom they treated with the utmost disrespect. They received nothing of the Old Testament but the Pentateuch; which should intimate them to have descended rather from the Samaritans than from the Jews. They agreed with the Nazarenes in using the Hebrew gospel of St Matthew, otherwise called the Gospel of the Twelve Apostles; but they had corrupted their copy in abundance of places; and particularly, had left out the genealogy of our Saviour, which was preserved entire in that of the Nazarenes, and even in those used by the Cerinthians. Some, however, have made this gospel canonical, and of greater value than our present Greek gospel of St Matthew: See Nazarenes. These last, whose sentiments, as to the birth of our Saviour, were the same with those of the Ebionites, built their error on this very genealogy. Besides the Hebrew gospel of St Matthew, the Ebionites had adopted several other books, under the names of St James, John, and the other apostles: they also made use of the Travels of St Peter, which are supposed to have been written by St Clement; but had altered them so, that there was scarce anything of truth left in them. They even made that saint tell a number of falsehoods, the better to authorise their own practices. See St Epiphanius, who is very diffusive on the ancient heresy of the Ebionites, Har. 30. But his account deserves little credit, as, by his own confession, he has confounded the other sects with the Ebionites, and has charged them with errors to which the first adherents of this sect were utter strangers. EBONY OF CRETE. See EBENUS, BOTANY Index. EBONY Wood is brought from the Indies, exceedingly hard and heavy, susceptible of a very fine polish, and on that account used in mosaic and inlaid works, toys, &c. There are divers kinds of ebony; the most usual among us are black, red, and green, all of them the product of the island of Madagascar, where the natives call them indifferently *hamon mainthi*, q. d. black wood. The island of St Maurice, belonging to the Dutch, likewise furnishes part of the ebonies used in Europe. Authors and travellers give very different accounts of the tree that yields the black ebony. By some of their descriptions, it should be a sort of palm tree; by others a cytisus, &c. The most authentic of them is that of M. Falcourt, who resided many years in Madagascar as governor thereof; he assures us, that it grows very high and big, its bark being black, and its leaves resembling those of our myrtle, of a deep dusky green colour. Tavernier assures us, that the islanders always take care to bury their trees when cut down, to make them the blacker, and to prevent their splitting when wrought. F. Plomier mentions another black ebony tree, discovered by him at St Domingo, which he calls *sportum portulacae foliis aculeatis ebeni materie*. Candia also bears a little shrub, known to the botanists under the name of *EBENUS Cretica*, above described. Pliny and Dioscorides say the best ebony comes from Ethiopia, and the worst from India; but Theophrastus prefers that of India. Black ebony is much preferred to that of other colours. The best is a jet black, free of veins and rind, very massive, astringent, and of an acrid pungent taste. Its rind, infused in water, is said to purge pitoita, and cure venereal disorders; whence Matthiolus took guaiacum for a sort of ebony. It yields an agreeable perfume when laid on burning coals; when green, it readily takes fire from the abundance of its fat. If rubbed against a stone, it becomes brown. The Indians make statues of their gods, and sceptres for their princes, of this wood. It was first brought to Rome by Pompey, after he subdued Mithridates. It is now much less used among us than anciently, since the discovery of so many ways of giving other hard woods a black colour. As to the green ebony, besides Madagascar and St Maurice, it likewise grows in the Antilles, and especially in the isle of Tobago. The tree that yields it is very bushy; its leaves are smooth, and of a fine green colour. Beneath its bark is a white blea, about two inches thick; all beneath which, to the very heart, is a deep green, approaching towards a black, though sometimes streaked with yellow veins. Its use is not confined confined to mosaic work: it is likewise good in dyeing, as yielding a fine green tincture. As to red ebony, called also grenadilla, we know little of it more than the name. The cabinet-makers, inlayers, &c., make pear tree and other woods pass for ebony, by giving them the black colour thereof. This some do by a few washes of a hot decoction of galls; and when dry, adding writing ink thereon, and polishing it with a stiff brush, and a little hot wax; and others heat or burn their wood black.

EBORACUM

Pages 555-555

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Brigantes in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the residence of Septimius Severus and Constantius Chlorus, and where they both died; a Roman colony; and the station of the Legio Sexta Victrix. Now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 50° Lat. 54°. Caer-frock, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Caer-effroc, in British (<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAMBRIA">Cambria</a>).

EBRO

Pages 555-555

anciently IBERUS, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, which, taking its rise in Old Castile, runs through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a> and Arragon, passes by Saragossa, and, continuing its course through Catalonia, discharges itself with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity into the Mediterranean, about 20 miles below the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Tortosa. EBUDÆ, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> HEBUGES, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the west of Scotland. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> differ greatly as to their situation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and names; said in general to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> and west of Scotland. Now called the Western Isles, also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>; this last a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name, the reason of which does not appear, unless it be a corruption of Hebudes. By Beda called Mevaniae, an appellation equally obscure.

EBULLITION

Pages 555-555

the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">Boiling</a>. The word is also used in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> with Effervescence.

EBUSUS

Pages 555-555

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the greater of the two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Pityussae, in the Mediterranean, near the east <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, to the south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>. Famous for its pastures for cattle, and for its figs. Now Ibiza, 100 miles in compass, without any noxious animals but rabbits, who often destroy the corn.

ECALESIA

Pages 555-555

Εκάλεσια, in antiquity, a festival kept in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, surnamed Hecalus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Hecalesius, from Hecale, one of the borough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>.

ECASTOR

Pages 555-555

in antiquity, an oath wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> was invoked. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the men never to swear by Castor, nor the women by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>.

ECATEA

Pages 555-555

Εκάτεια, in antiquity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> erected to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Hecate, for whom the Athenians had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration, believing that she was the overseer of their families, and that she protected their children.

ECATESIA

Pages 555-555

Εκάτεια, in antiquity, an anniversary solemnity, observed by the Stratonicensians, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Hecate. The Athenians likewise had a public entertainment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> every new <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, in honour of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. The supper was provided at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the richer sort; and was no sooner brought to the accustomed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people carried all off, giving out that Hecate had devoured it. For the rest of the ceremonies observed on this occasion, see Pott. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">Arch</a>. Graec. lib. ii. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 20. ECATOMBÆON, Εκατομβαῖον, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year. It consisted of 30 days, and began on the first new moon after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice, and consequently answered to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and beginning of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. The Boeotians called it Hippodromius, and the Macedonians <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>. See Month. The word is a derivation from the Greek ἱκάτεια, a hecatomb, because of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hecatombs sacrificed in it.

ECAVESSADE

Pages 555-555

in the mange, is used for a jerk of the cavesson.

ECBATANA

Pages 555-555

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Media, built by Deioces <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Medes, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>; Pliny says, by Seleucus; but that could not be, because it is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>. It was situated on a gentle declivity, distant 12 stadia from Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, and was in compass 150 stadia. Here stood the royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> and tombs. It was an open unwalled town, but had a very strong citadel, encompassed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> walls, one within and rising above another. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the outmost was equal to the whole extent of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, according to Herodotus; the situation favouring this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, as being a gentle ascent, and each wall was of a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>.—Another Ecbatana of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a> (Pliny).—A third of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. ECCENTRICITY. See Excentricity.

ECCHYMOSIS

Pages 555-555

from εκχυω, to pour out, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from εκ, out of, and χυω, juice. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of humours from their respective vessels, under the integuments; or, as Paulus Aegineta says, "When the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is bruised by the violent collision of any object, and its small veins broken, the blood is gradually discharged from them." This blood, when collected under the skin, is called ecchymosis, the skin in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> remaining entire; sometimes a tumour is formed by it, which is soft and livid, and generally without pain. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of blood is not considerable, it is usually resorbed; if much, it suppurates; it rarely happens that any further inconvenience follows; though, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a very bad <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body, a mortification may be the result, and in such case regard must be had thereto. ECCLAIRCISSMENT. See Esclaircissement.

ECCLESIASTES

Pages 555-557

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of which is to shew the vanity of all sublunary things. It was composed by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>; who enumerates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a>, an appellation given to whatever belongs to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>: thus we say, ecclesiastical polity, jurisdiction, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, &c. Ecclesiastical Courts. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Anglo-Saxons there was no sort of distinction between the lay and the ecclesiastical jurisdiction: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> was as much a spiritual as a temporal tribunal: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the church were ascertained and asserted at the same time, and by the same judges, as the rights of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>. For this purpose the bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in his absence the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the county, used to sit together in the county court, and had there the cognizance of all causes as well ecclesiastical as civil; a superior deference being paid to the bishop's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in spiritual matters, and to that of the lay judges in temporal. This union of power was very advantageous to them both: the presence of the bishop added <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and reverence to the sheriff's proceedings; and the authority of the sheriff was equally useful to the bishop, by enforcing obedience to his decrees in such refractory offenders as would otherwise have despised the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> ecclesiastical censures. But so moderate and rational a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was wholly inconsistent with those views of ambition that were then forming by the court of Rome. It soon became an established maxim in the papal system of policy, that all ecclesiastical persons, and all ecclesiastical causes, should be solely and entirely subject to ecclesiastical jurisdiction only: which jurisdiction was supposed to be lodged in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and immediately in the Pope, by divine indefeasible <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> from Christ himself, and derived from the Pope to all inferior tribunals. Hence the canon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> lays it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a rule, that "sacerdotes à regibus honorandi sunt, non judicandi;" and places an emphatical reliance on a fabulous tale which it tells of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine, That when some petitions were brought to him, imploring the aid of his authority against certain of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> accused of oppression and injustice; he caused, (says the holy canna) the petitions to be burnt in their presence, dismissing them with this valediction: "Ite, et inter vos causas vestras discutite, quia dignum non est ut nos judicemus Deos." It was not, however, till after the Norman conquest, that this doctrine was received in England, when William I. (whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was warmly espoused by the monasteries which he liberally endowed, and by the foreign clergy whom he brought over in shoals from France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and planted in the best preferments of the English church) was at length prevailed upon to establish this fatal encroachment, and separate the ecclesiastical court from the civil: whether actuated by principles of bigotry, or by those of a more refined policy, in order to discontinue the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward abounding with the spirit of Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, is not altogether certain. But the latter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the cause, was undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this separation: for the Saxon laws were soon overborne by the Norman justiciaries, when the county court fell into disregard by the bishop's withdrawing his presence, in obedience to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of the Conqueror; which prohibited any spiritual cause from being tried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> courts, and commanded the suitors to appear before the bishop only, whose decisions were directed to conform to the canon law. King Henry I. at his accession, among other restorations of the laws of King Edward the Confessor, revived this of the union of the civil and ecclesiastical courts. Which was, according to Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, after the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the conquest was past, only a restitution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law of England. This however was ill relished by the Popish clergy, who, under the guidance of that arrogant prelate Archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a>, very early disapproved of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> that put them on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the profane laity, and subjected spiritual men and causes to the inspection of the secular magistrates; and therefore, in their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> at Westminster, 3 Hen. I. they ordained, that no bishop should attend the discussion of temporal causes; which soon dissolved this newly effected union. And, when upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of King Henry I. the usurper Stephen was brought in and supported by the clergy, we find one article of the oath which they imposed upon him was, that ecclesiastical persons and ecclesiastical causes should be subject only to the bishop's jurisdiction. And as it was about that time that the contest and emulation began between the laws of England and those of Rome, the temporal courts adhering to the former, and the spiritual adopting the latter as their rule of proceeding; this widened the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> between them, and made a coalition afterwards impracticable; which probably would else have been effected at the general reformation of the church. Ecclesiastical courts are various; as the Archdeacon's, the Consistory, the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">Arches</a>, the Peculiars, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">Prerogative</a>, and the great court of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> in all ecclesiastical causes, viz. the Court of Delegates. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. As to the method of proceeding in the spiritual courts, it must (in the first place) be acknowledged to commend their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, that though they continue to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to decide many questions which are properly of temporal cognizance, yet <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is in general so able and impartially administered, in those tribunals (especially of the superior kind), and the boundaries of their power are now so well known and established, that no material inconvenience at present arises from this jurisdiction still continuing in the ancient channel. And, should any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> be attempted, great confusion would probably arise, in overturning <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> established forms, and new-modelling a course of proceedings that has now prevailed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> centuries. The establishment of the civil law <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in all the ecclesiastical courts was indeed a masterpiece of papal discernment, as it made a coalition impracticable between them and the national tribunals, without manifest inconvenience and hazard. And this consideration had undoubtedly its weight in causing this measure to be adopted, though many other causes concurred. In particular, it may be here remarked, that the Pandects, ECClesiastical or collections of civil law, being written in the Latin tongue, and referring so much to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and his delegated officers of justice, sufficiently recommended them to the court of Rome, exclusive of their intrinsic merit. To keep the laity in the darkest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, and to monopolize the little science which then existed entirely among the monkish clergy, were deep-rooted principles of papal policy. And as the bishops of Rome affected in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to mimic the imperial <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, as the spiritual prerogatives were moulded on the pattern of the temporal, so the canon law process was formed on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the civil law; the prelates embracing, with the utmost ardour, a method of judicial proceedings, which was carried on in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> unknown to the bulk of the people, which banished the intervention of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> (that bulwark of Gothic liberty), and which placed an arbitrary power of decision in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The proceedings in the ecclesiastical courts are therefore regulated according to the practice of the civil and canon laws; or rather to a mixture of both, corrected and new-modelled by their own particular usages, and the interposition of the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law. For, if the proceedings in the spiritual court be ever so regularly consonant to the rules of the Roman law, yet if they be manifestly repugnant to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> maxims of the municipal laws, to which, upon principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> policy, the ecclesiastical process ought in every state to conform (as if they require two witnesses to prove a fact, where one will suffice at common law); in such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, a prohibition will be awarded against them. But under these restrictions, their ordinary course of proceeding is, first, by citation, to call the party injuring before them. Then by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> ("a little book"), or by articles drawn out in a formal allegation, to set forth the complainant's ground of complaint. To this succeeds the defendant's answer upon oath; when, if he denies or extenuates the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, they proceed to proofs by witnesses examined, and their depositions taken down in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> by an officer of the court. If the defendant has any circumstances to offer in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, he must also propound them in what is called his defensive allegation, to which he is entitled in his turn to the plaintiff's answer upon oath, and may from thence proceed to proofs as well as his antagonist. The canonical doctrine of purgation, whereby the parties were obliged to answer upon oath, to any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, however criminal, that might be objected against them (though long ago overruled in the court of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, the genius of the English law having broken through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> imposed on it by its clerical chancellors, and asserted the doctrines of judicial as well as civil liberty), <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the middle of the last century to be upheld by the spiritual courts; when the legislature was obliged to interpose, to teach them a lesson of similar moderation. By the statute of 13 Car. II. c. 12. it is enacted, that it shall not be lawful for any bishop, or ecclesiastical judge, to tender or administer to any person whatsoever, the oath usually called the oath ex officio, or any other oath whereby he may be compelled to confess, accuse, or purge himself of any criminal matter or thing, whereby he may be liable to any censure or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. When all the pleadings and proofs are concluded, they are referred to the consideration, not of a jury, but of a single Ecclesiastic judge; who takes information by hearing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> on both sides, and thereupon forms his interlocutory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> or definitive <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, at his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, from which there generally lies an appeal, in the several stages mentioned in the articles above referred to; though, if the same be not appealed from him in 15 days, it is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a>, by the statute 25 Henry VIII. c. 19. But the point in which these jurisdictions are the most defective, is that of enforcing their sentences when pronounced; for which they have no other process but that of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>; which would be often despised by obstinate or profligate men, did not the civil law step in with its aid. See Excommunicatio. Ecclesiastical Corporations, are where the members that compose them are spiritual persons. They were erected for the furtherance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and perpetuating the rights of the church. See Corporations. Ecclesiastical State. See Clergy. Ecclesiasticus, an apocryphal book, generally bound up with the Scriptures; so called, from its being read in the church, ecclesia, as a book of piety and instruction, but not of infallible authority. The author of this book was a Jew, called <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> the son of Sirach. The Greeks call it the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> of the son of Sirach. Eccoprotics, in Medicine, laxative or loosening remedies, which purge gently, by softening the humours and excrements, and fitting them for expulsion.—The word is composed of the Greek particle εκ, and κοπτειν, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>. Ecdici, Ecdici, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, patrons of cities, who defended their rights, and took care of the public <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Their office resembled that of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> syndics. Echape, in the manege, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> begat between a stallion and a mare of different breeds and countries. Echaper, in the manege, a gallicism used in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, implying to give a horse head, or to put on at full speed. Echeneis, the Remora. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Ecchevin, in the French and Dutch polity, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> elected by the inhabitants of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town, to take care of their common concerns, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> and cleanliness of the city. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, there is a prevôt and four ecchevins; in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, a mayor and ecchevins. At <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, there are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> ecchevins; and at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, seven. In France, the ecchevins take cognizance of rents, taxes, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, they judge of civil and criminal causes; and if the criminal confesses himself guilty, they can see their sentence executed without appeal. Echinate, or Echinated, an appellation given to whatever is prickly, thereby resembling the hedgehog. Echinites, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> History, the name by which authors call the fossil centronia, frequently found in chalk pits. Echinophora. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Echinops. See Botany Index. Echinus.

ECHELLENSIS

Pages 555-555
ABRAHAM, a learned Maronite, whom the president Le Jai employed in the edition of his Polyglott Bible. Gabriel Sionita, his countryman, drew him to Paris, in order to make him his fellow labourer in publishing that Bible. They fell out; Gabriel complained to the parliament, and cruelly defamed his associate; their quarrel made a great noise. The congregation de propaganda fide associated him, 1636, with those whom they employed in making an Arabic translation of the Scriptures. They recalled him from Paris, and he laboured in that translation at Rome in the year 1652. While he was professor of the Oriental languages at Rome, he was pitched upon by the great duke Ferdinand II. to translate from Arabic into Latin, the 5th, 6th, and 7th books of Apollonius's Conics; in which he was assisted by John Alphonsus Borelli, who added commentaries to them. He died at Rome in 1644.

ECHINUS

Pages 558-558

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a member <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ornament near the bottom of the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite capitals. ECHITES. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ECHO

Pages 558-559
or ECHO, a sound reflected or reverberated from a solid, concave, body, and so repeated to the ear. The word is formed from the Greek ἠχος, sound, which comes from the verb ἤχω, echo. The ancients being wholly unacquainted with the true cause of the echo, ascribed it to several causes sufficiently whimsical. The poets, who were not the worst of their philosophers, imagined it to be a person of that name metamorphosed, and that she affected to take up her abode in particular places; for they found by experience, that she was not to be met with in all. (See below, Echo in fabulous history). But the moderns, who know sound to consist in a certain tremor or vibration in the sonorous body communicated to the contiguous air, and by that means to the ear, give a more consistent account of echo. For a tremulous body, striking on another solid body, it is evident, may be repelled without destroying or diminishing its tremor; and consequently a sound may be redoubled by the resiliency of the tremulous body, or air. But a simple reflection of the sonorous air is not enough to solve the echo; for then every plain surface of a solid hard body, as being fit to reflect a voice or sound, would redouble it, which we find does not hold. To produce an echo, therefore, it should seem that a kind of concameration or vaulting were necessary, in order to collect, and by collecting to heighten and increase, and afterwards reflect, the sound; as we find is the case in reflecting the rays of light, where a concave mirror is required. In effect, as often as a sound strikes perpendicularly on a wall, behind which is any thing of a vault or arch, or even another parallel wall, so often will it be reverberated in the same line, or other adjacent ones. For an echo to be heard, therefore, it is necessary the ear be in the line of reflection: for the person who made the sound to hear its echo, it is necessary he be perpendicular to the place which reflects it; and for a manifold or tautological echo, it is necessary there be a number of walls, and vaults or cavities, either placed behind or fronting each other. A single arch or concavity, &c., can scarce ever stop and reflect all the sound; but if there be a convenient disposition behind it, part of the sound propagated thither, being collected and reflected as before, will present another echo: or, if there be another concavity, opposed at a due distance to the former, the sound reflected from the one upon the other will be tossed back again by this latter, &c. Many of the phenomena of echoes are well considered by the bishop of Leighs, &c., who remarks, that any sound, falling either directly or obliquely on any dense body of a smooth, whether plain or arched, superficies, is reflected, or echoes, more or less. The surface, says he, must be smooth; otherwise the air, by reverberation, will be put out of its regular motion, and the sound thereby broken and extinguished. He adds, that it echoes more or less, to show, that when all things are as before described, there is still an echoing, though it be not always heard, either because the direct sound is too weak to beat quite back again to him that made it; or that it does return to him, but so weak, that it cannot be discerned; or that he stands in a wrong place to receive the reflected sound, which passes over his head, under his feet, or on one side of him; and which therefore may be heard by a man standing in the place where the reflected sound does come, provided no interposed body intercepts it, but not by him that first made it. Echoes may be produced with different circumstances. For, 1. A plane obstacle reflects the sound back in its due tone and loudness; allowance being made for the proportionable decrease of the sound, according to its distance. 2. A convex obstacle reflects the sound somewhat smaller and somewhat quicker, though weaker, than otherwise it would be. 3. A concave obstacle echoes back the sound, bigger, slower, and also inverted; but never according to the order of words. Nor does it seem possible to contrive any single echo, that shall invert the sound, and repeat backwards; because, in such case, the word last spoken, that is, which last occurs to the obstacle, must be repelled first; which cannot be. For where in the mean time should the first words hang and be concealed? or how, after such a pause, be revived, and animated again into motion? From the determinate concavity or archedness of the reflecting bodies, it may happen that some of them shall only echo back one determinate note, and only from one place. 4. The echoing body being removed farther off, it reflects more of the sound than when nearer; which is the reason why some echoes repeat but one syllable, some one word, and some many. 5. Echoing bodies may be so contrived and placed, as that reflecting the sound from one to the other, either directly and mutually, or obliquely and by succession, out of one sound, a multiple echo or many echoes shall arise. Add, that a multiple echo may be made, by so placing the echoing bodies at unequal distances, that they may reflect all one way, and not one on the other; by which means, a manifold successive sound will be heard; one clap of the hands, like many; one ha, like a laughter; one single word, like many of the same tone and accent; and so one viol, like many of the same kind, imitating each other. Lastly, Echoing bodies may be so ordered, that from any one sound given, they shall produce many echoes different both as to tone and intension. By which means a musical room may be so contrived, that not only one instrument playing therein shall seem many of the same sort and size, but even a concert of different ones, only by placing certain echoing bodies so, that any note placed shall be returned by them in 3ds, 5ths, and 8ths. Echo is also used for the place where the repetition of the sound is produced or heard. Echoes are distinguished into divers kinds, viz. 1. Single, which return the voice but once. Whereof some are tonical, which only return a voice when modulated into some particular musical tone: Others, polysyllabic, which return many syllables, words, and sentences. Of this last kind is that fine echo in Woodstock park, which Dr Plot assures us, in the day time, will return very distinctly seventeen syllables, and in the night twenty. 2. Multiple or tautological; which return syllables and words the same oftentimes repeated. In echoes, the place where the speaker stands is called the centrum phonicum, and the object or place that returns the voice, the centrum phonocampitium. At the sepulchre of Metella, wife of Crassus, was an echo, which repeated what a man said five times. Authors mention a tower at Cyzicus, where the echo repeated seven times. One of the finest echoes we read of is that mentioned by Barthius, in his notes on Statius's Thebais, lib. vi. 30, which repeated the words a man uttered 17 times: it was on the banks of the Nafta, between Coblentz and Bingen. Barthius assures us, he had proved what he writes; and had told 17 repetitions. And whereas, in common echoes, the repetition is not heard till some time after hearing the word spoke, or the notes sung; in this, the person who speaks or sings is scarce heard at all; but the repetition most clearly, and always in surprising varieties; the echo seeming sometimes to approach nearer, and sometimes to be further off. Sometimes the voice is heard very distinctly, and sometimes scarce at all. One hears only one voice, and another several; one hears the echo on the right, and another on the left, &c. At Milan in Italy, is an echo which reiterates the report of a pistol 56 times; and if the report is very loud, upwards of 60 reiterations may be counted. The first 20 echoes are pretty distinct; but as the noise seems to fly away, and answer at a greater distance, the reiterations are so doubled, that they can scarce be counted. See an account of a remarkable echo under the article Paisley. Echo, in Architecture, a term applied to certain kinds of vaults and arches, most commonly of the elliptic and parabolic figures, used to redouble sounds, and produce artificial echoes. Echo, in Poetry, a kind of composition wherein the last words or syllables of each verse contain some meaning, which, being repeated apart, answers to some question or other matter contained in the verse; as in this beautiful one from Virgil: Crudelis mater magis, an puer improbus ille? Improbus ille puer, crudelis tu quoque mater. The elegance of an echo consists in giving a new sense to the last words; which reverberate, as it were, the motions of the mind, and by that means affect it with surprise and admiration. Echo, in fabulous history, a daughter of the Air and Tellus, who chiefly resided in the vicinity of the Cephissus. She was once one of Juno's attendants, and became the confidant of Jupiter's amours. Her loquacity, however, displeased Jupiter, and she was deprived of the power of speech by Juno, and only permitted to answer to the questions which were put to her. Pan had formerly been one of her admirers, but he never enjoyed her favours. Echo, after she had been punished by Juno, fell in love with Narcissus; but being despised by him, pined herself to death, having nothing but her voice left.

ECHOMETER

Pages 559-559

among musicians, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rule, with several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> thereon, serving to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and length of sounds, and to find their intervals and ratios. ECHOUERIES. See under Trichecus.

ECKIUS

Pages 559-559

John, an eminent and learned divine, professor in the university at Ingolstadt, memorable for the opposition he gave to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, Melancthon, Caralostadius, and other leading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a> in Germany. He wrote many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> tracts; and among the rest, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUAL">Manual</a> of Controversies, printed in 1535, in which he discourses upon most of the heads contested between the Protestants and Papists. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of uncommon learning, parts, and zeal, and died in 1543.

ECLECTICS

Pages 559-559

(eclectici), a name given to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, who without attaching themselves to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, took what they judged good and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> from each. Hence their denomination; which, in the original Greek, signifies, "that may be chosen," <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "that chooses;" of the verb ελέγχω, I choose.—Laertius notes, that they were also, for the same reason, denominated analogetici; but that they call themselves Philalethies, i.e. lovers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> or founder of the eclectici was one Potaemon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, who lived under Augustus and Tiberius; and who, weary of doubting of all things with the Sceptics and Pyrrhonians, formed the eclectic sect; which Vossius calls the eclectic. Towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, a sect arose in the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> under the denomination of Eclectics, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Platonics. They professed to make truth the only object of their inquiry, and to be ready to adopt from all the different systems and sects such tenets as they thought agreeable to it.—However, they preferred <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> to the other philosophers, and looked upon his opinions concerning God, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and things invisible, as conformable to the spirit and genius of the Christian doctrine. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> patrons of this system was <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONIUS">Ammonius</a> Saccas, who at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> laid the foundation of that sect, afterwards distinguished by the name of the new Platonics, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> school. See Ammonius and Platonists. Eclectics were also a certain sect of physicians among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, of whom Archigenes, under Trajan, was the chief, who selected from the opinions of all the other sects that which appeared to them best and most rational; hence they are called eclectics, and their prescriptions medicina eclectic.

ECLIPSE

Pages 559-559

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the deprivation of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of some heavenly body, by the interposition of another heavenly body between our sight and it. See Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ECLIPTA

Pages 559-559

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of the polygamia superflua order, belonging to the syngenesia class of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The receptacle is chaffy; there is no pappus, and the corollae of the disk quadrifid.

ECLIPTIC

Pages 559-559

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle of the sphere, supposed to be drawn through the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, making an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the equinoctial of about

ECTHESIS

Pages 559-560

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a confession of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in the form of an edict, published in the year 639, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Heraclius, with a view to pacify the troubles occasioned by the Eutychian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> in the eastern church. However, the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> revoked it, on being informed that Pope Severinus had condemned it, as favouring the Monothelites; declaring at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that Sergius, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Constantinople, was the author of it.

ECTHILIPSIS

Pages 560-560
